title: Blue Energy And GVH Sign Agreement On Next Phase Of Gas-Plus-Nuclear Project
author: David Dalton
text: Approach aims to solve delays that have hit sector for decades

US companies Blue Energy and GE Vernova Hitachi Nuclear Energy (GVH) have signed an agreement that launches the next phase of their collaboration to deploy a 2.5 GW gas-plus-nuclear power plant in Texas.

A statement said the agreement advances engineering design, licensing, and safety analysis of the Victoria, Texas, project that will deploy both GE Vernova gas turbines and GVH BWRX-300 small modular reactors (SMRs), subject to a final investment decision in 2027.

Blue Energy said the agreement represents a significant step forward for its pairing of natural gas and nuclear generation to help meet surging US electricity demand driven by artificial intelligence and advanced manufacturing.
The collaboration combines Blue Energy’s project financing and nuclear construction techniques with GE Vernova’s reactor technology and turbines.
Blue Energy, a 2023 startup, is focused on building prefabricated nuclear power plants for faster deployment.

Its approach aims to solve delays that have affected nuclear projects for decades. Cost overruns and uncertainty have limited private capital in the sector. Blue Energy believes its model can remove these barriers.

“By collaborating with GE Vernova, we’re bringing together critical infrastructure, safe reactor technology, and a financeable delivery model,” said Blue Energy chief executive officer and co-founder Jake Jurewicz.

“We are shifting from the old way of building large reactor nuclear power to instead do it the ‘Blue Way’ that slashes costs and time to power and finally makes nuclear a financeable, repeatable product.”

For the Texas project Blue Energy will initially power a nearby data centre with approximately 1 GW of power using two GE Vernova gas turbines in 2030 and then add another 1.5 GW of power from up to five GE Vernova Hitachi SMRs beginning in 2032.
A rendering of a BWRX-300 small modular reactor nuclear power plant. Courtesy GVH.

title: Concreting Of Fourth Inner Containment Tier Completed At Egypt’s El Dabaa-1
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Russia supplying four VVER-1200 units for African nation’s first nuclear station

Concreting of the fourth tier of the reactor building inner containment has been completed at Unit 1 of the El Dabaa nuclear power station under construction in Egypt, Russian state-owned nuclear corporation Rosatom said.
El Dabaa is Egypt’s first nuclear power station and is being built at El Dabaa in Matruh province, on the Mediterranean coast about 300 km northwest of Cairo.
Rosatom is supplying four Generation III+ VVER-1200 pressurised water reactor units for the station, each with an electrical capacity of 1,200 MW.
Rosatom said the latest containment work on El Dabaa-1 took 30 hours and raised the reactor building elevation from 24.4 metres to 34 metres, with the height of the concreted tier being 9.6 metres.
Rosatom said it is planning to begin installation of the fifth tier around mid-August.
At a nuclear power reactor, the inner containment acts as a hermetic protection system, designed to withstand high external and internal pressures and protect against radiation release.

VVER-1200 plants have a total of seven cylindrical tiers for the inner steel containment, with the fifth one serving as a transition between the main part of the containment and its dome structure. The dome itself consists of a lower and upper tier.
Construction of El Dabaa-1 began in July 2022. In November 2025, the reactor pressure vessel was successfully lifted into place, becoming the latest construction milestone at the site.

Russia is supplying the El Dabaa reactor units under a set of contracts in force since 2017 and will provide nuclear fuel for the lifetime of the station. Under the contracts, it will also support Egypt with personnel training during the first 10 years of operation.
Rosatom said the latest containment work on El Dabaa-1 took 30 hours. Courtesy

title: Overwhelming Majority Of US Public Want Permanent Nuclear Waste Solution To Be ‘National Priority’
author: Nigel Davies
text: Respondents to survey also strongly backed the deployment of more reactors
A clear majority of the US public supports finding a permanent solution for nuclear waste in the country, with 81% of people in a YouGov survey believing it should be a national priority.

The survey, commissioned by nuclear waste management company Deep Isolation and conducted in April, also showed that 28% of people supported a continuation of storing spent nuclear at reactor sites over coming decades.

According to the US Nuclear Industry Council (USNIC) the US has an accumulated 92,500 tonnes of spent nuclear fuel, which is growing by 2,000 tonnes a year. Waste is stored in temporary facilities across 35 states in the US with an estimated liability for US taxpayers of over $150bn (€131bn).
The survey showed continuing strong support from the US public in using nuclear power, with 61% believing it should it be deployed heading into the future.

Respondents also supported, at 74%, the use of underground disposal techniques to reduce the need of transporting waste over long distances. In addition, 65% backed the use of deep borehole disposal, which Deep Isolation uses, when presented with information on the technology.

“This research comes at an important time as policymakers and industry leaders work to advance a long-term strategy for managing spent nuclear fuel,” said Todd Abrajano, president and chief executive officer of USNIC.
“As the US looks to expand nuclear energy to meet rising electricity demand, we must pursue practical, science-based pathways that address the back end of the fuel cycle,” he added.
Chris Parker, chief commercialisation officer of Deep Isolation, also welcomed the results of the survey.

“The results demonstrate that Americans recognise the importance of addressing the nuclear waste challenge and are looking for practical, science-based solutions to permanent waste disposal,” he said.
In 2002, Yucca Mountain in Nevada was identified as a potential deep geologic repository site for spent nuclear fuel, but a licence was never granted and the US Congress halted its funding in 2010.

In July, five states – Tennessee, Utah, Louisiana, Idaho and Oklahoma – signed agreements that would see them establish Nuclear Lifecycle Innovation Campuses hosting uranium disposal sites as well as enrichment, spent-fuel reprocessing and fuel fabrication facilities.

Deep Isolation’s borehole technology uses directional drilling to securely isolate waste deep underground, offering countries an alternative to conventional mined repositories. The technology features horizontal, vertical, or slanted boreholes deep underground.
The company has said borehole repositories can provide substantial isolation for many types of high-level waste in a wide range of locations.
Yucca Mountain was identified as a potential repository site, but a licence was never granted and the US Congress halted its funding in 2010. Courtesy US DOE.

title: Boost For Fermi With Appointment Of CEO And Lease Agreement With TensorWave
author: David Dalton
text: US nuclear startup developing ‘Project Matador’ hypergrid campus in Texas
US nuclear developer Fermi has named a new chief executive officer more than three months after firing co-founder Toby Neugebauer from the post.
Fermi said it has hired Lee McIntire, an independent member of the company’s board who has held chief executive positions at CH2M Hill and TerraPower, the nuclear power startup founded by Bill Gates.

Fermi, which was co-founded by former US energy secretary Rick Perry, is developing an AI campus in Amarillo, Texas, called Project Matador that will eventually use nuclear reactors to power data centres.
The company is planning a “hypergrid” campus – essentially a massive gas, nuclear and solar complex that could deliver its first power to onsite data centres by the end of 2026.
In April, Neugebauer and Miles Everson, the company’s chief financial officer, departed the company. Both remain on the company’s board.

The appointment of McIntire came as Fermi also announced it had signed a binding lease agreement with US cloud provider TensorWave for up to 650 MW of data centre capacity at the Project Matador site.
According to Fermi, the deal supports an initial 222MW of capacity beginning in the second half of 2027, but includes expansion rights for two additional data centres that would total 650 MW.
This week, Fermi said Project Matador is “well underway,” with approximately 6 GW of the planned 17 GW already permitted, and more than $1.5bn (€1.3bn) invested in the buildout to date.

The announcements provided a welcome boost to Fermi’s stock, which is up nearly 23% since Monday. The young company took a hit in April when Neugebauer and Everson were pushed out. At the time, the company described the executive shakeup, along with other plans including a corporate headquarters in Dallas, as “Fermi 2.0”.

“Fermi’s next chapter is a construction and power delivery story, and we believe Lee is the ideal executive to lead Fermi through that process,” Marius Haas, Fermi’s chairman of the board, said in a statement.

“The job now is to build on schedule, on budget, and safely. Lee has spent 40 years delivering exactly this kind of large, complex project. He also knows Fermi from the inside, having served on our board through our latest period of growth, and he brings a reputation for integrity that Fermi’s customers, employees, regulators, and neighbours can rely on.”
Fermi is developing an AI campus which will eventually use nuclear reactors to power data centres. Courtesy Fermi Inc.

title: Australia’s Opal Research Reactor Marks 20 Years Since First Criticality
author: David Dalton
text: Facility has supported production of more than 10 million lifesaving nuclear medicine doses

Australia’s Open Pool Australian Lightwater (Opal) reactor, which first reached criticality 20 years ago, has supported the production of millions of lifesaving nuclear medicine doses, irradiated over 900 tonnes of silicon ingots and created neutrons essential for enabling 8,000 cutting-edge scientific experiments, operator the Australian Nuclear Science and Technology Organisation’s (Ansto) said.
Opal, at Ansto’s campus at Lucas Heights in southern Sydney, first reached criticality on 12 August 2006. It is a 20-MW multi-purpose reactor that uses low-enriched uranium-235 fuel.

In 20 years, Opal has helped with the production of more than 10 million lifesaving nuclear medicine doses, used in the diagnosis and treatment of a range of medical conditions and diseases. Each week, these medicines are delivered to hospitals and medical clinics across the country.

As the world’s largest irradiator of neutron transmutation doped silicon, Opal helps produce high-performance semiconductors used in electric vehicles, smart grids, renewable energy infrastructure, robotics and aerospace technologies.
More than 900 tonnes of silicon ingots have been irradiated in the Opal pool and used worldwide in technologies supporting advanced manufacturing and the clean energy transition.
Ansto chief executive officer Shaun Jenkinson said for 20 years, Opal has been arguably, Australia’s most significant piece of scientific infrastructure.
Jenkinson said Opal supports healthcare, scientific research, advanced manufacturing and Australia’s nuclear expertise.
Opal, at Ansto’s campus at Lucas Heights in southern Sydney, first reached criticality on 12 August 2006. Courtesy Ansto.

title: Nuclear Energy Feasible And Advisable For Arkansas, Says Report
author: David Dalton
text: Aggressive timeline could see new reactor operating by mid-2030s
Six areas in the US state of Arkansas could be candidates for future nuclear power development with reactors “feasible and advisable”, according to a report.

The 533-page report, conducted by Maryland- based Excel Services Corporation, said the six areas are Flint Creek in Benton County; the existing Arkansas Nuclear One (Ano) nuclear power station site in Pope County; Central Arkansas, including areas south and southwest of Little Rock; Southwest Arkansas near Camden; Phillips County near West Helena; and Craighead County in northeast Arkansas.
The report noted that sites in the east and northeast parts of the state would require additional review due to their proximity to the New Madrid seismic zone.
The study, commissioned by the Joint Committee on Energy of the Arkansas General Assembly, has been presented to Arkansas lawmakers.

It concluded that nuclear can meet rising energy demand better than any alternative and nuclear plants can transform their host economy. It said: “The state needs the energy, workable sites exist, federal support is the strongest it has been in decades, and state law needs only modest changes.”
The report said that with an aggressive timeline, a new nuclear power plant could be operational in the state by the mid-2030s.

According to the study Arkansas power demand is surging with power needs projected to grow by more than 35% over the next five years, with longer-term projections indicating that the growth figure could more than double.

Nuclear fills the gap better than any alternative for a number of reasons. The US nuclear fleet ran at a 91% capacity factor in 2025, the highest of any generation source, against roughly 25% for utility-scale solar and 35% for onshore wind.

Nuclear produces no carbon dioxide during operation, and its lifecycle emissions are comparable to wind and generally less than solar generation. It has the smallest footprint and one of the lowest mortality rates per unit of energy of any electricity source.
The study said nuclear is also secure because uranium can be stockpiled on site for 18 to 24 months of operation. “No fossil plant can match that,” it said.
The study warned, however, that three elements must mature before reactor deployment becomes widespread: reactor designs, supply chains, and financing structures.
No current project is fully mature today in all three categories, though some are closer than others.

The first units of any design pay for the improvement in maturity. The Vogtle-3 and -4 AP1000 nuclear plants in Georgia, the only new large reactors completed in the US in decades, cost about $35bn (€30bn) against an original $14bn estimate and finished nearly seven years late.

“Repetition cures this,” the study said. Analysis of future AP1000 builds shows overnight cost falling from a first-of-a-kind (FOAK) anchor near $15,000 per kilowatt to roughly $6,200 by the fourth two-unit plant, trending towards $4,700 at nth-of-a-kind (NOAK).

Arkansas does not have to choose between building first at triple cost and doing nothing, the study said. The state can position itself for the NOAK price by supporting the acquisition, characterisation, and permitting of sites now.

The report made several recommendations, including the creation of legislation which would establish a nuclear development fund. The legislation would also expand the duties of the coordinator of atomic development activities, a position created by state law in the 1950s that has never been filled.

Ano is Arkansas’ only commercial nuclear power station. It has two pressurised water rector units that began commercial operation in 1974 and 1980. Ano-1 has a net capacity of 836 MW and Ano-2 of 988 MW.

A number of US states are looking at nuclear to provide energy for development and to reduce carbon emissions. New Jersey recently became the sixth state in the last decade, and the second this year, to fully repeal its moratorium on building new nuclear power stations.

New York is pushing ahead with plans for reactors and in April, governors from the six New England states – Maine, Connecticut, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, Rhode Island and Vermont – directed their state energy agencies to explore advanced nuclear technology.
The Arkansas Nuclear One power station is one of the suggested sites for new nuclear. Courtesy Entergy.

title: China Pours First Concrete For Unit 2 At Guangxi Bailong Nuclear Power Station
author: David Dalton
text: Massive project in south of country will eventually have six reactors
First concrete has been poured for the conventional island of a new commercial nuclear power plant at Guangxi Bailong.
Reports in China said the concrete was poured on 9 August for Unit 2 at Guangxi Bailong, also known as Bailong, in the autonomous region of Guangxi in the south of the country.

The conventional island is one of two primary zones of a power station. It houses the non-nuclear turbine generator and electrical balance of plant. The other zone, the nuclear island, houses the reactor core and safety systems.

Pouring the first concrete for the nuclear island represents the baseline event used by international regulators and industry databases to track a reactor’s official construction start date and schedule.

A total of six reactors are planned to operate at the Guangxi Bailong site. Units 1 and 2 are both CAP1000 pressurised waters reactor (PWR) units and units 3 to 6 are planned to be CAP1400 PWR plants. The CAP1000 is China’s indigenous version of the Westinghouse AP1000 PWR nuclear plant.
Guangxi Bailong is about 24 km from the border with Vietnam and about 30 km from the Fangchenggang nuclear power station, where four units began commercial operation from 2016 to 2024.

Guangxi Bailong is owned by the State Power Investment Corporation through its subsidiary Guangxi Nuclear Power Company. The massive six-unit project represents an estimated total investment of about $60bn (€51bn).
China’s state media has said the first two units at Guangxi Bailong will cost about $5.6bn and are expected to take 56 months to complete.

Guangxi Bailong-1 and -2 and a number of other units where construction began in recent months are is not listed in the International Atomic Energy Agency’s database of nuclear plants in China. The database says China has 60 plants in commercial operation and 37 under construction.
The Guangxi Bailong nuclear power station will evetually have six units. Courtesy Guangxi Nuclear Power Company.

title: US DOE Approves Nuclear Safety Design Agreement For Underground Reactor
author: David Dalton
text: Major milestone means Gravity plant warrants advancement, says Deep Fission

Deep Fission, a US advanced nuclear energy company developing small modular reactors installed one mile underground, announced that the US Department of Energy (DOE), has approved the company’s nuclear safety design agreement (NSDA) for its Gravity nuclear reactor.

The California-headquartered company, founded in 2023, said the approval marks a major regulatory milestone, confirming that the reactor design warrants advancement under the DOE’s Reactor Pilot Program, which establishes a fast-track pathway for advanced reactor demonstration and commercial licensing.
The NSDA approval establishes the safety framework that will guide the reactor’s continued development.

Deep Fission said that with the approval in place, it can move forward to the next phase of DOE authorisation, advancing towards demonstration and eventual deployment of its underground reactor technology.

Deep Fission was selected for participation in the DOE’s Reactor Pilot Program in 2025 and also in 2025 broke ground on its pilot project in Parsons, Kansas. The company has also announced a development pipeline representing 12.5 GW of future planned deployments.

Deep Fission and the Great Plains Development Authority have signed a letter of intent outlining their collaboration on the pilot and their intention to develop a full-scale commercial project at the same site.

The Great Plains Industrial Park, in Labette County, Kansas, is an established site for industrial and energy development. It offers Deep Fission the unique opportunity to scale onsite and potentially grow with the park “for decades to come”, Deep Fission said.
Earlier this year Deep Fission raised $80m (€69m) in new financing and formed a partnership with alternative asset manager Blue Owl.

Deep Fission plans to deploy 15-MW pressurised water reactors (PWR) one mile underground via 30-inch boreholes. Its reactor was previously referred to as the Deep Fission Borehole Reactor-1, or DFBR-1, but was renamed by the company to Gravity.
Deep Fission’s proprietary design combines PWR technology with deep borehole drilling techniques used in the oil and gas industry and heat-transfer methods drawn from geothermal applications.
Deep Fission plans to deploy 15-MW pressurised water reactors one mile underground. Courtesy Deep Fission.

title: From Fashion To Space, UK’s Harlette Capital Seeks Industry Support For Micro Lunar Nuclear Reactor
author: Nigel Davies
text: Company, until now best known for luxury clothing, says it has reached out to leading SMR developer

UK-based innovation company Harlette Capital has issued a request for information (RFI) as it seeks collaborators to help it develop a micro lunar reactor aimed at enabling sustained operations on the Moon.
The company, best known for its luxury Harlette fashion brand, has a separate innovation arm developing aerospace and energy assets and is developing its Alpha Lunar small modular reactor (SMR).
The company has a broader programme to support long-term lunar infrastructure, research and communications and future human exploration on the Moon.

Harlette Capital said the RFI had been sent to leading SMR developers including Rolls-Royce SMR and Westinghouse to better understand current technological capabilities, future development pathways and opportunities for collaboration.

“Reliable, compact nuclear power has the potential to become one of the foundational technologies enabling humanity's long-term presence on the Moon,” said Harlette and Harlette Capital founder Harlette DeFalaise.

“Through the RFI, Harlette is engaging with world-leading innovators to better understand how advanced microreactor and hydrogen technologies may contribute to future lunar infrastructure in a safe and responsible manner.
“We look forward to constructive engagement with industry, research organisations and international partners,” she added.

The company said it was reaching out not only to SMR developers, but also to organisations dealing in nuclear safety engineering, hydrogen energy systems, advanced materials, radiation shielding, lunar infrastructure and other areas of technology.
Harlette Capital aims to research technologies capable of delivering compact, lightweight lunar power systems providing continuous lunar operations.

There is growing interest globally in developing nuclear capacity for space missions. Earlier this month it was reported that US space agency Nasa was fast-tracking plans to deploy a nuclear energy source on the Moon by 2030 as it races with China to be the first.

In 2024 the head of Russia’s space agency said
Russia was working on plans with China on ways to deliver and install a nuclear power plant on the Moon by 2035.

In the UK, Rolls-Royce has unveiled a nuclear space microreactor concept model that is part of a UK Space Agency-backed research programme to deliver an initial demonstration of a UK lunar modular nuclear reactor.
UK-based Rolls-Royce has already unveiled a nuclear space microreactor concept model. Courtesy Rolls-Royce.

title: Cold Hydraulic Testing Begins At China’s Tianwan-8
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Construction of Russia-supplied unit began in 2022
China has completed cold hydraulic testing for Unit 8 at the Tianwan nuclear power station in Jiangsu province, eastern China, project owner China National Nuclear Corporation (CNNC) said.
Cold testing verifies that welds, joints, pipes and components in the primary circuit are able to withstand pressures higher than those during normal operation.
Tianwan-8 is a Russia-designed VVER-1200 pressurised water reactor (PWR) unit. Construction began in February 2022. Construction of twin unit Tianwan-7 started in May 2021.

With cold testing complete at Tianwan-8, the plant will move towards hot functional testing as the next phase of commissioning. Hot functional testing involves heating the reactor system to full operating temperature and pressure without fuel. The operation is usually the last major milestone before fuel loading and startup.

The Tianwan station has another six PWR units in commercial operation, with Units 1 to 4 having been built by Russia using its VVER-1000 PWR technology. Units 5 and 6 are of China’s indigenous CNP-1000 PWR design.

According to earlier reports, upon completion, the eight-unit Tianwan station is expected to generate about 70 TWh of electricity annually, which is equivalent to the annual electricity consumption of about 15 million households.

According to International Atomic Energy Agency data, China has 60 commercial nuclear plants in operation and 37 under construction. However, the 60 operational units do not include Taipingling-2, which according to Beijing has recently begun commercial operation.
Tianwan-8 is a Russia-designed VVER-1200 pressurised water reactor (PWR) unit.

title: Companies To Evaluate Opportunities For Holtec Reactor Deployment In US South
author: David Dalton
text: Initiative with Entergy and Hyundai reflects growing demand for baseload power

US nuclear reactor company Holtec International, power company Entergy Services and South Korea’s Hyundai Engineering & Construction are to evaluate opportunities to advance the potential deployment of Holtec’s SMR-300 advanced small modular reactor (SMR) for large-load customers across Entergy’s service territory in the southern US.

Holtec said the initiative reflects accelerating demand for reliable, carbon-free baseload power to support expanding industrial facilities, advanced manufacturing, and AI-driven data centres throughout the US Gulf South.

The collaboration, formalised through a non-binding memorandum of agreement (MOA), establishes a framework to jointly evaluate customer demand, candidate sites, and possible commercial structures for potential dual-unit SMR-300 projects.

Holtec said the objective is to identify commercially viable opportunities where advanced nuclear may be able to support economic growth while strengthening long-term grid reliability and energy security.
Entergy and its affiliates operate one of the nation’s largest fleets of nuclear power plants and electric utility systems serving customers in Mississippi, Louisiana, Texas, and Arkansas.
Together, the parties will evaluate whether, and if so, where SMR-300 deployment may best meet future customer demand.

Holtec’s SMR-300 is a Generation III+ pressurized water reactor that produces approximately 340 MW (net) per unit using proven pressurised water reactor (PWR) technology, standard nuclear fuel, and fully passive safety systems.
A standard dual-unit configuration provides approximately 680 MW of firm, carbon-free electricity in a scalable platform optimised for utilities, industrial facilities, and large-load customers.
Rendering of a Holtec SMR-300 nuclear power plant. Courtesy Holtec International.

title: US Fusion Company Chosen For US Project To Advance AI In Nuclear Fuel Recycling
author: David Dalton
text: Shine Technologies also joins federal-backed Prometheus consortium

US nuclear fusion company Shine Technologies has been selected for the US Department of Energy’s Genesis Mission to develop an AI-enabled system for designing more efficient nuclear fuel recycling processes, while also joining a national consortium focused on applying AI across the nuclear sector.
The Wisconsin-based company will lead a project called “AI-Guided Fuel Cycle Facility Optimization” with Argonne National Laboratory as its technical partner.
The project will use AI to help engineers evaluate fuel recycling facility designs by considering performance, product quality and waste at the same time.

Shine said the effort targets a significant US nuclear waste challenge. According to the company, the US has accumulated roughly 95,000 tonnes of used nuclear fuel. Shine is developing technology intended to recycle that material and recover usable components.

Rather than assessing individual process decisions separately, the new system is intended to examine multiple design options and weigh competing factors together. This could help engineers identify more effective recycling configurations while keeping a record of how the system arrived at its recommendations.

Shine will also participate in Prometheus, a Genesis Mission project led by Idaho National Laboratory. The Prometheus consortium brings together US national laboratories and industry to develop and apply AI across nuclear energy.

The initiative was awarded $60m (€52m) under the Genesis Mission, founded to support cooperation between national laboratories, industry, academia, and more to harness AI for breakthroughs across science.
Nuclear fusion company Shine’s headquarters in Janesville, Wisconsin. Courtesy Shine Technologies.

title: Key Step For Polish Nuclear Project As Site Is Handed Over To US Contractor
author: David Dalton
text: Warsaw planning three Westinghouse AP1000 reactors in north of Poland
The project to build Poland’s first commercial nuclear power station has reached a key milestone with the site in Pomerania handed over to general contractor Bechtel and earthworks underway.
US-based engineering company Bechtel replaces Polish state project company Polskie Elektrownie Jądrowe (PEJ) as coordinator of the project site, PEJ said.
In 2022 Warsaw chose US-based Westinghouse to supply three AP1000 pressurised water reactor units for the facility. In 2023, Westinghouse and Bechtel formed a consortium for the project.
The facility is to be built at the Lubiatowo-Kopalino site in the Pomeranian commune of Choczewo on Poland’s Baltic coast.
Earthworks at the site will be carried out by Budimex – one of the largest construction companies in Poland.

Poland’s energy minister Milosz Motyka said the nuclear project “strengthens Poland’s energy security and sovereignty, increases our independence from external factors, and creates conditions for ensuring stable and predictable energy prices for both households and businesses”.
Motyka said hundreds of Polish companies are already involved in the construction of the power plant, providing their services, technologies, and expertise.

“Our goal is to ensure that as much of the value generated by this project as possible remains in the country, strengthening the potential of local companies, creating high-quality jobs, developing domestic expertise, and building lasting competitive advantages for the Polish economy for decades to come,” he added.

PEJ submitted its construction licence application for the plant to the National Atomic Energy Agency (PAA) in March 2026. The first unit is scheduled to begin commercial operation in 2036, with the second and third units following in 2037 and 2038.

Poland’s parliament passed a law in early 2025 allocating 60.2 billion zloty (about €14bn, $16bn) from the state budget to finance investment in the project, covering about 30% of the costs. The remainder is to be financed through loans from international banks and export credit agencies.
In December 2025, the European Commission gave its approval for Poland to finance its first commercial nuclear power station with state aid.

PEJ’s president Marek Woszczyk told NucNet recently that PEJ is aiming to sign a general engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) contract for the nuclear power station with the Westinghouse and Bechtel consortium by the end of 2026.
Earthworks at the site will be carried out by Budimex – one of the largest construction companies in Poland. Courtesy PEJ.
The site for Poland’s first commercial nuclear power station. Courtesy PEJ.

title: Clean Core Signs Aneel Fuel Fabrication Agreement With BWXT Canada
author: David Dalton
text: US company preparing for irradiation in operating nuclear reactor

US-based Clean Core Thorium Energy (CCTE) has taken a significant step towards the commercial demonstration of its Aneel nuclear fuel platform through a fuel fabrication agreement with nuclear energy company BWXT Canada.

The agreement enables the fabrication of full-scale demonstration fuel bundles at Canadian Nuclear Laboratories (CNL), bringing together the final manufacturing capabilities required to prepare Aneel fuel for irradiation in an operating reactor.

Under the agreement, BWXT Canada will supply qualified fuel bundle hardware that will be integrated with Aneel fuel pellets and assembled into complete, reactor-representative fuel bundles at CNL’s Chalk River Laboratories.
Aneel fuel combines thorium and enriched uranium, with potential applications across pressurised heavy water reactors, Generation IV reactors, and light-water reactors.
According to CCTE it is designed to improve fuel utilisation, with the potential to reduce long-lived spent fuel volumes and strengthen safety margins and proliferation resistance.

Earlier this year, CCTE completed accelerated irradiation testing at Idaho National Laboratory’s (INL) Advanced Test Reactor, achieving burnups exceeding 60 GWd/MTU (gigawatt-days per metric ton of uranium). The programme generated reactor-based performance data under accelerated irradiation conditions and marked an important milestone in qualifying the technology.

CCTE said after that INL testing that, in simple terms, each fuel bundle produces more energy before it is replaced, fewer bundles are needed to generate the same electricity, and less spent fuel is produced per unit of energy
In parallel, CNL has begun fabrication of full-scale Aneel demonstration fuel bundles.
“With BWXT Canada’s qualified fuel bundle hardware now secured, the fabrication programme can progress to complete, reactor-ready fuel bundles for commercial reactor demonstration,” CCTE said.
“Qualification of an advanced nuclear fuel requires more than strong performance. It requires a supply chain capable of manufacturing, testing and ultimately deploying it at commercial scale.”
Earlier this year, CCTE completed accelerated irradiation testing at Idaho National Laboratory’s Advanced Test Reactor. Courtesy CCTE.

title: Westinghouse And Amentum To Cooperate On Common Engineering Platform For Nuclear Fleet Deployment
author: David Dalton
text: Collaboration also expected to accelerate licensing of AP300 SMR with Nuclear Regulatory Commission

Westinghouse Electric Company and Amentum have entered into a series of agreements supporting a technology platform which uses a common engineering platform for Westinghouse’s AP1000 and AP300 nuclear power plants.

Westinghouse said that by building the smaller AP300 small modular reactors (SMRs) around technology already proven in the large-scale AP1000, it hopes to streamline development, simplify future deployments and reduce the complexity of bringing new reactors to market.

Unlike many SMR developers pursuing entirely new reactor designs, Westinghouse has based the AP300 on the same core technology used in its AP1000 reactor. The shared platform – called the APX technology platform –extends across engineering, major components, fuel design, licensing strategies and parts of the supply chain.

That common approach could make it easier to deploy both reactor types without creating separate industrial ecosystems. Utilities could also benefit from technology that builds on an existing commercial reactor instead of an entirely new design.

Westinghouse said its collaboration with Amentum, the US-based engineering company, is expected to accelerate the licensing of the AP300 SMR with the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission. Separately, the two companies will work together to improve their engineering and execution capabilities for delivering AP1000 units at scale.

“The APX strategy offers the grid-scale, commercially available AP1000 reactor for near-term global fleet deployments, while developing the AP300 SMR to address additional market segments with smaller energy requirements,” Westinghouse said.

There are six AP1000 reactors in commercial operation worldwide. Four units operate in China – two at the Sanmen nuclear power station and two at the Haiyang nuclear power station. Two units operate in the US at the Vogtle nuclear power station in Georgia, where Vogtle-3 began commercial operation in July 2023 and Voglte-4 in April 2024.
Meeting Electricity Demand From AI
John Heller, Amentum’s chief executive officer, said the company supports nuclear projects across the entire project lifecycle and expects demand for firm baseload power to continue growing.

“There is an expanding global market for firm baseload power,” Heller said. He added that the collaboration with Westinghouse will help address electricity demand from AI and other energy-intensive industries.
The companies have worked together on nuclear projects for years, including power generation and decommissioning programmes in the US, the UK, Poland, Slovakia, Lithuania and South Africa.

Last year the US government and Westinghouse struck an $80bn (€69bn) deal
to build a fleet of new AP1000 nuclear reactors across the US, as Washington tries to quadruple its nuclear capacity by 2050.

Westinghouse filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in March 2017, primarily due to massive cost overruns and delays in building the Vogtle reactors. The bankruptcy severely impacted its parent company, Toshiba, which ultimately sold Westinghouse to Canada-based Brookfield Asset Management in 2018.
The two Vogtle plants were the last two commercial nuclear reactors built in the US.
There are six AP1000 reactors in commercial operation worldwide, including two at Sanmen, China. Courtesy Westinghouse.
Westinghouse plans to build the smaller AP300 small modular reactors (right) around technology already proven in the large-scale AP1000 (left). Courtesy Westinghouse.

title: Hungary's Paks Nuclear Plant Output Cut To Single Unit Amid Low Danube Levels
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Operator warns generation could stop if water drops further

Hungary’s Paks nuclear power station has reduced electricity generation to one unit operating at 50% capacity and faces a full halt in production if water levels in the Danube River fall further, operator MVM said.

MVM said the shutdown of the still operating turbine generator at Unit 4 was due to begin at 01:30 local time on 2 August, leaving only Unit 2 in operation at half capacity. The company said this production level can be maintained only as long as the water level allows safe operation of the pump impellers used to cool the unit.
Paks is Hungary’s only commercial nuclear power station with four 479-MW VVER V-213 pressurised water reactor units.
MVM had warned on 30 July that a complete shutdown of Paks could become unavoidable within 24 to 72 hours.

Last week, MVM said low-water conditions at Paks are divided into four stages, based on levels measured at the plant’s water intake on the Danube. It said the plant had reached stage three and there was a realistic chance of stage four, at which all units would have to be shut down.

The company said cooling of the shut-down units would still have to be maintained. It said the cooling of all four shut-down units would require a maximum of 2.5 cubic metres of water a second, compared with about 100 cubic metres a second needed by operating units.

MVM said emergency pumps installed in cooperation with Hungary’s water management authority are available to ensure that enough water remains available to cool the shut-down units even if the Danube falls to further extreme levels.
According to the company, the plant can be kept in a safe condition even during extremely low water levels lasting for weeks.
It said units could be restarted in stages within a few days once the required water level is reached, subject to strict operating rules.
Reuters quoted Hungarian prime minister as saying Hungary faces a "critical" five-day period starting on Monday (3 August).

The low water levels of the Danube River forced Romania to close Unit 1 at its Cernavodă nuclear power station last week. Unit 2 at the site remains operational despite warnings it too could be forced to shut down. Cernavodă operates two Candu heavy water reactor units.
In a statement yesterday Bulgaria’s Kozloduy nuclear power station, which also relies on the Danube for cooling, said operation of its two PWR units continues at full capacity.

Kozloduy said that if the average water level of the Danube from the past week remains unchanged, no actions are expected to be taken to significantly reduce the load factors at the station over at least the next three weeks.
The Danube River provides cooling water for the the Paks nuclear power station in southern Hungary. Image courtesy MVM Paks.

title: China’s Changjiang-3 Nuclear Power Plant Connected To Grid
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Construction of Hualong One unit in south of country began in 2021
Unit 3 at the Changjiang nuclear power station in Hainan province, southern China, has been connected to the national gird and has begun supplying electricity for the first time, local sources said.
State-owned China Daily said the domestic Hualong One, or HPR1000, pressurised water reactor (PWR) unit was connected to the grid of 1 August.
Changjiang-3 achieved first criticality on 10 July 2026, according to previous reports.
Construction of Changjiang-3 began in March 2021. Construction of an identical unit, Changjiang-4, began in December 2021.
Two CNP-600 PWRs have been in operation at the Changjiang site since 2015 and 2016.
Local reports said Changjiang-3 has become the first Hualong One unit in Hainan province to be connected to the grid.
The Hualong One PWR combines features from China National Nuclear Corporation’s ACP1000 and CGN’s ACPR1000+ designs.
Hualong One is now China’s flagship reactor technology, comprising about half of all reactor new-build projects in the country.
According to the International Atomic Energy Agency, China has 60 commercial reactor units in operation and 37 under construction.
The Changjiang-3 nuclear power plant in Hainan province. Image courtesy China Huaneng Group.

title: Italy Set To Approve Legal Framework For Advanced Nuclear, Says Report
author: David Dalton
text: Move could set in motion plans for crucial regulatory regime
Italy’s parliament is expected to approve legislation next week establishing a legal framework for advanced nuclear technologies, including small modular reactors (SMRs).
The measure would give the government a year to draft rules on reactor licensing, safety, waste management and site selection, Associated Press reported.

“The duty of the government at this moment is to create the conditions so that those who will eventually decide on installations will be able to do so,” Gilberto Pichetto Fratin, minister for the environment and energy security, told AP.

In June Italy’s lower house of parliament, the Chamber of Deputies, approved the legislation, which could pave the way for a return to nuclear power, nearly four decades after Italy shut down its last commercial reactors.

The legislation – passed by 155 votes for, 86 against and eight abstentions – does not restart nuclear power generation in Italy, but it does set in motion the creation regulatory process that might lead to its re-introduction during the first half of the next decade. The text has now moved to the Senate for a second reading and possible approval in the coming days.

The government of prime minister Giorgia Meloni has said it views the initiative as a component of a larger plan to equip the country with energy sovereignty, stabilise energy prices and speed up the reduction of greenhouse gases.

Italy was a pioneer of nuclear power and had four commercial nuclear plants – Caorso, Enrico Fermi, Garigliano and Latina – providing almost 5% of the country’s electricity production share at their peak in 1986-1987.
Italy shut down the last of the plants, Caorso and Enrico Fermi, in July 1990 following the 1987 referendum in the wake of the Chernobyl disaster.
There were later efforts to revive nuclear energy, but those plans were shelved after the 2011 Fukushima disaster in Japan.
Now, Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, concerns over energy security and rising electricity demand have prompted a major policy rethink.
Rather than returning to large conventional reactors, the government is focusing on SMRs and other advanced technologies, which supporters say are safer, quicker to build and more flexible.

“We are talking about the third advanced generation (of nuclear power), much more workable compared to what are the needs, much safer because it is small in size with very short construction times,” Pichetto Fratin said.
“When people ask me for a timeline, I say 2033, 2034, 2035,” he added, referring to when the first next-generation reactors could realistically begin operating.
Decommissioning of the reactor building at the Latina nuclear power station in Italy. Courtesy Sogin.

title: Malaysia’s PM Calls On Asean Countries Not To Sideline Nuclear Power
author: David Dalton
text: Comments follow calls by Philippines president to reconsider reactor deployment

Nuclear power should not be sidelined in the Association if Southeast Asian Nations’ (Asean) energy transition efforts as the region seeks a stable, affordable and reliable energy supply, Malaysia’s minister Anwar Ibrahim said at a regional energy conference.

Anwar said while Asean countries had increasingly focused on renewable sources such as solar and wind, nuclear energy appeared to have received less attention despite the region having regulatory experience and technical expertise.
He said nuclear power could play a role in supporting the objectives of the Asean Plan of Action for Energy Cooperation as countries seek to balance energy security with emissions reduction.
“Energy transition does not proceed in a straight line, nor can integration proceed in isolation,” he said.

“Even before the current energy crunch, overdependence on fossil fuels has drawn much of Asean's attention to alternatives such as solar and wind. Yet, nuclear power appears to have been relegated to lesser significance,” he said.
Anwar said this was unfortunate given the region’s experience and capabilities to explore options that could contribute towards achieving Asean's energy goals.

Reports in Malaysia earlier this year said the country had joined other Southeast Asian nations to consider introducing nuclear energy as many struggle with surging fuel prices caused by the war in Iran.

According to local news agency Bernama, Malaysia’s deputy prime minister Fadillah Yusof appointed MyPower, an agency under the country’s Ministry of Energy Transition And Water Transformation, to study the potential feasibility of nuclear power.
The study will include the legal and regulatory frameworks that would

The International Energy Agency said in a 2024 report that nuclear power plants could be commissioned in Southeast Asia beginning around 2035, primarily in Indonesia, increasing the region’s installed nuclear commercial capacity from zero to as much as 13 GW.
According to the Southeast Asia Energy Outlook 2024, two different scenarios show that Southeast Asia could have either 6 GW or 13 GW by 2050.

Philippines president Ferdinand Marcos Jr said in his state of the nation address this week that the time might be right for the Philippines to revisit nuclear energy production as an ongoing energy crisis caused by conflict in the Middle East continues to impact fuel prices.
A number of other countries in the region, including Vietnam, Thailand and Singapore, have said nuclear might be an option.

Vietnam has been the most active mover in the region since the start of 2026. It unveiled plans in April 2025 to build two nuclear power plants, Ninh Thuan-1 and -2, targeting commercial operation between 2030 and 2035 and providing 4,000-6,400 MW of baseload capacity.
To facilitate this, Vietnam passed the Law on Atomic Energy in June 2025, which took effect in January this year.
Malaysia’s prime minister Anwar Ibrahim said nuclear power appears to have been relegated to ‘lesser significance’. Courtesy Anwar Ibrahim.

title: Germany Announces National Hubs In Bid For Europe’s First Fusion Reactor In 2040s
author: David Dalton
text: Berlin has shut down its large-scale nuclear plants, but is backing advanced technologies

Germany has announced plans for three national fusion hubs with €125m ($143m) of initial funding planned for next month as Berlin aims to operate Europe’s first commercial nuclear fusion power plant to be operating in Germany in the 2040s.

Germany’s Federal Ministry for Rese arch, Technology and Space said the three national fusion hubs will consolidate research and development in the areas of laser fusion, magnetic fusion, fuel cycles and materials development.
One hub will be at will be at power company RWE’s former Biblis nuclear power station in the state of Hesse, central Germany.

Others will be at Karlsruhe, home to the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology, and Garching near Munich, where Proxima Fusion is building the Alpha fusion test reactor, the first fusion test plant in Germany.
Facilities in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Schleswig-Holstein and Hamburg will also be involved in the hubs
The German government said it wants the world’s first commercial nuclear fusion power plant to be operating in Germany in the 2040s.

It said the fusion hubs are designed as central locations where companies, research institutions and industry collaborate onsite and virtually on technological solutions for future fusion power plants.
It added: “The federal and state governments are working in close coordination on this.”
Federal research minister Dorothee Bär said: “Fusion could solve our energy problems in the future.” She said it was important “that we are the drivers, rather than just passengers”.
Germany has closed all its nuclear power plants, but the government has shown support for fusion research and aims to be the first country to connect a fusion reactor to the grid.

In February German company Proxima Fusion signed a memorandum of understanding with utility major RWE, the region of Bavaria, and the Max Planck Institute for Plasma Physics as it delivers a roadmap to build a nuclear fusion plant.

In January, the company laid out plans to build a test reactor called Alpha in Garching, to build a commercial scale fusion reactor plant called Stellaris within 15 years at a nuclear site at Gundremmingen being decommissioned by RWE, and to build a commercial reactor using laser-based technology in southern Bavaria.
Researchers at the Max Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Greifswald use the institute’s experimental Wendelstein 7-X (W7-X) stellarator for fusion research.

Last year they broke previous fusion records and set a new benchmark for reactor performance using the facility. In the experiments, the W7-X outperformed previous benchmarks, especially over how long plasma can be sustained.
This advancement is crucial because maintaining a hot, dense plasma long enough is the key to making fusion power viable.

In June Germany’s Focused Energy raised $240m (€206m) in an investment round led by RWE to support the construction of a laser fusion energy plant at the former Biblis nuclear power station in the region of Hesse, central Germany.
A view inside the vacuum vessel of the Wendelstein 7-X in Greifswald, Germany. Courtesy: Jan Hosan/Max Planck Institute for Plasma Physics.

title: Philippines Could Bolster Energy Security And Bring Down Costs By Revisiting Nuclear, Says Marcos
author: Nigel Davies
text: Country saw highest electricity rates in June among all members of Association of Southeast Asian Nations

The time might be right for the Philippines to revisit nuclear energy production as an ongoing energy crisis caused by conflict in the Middle East continues to impact fuel prices, president Ferdinand Marcos Jr has said.

In his state of the nation address to Congress, Marcos said: “Perhaps it is time to revisit nuclear energy production. After all, we are already using nuclear energy in the fields of medicine, in agriculture, water filtration and the upcycling of plastic.
“We are confident in its capacity to reinforce our energy security and bring down the cost of electricity in our country,” he added.

The Philippines relies heavily on imported fossil fuels for over half of its overall energy needs, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA), and prices have spiked due to the conflict in the Middle East.

According to the country’s department of energy, the Philippines saw the highest electricity rates in June among all members of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) as the country relied on more expensive power generation plants than its neighbours.

Residential electricity costs in the Philippines average about $0.20/kWh to $0.22/kWh. This is higher than many of its neighbours and sits well above the global residential average, which tracks closer to $0.176/kWh.
Its rates are comparable to high-cost developed nations like Singapore (about $0.23/kWh) and Japan (about $0.23/kWh), despite a significantly lower average local household income
In February the Philippines outlined a seven-phase process to construct nuclear power plants, with a focus on operating its first nuclear power plant by 2032.
The country has laid out clear targets it hopes to reach, planning to build 1,200 MW of nuclear capacity at the beginning, increasing to 2,400 MW by 2035, and 4,800 MW by 2050.

The country constructed a 621-MW Westinghouse nuclear power plant northwest of the capital Manila in Bataan, which was completed in 1984, but never commissioned because oif issues related to financing and  safety.

The Philippines has signed agreements with both South Korea and the US
as its looks for partners to help it to develop its nuclear industry.

According to London-based law firm Stephenson Harwood, the country’s procedural plans have helped to end ambiguity over nuclear progress and could allow it to meet its goal of receiving power plant applications by the end of 2026.

The law firm said the Philippines was also leveraging its regional influence, which was supported by holding the chairmanship of Asean in 2026 and holding the World Nuclear Supply Chain Conference in Manila in October later this year.

In a report on Asean countries’ nuclear development, Stephenson Harwood wrote: “The emergence of a clear, bankability‑focused framework for nuclear, combined with strong US and Korean engagement, is likely to draw increasing attention from small modular reactor (SMR) vendors and investors.”

“Whether targets can be met will turn on how efficiently it [the Philippines] can translate this institutional groundwork into site selection, permitting and long‑lead procurement over the next few years.”

The firm noted that a defining feature of nuclear power across Asean is that its nuclear future is being shaped as much in Moscow, Seoul, Washington, and Tokyo as in Hanoi or Manila, which makes vendor choice a geopolitical decision as much as an energy one.
The Bataan nuclear power station north of Manila never began operations. Photo: Creative Commons Licence.
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr delivers his state of the nation address to Congress in Manila on 27 July 2026. Courtesy Office of the President of the Philippines.

title: US Startup Raises $470 Million To Build Reactors For Military Bases
author: David Dalton
text: Antares Nuclear recently achieved criticality with Mark-0
US advanced nuclear power startup Antares Nuclear has raised $470m (€413m) to build micro nuclear reactors for US military bases.

The company said the Series C round, which was led by adventure capital firms Paradigm and Caffeinated Capital with participation from Industrious Ventures, Point72 Ventures, and Shine Capital, underscores investors' growing interest in advanced nuclear startups – a trend fuelled by an AI data centre building boom and demand for reliable new sources of low-carbon power.
The funding included $370m in equity and $100m in debt.

Antares announced on 4 June that its Mark-0 microreactor achieved initial criticality at Idaho National Laboratory (INL), making Antares the first private company to bring an advanced reactor to criticality under the US Department of Energy’s (DOE) push to deploy advanced plants.

The California-based company said the demonstration, backed by the DOE under its Reactor Pilot Program, meets an ambitious objective set by president Donald Trump and the DOE to reform how the federal government tests advanced reactors, and it establishes a replicable licensing pathway that the DOE and industry can use to accelerate future reactor demonstrations on commercial timelines.

The company is one of three finalists in the Pentagon’s Advanced Nuclear Power for Installations program, which will test SMRs on Air Force bases in Colorado and Montana. Antares aims to bring its first electricity-producing reactor online next year, with deployments at US military installations planned for 2028.
Antares is developing what it calls factory-produced, deployable fission microreactors of up to 1 MW to provide strategic energy for mission-critical systems across Earth, space and underseas.
In December Antares raised $96m in Series B funding as it pursues its reactor design.
In December Antares raised $96m (€82m) in Series B funding as it pursues its reactor design. Courtesy Antares/X.

title: Italy Announces Supply Chain Agreement As Efforts Continue To Deploy Nuclear
author: David Dalton
text: Global momentum creating ‘significant new opportunities’ for industrial sector

Italian state-owned energy company Ansaldo Energia and certification and engineering firm Rina have signed an agreement to develop the Italian nuclear industry supply chain as Rome steps up efforts to seize the opportunities of a rapidly growing nuclear market.
Ansaldo Energia said the initiative is primarily aimed at companies that are not currently active in the nuclear sector but possess transferable industrial capabilities.
The goal is to expand and strengthen the national industrial base, the company said.
The project includes preliminary assessments, gap analyses against international standards and pathways to access the nuclear market.

Rina will support companies throughout the certification and qualification process, while Ansaldo Energia will provide its industrial expertise, sharing market requirements and supporting the certification processes through potential financial backing from institutions and the public sector.
Ansaldo Energia said the agreement is set within a global context of strong nuclear growth, with nuclear energy playing an increasingly important role in energy security and decarbonisation.

Fabrizio Fabbri, chief executive officer of Ansaldo Energia, said: “Strengthening the country’s industrial capacity is an essential step to enable Italian companies to seize the opportunities of a rapidly growing nuclear market.”
Carlo Luzzatto, chief executive officer and general manager of Rina, said the renewed global momentum behind nuclear energy is creating significant new opportunities for Italy's industrial sector.
Italy is reversing its decades-long anti-nuclear policies by advancing a new legislative framework to reintroduce nuclear into its energy mix.
Prime minister Giorgia Meloni’s government is targeting a contribution of up to 22% of the nation’s electricity from nuclear power by 2050 to improve energy security and hit decarbonisation goals.

Italy was a pioneer of nuclear power and had four commercial nuclear plants – Caorso, Enrico Fermi, Garigliano and Latina – providing almost 5% of the country’s electricity production share at their peak in 1986-1987.
Italy shut down the last of the plants, Caorso and Enrico Fermi, in July 1990 following the 1987 referendum in the wake of the Chernobyl disaster.
There were later efforts to revive nuclear energy, but those plans were shelved after the 2011 Fukushima disaster in Japan.
Italy relies heavily on energy imports, including electricity generated by nuclear power in neighbouring countries such as France.
Italy shut down the last of its nuclear plants plants, Caorso (pictured) and Enrico Fermi, in July 1990. Courtesy Sogin.

title: Britain Needs Sweeping Policy Changes To Beat Russia And China In Civilian Nuclear Maritime Race, Says Report
author: David Dalton
text: Influential thinktank says nation has ‘narrow window’ in bid to capture markets and write rules
Britain has a narrow window to become a leading power in civilian maritime nuclear technology before Russia and China set global standards and dominate supply chains, a new report argues.

The report, produced by the Policy Exchange thinktank’s Nuclear Enterprise Commission, says nuclear-powered merchant ships and floating nuclear power plants are moving from technical possibility towards commercial deployment and urges the UK and the US to work together to develop “a functioning maritime nuclear cooperation programme”.

But the report, ‘Powering the Future: Leveraging the UK’s Nuclear and Maritime Heritage’, warns that deployment will depend on resolving legal and regulatory questions around safety, licensing, liability and insurability.

For the UK, alignment with the US to challenge Sino-Russian ambitions in maritime nuclear technologies presents a strategic opportunity, both to ensure control over contested regions and to lead the establishment of the required technical, commercial, and operational standards for the deployment of maritime nuclear.
“However, a clear route for British maritime nuclear applications, from concept to commercial operation, is currently absent from UK policies,” the report says.

Nuclear-powered ships and floating nuclear plants could operate for years without conventional refuelling, protect shipping from fuel-price shocks and provide reliable low-carbon power to ports, industry and remote infrastructure.

Advances in compact reactor design, modular construction and marine engineering are making maritime nuclear plants commercially credible just as global shipping and energy systems – especially for data centres – face growing pressure to become cleaner, more resilient and less dependent on vulnerable fuel supplies.

Floating nuclear power plants could supply firm, low-carbon energy to ports, remote settlements and critical infrastructure where land-based alternatives are difficult to build. Nuclear systems could allow states to sustain ships, infrastructure and wider economic activity across the Arctic, remote maritime regions and contested waters with far less dependence on vulnerable fuel logistics
According to the report, first movers will capture these markets and write their rules, shaping the standards, supply chains and operating assumptions of an important new global industry.
Russia has already moved, the report says. Russia possesses unrivalled operational experience through its nuclear icebreaker fleet and floating nuclear power programme.

It already operates the world’s only active civilian nuclear surface fleet, consisting primarily of specialised nuclear-powered icebreakers. Its floating nuclear power plant, the Akademik Lomonosov, has generated more than one billion kilowatt-hours of electricity.
China is following at scale, combining its expanding civil nuclear sector with the scale of the world’s largest shipbuilding industry.
Both nations recognise that maritime nuclear power can be used to support industrial development, secure access to remote regions and sustain a more persistent strategic presence at sea.
“Britain still has time to influence the outcome, but only if it acts before others define the sector’s standards and dependencies,” the report concludes.

“Britain cannot compete in mass shipbuilding, but over six decades of world-leading nuclear-submarine expertise, combined with strengths in maritime law, insurance, advanced engineering and nuclear fuel, offer it a credible route to leadership.”

The report says that with the international rulebook still being written, Britain can become the leading jurisdiction for deploying allied maritime nuclear technologies – securing a decisive strategic edge in an industry poised to reshape global shipping, energy and power projection.
The report says its recommendations are ambitious, but “grounded in Britain’s history and capabilities coupled with partnerships already underway”.

The recommendations include expanding the National Shipbuilding Office, a government agency, to cover maritime nuclear projects, preparing a full licensing roadmap, publishing an annually updated UK nuclear maritime code and developing a fleet licensing model based on approved vessel designs, reactor modules and operating envelopes. The aim should be to regulate serial deployment rather than treat each vessel as a first-of-a-kind case.

Other recommendations include using the London-based Nuclear Energy Maritime Organisation (Nemo) and other industry bodies to test emerging rules with those who will operate under them to identify practical gaps early and ensure that the regime is commercially usable.
The government should make London the centre for maritime nuclear liability and insurance.
“Liability must be predictable before civil nuclear maritime can scale,” the report says. “London should become the market in which this risk is understood and priced.”

The report also calls for cooperation with the US in the form of a partnership that establishes a legal, technical and commercial framework for the deployment of both nuclear-powered ships and floating nuclear power plants, ensuring these technologies are “predictable and insurable”.
The report urges the creation of a UK-US civil nuclear maritime work plan covering regulation, port access, liability, fuel, safeguards, workforce and demonstrator projects.
The UK and the US should create a shared safety case structure for marine advanced reactors. This would reduce duplication and make allied adoption easier.

Mikal Bøe, chairman and chief executive of Core Power, a London-based company developing maritime nuclear technologies for both grid-scale energy generation and commercial shipping, said Policy Exchange has asked the right question: not whether Britain should dominate every part of the maritime nuclear supply chain, but where it can become a valuable global partner.
He said: “The UK has the opportunity to rebuild its world-class strengths in nuclear engineering, maritime systems integration, international standards-setting, law, and insurance.

“The next step is coordinated action: a clear route from concept to operation, distinct but interoperable pathways for floating nuclear power plants and nuclear-powered commercial ships, and a practical UK–US programme covering regulation, port access, liability, workforce and demonstrator projects. Britain should help write the rules of this market, not wait to follow them.”
Russia’s Akademik Lomonosov floating nuclear plant, the only one operating in the world, has generated more than one billion kilowatt-hours of electricity. Courtesy Rosatom.
London-based Core Power is developing maritime nuclear technologies for both grid-scale energy generation and commercial shipping. Courtesy Core Power.

title: UK Startup Raises £15 Million For Novel Reactor Design Without Steam Turbines
author: David Dalton
text: Company says it has ‘flipped the script’ and solved critical cost and scale challenges

A UK startup developing compact advanced nuclear power systems has raised £15m ($19.9m, €17.5m) in a foundational fundraising round to advance and validate its novel reactor design, build large-scale test rigs and expand its team.

Manchester-based Nuclear Turbines, a spinout from Europe's largest aerospace and defence company BAE Systems, said the funding round was led by European deep tech venture capital firm IQ Capital, joined by Rhapsody Venture Partners, Zero Carbon Capital and Empirical Ventures.

The company said it is solving the nuclear sector’s “critical cost and scale challenges” by replacing steam turbine systems with highly efficient high-temperature turbine technology normally found in jet engines and gas-fired power plants.
Nuclear Turbines’ advanced nuclear reactor strips out the steam infrastructure that has kept nuclear prohibitively expensive and replaces it with novel technology found in jet engines.
This makes the reactors smaller, and cheaper to build and run, without sacrificing efficiency.
Once built, a single unit can generate electricity at a fifth of today’s cost and power factories at a tenth of current prices, Nuclear Turbines said.

The company said the solution is so compact that it could be deployed “behind the meter” on industrial sites, powering critical infrastructure such as industrial facilities and data centres and manufacturing facilities with a cost-effective alternative to grid-connected electricity.

It said the nature of its technology will make advanced nuclear power accessible and attractive to private finance, accelerating its deployment in energy-intensive sectors that are currently vulnerable to reliance on fossil fuels.

Jeremy Owston, the former BAE Systems principal engineer who is co-founder of Nuclear Turbines, said the nuclear industry has always designed reactors first, then figured out what to do with the heat.
“We flipped this script: we started with the cheapest way to generate power and designed a reactor to fit.
“If we’re serious about reindustrialising while meeting climate goals, we need energy that's clean and cheap. We’ve created the only tech that solves both, from the UK.”

Alongside the funding, Nuclear Turbines has appointed Lauren Dickerson as chief commercial and strategy officer. Dickerson joins from British multinational energy and services company Centrica, where she spent over four years as strategy director.

Today’s nuclear reactors generate electricity by boiling water to steam to drive a steam turbine. Steam turbines became the nuclear default because they work with the low-temperature heat produced by current water-cooled nuclear reactors. However, they are also large and relatively inefficient. They need large tanks and boilers, heat exchangers, and complex cooling systems all capable of handling high pressure water safely, which makes them expensive to build and difficult to shrink to an economically viable size.
In contrast, gas turbines, which power aeroplanes and are used in all gas-fired power stations, convert extremely hot air directly into power with very little energy loss.
This makes them highly efficient, compact and economically viable at small scales.

But they are not suitable for nuclear reactors because current designs cannot heat air to the high temperatures gas turbines need. Water-cooled reactors operate at low temperatures of below 300°C, while high-temperature reactors use graphite, which burns when exposed to air.

Nuclear Turbines’ novel reactor design bypasses the need for graphite. This means it can harness the efficiency of gas turbine tech for the first time, operate at higher temperatures and solve the critical scale and cost issues with steam systems.
L-R: Nuclear Turbines’ Lauren Dickerson, Jeremy Owston and Timothy Abram. Courtesy Nuclear Turbines.

title: Uranium Fundamentals Remain Strong Despite Disappointing Performance, Says Sprott
author: David Dalton
text: Nuclear power ‘has potential to provide solution’ to energy security woes
Uranium entered the middle of the year with a stronger fundamental backdrop than its market performance would suggest, according to mid-year analysis from Sprott Asset Management.

The Canada-based precious metals and critical materials investments company said that rising long-term prices, improving policy support, growing electricity demand and constrained supply have all continued to reinforce the investment case, even as returns across uranium mining equities have disappointed.
The first half of the year was marked by a growing, and at times frustrating, gap between uranium market fundamentals and price performance, Sprott said.

In June, the uranium spot price stayed relatively flat, edging up just 0.1%, while the long-term price advanced to its strongest level of the current cycle. Uranium mining equities, meanwhile, fell 14.4%, and junior uranium miners dropped 17.46%.
Year to date, the spot uranium price is up 4.28%, while uranium miners are down 3.91% and junior miners are down 7.43%.
Sprott described the gap as a matter of sentiment rather than substance.

“In our view, this performance divergence reflects a combination of near-term market uncertainty, risk-off positioning and subdued investor sentiment rather than any deterioration in the sector’s underlying fundamentals,” the report said.

It said policy support is turning into execution with the US, Canada and Europe moving from broad nuclear ambitions toward financing, regulatory reform, life extensions, restarts and fuel-cycle investment.
“For much of this year, investor attention has been largely focused on AI, geopolitical tensions in the Middle East, energy security and broader macroeconomic uncertainty,” Sprott said.
“Ironically, these same themes have reinforced the long-term investment case for uranium.
“The rapid expansion of AI data centres, reshoring, advanced manufacturing and electrification are accelerating the demand for reliable, baseload electricity.”
Sprott said the US-Iran conflict and concerns over the security of critical hydrocarbon transit routes have reinforced the strategic importance of energy security.
It added that nuclear power has the potential to provide a solution, offering large-scale, reliable, 24/7 generation with fuel requirements less susceptible to supply shocks.
Sprott said the fundamentals for the uranium market remain strong. Courtesy Kazatomprom.

title: EDF Extends Operations At Four More UK Nuclear Reactors
author: David Dalton
text: All nine commercial nuclear plants in country have now received lifetime extensions

EDF has extended the operating lifetimes of four nuclear units at two of its UK nuclear power stations by two years, a move that means all nine commercial reactors in the country have been granted extensions.

Heysham A in Lancashire, northwest England, and Hartlepool A in Teesside, northeast England, are now expected to produce electricity until March 2030, the French state company and UK nuclear fleet owner said.
It said extending the generating lives of the plants could boost nuclear output by 28 TWh over the two-year period, enough to power 8.4 million homes.
Before the decision to extend operations Heysham A and Hartlepool A were due to move into defueling in March 2028.

Heysham A has two advanced gas-cooled reactors (AGRs) that both began commercial operation in 1989. According to International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) data, Heysham A-1 has a net capacity of 485 MW and Heysham A-2 of 575 MW.
Hartlepool A also has two AGRs that began commercial operation in 1989. The IAEA says Hartlepool A-1 has a net capacity of 590 MW and Hartlepool A-2 of 595 MW.

EDF’s managing director of nuclear operations, John Munro, said: “We have been clear it is our ambition to generate from these stations for as long as it is safe and commercially viable to do so it is great to be able to confirm a further two-year extension for the plants.”
He said the AGR stations have been the backbone of secure, zero-carbon generation in the UK for five decades.

When EDF acquired the UK’s nuclear fleet in 2009 all the UK’s AGR plants were scheduled to be offline by 2023, but a series of life extensions mean four of those stations – Hartlepool A, Heysham A, Heysham B and Torness – are still generating with three now in various stages of defueling or decommissioning.

The UK currently operates eight AGRs across the four station sites. Originally, the UK had a fleet of 14 AGR reactors across seven sites, but several have reached the end of their operational lifespans and are undergoing defueling.

Munro said: “When nuclear goes offline it is often replaced with gas generation. If we are serious about reducing the UK’s reliance on gas and retaining system stability, it makes sense to keep these stations online to support energy security and our carbon targets.”
All nine commercial nuclear plants in the UK have now struck a deal with the government to continue running.
Earlier this month EDF announced that the Sizewell B nuclear power plant will produce electricity for a further 20 years after a deal was reached with the government.

The 1,198-MW pressurised water reactor unit, in Suffolk, eastern England, began commercial operation in 1995 and was due to be permanently shut down in 2035, but will now continue operating until 2055.
The plant produces 3% of Britain’s electricity, enough to meet the equivalent demand of 2.5 million homes.
According to the IAEA, the UK’s nuclear fleet produces about 10.7% of the country’s electricity.
The UK government is also pushing ahead with plans for two new units at Sizewell C, while two units at Hinkley Point C are under construction.
The UK’s nine commercial nuclear power reactors are: Hartlepool A-1, Hartlepool A-2, Heysham A-1, Heysham A-2, Heysham B-1, Heysham B-2, Sizewell B, Torness-1, Torness-2.
A control room at the Hartlepool nuclear site in northern England. Courtesy EDF.

title: US Signs Landmark Nuclear Deal With Saudi Arabia
author: David Dalton
text: Agreement paves way for reactor deployment and could also allow uranium enrichment

The US has signed a landmark nuclear deal with Saudi Arabia that paves the way for commercial nuclear reactor deployment, but US president Donald Trump has denied reports the deal allows for uranium enrichment.

In a statement on 22 July, the US Department of Energy (DOE) said its secretary, Chris Wright, and his Saudi counterpart, Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman, signed a “peaceful nuclear cooperation agreement” along with a “bilateral safeguards agreement”.
According to the DOE the agreement, commonly known as a 123 agreement, will provide “great access” for US firms to the Saudi nuclear energy programme.

The full details of the deal have yet to be released, but the timing of the announcement is seen as controversial because the US’s war with Iran is being fought in part to prevent Tehran enriching uranium and to make it difficult for Iran to build a nuclear weapon.

US media reported before the deal was announced that it could potentially allow Saudi Arabia to enrich uranium, although this has not been confirmed. Trump posted on Truth Social today that the deal does not allow the enrichment of uranium.

Earlier reports had suggested that, after undertaking a joint study with the US, Saudi Arabia may be allowed to enrich uranium on its soil to produce fuel at a US-built enrichment facility, instead of relying on imported fuel.

A civil nuclear deal with Saudi Arabia has been in the works for years during both Trump’s first administration and that of former president Joe ⁠Biden. No deal has been finalised before now, in part because of concerns that it could offer Saudi Arabia a path to develop a nuclear weapon.

The deal will be submitted to Congress for review, where it could face opposition among lawmakers who fear a lack of monitoring safeguards to restrict Saudi Arabia’s uranium enrichment.
