The BBC said it appears lawmakers do not have the votes needed to block Trump from putting the agreement in place.
The DOE said the 123 agreement will benefit US industry, workers and supply chains while helping to meet Saudi energy needs.

It said the two agreements advance US and regional security by upholding high standards of nuclear safety, security, and nonproliferation and strengthening the US’s competitive edge in civil nuclear technology.
“These agreements reflect our two nations’ shared commitment to strengthening US-Saudi commercial relations, delivering prosperity at home and security to our allies abroad,” said Wright.

“Rest assured, these agreements uphold the highest standards of nuclear safety and nonproliferation, while relying on the world’s best nuclear technology and scientists, designed right here in the United States.”
The Saudi Arabian government said in a statement that it had signed the agreement, finalising negotiations over the peaceful uses of nuclear energy.

It said the deal will contribute to developing joint cooperation regarding nuclear security, safety and non-proliferation, adding that it reflects the shared vision of both countries to expand cooperation in the fields of energy and future technologies and support sustainable development.

A 123 agreement, named after Section 123 of the US Atomic Energy Act, sets out the framework for peaceful nuclear cooperation between the US and other countries, allowing the transfer of nuclear material, reactors, and technology while ensuring safety and non-proliferation.
They are designed to govern how US companies can export nuclear technology while preventing partner countries from developing nuclear weapons.
Key aspects of 123 agreements include non-proliferation criteria and International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) oversight to monitor nuclear activities.

Reports suggest the Saudi agreement would not require the IAEA’s additional protocol, which gives inspectors broader powers to verify that nuclear material is not being diverted for military purposes.

A 2009 123 agreement with the United Arab Emirates, which has since become the only nation in the Arab World to have built commercial nuclear plants, included an explicate agreement that the UAE would forgo domestic uranium enrichment entirely.

Saudi Arabia, the world’s largest oil exporter, is seeking to generate substantial renewable energy and reduce emissions, under its Vision 2030 reform plan. At least some of this is expected to come from nuclear energy.

In 2022, Saudi Arabia established a national nuclear energy company to develop and operate nuclear facilities. Riyadh said the Saudi Nuclear Energy Holding Company would participate in nuclear projects locally and internationally.
Also in 2022, the kingdom began the process to issue a licence to build its first nuclear station, which reports said could cost about $14bn (€12.2bn).
According to local media, the nuclear station is projected to have a capacity of 2,800 GW.
Earlier reports said bids had been received by South Korea, France, China and Russia, but that information has not been officially confirmed.

File photo of US energy secretary Chris Wright with Donald Trump. Wright said the deal with Saudi Arabia upholds the highest standards of nuclear safety and nonproliferation. Courtesy The White House.

title: Rosatom Points To Poor Economic Conditions As Doubts Cast On Nuclear Projects
author: David Dalton
text: Budget cuts call plans for reactors in Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan into question, say reports
Russia’s state-owned nuclear corporation has at least 18 new nuclear projects underway at home, but is cutting its investment programme by nearly 50% this year due to “poor economic conditions”.

The company said the projects are in “various stages of implementation” throughout Russia, and do not count the more than two dozen under construction overseas in places including Bangladesh, India and Turkey. Projects are also in the early stages in Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan.

In an article published in the company’s in-house magazine, Rosatom director-general Alexey Likhachev said the company aims to increase revenues to $51.3bn (€44.9bn) by 2028 – a nearly 18% increase from this year. Improving profits, however, means reducing costs by 5% that same year.
Likhachev also said Rosatom would strive to cut operating costs by 10% within the next 18 months.

“We immediately abandoned a number of projects or shifted the deadlines for their implementation to a later date, guided by several criteria, the main of which is efficiency in the horizon until 2030, that is, more profit and revenue per ruble of investment,” Likhachev was quoted as saying by Reuters.

Press reports said the company’s troubles are widely linked to the Kremlin’s ongoing campaign in Ukraine, which has generally sapped Russia of its financial strength. International sanctions have also hampered Rosatom.
Likhachev did not specify which projects are being abandoned delayed.
In 2025 Kazakhstan awarded Rosatom a contract to build the Central Asian state’s first nuclear power station on the shores of Lake Balkhash.
Rosatom has also begun construction in Uzbekistan of an integrated nuclear plant with both large-scale and small modular reactor (SMR) units.
The independent news organisation Eurasianet reported that both Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan have alternatives to Rosatom.

Kazakhstan already has an agreement in place for a Chinese company to build two nuclear plants in the country. And both Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan have expressed interest in working with the US to develop SMRs.
Russia’s president Vladimir Putin recently oversaw by video link the official start of reactor construction in Uzbekistan. Courtesy Rosatom.

title: Advanced Nuclear Company Unveils Generation IV Reactor Project For Southern France
author: David Dalton
text: Stellaria signs MOU as plans progress for ‘sovereign French energy infrastructure’

French advanced nuclear reactor developer Stellaria has signed a memorandum of understanding to develop an integrated energy hub, marking what it said is another step towards its aim of deploying a sovereign French energy infrastructure for electricity and industry.
The MOU, signed with Unitel Group and Energie Hub, is for the progressive deployment of several Stellarium nuclear units in the Fos-sur-Mer area of southern France.

Unite group is an AI, digital infrastructure and technology company. It formed the Energie Hub consortium for the development, financing, construction and operation of strategic energy infrastructure.
Stellaria said the phased approach to deploying its reactors in Fos-Sur-Mer This will allow each stage of the project to be validated while ensuring safety and industrial control.
It said the units will supply low-carbon electricity, industrial heat, and grid flexibility and support services for the Fos-sur-Mer area.

The MOU includes the development of an AI-powered digital energy management platform that will optimise energy production and consumption, manage networks in real time, oversee storage capacity and anticipate industrial demand.

It also covers the structuring of the project’s financing, preparations for creating a dedicated entity for project development and operation, and the establishment of a strategic partnership between the three companies.

Earlier this year Stellaria and the French Alternative Energies and Atomic Energy Commission (CEA) signed a letter of intent (LOI) for a feasibility study into the construction of key Stellaria testing facilities at CEA’s Cadarache site.

Stellaria said the signing of the LOI lays the foundations for critical experiments, scheduled for 2030, using the Alvin prototype plant. The Alvin experiments will allow Stellaria to validate its modelling and calculations.

Stellarium is a Generation IV molten salt design. Molten salt reactors are said to have advantages over more traditional water-cooled plants, including improved safety and higher efficiency. Inherent safety features include low-pressure operation, reduced waste and the use of standard low-enriched uranium fuel.
Stellaria raised €23m ($26.2m) in 2025 to support technical and regulatory studies and has previously signed a power pre-order agreement with data centre operator Equinix.
The company also received €10m in public funding under the federal France 2030 programme in 2024, supporting technical studies and regulatory preparation for its prototype reactor.
In February Stellaria submitted an application to the French authorities for the potential construction the Alvin prototype.
A computer-generated image of Stellaria’s planned Alvin demonstration plant. Courtesy Stellaria.

title: Impact Of Heatwave On French Nuclear Plants ‘Limited’ With Exports Continuing
author: David Dalton
text: Analysis shows reactors remained a foundation of electricity system

The impact of the recent heatwave in France on the country’s nuclear plants was limited, with around 5.5 GW of capacity temporarily unavailable in order to comply with regulatory constraints relating to river temperatures, the Paris-based nuclear group Sfen has said, quoting research by UK-based Aurora Energy Research.
Three commercial nuclear plants were affected by shutdowns due to rising river temperatures: Nogent, Bugey and Golfech.
But France remained an exporter of electricity throughout the heatwave at the end of June.
Sfen said the “exceptional” heatwave was a test for the French power system.
Strong demand was linked to air conditioning, weak wind generation and constraints on certain nuclear reactors.
“Despite this unfavourable combination, France remained a net electricity exporter thanks to its nuclear fleet,” Sfen said.
“This analysis shows that the nuclear fleet, despite limited production restrictions, remained a foundation of the power system.

“It enabled France to remain an exporter during the period and to support its neighbours, in particular Belgium and Germany, which were exposed to very high market prices in the late afternoon and forced to rely heavily on fossil fuels.”
The Aurora research showed that electricity demand reached up to 12 GW above seasonal norms, driven by air conditioning, without ever approaching winter peaks or threatening security of supply.
Aurora said the heatwave affected all generation technologies. Nuclear availability was reduced, mainly due to long-planned outages and restrictions linked to river water temperatures.

A comparison with Germany and Belgium illustrates France’s role in the functioning of the European electricity market. Both countries relied more heavily on imports – particularly from France – and on thermal power plants, and faced average prices between 18:00 and 21:00 of €369/MWh and €424/MWh respectively, compared with €222/MWh for France.

Aurora said the heatwave confirms the need to adapt the electricity system to heat events that are set to recur and intensify. It called for nuclear plants to deploy additional cooling solutions for reactors – following the example of the system already in place at the two-unit Civaux nuclear station in central France.

Civaux uses a specialised hybrid cooling tower system to process water from the Vienne River. It is designed to handle the river’s low summer flow by chilling the water with large ventilators before discharging it back, ensuring it does not overheat the environment.
France has 57 nuclear units generating about 67% of its electricity production, the highest percentage ahead of Slovakia 60% from five plants and Hungary with 47% from four plants.

The newest 57th unit, Flamanville-3, was connected to the grid in December 2024 after years of delays and cost overruns, but though it recently reached full power, has not yet begun commercial operation.

France has ambitious plans for new nuclear power plants with state power company EDF aiming to begin preparatory works for a new EPR2 nuclear plant at the existing Penly nuclear site in northern France.
The Nogent, Bugey (pictured) and Golfech nuclear power stations were affected by shutdoiwns. Courtesy Bernard Gaetan/EDF.

title: European Nuclear Industry Group Backs Bloc’s Electrification And ETS Proposals
author: David Dalton
text: More nuclear and renewables ‘bring electricity prices down and drive fossil fuels out’

The Brussels-based nuclear group nucleareurope has welcomed both the bloc’s electrification action plan and revised EU emissions trading system (ETS) proposals, both of which it said have the potential to accelerate a shift to electrification, reduce CO2 emissions and ultimately strengthen the competitiveness of Europe’s industries.
“One of the best ways of reducing our CO2 emissions – and our dependence on energy imports – is to electrify what can be electrified,” said nucleareurope director-general Emmanuel Brutin.
He said the long-awaited electrification action plan is key in this respect and “we therefore fully support the idea of establishing an indicative electrification target for 2040”.

“At the same time, industry needs support to help decarbonise its manufacturing processes (either through electrification or shifting to clean heat or hydrogen). We are therefore very much in favour of an EU ETS which redirects revenues back into industries with clear decarbonisation plans.”
The two sets of proposals were published on 17 July by the European Commission.

The aim of the electrification action plan is to make Europe the world’s first “electro-powered” continent by aiming to increase electrification from today’s 23% of energy use to 46% by 2040. The commission said that by reaching this goal, the EU could save €260bn ($297bn) per year in fossil fuel imports.
According to the electrification action plan, more nuclear and renewables bring electricity prices down and drive fossil fuels out.

“We therefore support the idea of an indicative electrification target by 2040,” nucleareurope said. “In addition, and as recognised in the communication, taxes on gas are lower than electricity.  Reducing taxes on electricity and ensuring it is not taxed more than gas is another proposal which we fully support.”
The ETS reforms would relax the rules of the system to give businesses more time to reduce their carbon output than previously planned.
The changes would mean some industries could obtain emission allowances until 2038 instead of 2034, if they commit to investing in decarbonisation efforts.
The ETS, which was introduced in 2005, is the EU's main tool for curbing greenhouse gases.
But it has come under criticism from a number of member states, with Italy in particular condemning the trading scheme as a de facto tax that has helped keep energy prices artificially high.

Under the ETS, Europe's industries and power plants are required to buy a permit, or allowance, for every tonne of carbon dioxide they emit, creating a financial incentive to invest in cleaner technologies.
Companies can buy extra permits or trade them. Some businesses are given permits for free to help them compete with foreign firms that do not pay carbon costs.
The ETS also caps the number of permits released each year to make sure missions decrease.
Photo courtesy National Grid.

title: Kyoto Fusioneering Signs Partnership With NGK To Develop Flibe For Nuclear Fusion Plants
author: David Dalton
text: Molten salt is prized in advanced reactors for safety, thermal capacity and low-pressure operation

Japanese fusion energy company Kyoto Fusioneering (KF) has signed an agreement with industrial company NGK Corporation to develop and commercialise Flibe required for fusion plants to extract heat from plasma.
Flibe is a molten salt made from lithium fluoride and beryllium fluoride and is seen as a method to extract heat away from a reactor and breed the tritium fuel needed to sustain a fusion reaction.

It is essentially both a nuclear reactor coolant and a solvent for fertile or fissile materials. The companies will produce, refine, and test the molten salt. They will also build the circulation systems needed to use it in commercial fusion reactors.
Flibe was first used in the 1960s at the Oak Ridge National Laboratory in Tennessee. It is prized in advanced nuclear reactors for its safety, high thermal capacity and low-pressure operation.

It can perform several critical functions at the same time. Apart from transferring heat away from the reactor, the molten salt can breed tritium, an essential fuel for sustaining fusion reactions. This makes Flibee well suited for future fusion reactors.

KF said that under the partnership it would lead the design of a Flibe production and refining facility, which NGK would then operate at its beryllium facility in Nagoya, Japan. The aim would be to serve both Japanese and global customers.

“By combining the beryllium-handling expertise NGK has built over many years with the system-integration know-how we have accumulated through fusion plant design, we aim to accelerate the industrial foundation for Flibe-related technology and take an important step toward the societal implementation of fusion energy,” said Kiyoshi Seko, president of KF.

KF said that bringing fusion to commercial reality depended more than just on the plasma-confinement technology at the heart of the reactor, but also solving how heat could be extracted from the plasma, how to breed and recover the tritium fuel of a reactor, and how to build the circulation systems that bring a plant together.

According to KF, Flibe was a leading candidate to do this. However, to realise its potential would also require mastering the safe handling, purification and quality control of beryllium, which it described as a rare and technically demanding material.

Founded in 2019, KF specialises in developing advanced technologies for commercial fusion power plants such as gyrotron systems, tritium fuel cycle technologies, and breeding blankets for tritium production and power generation.

KF is also progressing its own privately led demonstration programmes. Unity-1, an engineering test facility focused on fusion plant subsystems such as the tritium fuel cycle, is already operational in Japan, while Unity-2, a larger integrated demonstration project, is currently under construction in Canada as a joint venture with Canadian Nuclear Laboratories.
Unity-1, an engineering test facility focused on fusion plant subsystems, is already operational in Japan. Courtesy Kyoto Fusioneering.

title: US Nuclear Leader Constellation Makes Strategic Investment In Startup SMR Developer
author: Nigel Davies
text: Blue Energy aims to develop financeable, turnkey nuclear plants compatible with leading reactor technology

US utility major Constellation Energy has made a strategic investment in small modular reactor (SMR) developer Blue Energy through its venture capital arm as the startup company aims to accelerate the rollout of nuclear plants fabricated largely in shipyards.

The investment is the first by Constellation, the largest operator of nuclear energy in the US, in an SMR developer and was made through its Constellation Technology Ventures investment arm. No value for the investment was announced.
Blue Energy was established in 2023 and aims to build the bulk of its SMRs at shipyards and then send them by barge to their final locations to save on costs and time to deployment.
It plans to develop financeable, turnkey nuclear power plants compatible with leading reactor technology such as GE Vernova Hitachi’s BWRX-300.

The company said the investment would help it to scale its efforts towards commercialisation, and follows a partnership signed earlier this year with GE Vernova to develop a gas-to-nuclear plant with a capacity of 2,500 MW.

“This relationship helps us leverage an established operator, proven technology, and innovative, project-financeable deployment models to expand access to nuclear energy,” said Jake Jurewicz, chief executive of Blue Energy.
Constellation also welcomed the investment.

“Constellation is committed to exploring innovative pathways that can help accelerate the deployment of advanced nuclear technologies in the US and allocate risk appropriately,” said vice-president David Dardis.

“The Constellation Technology Ventures investment in Blue Energy supports its deployment plans for the GE Vernova Hitachi BWRX-300, a proven technology with a potential path to scale for the next generation of nuclear energy,” he added.
Blue Energy's model is designed to address one of the biggest challenges facing the nuclear industry: how to finance and deploy new nuclear generation at the speed required to meet growing demand.

By using proven nuclear technology​ and​ employing an innovative large-format robotic prefabrication and assembly methods inspired by offshore oil and gas and LNG projects, the company plans to unlock project financing ​​for the first time in the nuclear sector​ and accelerate deployment timelines.

The company said it can accelerate deployment of new nuclear power with the potential to eliminate at least half a decade off the conventional 10-year-plus nuclear timeline, slashing time to power to 48 months or less by energising turbines with a “natural gas bridge” that converts to nuclear power.

The US Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) recently approved Blue Energy’s approach to resequencing major phases of nuclear plant construction that supports large module and gas-to-nuclear delivery schedules.
Blue Energy could begin early site works on its first planned project in Texas in 2026.
The company will ​then apply to the NRC for a construction permit in 2027.
Blue Energy is focused on building prefabricated nuclear power plants for faster deployment. Courtesy Blue Energy.

title: Russia’s Nuclear Regulator Issues Site Licences For Two New Reactors At Kola
author: David Dalton
text: Aim is to replace ageing units at existing site near border with Finland

Russia’s federal nuclear regulator Rostekhnadzor has issued site licences for the first two proposed units at the new Kola nuclear power station, about 150 km from the border with Finland in northwest Russia, state nuclear corporation Rosatom said.
The decision means that the site, 10 km south of the existing Kola nuclear station on the shores of Lake Imandra in the Murmansk region, meets requirements.
The general contractor, Titan-2, will start site preparation by laying access roads, clearing forests and creating a construction and installation base.

“In preparation for the plant’s construction, we are working with the general designer and general contractor to develop the construction technology, timeframe, and safety issues,” said Nikolai Rusakov, deputy director for capital construction at Kola.
“I am confident that the coordinated work of all participants will allow us to begin the main construction phase on schedule.”

Rosatom has said it is planning to build four new units at Kola. They will be VVER-S plants, a 600 MW pressurised water reactor under development, with the first two to be built between 2027 and 2037.
The new units are intended to replace the existing four Kola units as they come to the end of their operating lives.
They are VVER-440 reactors at the existing Kola site. They each have a capacity of 411 MW and according to International Atomic Energy Agency data began commercial operation between 1973 and 1984.
Rosatom said the construction of the Kola NPP-2 is a project that will shape the future of the Murmansk region for decades to come.
“The new power units will replace the decommissioned capacity of the existing plant, which is nearing the end of its service life, and maintain the region's energy balance,” it said.
The existing Kola nuclear power station in northwest Russia. Courtesy Rosenergoatom.

title: Newcleo Submits Regulatory Engagement Plan For US Nuclear Reactor Licensing
author: David Dalton
text: French company working on basic design of LFR-AS-200

France-based advanced modular reactor technology and nuclear fuel company Newcleo has submitted a regulatory engagement plan (REP) to the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) for its LFR-AS-200 lead-cooled fast reactor.
The REP sets out the proposed framework for Newcleo’s pre-application engagement with NRC staff in support of the future licensing of the LFR-AS-200.
It provides an overview of the company’s proposed licensing approach and an indicative schedule for technical submissions and interactions with the NRC.
“This submission to the NRC reflects years of dedicated research and engineering behind the LFR-AS-200," said Newcleo chief executive officer Stefano Buono.
“Lead-cooled fast reactor technology offers a uniquely safe and efficient path to clean, reliable energy, and we look forward to a constructive dialogue with the NRC as we advance toward licensing.”

To support the development and licensing of its reactor technology, Newcleo has established an extensive international research and development programme, in collaboration with national laboratories in Italy, France and Japan
Newcleo is working on the basic design of its demonstrator LFR-AS-30 reactor.
Newcleo’s LFR technology is designed to operate with recycled nuclear fuel, offering the promise of greater sustainability and reduced waste in nuclear energy production.
The company is planning to deploy a pilot LFR-AS-30 plant as a demonstrator in France in the early 2030s.
The facility, known as Precursor, will emulate the size, complexity and thermal hydraulic performances of the LFR-AS-30 reactor design.
The main vessel for Newcleo’s Precursor non-nuclear test facility arrives at the Brasimone research centre in Italy. Courtesy Newcleo.

title: Serbia Plans To Start Construction Of First Nuclear Plant By 2035
author: David Dalton
text: Belgrade continues with plans to reassess long-term energy strategy

Serbia expects to start the construction of a nuclear power plant by 2035, after completion of the initial phase of its nuclear energy initiative planned for next year, energy minister Dubravka Djedovic Handanovic said.
Djedovic Handanovic said in a statement on 13 July that Serbia’s goal is to complete the first phase of its nuclear energy initiative by the middle of next year.

The first phase will include a comprehensive analysis of the legal and regulatory framework required for construction of a nuclear power plant and will mean Serbia has all the information it needs to make a decision on further development.
“By 2032, we expect to be ready in institutional, regulatory, and professional terms to select the technology and begin the construction process by 2035,” Djedovic Handanovic said.
In March Serbia’s ministry of mining and energy presented a preliminary technical study on nuclear energy that laid out a roadmap towards a possible first nuclear power plant by around 2040.

The study, completed in June 2025 by France’s EDF, said all studies necessary for a government decision on whether to proceed with a nuclear programme should be completed by mid-2027 with institutional, regulatory and workforce capacity-building to follow.
This would allow Serbia to select a technology and enter construction contracting by 2032.

The study did not prioritise a single reactor technology, but provided a comparison of large nuclear power plants and small modular reactors (SMRs). The study found both options could support Serbia’s energy system.

Serbia has no commercial nuclear power plants. Under a law adopted in 1989 following the Chernobyl disaster, the country imposed a moratorium on nuclear power development and the construction of nuclear facilities.
However, the government has recently taken steps to reassess nuclear energy as part of its long-term energy strategy.
In 2024 Serbia lifted the decades-long ban on nuclear power development and signed cooperation agreements with several countries and companies to explore potential nuclear projects.
Energy minister Dubravka Djedovic Handanovic said Serbia’s goal is to complete the first phase of its nuclear energy initiative by the middle of next year. Courtesy Serbia Energy Ministry.

title: TerraPower Holds Positive Talks With UK, Targets Early To Mid-2030s For Reactor Launch
author: Nigel Davies
text: First British office expected to be in Liverpool, close to regulator carrying out Natrium nuclear plant design assessment

US advanced nuclear innovation company TerraPower aims to export its Natrium reactor to the UK by the early to mid-2030s as the country strengthens its policy support for nuclear, a senior executive for the Washington-state based firm said.

The company, co-founded by Bill Gates, who serves as chairman, recently established a UK subsidiary, TerraPower UK Ltd, and announced the beginning of a UK regulatory review for its 345-MW Natrium reactor. The review will assess the safety, security and environmental implications of the Natrium technology.

In conversation with NucNet, TerraPower’s vice-president for government affairs, Andrew Richards, said the company was encouraged by recent policy steps in the UK, including a nuclear framework that aims to promote a new era of British nuclear energy generation.

“We’ve had a lot of really positive engagements with the government, and there does seem to be a strong interest to deploy advanced nuclear in the United Kingdom. So we do see some promise there to be able to proceed with exporting Natrium,” said Richards.
TerraPower is building its first Natrium sodium-cooled fast reactor at a retiring coal site in Kemmerer in Wyoming. The nuclear plant is expected to become operational around 2031.
This would give time for its subsidiary to develop in the UK, with a target of the early to mid-2030s for a first reactor launch, according to Richards.
The company has hired Ian Hudson as the head of its UK business, with an office targeted first in the north of England.
“We’ll likely open office space in Liverpool, close to the UK’s Office for Nuclear Regulation [ONR],” said Richards, adding that a further London office would likely follow.
The ONR is responsible for the Natrium regulatory review, known as a generic design assessment (GDA).

Richards said the company was working with the government to help develop some level of local supply chain in the UK, as it would do in other countries such as South Korea, where TerraPower also expects to deploy its reactors.
“We’ve been in early discussions and we’re looking at the requirements for the UK, and we do see an interest from the government to see what can be sourced in the UK,” said Richards.
Richards said that by the time a reactor was launched in the UK, the company would expect to have guaranteed a “robust supply” of high-assay low-enriched uranium (Haleu) required for its reactors.
As for the first Natrium reactor, Richards said that work was continuing at the Kemmerer site, where initial construction began on the non-nuclear part of the facility in June 2024.

He said that the walls were installed for the sodium test and fill facility, where tests would be carried out on how the plant’s nuclear components engage with sodium. This building is now 15-storeys high, and is expected to be operational in 2027.
Richards also said that work was beginning on the nuclear site following the construction permit granted by the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) in March.
“We have spent the last few weeks since receiving the construction permit moving a lot of earthwork and preparing the site to begin nuclear grade construction,” he said.
Richards said that work would begin on the energy island later this year, and by early 2027 the construction of the nuclear island would start.
Construction is expected to  take until 2030, fuel loading would begin at the end of that year, and commercial operations would begin in 2031.
Richards said the company’s biggest construction challenges so far had been in hiring the skilled workforce and creating a supply chain for the reactors.
“We’re building one reactor now, but we want to have 10 by 2035. So, to be able to build this around the country and be able to move the workforce is going to be a challenge.”
Discussions were also continuing with technology giant Meta, which has an agreement with TerraPower to acquire up to eight reactors by 2035.
“We don’t have any sites to announce yet, but I can tell you that we are working very closely with Meta to find out where it would best fit .”
TerraPower said that fuel for its Kemmerer plant would be sourced through its partnership with ASP Isotopes, an American company with operations based in South Africa.
TerraPower’s long-term aim, however, is to buy fuel sourced in the US.
“We’ve worked very closely with the nuclear industry in the US, the Department of Energy, as well as the US Congress, as they work to onshore and reestablish a domestic uranium enrichment supply.”

TerraPower says its Natrium technology is well positioned to support rapidly increasing energy demand. The Natrium plant design features a 345 MW sodium-cooled fast reactor with a patented molten salt-based energy storage system.

The storage technology can boost the system’s output to 500 MW of power when needed because it is designed to keep base output steady, ensuring constant reliability, and can quickly ramp up when demand peaks. It is the only advanced reactor design with this unique feature.
A rendering of a TerraPower Natrium nuclear power plant. Courtesy TerraPower.

title: New Legislation Paves Way For At Least 1,100 MW Of Nuclear Construction In New Jersey
author: Nigel Davies
text: Bipartisan bill launches state’s reactor procurement process and comes after recent lifting of moratorium

The US state of New Jersey aims to build at least 1,100 MW of new nuclear and companies will have until the start of next year to present their plans following the passing of key nuclear procurement legislation.
The Power NJ Act, which has been signed into law by state governor, the Democrat Mikie Sherrill, follows the lifting of a 50-year moratorium on new builds in New Jersey in April.
The legislation launches the state’s procurement process for new nuclear energy and will establish a transparent, competitive process to evaluate proposals.
The bill passed both houses of the legislature unanimously with strong bipartisan support.

“This is how we don’t kick the can down the road, and we make sure in 10 years we’re not still facing a power generation problem or affordability crisis,” Sherrill said at the bill signing event at the Statehouse dubbed Nuclear Power Generation for Generations.

The legislation aims to build out new nuclear in the state, and follows the path of five other states (Wisconsin, Kentucky, Montana, West Virginia, Illinois) that have also withdrawn moratoriums on additional nuclear capacity.

The law will create a process for evaluating and approving projects that can help address growing energy demands while ensuring benefits for ratepayers and maintaining system reliability, Sherrill said.
Land next to New Jersey’s existing Salem and Hope Creek nuclear stations has long been designated by the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) as a potential location for an additional reactor.

Estimates are that it would take at least 10 years and about $24bn (€20.9bn) to build a large convention nuclear power reactor in New Jersey. Federal financing programmes may guarantee or finance up to 80% of a project’s cost, Sherrill’s office said

The Power NJ Act says companies will have until 9 January 2027 to submit proposals including regulatory, environmental, financial and workforce information to build at least 1,100MW of new capacity in the state.
The proposals will be evaluated by the New Jersey Board of Public Utilities (NJBPU) and the New Jersey Economic Development Authority (NJEDA).
The legislation says that within the next 12 months negotiations and stipulations would then begin with selected companies to set accurate cost estimates, the price of electricity and other terms.
According to the governor’s office, the legislation will also require projects to secure federal financing, which would shift the risk away from taxpayers in the state.
New Jersey’s two operating nuclear power stations, Salem and Hope Creek, have three units between them – two at Salem and one at Hope Creek.
Both stations are run by utility company PSEG and produce around 40% of the state’s electricity and over 80% of its clean energy supply.
The news was welcomed by both Democrat and Republican policymakers in the state as well as business groups and energy focused initiatives.

“This new law is an important step toward increasing base load capacity, improving grid reliability, and ensuring our state has the energy needed to support residents, businesses, and economic growth,” said Erick Ford, president of the New Jersey Energy Policy Coalition.

Numerous states across the US are advancing plans to build out new nuclear plants. Neighbouring New York this year unveiled plans to build 4GW of new nuclear power, in addition to a 1GW announcement made in 2025.
Mikie Sherrill visits the Salem nuclear power station in April. Courtesy Mikie Sherrill.
New Jersey governor Mikie Sherrill signs into law the the Power NJ Act. Courtesy Mikie Sherrill/X.

title: China’s Changjiang-3 Nuclear Power Plant Reaches First Criticality
author: David Dalton
text: Construction of Hualong One unit in south of country began in 2021
Unit 3 at the Changjiang nuclear power station in Hainan province, southern China, has reached first criticality, state-owned China National Nuclear Corporation (CNNC) said.
The nuclear plant, being constructed by CNNC Engineering, achieved first criticality at 18:00 local time on 10 July, CNNC said.

It added: “This marks the official attainment of a self-sustaining and controllable chain fission reaction capability for the Hainan Unit 3 reactor, laying a solid foundation for subsequent grid connection and commissioning.”
Changjiang-3 is a domestic Hualong One, or HPR1000, pressurised water reactor (PWR) unit with a gross design capacity of 1,200 MW.
Construction of Changjiang-3 began in March 2021. Construction of an identical unit, Changjiang-4, began in December 2021.
Two CNP-600 PWRs have been in operation at the Changjiang site since 2015 and 2016.

China is moving forward with its indigenous Hualong One reactor technology, with 21 such units now either operational or under construction in the country. According to CNNC, there are 41 Hualong One reactors either under construction or in operation globally,
According to International Atomic Energy Agency data, China has 37 reactors under construction and 60 in operation.
October 2024 file photo of construction at the Changjiang-3 nuclear power plant in China. Courtesy CNNC.

title: European Commission’s SMR Alliance Launches Second Call For Reactor Projects
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Group set up to support rollout of small modular reactors across bloc
The European Commission has opened a second call for projects under the European Industrial Alliance on Small Modular Reactors (SMRs).

The call, published on 6 July, aims to select a limited number of additional projects that can contribute to the alliance’s objective of developing and deploying the first SMR projects in Europe in the early 2030s.
The deadline for applications is 11 September 2026, with proposals to be reviewed in September and October. The commission said results are expected by the end of October.
The European Industrial Alliance on SMRs was established in February 2024 to support SMR development and deployment in Europe.

The commission said it was looking for projects that can “join and reinforce” one of the existing project working groups, particularly where they involve the same SMR technology, and also for projects representing technologies not covered by the existing working groups. It said joint applications were “strongly encouraged”.
Projects will be assessed by the alliance’s governing board, supported by the secretariat.

According to the commission, eligibility criteria include added value for the European economy, support from European stakeholders, compliance with EU legislation on nuclear safety, waste, safeguards and environmental requirements, and contribution to net-zero objectives.

The alliance, which brings together more than 350 SMR stakeholders, initially selected nine project working groups in October 2024, but after a 2025 progress review confirmed eight: Nuward, European BWRX-300, Rolls-Royce SMR, CityHeat, NuScale Voygr, Eagles, Newcleo European LFR AS and Thorizon One. Project Quantum, led by Last Energy, was suspended
pending clarification of its status.
European Commission headquarters in Brussels. Courtesy Emdee/Creative Commons 4.0 Licence.

title: Australia And India Sign Key Agreement On Uranium Exports During Modi Visit
author: David Dalton
text: New Delhi needs fuel for ambitious nuclear reactor new-build programme
Australia and India have signed an agreement to export Australian uranium to India for use in the south Asian nation’s expanding nuclear energy industry.
“We have signed an important agreement today on nuclear energy,” Indian prime minister Narendra Modi said on 9 July after talks with his Australian counterpart, Anthony Albanese, in Melbourne.
“This will pave the way for uranium supplies from Australia to India and give our clean energy objectives fresh momentum.”
A joint statement said the arrangement allowed long-term uranium exports for “exclusively peaceful purposes”.

The deal is expected to provide a boost to Australia’s mining industry while helping India meet the target of installing 100 GW of nuclear energy capacity by 2047, an ambitious target from around 7.7 GW today.
New Delhi has said its next step on the road to the 100 GW target is to hit 22 GW of nuclear power by 2032.
India operates 23 commercial nuclear reactors and has eight under construction.
The government recently enacted the Shanti Act, a major reform designed to facilitate greater private sector participation – including foreign investment – in India’s nuclear energy sector.

The Shanti (Sustainable Harnessing and Advancement of Nuclear Energy for Transforming India) Act ended the state monopoly on nuclear power in India, permitting up to 49% private and foreign equity in civilian nuclear projects.

The Nuclear for Australia (NFA) lobby group had said Modi’s visit was an opportunity to reopen discussions about how Australian critical minerals like uranium could help fuel clean energy solutions around the world.
According to NFA, Australia is home to the world’s largest known uranium deposits and is perfectly placed to capitalise on increasing global interest in uranium to fuel nuclear energy.
The group said removing policy barriers would allow more states and territories to participate in the uranium cycle, positioning Australia as a major uranium exporter.
Only one Australian state, South Australia, and one territory, the Northern Territory, allow uranium mining.

In May the New South Wales legislative council, or upper house, voted for a bill to lift the prohibition on nuclear energy and uranium mining in the state. The bill now awaits debate in the legislative assembly (lower house), where it faces resistance.
India’s prime minister Narendra Modi and his Australian counterpart Anthony Albanese held talks in Melbourne. Courtesy Govt of India X account.

title: NRC Proposes Most Significant Environmental Review Regulation Changes In Decades
author: David Dalton
text: Planned changes will make safety decisions faster, says US regulator
The US Nuclear Regulatory Commission is proposing changes to its environmental review regulations that agency officials call the most significant in decades.

The proposed changes, published in the Federal Register on 7 July, would end the requirement for draft environmental impact statements (EIS) and add exclusions that exempt licensing actions from National Environmental Policy Act (Nepa)  review.
The proposals would reduce the regulatory burden in its environmental reviews, the NRC said.

NRC chairman Ho Nieh said the proposed changes will help narrow Nepa-related reviews to impacts within the agency’s authority, which is in radiological safety. For many years, the NRC has done much more than required under Nepa, he said.
“This really brings us back to what Nepa demands – nothing more, nothing less. Doing it this way, we’ll be able to issue our safety decisions faster without compromising safety at all,” Nieh said.

For instance, the NRC can issue construction permit decisions without considering non-radiological issues like dust, noise, and non-radiological water. Nevertheless, NRC reviews have addressed those topics.

Kimyata Savoy, NRC chief environmental review and permitting officer, said the agency’s focus will now be on radiological safety issues. Other federal agencies may still assess non-radiological impacts as part of their respective reviews.

According to the proposed rule’s regulatory analysis, the changes could save roughly $135m (€118m) over a 10-year period. Savoy said the proposed rule would allow one year for a review of an environmental assessment and two years for an EIS.
The NRC will accept public comments on the proposed rulemaking until 21 August, with plans to hold a public hearing during the comment period.
Image courtesy NRC.

title: US, Japan And South Korea Agree To Cooperate On SMR Deployment
author: David Dalton
text: Countries aim to foster fleet deployment models that de-risk project development

The foreign ministers of the US, Japan and South Korea signed an agreement to cooperate on the deployment of small modular reactors (SMRs) in third countries on the sidelines of the Nato summit in Turkey, the US state department said on 8 July.

US secretary of state Marco Rubio, Japanese foreign minister Toshimitsu Motegi and South Korea’s foreign minister Cho Hyun agreed the allies will work together to provide competitive options on meeting energy demands in the Asia-Pacific region and beyond, a statement said.

The US state department said the agreement aims to foster fleet deployment models that de-risk project development, achieve economies of scale, catalyse private investment, streamline licensing processes, and optimize supply chains.

“A coordinated trilateral approach positions American, Japanese, and Korean firms to provide partners in the region with more competitive alternatives to meet their growing energy demands and to uphold the highest standards of nuclear safety, security, and non-proliferation as new reactor technology increasingly comes online,” it said.

In support of the initiative, the US is committing over $10m (€8.7m) in new funding for the department of state’s Foundational Infrastructure for Responsible Use of Small Modular Reactor Technology (First) Program to provide technical support to countries in Asia-Pacific region for the deployment of nuclear energy.  Funds will advance SMR project development activities and establish an SMR regional training hub for workforce development.
The US also announced an industry initiative agreed upon among GE Vernova, Hitachi, Samsung C&T, and SGE to advance deployment of GE Vernova Hitachi Nuclear Energy’s BWRX-300 SMR across Europe.

Left to right: Japanese foreign minister Toshimitsu Motegi, US secretary of state Marco Rubio and South Korea’s foreign minister Cho Hyun sign the SMR agreement in Ankara, Turkey. Courtesy US department of state.

title: UK’s Sizewell B Nuclear Power Plant Granted A 20-Year Life Extension
author: David Dalton
text: Move comes as government encourages ‘golden age of nuclear’ to meet country’s growing need for electricity
The Sizewell B nuclear power plant in the UK will produce electricity for a further 20 years after a deal was reached between its owner, the French state utility EDF, and the government.

The 1,198-MW pressurised water reactor unit, in Suffolk, eastern England, began commercial operation in 1995 and was due to be permanently shut down in 2035, but will now continue operating until 2055.
The plant produces 3% of Britain’s electricity, enough to meet the equivalent demand of 2.5 million homes.

The government approved plans by EDF to extend its life. The government has said that a “golden age of nuclear” will help the UK meet the growing need for electricity to power electric vehicles, low-carbon heating and AI datacentres while keeping its climate commitments intact.
Ed Miliband, the energy secretary, said: “Nuclear power is vital for our energy security, and this extension will help produce the clean power our country needs.”

Chancellor Rachel Reeves said the life extension was “a real vote of confidence in the hundreds of skilled workers in Suffolk who will power Britain’s clean energy future, delivering the long-term certainty that businesses and workers need”.

EDF UK chief executive officer Simone Rossi said : “Global events demonstrate time and again how vital it is for the UK to secure long term, low -carbon, homegrown electricity which protects British households and businesses from market volatility. Extending the life of the plants we already have alongside building new ones is central to EDF ’s strategy.”

Under the deal, EDF will receive £70.50 (€82.7, $94.6) for every megawatt-hour Sizewell B generates, starting from 2035, when it was originally due to close. The extra investment needed to maintain the plant will come from British multinational energy company Centrica, which owns a 20% share in EDF’s reactors in the UK.

All nine commercial nuclear plants in the UK have now struck a deal with the government to continue running, following the decision last year to extend the life of eight units at four nuclear stations built across the country in the 1980s.

EDF Energy said in 2024 that two stations due to close in March 2026 – Hartlepool A and Heysham A – would remain online until March 2027. Two more stations, Heysham B and Torness, which were scheduled to close in March 2028, will stay online until March 2030.
Each station has two Generation II advanced gas-cooled reactor units. According to International Atomic Energy data the eight units have a combined net capacity of 4,685 MW.
The UK has nine operational reactors* across five nuclear sites providing around 14% of the country’s electricity. Thirty-six reactors have been permanently shut down.
The government is also pushing ahead with plans for two new units at Sizewell C, while two units at Hinkley Point C are under construction.

Tom Greatrex, chief executive of the London-based Nuclear Industry Association, said Sizewell B is the cleanest, most productive and most reliable plant in the whole country, so extending its life is “one of the best things we can do to build an affordable and reliable clean power system”.

The NIA said that since 1995, Sizewell B has produced over 270 TWh of low-carbon electricity, enough to meet the needs of every household in the counties of Suffolk and Norfolk for more than 100 years.
* The UK’s nine commercial nuclear power reactors are: Hartlepool A-1, Hartlepool A-2, Heysham A-1, Heysham A-2, Heysham B-1, Heysham B-2, Sizewell B, Torness-1, Torness-2.
Sizewell B has produced enough electricity to meet the needs of every household in Suffolk and Norfolk for more than 100 years. Courtesy EDF.
The single-unit Sizewell B plant will now continue operating until 2055. Courtesy EDF.

title: Companies Sign Agreement For Siting Odin Nuclear Microreactor In England
author: David Dalton
text: Letter of intent could see nuclear plant R&D taking place at new energy ‘super cluster’

UK-based Chiltern Vital Group (CVG) and Cambridge Atomworks have signed a letter of intent to carry out research and development into Cambridge Atomworks’ Odin nuclear microreactor at the planned Berkeley Green Science and Technology Park in Gloucestershire, southwest England.

Chiltern Vital Berkeley (CVB), the CVG subsidiary that owns and is developing the Berkeley project, said it is in final stage negotiations with multiple nuclear and energy technology companies wishing to open facilities on the Berkeley Green site.
CVB has announced its intention to create a low-carbon technology “super cluster” at the site, and develop it into a centre of excellence for nuclear power R&D.
The technology park is being planned on a site next to the Berkeley nuclear station. Berkeley was home to two gas-cooled Magnox nuclear plants of 138 MW each that operated from 1962 to 1989.

Chris Turner, chief executive officer of both CVG and CVB, said Cambridge Atomworks agreeing to site their prototype research and development facility at Berkeley represents another important step forward for the development of the Berkeley Green Science and Technology Park as a global energy technology, education and training hub.

Cambridge Atomworks chief executive officer Ian Farnan said this is a major step forward in the regulatory development of the Odin microreactor and will provide key answers about the combined physics and thermal hydraulics of the plant required by regulators across the world.

Farnan said: “After our physics demonstration campaign has been completed, our objective is to use the Berkeley-based prototype reactor as a training facility for our global workforce and the UK nuclear workforce. Currently, there is no reactor training facility for this purpose in the UK.”

The Odin microreactor is a portable, low-pressure coolant micro nuclear reactor originally developed by US-based Nano Nuclear Energy. It is designed to fit within standard shipping containers to provide energy for remote communities, disaster relief and industrial sites.

In 2025 Nano Nuclear announced it was selling the Odin design and all associated intellectual property to Cambridge Atom Works, which had already been developing Odin for Nano Nuclear on an outsourced consulting basis.
The total purchase price was $6.2m (€5.4m) and future royalties for Nano Nuclear based on net sales if and when Odin is commercialised.
A rendering of the planned Berkeley Green Science and Technology Park in Gloucestershire, southwest England. Courtesy CVG.

title: Containment Ring Installed At China’s Lufeng-2 Nuclear Power Plant
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Four CAP1000 units planned at site in Guangdong province

The first ring of the steel containment vessel has been installed at Unit 2 of the Lufeng nuclear power station in Guangdong province, southern China, the official China National Nuclear Power News Network (CNNPN) said.
CNNPN said the operation marks the start of a peak construction phase for civil engineering and installation work on the unit’s nuclear island.
Lufeng-2 will be a Generation III, 1,161-MW CAP1000 pressurised water reactor (PWR), China’s indigenous version of US-based Westinghouse’s AP1000 design.
Construction began in December 2025 with pouring first concrete for the nuclear island foundation slab.

CNNPN said the first containment ring is the largest and heaviest of six main steel containment vessel rings, also called tiers. It is made from four layers of steel plates and weighs about 1,029 tonnes.
Four CAP1000 units are planned at the Lufeng site. Construction of Lufeng-1 began in February 2025 and of Lufeng-2 in December 2025.
Construction of the two additional units, Lufeng-3 and Lufeng-4, has not yet begun.
Two domestic Hualong One PWR units are also under construction at the site. Construction of Lufeng-5 began in September 2022 and Lufeng-6 in August 2023.

The International Atomic Energy Agency’s database of nuclear plants in China says China has 60 plants in commercial operation and 37 under construction. About half of those under construction are domestic Hualong One units and nine are CAP1000 units
The first containment ring is lowered into place at Lufeng-2. Courtesy CNNPN.

title: West Must Follow Example Of South Korea And China To Reduce Nuclear Plant Costs
author: Nigel Davies
text: Report by McKinsey shows huge gulf in new-build costs between US and Asia

Western countries must follow the lead of South Korea and China by standardising and replicating reactor designs to bring down costs and the time it takes to see them operating, a report by business consultancy McKinsey says.

The report, titled Nuclear power: A renaissance in the making said that nuclear capacity was expected to at least double by 2050, and potentially triple to reach 1200 GW. According to the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), nuclear capacity today stands at 379 GW.

McKinsey, a New York-based global management consulting firm, said that momentum for nuclear power was stronger in Asia than in Western economies, with China accounting for half of new nuclear power coming online. The report said China would soon overtake France in terms of capacity, and the US by 2035.
The report also highlighted a stark contrast in the costs of bringing reactors online between the West and Asia.

McKinsey said that the levelised cost of energy (LCOE) for a new Generation III 1,000 MWh reactor was $63/MWh (€55/MWh) in China, $65/MWh (€57/MWh) in South Korea, $154/MWh (€135/MWh) in the US, and $190/MWh (€166/MWh) in France.

LCOE captures both capital and operating costs that need to be covered and is a standard measure of nuclear new-build costs. It is essentially the long-term price at which the electricity produced by a power plant will have to be sold at for the investor to cover all their costs.

The authors also noted a sharp contrast in time to market between East and West. The report said that South Korea has construction times of six to eight years, compared to close to two decades for recent projects in the US and Europe. China was far in front with delivery times of 70 months.
McKinsey said companies and policymakers must follow the example of those Asian nations by taking steps to make sure projects are economical.

“Companies can build fleets of plants to reduce cost and time to market. Repeating standardised designs across multiple projects, as China and South Korea do, reduces costs and compresses schedules,” the report said.
It said that since 2000, China had deployed a single reactor design for over a third of units, and successive models made up nine in every 10 reactors under construction.

The report added: “Modular construction, integrated project delivery, and aligned incentives across owners and contractors reduce change orders, decrease labour hours, and make execution more predictable.”
McKinsey said policymakers could help nuclear projects to flourish by completing licensing before construction begins and not allow it to change during construction, which adds to delays and costs.
The report also said nuclear projects need lower operation and market risks in order to attract private investment.

“Sovereign support, export-credit financing, loan guarantees, indexed power purchase agreements, and contracts for difference can reduce financing costs. These tools matter most for first-in-country or first-of-a-kind projects that have high execution risk.”
The report suggested that small modular reactors (SMRs) could provide the answer for nuclear growth.

“SMRs, which typically produce less than 300 megawatts, could reshape the industry by enabling more standardisation, offsite manufacturing, and serial production, potentially trimming construction times and fitting into regional grids or industrial hubs where gigawatt-scale reactors would not fit,” the report said.
The report also cautioned that countries including the US also had more work to do to rebuild a secure supply of fuel for new reactors.

McKinsey said that enrichment was the most costly part of the fuel supply chain process, and that demand for high-assay low-enriched uranium (Haleu) required by advanced reactors threatened to outstrip capacity.
The company’s analysis said that the US alone would need to invest $105-$170 billion across the fuel cycle to meet its 2050 ambitions.
China accounts for half of new nuclear power coming online, the McKinsey report says. Courtesy Rosatom.

title: Finland’s Regulator Publishes Joint Early Review Of Steady Energy Small Modular Reactor
author: David Dalton
text: Voluntary collaboration involved five European nuclear safety authorities
The Finnish Radiation and Nuclear Safety Authority (Stuk) has published a summary report of an international joint early review of Steady Energy’s LDR-50 small modular reactor (SMR) design
The review concludes that no fundamental issues were identified that would prevent the reactor concept from being further developed and deployed.

The review was a voluntary collaboration involving five nuclear safety authorities: Stuk, the Swedish Radiation Safety Authority (SSM), Poland’s National Atomic Energy Agency (PAA), the Czech State Office for Nuclear Safety (SÚJB) and Ukraine’s State Nuclear Regulatory Inspectorate (SNRIU).
Each independently assessed the LDR-50 reactor concept against their respective national regulatory frameworks.
Steady Energy said the review was not part of a formal licensing process and does not constitute regulatory approval or a licensing decision in any of the participating countries.
The assessment was based on LDR-50 design documentation first made available in early 2025 together with STUK’s early-stage concept assessment completed in the summer of 2025.
Steady Energy said that since then, the design has continued to mature significantly.

It said: “As expected for a concept at this stage of development, the review concluded that the available documentation was not yet sufficiently detailed to support the launch of a formal licensing process.

“At the same time, all participating regulators reached broadly consistent conclusions: none identified any fundamental nuclear safety issues that would prevent the concept from progressing to the next stages of development.”
The LDR-50, the size of a shipping container, can be built underground in cities, and is designed to be particularly well suited to district heating.
A pilot version of the reactor is being built in the Finnish capital Helsinki, inside a decommissioned coal plant.

District heating, also known as a heat network, is a centralised system that generates heat in one location and distributes it – via a network of insulated underground pipes – to multiple residential, commercial, or public buildings for space heating and hot water. It acts like “central heating for cities”, eliminating the need for individual boilers in every home.
According to Finnish utility and nuclear operator Fortum, district heating is the most common heating method in Finland, providing heat to about 45% of residential, commercial, and public buildings.
The LDR-50, the size of a shipping container, can be built underground in cities. Courtesy Steady Energy.

title: Holtec Announces ‘Watershed Moment’ In Bid To Restart Palisades Nuclear Plant
author: David Dalton
text: Last of major projects closed out at shut-down Michigan facility

Holtec International said it has reached a “watershed moment” in its project to restart the single-unit Palisades nuclear power station in the US state of Michigan with the last of the major projects closed out.
New Jersey-based Holtec said the site has transitioned from large-scale activities to the remaining routine maintenance, testing, inspection, and operational readiness work required before startup.
More 5,000 individual work activities remain, but the transition represents an important milestone in the historic restart effort, Holtec said.

Among the final accomplishments in this “project phase” of restart was placement of the plant’s turbine-generator onto its turning gear following extensive inspections, maintenance, testing and refurbishment activities.
Another major achievement was installation and testing of a new fuel handling machine, completing the upgraded fuel handling system.

Holtec said the projects represent the culmination of a series of major efforts carried out across the station. Other work included reactor vessel inspections and replacement of reactor head penetrations, primary system chemical decontamination and passivation, steam generator tube refurbishment and secondary-side cleaning, fuel receipt and inspection, operator training and requalification, and numerous equipment upgrades and modernisation projects.
Palisades, an 805-MW pressurised water reactor unit which began commercial operation in 1972, ceased operations in May 2022.

Holtec bought Palisades to decommission the facility, which had struggled to compete with natural gas-fired plants and renewable energy, but in early 2023 applied to the DOE for federal loan funding to repower the plant.
In late 2023, Holtec began filing licensing and regulatory requests to support returning the plant to operational status.
The Biden administration finalised a $1.52bn loan guarantee for the project in September 2024.
If Holtec succeeds, Palisades will be the first nuclear plant in the US to restart after going into decommissioning.
The new fuel handling machine installed as part of Palisades’ upgraded fuel handling system. Courtesy Holtec.

title: Uzbekistan Has Made Significant Progress On Developing Nuclear Infrastructure, Says IAEA
author: David Dalton
text: Expert agency mission highlights key areas for improvement

Uzbekistan has made significant progress in developing the infrastructure needed for the implementation of its nuclear power programme, an International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) team of experts has found.

The conclusion followed an IAEA follow-up Integrated Nuclear Infrastructure Review (INIR) mission, carried out at the request of Uzbekistan from 22 to 26 June, which reviewed progress in addressing recommendations and suggestions from a 2021 Phase 2 INIR mission. Phase 2 missions assess the country’s preparedness for implementing a nuclear power project.

The INIR team said Uzbekistan has joined international legal instruments, revised its national nuclear legislation and developed its regulations for licensing and oversight, management systems and the necessary electrical grid studies and enhancement plans.
The team said that further work is needed to strengthen the nuclear regulatory body and finalise feasibility studies.
In 2018, Uzbekistan decided to develop a nuclear power programme to help meet growing electricity demand and diversify its energy mix.
Last month Russia and Uzbekistan began construction of an “integrated” nuclear power plant in Uzbekistan, the first of its kind in ​post-Soviet Central Asia, the Kremlin said.
Russian president Vladimir Putin and Uzbek president Shavkat Mirziyoyev oversaw the start of the construction via video link from St ​Petersburg.
The ⁠project is in Uzbekistan’s central-eastern Jizzakh Region, which borders both ​Tajikistan and Kazakhstan.

The project, being developed by Uzbekistan’s state nuclear project company Uzatom and Russia’s state nuclear corporation Rosatom, will include two high-capacity power units based on Russia’s VVER-1000 Generation III+ reactors and two power units with small-scale RITM-200N reactors, each with a capacity of 55 MW.

Russian president Vladimir Putin and Uzbek president Shavkat Mirziyoyev oversaw the start of the construction of Uzbekistan’s first nuclear power station via video link from St ​Petersburg. Courtesy IAEA.

title: No Need For Blanket Ban On An Entire Technology, Says Swiss Nuclear Forum
author: David Dalton
text: Nation facing referendum on plans to end ban on nuclear reactor construction

A planned referendum in Switzerland next year on lifting the ban on building new nuclear power plants brings the country’s long-running energy policy debate back to the ballot box, but there is no need for a blanket ban on an entire technology, the Swiss Nuclear Forum has said.
The forum, a pro-nuclear group which has individual and collective members, said it will participate in the debate, relying on “facts and objective arguments”.

The forum said objections to new nuclear power plants often concern specific projects, costs or construction timelines. It said these issues will need to be addressed within the framework of any potential permitting procedures.
However, it added, they do not constitute arguments for a blanket legal ban on an entire technology.

“Lifting the ban on building new nuclear power plants does not lead to the construction of new plants, but rather creates the necessary conditions for us to respond to the evolving context and make decisions without excluding any technology a priori.”

Despite a long tradition of nuclear power production, Switzerland voted in 2017 to no longer allow construction of new nuclear power plants. That law was the result of a long process initiated after the 2011 Fukushima-Daiichi nuclear accident in Japan.
However, there is no clear timetable for shutdowns, and the country’s four nuclear units can remain operational as long as they meet legal safety requirements.
Switzerland’s nuclear operators have said they are considering keeping nuclear plants in use longer than previously expected over fears of electricity shortages.

Earlier this month Switzerland’s lower house of parliament, the National Council, approved plans to allow the construction of new nuclear power plants, with a national referendum likely to decide the issue.
An industry spokesperson told NucNet that the referendum is expected to take place on 28 February 2027.
Switzerland’s four nuclear plants are Beznau-1, Beznau-2, Gösgen and Leibstadt. They produce about a 27% share of the country’s electricity production.
The two-unit Beznau nucleaqr power station in Switzerland. Courtesy Axpo.

title: Urenco USA Continues Capacity Programme With Startup Of New Cascade
author: David Dalton
text: Company making major commitment to strengthening US nuclear fuel supply chain
Urenco USA announced the startup of the fifth cascade of new US uranium enrichment capacity at its New Mexico facility.
The company said the cascade began production on 22 June, continuing its track record of bringing new cascades online ahead of schedule and on budget.

The new cascade is part of the current capacity programme at the facility to install 700,000 separative work units (SWU)* of enrichment capacity over a two-year period, including three further cascades, by early 2027. The facility has an existing annual capacity of 4.3 million SWU, which is approximately one-third of current US demand.

Urenco USA said its capacity programme supports the US Department of Energy’s goals to accelerate the deployment of new domestic capacity and to strengthen the US nuclear fuel supply chain to meet the expected increase in demand from utilities operating nuclear plants in the US and “allied nations”.
Starting in 2027, Urenco USA will also begin to refurbish existing cascades at the site as part of ongoing capital investments in the facility.
In support of that project, Urenco USA has begun construction of a centrifuge storage building at the site, which will house equipment removed from existing cascades until future disposal.

Urenco USA announced last month that it will expand the capacity of the facility by nearly 50%, marking a major commitment to strengthening the US nuclear fuel supply chain as the country expands the use of nuclear power.
Installed capacity will grow to more than seven million SWU over the next 10 years.

* A separative work unit (SWU) is the standard measure of the effort required to separate uranium-235 (U-235) and uranium-238 (U-238). Both are isotopes of uranium, but they differ in the number of neutrons in their nuclei and have different properties and uses. U-235 is used as fuel in nuclear power plants, naval ships and submarines, and in nuclear weapons. U-235 must be separated from the more plentiful isotope U-238 for its various uses.
The new cascade is part of a capacity expansion programme at the New Mexico facility. Courtesy Urenco USA.

title: Poland’s OSGE Begins State Support Bid For Construction Of Small Modular Reactor Fleet
author: David Dalton
text: Company applies for CfD for 14 units across three locations in European country

Orlen Synthos Green Energy (OSGE) has asked Poland’s energy ministry to begin work on a state support scheme for the construction of a fleet of GE Vernova Hitachi BWRX-300 small modular reactors (SMRs) in the European country.

The company said it had applied for a contract for difference (CfD) for 14 units across three locations – Wloclawek, in central Poland, Stawy Monowskie, in the south of the country, and Stalowa Wola, southeastern Poland.

According to OSGE, a joint venture between the private industrial group Synthos Green Energy (SGE) and Poland’s state-controlled energy giant Orlen, the first BWRX-300 unit will be commissioned in 2032 in Wloclawek.
OSGE said the government will notify the European Commission of the plans for state support.
The units listed in the application are the first phase of a broader OSGE SMR deployment programme, which ultimately includes the construction of 26 BWRX-300 units.
“The contract for difference for 14 units will enable us to build a fleet of BWRX-300 reactors in Poland,” said OSGE chief executive officer Rafał Kasprów.

“Thanks to economies of scale, standardisation and modularisation, we will reduce unit cost and, as a result, create a cost-attractive electricity generation model for both individual and industrial customers.
“At the same time, the approval of the contract for difference will be a significant step toward building a robust SMR supply chain in Poland,” he added.

A CfD is a financial mechanism that allows an energy generator and the government to agree on a fixed “strike price” for their electricity. If the wholesale market price of electricity falls below the strike price, the government pays the generator the difference, guaranteeing their revenue. If the wholesale price goes above the strike price, the generator pays the excess back to the government. This protects both developers from market volatility and consumers from high bills.
The 3,400-MW Hinkley Point C nuclear power station, under construction in the UK, is funded by a CfD with a strike price of £92.50/MWh (€107, $122).
The 300-MW BWRX-300 is based on an existing boiling water reactor design – the ESBWR – that is licensed in the US.

Poland is building three Westinghouse-supplied large-scale reactors in Pomerania in the north of the country as it aims to phase out its heavy reliance on coal, reduce carbon emissions and guarantee long-term energy independence. Coal accounts for about half of Poland’s electricity generation, which is by far the highest proportion in the European Union.
The government recently released an updated nuclear power policy which says it is aiming to choose a partner and technology for a second nuclear station scheduled for 2027.
OSGE said the first BWRX-300 unit in Poland will be commissioned in 2032 in Wloclawek. Courtesy OSGE.

title: Industry Group Calls For Flexible ‘Made In EU’ Criteria For New Nuclear Projects
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Proposed legislation sets out mandatory trusted partner origin criteria

Brussels-based nuclear industry group nucleareurope has called for the EU’s Industrial Accelerator Act to use flexible “Made in EU” criteria for nuclear new-build projects instead of component-based rules.
The group said in a position paper that nuclear projects are “large strategic” developments involving many components and subcomponents, long delivery timelines and strict safety requirements.
It said a component-based approach would not fully reflect the complexity of nuclear new-build projects.

The act aims to introduce Made in EU requirements for some specific net-zero technologies components, in order to prevent circumvention, further build EU manufacturing capacity as well as resilient and competitive domestic value chains.
It says that member states shall ensure that at least two main specific components of the nuclear fission technology final products originate in the EU.
Nucleareurope said a more suitable approach would be to replace component-based rules with broader Made in EU criteria that could be used by EU and national authorities to evaluate full projects.

According to nucleareurope, these criteria could include ownership and control of intellectual property rights, the European origin of materials, the European location of manufacturing and processing, use of local workforce, gross value added in the EU, and the location of long-term maintenance and service contracts. The criteria could be tailored by national administrations depending on each project.
Nucleareurope said “such an incentive-based approach would provide greater flexibility” while supporting the objective of strengthening Europe’s industrial base.

The group said Made in EU requirements should apply only to nuclear new-build projects, but not to research, development and innovation projects, including first industrial deployment of nuclear reactors, or to existing nuclear reactors.
Nucleareurope data shows more than 5,000 companies across all EU member states supply equipment, materials, digital technologies and specialist services to the nuclear sector.

The group said significant nuclear investments are planned in the coming years, with installed EU nuclear capacity expected to grow from about 100 GW to close to 150 GW by 2050, according to a recent report.

The proposed Industrial Accelerator Act sets out mandatory “Made in EU” (or trusted partner) origin and low-carbon criteria for public procurement, auctions, and state-aid schemes, including for nuclear power plants.
The act has not yet been adopted and must still be negotiated and approved by the European Parliament and EU member states, meaning the final rules could still change.
Nuclear power provides about a quarter of the EU’s electricity from about a one hundred commercially operating reactor units in 12 of 27 member states.

title: MOU Strengthens Transatlantic Cooperation On Deployment Of Fusion Energy
author: David Dalton
text: Agreement will focus on advancing physics and technology

Transatlantic cooperation on fusion energy has been strengthened by the signing of a memorandum of understanding that sets out a programme of collaboration spanning a wide range of fusion disciplines to support ambitions to deliver commercial fusion energy
The MOU was signed between the US Department of Energy’s Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory (PPPL) and the UK Atomic Energy Authority (UKAEA).

The UKAEA said the agreement builds on King Charles’s address to the US Congress in Washington in April, which highlighted new partnerships between the UK and the US on fusion energy, ensuring that “British and American ingenuity continues to lead the world”.
The agreement will focus on advancing the physics and technology basis for future fusion power plants.
Under the agreement, PPPL and UKAEA will work together to expand scientific, academic, and educational cooperation across fusion science and technology.

This work will include reciprocal staff exchanges, access to major research facilities, joint projects, exchange of academic information, collaboration on International Thermonuclear Experimental Reactor (Iter) diagnostics, advanced computing programmes and wider information sharing over the coming years.

Fulvio Militello, executive director of plasma science and fusion operations at UKAEA, said the agreement with PPPL confirms the positive working relationship between the US and UK fusion communities.
The control room at a UKAEA fusion faclity in England. Courtesy UKAEA.

title: Reactors Shut Down As France’s Nuclear Output Hit By European Heatwave
author: David Dalton
text: Latest closures follow decision earlier this week to take Golfech unit offline
