France’s state-owned energy company EDF has temporarily shut down two more nuclear reactors as a precautionary environmental measure, as the country grapples with a record-breaking heatwave.
The plants taken offline on 25 June were at the two-unit Nogent nuclear station on the Seine River north of Paris, and at the four-unit Bugey facility on the Rhone near Lyon in the southeast.
Both shutdowns were triggered by rising river temperatures, which EDF is required by law to monitor to avoid discharging water that could harm aquatic ecosystems.
The latest closures follow the shutdown earlier this week of a reactor at the Golfech nuclear power plant in southwestern France.
France’s 57 nuclear reactors are subject to strict environmental thresholds governing the temperature of nearby rivers.
EDF said on social network X that some reactors may be forced to reduce their output, or even shut down temporarily, to comply with regulatory limits and protect wildlife and vegetation.
Reports in France said regulations at the Golfech plant require that the temperature of the Garonne River not exceed 28°C after cooling water is discharged.
At Nogent, rules require that the temperature of the Seine River not rise by more than 3C downstream of the plant and remain below 28°C on average.
Reuters reported that output was reduced by 4.1 GW, or 7%, of total power demand, at midday on 25 June, citing data from EDF.
The four-unit Bugey nuclear power station on the Rhone near Lyon. Courtesy Bernard Gaetan/EDF.

title: Newcleo Installs Main Vessel For Non-Nuclear ‘Precursor’ Test Facility In Italy
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Project is demonstrator for company’s lead-cooled fast reactors
European advanced reactor developer Newcleo has completed installation of the main vessel for its Precursor non-nuclear test facility at the Brasimone research centre in Italy, the company said.
Newcleo said Precursor is a 10-MWt non-nuclear demonstrator for its planned commercial lead-cooled fast reactors (LFRs).

The Precursor main vessel is the non-nuclear equivalent of the vessel for LFRs and will host key systems including steam generators, decay heat removal dip coolers, the inner vessel and the electrical core simulator.
Although the Brasimone facility will not use nuclear fuel, Newcleo said it is designed to be fully representative of the plant operating cycle, including electricity generation.

Newcleo said the component was engineered by the company and SRS Servizi di Ricerche e Sviluppo, and manufactured by Fucina Italia with support from ENEA, the Italian national agency for new technologies, and energy.
The next step for Precursor will be delivery and installation of the turbine as Newcleo moves towards electricity generation from the demonstrator.

Newcleo is working on the basic design of its demonstrator LFR-AS-30 reactor. Newcleo’s LFR technology is designed to operate with recycled nuclear fuel, offering the promise of greater sustainability and reduced waste in nuclear energy production.
The company is planning to deploy a pilot LFR-AS-30 plant deployed as a demonstrator in France in the early 2030s.
The company has said the Precursor facility will emulate the size, complexity and thermal hydraulic performances of the LFR-AS-30 reactor design.
The main vessel for Newcleo’s Precursor non-nuclear test facility arrives at the Brasimone research centre in Italy. Courtesy Newcleo.

title: IAEA Completes Key Safety Related Repairs At Zaporizhzhya Nuclear Power Station
author: David Dalton
text: Work carried out on frontline in Ukraine under protection of localised ceasefire

Repairs have been completed on a key power line and other energy infrastructure vital for nuclear safety at the Russia-controlled Zaporizhzhya nuclear power station in Ukraine, as part of efforts to strengthen its access to the electricity grid and help reduce the risk of a nuclear accident during the military conflict, International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) director-general Rafael Grossi said.
The technically complex repairs, preceded by extensive de-mining, were carried out on the frontline under the protection of a localised ceasefire mediated by the IAEA.
Agency teams monitored the work in challenging conditions, including nearby drone activity and the sound of military activity in the area.

The ceasefire enabled repairs at two separate locations, both of them essential components of the Zaporizhzhya’s energy infrastructure: the 750 kilovolt (kV) Dniprovska power line, which has been disconnected since March this year, and the switchyard of the Zaporizhzhya thermal power plant, which helps supply electricity to Zaporizhzhya through the back-up 330 kV Ferosplavna-1 line.
The Ferosplavna-1 line is currently the only line available to Zaporizhzhya and has been repeatedly disconnected in recent weeks.
At the thermal power plant, repairs were completed both on switchyard equipment and on a back-up transmission line connecting the Ferosplavna-1 line to the plant, making it more robust.

However, the 750 kV Dniprovska line has not yet been brought back into operation because of extensive damage to its connecting substation, more than 100 km northwest of Zaporizhzhya. The substation was reportedly damaged during military activity in late May, and IAEA staff experts who visited the facility this week observed severe damage to essential equipment.
Repair efforts are not expected to be completed in the near term, but are ongoing, and the agency said it will continue to monitor the situation closely.

“The line has been repaired, but it still needs to be brought back into operation,” Grossi said. “Repeated damage to the electrical infrastructure on which nuclear power plants depend continues to create serious nuclear safety and security risks. I once again call for maximum military restraint around all nuclear facilities and the power infrastructure they require.”

“Of the six temporary ceasefires that we have negotiated since late last year to help protect nuclear safety at the Zaporizhzhya Nuclear Power Plant, this was the most challenging to implement,” Grossi said. It required several months of delicate negotiations, followed by mine clearance and repairs on high pylons across the Dnipro River.
“It is an important step for nuclear safety at the plant, where reliable access to off-site power remains essential as all six reactors are in shutdown,” Grossi added.

Elsewhere in Ukraine, IAEA teams continued to report military activity near nuclear facilities. The South Ukraine nuclear power station told the agency that 11 drones had been detected in its monitoring area on Sunday, some as close as 3.5 km from the site. During this period, the IAEA team at the plant heard gunfire and the sound of drones.
The Chornobyl site reported detecting 10 drones in its monitoring area over the past week, as well as three fire spots in the exclusion zone caused by falling drone impacts.
All six units at the Zaporizhzhya nuclear power station in Ukraine are shut down. Courtesy IAEA.

title: Sweden Agrees Financing Plan For Small Modular Reactors At Ringhals
author: David Dalton
text: ‘Statement of strength’ as project for three Rolls-Royce nuclear plants takes crucial step

Sweden’s government has agreed on ​the details of a first financing package to ‌build new nuclear power reactors with project developer Videberg Kraft, prime minister Ulf Kristersson said on ​25 June.
“The state will also go in ​as an owner in this project,” Kristersson ⁠told reporters.
Kristersson gave no details of ​the financing package, which has to be ​approved by the European Commission.

State utility Vattenfall had already requested state financing to build three small modular reactors (SMRs) near the existing Ringhals nuclear site on the Värö peninsula, on Sweden’s west coast, with the first scheduled to begin commercial operation in the mid-2030s.

The government said in a statement it will take a 60% stake in Videberg Kraft, ​currently 80% owned by Vattenfall ​and 20% by the Industrikraft consortium of industrial companies. Vattenfall’s ‌stake ⁠will drop to 20%, the government added.
“Building new nuclear power is expensive and complicated, but important for us to have a better functioning energy system,” said minister for financial markets Niklas Wykman.
“The fact that the state, Vattenfall and the large industrial companies in Industrikraft have now agreed is a statement of strength for Sweden.”
Wykman said the agreement enables new nuclear power while protecting taxpayers’ money and ensuring order in public finances.
“We can now move forward and take this to the EU Commission for consideration,” he added.
Last week Videberg Kraft announced the selection of Rolls-Royce SMR as its partner to deliver the project.

UK-based Rolls-Royce SMR, a subsidiary of the UK engineering giant Rolls-Royce, said the decision underlined its position as Europe’s leading SMR technology, following recent contract awards in both the UK and Czech Republic.

Sweden’s government made new nuclear power one of its key pledges during campaigning for a general election in 2022. The move reversed a decades-long policy to shut down the country’s ageing reactors and replace them with renewable energy.

Sweden’s parliament last year passed legislation to finance a new generation of reactors, the first built ​in Sweden ​for more ⁠than 40 years. The government says the new plants are needed ​for energy security and achieving net ​zero ⁠emissions by 2045.

Sweden has six large-scale reactor units in commercial operation at three sites: Forsmark, Oskarshamn and Ringhals. According to International Atomic Energy Agency data, nuclear energy provided 29% of the country’s electricity generation in 2024.
Sweden previously operated 12 commercial reactors, but permanently shut down six due to economic factors and shifting political goals.
The government wants to attract more players to build new nuclear by streamlining its licensing process and opening up its coastline to build capacity in the sector.
Earlier this month energy company Nordic Baseload Power applied for financial ​support to build two large-scale nuclear reactors at ‌Barseback, close to Malmo in southern Sweden.
The ⁠application was the fourth received by the government for new nuclear power plants.

The other three are Videberg Kraft, Blykalla and Studsvik. Blykalla submitted an application for government financing for an advanced nuclear reactor park in Norrsundet, two hours north of Stockholm. Studsvik applied to the government for state support to develop up to 1,400 MW of new nuclear capacity using SMRs.

Left to right: Sweden’s minister of labour Johan Britz, prime minister Ulf Kristersson, minister of energy and enterprise Ebba Busch, and Sweden Democrats’ party secretary Mattias Bäckström Johansson at a press conference announcing the financing plans. Courtesy: Swedish Government.

title: Canada Announces Bold Strategy For 10 New Large-Scale Nuclear Reactors
author: David Dalton
text: Ottawa also targets first microreactor for remote community
Canada has unveiled a strategy ​to accelerate the development of ‌nuclear power, setting out a goal of building up to 10 ​new large-scale reactors and ​streamlining approvals for future projects.

The strategy, ⁠announced on 22 June by Natural Resources ​Minister Tim Hodgson, calls for construction to start on two new large-scale reactors by 2035, for five more to be planned or under development by 2040 and for at least one reactor to be under construction outside Ontario by 2035.
It also calls for a Canadian-made microreactor to be finalised by 2035 and deployed to a remote community by the late 2030s.

The strategy does not include details of new funding, but ‌the ⁠government said it will release a policy by April 2027 outlining conditions for federal support ​and the ​financing ⁠tools available for new nuclear projects.
Hodgson called the strategy a plan for a “new civilian nuclear renaissance” as the federal government looks to double the capacity of the country's electrical grid by 2050.

“If our goal is to double our grid and build a low-carbon economy in less than 25 years, there is no credible plan to do that without nuclear energy and the clean, reliable baseload power it provides,” Hodgson said.
“There is no credible plan for Canada to become an energy superpower if we choose not to build upon one of the strongest energy advantages we have.”

The government said the strategy sets out how it will strengthen energy affordability, security and sustainability at home and abroad by “building big” – from new reactors to uranium development and beyond.

“We will start by building on what we have, including Candu reactor technology, world-class uranium deposits in Saskatchewan, a top-tier Canadian nuclear workforce and supply chain, proven refurbishment expertise, medical isotopes and other nuclear innovations,” the government said.
Nuclear power generates approximately 13% of Canada’s electricity from 17 Candu reactors in Ontario and New Brunswick.
Canada’s Candu technology is also used around the world, powering a total of 26 reactors across six countries, including 17 at home and nine in South Korea, China, Romania, Argentina and India.

With an endowment of the world’s highest-grade uranium, and as the world’s second-largest producer, Canada produced roughly 24% of total global uranium output in 2024. About 90% is exported to other countries, where it is used as fuel in nuclear power plants.
Canada has been bullish about the prospects for nuclear energy, including large-scale units and small modular reactors (SMRs).

In May the government of Ontario said it was moving ahead with plans to build the province’s first large-scale nuclear power generation project in three decades with four new reactors at the Bruce nuclear power station.

Meanwhile, Ontario Power Generation is building the first unit of the Darlington BWRX-300 SMR project in Canada. Darlington is being developed as a four-unit SMR site to provide low-carbon electricity and support growing demand in Ontario, said OPG.
Other provinces, including Saskatchewan, have also said they are considering the possibility of deploying nuclear plants.

Nuclear refurbishments at the Bruce and Darlington nuclear stations have been delivered ahead of schedule and on budget, with Darlington-4 completed four months early and CAD150m (€92m, $105) under budget, concluding the world’s largest completed nuclear refurbishment.
A Cameco uranium facility in Canada. Courtesy Cameco.
The Pickering nuclear power station in Ontario, Canada. Courtesy OPG.

title: UK Startup Secures £23 Million In Bid To ‘Put Nuclear Fusion To Work’
author: David Dalton
text: Astral Systems developing ‘commercially viable technology with near term applications’

Astral Systems, the UK company pioneering multi-state fusion (MSF) technology, has secured a £23m (€26m, $30m) investment that supports plans to put nuclear fusion to work in the near-term and run compact fusion reactors at full capacity by the end of 2026.

The Series A funding round was led by British venture capital firm Mercia Ventures and supported by prominent tech investors including Tees River, Daphni, and Blast Club, alongside previous investors Speedinvest and Playfair. It brings the total funding of Astral Systems to over £28m.

Astral Systems said the financing supports plans to put fusion to work now by using its proprietary multi-state fusion technology. This includes bringing critical medical radioisotopes to market by early 2027, scaling the production of its modular MSF reactors and advancing fusion research.

The Bristol-based company said it is cementing its reputation as one of Europe’s flagship fusion pioneers, turning breakthrough physics into a new class of commercially viable fusion technology with near term applications.

The company claims its unmatched fusion capabilities put it in a strong position to tackle the fragile supply chain and potential global shortages of medical radioisotopes that severely impact cancer diagnosis and treatments.

With this new capital and its new facility being developed at the former Berkeley nuclear power station, Astral Systems intends to run multiple next-generation compact fusion reactors at full capacity by the end of 2026.

In 2023, Astral, co-founded by University of Bristol research associate Tom Wallace-Smith, developed and demonstrated a first-of-its-kind MSF reactor which can be used to create vital medical radioisotopes.

The company said in 2023 that its prototype compact MSF reactors – small enough to fit on a desktop – were being tested at its facility in the UK with members from external independent institutions verifying fusion performance.

The company aims to build small fusion reactors that could be installed in regional radioisotope factories around the UK and internationally, providing cheaper access to radioisotopes on a more flexible timeline.
Rather than requiring a new nuclear plant, which would cost about £400m to build, radioisotopes could be produced in small plants “right by hospitals” for about £1m, Wallace-Smith said.
The world has been facing a shortage of radioisotopes and the onsite production from small reactors being proposed by Astral could change the nature of the supply chain.

Recent shortages have been due to a temporary reduction in the production of molybdenum-99 which is used to generate technetium-99m, a radioisotope used for diagnostics. This issue impacted countries across Europe, and worldwide.
Astral Systems says it has established three commercial fusion facilities and generated more than £3m in revenue via research contracts that utilise MSF technology.
It has been working on producing actinium-225 and lead-212, two highly sought-after radioisotopes critical to new cancer treatments.
UK-based startup Astral Systems is scaling up the production of its modular MSF reactors and advancing fusion research. Courtes Astral Systems.

title: Deployable Energy Reaches Regulatory Milestone For Microreactor Plans
author: Kamen Kraev
text: US company to perform Unity nuclear battery test at Idaho National Laboratory

US advanced reactor company Deployable Energy announced that the US Department of Energy (DOE) has approved the documented safety analysis for its Unity nuclear battery test at Idaho National Laboratory (INL).
The company said the approval is a regulatory milestone before proceeding to criticality and follows completion of a DOE safety review process.

A statement said the documented safety analysis covers core engineering and safety analysis for the planned test and supports continued work towards deployment of the company’s microreactor technology.
According to earlier reports, the criticality test aims generate early data for design, manufacturing and future licensing work.
Bobby Gallagher, co-founder and chief executive of Deployable Energy, said the milestone positions the company to move towards criticality and later operational testing.
Deployable Energy said its 1-MW gas-cooled microreactor technology is designed to provide power in locations where traditional energy infrastructure may be “unavailable, vulnerable or impractical”.

The company said it has also received the full core of low-enriched uranium fuel for the Unity nuclear battery and will proceed with final preparations towards DOE authorisation and commissioning activities at INL.
Earlier this year, the company delivered its criticality test rig to INL following a cross-country road trip in a Ford truck, underscoring the compact and deployable nature of the Unity system.

In April, Deployable Energy was selected for the DOE’s Nuclear Energy Launch Pad, an INL-based programme designed to give private developers access to national laboratory expertise, infrastructure and testing for advanced nuclear technologies.
Deployable Energy and NRC officials observing the DOE authorisation process of the Unity nuclear battery test at INL Courtesy Deployable Energy.

title: Elementl Announces Plans For 1.5 GW SMR Nuclear Plant In Ohio
author: David Dalton
text: Company has signed agreement to use BWRX-300 reactor technology

Elementl Power, a US-based independent developer of utility-scale nuclear power projects, announced that it is pursuing development of a nuclear power plant with a planned capacity of up to 1.5 GW in Ohio.

Elementl has signed an early works agreement with GE Vernova Hitachi Nuclear Energy to use the company’s BWRX-300 small modular reactor (SMR) technology for the project, making it among the first new SMR projects in the US.

The nearly 700-acre (283-hectare) Meigs County property is situated along the Ohio River, approximately 100 miles southeast of Columbus. Elementl has agreed to buy the site from nonprofit wholesale power supplier American Municipal Power (AMP).

Elementl recently filed a request with regional transmission organisation PJM Interconnection to connect the site into the regional transmission system for the first 600 MW of output from the facility. PJM will review Elementl’s application and is expected to respond later this year.

If Elementl moves forward with the project, the site will require regulatory approvals from multiple state and federal agencies, including the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) and the Ohio Power Siting Board.
As a private development project, Elementl plans to finance the cost of the proposed plant. It said the project will not be funded through electric customer rates.
Construction on the first unit is expected to begin in 2030, subject to a final investment decision and regulatory approvals, with an anticipated completion date of 2034.
Elementl Power says it has a technology-agnostic approach to its projects. It offers expertise in capital formation, project execution and regulatory strategy.
The small modular reactor project site in Meigs County, Ohio. Courtesy Elementl Power.

title: Fusion Spending Increases, But Incentives Needed In Bid To Boost Supply Chain
author: David Dalton
text: Bottlenecks remain in key areas, which could constrain progress, warns FIA report

Supply chain spending by the nuclear fusion industry increased by 24% in 2025, but targeted incentives are needed as the sector aims for “serious capacity building” in the next decade, according to The Fusion Industry Supply Chain 2026, the annual report from the Fusion Industry Association (FIA), published today.

Around half of the world’s private fusion companies shared their supply chain spending data for the report, reporting a total spend of $538m (€471m) and projecting this to jump a further 27% in 2026, to $681m.
The report was launched at The Fusion Supply Chain Trade Show in the US state of New Mexico and is based on interviews and surveys with 25 fusion companies and 67 fusion suppliers.

The Washington, US-based FIA said the annual report has long noted a “chicken and egg” gridlock, where fusion companies need serious supply chain capacity building in the next decade, but struggle to give suppliers the long-term confidence to make these investments.

The 2026 report shows signs that the gridlock is easing, with 70% of fusion companies seeing an increase in established suppliers pivoting to fusion, and 25% observing existing suppliers successfully scaling up capacity to meet their needs.
Meanwhile, 75% of suppliers made investments to expand fusion capacity in the last year, ranging from $30,000 to $65m.

The report warned that the industry has not yet reached the transformative inflection point when large-scale investment in commercial fusion machines drives a step change in supply chain demand. At that stage, annual procurement programmes are expected to reach into the billions, with sustained demand for high-volume manufacturing of materials, components, and power systems, alongside large EPC contracts for plant construction.
While this shift has not yet occurred, it is anticipated to start within the decade and is “front of mind for both fusion companies and suppliers”, the report said.

Suppliers report that the frequency and substance of their conversations with fusion companies have notably improved over the last year. However, there is still work to do, as 69% continue to report a lack of long-term visibility of fusion needs, making planning and investment difficult.

Bottlenecks remain in key areas, which could constrain progress. Many respondents face constraints in power systems and power components (48%), heat management technologies (44%) and vacuum vessels and pumps (both 32%).

A particular worry was fusion fuel cycle systems, named by 48% of fusion companies as a major future concern. Fuel cycle systems underpin the production of fusion fuels and will be essential to sustaining long-term operations at commercial scale.

In response to these concerns, 54% of fusion companies plan to work with external suppliers to develop fusion fuel cycle technologies, and the same number plan to develop these in-house. Some plan to use both approaches.
A final challenge of note is commercial-scale access to materials that can withstand extreme conditions, with first-wall materials named by 40% as a future concern.

The FIA called for governments and investors to nurture specialist fusion suppliers through a mix of targeted incentives such as tax credits, grants, loan guarantees) and public-private partnerships (PPPs). PPPs can de-risk early capital investment, aggregating demand, and accelerating capability development.

It warned that there is a mismatch between funding for fusion developers and their suppliers. Policymakers and investors should expand dedicated financing for supply chain scale-up, including investment, grants, loan programmes, and blended finance models.

In some areas, regulatory uncertainty and tariff barriers are slowing supply chain development, the report said. Governments should pursue harmonised regulatory frameworks, targeted tariff exemptions and support for cross-border collaboration.
Courtesy General Atomics.

title: Finland’s Steady Energy Gets €10.5 Million Loan For Helsinki Pilot Nuclear Reactor
author: David Dalton
text: Facility being built in turbine hall of Salmisaari B coal-fired power plant

Steady Energy, the Finnish small nuclear power developer, has been granted a loan of €10.5m ($12m) by innovation funding agency Business Finland for construction of a pilot plant in Salmisaari, Helsinki.
Construction of the test facility has begun and operations are scheduled to begin in spring 2027.
The facility is being built in the turbine hall of the Salmisaari B coal-fired power plant, which power utility Helen recently decommissioned.

Instead of a reactor core, the full-scale pilot of Steady Energy’s LDR‑50 fission nuclear plant, will use an electric resistor that simulates the decay heat produced by an actual reactor. The main purpose of the pilot is to demonstrate that safety features operate as designed.
During the testing period, the heat generated as a by-product will be supplied to Helen’s district heating network.

Steady Energy said no nuclear technology developer has previously built a full‑size pilot plant of its reactor before commercial delivery. The project will also help prepare future supply chains and industrial‑scale deployment.

“Our plant is small and probably the simplest in the world,” said Hannes Haapalahti, chief technology officer at Steady Energy. “This means we can build a full-scale unit specifically for safety testing.

“In terms of design, our goal is to be ready to begin building the first [commercial nuclear] plant within three years,” Haapalahti said. Real-world testing significantly reduces schedule risks of the kind traditionally associated with large nuclear plant projects.

Steady Energy is developing the pilot plant before intending to roll out its LDR-50 reactor, which is designed to be installed underground and primarily aimed at providing 50 MW of heat for district heating systems common in Nordic, eastern European countries, as well as in South Korea.
The plants, the size of a shipping container, can be built underground in cities, close to district heating networks.
The technology is particularly well suited to district heating. Heating accounts for around 40% of global energy use.
In Finland, the cities of Helsinki, Jyväskylä, Kerava and Kuopio are exploring the use of small nuclear power for district heating.
The pilot plant is being built in the turbine hall of the Salmisaari B coal-fired power plant. Courtesy Helen.
The Steady Energy plants, the size of a shipping container, can be built underground in cities. Courtesy Steady Energy.

title: US Steps Up Support With Streamlined Civil Nuclear Exports To Thailand
author: David Dalton
text: Move follows Trump executive order on promoting American technologies overseas

The US has added Thailand to the list of destinations to which US companies are allowed to export nuclear technology and assistance, stepping up support for the deployment of US reactor technology overseas.

The Department of Energy (DOE) said in a statement these exports do not require advance DOE approval, though they are subject to reporting requirements. With the addition of Thailand, the total number of eligible destinations is 51.

The exports are controlled under the DOE’s regulation on assistance to foreign atomic energy activities. Under the regulation, energy secretary Chris Wright authorises specific activities that are not harmful, adverse, or hostile to the interest of the US, including assistance or transfers of technology.

The DOE said it continues to make progress implementing president Donald Trump’s executive order 14299, ‘Deploying Advanced Nuclear Reactor Technologies for National Security’, and specifically section 8 on promoting American nuclear exports.

Section 8 says the energy secretary will lead diplomatic engagement and negotiations for so-called 123 Agreements, the bilateral pacts between the US and other countries that provide the legal framework for the US to export nuclear material, reactors and critical components while preventing nuclear weapons proliferation. The US already has a 123 Agreement with Thailand.

Section 8 says the US will “aggressively pursue” at least 20 new 123 Agreements by the close of the 120th Congress in January 2029 to enable the US nuclear industry to access new markets in partner countries;
It also says the US will aggressively renegotiate 123 Agreements set to expire within the next decade.
Thailand has no commercial nuclear facilities, but according to a 2025 draft energy policy it plans to introduce two small modular reactor (SMR) plants in the northeast and south of the country.

The Electricity Generating Authority of Thailand has said it is studying SMR designs as it pushes ahead with plans to deploy “a sustainable alternative for Thailand’s green future” that helps boost the country’s competitiveness with affordable energy prices.
In 2024 Thailand’s nuclear regulator, the Energy Regulatory Commission, said it was looking into the legal aspects of an SMR programme.
Thailand has never had commercial nuclear plants, but is considering small modular reactors. Courtesy Preecha.MJ/Creative Commons Licence.

title: Zeno Power To Establish Nuclear Battery Production Centre At Historic Vallecitos Site
author: David Dalton
text: Project ‘addresses national need’ and reinvigorates nuclear industry base
US-based Zeno Power is establishing a nuclear battery manufacturing facility at the Vallecitos Nuclear Center in Sunol, California.

The company said it has partnered with NorthStar, a leader in nuclear decommissioning, to restore specialised hot cell infrastructure to produce nuclear batteries that will power critical defence, space, and commercial missions.
This lease agreement with NorthStar enables Zeno to fulfill initial deliveries to government customers in 2027 and then quickly scale production.

With more than $60m (€52m) in contracts with the Pentagon and Nasa, and strong follow-on demand from government and commercial partners, Zeno believes it is positioned to deliver nuclear batteries at scale beginning in 2028.

The 1,600-acre (647-hectare) Vallecitos complex was established in 1956 and was home to the Vallecitos boiling water reactor unit, the first privately owned and operated nuclear power plant to deliver significant quantities of electricity to a public grid. It was also the first nuclear power plant to be licensed by the US Atomic Energy Commission. The plant operated from 1957 until 1963.
The site was at the forefront of innovation at the US nuclear industry’s inception through fuel testing, isotope production and reactor research.
In March of 2024, the former operators of Vallecitos closed a deal with NorthStar to complete nuclear decommissioning and eventual site restoration at Vallecitos.
NorthStar’s decommissioning work will continue across the broader site in parallel with Zeno’s manufacturing activities in the discrete hot cell portion of the complex.

Zeno recently took possession of initial decontaminated hot cells – thick-walled, robustly shielded rooms designed for safe handling of radioactive materials. Non-radiological operations have begun at the facility, with radiological operations expected later this year, pending regulatory approval.

Vallecitos Nuclear Center has existing decommissioning licences from the Nuclear Regulatory Commission and California, with dedicated hot cell infrastructure already in place, a rare and valuable asset in the US. Hot cells allow technicians to safely build nuclear batteries by remotely handling radioactive materials through thick lead-glass windows and mechanical arms.

Zeno said its nuclear battery production at Vallecitos addresses a national need: ensuring domestic radiological infrastructure to meet the burgeoning demand for nuclear power. It said the effort aligns with the White House’s executive order 14302 to usher in the American nuclear renaissance.

“By establishing secure US production of nuclear batteries at an existing, licensed facility, Zeno is reinvigorating the nuclear industry base to provide decades of reliable energy for America's most critical missions,” the company said.
Nuclear batteries, also known as radioisotope power systems, convert the natural decay of radioisotopes into years of uninterrupted power.
Unlike conventional batteries or solar panels, these microwave-sized systems operate continuously in extreme environments – from the deep ocean to spacecraft exploring the outer solar system.
The Vallecitos Nuclear Center already has dedicated hot cell infrastructure in place. Courtesy Zeno Power.
The Vallecitos Nuclear Center in Sunol, California. Courtesy Zeno Power.

title: Switzerland’s Lower House Backs Plans To Allow Construction Of New Nuclear Plants
author: David Dalton
text: Legislation, which could now go to an optional national referendum, has proved divisive

Switzerland’s lower house of parliament, the National Council, has approved plans to allow the construction of new nuclear power plants, with a final vote due on Friday and a national referendum likely to follow.
The 200-seat council approved the plans, which have provided divisive, by a vote of 100 to 98, with two abstentions.

It rejected a motion to refer the matter back to the Federal Council – the seven-member executive cabinet and collective head of state and government – for clarification of financing issues for new reactors.

The plans are part of a counter-proposal linked to a popular initiative titled “Electricity for everyone at all times (Stop the blackout)”, launched by right-leaning lawmakers and representatives of the business sector.
That initiative sought to amend the constitution to ensure that all forms of electricity production that respect environmental and climate standards are allowed, including nuclear power.

Instead, the Federal Council put forward a counterproposal to the popular initiative that proposed to amend existing law rather than the constitution, and allow for different electricity generation technologies, including nuclear.

On Monday, following a marathon debate, the National Council had voted by a narrow margin of 100 to 97 with two abstentions in favour of a motion to refer the proposal back to the Federal Council for clarification on financing issues.

The upper house – the 46-seat Council of States – subsequently rejected the referral motion by a clear majority, paving the way for the National Council to fall in line and narrowly vote for approval of the pro-nuclear plans.
The legislation still needs a final vote – scheduled for Friday – in both the upper and lower houses, although this is likely to be a formality.

As a compromise, the Council of States’ environment, energy and spatial planning committee commissioned a report from the energy minister Albert Rösti which will outline the financial consequences of new nuclear power plant construction projects. The report is due by the end of the year.
“This report would therefore be available before a referendum could be held,” a Swiss parliament statement said.
“This convinced some centrist members of the National Council to vote differently on Thursday than they had earlier in the week. The proposal is thus ready for the final votes on Friday.”

The Swiss Nuclear Forum welcomed the National Council’s decision, saying it strengthens the long-term capacity of Swiss energy policy and lays the groundwork for a pragmatic and factual discussion about the country’s energy future.
“Switzerland should not rule out major options from the outset,” said forum president Hans-Ulrich Bigler.
“If it turns out that renewable energies alone cannot cover our electricity needs at all times in the future, then we will have to be able to resort to nuclear energy.”

The forum pointed out that lifting the construction ban does not mean that new nuclear reactors will be built in the near future. Rather, it is about maintaining flexibility and allowing for democratic decisions on potential projects.

The legislation is subject to an optional referendum which will be triggered if 50,000 eligible voters or eight of the country’s 26 cantons request a vote within 100 days of the official publication of the proposals.
Opponents to the legislation have already said they are likely to succeed in collecting the signatures needed for a referendum.
An industry spokesperson told NucNet that the referendum is expected to take place on 28 February 2027.

Despite a long tradition of nuclear power production, Switzerland voted in 2017 to no longer allow construction of new nuclear power plants. That law was the result of a long process initiated after the 2011 Fukushima-Daiichi nuclear accident in Japan.
However, there is no clear timetable for shutdowns, and the country’s four nuclear units can remain operational as long as they meet legal safety requirements.
Switzerland’s nuclear operators have said they are considering keeping nuclear plants in use longer than previously expected over fears of electricity shortages.
Switzerland’s four commercial nuclear plants are Beznau-1, Beznau-2, Gösgen and Leibstadt. They produce about a 27% share of the country’s electricity production.
Switzerland is now expected to hold a national referendum on the nuclear plans. Photo courtesy Khairul Abdulah. Creative Commons Licence.
The chamber of the Swiss National Council. Courtesy Peter Mosimann/Swiss Parliament

title: Estonia Study Shows ‘No Fundamental Technical Barriers’ To New Nuclear
author: David Dalton
text: Baltic country’s parliament recently passed crucial nuclear energy and safety act
There are no fundamental technical barriers that would prevent the development of a first commercial nuclear power plant in Estonia, a pre-feasibility site study has shown.
The study was carried out between December 2025 and April 2026 and provided input for the national planning process and the related environmental assessment.
The work focused on key technical areas including construction logistics, site layout, reactor building foundations and construction organisation.

Geological and geotechnical conditions were assessed as suitable with appropriate engineering solutions, while key challenges such as groundwater pressure and deep excavation can be addressed using established methods, the study showed.
The study also analysed how large components and construction materials could be delivered, identifying multiple viable logistics solutions combining maritime, rail and road transport.

According to Estonia-based nuclear company Fermi Energia, environmental aspects of reactor construction, including protected species and construction impact, were assessed “at a preliminary level” and are expected to be further analysed in subsequent stages.

Conceptual layouts for a two-unit nuclear power plant were developed, including alternative cooling solutions, indicating that different technical configurations remain possible depending on future site selection.
The study was commissioned by Fermi Energia and Samsung C&T Engineering & Construction Group.
The results will be used in the next stages of Estonia’s planning process, which aims to identify a suitable location and define the conditions for possible nuclear power plant development.

The results of the study came soon after Estonia’s parliament passed a nuclear energy and safety act
which creates the Baltic country’s first complete set of rules for producing nuclear energy and for overseeing its safety.
The government approved the draft of the legislation and sent it to parliament in March. If the president proclaims the act within 14 days, it will take effect on 1 January 2027.
The legislation was supported by both coalition and opposition parties. It reflects public support for adopting nuclear energy, which stood at 71% in January.
Fermi Energia is looking to deploy two 300-MW GE Vernova Hitachi Nuclear Energy BWRX-300 small modular reactors (SMRs) in Estonia by 2035
Estonia relies heavily on imported electricity and domestically produced oil shale – a highly polluting fossil fuel.

SMRs are emerging as a viable long-term solution as Estonia seeks to find what the government has called “controllable and continuous generation capacity” to balance fluctuations in renewable energy generation.
Fermi Energia is working towards the deployment of BWRX-300 SMRs in Estonia. Courtesy Fermi Energia/GE Vernova Hitachi Nuclear Energy.

title: India Announces RPV Landmark At Kudankulam-5 Nuclear Power Plant
author: David Dalton
text: Site in Tamil Nadu state will have six reactor units

The Nuclear Power Corporation of India Limited (NPCIL) has reached a major construction milestone at Kudankulam-5 nuclear power project with the successful placing of the reactor pressure vessel (RPV) inside the reactor building.
NPCIL said the landmark is a critical transition in the project’s construction phase.
The RPV weighs approximately 320 tonnes and is considered the heart of a nuclear power plant. It houses the reactor core where nuclear fission takes place.
Construction of Kudankulam-5, a Russia-designed VVER-1000 pressurised water reactor unit, began in June 2021.

There are three other reactor units of the same design under construction at the site, in Tamil Nadu state, southern India. Construction of Kudankulam-3 and -4 began in 2017 and of Kudankulam-6 in 2021.
Kudankulam-1 and -2 began commercial operation in 2014 and 2017 respectively.
NPCIL said the Kudankulam site is “steadily moving towards its full potential of 6,000 MWe installed capacity, reinforcing India’s long-term commitment to reliable, clean, and sustainable energy”.
India has eight commercial nuclear plants under construction and 21 in operation, providing about 3.3% of its electricity generation.
The RPV weighs approximately 320 tonnes and is considered the heart of a nuclear power plant. Courtesy NPCIL.

title: Switzerland’s Upper House Rejects Motion To Call For More Information On New Nuclear
author: David Dalton
text: Vote on divisive reactor bill could now take place this week

Switzerland’s Council of States, its upper house of parliament, has rejected a motion to refer a divisive nuclear bill back to the Federal Council with a vote now expected this week on whether the European country will allow the construction of new reactors.
The National Council had earlier asked for additional information from the Federal Council on the financial implications of the proposal to allow the construction of new nuclear power plants.

The National Council said it had referred a counter-proposal from the Federal Council back to the Federal Council. The Council of States has now narrowly voted by 28 to 16, with one abstention, to reject that motion.
On Monday, following a marathon debate, the National Council had voted by a narrow margin of 100 to 97 with two abstentions in favour of referral.

The counter-proposal was linked to a popular initiative titled “Electricity for everyone at all times (Stop the blackout)”, launched by right-leaning lawmakers and representatives of the business sector.
That initiative sought to amend the constitution to ensure that all forms of electricity production that respect environmental and climate standards are allowed, including nuclear power.

Instead, the Federal Council – the seven-member executive cabinet and collective head of state and government – put forward a counterproposal that would amend existing law rather than the constitution, and allow for different electricity generation technologies, including nuclear.

The National Council said it wanted clarification on the financial aspects of new nuclear. A statement said the council will have to vote on the matter again this week, but a second postponement would be “final”.
The 200-seat National Council is the larger, lower house of the Swiss parliament, or federal assembly. The other house is the upper house – the 46-seat Council of States.

For any federal law or amendment to pass, it must be debated and approved in identical form by both the National Council and the Council of States. If not, the law or amendment follows what is known as a “procedure for reconciling differences” of both councils.

Thierry Burkart, a member of the centre-right Radical-Liberal Party on the Council of States and a supporter of nuclear new build plans, said the issue of financing did not need to be looked at in advance and could be thoroughly examined “during the development of a concrete project”.
He said nuclear power plants were needed for security of energy supply and warned of “serious problems” if existing plants are not extended and if consideration is not given to additional capacity.

Burkart said that at this stage, the question is whether to decide on the principle of being able to build new nuclear power plants. “We must leave the door open to this option, especially given the technological advances in this area,” he said.

The Social Democratic Party’s Mathilde Crevoisier Crelier, a member of the Council of States, said she was against giving a “blank check” for new nuclear based on the assumption that the issue would be resolved later. She pointed out that the management of nuclear waste remained unresolved.
The Swiss Nuclear Forum earlier said it regretted the National Council’s decision and hoped that the Council of States would uphold the lifting of the ban on building new power plants.
““Without technological openness, there’s no point in considering the financing of new nuclear power plants,” said forum president Hans-Ulrich Bigler.
“Today, we don’t know if, when, or where new nuclear power plants will be built, and we know neither the reactor technology nor the scale of any future project.

“The question of financing is pure speculation. This argument is nothing more than a delaying tactic. Making prior clarification of financing a condition for lifting the construction ban would constitute a special rule that doesn’t apply to any other electricity generation technology.”

Despite a long tradition of nuclear power production, Switzerland voted in 2017 to no longer allow construction of new nuclear power plants. That law was the result of a long process initiated after the 2011 Fukushima-Daiichi nuclear accident in Japan.
However, there is no clear timetable for shutdowns, and the country’s four nuclear units can remain operational as long as they meet legal safety requirements.
Switzerland’s nuclear operators have said they are considering keeping nuclear plants in use longer than previously expected over fears of electricity shortages.
Switzerland’s four commercial nuclear plants are Beznau-1, Beznau-2, Gösgen and Leibstadt. They produce about a 27% share of the country’s electricity production.
Photo courtesy Khairul Abdulah. Creative Commons Licence.

title: TerraPower Announces ‘Major Milestones’ In Bid For UK Nuclear Reactor Rollout
author: David Dalton
text: Bill Gates-founded company begins Step 1 of generic design assessment process

US nuclear technology company TerraPower has announced major milestones in its UK reactor deployment programme with the formal commencement of the UK regulatory review for its Natrium plant, and the launch of its UK subsidiary, TerraPower UK Ltd.

TerraPower, which was co-founded by Bill Gates, said these regulatory and commercial activities mark the company’s most significant steps to date towards deploying a fleet of Natrium reactors in the UK.

Chris Levesque, TerraPower president and chief executive officer, said: “TerraPower is entering the UK market with a long-term commitment to supporting the nation’s clean energy future and establishing ourselves as a serious and reliable deployment partner.”
The company has begun Step 1 of the three-step regulatory review process, known as the generic design assessment, or GDA.

The company submitted its GDA application in October 2025, its first international regulatory filing for the Natrium technology. In February the UK announced its readiness to begin the GDA process for the Natrium reactor after the company’s application was accepted for review.

The voluntary GDA process is used by the UK’s joint nuclear regulators to assess new nuclear power station designs. It allows the regulators to assess the safety, security and environmental implications of new reactor designs, separately from applications to build them at specific sites.
The start of Step 1 of the GDA process marks a significant step toward Natrium advanced reactor deployment in the UK, TerraPower said.
“Confirming arrangements is an important enabling step for ONR to engage with and assess TerraPower’s Natrium design,” it said.

Diego Fernandez Lisbona, the UK Office of Nuclear Regulation’s head of regulation for the TerraPower Natrium GDA and advanced nuclear technologies, said: “Interactions in 2025, through our framework for early engagement, have provided early design familiarity and we will continue to engage closely with TerraPower and broader stakeholders as GDA progresses.”
The GDA’s purpose is to de-risk future Natrium projects by ensuring that environmental protection is built into the design from the start.

Alan McGoff, the Environment Agency’s policy lead for new nuclear build, said: “This is the first GDA where we can take advantage of our arrangements for enhanced cooperation between international regulators following the UK and US governments’ signing last year of the Atlantic Partnership for Advanced Nuclear Energy.”
TerraPower UK will serve as the company’s operational base for all UK activities including GDA engagement. It is the company’s first office outside the US.
Ian Hudson has been appointed head of TerraPower UK. He brings more than 30 years of leadership experience in the nuclear industry.

TerraPower has been working through regulatory requirements in the US, where the first Natrium plant is being built at a former coal site in Kemmerer, Wyoming. That project is expected to be completed in 2030 and will be the first utility-scale advanced nuclear power plant in the US.

The US work includes recent approval by the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission to begin building the plant. The UK’s GDA process will expand on the company’s experience and efforts in the US and will allow TerraPower to establish deployment timelines for Natrium sites in the country.

TerraPower says its Natrium technology is well positioned to support rapidly increasing energy demand. The Natrium plant design features a 345 MW sodium-cooled fast reactor with a patented molten salt-based energy storage system.

The storage technology can boost the system’s output to 500 MW of power when needed because it is designed to keep base output steady, ensuring constant reliability, and can quickly ramp up when demand peaks. It is the only advanced reactor design with this unique feature.
TerraPower said it is rapidly commercialising the Natrium technology, including an agreement with Meta for up to eight Natrium plants in the US by 2035.

title: Southeast Asia Could Meet 8% Of Electricity Demand Growth By 2050 If It Meets Nuclear Targets
author: David Dalton
text: IEA report says Indonesia, Philippines and Vietnam most advanced in plans, but warns on cost

Southeast Asian countries could meet around 8% of total electricity demand growth by 2050 if announced targets for nuclear deployment are met, a report from the International Energy Association (IEA) says.

The Paris-based organisation’s Southeast Asia Energy Outlook report for 2026 said that in terms of generation, announced nuclear output so far would be the equivalent of installing 130 GW of solar energy or 70 GW of wind energy capacity.

The IEA said that Indonesia, the Philippines and Vietnam have all set clear nuclear targets. A growing number of other countries including Malaysia, Myanmar, Singapore and Thailand, are also all considering developing nuclear power, with a particular focus on small modular reactors (SMRs).

There are no commercial nuclear plants under construction or operating in the region. The Philippines built a Westinghouse-supplied 621-MW pressurised water reactor at Bataan, northwest of Manila, which was completed in 1984, but never commissioned.
“The development of nuclear energy in Southeast Asia could bring a range of benefits for electricity systems undergoing rapid growth and transformation,” the report said.
“By diversifying the generation mix, nuclear energy can complement renewables while reducing reliance on a narrower set of technologies.”

The report added that nuclear generation could displace a heavy reliance on fossil fuel used in the power sector. It said that by 2050 nuclear power could displace the need for 35 Mtce (million tonnes of coal equivalent) of coal use and close to 20 bcm (billion cubic metres) of natural gas.

“In all cases, the displacement of coal or natural gas would enhance energy security by reducing reliance on imported fossil fuels, lowering exposure to price volatility, and mitigating long-term supply risks,” the report said.

The report highlighted the impact on the region of the conflict in the Middle East and said that following measures to alleviate short-term consquences, it was now a priority for the region to diversify with clean energy, electrification and efficiency as key levers.
The report said that countries could move from considering nuclear power to operating first reactors in a period of around 10-15 years.
Key priorities to doing this included establishing a robust nuclear regulatory framework, aligned with the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) milestones approach.

This approach includes the creation of an independent regulator with a clear separation between promotion and oversight, backed by emerging regional and international cooperation on safety and emergency protocols.
The report suggested that countries would need to develop nuclear skills, strengthen institutional and industrial capabilities, share and diversify risks, as well as achieving broad public support.

“These steps are critical to translating stated ambitions for nuclear energy into reality across the region, provided that the countries are able to avoid undue delays and make clear and timely decisions at each stage of the process.”
The IEA said nuclear can be cost competitive in the region, but this would be dependent on delivering on time and budget, as well as keeping financing costs low.

The report said that the levelised cost of electricity (LCOE) for nuclear power was just below $100/MWh (€86.2/MWh) given high upfront investment costs and financing costs. This compared with average electricity generation costs in the region of around $70/MWh.

LCOE captures both capital and operating costs that need to be covered. It is essentially the long-term price at which the electricity produced by a power plant will have to be sold at for the investor to cover all their costs.
The IEA said that construction costs and financing would have to fall to bring costs closer to the $70/MWh average. SMRs could also help to bring the cost of nuclear down.

“Nuclear projects delivered closer to this range would therefore strengthen long‑term electricity affordability while providing firm, low‑emissions power that strengthens system adequacy and supports grid stability.”
The report did caution that LCOE was not always the best benchmark to compare all technologies and cost options.

In terms of nuclear commitments to date, the IEA said that Indonesia planned to have 0.5 GW by 2032, rising to 7 GW by 2040. The Philippines plans 1.2 GW of capacity by 2032, rising to 4.8 GW in 2050. Vietnam projects to have 4-6.4 GW of capacity by 2030, increasing to 10.5-14 GW by 2050.
The Philippine capital Manila. The Philippines is one of several countries in the region considering nuclear. Courtesy Jopey Sy/CC Licence.

title: Rolls-Royce Broadens Nuclear Ambitions With Trilateral Agreement On Advanced Modular Reactors
author: David Dalton
text: Cooperation with Japan builds on plans for three of UK company’s SMR plants in Wales

Rolls-Royce has taken a significant step towards broadening its nuclear portfolio by signing two trilateral memorandums of cooperation with United Kingdom National Nuclear Laboratory (UKNNL) and Japan Atomic Energy Agency (JAEA) to accelerate the introduction of advanced nuclear technologies in the UK.

The three parties said they will cooperate to advance high-temperature gas-cooled advanced modular reactor (AMR) technology and the next generation coated particle fuel (CPF) that powers them. He reactors could provide power for industrial clusters, remote industry and off-grid communities.

A high-temperature gas-cooled reactor (HTGR) is a type of gas-cooled nuclear reactor which uses uranium fuel and graphite moderation to produce very high reactor core output temperatures. According to the International Atomic Energy Agency, interest in HTGRs is increasing because they can provide efficient and cost-effective electricity and produce high-temperature process heat usable for various industrial applications.
A formal signing ceremony was held on 14 June at the UK prime minister’s residence, Number 10 Downing Street, during the visit of to London of Japan’s prime minister Sanae Takaichi.

Rolls-Royce said the cooperation builds on the success of subsidiary Rolls-Royce SMR, which in April signed a contract with UK government body Great British Energy - Nuclear that enables work to start immediately on the delivery of three Rolls-Royce small modular reactors (SMRs) at Wylfa, on the coast of Ynys Môn (Anglesey) in North Wales.
The company said the parties have a collective ambition to accelerate the research and development required for deployment of AMRs and to progress the qualification and manufacture of CPF.

The UK’s Nuclear Regulatory Taskforce, commissioned by prime minister Keir Starmer, recently identified nuclear technology as being vital to the UK’s economic growth, energy security and national defence.

Rolls-Royce said the new trilateral relationship will advance the UK’s sovereign nuclear technology capability and demonstrate a commitment to strengthening the UK and Japan’s cooperation on clean energy and nuclear technologies.

The company said AMRs can deliver energy resilience and enable decarbonisation across civil, defence and industrial applications. They represent a compact and rapidly deployable nuclear energy solution for off-grid customers who require flexible heat and power that is safe, secure and reliable.

Coated particle fuel is a key component in the inherent safety of AMRs. Within its core, each particle of uranium is surrounded by protective layers, allowing it to withstand even the most extreme conditions.

Rolls-Royce said: “To be a fully capable nuclear nation and secure the full economic and security benefits from these technologies, the UK needs end-to-end capability in advanced nuclear technologies and a supportive ecosystem.”

JAEA president Masanori Koguchi said he hopes the collaboration will lead to the early deployment of high-temperature gas-cooled advanced modular reactor technology, which he called “a significant step towards net zero”.
A rendering of a Rolls-Royce AMR used to provide power for industry. Courtesy Rolls-Royce.
A Rolls-Royce AMR could provide power for remote industries or communities. Courtesy Rolls-Royce.

title: Poland To Choose Partner And Reactor Technology For Second Nuclear Station In 2027
author: David Dalton
text: Updated policy confirms schedule and two preferred locations for project

Poland has released an updated nuclear power policy which says its goal of building two large-scale nuclear power stations remains unchanged with selection of a partner and technology for a second nuclear station scheduled for 2027.

A government statement said the update of the Polish nuclear power programme (PNPP), prepared by the ministry of rnergy, marks the next stage in the implementation of “one of the most important strategic and development projects in Polish history”.
It said nuclear will support energy security, help transform the energy sector and help create conditions for further economic development.
The statement said the project for the first nuclear power station has moved from the preparation phase to the implementation phase.

Work is underway on the construction of the second nuclear station with selection of a strategic partner and reactor technology planned in 2027. Construction is scheduled to start around 2032 and launch of the first unit will be around 2040.
An earlier PNPP said the tender for technology and investors for the second facility would be launched in 2025-26, with construction from 2032 and the first reactor expected online in 2040.
As with Poland’s first nuclear station, the second will use proven Generation III+ large-scale light-water reactor technology.

Two coal-generation sites, Bełchatów and Konin, both in central Poland, remain the preferred locations. The government said they are regions with adequate energy infrastructure and years of experience in electricity production. The final location selection will be made after detailed analyses and field studies.
Work has begun to select a technology supplier and project contractor. The US, France and Canada have joined the process.

Energy minister Miłosz Motyka told a press conference that state-owned project company Polskie Elektrownie Jądrowe (PEJ) will coordinate work on the second facility. State-controlled utility Polska Grupa Energetyczna (PGE) had been seen as the possible project leader. Motyka said: “We also see a very important role here for PGE, which is currently present in the locations indicated for the construction of the second Polish nuclear power plant.”
The government said the goal is to select a comprehensive offer encompassing both technology and project financing under the best possible terms.

The update of the PNPP takes into account the changes that have affected the European energy market in recent years – from the energy crisis and Russia’s aggression against Ukraine to the growing industrial demand for predictable and low-emission energy.

In the plan, nuclear energy remains one of the pillars of Poland’s energy security. Nuclear will diversify energy sources, reduce dependence on fossil fuels, replace shut-down coal-fired units with new, stable capacity, and increase the resilience of the power system to crises and market disruptions, the plan says.
It says nuclear power plants ensure energy production regardless of weather conditions, and support the development of renewable energy sources and the stability of the national power system.
The development of nuclear energy also creates conditions for “industrial development and new investments”, according to the plan.

Poland’s first nuclear project, on the country’s northern coast in the province of Pomerania, is being carried out by PEJ. It involves the construction of three Westinghouse AP1000 reactors with a total capacity of approximately 3,750 MW.

In recent months, the project has reached a number of key milestones. In December 2025 the European Commission approved the public support model for investments and in March 2026 PEJ submitted an application to the National Atomic Energy Agency for a construction permit for the facility. Preparatory work has begun at the site and so has work on supporting infrastructure.
“The process of contracting and preparing the next stages of the investment is continuing,” the government said.
Poland has already approved 60.2 billion zloty (€14.1bn, $16.3bn) in equity funding, subject to state aid decision, to cover up to 30% of the expected cost of the project
The first unit is scheduled to start commercial operation in 2036 and the facility is expected to reach full capacity by 2038.
Preparatory work has begun at the site of the first nuclear station. Courtesy PEJ.
Energy minister Miłosz Motyka (left) told a press conference that state-owned project company PEJ will coordinate work on the second facility. Courtesy Ministry of Energy of Poland.

title: US Lays Out Fusion Roadmap With Aim Of Scaling Up Private Sector By Mid-2030s
author: David Dalton
text: Strategy warns of critical science, materials and technology gaps on road to deployment

The US Department of Energy has released a finalised national roadmap to accelerate the development and commercialisation of fusion energy on the most rapid, responsible timeline in history, with the goal of scaling up the private fusion sector by the mid-2030s.

Released on 9 June, the Fusion Science and Technology Roadmap builds on an earlier roadmap released by the DOE in October 2025. That roadmap warned that there remain critical science, materials and technology gaps that must be closed for fusion to succeed.

The new roadmap echoes those findings. It says the US private sector has attracted more than $10bn (€8.6bn) in cumulative private investment to commercialise fusion technology and deliver fusion energy to the grid. But it adds: “There remain critical science, materials, and technology gaps, such as the breeding and handling of fusion fuels, developing materials that can withstand fusion conditions, and increasing plasma performance, all of which must be closed. These critical gaps require innovation and bridging of the public and private sectors.”

The roadmap outlines plans for the US to build key infrastructure to address critical fusion materials and technology gaps. The US will “innovate and advance the science and engineering of fusion energy and grow the US fusion ecosystem”, it says.

“Growth strategies include expanding domestic and international public-private partnerships and regional consortia, and building critical research infrastructure, supply chains, and fusion manufacturing networks.”

The roadmap charts a path for the public and private sectors to work together with a unified strategy to ensure that the US is progressing towards fusion commercialisation “on the most rapid, credible timeline in history”.
It targets actions and milestones out to the mid-2030s, providing the scientific and technological foundation to support a competitive US fusion energy industry.

According to the DOE, the roadmap brings together fusion science, technology, infrastructure, workforce development, and commercialisation priorities into a single national strategy, outlining how the DOE, industry, universities, and national laboratories will work together to accelerate the path toward US commercial fusion energy.
The roadmap is built around three primary drivers:
- Building critical infrastructure to close fusion materials and technology gaps.
- Innovating through advanced research, high-performance computing, and AI.
- Growing the US fusion ecosystem through public-private partnerships, supply chain development, workforce growth, and commercialization pathways.

The DOE said its ability to support the roadmap’s milestones and timelines is contingent on future public-private partnerships and future congressional appropriations, and that the document does not commit the department to specific funding levels.
“Fusion energy has entered a new era defined by extraordinary scientific progress and public-private momentum,” said DOE undersecretary for science Darío Gil.
“With this roadmap, we now have the clarity, coordination, and sustained commitment needed to turn the promise of fusion into a reality for the American people.”

The roadmap was developed with input from more than 800 scientists and engineers across the public and private sectors, with contributions from more than 15 private companies, over 10 national laboratories and more than 70 universities.
The roadmap charts a path for the public and private sectors to work together on nuclear fusion.

title: DOE Approves Key Safety Analysis For Oklo Aurora Nuclear Plant In Idaho
author: David Dalton
text: Project advancing alongside advanced reactor company’s ‘broader work’ in US state

US advanced reactor company Oklo announced that the US Department of Energy’s (DOE’s) Idaho Operations Office has approved the preliminary documented safety analysis (PDSA) for Oklo’s Aurora powerhouse at Idaho National Laboratory (INL).

The PDSA is a major step under DOE’s Reactor Pilot Program authorisation pathway and represents a detailed review of the preliminary safety basis for the Aurora-INL plant, including the project’s hazard analysis, accident analysis, safety controls and design commitments.

Oklo said the approval advances Aurora-INL through a federal process designed to unlock US industrial capacity by enabling an accelerated deployment of scalable generation capacity under rigorous federal oversight.

Aurora-INL will be the first of Oklo’s planned fast fission power plants. The company has been granted access to recovered fuel from the Experimental Breeder Reactor-II (EBR-II)* following a competitive DOE process launched in 2019, the same year Oklo received a site-use permit at INL for the Aurora powerhouse.

Aurora-INL is advancing alongside Oklo’s broader work in Idaho, including the Aurora fuel fabrication facility (A3F) where it will be fabricating the initial fuel assemblies for Aurora-INL from EBR-II fuel.

* The Experimental Breeder Reactor-II was a sodium-cooled fast reactor designed, built and operated by Argonne National Laboratory at the National Reactor Testing Station in Idaho. It was shut down in 1994. Custody of the reactor was transferred to INL after its founding in 2005.
Aurora-INL will be the first of Oklo’s planned fast fission power plants. Courtesy Oklo.

title: Focus On Design Documentation As Russia Continues Preparations For Beloyarsk BN-1200 FBR
author: David Dalton
text: Rosenergoatom boss sets deadline for first concrete at Generation IV nuclear plant

Rosenergoatom’s primary focus is on finalising the design documentation as preparations continue for the construction of the Beloyarsk-5 nuclear plant – the first unit in the country with a Generation IV BN-1200M reactor.

The state nuclear power development and operations company said it was aiming to submit the documentation to the Main Directorate of State Expertise of Russia, with the goal of receiving a final opinion by the end of 2026. The directorate, known as Glavgosexpertiza, is the federal executive institution authorised to examine project documentation for significant infrastructure projects.
Rosenergoatom said once the documentation is approved the next step will be to obtain a licence to construct the power unit. That licence could be issued in the spring of 2027, Rosenergoatom said.

The update on the project came as Rosenergoatom chief executive officer Alexander Shutikov paid a working visit to the Beloyarsk site, near Yekaterinburg in southwest Russia, where he held a series of meetings on preparations for construction.
Shutikov said the deadline for pouring first concrete was the end of 2027.
To date, more than 1.4 million cubic meters of waste soil have been cleared, and the site has been cleared of vegetation.
According to Yuri Nosov, director of the Beloyarsk nuclear power station, the site will now be prepared for drilling and blasting operations.

Russia’s sodium-cooled BN-series fast breeder reactors (FBRs) are part of state nuclear corporation Rosatom’s project to develop fast reactors with a closed fuel cycle whose mixed-oxide (MOX) fuel will be reprocessed and recycled.

An FBR is an advanced nuclear reactor that generates more fissile material – nuclear fuel – than it consumes while producing electricity. By converting non-fissile materials into usable fuel, it drastically improves resource efficiency and extracts far more energy from uranium reserves than conventional reactors
The Beloyarsk-3 BN-600 FBR began commercial operation in 1981 and the BN-800 Beloyarsk-4 FBR in 2016.
Beloyarsk-4 is seen as a demonstration unit for the larger BN-1200 FBR at Beloyarsk-5.
Rosenergoatom chief executive officer Alexander Shutikov paid a working visit to the Beloyarsk site, near Yekaterinburg in southwest Russia. Courtesy Rosenergoatom.

title: Loading Of Dummy Fuel Completed At Akkuyu-1 Nuclear Plant In Turkey
author: David Dalton
text: Landmark is key element of commissioning process for Russia-supplied reactor
A batch of 163 dummy nuclear fuel assemblies has been loaded at Turkey’s Akkuyu-1 nuclear power plant in the southern province of Mersin as a key part of the commissioning process.

Russia’s state nuclear corporation Rosatom said the dummy fuel is designed to be an exact replica of nuclear fuel in design, weight and dimensions. Its loading is key to checking systems for loading the real fuel as well as confirming readiness for the next stage of commissioning operations.

The dummy fuel does not contain any nuclear materials and its loading precedes the cold and hot running tests of reactor plant equipment during the commissioning process for new units, before the reactor starts up.

Sergei Butckikh, chief executive officer of project company Akkuyu Nuclear, said: “The completion of loading of dummy fuel assemblies at Akkuyu NPP Unit 1 is a full rehearsal for loading nuclear fuel.

“Using the dummies, we work out procedures for handling nuclear fuel in conditions as close to operational as possible, and confirm the readiness of equipment and personnel for the next pre-launch stage.”
Akkuyu, Turkey’s first nuclear station, will have four Russia-supplied Generation III+ VVER-1200 pressurised water reactor units. Construction of Akkuyu-4 started in July 2022.
Akkuyu-1, the first unit, was expected to be online in late 2025 or early 2026, but the latest schedule eyes first power generation by the end of 2026.
According to reports in December 2025, Russia had provided an additional $9bn (€7.7bn) for the Akkuyu plant, with total financing valued at $20bn.
The dummy nuclear fuel assemblies being loaded at Turkey’s Akkuyu-1. Coyurtesy Rosatom.

title: Switzerland Extends ‘Highly Controversial’ Debate On Lifting Nuclear Power Ban
author: David Dalton
text: Proposal would reverse phaseout policy endorsed by voters in 2017
Switzerland’s high-profile debate on lifting a ban on nuclear power will continue beyond is scheduled days after about 100 elected officials and several minority groups asked to be heard.

The National Council, Switzerland’s lower house of parliament, said the debate, originally scheduled to end after two days on 9 June, will continue on 15 June. It said the issue is “highly controversial” and the Swiss People's Party (SVP) and the Liberal Party (FDP) need the support of the Centre party to get the proposal approved.
Between them the SVP and FDP hold 90 seats in the 200-seat chamber. The Centre party holds 29 seats. The left, the Green Liberal Party, and a minority of centrists opposed the proposal.
In an earlier statement on 8 June the National Council said the possibility of building new nuclear power plants in Switzerland was causing division in the federal parliament.
At the core of the debate is an initiative that revolves around the question of whether Switzerland should lift a ban on the construction of new nuclear power plants.
Earlier this year Switzerland’s upper house of parliament supported lifting the ban on new nuclear.
The proposal, which would reverse the nuclear phaseout policy endorsed by voters in 2017, must be approved by the lower house and is widely expected to be put to a national referendum.

Despite a long tradition of nuclear power production, Switzerland voted in 2017 to no longer allow construction of new nuclear power plants. That law was the result of a long process initiated after the 2011 Fukushima-Daiichi nuclear accident in Japan.
However, there is no clear timetable for shutdowns, and the country’s four nuclear units can remain operational as long as they meet legal safety requirements.
Switzerland’s nuclear operators have said they are considering keeping nuclear plants in use longer than previously expected over fears of electricity shortages.
Switzerland’s four commercial nuclear plants are Beznau-1, Beznau-2, Gösgen and Leibstadt. They produce about a 27% share of the country’s electricity production.
Nearly 60% of the Swiss population supports the construction of new nuclear power plants, according to a survey commissioned by the Swiss Association of Electricity Companies.

According to the survey, conducted by the GFS.bern research institute, 79% of respondents want to continue operating nuclear power plants as long as they remain safe, while the construction of new generation facilities receives 59% support.

GFS.bern said the popularity of nuclear power in its survey reflects a growing fear of electricity shortages, but added the research found that most people still opt for renewables to cope with the shortage.
Photo courtesy Khairul Abdulah. Creative Commons Licence.

title: European Conference Calls For Coordinated Action On Molten Salt Reactors
author: David Dalton
text: Joint Research Centre says deployment no longer a distant aspiration
The deployment of molten salt reactors (MSRs) is no longer a distant aspiration, but coordinated action will be needed if projects are to be delivered on time, a conference in Germany has concluded.

Delegates at the 1st European Conference on Molten Salt Reactor Technology said action that needs to be taken includes shared standards, bankable projects, integrated licensing strategies and a European ecosystem that can efficiently deliver on time.
The conference, in Baden-Baden, was organised by the European Commission’s Joint Research Centre (JRC), which carries out research in various fields to provide independent advice to EU policymakers.
