The JRC said: “The science is mature, the engineering is in hand, and private capital is ready to commit.
“The field has the concepts, the growing political will, and the industrial players.”

The JRC said the nuclear sector is becoming increasingly important in Europe’s clean technology and sustainable energy agenda. It warned that first of a kind projects require stable policies, risk reduction mechanisms, and viable partnerships.

MSRs have progressed from the conceptual stage to the point where real deployment questions are being asked, but qualified evidence is still needed, the JRC said. Fuel salt chemistry, materials corrosion and component lifetime are key challenges, but the EU “has the right competence to address them”. Safety, security and safeguards must be integrated from day one.
On deployment, the JRC said early regulatory dialogue and graded licensing are essential.

MSRs are nuclear fission reactors in which either the fuel and/or the coolant is a molten salt. Molten salt is salt which liquifies at elevated temperatures and can store massive amounts of thermal energy at atmospheric pressure.

The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) says international interest in MSRs is increasing because they have the potential to provide large amounts of efficient and cost-effective electricity and produce high-temperature process heat usable for various industrial applications.

According to the IAEA, several MSR designs are under development and approaching deployment readiness. In Canada, a molten salt-based small modular reactor (SMR) concept passed a crucial pre-licensing vendor design review in 2023, the first such review completed for an MSR. Other projects, including in China and the US, continue to make progress, with the hope that MSRs could begin to see deployment as soon as the mid-2030s.
The conference, in Baden-Baden, was organised by the European Commission’s Joint Research Centre. Courtesy JRC.

title: Port Operator DP World Launches SMR Study For Port Of Constanța in Romania
author: Nigel Davies
text: Company teams up with France’s CEA to evaluate nuclear

Dubai-based global port operator DP World has launched a study alongside French research organisation the Commisariat à l’Energie Atomique et aux Energies Alternatives (CEA) into the use of a small modular reactor (SMR) at the Romanian port of Constanța.

In a statement, DP World, which is also working on the study with France-based thinktank TerraWater Institute, said it would assess the projected energy demand for the port from 2030-2050 and evaluate the technical, strategic and economic feasibility of deploying an SMR.
DP World said that SMRs have the potential to provide low-carbon electricity for port operations, as well as wider industrial use.

The study, supported by the CEA’s knowledge of SMR designs, will examine standards and issues for the surrounding environment of the port, on the Black Sea in eastern Romania. Future development at the port would be dependent on further technical assessment, regulatory reviews and stakeholder engagement.

“SMRs are not just energy projects for our ports, they are a competitive infrastructure differentiator,” said Nicholas Mazzei, vice president of sustainability for Europe at DP World. “This study will help us better understand how nuclear energy can strengthen operational resilience and help meet rising demand.”
The CEA said that the study would assess how SMRs could be integrated into a real port environment.

DP World is already planning for the development of nuclear-powered ports in the UK. Working with US reactor manufacturer Last Energy it plans to install a microreactor to expand its London Gateway port and business park.
Romania has one commercial nuclear reactor at Cernavodǎ, which uses two 650-MW Canada-designed Candu6 plants that began commercial operation in 1996 and 2007.

However, the country is committed to developing a 462 MW SMR project using six 77-MW reactors developed by NuScale, built on the site of the former Doicești coal plant about 90 km northwest of Bucharest.
The port of Constanța on Romania’s Black Sea coast in the east of the country. Courtesy DP World.

title: UK National Nuclear Laboratory Chooses Actemium As Partner For Advancing Nuclear Energy Independence Plans
author: David Dalton
text: Contract will support efforts to develop sovereign Haleu supply

Actemium Design UK, part of Actemium UK, has been selected by United Kingdom National Nuclear Laboratory (UKNNL) as its design partner to support the development of high assay low enriched uranium (Haleu) capability at UKNNL’s Springfields site in northwest England.
The four-year partnership will provide engineering design support to help develop this critical UK Haleu capability.

The contract will support UKNNL in advancing the R&D needed to develop a UK sovereign capability to produce Haleu in the quantities required to fuel the next generation of advanced modular nuclear reactors.

Actemium noted in a statement that currently, only two other nations are capable of producing Haleu at commercial scale. It was most likely referring to Russia and China. Western nations do not yet produce Haleu at commercial scale, although several are developing or funding domestic production facilities to meet potential demand for advanced nuclear reactors.

Haleu is a nuclear fuel with a higher concentration of the fissile isotope uranium-235 (U-235) (5-20%) than traditional reactor fuel (3-5%). It will be crucial for advanced reactors like small modular reactors (SMRs) and microreactors. Most new reactor designs, especially SMRs, require Haleu to achieve their advanced performance goals.

Actemium Design UK will help UKNNL develop the new Haleu production process. The work will include defining the technical scope, producing detailed designs and shaping the overall manufacturing approach.

UKNNL is the government’s lead civil national laboratory for nuclear fission, with a twofold mission: to enable and deliver nuclear outcomes for government, and to support growth of the UK nuclear sector.
UKNNL plays a central role in maintaining the country’s nuclear fuel expertise. It is expanding its support to the development of advanced fuels, including Haleu.

title: Russian Drone Hits Building Storing Spent Nuclear Fuel Near Chornobyl
author: David Dalton
text: Attack was ‘extremely vile’ and deliberate, says Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy

The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) said on Sunday (7 June) it had been informed by Ukraine of a drone attack early this morning on the central spent fuel storage facility within the Chornobyl nuclear power station exclusion zone.

The IAEA said the attack, which took place at about 02:00 local time, caused significant damage to the facility’s fuel reception building – including to the facade, windows and doors – and nearby buildings were also affected by the blast wave.
A fire covering about 40 square metres broke out after the attack and was extinguished, said state nuclear power operator Energoatom. No personnel were injured.
Radiation levels at the facility remain within established limits, Ukraine said. The IAEA team at the Chornobyl site will soon visit the facility to inspect the impact.
Unconfirmed reports said the attack was by a Shahed drone, a type manufactured in both Russia and Iran.

IAEA director-general Rafael Grossi said the incident was “deeply concerning” because it occurred at a facility containing large amounts of nuclear material, held in storage just metres away from the attacked building.

“Attacks on nuclear sites are completely unacceptable and in direct contravention of key nuclear safety principles, notably the Seven Indispensable Pillars for nuclear safety and security during a military conflict, Grossi said.
Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy described the attack as deliberate and “extremely vile”.

“As of now, there is no heightening of radiation safety limits. But there is clearly a heightening of Russia’s already sky-high arrogance,” Zelenskyy said after the attack. “It was [a] critical infrastructure facility. And an extremely vile Russian attack.”

Andrii Sybiha, Ukraine’s foreign minister, posted on X: “This is not the first time Russian forces are putting Ukrainian nuclear facilities at risk. Russia’s nuclear blackmail and threats to nuclear safety are systemic, deliberate, and unacceptable.”
The spent fuel storage facility is about nine miles from the Chornobyl plant that in 1986 was the scene of the world’s worst nuclear accident.

Energoatom said: “The strike on a nuclear infrastructure facility has once again shown the world the true face of the Kremlin regime, which deliberately poses threats to nuclear and radiation safety.”

In February 2025, a Russian attack drone damaged the containment arch, known as the New Safe Confinement, that was built over the Chornobyl reactor that was destroyed in the 1986 explosion and meltdown. Russia denied responsibility.
Kyiv and Moscow have also traded accusations of attacking the Russian-occupied six-unit Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant in south-eastern Ukraine, Europe’s largest.
The IAEA said the attack caused significant damage to the fuel reception building. Courtesy Energoatom.

title: Japan Aims To Replace 14 Ageing Nuclear Reactors By 2050s
author: David Dalton
text: Official target is first released since 2011 Fukushima accident

Japan plans to rebuild between two and five ageing nuclear reactors by the 2040s and as many as 11 to 14 by the 2050s as it aims to secure stable power supply, public broadcaster NHK reported, citing a draft policy presented on 5 June.

The proposal, outlined by the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry (Meti) at a meeting on nuclear policy, reflects a shift towards greater reliance on nuclear energy to help meet rising power demand and reduce costly fuel imports.

It is the first official numerical target for reactor replacement released since the March 2011 accident at the Fukushima-Daiichi nuclear power plant owned and operated by Tokyo Electric Power Company.
By setting a concrete goal, the ministry will make it easier to secure human resources in the nuclear power industry, a statement said.
Meti said it plans to rebuild an additional nine reactors by the 2050s, bringing the total number of reactors subject to replacement to 11-14.

The government’s latest energy plan, adopted in February 2025, calls for nuclear electricity generation to increase from 8.5% in fiscal 2023 to about 20% in fiscal 2040. Renewable energy’s share of electricity production is expected to increase from 22.9% to 40%-50%, with fossil fuels’ share falling from almost 69% to 30%-40%.
Japan has 15 reactor units in commercial operation, while its potential complete fleet has 33 units including 18 units where operations are suspended pending post-Fukushima restart approvals.

The 15 restarted reactors have a combined capacity of 14.6 GW. The restarted units are Onagawa-2, Kashiwazaki Kariwa-6, Mihama-3, Takahama Units 1-4, Ohi Units 3-4, Shimane-2, Ikata-3, Genkai Units 3-4, and Sendai Units 1-2.
Before the Fukushima disaster Japan’s fleet of 54 nuclear plants generated about 30% of the country’s electricity, but were all shut down for safety checks following the accident.
Japan’s prime minister Sanae Takaichi has said she will push for the accelerated revival of nuclear power with reactor restarts key to reducing costly fuel imports.
Units at the Takahama nuclear power station are among those to have restarted since the Fukushima disaster. Courtesy Kansai Electric.

title: Sweden’s Blykalla Applies For Financing For Advanced Nuclear Reactor Park Near Stockholm
author: David Dalton
text: Application first to be submitted under government’s new financing model

Sweden-based advanced nuclear reactor company Blykalla today submitted an application for Swedish government financing for its planned advanced nuclear reactor park in Norrsundet, two hours north of Stockholm.
The proposed advanced nuclear facility in Sweden would be powered by six Sealer reactors, which are Blykalla’s lead-cooled advanced modular reactors (AMRs).

The nuclear reactor park in the municipality of Gävle is intended to have a total installed capacity of up to 330 MW and an estimated annual production of 2.76 TWh, which would make up approximately 13% of Sweden’s target of 2,500 MW of new nuclear power by 2035.

Blykalla said the application is the first to be submitted for advanced nuclear power under a new Swedish financing model, which came into effect on 1 August 2025. It follows submission of an application last month to the Swedish government to build the facility.
“This application is a major milestone toward building the clean baseload power Sweden needs,” said Blykalla chief executive officer Jacob Stedman.

“The new financing model is designed to enable exactly what we plan to build, an advanced nuclear reactor park that can meet Sweden’s rapidly growing electricity needs as industry is electrified and we increasingly rely on a digital infrastructure.
“For our reactor park in Norrsundet, it also means that we can expand supply chains with partners and suppliers, and thus take important steps towards commercial series production.”

According to Blykalla, Sweden is facing a doubling of its electricity demand by 2045, driven by industrial electrification, data centres and AI. Clean and predictable baseload power is central to the Swedish electricity system, and with a new financing model for investments in nuclear power, Sweden has taken a decisive step towards a stable and robust electricity grid, the company said.

The financing model consists of three instruments: government loans, a contract for difference (CfD), and a risk and profit-sharing mechanism. The parameters – particularly interest rate, strike price and contract length – are negotiated project by project and tested by the European Commission.

Blykalla says its Sealer AMR is a small modular reactor (SMR) that uses proven lead-cooling technology. By incorporating its proprietary and patented aluminium alloyed steels into its Sealer reactor, Blykalla has developed an AMR that it says can withstand the corrosive nature of liquid lead, enabling the commercialisation of lead-cooled fast reactors.

AMRs, and lead-cooling in particular, offer significant advantages, including rapid deployment and flexible siting due to their compact design and passive safety features. This enables co-location with industrial facilities, delivering power where and when it’s needed.

Blykalla said the next step in the funding process is to negotiate with the Swedish government about the parameters of the financing model. Parallel applications are underway for permits and the company is cooperating closely with Gävle municipality.

Sweden has six large-scale reactor units in commercial operation at three sites: Forsmark, Oskarshamn and Ringhals. According to International Atomic Energy Agency data, nuclear energy provided 29% of the country’s electricity generation in 2024.

Sweden’s centre-right government made new nuclear power one of its key pledges during campaigning for a general election in 2022. The move reverses a decades-long policy to shut down the country’s ageing reactors and replacing them with renewable energy. Sweden previously operated 12 commercial reactors, but permanently shut down six due to economic factors and shifting political goals.
The government wants to attract more players to build new nuclear in the country by streamlining its licensing process and opening up its coastline to build capacity in the sector.

State-controlled utility Vattenfall has requested state financing to build SMRs near the existing Ringhals nuclear power station. Sweden-based SMR project development company Kärnfull Next has submitted an application for an SMR project in the south of the country.
A rendering of Blykalla’s planned Sealer nuclear plant project in Norrsundet, Sweden. Courtesy Blykalla.

title: Head Of Nuclear Industry Group Calls For Europe To Get On Right Track With Climate Target
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Brussels conference told reactors can deliver and are needed alongside renewables

The European Commission’s commitment to technology neutrality will be judged by how it designs the rules behind its 2040 climate target to reduce net greenhouse gas emissions by 90%, the president of Brussels-based industry group nucleareurope Xavier Ursat has said.

Ursat, also an EDF senior executive vice-president in charge of innovation, corporate social responsibility and strategy, told the nucleareurope conference in Brussels this week that “the first demonstration of the sincerity of the European Commission” would be the shape of the 2040 target.
If it remained a renewables target rather than one built around clean energy, “we are on the wrong track”, he said, adding the measure should be the share of clean energy in each member state.
Ursat said nuclear “is not a religion, it’s an energy, but it’s first an industry that delivered when built in series, faster and cheaper with repetition”.

The Dutch state secretary for climate policy and green growth, Jo-Annes de Bat, struck a similar note, telling the conference that for the Netherlands “this is not a discussion about renewables versus nuclear. We need both”.

The focus should not be on renewable targets alone but on a clean, reliable and affordable system, de Bat said, and member states should have “flexibility to choose the technology that best fits their energy system”.
The Dutch government was taking the next step towards new large-scale reactors and exploring small modular reactors, he said.
Cristian Bușoi, state secretary at Romania's energy ministry, made the same argument, saying that in Romania, as in many European countries, the question was “not nuclear versus renewables” but both.
He said he saw no contradiction between the EU’s renewable energy rules and a push for greater electrification, and that nuclear was low-carbon and would help meet the 2030 and 2040 targets.
The EU wrote a binding target to cut net emissions by 90% by 2040 relative to 1990 levels into its climate law in March, but the legislation on how to deliver still needs to be drafted.

The commission opened consultations in March on a renewable energy framework for the next decade, a successor to the Renewable Energy Directive due to be proposed by the end of 2026, with the consultation period closing on 12 June.

The nuclear industry and several member states have already called on the Commission to make the post-2030 framework technology-neutral, warning that excluding any clean-energy source would undermine competitiveness and affordability.

Ursat also called on the commission to speed up, saying Europe was competing with countries able to move “two or three years faster”, not because of construction times but because of financing and regulatory procedures.

He put the scale of the sector in Europe at more than 5,000 companies and around 900,000 jobs, a figure he said could reach 1.5 million within a decade, and said nucleareurope had a responsibility, alongside the commission, to strengthen the European nuclear supply chain.
*Updated 9 June 2026: Cristian Bușoi is one of three state secretaries at Romania's energy ministry. A previous version of the article erroneously referred to him as Romania's energy minister.
Xavier Ursat speaking at the nucleareurope 2026 conference in Brussels. Image courtesy nucleareurope/Pauline Leclère.

title: Russia And Uzbekistan Begin Construction Of First ‘Integrated’ Nuclear Power Plant
author: David Dalton
text: Facility will combine both large-scale VVER-1000 reactors and smaller RITM-200N units
Russia and Uzbekistan on 4 June began construction of an “integrated” nuclear power plant in Uzbekistan, the first of its kind in ​post-Soviet Central Asia, the Kremlin said.

Russian president Vladimir Putin and Uzbek president Shavkat Mirziyoyev oversaw the start of the construction via video link from St ​Petersburg where they held talks on the sidelines of Putin’s ​annual economic forum, the Kremlin said.
The ⁠project is in Uzbekistan’s central-eastern Jizzakh Region, which borders both ​Tajikistan and Kazakhstan.

The project, being developed by Uzbekistan’s state nuclear project company Uzatom and Russia’s state nuclear corporation Rosatom, will include two high-capacity power units based on Russia’s VVER-1000 Generation III+ reactors and two power units with small-scale RITM-200N reactors, each with a capacity of 55 MW.
Once fully operational, the facility will generate approximately 17.2 billion kWh per year, accounting for up to 14% of Uzbekistan’s total energy consumption, Rosatom said.
Alexey Likhachev, director-general of Rosatom, said the integrated model will provide baseload power through high-capacity generation, while peak demand surges will be offset by smaller capacities.
“The shared plant infrastructure, which will be used jointly by both categories of units, will create conditions for resource conservation during construction and operation,” he said.

The RITM-200N is an adaptation of marine technology for land-based deployment. RITM-200 reactors, on which the RITM-200N is based, have been used on Russian icebreakers. Since 2012, 10 RITM-200 reactors have been manufactured with the first three already in operation on vessels in the western Arctic.
Uzbekistan, a country of 33 million people, is looking to nuclear power as a low-carbon energy source to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and boost electricity generating capacity.

There are no nuclear power plants in any of the five ex-Soviet Central Asian republics, although Uzbekistan and its neighbour Kazakhstan, both uranium producers, have long said their growing economies need them.
The project was officially started by video link from St ​Petersburg where the presidents of Russia and Uzbekistan were holding talks. Courtesy IAEA.

title: Nuclear Essential For Europe, But More Work Needed To Reduce Reliance On Russia, Says Energy Commissioner
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Dan Jorgensen underlines scale of investment challenge facing sector

Nuclear is essential to Europe's energy autonomy, but the bloc must do further work to replace Russian fuel-cycle services such as enrichment and conversion before nuclear can play that role, European commissioner for energy and housing Dan Jorgensen told a conference in Brussels.

Speaking at the Brussels-based nuclear industry group nucleareurope’s 2026 conference on 1 June, Jorgensen said safety and security of supply were the “foundational blocks” of the sector, and that diversification was “a long-standing EU policy”.

Jorgensen described a mix of renewables and nuclear as central to Europe’s energy autonomy, saying it offered the chance to free the bloc from “the volatility of fossil fuels” and to secure “a level of autonomy never before experienced in Europe,” powering households and businesses with “homegrown and affordable energy”.
“To deliver on these goals, Europe needs nuclear,” he said.

Jorgensen said that through the REPowerEU
programme the EU had made progress in diversifying nuclear fuel supplies for Russian-designed reactors in Europe. “However, as you know, more work is needed,” he said.

Further efforts were needed to obtain spare parts and to develop alternatives in nuclear fuel services, including for enrichment and conversion, he said. The commission was working with member states and industry to address these issues and to ensure that the phaseout of Russian nuclear supplies was “gradual and successful”.
On safety, he said Europe had “an impressive record” and needed to maintain its global leadership, upholding the highest standards and aligning with the internationally agreed safety framework.

He called for further steps in the safe and permanent disposal of radioactive waste, saying the EU could become “a model of scientific responsibility, public trust, and sustainability” by leading on deep geological repositories.

The REPowerEU roadmap, adopted in May 2025, set out plans for a gradual removal of Russian oil, gas and nuclear energy and required member states to submit national diversification plans by March 2026.

But the commission has consistently framed the nuclear part of its Russian energy phaseout as more complex than gas or oil and no binding targets have been introduced despite some discussion between EU institutions.

Five EU countries operate Russia-designed VVER units: Bulgaria, Czechia, Finland, Hungary, and Slovakia. Utilities in all five countries have signed contracts for non-Russian reactor fuel since 2022, and most have gradually begun loading non-Russian fuel assemblies.

Russia accounted for around 23% of the EU’s enriched uranium supply in 2024, down from 38% in 2023, according to Euratom Supply Agency data. New enrichment capacity in Europe is being developed by European companies Urenco and Orano but is expected around 2027.
Jorgensen also repeated the findings of the commission’s 2025 Pinc nuclear illustrative programme, which he said confirmed the scale of the investment challenge facing the sector.

Under a base case of about 109 GW of installed capacity by 2050, total investment needs were estimated at around €241bn ($280bn), he said. The 2050 scenarios ranged from 70 GW to 144 GW, with member states able to choose a combination of lifetime extensions, new large-scale reactors and the gradual deployment of small modular reactors (SMR) and advanced modular reactors (AMR).

On financing, Jorgensen said the commission had committed €200m in guarantees to de-risk investment in first-of-a-kind SMR and AMR installations, and that its proposal for the next multiannual financial framework allocated €6.7bn to the Euratom research and training programme.

He said the commission’s SMR strategy, was built on the European Industrial Alliance on SMRs, which now brings together around 400 members with the aim of deploying Europe’s first SMR project by the early 2030s.

The strategy was structured around “focus, scale, and coordination,” he said, concentrating EU support on a limited number of the most promising designs. Member states’ plans put EU SMR capacity at between 17 GW and 53 GW by 2050, according to PINC.
However, the president of nucleareurope, Xavier Ursat, told the conference that the commission's commitment to low-carbon technology neutrality would be judged by the shape of its 2040 target.

Ursat, also an EDF senior executive vice-president in charge of innovation, corporate social responsibility and strategy, said the first demonstration of “the sincerity of the European Commission” would be whether that target was built around clean energy or renewables.
If it remained a renewables target, “we are on the wrong track”, he said, arguing the measure should be the share of clean energy in each country.
He said Europe was competing with “countries able to move two or three years faster”, referring to financing and regulatory procedures before actual construction.

In March the EU adopted a binding target to cut net emissions by 90% by 2040 on the path to climate neutrality by 2050. But the focus is expected to shift to the actual set of binding rules the commission will propose post-2030 to help meet these targets.
The nuclear industry and several member states are pressing for technology-neutral rules that treat all low-carbon sources equally rather than favouring renewables alone.
Dan Jorgensen told the conference that to deliver on its goals, Europe needs nuclear. Courtesy nucleareurope.

title: Kenya Responds To Protests With Plans For Educational And Engagement Campaign Over Nuclear Plans
author: Nigel Davies
text: African country planning a 2,000 MW plant on shores of Lake Victoria in Siaya County

Kenya’s Nuclear Power and Energy Agency (NuPEA) has promised it will begin a thorough educational and engagement campaign on the benefits of building a nuclear power station on the banks of Lake Victoria.
Kenya plans to build a 2,000 MW nuclear plant in Siaya County, in the west of the country, with construction pencilled to begin in 2027 and delivery of first power by 2034.
However, recent protests in Sakwa, Siaya County over the plans, led to NuPEA saying that the plant would not go ahead without broad local support.

In a statement, Justus Wabuyabo, chief executive officer of NuPEA, said the agency heard and respected the voices of the people of Siaya. “Public participation is not a mere procedural formality. It is a constitutional right and a technical necessity for a successful national nuclear programme.”

In April, Kenyan president William Ruto confirmed plans to build a 2,000 MW plant in Siaya. The country forecasts power capacity to grow from 3,300 MW to 10,000 MW in the next five to seven years, with 3,000 MW coming from nuclear.

“No infrastructure will be built without the broad, informed consent of the community. We are fully committed to executing a robust, transparent, and multi-layered educational campaign to address all anxieties regarding safety, livelihoods, and land,” said Wabuyabo.

Nuclear energy is gathering increasing interest across Africa. According to the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) a high case scenario would see nuclear capacity triple from 2024 to 2030 in the continent and sixteen-fold by 2050.
The IAEA also said in a report in 2025 that small modular reactors might prove attractive in Africa to reach remote areas where grid expansion wasn’t feasible.

The IAEA says that around 500 million people do not have access to electricity in Africa with the continent reliant on fossil fuels. In order to improve energy security and lower emissions, more African states are looking to install nuclear power.

South Africa is the only African country with an operational nuclear station, at Koeberg, near Cape Town. Egypt is building a four-unit plant at El Dabaa, expected to be ready by 2028. Ghana, Nigeria and Kenya plan to adopt nuclear technology, and 10 other countries are considering it.
Last year, the IAEA and World Bank also announced an agreement to cooperate on the development and financing of nuclear power for developing countries.
Courtesy IAEA.

title: Tepco Announces Start Of Spent Fuel Removal From Fukushima-Daiichi Unit 2
author: David Dalton
text: Major step forward for decommissioning, but operation is one of most technically challenging at Japan nuclear site

The long-running decommissioning effort at Japan’s Fukushima-Daiichi nuclear power station has reached an important milestone with the start of removal of nuclear fuel from the spent fuel pool of Unit 2.
The operation is one of the most technically challenging phases of the site’s decades-long cleanup programme following the catastrophic 2011 earthquake, tsunami and nuclear accident.
Owner and operator Tokyo Electric Power Company (Tepco) intends to complete the removal of all fuel assemblies from the Unit 2 pool by fiscal year 2028.

The Unit 2 reactor’s spent fuel pool currently stores 587 spent fuel assemblies, which are highly radioactive, and 28 unused fuel assemblies, according to Tepco. The unused fuel is being removed first because it poses a lower risk in the event of an accident.

Radiation levels at the Unit 2 reactor building are still high after the nuclear fuel in the reactor melted down in the March 2011 accident. Radiation on the fifth floor, where the fuel pool is located, measures as high as 3 to 5 millisieverts per hour, making it difficult for workers to stay there for a long time.

Tepco is using a remotely controlled crane to remove the fuel assemblies, which are placed one by one in a transport container called a cask inside the pool. The cask will be lifted out of the pool and then lowered onto a trailer from a platform installed next to the building.
The trailer carrying the cask will move to a common pool at the plant to cool and store the fuel.

Since spent fuel continues to generate heat, it must be continuously cooled. At the time of the accident at the plant, the loss of power prevented the pools from being cooled, so Tepco injected seawater.

As the common pool has limited capacity, Tepco plans to transfer fuel that no longer generates significant heat to containers called dry casks, which can be cooled by air, in order to secure storage space in the common pool.
The Fukushima-Daiichi decommissioning programme remains one of the largest and most complex nuclear cleanup projects ever undertaken. The total cost has been estimated at $76bn (€65bn).

Significant progress has been made in stabilising the site since the 2011 disaster, but the removal of spent and unused nuclear fuel from reactor buildings remains a top priority due to the potential safety risks posed by fuel stored above ground in spent fuel pools.

Spent fuel has already been removed from pools at Units 3, 4 and 6 at the six-unit facility, with removal work underway at Unit 5. Tepco has said removal of spent nuclear fuel from the Unit 1 pool is scheduled to begin between 2027 and 2028.
Tepco is using a remotely controlled crane to remove the fuel assemblies. Courtesy Tepco.

title: Lloyds Register Meeting Highlights Absence Of International Framework For Maritime Nuclear
author: David Dalton
text: Participants told regulation must move in parallel with technology development

A meeting of senior leaders from maritime, the nuclear industry and international regulation has highlighted the absence of an established international framework tailored to civil nuclear applications at sea.

Participants at the Lloyds Register nuclear roundtable in Athens, Greece, highlighted the mounting interest in nuclear energy for the maritime industry from governments, including the government of Greece, and operators looking for scalable, zero-emission propulsion options.
But participants stressed that regulation must move in parallel with technology development, rather than waiting for mature designs to emerge.
Lloyds Register said the closed-door gathering was convened to examine what needs to happen next to make nuclear propulsion a viable option for commercial shipping.
The session gathered around 20 senior representatives from shipowners, regulators, reactor developers and industry bodies, alongside invited observers.

Participants examined how regulatory frameworks can evolve to support controlled demonstration without compromising safety, how commercial models might develop to manage the high upfront costs, and where nuclear may have advantages over other zero-carbon fuel options.

The economic case for nuclear also came under scrutiny. Participants explored potential cost drivers, investment models and areas of disruption across ship design, operations and infrastructure. While recognising the significant barriers to entry, the meeting acknowledged that early adopters could gain a competitive advantage as technologies mature, Lloyds Register said.

The meeting came as the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) announced its Atomic Technologies Licensed for Applications at Sea (Atlas) initiative to support the maritime industry’s exploration of small modular reactors (SMRs) to power civilian ships and to provide offshore energy, as operators consider alternative fuels and seek to strengthen long-term energy security.
The initiative will be officially unveiled at an IAEA ministerial-level event hosted by the US in Washington on August 26-27.
The IAEA said nuclear energy is being explored as a safe, viable option for commercial shipping, offering the potential for higher-speed maritime transport without the need for frequent refuelling.
At the same time, innovations such as floating nuclear power plants provide versatile energy sources through advanced SMRs and could deliver energy to coastal or remote communities and industry.

Last year Lloyd’s Register published a guidance document, Navigating Nuclear Energy in Maritime, providing what it said is the first roadmap for the use of nuclear technology in commercial shipping and offshore industries, but warning of “considerable challenges”.
Nuclear energy is being explored as a safe, viable option for commercial shipping. Courtesy Maersk.

title: New York Takes ‘Significant’ New Steps Towards Governor’s Plans For Nuclear Deployment
author: David Dalton
text: Kathy Hochul has set statewide goal to add 5 GW of reactor capacity to grid

New York state governor Kathy Hochul took two “significant” steps on 2 June towards her goal of deploying new commercial nuclear reactors, announcing solicitations for work force training and for a developer to start construction of at least one new reactor by 2032.

The state-owned New York Power Authority (NYPA) will spend up to $40m (€34m) to develop training programmes for a wide variety of nuclear jobs, ranging from welders and pipefitters to engineers and radiation protection technicians, Hochul announced.
The power authority issued a request for applications from colleges, trade unions, community-based organisations or others interested in providing the training.

NYPA also issued a request for qualifications (RFQ) for firms who are interested in building 1 GW (1,000 MW) of new nuclear power that Hochul has ordered the power authority to develop. The document states that firms must be able to begin construction no later than 2032 so they would qualify for federal tax credits.
The RFQ follows on a request for information last year, to which 23 parties responded.

Hochul has set a statewide goal to add 5 GW of nuclear power to the state electric grid, to more than double nuclear capacity from 3.4 GW to 8.4 GW. Of that, NYPA has been directed to build at least 1 GW.
The governor said nuclear provides the base of her “all of the above” energy strategy, which favours power sources that do not emit greenhouse gases.

“The solicitations announced today will help ensure New York is poised to lead the nation in new nuclear development that, along with renewables, will provide needed power in the face of increasing demand,” Hochul said in a news release.

In her 2025 State of the State address, Hochul announced the development of a master plan for advanced nuclear development in New York. The New York State Energy Research and Development Authority (Nyserda), together with the Department of Public Service other state agencies, is leading the development of the master plan. As a first step, Nyserda published a blueprint for advanced nuclear energy technologies that sets out the scope of issues to be considered throughout the master plan process.

The development of the master plan will provide a framework for in-depth examination into the key issues raised by the blueprint to develop recommendations for implementation of advanced nuclear technologies in New York State. The master plan development process is expected to conclude with publication by the end of 2026.
In January Hochul’s office said 23 developers and partners had expressed interest in the NYPA plans to develop a 1 GW nuclear plant in the state.
Among those to express interest in collaborating with the project were Acccenture, Aecom, GE Hitachi Nuclear Energy, Holtec, NextEra Energy Resources, Rolls Royce and Westinghouse.

In addition, eight communities expressed their interest in hosting the project. These were Broome County, Jefferson County, Oswego County, Schuyler County, St. Lawrence County, Wayne County, City of Dunkirk and RED-Rochester, which manages energy use at Eastman Business Park, near the Ginna nuclear station.
New York has about 3.4 GW of nuclear power in operation through its Ginna, Nine Mile Point and FitzPatrick plants, which have four units between them and are all run by utility company Constellation.
In December 2025, NYPA signed a memorandum of understanding with Ontario Power Generation to collaborate on the development of both large-scale and small modular reactors in New York.
New York has about 3.4 GW of nuclear power in operation through its Ginna (pictured), Nine Mile Point and FitzPatrick plants. Courtesy Constellation.

title: Slovenia’s Jožef Stefan Institute Awarded Golden Order Of Merit As Triga Reactor Reaches Landmark
author: David Dalton
text: Country’s president says facility serves as ‘a guide in shaping our nuclear future’

Slovenia has marked the 60th year of operation of the Triga research reactor with a ceremony at which Slovenia’s president Nataša Pirc Musar awarded the Golden Order of Merit to the Jožef Stefan Institute.

The order was awarded to the institute for its exceptional contribution to the development of Slovenian science, nuclear safety, energy independence and the international recognition of Slovenia, a statement said.
The Triga reactor is at the Jožef Stefan Institute near the Slovenian capital of Ljubljana. It first reached criticality on 31 May 1966.

Triga was designed as a facility for research, education and practical applications. The reactor is owned by Slovenia’s Ministry of Higher Education, Science and Innovation, and operated by the Jožef Stefan Institute, Slovenia’s leading scientific research institute.

Pirc Musar said: “Sixty years of the operation of the Triga reactor is a milestone that underscores the exceptional importance of scientific progress and investment in research. At the same time, it serves as a guide in shaping our nuclear future.”

During its first decades of operation, the reactor has played a pivotal role in educating nuclear scientists in Slovenia. It served as a training ground for generations of researchers, engineers, and operators working in nuclear energy, medicine, radiation protection and other fields. It contributed to the development of neutron activation analysis, neutron radiography and the production of radioactive isotopes for medicine and industry. It also served as an important hub of knowledge, giving rise to numerous fundamental research and technological achievements.

Jožef Stefan Institute director Leon Cizelj, who also serves as president of NucNet, said that in 60 years of operation of the Triga reactor, the Jožef Stefan Institute has experienced unprecedented development.

He said: “Today, we are an internationally renowned research institution exploring numerous areas that are not even directly connected to nuclear energetics: from artificial intelligence and new materials to biotechnology and physics, energy, environment, and robotics.”

The Jožef Stefan Institute said Triga contributes to all the key elements of the institute’s operations, including research infrastructure, achievements in science, collaboration with the industry, integration of various disciplines, education and training new generations of researchers and experts, and science communication and engaging the public in understanding the technologies of the future.

“The fact that the reactor along with all its research and experiments continues to be relevant today is because it is constantly opening up to new areas, from education and isotope production to the current highly specialised research,” the institute said. “Today, Triga is focused on cutting-edge research and has a distinctly international role.”

Head of the Triga reactor, Anže Jazbec, said: “We participate in projects such as upgrades at Cern and the development of the Iter fusion reactor, but we have also established ourselves as a leading facility for neutron irradiation and the testing of detectors and electronic components under extreme conditions.

“We are also a key partner to the French CEA [French Alternative Energies and Atomic Energy Commission]. Yet, what remains crucial today is the same as it was 60 years ago: knowledge, teamwork, and responsibility. This ensures the reactor remains safe, reliable, and scientifically relevant even today, and provides a solid foundation for its further development.”

The Triga reactor is part of a family of research reactors renowned for their inherent safety and exceptional robustness. The fuel, made of uranium alloy and zirconium hydride, enables a fast negative feedback loop, meaning that the reactor remains safe even during rapid changes in power.

It has a nominal thermal power of 250 kW, and a unique capability for pulsed operation, during which the power can briefly increase to 1 GW. These characteristics have made Triga an ideal tool for experimental reactor physics, materials testing, and education for decades.

Earlier this year Slovenia said financing conditions for a new reactor unit at the Krško nuclear power station look favourable as the country begins planning for the potential unit before a national referendum on its development no later than early 2028.

The Slovenian government said it will proceed with a national spatial plan (NSP) for the plant, which would provide all the details regarding the location of the new reactor, financing, technology and suppliers.

Krško is owned equally by Croatian utility Hrvatska Elektroprivreda and Slovenia’s state-owned power generator, GEN Group, the parent company of power company Gen Energija. However, current plans for a new Krško reactor are being pursued solely by Slovenia.
Krško supplies around 20% of Slovenia’s electricity needs and 16% of Croatia’s.
Slovenia’s president Nataša Pirc Musar arrives at the Jožef Stefan Institute near Ljubljana. Courtesy Jožef Stefan Institute/Marjan Verc.
Slovenia’s president Nataša Pirc Musar presents the Golden Order of Merit Jožef Stefan Institute director Leon Cizelj. Courtesy Jožef Stefan Institute/Marjan Verc.

title: Eden Radioisotopes Files Construction Permit Application For New Mexico Facility
author: David Dalton
text: Company will use reactor concept optimised for high-yield production
US-based Eden Radioisotopes has filed a construction permit application with the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission for an isotope production complex near Eunice, New Mexico.
This purpose-built facility is designed to produce a domestic source of life-saving medical isotopes – something currently unavailable at scale in the US.

The company proposes to use a small, nonpower, open-pool reactor design that is optimised for high-yield isotope production. The reactor will use low-enriched uranium and operate at 1.8 MWt. Eden expects to operate it for 22 hours per day, using the downtime to replace targets.

Eden will use an “all-target” reactor concept exclusively licensed from Sandia National Laboratories and optimised for high-yield isotope production. The company said the technology generates no spent fuel, and with a co-located processing facility, improves the domestic supply of isotopes for US patients.

According to Eden’s NRC regulatory engagement plan, the new facility will produce molybdenum-99 (Mo-99), iodine-131 (I-131), and xenon-133 (Xe-133) through the fission process and other isotopes, such as lutetium-177 (Lu-177), through neutron activation.

When approved, the Eden facility will be positioned to deliver up to 50% of global demand for Mo-99, the isotope behind more than 40,000 diagnostic imaging procedures performed in the US each day. It would also be a key producer of more than 3.5 million annual doses of isotopes such as Lu-177, an advanced form of targeted cancer treatment.

The US imports 100% of its Mo-99 from aging foreign reactors. Because medical isotopes decay within hours or days of production, they cannot be stockpiled. Any disruption outside of the US can result in immediate cancellation of patient procedures domestically.

Eden said in a statement that the shortage has drawn federal attention. Congress passed the 2012 American Medical Isotope Production Act, which promotes the development of a reliable domestic supply. However, more than a decade later, the US still lacks sufficient domestic production capacity for both diagnostic and therapeutic isotopes.

“For decades, the American medical system has operated at the mercy of a fragile, foreign-dependent supply chain,” said Eden chief executive officer Carrie Freeman. “Eden will permanently reshore this capability – establishing a domestic supply of Mo-99 and Lu-177 and bringing proven nuclear technology directly to the fight against cancer and heart disease.”
A rendering of the planned Eden Radioisotopes facility in New Mexico. Courtesy Eden Radioisotopes.

title: US DOE Approves PDSA For Last Energy Pilot Nuclear Reactor At Texas University
author: David Dalton
text: PWR-5 will act as ‘direct bridge’ to PWR-20 commercial unit

US-based advanced nuclear technology company Last Energy announced that the US Department of Energy (DOE) has approved the company’s preliminary documented safety analysis (PDSA) for its PWR-5 pilot reactor at Texas A&M-Rellis university.
The PDSA establishes the preliminary safety basis for Last Energy’s reactor, facility, and planned operations, marking a critical step in the DOE authorisation process.
The approval means Texas-headquartered Last Energy advances towards DOE authorisation to bring nuclear fuel on site, demonstrate criticality, and operate the reactor.
“PDSA approval is a major step in moving the PWR-5 from construction into operations,” said Adam Lenarz, vice-president of development at Last Energy.

“Our team has advanced building construction, equipment procurement, fuel fabrication, and safety documentation in parallel, reflecting the disciplined execution this project requires. With this milestone complete, we are focused on finalising the DSA, the final safety analysis needed to secure DOE authorisation for fuel receipt, criticality, and reactor operations.”

In August 2025, Last Energy was selected to participate in the DOE’s Reactor Pilot Program. The programme is designed to accelerate reactor demonstration by authorising test reactors through DOE’s process.

Since then, Last Energy signed its land lease with Texas A&M-Rellis, began construction in 2026, procured and delivered key reactor components to site, and advanced construction of the reactor building. Last Energy said its reactor fuel has been manufactured.

The PWR-5 uses the same physical reactor geometry as the company’s commercial PWR-20, with reduced fuel enrichment scaled for 5 MW of electrical output. The pilot reactor will demonstrate low-power criticality before progressing to electricity generation designed for commercial deployment.

The PWR-5 pilot project is a “direct bridge” to Last Energy’s commercial PWR-20 deployment model, the company said. The PWR-20 is a 20 MW micro modular nuclear plant designed for factory fabrication, standard road transport, rapid on-site assembly, and 24/7 baseload power delivery to industrial customers, data centres, and other high-energy users.

Last Energy said it intentionally uses proven pressurised water reactor technology, standard low-enriched uranium fuel, and existing supply chains to reduce technical risk and accelerate project delivery.

In February the Texas A&M University System selected an additional four companies to explore developing advanced nuclear power reactors on the Rellis campus, about 15 km west of Texas in Brazos County.
Ultimately, the goal is to create an “energy proving ground” at the campus that can serve as a test bed for cutting-edge energy technologies.
Construction progress on Last Energy’s PWR-5 pilot at the Texas A&M–Rellis Campus. Courtesy Last Energy.

title: Fulcrum Announces Agreement To Advance Blue Castle SMR Project In Utah Using Holtec Technology
author: David Dalton
text: Proposed multi-unit facility could add 2,200 MW of installed electrical capacity

US-based Fulcrum Point Holdings has announced an agreement with Blue Castle Holdings to advance the existing Blue Castle nuclear project near the city of Green River in Utah through the next stages of site development, NRC licensing and eventual reactor deployment.
Fulcrum Point, headquartered in Salt Lake City, Utah, develops, finances and operates energy generation assets with a focus on power projects in the eight states of the Mountain West region.

The company said in a statement that the project represents a significant economic development opportunity for the region, with the expectation to support construction jobs, long-term skilled energy sector jobs, and more demand for energy as Utah grows.

Fulcrum Point will work with Blue Castle using SMR-300 nuclear plant
technology and equipment to be provided by Holtec International.

Holtec welcomed the announcement and said the SMR-300 stands out with its advanced design rooted in 80 years of proven pressurised water reactor technology. Holtec said the SMR-300 offers a unique optional air-cooled condenser system, enabling operation in arid environments like Utah, where water resources are scarce. This flexibility means SMR-300 can effectively operate in desert climates, providing a reliable and environmentally responsible energy source.
Blue Castle Holdings is a Utah-based energy infrastructure development company focused on bringing commercial nuclear power to the Mountain West.
The proposed multi-unit Blue Castle nuclear project would increase the electricity generated in Utah by up to 2,200 MW of installed electrical capacity.
An artist’s rendering of Holtec SMR-300 nuclear plant using air-cooled condenser technology. Courtesy Holtec International.

title: Nuclear Fuel: The Five Companies Chosen To Negotiate Receipt Of Surplus US Plutonium
author: David Dalton
text: Aim of federal-backed programme is to fabricate fuel for advanced nuclear technologies

Nuclear start-ups Oklo and Flibe Energy both announced this week that they have been selected by the US Department of Energy for advanced negotiations under the DOE’s surplus plutonium utilisation programme, which aims to make surplus US plutonium available to the nuclear industry for advanced reactor fuels.

The American Nuclear Society said that according to multiple reports, three other companies – Exodys Energy, Shine Technologies, and Standard Nuclear – have also been selected for advanced negotiations under the programme, which is being led by the DOE’s Office of Nuclear Energy.

The DOE established the programme last year with a request for applications from prospective companies interested in receiving almost 20 tonnes of DOE-owned plutonium materials for “recycling, processing, and manufacturing” into nuclear fuel for advanced reactors.

The programme follows president Trump’s Executive Order 14302, ‘Reinvigorating the Nuclear Base’, which ordered the DOE to halt its Biden-era “dilute and dispose program” and to “establish a program to dispose of surplus plutonium by processing and making it available to industry in a form that can be utilized for the fabrication of fuel for advanced nuclear technologies”.

In 2024, the DOE’s National Nuclear Security Administration issued a decision to dispose of up to 34 tonnes of surplus defence-related plutonium at the Waste Isolation Pilot Plant in New Mexico using a “dilute-and-dispose” strategy. Also known as plutonium downblending, the strategy was adopted after the cancellation of the DOE’s mixed oxide (MOX) fuel project in 2018.
The DOE has declared it has about 61.5 tonnes of weapons-grade plutonium as surplus to national security needs.

On 26 May 26, Oklo announced that its selection for surplus plutonium negotiations with the DOE supports the company’s “broader fuel strategy, which includes multiple pathways to source fuel to support advanced reactor deployment while domestic enrichment and fuel infrastructure continue to scale”.

“Fuel supply constraints are a key throttle to advanced reactor development,” said Oklo chief executive officer Jacob DeWitte. “This program creates a pathway to use existing surplus material as bridge fuel for advanced reactors to bring more reactors on line sooner. Material that has been set aside for disposal can instead be converted into fuel to produce electricity through fission.”
Oklo said it would work in partnership with Newcleo, a Europe-based developer of advanced reactors and MOX nuclear fuel, on the programme.

Alabama-based Flibe Energy, which announced on 27 May that it was selected for negotiations by the DOE, said the programme complements the company’s study of the use of electrochemical methods to process spent nuclear fuel.

Flibe, along with Oklo, Shine, Alpha Nur, and Curio Solutions, was one recipient of a total of $19m (€16.3m) awarded by the DOE in February for research and development of spent fuel recycling technologies.
Flibe also said the surplus plutonium is ideal for the lithium fluoride thorium reactor technology being developed by the company.
A rendering of a planned Oklo nuclear fuel facility. Courtesy Oklo.

title: Russia Ships First Reactor Unit For Far East Floating Nuclear Plant
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Rosatom hails significant milestone in small-scale nuclear energy programme

Russian state-owned nuclear corporation Rosatom announced it has completed manufacturing and shipped the first RITM-200S small reactor unit for a new floating nuclear power unit being built for industrial operations in Russia’s Far East.
Rosatom described the move as a significant milestone in the development of its small-scale nuclear energy programme.

A statement said the reactor was produced at the ZiO-Podolsk plant near Moscow, part of Rosatom’s machine-building division. It will be installed on a lead floating power unit known as PEB-106 (Floating Power Unit-106).
Rosatom said completion of the reactor allows the project to move to the next construction stage, including installation of power equipment inside the vessel hull.
The floating power units are being built to supply electricity to the Baimsky copper mining cluster in the Chukotka region.
Each PEB-106 barge will house two RITM-200S reactors, each with an electrical output of 58 MWe, Rosatom said.
The RITM-200S is derived from the RITM-200 reactor used on Russia’s latest generation of nuclear icebreakers.

The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) small modular reactor catalogue describes the RITM-200 family as using an integrated reactor layout, with key primary circuit equipment arranged in or directly around the reactor vessel, making the unit more compact than loop-type marine reactor designs.

Igor Kotov, head of Rosatom's machine-building division, said the reactor completed for PEB-106 was the 14th RITM unit to be built by the division. A further 14 RITM-200 reactor units for icebreakers and floating power units are currently at various stages of manufacture at the division's facilities, he said.

According to project materials shared with the IAEA by Rosatom in 2023, the floating power unit programme for the Baimsky mining project began in 2021 with the signing of an agreement with operator GDK Baimskaya.
Detailed design approval followed in 2022 and construction of two hulls started in China later that year.
According to the materials, commissioning of the first two floating PEB-106 plants is planned for 2027, followed by a third plant in 2028 and a fourth in 2032.

In 2020, Russia was first in the world to commission a floating nuclear power plant, the Akademik Lomonosov, which supplies energy to consumers in the remote city of Pevek in Chukotka. The plant has two 35-MW KLT-40S commercial reactor units onboard.
The 55-MW RITM-200 design is a successor of the KLT-40S and is being developed for both maritime and land-based deployment.

Rosatom plants to deploy the first commercial land-based RITM-200N reactor in 2028 near Ust-Kuyga, Yakutia, 4,000 km to the east of Moscow in the country’s Far East. In 2024, Russia and Uzbekistan signed a protocol for the start of work on a project to build a nuclear station that would house six RITM-200N units.
The reactor will be used to supply electricity to the copper mining industry. Courtesy Rosatom.

title: No Fundamental Barriers To Floating Nuclear Power Plants In Greece, Says Thinktank
author: David Dalton
text: Challenge to deployment ‘is not one of feasibility’

There are no fundamental barriers to deployment of floating nuclear power plants (FNPPs) in Greece, but clearer assessment and regulatory pathways are needed, including coordination across maritime, nuclear and energy authorities, according to a report.

The report, published by the Deon Policy Institute, a US-based thinktank founded by Greek academics, entrepreneurs, and professionals, suggests that the challenge to deployment in Greece is not one of feasibility, but of framework development.

“Policy, legal and regulatory frameworks in Greece do not yet substantively address nuclear energy or FNPP deployment, reflecting a broader gap in European energy and maritime policy discussions,” the report concludes.
It says there are no major technical barriers to FNPP deployment given the maturity of the technology. However, there is a need for the development of local value chains and workforce capability.

The report notes that social acceptance of nuclear energy remains low in Greece compared with other countries, even though FNPPs are perceived more positively, implying a need for further education and engagement with both the broader public and key stakeholders.
It says: “Given Greece’s long maritime heritage, developed port infrastructure and reinvigorated shipbuilding industry, the potential for deploying FNPPs warrants consideration.
“FNPPs are also compatible with Greece’s geography and energy markets, given the large number of inhabited islands, the increasing need for desalination and the country’s climate goals.”
Georgios Laskaris, a nuclear physicist who is president of Deon Policy Institute, said the study shows that FNPPs are not a distant or purely theoretical option for Greece.

He said: “No fundamental technical or institutional barriers were identified. The real challenge is building the policy, regulatory, financial and social foundations needed for responsible assessment.
“For Greece, FNPPs sit at the intersection of energy security, decarbonisation, maritime capability and industrial policy.”
Greece has no nuclear power plants and the 5 MW Greek Research Reactor-1 (GRR-1) at the National Centre of Scientific Research is currently licensed for extended shutdown.

In 2022 Bulgaria said it had begun negotiations with Greece for the potential construction of a new nuclear power station in Bulgaria which would supply electricity to both countries, but progress on the project seems to have been limited.
The bulk of Greece’s electricity is generated from natural gas, followed by renewables, but the country also traditionally imports electricity from Bulgaria.
The Paris-based Nuclear Energy Agency has said nuclear energy is not considered as an option for Greece “in the foreseeable future”.
The report says floating nuclear power plants could serve Greece’s large number of inhabited islands. Courtesy Visit Greece/Greece Government.

title: Advanced Nuclear Startup Newcleo To Go Public Through Blank-Cheque Deal
author: David Dalton
text: Merger will support European company’s push into US market
Nuclear power developer Newcleo said on 27 May that it plans to go public through a merger with a blank-cheque company* in a deal valuing it at about $2.4bn (€2.06bn).
The Paris-based company, which operates in seven countries, said the merger would support its entry into the US power market and fund existing projects in Europe.
In a statement Newcleo said it generated approximately $80m in revenue, other income and financial income in 2024 from its nuclear equipment supply chain operating companies.

Newcleo has made substantial R&D investments since its founding in 2021 by physicist Stefano Buono and has a patent portfolio covering 31 patent families across both its lead-cooled fast reactor (LFR) design and mixed-oxide (MOX) fuel processing.
The company has raised approximately $780m of private funds to fund this growth as well as its licensing and siting progress.
In October 2025 Newcleo announced plans to form a partnership with US-based advanced nuclear technology company Oklo to build advanced nuclear fuel manufacturing infrastructure.
Newcleo says it is pioneering the next generation of nuclear technologies through its advanced modular LFRs, which use MOX fuel.

MOX fuel is a proven nuclear fuel made from reprocessed nuclear waste and nuclear materials. It is said to be a sustainable, low-carbon alternative to standard low-enriched uranium fuel and is widely used in commercial reactors to recycle nuclear waste and repurpose surplus weapons-grade plutonium.

Newcleo’s 200 MWe (480 MWth) commercial reactor design is aimed at addressing critical industry needs by supplying combined electricity and high-temperature heat to energy intensive off-takers across industries, including data centres, chemicals, steel, glass, ceramics and paper manufacturing.
The company’s LFRs are designed to reduce certain severe accident risks by design by combining the intrinsic properties of lead with passive safety systems and atmospheric pressure operations.

“This transaction represents a pivotal moment for Newcleo as we accelerate our mission of closing the nuclear fuel cycle and safely producing clean and competitive low carbon energy," said Buono, who serves as CEO.

“The capital raised as part of this strategic transaction, combined with public market access, will enable us to rapidly advance our reactor deployment and fuel manufacturing capabilities across Europe and the United States.
“Newcleo is positioned to deliver a competitive solution to the world’s clean energy needs while reducing existing and future nuclear waste liabilities.”

* A merger with a blank-cheque company – formally known as a special purpose acquisition company (Spac) – is a financial manoeuvre where an existing publicly traded shell company merges with a private company to take the private company public, thereby bypassing the traditional initial public offering (IPO) process.
Stefano Buono: Newcleo is positioned to deliver a competitive solution to the world’s clean energy needs while reducing existing and future nuclear waste liabilities.

title: Could Ireland Follow Finland’s Model For Nuclear Energy?
author: David Dalton
text: Nordic country offers lessons on policy, says legislator

The countries that will enjoy affordable and secure energy in the 2040s and 2050s are making their decisions now and Ireland cannot afford another decade of avoiding difficult conversations simply because the solutions – such as nuclear power – are politically challenging, a member of the lower house of the Irish parliament has said.
James O’Connor said in an article in the Irish Examiner that Ireland’s electricity prices are now the highest in the EU, almost double the electricity costs of some EU states.
O’Connor is bringing forward legislation to address Ireland’s statutory ban on energy generation by nuclear fission.

He said: “We speak constantly about the ‘cost of living crisis’, but too often our political debate avoids confronting the difficult long-term decisions required to bring meaningful relief to households and businesses. Energy policy is one of those decisions.”

He added: “If we are serious about reducing electricity prices, improving energy security and maintaining competitiveness, then every viable option must at least be examined honestly, including nuclear power.”

O’Connor said that for years, nuclear energy has effectively been treated as politically untouchable in Ireland. The debate has often been reduced to slogans and fears rather than facts and economics. But across Europe, attitudes are changing rapidly. One country in particular offers lessons for Ireland: Finland.

Like Ireland, Finland has a population of roughly 5.5 million people. O’Connor said it has invested heavily in renewable energy, particularly wind power, and shares many of the challenges faced by smaller European states operating on the edge of larger continental markets.

“Unlike Ireland, however, Finland made the strategic decision not to rely solely on intermittent renewables and imported energy,” O’Connor said. “It chose to combine renewables with long-term nuclear generation.”
“The result is a far more stable and affordable electricity system.”
O’Connor said that combined with renewables, nuclear has allowed Finland to reduce reliance on imported fossil fuels while strengthening energy security and lowering wholesale electricity costs.

Meanwhile, Ireland remains heavily dependent on gas-fired generation to stabilise the grid whenever wind output falls. “Our undersea gas interconnects to Britain are hopelessly exposed to malign foreign influence,” O’Connor said. “We are building a system that is renewable in ambition but fragile in practice.”

Last month the London-based Nuclear Industry Association said in evidence to a parliamentary inquiry that small modular reactors (SMRs) would help Ireland to meet rising electricity demand and energy security.

The British-Irish Parliamentary Assembly opened the inquiry in January to look at the role of nuclear power generation in long-term energy security. It called for submissions looking at the advantages of nuclear, its environmental impact, and the potential for cooperation between the UK and Ireland.N

Finland recently submitted an amended Nuclear Energy Act which aims to streamline the licensing process for nuclear plants, manage project risks and spur the use of new technology including small modular reactors (SMRs).
Finland has five commercial nuclear plants that produce almost 40% of its electricity generation. The most recent unit, the Olkiluoto-3 EPR, began commercial operation in 2023.
The London-based Nuclear Industry Association has said in evidence to a parliamentary inquiry that small modular reactors would help Ireland to meet rising electricity demand and energy security.
Finland’s newest nuclear plant, the Olkiluoto-3 EPR, began commercial operation in 2023. Courtesy TVO.

title: US Advanced Reactor Company Receives Key Approval For Criticality Test
author: David Dalton
text: Deployable Energy team working ‘urgently’ towards demonstration

US advanced reactor company Deployable Energy announced that it has received approval of its preliminary documented safety analysis (PDSA) for its Unity microreactor criticality test, marking a critical milestone in the US Department of Energy (DOE) safety authorisation process and enabling the company to proceed towards reactor demonstration.

The approved PDSA establishes the preliminary safety basis for the Unity reactor criticality test, documenting how the design meets DOE requirements for hazard analysis, accident mitigation, and operational controls.

Completed in just 106 days, the review reflects “extensive engineering and safety evaluation and provides the formal foundation required to advance toward reactor startup and operations”, Washington-based Deployable Energy said.

“The PDSA approval is an important step in bringing a new reactor to life,” said Deployable Energy’s chief executive officer Bobby Gallagher. “Completing this review in 106 days since program kick-off demonstrates both the strength of our safety approach and the urgency with which our team is executing toward demonstration.”

Deployable Energy said that with the PDSA in place, it is now positioned to complete final preparations for its upcoming demonstration, including commissioning and startup activities under DOE oversight.

The company recently delivered its criticality test rig to Idaho National Laboratory following a cross-country road trip in a Ford F-150 truck, underscoring the compact and deployable nature of the Unity system. The manufacturing of the fuel that will be used during the initial criticality test has also been completed.

Deployable Energy’s Unity microreactor is a compact, factory-built nuclear system designed to deliver reliable, transportable power in remote and infrastructure-constrained environments, supporting applications across defence, commercial, maritime, and industrial sectors.
Deployable Energy co-founder and chief executive officer Bobby Gallagher at Idaho National Laboratory earlier this month. Courtesy Deployable Energy.

title: US Could Save Time And Money By Cutting Out Reviews For Already-Licensed Nuclear Plants, Says Columbia Report
author: Nigel Davies
text: Advisory committee on reactor safeguards could cut costs by potentially millions

The US could help to accelerate and cut costs of the licensing process for reactor designs by cutting out safety reviews by the advisory committee on reactor safeguards (ACRS) for reactor designs have already been approved, a Columbia University report has said.

The report from the Center on Global Energy Policy (CGEP) at Columbia said that the longest single element of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) reactor licensing process was its safety evaluation.

Part of this evaluation is a report from the ACRS which follows the NRC’s draft safety evaluation report. The independently-led ACRS can make recommendations on reactor safety design, which the NRC can then decide to act on or say why it does not think any change is warranted.

The CGEP report said it is essential that the ACRS remains independent and it is important with new reactor designs coming through that the body could examine NRC safety evaluations, which enhance safety and public confidence.

Since 1957, the advisory committee on reactor safeguards has had a statutory responsibility for providing independent reviews of, and advising on, the safety of proposed or existing reactor facilities and the adequacy of proposed reactor safety standards in the US.
“Preserving the ACRS’s independence can provide some protection against the prospect of NRC decisions being influenced by political considerations, the report said.

However, the report said that legislation could be passed so that the ACRS could decline reviews of an already certified reactor design. It did caution that this would have only a limited impact on accelerating the process.

“Explicitly giving the ACRS flexibility to decline reviews associated with new reactor licensing could speed up new reactor licensing actions in the future, though… perhaps only by 3 to 11 percent,” the report said.
The CGEP said that not having an ACRS review in cases of an already certified reactor could reduce licensing costs “likely by hundreds of thousands to millions of dollars”.

The CGEP also recommended that the ACRS help to clear up any misconceptions by providing estimates of the cost of future reviews of construction permits, operating licenses, early site permits, and combined licenses.
It added that the NRC could also disclose how much staff time and costs it took for it to respond to ACRS reviews if it possessed the relevant data.
On staff issues, the CGEP report said that the ACRS must continue to ensure that its membership consists of individuals with independence, integrity and technical expertise.
According to the report, the NRC could also consider developing an internal process whereby its staff met with the ACRS earlier to discuss whether an ACRS review would be a good use of resources.

“If the United States ever finds itself in a position where the NRC is evaluating applications for the same reactor design, it will likely not be a good use of ACRS resources to review every construction permit or operating license application with that design,” the report stated.
“On the other hand, the ACRS should be allowed to determine the matters of safety significance that warrant its examination.”

title: UK Nuclear Industry Welcomes Plans To End Judicial Reviews For Critical Clean Energy Infrastructure
author: Nigel Davies
text: Changes aim to ensure key projects ‘cannot be left stuck in the slow lane’

The UK government’s proposed policy change taking away the right to judicial reviews for major clean energy infrastructure projects in order to stimulate development and economic growth has been welcomed by the country’s Nuclear Industry Association (NIA).

A policy paper published by the government proposes that the country’s parliament would be able to designate the most important of clean energy projects as being of “critical national importance”, which would reduce their exposure to judicial review apart from on human rights grounds.

The government said the policy move added to its Planning and Infrastructure Act of 2025 aimed at speeding up major projects by an average of 12 monthsand unlocking £7.5bn ($10bn, €8.7bn) in economic benefits over the next decade.

The UK aims to boost a new age of British nuclear energy generation, and a government review recognised nuclear power as being vital to meet its 2050 net zero commitment and a forecast doubling of electricity demand.

A Treasury spokesperson said the UK chancellor Rachel Reeves was ensuring that parliament was taking back control so the UK could build power plants, wind farms and grid connections to reduce consumer bills.
The policy paper stated: “Building a modern, competitive and resilient economy demands that we get better and faster at delivering the infrastructure required to power it.”
“Delay has a cost, undermines investor confidence, and slows our transition to homegrown clean energy that protects households from volatile global prices.”
The government said that the changes would go further by ensuring that a legal challenge did not create unnecessary delay to nationally important infrastructure.

In addition to parliamentary authorisation for criticial energy projects, the policy change would also open a “challenge window” mechanism whereby secretaries of state could respond in a more agile way to potential issues and limit the ability to raise other issues once final consent was granted.
The policy moves were welcomed by the UK’s NIA chief executive Tom Greatex.

“New nuclear projects are vital national infrastructure, delivering reliable clean power, skilled jobs and major investment across the country. Giving developers and investors the confidence to move ahead is essential if the UK is to build at the pace this moment demands,” Greatex said.
“These reforms rightly recognise that nationally important infrastructure cannot be left stuck in the slow lane,” he added.

Trade association Energy UK struck a similar tone. Its chief executive Dhara Vyasa, said: “Planning reform for clean energy is critical and still needs to strike a balance between a process that allows proper scrutiny of applications without unduly restricting the country’s ability to build the infrastructure necessary to strengthen our energy security, boost our economy, and help stop energy bills being at the mercy of global events.”

The only nuclear station under construction in the UK is the two-unit Hinkley Point C,  the first nuclear plant to be built in the UK in two decades. It is also planning new large-scale units at Sizewell C and small modular reactors at Wylfa in Wales.
File photo of construction at the Hinkley Point C nuclear power station in the UK. Courtesy EDF Energy.

title: TerraPower Announces Key Natrium Reactor Agreements With South Korea Companies
author: David Dalton
text: Bill Gates-founded nuclear company aims for ‘rapid deployment’ in coming years

TerraPower, the US nuclear company co-founded by Bill Gates, announced it has signed agreements with South Korea’s HD Hyundai and Hyundai Engineering & Construction (HDEC) to support the rapid commercialisation and deployment of a fleet of Natrium reactor and integrated energy storage plants in the coming years.

During a signing ceremony in New York, TerraPower and HD Hyundai signed a supply framework agreement that establishes HD Hyundai Heavy Industries (HHI), a shipbuilding subsidiary of HD Hyundai, as a preferred manufacturer for Natrium reactor enclosure system components.
