In 2022, in light of concerns about security of supply in the context of the energy crisis and the Russian war against Ukraine, the government decided to keep Doel-4 and Tihange-3, the two newest plants, in operation for an additional 10 years.
The Belgian Nuclear Forum (BNF), the federation of the nuclear sector in Belgium, said it welcomed the announcement “with great satisfaction”.

BNG called the move “a courageous and strategic decision. BNF chief executive officer Serge Dauby said: “This step demonstrates political determination and vision within the government. It reinforces a new and positive perspective on Belgium’s security of energy supply.”

BNF said: “It is time to take greater control of our energy supply again. This decision provides prospects for our industry, which can once again look to the future in Belgium with greater confidence.
“It is also good news for the Belgian population, which, according to various opinion polls, is largely in favour of nuclear energy.
“In recent months and years, we have been confronted with high energy prices as a result of a complex geopolitical context.

“Both industry and the population attach importance to security of energy supply at a competitive price. In this regard, the takeover of nuclear activities by the Belgian State will play a positive role.”
The Tihange nuclear power station, where a shut-down reactor could be restarted. Courtesy Engie.

title: Diablo Canyon Lobby Group Launches Push For State Approval Of Plant Lifetime Extension
author: Nigel Davies
text: NRC approved renewal of operating licence for 20 years, but backing needed from California

A group of business, labour and regional organisations have formed a coalition called Diablo Canyon 2045 to push for the state of California to amend its legislation so it can grant a lifetime extension to its sole commercial nuclear power station.

In early April, the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) granted a 20-year extension to the 1,138 MW Diablo Canyon-1 reactor to 2044, and the 1,118 MW Diablo Canyon-2 reactor to 2045. Both plants are owned and operated by Pacific Gas & Electric (PG&E).
However, California would need to amend its own state legislation, which currently allows the plants to operate until 2030, for operations to continue until the mid-2040s.

The Diablo Canyon 2045 group, which is supported by the regional Bay Area Council and the California Electric Utility Industry Labor-Management Cooperation Committee, said “failure to act will drive up electricity costs today as California makes long-term power supply decisions and investments beyond 2030”.
Diablo Canyon provides around 9% of the state’s electricity demands.

The campaign group said that according to an independent study by the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, the extension of Diablo Canyon would save customers over $1.3bn (€1.1bn) a year.  It also saves around seven million tons of greenhouse gases annually through its operations.

“Extending the life of Diablo Canyon this year will set California on a path to save customers money on their bills and ensure the state has a reliable source of clean energy as demand is expected to double by 2045,” said John Grubb, Bay Area Council interim president and chief executive officer.
According to the California Energy Commission, electricity demand is expected to grow in the state by over 20 GW by 2045.
The 20-year lifetime extension to the plants marked the 99th and 100th commercial reactor renewals granted by the NRC in the country.

Diablo Canyon is the last operating nuclear plant in the country’s most populous state. The three other nuclear plants in the state –the three-unit San Onofre, the single-unit Humboldt Bay and the single-unit Rancho Seco – have all been shut down.
The two-unit Diablo Canyon nuclear power station provides around 9% of California’s electricity demands. Courtesy PG&E.

title: Fuel Loading Begins At Bangladesh’s First Nuclear Power Plant
author: David Dalton
text: Two VVER-1200 units being provided under contract with Russia’s Rosatom
Fuel loading has begun at the first commercial nuclear power plant to be built in Bangladesh, Russia's state nuclear corporation Rosatom has said.
According to reports in Bangladesh, fuel loading at Rooppur-1 is expected to be completed in less than 45 days.
Rosatom said fuel loading is the first phase of the key commissioning stage of the unit.

Later, the reactor will be brought to minimum controlled level, after which a gradual increase of power will begin. The next stage will be power startup when the generated electricity will be transmitted to the power grid of Bangladesh, Rosatom said.
It said a ceremony to mark first fuel loading was attended by Rosatom director-general Alexey Likhachev and Bangladesh’s minister of science and technology, Fakir Mahbub Anam.

Rosatom is building two VVER-1200 pressurised water reactor units at the Rooppur site, about 150 km west of the capital Dhaka, under a general contract signed in 2015.Russia’s state-run Tvel nuclear fuel company is providing the nuclear fuel. Spent fuel will be returned to Russia.

“If the commissioning progresses smoothly, we expect to add a minimum of 300 megawatts by late July or early August to the national grid.” Anwar Hossain, secretary at the science and technology ministry, told The Daily Star.
“Production will then gradually increase by 10 to 15 percent, reaching the ceiling of 1,200 megawatts by late 2026 or early 2027.”

Zahedul Hasan, managing director of the Nuclear Power Plant Company of Bangladesh Ltd (NPCBL), said: “We must navigate a challenging test phase during commissioning. Tests will be conducted at various stages to prepare the final safety analysis report.”
Initial concrete pouring for Rooppur-1 took place in November 2017, followed by Rooppur-2 in July 2018.
The Rooppur nuclear power station is about 150 km west of the capital Dhaka. Courtesy Rosatom.

title: AtkinsRéalis And Oxford Robotics To Collaborate On Autonomous Robotics Solutions
author: David Dalton
text: Technologies are intended for nuclear and energy industries

Canadian engineering services and nuclear company AtkinsRéalis and Oxford Robotics Institute (ORI), the University of Oxford’s centre for robotics and artificial intelligence, have announced a new global partnership to accelerate the adoption of autonomous robotic solutions for the nuclear and energy sectors.

Through the partnership, advanced autonomous robotic solutions will be developed and tested, supporting the emerging field of physical AI, where intelligent systems are deployed safely and reliably in real‑world, safety‑critical environments.

The collaboration builds on a successful period of joint work in the UK, where ORI systems have been integrated into AtkinsRéalis robotics platforms for autonomous navigation, advanced mapping and hotspot detection at nuclear sites, including Sellafield in northwest England.
The new partnership expands this work internationally, focusing on improving safety by reducing the time people need to spend in hazardous environments while improving capability and efficiency.

Initially, the partnership will focus on scaling proven UK deployments, including autonomous mobile inspection platforms and robotic manipulation systems. Solutions will be tested and refined at ORI’s robotics facilities.

Sam Stephens, head of digital – nuclear at AtkinsRéalis, said: “This partnership allows us to rapidly move autonomous robotics from research to operational deployment on nuclear power plants around the world.”
The Oxford Robotics Institute is the University of Oxford’s centre for robotics and artificial intelligence. Courtesy ORI.

title: France’s Stellaria Signs LOI On Feasibility Studies For Key Reactor Facilities
author: David Dalton
text: Company planning commercial advanced molten salt nuclear plant by 2035

French advanced nuclear reactor developer Stellaria and the French Alternative Energies and Atomic Energy Commission (CEA) have signed a letter of intent (LOI) for a feasibility study into the construction of key facilities at CEA’s Cadarache site.

Th LOI is for an Alpha basic nuclear installation (installation nucléaire de base, or INB) housing a test model, a fast-spectrum molten salt demonstration reactor and a salt fabrication facility to supply the prototype and demonstration reactor.

Stellaria said the signing of the LOI lays the foundations for critical experiments known as Alvin, scheduled for 2030 at the Alpha INB facility. The Alvin experiments will allow Stellaria to validate its modelling and calculations.
Once the Alvin experimental programme is complete the Alpha INB will also house the MegAlvin prototype reactor. Modification of the facility so it can house MegAlvin will begin around 2032.

The main objective of the MegAlvin project are to conduct endurance and qualification tests on fuel, testing structural materials and systems specific to molten salt reactors, and obtain operational feedback for the commissioning of Stellaria’s first commercial reactor, the Stellarium, in 2035.

Stellarium is a Generation IV molten salt design. Molten salt reactors are said to have advantages over more traditional water-cooled plants, including improved safety and higher efficiency. Inherent safety features include low-pressure operation, reduced waste and the use of standard low-enriched uranium fuel.
The startup raised €23m ($26.8m) in 2025 to support technical and regulatory studies and has previously signed a power pre-order agreement with data centre operator Equinix.
Stellaria also received €10m in public funding under the federal France 2030 programme in 2024, supporting technical studies and regulatory preparation for its prototype reactor.
In February Stellaria submitted an application to the French authorities for the potential construction the Alvin prototype.
A computer-generated image of Stellaria’s planned Alvin demonstration plant. Courtesy Stellaria.

title: EDF Announces €100 Million Investment In Factory For EPR2 Equipment
author: David Dalton
text: Project part of France’s ambitious plans for rollout of new nuclear plants

France’s state-owned energy company EDF has announced an investment of nearly €100m ($117m) for the construction by subsidiary Arabelle Solutions of a new factory for the production of key equipment for an ambitious programme of new nuclear reactor construction.

The factory, in Chalon-sur-Saône, eastern France, will produce the equipment for the planned construction of six EPR2 reactors and eight potential additional EPR2 reactors in France, as well as for new construction programmes internationally.
This investment will be accompanied by approximately 160 local job creations by 2030, EDF said in a statement.

EDF said the plant will produce equipment that optimises heat exchange in the turbine section of a nuclear power plant, where electricity is generated. This includes superheater dryers and high- and low-pressure heaters.
The first equipment is scheduled to be manufactured starting in 2030. The new plant in will have the production capacity to supply all of this equipment for a nuclear power plant each year.

The project is part of Arabelle Solutions’ investment plan for new EPR2 nuclear plants and complements recent investments for the Belfort site in northeastern France, where turbines and generators are designed and made.

“These investments will ensure the equipment for future EPR2 nuclear power plants is supplied via a French production line,” EDF said. “Arabelle Solutions will be able to supply and integrate all the turbine hall equipment for nuclear power plants.”
EDF has already submitted an application for authorisation to build two EPR2 plants at Penly in Normandy. A second pair of EPR plants is being planned for Gravelines, about 170 km northeast of Penly.
EDF said in October that it was planning to submit an application for an environmental permit and begin preparatory work as early as 2027 for a two EPR2s at the Bugey site, in southeastern France.
Bugey would be the third project in a major French plan to deploy new EPR2 units.
France’s president Emmanuel Macron said recently that the world cannot achieve decarbonisation, energy independence, and economic competitiveness without nuclear energy.

France operates 56 commercial reactors units, providing about 70% of the country’s electric generation. The newest unit, the 57th, is Flamanville-3, which was connected to the grid in December 2024 after years of delays and cost overruns. It recently reached full power, but has not yet begun commercial operation.
A nuclear power plant steam turbine manufactured by Arabelle Solutions. Courtesy GE.

title: Ur-Energy Announces Start Of Uranium Mining At Shirley Basin In Wyoming
author: David Dalton
text: Company welcomes ‘pivotal moment’ in bid to expand US production capacity
US uranium company Ur-Energy has announced the start of uranium mining operations at its Shirley Basin project in Wyoming.

The company, which says it has in-situ recovery (ISR) projects that are among the largest and lowest-cost in the US, said uranium bearing solution is now being captured from Mine Unit 1 at Shirley Basin after the successful completion of significant construction, wellfield installation and permitting.
Uranium bearing solution is used in ISR mining to dissolve uranium from underground ore bodies, turning it into a “pregnant solution” or that is pumped to the surface.

Ur-Energy, which is headquartered in Colorado and has a regional office in Wyoming, said uranium concentrations in recovered solutions are expected to increase over time as it further conditions the wellfield and all production circuits are brought online.
It said it expects to transport uranium loaded resin to its Lost Creek facility for processing this summer, “subject to an additional regulatory inspection and approval”.
The Shirley Basin project has licensed annual wellfield and toll processing capacity of up to two million pounds equivalent of triuranium octoxide (U3O8).
Measured and indicated mineral resources total approximately 9.1 million pounds U3O8.
Ur-Energy said anticipated mine life is approximately nine years across three shallow mining units.
Uranium is captured on ion exchange resin and transported to Lost Creek for final processing, drying, and packaging.

The company said in a statement that this milestone marks the successful transition of its second ISR mine – following Lost Creek*, also in Wyoming – from development to initial operations and represents a significant expansion of its uranium production capacity.

“Our Shirley Basin Project is situated in the Shirley Basin district, widely recognised as the birthplace of ISR mining, is now returning to active operations under Ur-Energy's stewardship,” it said. “With new production anticipated from Shirley Basin, Ur-Energy is well positioned to contribute to growing global uranium demand amid a nuclear energy renaissance.”

Ur-Energy chief executive officer and president Matt Gili said: “Launching initial operations marks a pivotal achievement in Ur-Energy’s growth strategy and plan to expand US uranium production capacity.”

Washington has been trying to boost domestic uranium production and reduce reliance on foreign imports, particularly from Russia. President Donald Trump issued executive orders in 2025 that included efforts to fast-track mining on federal lands.

Earlier this month Uranium Energy Corp received approval from the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality to begin production at its Burke Hollow ISR uranium project in Texas. The company said Burke Hollow was the first new US ISR operation in over a decade.
* Production at the Lost Creek officially began in 2013. After reducing operations in late 2019 due to market conditions, the mine returned to full commercial production in 2023.
Ur-Energy’s Shirley Basin uranium facility in Wyoming. Courtesy Ur-Energy.

title: Spanish Industry Group Foro Nuclear Urges Country To Align With EU On Calls Against Plant Closures
author: Nigel Davies
text: New president Marta Ugalde says nuclear is part of climate and energy solutions

Spain’s nuclear industry group Foro Nuclear says the country should now align with the European Union following strong calls against the premature closure of plants which provide a clean energy solution in times of energy crisis.
On 22 April the European Commission said it would deliver a package of measures to alleviate the impact of surging fossil fuel prices caused by the conflict in Iran.

The EC also said that new small modular reactors (SMRs), and avoiding the premature retirement of existing nuclear capacity, could help reduce dependency on fossil fuels and help drive a clean energy transition.
The recently appointed Foro Nuclear president, Marta Ugalde, welcomed the support of nuclear energy made by the EU.

“Spain has the opportunity to align with Europe on this issue, making the most of the added value that nuclear energy brings to a robust, sustainable and forward-looking electricity system,” said Ugalde.

Spain plans to shutter its fleet of seven commercial nuclear reactors between 2027-2035. Already, operators of those plants have called for lifetime extensions to be made because reactors account for around 20% of electricity production in the country.

Ugalde added: “Europe is facing a decisive moment. Accelerating the energy transition requires realistic decisions, mature technologies and regulation that is aligned with climate and industrial goals. Nuclear energy is part of that solution.”
EU president Ursula Von der Leyen stated in March that it was a “strategic mistake” for Europe to have turned its back on nuclear energy.
At that time, she said nuclear power accounted for around 15% of the bloc’s electricity mix, down from around a third in 1990.
Marta Ugalde said Spain has the opportunity to align with Europe on nuclear. Courtesy Foro Nuclear.

title: US Air Force Chooses Three Microreactor Manufacturers For Onsite Nuclear Power
author: Nigel Davies
text: Radiant, Westinghouse and Antares have each been paired with a miltary installation
The US Department of the Air Force (DAF) has selected three nuclear reactor manufacturers to develop microreactors for three air bases as part of efforts to support energy needs.
The DAF said that under its Advanced Nuclear Power for Installations Initiative (ANPI), it had selected Radiant Industries to install its technology at the Buckley Space Force Base in Colorado.
Meanwhile, Westinghouse Government Services was chosen for the installation of a microreactor at the Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana.

Since the DAF announced those two air force bases as microreactor sites earlier in April, it also added a third site at the Joint Base San Antonio in Texas. This site would deploy technology from Antares Nuclear, DAF confirmed.
“The future of air and space dominance is powered by resilient energy,” said Michael Borders, assistant secretary of the Air Force for energy, installations and environment.

“By integrating advanced nuclear technology, we are not just keeping the lights on, we are guaranteeing that our most critical national security missions will never be held at risk by a power outage. This is a pivotal moment for the DAF.”

The ANPI initiative aims to have at least one advanced nuclear reactor operating at an air force base by 2030. The next step in the process will cover siting and environmental analyses as part of the National Environmental Policy Act process.

The DAF said this initiative was separate from the microreactor pilot program at Eielson Air Force Base, Alaska, which is a standalone effort focused on demonstrating the feasibility and operational benefits of a microreactor at a single installation.
In a statement, Radiant welcomed news of its selection to roll out its Kaleidos 1 MW microreactor at the Buckley Space Force Base.
“Together with our incredible government partners, Radiant is making the nuclear renaissance a reality,” said Mike Starrett, chief revenue officer at Radiant.
“The American energy industry needs to make progress now, not in five or 10 years. With a full-power reactor already under assembly, Radiant will deliver,” he added.

In Radiant’s statement, Colonel Eamon Murray, a Space Base Delta 2 commander at Buckley, said: “A secure and reliable power source will enable Buckley’s warfighters from all six services and allied nations to support the Joint Force in all situations.”

Antares, meanwhile, said that it expected to deliver its R1 sodium pipe-cooled microreactor by 2028 or earlier. The company is targeting criticality for its first reactor by 4 July 2026, to meet the Department of Energy’s target under its Reactor Pilot Program.

The US military has already shown its willingness to deploy nuclear power to aid its energy requirements. It wants to deploy small microreactors and small modular reactors (SMRs) to ensure energy resilience, reduce reliance on fossil fuels and power remote bases.
In February, it conducted its first air transport of a microreactor to show how such facilities could be rapidly deployed for both military or civilian needs.
A standalone microreactor pilot programme has already begun at a fourth site – Eielson Air Force Base in Alaska. Courtesy Eielson Air Force Base.
Joint Base San Antonio in Texas has become the third base to be earmarked for a microreactor. Courtesy Joint Base San Antonio.

title: Vietnam And South Korea To Consider Development And Financing Of New Nuclear Power Station
author: David Dalton
text: Hanoi has already signed agreement with Russia for cooperation on first reactors

Vietnam and South ‌Korea’s leaders agreed to boost cooperation in nuclear energy at a meeting in Hanoi on 22 April including the possibility of the development and financing of a new nuclear plant for Hanoi.

In their second meeting since August, Vietnam’s president To Lam and South Korean counterpart Lee Jae Myung attended the signing of 12 non-binding documents, including on energy, technology and security cooperation.
Lee said that amid the current conflict in the Middle East, “the need for cooperation between our nations has grown even greater”.
The documents included plans to ⁠cooperate on nuclear power plant development and financing for Vietnam.

The southeast Asian nation has already signed an intergovernmental agreement with Russia to cooperate on the construction of its first commercial nuclear power station, Russian state-owned nuclear corporation Rosatom said last month.
That project, the Ninh Thuan nuclear power station, foresees the construction of two Russia-designed VVER-1200 pressurised water reactor units with an installed capacity of 2,400 MW.
Russia and Vietnam are also cooperating on the construction of a nuclear science and technology centre in Vietnam, which will include a Russian-designed research reactor, said Rosatom.

According to earlier reports, Vietnam aims to have Ninh Thuan online in before the end of 2031 and a second nuclear station in operation between 2036 and 2040, although the 2031 target seems ambitious given that development is in the early stages.

In April 2025, the government approved a revised version of its national power development plan, allocating $136bn (€117bn) by 2030 to strengthen long-term energy security and including nuclear power for the first time.
The government had said its planned nuclear programme would involve building two nuclear power stations with a combined capacity of about 4,000 GW.

Vietnam had planned the two stations as far back as 2009, but the National Assembly rejected the proposal in 2016 on cost grounds. Hanoi had selected Rosatom and Japan Atomic Power Company to build the stations, agreeing to a loan of $8bn from Russia for the first facility, with construction originally planned to start in 2014.
In December 2024, lawmakers asked the government to resume the development of the nuclear power programme and Vietnam reached out to foreign reactor technology partners.
In June 2025, Bloomberg reported Vietnam was seeking urgent discussions with Russia to accelerate its nuclear programme and sign an investment cooperation agreement for a first nuclear power station.

According to a report by accountancy company PwC, Vietnam’s expected economic growth over the next three decades means a need for 150 GW in installed energy generation capacity by 2030, and 500 GW by 2050, from about 80 GW today.

Southeast Asia's fastest-growing economy has at times struggled to meet growing power demand as its industrial base expands. According to Reuters, South Korea is the largest investor in Vietnam, with multiple South Korean multinationals having large manufacturing operations in the country.

Also in Hanoi this week, the International Atomic Energy Agency handed over to Vietnam the final report of a peer review mission that assessed the country's development of the infrastructure needed for a nuclear power programme.

The mission team concluded that Vietnam has taken major steps to restart and accelerate the Ninh Thuan project and the development of the required infrastructure. In 2025, Vietnam enacted a new atomic energy law and adopted special mechanisms to facilitate financial and contractual arrangements for nuclear power plants.

The IAEA team identified good practices in government-enabling mechanisms for financing and procurement, as well as in leveraging existing expertise in environmental monitoring for nuclear projects, practices that could benefit other countries developing nuclear power.
South Korean President Lee Jae Myung attends a wreath-laying ceremony at the Ho Chi Minh Mausoleum in Hanoi, Vietnam, on 22 April. Courtesy Lee Jae Myung/X.

title: US Support For ‘Greater Emphasis’ On Nuclear Is Highest To Date, Says Gallup
author: David Dalton
text: Americans remain ‘broadly resistant’ to reactors in their area

Most Americans continue to prefer that the US put more emphasis on solar and wind power for domestic energy production, but at the same time, support for greater emphasis on nuclear power has risen to its highest point to date, at 46%, Gallup has said.
According to the polling company, fewer now hold the view that solar and wind should be emphasised than in any of five measurements over the past 13 years.
Levels of support for increased use of fossil fuels like oil, coal and natural gas remain well below their highs.

Democrats are more likely than Republicans to favour more emphasis on renewable energy sources, while Republicans are more likely to back greater emphasis on fossil fuels. Cross-party views are most similar on nuclear energy.
Even as there is growing support for more emphasis on nuclear energy, most Americans remain broadly resistant to the construction of a nuclear power plant in their area, Gallup said.
The latest findings are from Gallup’s March 2-18 annual Environment poll.

When asked whether the US should put more emphasis, less emphasis or about the same emphasis as it does now on producing domestic energy from each of six sources, 66% of Americans prefer more emphasis on solar energy and 55% on wind. Though still majorities, both have slipped considerably since the previous reading in 2021, with solar down seven percentage points and wind down 11 points.

Meanwhile, nuclear energy is the only one of the six sources to see support grow since 2021, rising seven points to 46%, making it the plurality response. “This shift is notable given that preferences for nuclear energy had historically been more evenly divided among responses of more, less and the same,” Gallup said.

Support for more emphasis on natural gas remains even between Democrats and Republicans, at 42%, but is down seven points from the previous measurement. Twenty two percent prefer less emphasis on natural gas and 37% prefer the same level.

Views on oil are divided, with 34% preferring more emphasis on it, 37% less and 28% no change. Coal draws the least support of any source asked about, with just 23% of Americans favouring more emphasis, half preferring less and 25% the same amount. These figures have held roughly steady since 2013, with slightly more now preferring less emphasis.
The Vogtle nuclear power station in the US state of Georgia. Courtesy Georgia Power.

title: After ‘Optimisation’ Delay, France’s Nuward Targets New Conceptual SMR Design This Year
author: Rachel Rigby
text: First fleet of three to four reactors could be deployed in one or two European countries

The conceptual design for the French Nuward small modular reactor (SMR) should be completed by the middle of 2026 with a detailed design ready in 2031 following a recent project pause, a company representative has said.

The Nuward project was launched in September 2019 by France’s Alternative Energies and Atomic Energy Commission, EDF, Naval Group and TechnicAtome. The plant consists of a 340 MW SMR plant with two pressurised water reactors (PWRs) of 170 MW each.
The technology was developed using France’s experience in PWRs. Nuward is a subsidiary of French state-owned nuclear power company EDF.

The technology is intended to replace carbon-dioxide-emitting coal, oil and gas plants and support other applications such as hydrogen production, urban and district heating or desalination facilities, according to EDF.

After early development of the technology and a shortlisting in the UK’s SMR competition, the Nuward project was paused in July 2024. EDF said at the time that this was in response to feedback from potential European customers, adding at the time that it planned to “optimise” the Nuward design, focusing on existing and proven technologies, in order to guarantee that future project deadlines and budgets were met.
The aim is that the revised concept design “will be finalised by mid-2026. The aim is to finalise the basic design in 2028 and detailed design in 2031,” the EDF representative said.

Juliet Reingold, a lawyer at UK-based law firm Simmons & Simmons, said in an email that Nuward was “formally relaunched in 2025 after a strategic refocusing on feasibility and market readiness and is now in a more mature, “proven-technology development phase, rather than an exploratory concept phase”.
“The new design emphasises industrial feasibility and regulatory predictability, rather than experimental innovation,” Reingold said.

“The practical implication is that the programme is now optimising for industrial realism: existing supply chains, lower technical novelty, and a clearer licensing path. That is a different posture from the earlier ‘new concept’ approach, which had to prove too many things at once and therefore carried more technical and scheduling risk,” she added.
The Nuward representative noted that six European safety authorities had undertaken a joint early review of the Nuward reactor technology.

They were the French nuclear Safety authority ASNR, the Czech Republic’s nuclear safety authority SUJB, the Finnish nuclear safety authority STUK, the Polish nuclear safety authority PAA, the Swedish nuclear safety authority SSM and ANVS, the Dutch nuclear safety authority.

All of these authorities are “members of the joint early review, a Nuward-led initiative,” the representative noted, adding that the “feedback and consultations of its members help anticipate the regulatory expectations in target European markets and contribute to the ambition of stronger regulatory harmonisation for SMRs in Europe”.
Nuward and the six regulators published a joint early review for the Nuward plant in December 2025, presenting the conclusions of a “Phase 2” review of the unit and its regulatory preparedness.
A Phase 3 review, in which Belgium nuclear regulator Fanc and Italian regulator ISIN joined the regulatory review as observers, began in January 2026.

Phase 1 took place between June 2022 and June 2023 and consisted of a series of technical exchanges took place between Nuward, EDF, the safety authorities and their technical support organizations. These discussions, held outside any formal licensing process, made it possible to receive early feedback.
“The joint European effort is key to EDF’s thinking with regard to this reactor,” said a source at EDF Energy who is familiar with EDF’s thinking on the development of the Nuward unit.
The source asked to speak on the condition of anonymity to discuss commercially sensitive matters. EDF Energy is the wholly-owned UK subsidiary of EDF.

EDF would have liked to develop this unit as the flagship design for the European SMR Alliance. I think they still would like to pursue the unit on that basis but they have maybe lost a little bit of the momentum with the delay in the project’s development.”

The European Industrial Alliance on Small Modular Reactors “aims to facilitate and accelerate the development, demonstration, and deployment of SMRs in Europe by the early 2030s,” according to the website of the European nuclear companies are members of the alliance, as are a series of non-governmental organisations, trade bodies and government bodies.

The “revised version of the Nuward SMR is “based on mature, proven technologies, eliminating the risk of technical non-feasibility and ensuring safe and rapid development with an industrial supply chain that already exists,” the EDF representative added.
The “objective is to meet market needs while delivering technology which will be ready for commercialisation in the next decade,” the representative said.

The “insights provided by experts on the Nuward International Advisory Board (NIAB) also offer valuable guidance for shaping Nuward’s product development strategy and defining its major priorities,” the Nuward representative also said. The NIAB includes representatives from the nuclear industry, academia and research.

The Nuward representative confirmed that the “objective is to… bring a commercial product to the market in the 2030s, with a first-of-a-kind unit to be built in France and Europe, supplying decarbonised electricity and heat for industrial applications.”

EDF’s priority for Nuward is the “European market where the demand for decarbonised energy solutions is high, notably from data centres. We have carried out an in-depth assessment of the needs of the 80 largest industrial clusters in Europe,” the representative said.

“In the short-term our aim is to co-develop with clients and partners and deploy a first fleet of three to four reactors in one or two European countries, including France,” the representative said, adding that EDF is “actively involved as a member of the European Industrial Alliance on SMRs, established by the European Commission in 2024”.

“I think this is still a very strong reactor design which has a good chance of deployment,” The EDF Energy Source said. “EDF is the strongest nuclear power company in Europe, without question and their full weight is behind this project.”

“The pause in the project was unfortunate, but Nuward and EDF have been quite clear that the purpose of it was to rationalise the design and make it more conventional. At the end of the day, that may make the reactor design more marketable. We will see,” the source said.
EDF is said to be putting its full weight behind the Nuward project. Courtesy Nuward.
A rendering of a Nuward small modular reactor nuclear power station. Courtesy Nuward.

title: Unit 1 At China’s Taipingling Nuclear Power Station Begins Commercial Operation
author: David Dalton
text: Reactor part of Beijing’s plans to boost power in booming Yangtze Delta region

Unit 1 of the Taipingling nuclear power station project in Guangzhou province, southern China, has begun commercial operation, China General Nuclear Power (CGN), the state-owned energy developer, has announced.
The 1,116-MW domestic Hualong One pressurised water reactor (PWR) unit was initially connected to the grid and produced its first electricity on 13 February.
The Hualong One, also known as the HPR1000, is a domestically developed PWR that combines features from China National Nuclear Corporation’s ACP1000 and China General Nuclear’s ACPR1000+ designs.

Taipingling-1, built by CGN Huizhou Nuclear Power, a subsidiary of CGN, completed all commissioning work and met the conditions for commercial operation on 19 April, the Shenzhen-based parent firm noted.
CGN said Taipingling-1 is the first domestic Hualong One reactor unit to begin operation in the greater Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macau bay area of southern China.

It said the area is seeing the emergence of a number of leading artificial intelligence companies such as DeepSeek. The “explosive” growth in computing power demand has led to a continuous increase in energy consumption, CGN said.

The International Atomic Energy Agency’s (IAEA) database of nuclear plants in China says China has 60 plants in commercial operation and 35 under construction. About half of those are domestic Hualong One units.

CGN previously said there will be six domestic Hualong One PWR units at the Taipingling site with a total project cost estimated at CNY120 billion (€14.9bn, $17bn). Construction of Unit 1 began in December 2019. Construction has also begun of Units 2 and 3.

China is aiming for 200 GW of nuclear capacity by 2035, up from around 57 GW today. Nuclear is expected to contribute about 10% of power generation in the country by 2035 – up from around 4.5 today – and 18% by 2060, with a total generation capacity of 400 GW by 2060, the China Nuclear Energy Association has said.
The control room at the Taipingling-1 nuclear power plant. Courtesy CGN.
The Taipingling nuclear power station will eventually have six Hualong One unts. Courtesy CGN.

title: Italy Should Reconsider Ban On Nuclear Power, Says IEA Head
author: David Dalton
text: Fatih Birol highlights need for ‘stable and continuous production’

Italy should reconsider its ban on the construction of new nuclear power plants as it seeks greater energy security and economic stability, the head of ​the International Energy Agency said in an interview.
Italy has no operating commercial nuclear reactors and relies heavily on energy imports, including electricity generated by nuclear power in neighbouring countries such as France.
Nuclear plants ​are prohibited following referendums in 1987 and 2011, ​but the government has been drafting rules to lift the ⁠ban through the use of new nuclear power technologies.

Asked whether the debate ​in Italy over a possible return to nuclear power was the right choice, ​IEA executive director Fatih Birol told Italian daily La Stampa: “I know that Italy rejected nuclear power in two referendums. But already two years ago, in Rome, ​I said that, if I were [Italy’s] government, I would reconsider that ​choice and look more closely at nuclear energy”.
Birol said Italy did not have abundant ‌energy ⁠resources and that although it was doing very well on renewables it also needed “stable and continuous production”.
“For economic prosperity, energy security and national sovereignty, Rome should evaluate nuclear power carefully, both in its traditional ​form and with ​new modular reactors,” ⁠he said.

Italy was a pioneer of nuclear power and had four commercial nuclear plants – Caorso, Enrico Fermi, Garigliano and Latina – providing almost 5% of the country’s electricity production share at their peak in 1986-1987.

Italy shut down the last of the plants, Caorso and Enrico Fermi, in July 1990 following the 1987 referendum in the wake of the Chernobyl disaster. The second referendum in 2011 followed the Fukushima disaster in Japan.
File photo from earlier this year of IEA executive director Fatih Birol (centre) with US energy secretary Chrtis Wright. Courtesy IEA.

title: Bruce Power To Share Nuclear Expertise As SaskPower Evaluates Reactor Technologies
author: David Dalton
text: Saskatchewan’s energy policy sets out pathway to nuclear generation

Canadian electricity company and nuclear operator Bruce Power has signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with utility SaskPower to share its expertise in nuclear generation, project development and long-term operations as Saskatchewan evaluates large nuclear technologies for potential use in the province.
In January, the government of Saskatchewan and SaskPower announced plans to formally evaluate large nuclear reactor technologies.

Saskatchewan’s energy security strategy sets out a pathway to nuclear power generation from both large nuclear reactors and small modular reactors (SMRs) to prepare for rising electricity demand and future export opportunities, including electricity and critical minerals such as potash and uranium, minister responsible for SaskPower Jeremy Harrison said.
“Collaboration is key to ensure we make informed, future-focused decisions that benefit our provinces and our country,” Harrison said.

With most of Canada’s nuclear industry and supply chain focused in Ontario, the MoU with Bruce Power will formalise information-sharing, enable alignment on federal and provincial nuclear strategy, and make use of Bruce Power’s national leadership in nuclear expertise, a Bruce Power statement said.

“We’re uniquely positioned to collaborate with SaskPower as it explores new nuclear to power the province with clean energy for the next generation,” said James Scongack, Bruce Power’s chief operating officer and executive vice-president. “We will share what we’ve learned in 25 years of operating the Bruce site and in planning projects and planning for new nuclear.”

The Bruce Power site was home to Canada’s first commercial reactor, Douglas Point, which operated from 1967 to 1984, and its current fleet of eight Candu pressurised heavy water reactors are being renewed to operate for several decades to come. Bruce Power is also exploring the option for a Bruce C project and up to 4,800 MW of new nuclear on its site.
The Bruce Power site has a fleet of eight Candu pressurised heavy water reactors. Courtesy Bruce Power.

title: Indiana Governor Signs Letter Of Intent On Nuclear Projects With Eli Lilly
author: David Dalton
text: US pharmaceutical company planning facilities for which energy needs will be substantial

The governor of the US state of Indiana, Mike Braun, has signed a nonbinding letter of intent that will see the state’s Office of Energy Development (OED) and Indiana-based pharmaceutical company Eli Lilly collaborate to explore potential nuclear projects.
The projects will focus on “small modular reactors and other advanced nuclear technologies” that could provide “baseload power for industrial, research, and community uses”, according to the LOI.

This partnership will tackle each major component of early-stage project development: evaluating technologies, regulatory pathways, opportunities to attract private capital and federal support, and workforce supply chain needs and opportunities.
The parties tentatively plan to collaborate on a variety of assessments covering grid siting, grid interconnection, infrastructure needs, overall costs, scheduling and project risks.
The LOI puts the OED in charge of coordinating with state and federal agencies; facilitating policy, permitting, and siting work; and supporting workforce and economic development initiatives.

For its part, Eli Lilly will evaluate technologies, provide input on energy demand, engage in discussions on long-term energy procurement deals, and collaborate on “onsite screening discussion for the Leap Research and Innovation District or other Lilly-affiliated locations”.

The Leap (Limitless Exploration Advanced Pace) Innovation and Research District is a parcel of land in the central Indiana city of Lebanon and the broader Boone County that is being developed by the Indiana Economic Development Corporation. The corporation aims to turn Leap into a hub for manufacturing and R&D facilities, along with corporate campuses.

In February, Meta broke ground in the Leap District on a $10bn (€8.5bn) data centre campus. Eli Lilly has announced more than $13bn in investment in Leap for various drug manufacturing facilities, for which energy needs are expected to be substantial
Indiana is not home to any commercial nuclear power plants, but the Eli Lilly agreement is not its first foray into nuclear project development in recent months.

In November, the state partnered with reactor start-up First American Nuclear, which plans to site its headquarters, manufacturing facilities, and a nuclear power plant in Indiana. First American Nuclear is developing the EAGL-1, a small, fast-spectrum reactor.
On 15 April, First American Nuclear announced that it has submitted its pre-licensing regulatory engagement plan for the EAGL-1 to the Nuclear Regulatory Commission.
Eli Lilly has announced more than $13bn in investment in the Leap district, for which energy needs are expected to be substantial. Courtesy Eli Lilly.

title: SMRs In Ireland Would Offer Energy Security And Help Meet Rising Demand, NIA Tells Inquiry
author: Nigel Davies
text: Nuclear association says small nuclear reactors could power needs of AI data centres

Small modular reactors (SMRs) would help Ireland to meet rising electricity demand and energy security, the London-based Nuclear Industry Association (NIA) has said in evidence to a parliamentary inquiry.

The British-Irish Parliamentary Assembly opened the inquiry in January to look at the role of nuclear power generation in long-term energy security. It called for submissions looking at the advantages of nuclear, its environmental impact, and the potential for cooperation between the UK and Ireland.
The assembly was established in 1990* as a link between the parliaments of the UK and Ireland to promote cooperation between the countries.

Ireland has no nuclear research reactors or commercial nuclear power plants. The country prohibits nuclear power generation under current legislation, although it engages in nuclear fusion research, such as the Iter project, via the National Centre for Plasma Science and Technology at Dublin City University.
In response to the inquiry, the NIA said the smaller size of both advanced modular reactors (AMRs) and SMRs made them particularly well suited for Ireland.

The NIA said that with peak demand in Ireland at 5-6 GW, a large-scale reactor being offline could cause a power outage, while a bundle of smaller 200-400 MW reactors would provide reliable clean power and strengthen grid stability.

The NIA said smaller reactors would also meet rising electricity demand in Ireland from industry, particularly from AI data centres. Electricity demand is forecast to be 2.5 times higher in Ireland by 2050 at around 82.25 TWh.
According to the International Energy Agency, Ireland derives around 41% of its electricity from natural gas, with an increasing expansion of renewables accounting for around 40% of demand.

The NIA said that to some extent Ireland already sourced some of its electricity demand through interconnections with Europe, and this would increase if proposals to create an interconnection with France were realised.

“Since France gets nearly 70% of its electricity from nuclear, this is an implicit recognition by the Irish government of the benefits of nuclear power generation for reliability, security and sustainability of power supplies,” the NIA said.
The NIA said it supported a rollout of another interconnection between the UK and Ireland.

“With the development of the Great British Energy-Nuclear and Rolls Royce SMR programme at Wylfa underway in North Wales, we would encourage the governments to explore deploying an interconnector to strengthen collective energy security.”
The NIA also argued that electricity bills would fall in Ireland if it adopted nuclear power, which would also promote investment and highly skilled jobs.

It said that according to data from the United Nations Economic Commission for Europe, nuclear has the lowest land use, lowest ecosystem impact and the lowest lifecycle carbon of all generating technologies at 5.1-6.4g CO2/kWh. The average carbon intensity of electricity is commonly measured in CO2/kWh (grams of equivalent per kilowatt-hour).

The NIA also urged a rethink in Scotland, which has also banned new nuclear capacity being built. It said that both Ireland and Scotland should look at Germany’s phaseout of nuclear energy, which had led to increasing electricity prices and had damaged its industrial competitiveness.
The NIA said both Scotland and Ireland would benefit from energy security and to meet their respective emissions goals by reversing policy on nuclear energy.

“To achieve net zero by 2050 with energy security and strong economic growth, we would strongly encourage the Republic of Ireland and the Scottish government to consider nuclear deployment alongside renewables,” the NIA said.

* In 2001 membership of the assembly was enlarged to include the Scottish Parliament, Senedd Cymru (the Welsh Assembly), the Northern Ireland Assembly, the Isle of Man’s parliament, the Tynwald and the legislatures of Guernsey and of Jersey.
The British government is backing plans for the deployment of Rolls-Royce small modular reactors in Wales. Courtesy Rolls-Royce SMR.

title: White House Releases Policy Designed To Launch Space Nuclear Power Systems By 2028
author: David Dalton
text: Nasa directed to start work within 30 days on ‘mid-power’ reactor with variant for lunar surface
The White House has released a policy directing Nasa, the Pentagon and the Department of Energy (DOE) to develop space nuclear power systems that could launch as soon as 2028.
The six-page policy, released on 14 April, follows an executive order issued by president Donald Trump in December that also set out plans for nuclear reactors on the moon.
The goal is to start launching reactors into space as soon as 2028, with a lunar surface version ready as early as 2030.

Reactors would be necessary for any lengthy stay on the moon because each lunar day and each lunar night lasts about 14 Earth days. That means any moon base will experience two weeks of darkness followed by two weeks of light, ruling out solar power as a reliable and permanent source of energy. There are no fossil fuels, wind or flowing water on the moon to otherwise generate power.

The new White House policy directs the Pentagon, Nasa and the Department of Energy (DOE) to run design competitions “to enable near-term demonstration and use of low- to mid-power space reactors in orbit and on the lunar surface.” Ultimately, the White House wants “high-power reactors” on the moon as soon as the next decade.

Under the plan, Nasa would start building a “mid-power” space reactor that would generate at least 20 kW of electrical power and could operate on the moon. The space agency would also work with outside companies to develop smaller reactors with the goal of launching them to the moon as soon as 2030. Eventually, these mini reactors would be scaled up, the plan states.

Michael Kratsios, director of the White House’s Office of Science and Technology Policy, announced the policy in a speech at the 41st Space Symposium, describing it as part of the implementation of the space policy executive order in December.
“Nuclear power in space will give us the sustained electricity, heating and propulsion essential to a permanent robotic and eventually human presence on the moon, on Mars and beyond,” he said.
The policy, he added, “creates the roadmap for the federal government to develop and deploy nuclear reactors on the moon and in orbit.”

The policy, designated NSTM-3, directs “parallel and mutually reinforcing” design competitions by Nasa and the Defense Department “to enable near-term demonstration and use of low- to mid-power space reactors in orbit and on the lunar surface, and prepare to deploy high-power reactors in the 2030s”.
The policy directs Nasa to start work within 30 days on a “mid-power” space reactor generating at least 20 kW of power, with a variant that can operate on the lunar surface.
It calls on the agency to work with multiple companies on reactor designs, including for a low-power system that produces as little as one kW “if doing so offers lower cost and schedule risk”.
Under the policy, Nasa would pick no more than two designs in one year for development, with a preference toward systems that can be later scaled up to 100 kW or more.
The policy calls on the Defense Department to provide a briefing to the White House in 90 days on potential uses and payloads for space nuclear systems of varying power levels.
The Pentagon will, in the first year of the policy, use its space nuclear funding to support Nasa’s efforts, then conduct its own competition for space nuclear power systems.

The DOE will provide its expertise in nuclear power systems, including a 60-day assessment of the readiness of the nuclear industrial base. It would also conduct “cross-cutting and mission-independent” research and development of space nuclear power technologies.

Nasa has already begun work on nuclear power technologies relevant to the policy when it announced last month a series of “transformative” initiatives including plans to launch a nuclear electric propulsion spacecraft to Mars in December 2028 and a three-phase plan to establish a lunar base incorporating nuclear-driven heat and power.
Nasa’s plans include launching Space Reactor-1 Freedom (SR-1 Freedom), the first nuclear powered interplanetary spacecraft, to Mars in December 2028.

NASA has released a ‘user’s guide’ that sets out three phases during which the agency will develop the capabilities, infrastructure and resources needed for a moon base. Ultimately, the goal is to set up the moon as a jumping-off point for an eventual Mars mission.

Kratsios noted that Nasa has spent more than $20bn (€16.9bn) on various nuclear power and propulsion projects over the last several decades, none of which flew. The new policy is intended to reverse that long-running trend.
Illustration of a conceptual nuclear-powered spacecraft. Courtesy Nasa.
An artist’s concept of a nuclear-powered moon base. Courtesy Nasa.

title: US Needs Comprehensive Nuclear Waste Strategy Incorporating Recycling and Disposal, Says Report
author: Nigel Davies
text: New analysis points to ‘strategically significant opportunity’ for Washington

The US must create an integrated nuclear waste strategy that combines recycling with disposal and that can help the country regain leadership in the industry, a report from the Washington-based thinktank Energy Innovation Report Project (EIRP) said.

The report, written in collaboration with advanced nuclear reactor manufacturer Oklo, said the economics of recycling have improved, recycling technologies have progressed and there are more advanced safeguards to limit proliferation concerns.

The report said that with approximately 94,000 metric tonnes of used nuclear fuel (UNF) accumulated in the US, and with no operational deep geologic repository (DGR), Washington must look to recycling to reduce permanent disposal levels. This would also help it recover valuable isotopes with energy, space, medical and industrial uses.

“Technological advances, new market dynamics, and high-assay low-enriched uranium (Haleu) supply constraints have created a strategically significant opportunity for the US to implement commercial nuclear fuel recycling,” the report said.

“By enacting supportive policies and taking associated federal actions, the US can responsibly reduce the burden of nuclear waste, enhance energy security, secure critical minerals, and reestablish global leadership in nuclear innovation – all steps that could have far-reaching economic and security benefits.”

However, it said the government should adopt a national policy statement for UNF, which would “provide strong signals to Department of Energy, industry and investors to accelerate commercial recycling efforts.”
In turn, the report recommended the creation of a national long-term waste strategy, with both recycling of UNF and the creation of a DGR as “critical elements of a comprehensive strategy”.

The EIRP report said a repository is needed in the US, but cautioned that current used fuel levels would already surpass the capacity of the abandoned Yucca Mountain repository project. For that reason, successful waste disposal would be easier to achieve if the quantity of waste was reduced through recycling.

Nuclear fuel recycling – or reprocessing – is the process of treating spent nuclear fuel to recover reusable uranium and plutonium, separating them from waste materials. By treating this fuel, roughly 96% of the spent material can be repurposed into new fuel.
In 2002, Yucca Mountain in Nevada was identified as a potential repository site, but a licence was never granted and the US Congress halted its funding in 2010.
Bi-partisan groups in the US have called for a company to lead waste management in the country and find a permanent solution.

The report suggested the government should support the construction of production-scale commercial recycling facilities led by the DOE, issuing service contracts to companies for UNF recycling services and providing tax credits for utilities recycling waste.

The report said that commercial recycling in the US would allow companies to recover uranium and transuranic elements from used fuel to enable the production of uranium/transuranic fuel, which can be used in certain advanced reactors instead of Haleu.
“This could serve as a stopgap fuel until sufficient domestic Haleu enrichment capabilities are established and could continue to supplement fuel material needs thereafter.”

The authors of the report argued that recent strong growth in the nuclear sector and expected demand for advanced reactors could change the economics of recycling, lowering the costs for recycling facilities.
Several companies in the US, including Oklo, are looking to establish the commercialisation of advanced recycling technologies.

The report added that the nuclear industry must continue to find new fuel sources. It said that in 2024, global annual uranium demand was 67,500 million tonnes, and that with an expected increase in reactor construction, existing uranium supplies would not last as long as the forecast 90 years.
In 2002, Yucca Mountain in Nevada was identified as a potential repository site, but funding eas stopped in 2010. Courtesy US DOE.

title: South Africa Study Recommends Thyspunt Site For New Nuclear Power Station
author: David Dalton
text: Gov’t has called for ‘thorough investigation’ into costs, financing, safety and benefits of reactors

Further studies on which site to select for state power company Eskom’s proposed 5,200 MW nuclear power station in South Africa should be limited to Thyspunt, about 700 km east of Cape Town, according to a draft environmental scoping report released for public comment.
The report says further investigation at the only other proposed site, Bantamsklip about 200 km east of Cape Town, should not be prioritised because of the area’s cultural landscape status.

Both sites encompass landscapes that have “a sense of place with strong coastal wilderness qualities”. Both would require overhead powerlines to connect the new plant to the national grid, the report says.
Bantamsklip is in “a very remote location” and constructing the new plant here would have “an acute impact” as there are few large distribution lines or load centres nearby.
However, at Thyspunt the rapid development of wind farms has created a large network of new powerlines that have already “severely degraded” that rural setting.
“From a spatial, technical, and infrastructure perspective [Thyspunt offers] clear advantages,” the report says.

Any project likely to cause significant environmental, social, heritage and economic impact – as defined in the National Environmental Management Act (Nema) – is subject to a formal environmental impact assessment (EIA). Scoping is the critical first screening step in this statutory process.
Eskom Holdings appointed WSP Group Africa to manage the new nuclear build impact assessment process.
The draft scoping report, which runs to 776 pages and scores of appendices, is available for public review and comment until 5 May.
It says that Thyspunt is already owned by Eskom and is appropriately zoned for nuclear development.

Thyspunt’s “reasonable proximity” to existing transmission infrastructure and load centres reduces the need for extensive new infrastructure and limits further land acquisition. It also lowers the potential for additional environmental and social impacts associated with grid connection, the report says.

“Specialist screening undertaken to date has not identified any unmitigable environmental constraints at Thyspunt,” the report says. It “is therefore recommended as the preferred site to be taken forward in the assessment process”.
This does not however mean Bantamsklip will never be considered for a future nuclear power plant, the report concludes. “This site is not fatally flawed and remains a viable site,” it states.

If the draft scoping report is accepted by South Africa’s Department of Forestry, Fisheries and the Environment, an EIA will then be carried out with independent specialist studies including air quality, water resources, biodiversity, heritage, land use, human health and socioeconomic conditions.

There is at least one potential stumbling block for Thyspunt. In January 2025, all Eskom’s properties at Thyspunt were collectively declared a provisional Grade I Cultural Landscape by the South African Heritage Resources Agency. This protection remains in place until 1 February 2027 and could be renewed.

The report says South Africa’s National Development Plan 2030 emphasises a diversified, secure, and sustainable energy mix, promoting renewables and clean coal, while calling for “a thorough investigation” into nuclear energy’s costs, financing, safety, and benefits as a potential baseload option, rather than an immediate commitment. The report notes that government policy has shown interest in nuclear procurement alongside a “just energy transition” to meet climate goals and ensure energy security, job creation, and industrial development.

Electricity and energy minister Kgosientsho Ramakgopa said last year that South Africa would move forward with plans to build a new nuclear power station and revive its pebble bed modular reactor (PBMR) programme.
He said a new plant would be built in Duynefontein near Cape Town, next to the existing Koeberg nuclear power station.

Reports said the facility will add 2.4 GW of nuclear capacity initially, suggesting it could have two large-scale units of around 1,200 MW each. Some reports quoted Ramakgopa saying the plant could add as much as 4 GW of capacity. It is unclear if this project is still being considered.

South Africa relies on coal to generate the bulk of its electricity and has suffered from blackouts caused by a combination of factors including insufficient generation capacity, ageing and poorly maintained coal power plants and a lack of new investment.
The two-unit Koeberg is South Africa’s only commercial nuclear power station and the only such facility in Africa, although Russia is building a new nuclear station in Egypt.
According to International Atomic Energy Agency data, nuclear energy provided about 5% of South Africa’s electricity generation in 2023.
The two-unit Koeberg is South Africa’s only commercial nuclear power station. Courtesy Eskom.

title: Outer Steel Dome Lifted Into Place For China’s Changjiang-4 Nuclear Plant
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Two indigenous Hualong One plants under construction at site

The outer steel dome of the nuclear island containment building has been lifted into place for Unit 4 of the Changjiang nuclear power station under construction in Hainan province, southern China, developer CNNC) said.
Changjiang-4 is a domestic Hualong One, or HPR1000, pressurised water reactor (PWR) unit with a gross design capacity of 1,200 MW. Construction began in December 2021.

The dome forms part of the reactor’s double containment building, which is designed to protect the reactor from external effects and withstand high external and internal pressures and protect against radiation release.
In April 2025, workers completed welding of the main circulation pipeline for Changjiang-4.
Two CNP-600 pressurised water reactors have been in commercial operation at the Changjiang site since 2015 and 2016.
A fourth unit at the site, Changjiang-3, also a Hualong One, has been under construction since March 2021.

China is moving forward with its indigenous Hualong One reactor technology, also known as the HPR1000. It is a Generation III pressurised water reactor technology jointly developed by CNNC and China General Nuclear Power Group.

According to the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), China has 60 commercial nuclear power plants in operation and 35 under construction, but the figure does not include the recent start of construction of Jinqimen-2.
An aerial view of the Changjiang-4 outer dome lifting operation on 13 Apr 2026. Image courtesy CNNC.

title: First-Of-A-Kind Microreactor Test Bed ‘Open For Business’ At US Idaho Laboratory
author: David Dalton
text: Facility ‘essential’ for testing and validation of new reactor designs

A “first-of-its-kind” microreactor test bed that will enable rapid development, testing and demonstration of privately developed advanced nuclear reactors has opened at the federal Idaho National Laboratory (INL) in the US.
INL said in a statement that the “highly anticipated” Demonstration of Microreactor Experiments (Dome) test bed at INL’s National Reactor Innovation Center (NRIC) is “open for business”.
The test bed will play a role in reinvigorating the American nuclear energy industry and meeting the nation’s need to produce abundant, affordable and reliable power, the statement said.

Dome was developed as a hands-on demonstration facility for industry. INL said the nation’s growing demand for advanced nuclear energy required a dedicated, world-class testing environment that only a US Department of Energy national laboratory could provide.

Following a number of executive orders issued by president Donald Trump in an effort to speed up nuclear development and deployment, construction of the test bed was accelerated by nearly a year to enable industry to meet the urgent need for advanced nuclear energy in the US.

“The Dome test bed will be a cornerstone of the Department of Energy’s comprehensive strategy to re-establish US. leadership in advanced nuclear technologies,” said Rian Bahran, deputy assistant secretary for nuclear reactors.

“By providing essential infrastructure for testing and validation of new reactor designs, Dome directly supports our programmatic goals, accelerating the development and deployment of innovative solutions vital for energy security and economic growth for the United States.”

Built from the repurposed Experimental Breeder Reactor-II dome, a former reactor facility at INL, the test bed provides a safe, flexible and capable environment for testing experimental reactor concepts and gathering performance data, INL said
Reactor developers will use that data to support design verification and future licensing.
According to INL, by offering real-world operating conditions and expert support, Dome is poised to significantly reduce the time and cost required to deploy next-generation nuclear technologies.
It is designed to host microreactor experiments generating up to 20 MW of thermal energy.

Dome experiments will be scheduled through an annual competitive application process. The sequencing of experiments is based on several criteria, including technology readiness, fuel availability and a regulatory approval plan. Applicants will fund their testing campaigns.
INL is preparing for Dome’s inaugural experiment, using nuclear fuel, this year. Radiant’s Kaleidos demonstration unit plans to start a year-long testing programme this spring.
California-based Radiant was selected by the DOE among 10 others under the 2025 reactor pilot programme which aims to see at least three advanced reactors reach criticality by 4 July 2026.

In April 2025, the DOE shortlisted Radiant as one of five companies for the first round of conditional Haleu (high-assay low-enriched uranium) allocations. The allocations aim to pull from existing DOE and National Nuclear Security Administration stockpiles to support near-term advanced reactor demonstrations.
The Demonstration of Microreactor Experiments (Dome) test bed at INL’s National Reactor Innovation Center. Courtesy INL.
Construction of the Dome test bed was accelerated by nearly a year. Courtesy INL.

title: South Korea’s Saeul-3 Nuclear Plant Gets Approval For First Criticality
author: David Dalton
text: Indigenous APR1400 PWR unit could begin commercial operation in September
South Korea’s nuclear regulator has completed all required inspections for first criticality of the Saeul-3 nuclear power plant, a key step towards commercial operation, potentially in September.
The Nuclear Safety and Security Commission (NSSC) said its inspections at Saeul-3, near Busan in the south of the country, showed the reactor can safely achieve a sustained nuclear chain reaction.
The NSSC began pre-operational inspections after issuing an operating licence in December.
The latest checks focused on systems required before the reactor reaches criticality.

“During this process, inspections were conducted on items that must be performed before criticality, such as nuclear fuel loading inspections and high-temperature functional tests,” the NSSC said. “As a result, it was confirmed that reactor criticality can be safely achieved.”

Construction of the indigenous 1,340-MW APR1400 pressurised water reactor unit at the Saeul nuclear station, formerly known as Shin-Kori, began in April 2017, but has been delayed by changes in government policy.
State nuclear operator Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power (KHNP) applied for the licence on 5 August 2020, alongside one for the identical Saeul-4 unit, construction of which began in September 2018.
The move comes as president Lee Jae Myung pushes for renewable energy, reversing course from the more pro-nuclear stance of his predecessor Yoon Suk Yeol.

Lee said in September that building more nuclear power plants is not realistic because it takes more than 15 years to construct a new facility from scratch. However, his government has been supportive of using reactors that are already online or have started construction.
Yoon, who served from 2022 until he was impeached and removed from office in 2025, resumed construction of nuclear reactors and planned to expand nuclear output.
Moon Jae-in, who served as president from 2017 to 2022, had overseen a nuclear phaseout policy that drew fierce resistance from industry and labour unions.

According to the International Atomic Energy Agency, South Korea has 26 nuclear units in commercial operation and two, Saeul-3 and -4, listed as under construction. The 26 plants provided 31.7% of the country’s electricity production share in 2024, the IAEA said.
Apart from Saeul-3 and -4, the previous government also wanted to complete construction of two additional delayed plants, Shin-Hanul-3 and -4.
Construction of Unit 3 at the Saeul nuclear station began in April 2017. Courtesy KHNP.

title: France Confirms Latest Cost Estimate Of €37 Billion For Cigéo Nuclear Repository
author: David Dalton
text: Regulator ASNR continuing review of construction licence application

A ministerial decree published in France has confirmed the latest cost estimate of the planned Cigéo deep geologic spent nuclear fuel repository at €33.4bn ($39bn) – €37bn including taxes – of which €9.7bn is for initial construction.
National nuclear waste agency Andra, which is responsible for the Cigéo project, said amount was calculated using economic conditions of January 2025.
The €37bn represents an increase of approximately 15% compared to the previous assessment in 2016, Andra said.

The cost was determined on the basis of an estimate submitted by Andra in May 2025. France’s three main producers of waste for the repository – state nuclear operator EDF, nuclear fuel cycle corporation Orano and the French Alternative Energies and Atomic Energy Commission – also gave input, along with the country’s nuclear regulator, the French Nuclear Safety and Radiation Protection Authority (ASNR).
Andra said in a statement after publication of the confirmed cost by the government that it will “strive to continue its cost control and optimisation efforts while maintaining safety as a priority”.

Andra said the cost of the Cigéo project will not be a burden for future generations. EDF, Orano and CEA have set aside reserves for the project which are regularly updated and dedicated funds have been allocated under the control of the state and ASNR.
The latest cost estimate provides waste producers with the information needed to adjust their provisions and dedicated funds.
Cigéo will be France’s centralised facility for long-term storage of high-level radioactive waste from nuclear power plants and other reactor facilities.
The facility is planned near the border of the Meuse and Haute-Marne departments in northeastern France, within the communes of Ribeaucourt, Bure, Mandres-en-Barrois, and Bonnet.

In June 2023 ASNR (then known as ASN) accepted and said it would begin reviewing an application by Andra for the construction of Cigéo. ASNR said a public inquiry is anticipated in the second half of 2026, targeting construction to potentially start around 2027.
Cigéo is for the disposal of the most high-level radioactive waste, which is also very long-lived.
There are no long-term waste facilities in operation anywhere in the world for high-level waste from civil nuclear power programmes.
According to the International Atomic Energy Agency, France, Finland and Sweden are the three countries that have made the most progress towards operating such facilities.
The Onkalo repository in Finland is likely to become the first operational deep geological disposal facility in the world with full startup scheduled for this year.

A rendering of Cigéo, which is planned to be France’s centralised facility for long-term storage of high-level radioactive waste from nuclear power plants and other reactor facilities. Courtesy Andra.

title: Return To Nuclear Sees Belgium Step Up Efforts On Innovative Therapies
author: Carl Deconinck
text: Conference hears call for more European cooperation and ‘encompassing regulatory framework’

The return of interest in nuclear energy has once again given Belgium “leverage” in the supply chain with tools available for innovative nuclear medicine treatments such as radioligand therapy, Stien Schrauwen, a member of energy minister Mathieu Bihet’s cabinet has said.
Schrauwen said an investigation into and production of radioligand therapy was “a strategic priority” with scientific value and a matter of national sovereignty in “a critical sector”.
Schrauwen said that in 2025, Belgium helped to treat almost 13 million patients worldwide by producing medical radioisotopes.

“Nuclear medicine is a true sector of excellence for our country,” she said. “We benefit from a unique ecosystem that brings together cutting-edge institutions, high-quality infrastructure, and internationally recognised expertise.

“This gives us a responsibility and an opportunity: to continue playing a leading role in Europe and around the world by making the most of our expertise. After all, behind these applications lie lives, hopes and care pathways.”
Schrauwen called for more European cooperation and an encompassing regulatory framework.
Schrauwen was speaking at a conference, ‘Scaling up nuclear medicine’, organised by the Belgian nuclear research centre SCK CEN.

SCK CEN said Belgium’s ambition is to embed radioligand therapy in Belgian cancer policy, prepare the healthcare system for the wide-scale deployment of radioligand therapy and position the country as an “international pioneer”.
Radioligand therapy is a precision cancer treatment that delivers radiation directly to cancer cells while minimising damage to healthy tissues and often resulting in fewer side effects.
It is used to treat neuroendocrine tumours and metastatic prostate cancer.
SCK CEN said around 400 clinical trials are underway worldwide to extend radioligand therapy to other types of cancer. Several of those are in the final clinical phase.

“The number of patients eligible for radioligand therapy is expected to increase tenfold or even fifteenfold by 2035 and we need to prepare for that now,” said Sarah Baatout, deputy director of the Nuclear Medical Applications Institute at SCK CEN. “The prospect of so many patients being able to benefit from this treatment is gaining increasing political traction.”
The conference heard that issues potentially hindering the expansion of radioligand therapy include infrastructure, long-term vision and legislation.
MEP Wouter Beke of the European People’s Party warned that the European market is fragmented and there are a lack of breakthrough companies in the bloc.

This is because research often does not cross over from universities to the market and scale ups do not happen enough. Beke said that in China, after clinical trials, new technologies can hit the market in around 30 days, while in the EU, it takes around 600 days.

Belgium has officially reversed its 2003 nuclear phaseout policy. In May 2025, parliament formally abandoned the exit, opting to extend the operational lives of its two remaining reactors, Doel-4 and Tihange-3 for 10 years until 2035.
The government is focussed on maintaining existing capacity and constructing new nuclear units.
International Atomic Energy Agency data shows that nuclear power generated about 42% of Belgium’s electricity in 2024, when five reactors were in commercial operation.

Radioligand therapy combines two essential components: a ligand* that binds to specific receptors on cancer cells and a radioactive substance – or radioisotope – that delivers targeted irradiation to those cells.
Once injected into the bloodstream, this combination navigates to the tumour and any metastases.
Once bound, the radioisotope irradiates the cancer cells in a precise way, causing them to die and the tumour to shrink.
Thanks to this precision approach, as much healthy tissue as possible is spared, resulting in fewer side effects and a better quality of life for the patient.
Belgium has two institutes – SCK CEN in Mol and the Institute for Radioelement in Fleurus – that are playing a vital role in the global production of medical radioisotopes.
* A ligand in biology is a molecule – such as a neurotransmitter, hormone, or drug – that binds specifically to a target protein, known as a receptor, to trigger a physiological response or signal.
Stien Schrauwen said an investigation into and production of radioligand therapy was ‘a strategic priority’. Courtesy SCK CEN.

title: Rolls-Royce SMR Signs Landmark Agreement For Three Reactors At Wylfa
author: David Dalton
text: Contract ‘unlocks delivery’ and is tangible example of government’s ‘golden age’ of new nuclear

Rolls-Royce SMR and UK government body Great British Energy - Nuclear (GBE-N) have signed a contract that enables work to start immediately on the delivery of three Rolls-Royce small modular reactors
(SMRs) at Wylfa, on the coast of Ynys Môn (Anglesey) in North Wales.
The three-unit project at Ynys Môn will generate at least 1,400 MW, supplying enough stable, clean electricity to power the equivalent of around three million of today’s homes for more than 60 years.
