Russia and Vietnam are also cooperating on the construction of a nuclear science and technology centre in Vietnam, which will include a Russian-designed research reactor, said Rosatom.
A feasibility study for the centre is expected to be completed in April 2026.
According to earlier reports, Vietnam aims to have its first nuclear power station online in Ninh Thuan before the end of 2031 and a second between 2036 and 2040.

In April 2025, the government approved a revised version of its national power development plan, allocating $136bn (€117bn) by 2030 to strengthen long-term energy security and including nuclear power for the first time.
The government had said its planned nuclear programme would involve building two nuclear power stations with a combined capacity of about 4,000 GW.

Vietnam had planned the two stations as far back as 2009, but the National Assembly rejected the proposal in 2016 on cost grounds. Hanoi had selected Rosatom and Japan Atomic Power Company to build the stations, agreeing to a loan of $8bn from Russia for the first facility, with construction originally planned to start in 2014.
In December 2024, lawmakers asked the government to resume the development of the nuclear power programme and Vietnam reached out to foreign reactor technology partners.

In January 2025, Vietnam and Russia signed an agreement to deepen cooperation on nuclear power, marking a potentially crucial development in Hanoi’s plans to revive abandoned plans to build commercial reactors.
In June, Bloomberg reported Vietnam was seeking urgent discussions with Russia to accelerate its nuclear programme and sign an investment cooperation agreement for a first nuclear power station.

According to a report by accountancy company PwC, Vietnam’s expected economic growth over the next three decades means a need for 150 GW in installed energy generation capacity by 2030, and 500 GW by 2050, from about 80 GW today.
The intergovernmental agreement was signed in Moscow on 23 March 2026. Image courtesy Rosatom.

title: EU Must Prioritise First SMR Irrespective Of Origin But With Key European Components, Says Commission Official
author: Nigel Davies
text: Bloc needs to have ‘fastest possible deployment,’ event hears

Europe must strive to establish its first small modular reactor (SMR) irrespective of where the technology comes from, as long as it is manufactured using key European components, deputy head of unit for Euratom Research at the European Commission Domenico Rossetti di Valdalbero said.

Speaking at an event organised by Brussels-based thinktank CEPS to discuss the EU’s recently announced SMR strategy, Rossetti said that the subject of SMRs was also heatedly discussed by the EU before the introduction of the Industrial Accelerator Act, which aims to advance industrial capacity and decarbonisation in Europe.
“There was a big tension at the EU level – should we have a European built SMR or would be prefer just to see a first deployment, even if it’s with an American or British design or others,” he said.

“The first priority for the EU is to have the fastest possible deployment, whatever the origin of the SMR, but with the Industrial Accelerator Act we mustn’t be naïve – that means that we want key components of an SMR being manufactured in Europe. That is quite important.”

He added that the EU’s research budget would be doubled in the areas of nuclear fission and fusion. For fission research that would mean going to €100m ($115m) from €50m a year. The budget for fusion was not specified but the Commission said
last week its fusion work programme will receive €220m over 2026 and 2027.

He said that while this was not enormous, on top of the proposed €200m guarantee fund recently announced under the EU’s SMR strategy, that it would provide a lever for other private investment to come into the sector.

Speaking at the same event, participants largely welcomed the EU’s SMR strategy, but several said there were many technologies being developed and the EU must end up converging on the best to become more competitive and standardised.
Andrei Goicea, member of the steering committee of the Industrial Alliance for SMRs at industry body Nucleareurope, argued that to some extent this was already beginning to happen.

He cited the example of SMRs for district heating by companies such as France’s Calogena and Finnish Steady Energy, who were collaborating together. In addition, France’s Newcleo was working with Eagles, with both companies developing lead-cooled fast reactor (LFR) technology.
“I think we are seeing that this sort of collaboration, and prioritisation of technologies in Europe has started,” said Goicea.

title: Second Tier Of Inner Steel Containment Installed At Russia’s Leningrad 2-3 Nuclear Plant
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Construction of VVER-1200 unit on Gulf of Finland began in 2024
The second tier of the inner steel containment has been installed for Unit 3 of the Leningrad 2 nuclear power station on the Gulf of Finland in Russia, state nuclear corporation Rosatom said.

The inner containment is part of the plant’s safety systems and, together with the outer containment, forms a double barrier designed to ensure leak-tightness under all operating conditions and protection against external impacts.
Leningrad 2-3 will be a VVER-1200 pressurised water reactor with a net capacity of 1,150 MW. Construction began in March 2024.

The installed segment weighs about 260 tonnes, said Rosatom, adding that following the latest works, the height of the reactor building has reached 22 metres out of a planned total of around 70 metres.

The full double containment structure is expected to be completed in 2028, said Rosatom. Installation of large nuclear island components, including the reactor pressure vessel and steam generators usually takes place before the containment is capped.
The Leningrad site has four units in operation and two that are permanently shut down. The operational units are Leningrad-3 and Leningrad-4, Leningrad 2-1 and Leningrad 2-2.

Leningrad-1 and Leningrad-2, both Soviet-era RBMK-1000 light-water graphite units, were permanently shut down in 2018 and 2020 respectively.Leningrad-3 and Leningrad-4, also of the RBMK-1000, are scheduled for retirement.
Concrete was poured in March 2025 for an eight unit at the site, Leningrad 2-4.
The second tier of the inner steel containment has been installed for the Leningrad 2-3 nuclear power plant Courtesy Rosatom.

title: US Enrichment Company General Matter To Export Nuclear Fuel To Japan
author: David Dalton
text: Move aims to reduce reliance on ‘adversarial supply chains’
US uranium enrichment company General Matter will export US nuclear fuel to Japan in a plan supported by up to $2.4bn (€2.09bn) in financing from the Export-Import Bank of the US.
The financing would support the purchase of General Matter enriched uranium by Japanese utilities.
General Matter said in a statement that Japan is advancing its 7th Strategic Energy Plan, which calls for nuclear power to play a central role in the country’s energy future.

It said US-made fuel gives Japanese operators a safe, secure alternative to Russian and Chinese enrichment, strengthening the alliance between the US and Japan while reducing both nations’ exposure to adversarial supply chains.
“American energy dominance means displacing Russia and other foreign producers who dominate global nuclear fuel markets,” General Matter said.
“Every ally that sources American fuel strengthens America's domestic supply chain and the resilience of our allies.”
General Matter says it is enriching uranium in the US to reshore nuclear fuel production and power the US energy production needed to lead in AI, manufacturing, and other critical industries.

The company’s first facility is under development in Paducah, Kentucky — the site where the US first industrialised uranium enrichment — and will be the nation’s first US-owned, privately developed uranium enrichment facility.
A nuclear plant in Japan, where the government wants nuclear power to play a central role in the country’s energy future. Courtesy Kansai Electric.

title: Swedish Nuclear Company Blykalla To Proceed With Planning For Small Modular Reactor Park
author: David Dalton
text: Facility to north of Stockholm could host six lead-cooled Sealer plants

Sweden-based nuclear reactor company Blykalla has said it will proceed with the next phase of planning for a small modular reactor (SMR) park in Norrsundet, Gävle, about 200 km north of Stockholm in southeast Sweden.
The company said it aims to begin the permitting process this year, following initial assessments confirming that the site offers suitable conditions for fossil-free energy production.

The proposed park is envisioned to consist of six of Blykalla’s lead-cooled Sealer reactors, with a total capacity of approximately 300 MW. This corresponds to the electricity demand of around 150,000 households, a large-scale industrial operation, or a medium-sized data centre. Blykall said the project is expected to generate 300-400 direct jobs and several thousand indirect employment opportunities in the region.

“The decision to move forward in Norrsundet is based both on the site’s favourable conditions and the growing need for stable, fossil-free electricity to enable industrial development,” said Blykalla chief executive officer Jakob Stedman “Gävle is a strategically important location where new power generation can support long-term growth and strengthen competitiveness.”
The project is subject to approvals from several authorities, including the Swedish Radiation Safety Authority, the Land and Environment Court, the Swedish Government, and Gävle Municipality.
Subject to the permits and final investment decisions, the facility could become operational in the first half of the 2030s.
Blykalla said it will now continue site investigations and detailed studies, alongside maintaining a dialogue with local stakeholders as the project progresses.

Blykalla is focused on two projects – the construction of an electric non-nuclear prototype test reactor at Oskarshamn and the development of a proposed flagship advanced reactor design demonstrator known as the Sealer-One.

The company will use the Sealer-One prototype to prepare for mass production of the 55-MW Sealer-55, which will be used for both industrial processes and electricity production. Due to their modular structure these SMRs can be produced in factories and shipped to their final locations.
Lead-cooled nuclear plants such as that being developed by Blykalla are not yet operating, but are being developed as next-generation, or Generation IV, reactors.
In December Blykalla raised $50m (€42m) of fresh capital to accelerate its work on the Sealer SMR, which it says could help power data centres and other big tech or industrial facilities.
A rendering of a Blykalla small modular reactor nuclear power plant. Courtesy Blykalla.

title: NRC Seeks Industry Input On Future New Reactor Licensing Plans
author: David Dalton
text: Move is part of efforts to safely enable nuclear technologies

The US Nuclear Regulatory Commission is asking applicants for new reactor-related activities to share planning information so it can set budgets for licensing reviews and inspection support needed to safely enable new nuclear technologies.
The commission said it is asking for the information through fiscal year 2028.

NRC staff published a regulatory issue summary (RIS) so the agency can “best understand industry interest in order to most effectively set budgets for licensing reviews and inspection support needed to safely enable new nuclear technologies”.
The RIS reminds potential applicants that the earliest possible engagement with the NRC helps produce the most efficient reviews.

The RIS asks reactor developers, existing licence holders and existing or potential licensing applicants to voluntarily outline the types, quantity and timelines of expected requests for licence amendments, preapplication interactions or new licensing applications.
Additional topics include potential reactor technologies and fuels, collaboration with the Department of Energy or academic institutions, and projected construction schedules.
The NRC is also reminding advanced reactor applicants and pre-applicants that they may qualify for reduced licensing fees under provisions of the Advance Act, passed in 2024.
A statement said advanced nuclear pre-applicants are encouraged to submit a licensing project plan or regulatory engagement plan and
periodically submit updates with planned activities to qualify for the reduced licensing fees.
Courtesy American Nuclear Society.

title: APS To Seek Licence Renewal For All Three Units At Palo Verde Nuclear Station
author: David Dalton
text: Move could extend operations at Arizona facility until the mid-2060s

Energy company Arizona Public Service (APS) has officially notified the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) of its intent to renew the operating licences for all three units at Palo Verde nuclear power station, which could extend operations from the mid-2040s to the mid-2060s.
The facility, to the west of Phoenix, has three large pressurised water reactor units that began commercial operation between January 1986 and January 1988.

APS said Palo Verde is the heart of its energy mix, playing a vital role in supporting Arizona’s economic development by providing 24/7 reliability. With the capacity to produce 4,200 MW of clean, carbon-free electricity for four million homes and businesses, Palo Verde is the largest power generator in the western US.

In the 1980s, the NRC licensed Palo Verde’s nuclear units to operate for 40 years. In 2011, the NRC approved APS’s renewal application to extend the operating licences 20 years, allowing the three units to operate through the mid-2040s.

On 13 March 2026, APS filed a notice of intent to submit a subsequent licence renewal application to the NRC in late 2027. The application will seek to renew Palo Verde’s operating licence for an additional 20 years, allowing Unit 1 to operate until 2065, Unit 2 until 2066 and Unit 3 until 2067.

After APS files the application, the NRC will evaluate Palo Verde’s strategy to maintain the plant over time, plan for environmental protection and ability to operate safely. APS said public participation is an important part of the licence renewal process, and the NRC will hold public meetings to share information and seek input.

APS said that as nuclear power continues to support the nation’s energy needs, a licence renewal would extend Palo Verde’s life to 80 years. APS is following the NRC’s established licence renewal process, which has resulted in renewing licences to 80 years for 10 stations across the country. The NRC is currently reviewing applications for three stations.
APS is also assessing new nuclear technologies and leading a collaborative effort with Salt River Project and Tucson Electric Power to explore and advance additional nuclear generation in the state.
In 2025, the utilities teamed up to apply for a grant from the US Department of Energy for funding to support the evaluation of possible sites.

APS said that while awaiting a decision, the three utilities continue to move forward with their siting efforts as they consider many types of nuclear energy solutions, including small modular reactors and large reactor projects.
The three-unit Palo Verde nuclear power station. Courtesy APS.

title: Thorizon And Hyundai E&C To Work Together On MSR Development And Deployment
author: David Dalton
text: Dutch-French company developing Thorizon One nuclear plant

Thorizon, the Dutch-French nuclear technology company developing molten salt reactors, and South Korea-based Hyundai Engineering & Construction (Hyundai E&C), have signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) to jointly advance the development and future deployment of molten salt reactor (MSR) technology.

The agreement was signed at Thorizon’s headquarters in Amsterdam by Thorizon chief executive officer Kiki Lauwers and Thorizon founder Sander de Groot, Founder of Thorizon, with Young Choi, Hyundai E&C chief operating officer.

Under the MOU, the companies will explore areas of cooperation related to the development and commercialisation of Thorizon reactors. This includes collaboration on engineering and design activities, preparation for participation in future reactor projects and joint engagement with industrial energy users.

Thorizon said the collaboration reflects the growing global momentum behind advanced nuclear technologies and the importance of combining breakthrough reactor technologies with experienced industrial partners capable of delivering large-scale energy infrastructure.
Thorizon is developing the Thorizon One, a modular molten salt reactor designed to provide reliable carbon-free electricity and industrial heat for energy-intensive sectors.

Thorizon said the reactor operates at low pressure and high temperature and is designed to contribute to a stable and sustainable energy system. It has the potential to reuse spent fuel from conventional reactors to extract remaining energy from it.

Thorizon, originally a spin-off from the Dutch nuclear research institute NRG, said recently that several Dutch provinces have confirmed their engagement and are now assessing potential sites for a demonstrator plant, as well as opportunities to establish an innovation hub around the facility with testing capabilities for materials and components.
Thorizon chief executive officer Kiki Lauwers and Hyundai E&C chief operating officer Young Choi. Courtesy Thorizon.

title: US And Japan Companies Announce Partnership To Accelerate ‘Global Commercialisation’ Of Fusion Energy
author: David Dalton
text: Agreement outlines several key areas of nuclear reactor development
US-based Realta Fusion and Kyoto Fusioneering (KF) have announced a bilateral partnership designed to accelerate the global commercialisation of fusion energy.
Realta said the agreement outlines several areas of joint technological development that builds on the strengths of both companies.

KF, a Japan-based fusion engineering and integrated systems company, will bring its expertise to the design, engineering and fabrication of plasma heating systems optimised for use in Realta’smagnetic mirror nuclear fusion machines.

Realta and KF will also explore the design and deployment of mirror-based neutron sources that can be used to qualify materials and de-risk the development of tritium blanket breeding and fuel cycle systems for fusion reactors.
In the first phase of the partnership, Realta has purchased gyrotrons – the high-powered microwaves that help heat fusion plasmas to many times the temperature of the sun – from KF.
The gyrotrons will be installed on Realta's first commercial-grade fusion machine, which will be located in their planned research and development facility known as The Realta Forge.
Pictured, left to right: Keishi Sakamoto (KF), Dominick Bindl (Realta), Kieran Furlong (Realta), Kiyoshi Seko (KF), Yuhei Nozoe (Fusion Fuel Cycles), Yuto Yoshioka (KF). Courtesy Realta Fusion.

title: New Strategy Makes UK ‘First Country’ To Establish Clear Path Towards Nuclear Fusion
author: David Dalton
text: Government also awards £200 million contract for construction of Step reactor

The UK government has launched a nuclear fusion strategy that it says makes the country the first to establish a clear national path towards commercial fusion energy in a bid to contribute to energy security.
The plan involves creating a market framework intended to attract private investment into fusion electricity.
A central project is the Step prototype fusion power plant, planned for a former coal facility at West Burton in Nottinghamshire, northern England.

The government said UK Industrial Fusion Solutions will appoint a consortium called Ilios as construction partner for the Step programme under a £200m (€231m, $266m) contract that is a “major milestone” in transforming the West Burton site into the UK’s world-leading prototype fusion energy plant.
The announcement follows the publication of the government’s new fusion strategy, setting the direction for the UK’s long-term approach to developing and delivering fusion energy.
Ilios is a consortium led by a joint venture between Kier and Nuvia, and supported by AECOM, AL_AArchitects and Turner & Townsend.

The appointment comes as UK Industrial Fusion Solutions Ltd, soon to be known as UK Fusion Energy Ltd, enters the next phase of delivery for the Step programme. The government said the name change reflects the organisation’s growing focus on delivering the prototype fusion plant at West Burton in Nottinghamshire, northern England, and its ambition to lead the industrial team that will design and build future commercial fusion facilities.
UK Industrial Fusion Solutions Ltd is a wholly owned subsidiary of the  UK Atomic Energy Authority, which is responsible for delivering the  Step programme.
Step is the Spherical Tokamak for Energy Production, a prototype power plant at the now decommissioned West Burton coal-fired power plant. The aim is to have the plant online by 2040.

Paul Methven, chief executive officer of UK Industrial Fusion Solutions and responsible officer for Step Fusion, said the appointment of Ilios as construction partner marks a significant milestone for the Step programme. He said: “Their combined experience in major infrastructure, safety-critical engineering and complex site transformation gives us real confidence as we move from planning into delivery. This partnership will help ensure that West Burton becomes a leading centre of fusion innovation and a cornerstone of the UK’s future clean energy landscape.”
Ilios will be responsible for every aspect of construction at the West Burton site, including acting as principal design and build contractor and delivering all construction work.
Last year the UK government announced over £2.5bn of funding in support of the Step programme. Earlier last year the government promised £410m in fiscal year 2025 for the project.

“Britain is another step closer to a future powered by clean, virtually limitless energy as the government launches its fusion strategy, backing British jobs, investment and energy sovereignty and delivering on its industrial strategy,” a statement said.

“The current conflict in the Middle East shows the only route to energy sovereignty for the UK is to end its dependence on fossil fuel markets and accelerate the transition to clean homegrown power, with fusion holding the potential to revolutionise the energy system and ensure lasting energy abundance and security.”

Welcoming the fusion strategy announcement, Tom Greatrex, chief executive of the London-based Nuclear Industry Association, said the government’s continued investment in fusion is a welcome signal of the UK’s ambition to lead in one of the most exciting clean energy technologies.
“Sustained funding is essential to turn the UK’s world-leading research into commercial projects, new supply chains and high-skilled jobs across the country,” he said.
“Backing programmes such as Step and the wider capabilities needed for fusion development will help ensure the UK remains at the forefront of the global race to bring fusion energy to market.”
A rendering the prototype Step nuclear fusion reactor planned in the UK. Courtesy UKAEA.

title: NRC Annual Assessment Places 5 of 95 US Reactors in Second Performance Category For 2025
author: Nigel Davies
text: Five reactors will need additional inspection and corrective actions

The US Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) said that five of the country’s 95 operational reactors came in the second-of-five performance safety and security categories in 2025, meaning they would require additional inspection and follow-up corrective action.
The NRC said in a statement that the five in the second category were Hope Creek (New Jersey), South Texas Project Unit 2, Summer (South Carolina) and Watts Bar-1 and -2 (Tennessee).
The regulator said that “five reactors were in the second performance category for 2025 as they need to resolve one or two items of low safety significance”.

The country’s other 90 reactors were all ranked in the top category for their safety and security. The NRC said that the Waterford-3 site in Louisiana was also ranked in the top band, having resolved issues of low safety significance over the year.
No reactors were ranked in the lowest three categories, with the lowest requiring a reactor to shut down in order to address performance problems.

The NRC said it would host meetings in the spring and summer to discuss the annual assessments for each plant. Plants will also receive an NRC inspection plan for the year ahead, with ongoing updates available.
Watts Bar-1 and -2 in Tennessee were among five nuclear plants in the second category. Courtesy Bechtel.

title: Russia’s Kursk 2-1 Nuclear Plant Reaches Full Power Ahead Of Commercial Operation
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Site near border with Ukraine will be home to four VVER-TOI power reactors

Unit 1 of the new Kursk 2 nuclear power station in Russia has reached 100% of its design output as part of commissioning tests before entering commercial operation, a statement by operator Rosenergoatom said.

Rosenergoatom said the VVER-TOI pressurised water reactor unit, which is currently in pilot industrial operation, has gradually increased output from 40% to full power since it was first connected to Russia’s power grid in December 2025.
Construction of the 1,200-MW Kursk 2-1 began in 2018, and the unit reached first criticality in May 2025.

Plant director Alexander Uvakin said further tests at full power will examine the reactor core’s neutron-physical characteristics, the performance of reactor monitoring systems and the plant’s behaviour under different operating conditions, including a simulated complete loss of external power.
The tests will also verify the effectiveness of radiation protection systems and assess the radiological conditions at the plant.

Rosenergoatom said final approval for commercial operation will be granted by Rosenergoatom after Russia’s nuclear regulator Rostekhnadzor confirms that all systems of the start-up complex are ready. The unit is expected to enter commercial operation later this year.
The Kursk 2 nuclear power station is being built to replace four existing RBMK graphite-moderated reactors at the site. Two of those RBMK units, Kursk-1 and -2, were shutdown in 2021 and 2024.
Kursk 2 will have four VVER-TOI units, with the first two under construction, and an additional two under planning and preparation.
According to International Atomic Energy Agency data, Russia has 34 nuclear plants in commercial operation and four – not including Units 3 and 4 at Kursk 2 – under construction.
The Kursk 2-1 control room. Image courtesy Rostom / Alexei Duginov.

title: Study Highlights Economic Benefits Of Proposed AP1000 Buildout In US
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Construction of ten reactors could generate billions in GDP

Building a fleet of ten AP1000 nuclear reactors in the US could generate $92.8bn (€85bn) in gross domestic product (GDP) and support an average workforce of more than 44,000 jobs annually during a 13-year construction phase, according to a PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC) study conducted for Westinghouse.

Westinghouse announced plans in July 2025 to deploy ten AP1000 units in the US, with construction intended to begin by 2030. The 11.5 GW fleet is expected to support the US government's aim to quadruple nuclear energy capacity from around 100 GW today to 400 GW by 2050.

The PwC analysis, based on economic modelling using Westinghouse data, calculates economic impacts at three levels: direct effects from spending on labour and capital; indirect effects from activity in the supply chain; and induced effects from consumer spending by employees in those supply chains.

The report found that during construction, direct GDP impact alone is projected at $39.2bn, with indirect and induced effects adding a further $53.6bn. The study estimates $20.1bn in tax revenues over the construction period.

Over a minimum 80-year operating lifespan, the cumulative GDP impact is estimated at $1.03tn, the report said. Over the same period, estimations are also for $329bn in labour income and $271bn in tax revenues.
PwC also said it projects around 5,000 direct operational jobs once the AP1000 fleet is running, with the total workforce including indirect and induced roles estimated at 22,500.
The AP1000 is a Generation III+ pressurised water reactor with net electrical output of 1,117 MW.

Six AP1000 reactors are currently in operation worldwide. Two units are operating at the Vogtle nuclear station in the US state of Georgia. Four units are operating in China at the Sanmen and Haiyang nuclear power stations.
Two additional AP1000 units at the V.C. Summer project in South Carolina were suspended in 2017 after cost overruns.
Westinghouse said it has 14 additional AP1000 under construction, all in China, and five more under contract in Poland and Bulgaria.
There are two commercially operational AP1000 reactors in the US: Units 3 and 4 at the Vogtle nuclear power station in Georgia. Image courtesy Georgia Power.

title: Germany Pushes Back On EU SMR Strategy Amid Domestic Debate
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Berlin signalled nuclear debate shift, but no reversal planned

Germany’s government has reacted critically to the European Commission’s new strategy for small modular reactors, with environment minister Carsten Schneider rejecting plans for further support for nuclear power and describing the initiative as a “backward-looking strategy”.

The strategy, announced by European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen at the Nuclear Energy Summit in Paris on 10 March, proposed a framework to support the development and deployment of SMRs in Europe during the 2030s.

In a statement responding to von der Leyen’s remarks about the retreat from nuclear energy being “a strategic mistake”, Schneider said the proposal relied on additional subsidies for a technology that has struggled to demonstrate commercial viability.
“If a risky technology is still dependent on state support after three-quarters of a century, and better alternatives have long existed, then consequences should be drawn,” Schneider said.
He said Germany would continue to rely on wind and solar, which he called cleaner, safer and cheaper.
Chancellor Friedrich Merz, leader of the conservative Christian Democrats and Schneider's Social Democrats’ senior coalition partner, has given mixed signals on nuclear power.

In September 2025, Merz and France’s president Emmanuel Macron agreed to recognise the role of nuclear power in Europe’s energy transition, potentially ending years of friction between the countries over energy policy, including subsidies for reactors.

In January, Merz called the nuclear phaseout "a serious strategic mistake" and said Germany simply did not have enough generation capacity. "To have acceptable market prices for energy production again, we would have to permanently subsidise energy prices from the federal budget," he said. "We can't do this in the long run."
But during a visit to the Czech Republic this week, Merz said rolling back the phaseout was not possible.
"I regret this," he said, "but it is the way it is, and we are now concentrating on the energy policy we have."

According to public broadcaster Deutsche Welle (DW), Germany’s Christian Democrats and ally allied Bavarian Christian Social Union have been supportive of nuclear power. The parties included nuclear power in political campaigning prior to the February 2025 federal elections.
However, DW said a reversal would need a majority in the Bundestag, Germany's lower house, and would require the votes of the far-right Alternative for Germany, which Merz has ruled out working with.

The German nuclear industry group KernD struck a more pragmatic note. It said Germany, with its large industrial base, could in theory benefit directly from SMR deployment. But even if domestic construction remained politically impossible, German companies and universities still held relevant competencies ranging from enrichment and fuel development to primary circuit components, pumps, instrumentation and control systems.
KernD said participation in Europe's nuclear supply chain would contribute to industrial value creation, maintain employment and preserve nuclear competency in Germany.

The country’s last three nuclear power plants, Isar-2, Neckarwestheim-2 and Emsland, were permanently shut down in April 2023, making good on the country’s delayed nuclear phaseout even amid Europe’s energy crisis caused by Russia’s war in Ukraine.

Until March 2011, when Germany’s older reactors were shut down immediately after the Fukushima disaster in Japan, Germany generated one-quarter of its electricity from nuclear energy with 17 reactors.
In June 2011, Berlin ordered the immediate shutdown of eight of the country's 17 commercial reactors. The decision also outlined a timeline for taking the rest of the nuclear plants offline by 2022.

The International Energy Agency said in its 2025 energy policy review for Germany that variable renewable generation had already exceeded 60% in 2024 but that Germany had "relatively low levels of large-scale electricity storage." The agency also flagged concerns about generation adequacy as coal and gas plants close and demand rises.

The EU's recent SMR strategy calls on member states to coordinate on reactor designs, licensing and supply chains and warns that a fragmented approach would lead to higher costs and slower deployment. Preliminary estimates put expected EU SMR capacity by 2050 at between 17 GW and 53 GW. SMR plants have not been commercially deployed in the Western world.

Germany closed its last nuclear power plants in April 2023​ as part of the Energiewende (energy transition) policy, which aims to shift the country towards renewable energy sources. Berlin had the second largest nuclear fleet in Europe. Image courtesy i_aoquadrado / Flickr. CC BY-SA 2.0.

title: Bulgaria Says New Kozloduy Reactors Could Add €55Bn To Economy
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Financing structure to rely on export credit agency loans, say reports

The planned construction of two new nuclear reactor units at the Kozloduy nuclear power station in Bulgaria could generate more than €55bn ($63bn) in economic value for the country over a lifetime of at least 60 years, according to an analysis presented by the project developer.

Petyo Ivanov, chief executive of state-owned Kozloduy NPP-New Build, told a conference earlier this week that Units 7 and 8 could contribute more than €9bn to the country’s gross domestic product during the construction phase alone.

US-based Westinghouse Electric was selected in 2023 to supply its AP1000 pressurised water reactor technology for the project. In early 2024, Sofia chose South Korea’s Hyundai E&C for the construction, delivery and eventual commissioning of the two proposed units, to be known as Kozloduy-7 and -8.

Speaking at the Regional Energy Summit 2026 in Sofia organised by the Bulgarian daily Kapital, Ivanov said every euro invested in the two new reactors could generate about €2.7 for the Bulgarian economy.
Ivanov said the project could create around 7,000-8,000 jobs during construction and around 1,200 long-term positions once the units begin operation, which is expected in the later 2030s.

Referring to the Europaen Union’s emission trading system, Ivanov told Kapital
that two new reactor units are expected to deliver annual savings of more than €500m to €600m by avoiding carbon emissions costs.

"On an annual basis, we expect savings of over €600m with just one unit in operation," Ivanov was quoted as saying by Kapital. "Even at the current price of over €70 per tonne of CO2, the value exceeds €500m."

Kapital reported that the project is still preparing key steps ahead of a final investment decision, which must be approved by the Bulgarian parliament and will determine the final cost of the project. According to the report, the financial structure could include about 20-30% equity financing and 70–80% debt, with loans expected to be provided mainly through export credit agencies.

The project company is also preparing
documentation for a state aid notification to the European Commission, a required step before the project can move forward.

Press reports said that so far about BGN 500m (€255m, $304m) has been spent on preparatory activities under contractual obligations including the engineering services contract signed in November 2024 with Westinghouse and Hyundai.

The first concrete for Unit 7 could be poured around 2030, subject to regulatory approvals and a final investment decision, Kozloduy NPP-New Build officials said earlier. Operation is not expected before 2036.

According to 2023 reports, Sofia had expected the cost of the Kozloduy new-build project to remain around $14bn. However, media reports in Bulgaria have said a more recent estimate for the proposed two new units may now be closer to $16bn.

Kozloduy, on the Danube River in northern Bulgaria, is the country’s only commercial nuclear power station and provides about a third of its electricity. There are two 1,000-MW Russia-designed VVER units in operation at the site and four older VVER-440 PWRs under decommissioning.
Kozloduy NPP-New Build CEO Petyo Ivanov at the Regional Energy Summit in Sofia on 10 March 2026. Image courtesy Kozloduy NPP-New Build.
The Kozloduy nuclear power station in northern Bulgaria.

title: Rolls-Royce SMR, Equilibrion To Study Nuclear-Powered Aviation Fuel Production
author: Kamen Kraev
text: IEA says supply of sustainable aviation fuel remains limited

UK small modular reactor developer Rolls-Royce SMR and project development company Equilibrion have signed an agreement to study the potential for producing sustainable aviation fuel using nuclear energy.

Equilibrion said in a statement that under the memorandum of understanding, the companies will carry out a technical and economic assessment of producing power-to-liquids sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) using electricity and heat from small modular reactors.

The study will examine how Rolls-Royce SMR power plants could supply the energy needed for Equilibrion’s Eq.flight system, a modular technology designed to produce synthetic aviation fuel at commercial scale.

According to the companies, one SMR could support production of more than 160 million litres of sustainable aviation fuel a year, potentially meeting about one-third of the UK’s projected power-to-liquids SAF demand by 2040.

The project is supported by a grant from the UK government’s Advanced Fuels Fund administered by the UK Department for Transport. Equilibrion and its partners plan to demonstrate the Eq.flight system in the UK by 2030 to confirm both the technical viability and economic case of the system.
The companies said nuclear energy could provide stable and low-carbon electricity and heat needed for large-scale production of synthetic fuels for aviation.

Global supply of sustainable aviation fuel currently accounts for less than 1% of aviation fuel demand, while the UK has set a target for SAF to make up 22% of aviation fuel use by 2040, said Equilibrion.

Sustainable aviation fuel is produced from renewable or low-carbon sources such as biomass, waste oils or synthetic fuels and can significantly reduce lifecycle emissions compared with conventional jet fuel, according to the International Energy Agency (IEA) and the International Air Transport Association.

The IEA says sustainable aviation fuel supply remains limited because production costs are higher than conventional jet fuel and scaling output requires major investment in new facilities, feedstocks and low-carbon energy sources.
Sustainable aviation fuel currently accounts for less than 1% of aviation fuel demand. Image courtesy Creative Commons. AI used in generation.

title: NuScale And Framatome Expand Partnership On SMR Fuel Supply
author: Nigel Davies
text: Agreement to see extended manufacturing in Europe and US
US small modular reactor (SMR) developer NuScale has extended its fuel supply agreement with Framatome to cover projected demand in both the US and Europe.
NuScale said that under the agreement, Framatome would produce fuel for its European SMR customers at its facilities in Europe.
The company also said that Framatome will be expected to supply at least 444 fuel assemblies for its first US customers as early as 2030 from its Richland, Washington, manufacturing site.
Framatome’s Richland facilities would produce NuScale’s NuFuel-HTP2 fuel based on its HTP fuel and spacer grid technology, said a statement.
HTP is a Framatome pressurised water reactor fuel design used in many operating reactors worldwide, using advanced zirconium-alloy cladding and spacer-grid structure.
The agreement will support NuScale’s “supply chain and manufacturing milestones,” said Carl Fisher, chief operating officer at NuScale.
Framatome plans to modify its fuel licence in the US to deliver low-enriched uranium fuel fuel above 5% of U-235 under its advanced fuel management programme.

NuScale’s most advanced project is a 462-MW nuclear generation facility in Romania on the site of a former coal-fired plant. A final investment decision was approved by the country’s government in February.

Under the plan for the site, project company RoPower Nuclear would use six of NuScale’s 77-MW SMR modules. The first SMR module is scheduled for operation in July 2033, with the entire facility completed by the end of 2034.
Energy developer Entra1 owns the global rights to the commercialization and distribution of NuScale’s SMRs.
In Europe, Framatome has fuel production sites in France and Germany. The company is owned the EDF Group (80.5%) and Mitsubishi Heavy Industries (19.5%).
Framatome’s HTP fuel design modified for NuScale’s SMR design. Image courtesy NuScale/Framatome.

title: Amentum To Lead Decommissioning Services At EU Nuclear Research Centres
author: Nigel Davies
text: Contract for $112m across four sites

US-based engineering company Amentum will lead a joint venture which has been awarded a $112m (€96m) contract by the European Commission Joint Research Centre for decommissioning and waste management work at four of its sites across the EU, a statement said.
The two-year extendable joint venture contract will also include engineering company WSP Italia and subcontractors TUV Rheinland and Protection Solution SRL, said the statement.
Together the companies will provide decommissioning solutions to accelerate the cleanup efforts at sites in Ispra (Italy), Karlsruhe (Germany), Geel (Belgium) and Petten (Netherlands).
This work will include the decommissioning of research reactors, hot cells, accelerators, laboratories and other infrastructure at these sites.
Amentum said the contract can be extended by two years a total of three times to cover the timeframe of full decommissioning, and that it already had experience working at the Ispra site in Italy.
The EU has also set up initiatives such as the Nuclear Decommissioning Knowledge Management initiative to learn from the decommissioning at the four sites.
The JRC Ispra site (foreground) near Lake Maggiore in northern Italy.

title: Macron Says Nuclear Key To Meeting Climate Goals And Powering Future Industries
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Paris summit speech highlights financing barriers, cooperation, and uranium independence
The world cannot achieve decarbonisation, energy independence, and economic competitiveness without nuclear energy, French president Emmanuel Macron said.

Speaking at the Nuclear Energy Summit in Paris today, Macron said nuclear energy was “uniquely placed” to reconcile three objectives shared by all countries: affordable and competitive energy, low-carbon electricity production, and strategic independence from fossil fuel imports.
"Without nuclear, we will not be able to meet the objective of decarbonisation and carbon neutrality by 2050 while continuing to create jobs and having dispatchable and abundant energy," he said.

Macron also pointed to the growing demands of artificial intelligence and digital infrastructure as a new argument for nuclear. Countries that tried to develop AI capacity using fossil fuels or new drilling would deepen “the climate dilemma” he said.

On France's own programme, Macron said the country had already decided to build six new EPR2 reactors and was programming eight more. A nuclear policy council would take place in two days to take further decisions based on the multiannual energy programme approved in February.
"Things are moving as they should," he said.

France operates 56 commercial reactors units, providing about 70% of the country’s electric generation. The newest 57th unit, Flamanville-3, was connected to the grid in December 2024 after years of delays and cost overruns, but though it recently reached full power, has not yet begun commercial operation.
On financing, Macron said Europe had spent years methodically constructing rules that prevented banks and insurers from financing nuclear.

"We had methodically done everything so that our banks and insurance companies could never finance nuclear," he said. "We were not in agreement among ourselves, so there was no technological neutrality in our financing rules. We come from very far back. We were very bad."
He welcomed the return of private capital to the sector and the European Investment Bank's recent support, but said European banks and insurers needed to do far more.
Macron called for a major European project of common interest for nuclear, equivalent to those already established for hydrogen and batteries, with a particular focus on SMRs.

On uranium supply, Macron issued a warning about Europe's dependence on Russia, which he said accounts for 40% of global enrichment capacity. "We must cooperate at the international level to diversify our supply," he said. He named Mongolia, Kazakhstan, Canada, Australia and Uzbekistan as countries with uranium reserves that could help reduce that dependence.
Rafael Grossi, director-general of the International Atomic Energy Agency said the conditions today clearly pointed toward the full integration of nuclear energy into the global energy mix.

Grossi said: "Nuclear power is not simply a nice-to-have, or a cleaner option. It is a strategic opportunity and we know it. When we speak about development, we speak about electrification, digitalization and artificial intelligence; in all these areas, we will need reliable and predictable answers. Nuclear energy is one of those answers."

He gave Ukraine as a “powerful example” of nuclear's reliability, noting that 70% of the country's electricity currently comes from nuclear power. In February 2022, Russian forces invaded Ukraine and currently hold about a fifth of the country’s territory in the east and southeast.
"When we say predictability, when we say reliability, we know what we are talking about," he said.

Grossi said the sector's two biggest practical challenges were harmonising licensing and regulation unlocking financing, but without lowering safety standards. He welcomed a shift in attitude among international development banks, citing agreements with the World Bank, the Asian Development Bank and the Latin American development bank as signs that the financing barrier was beginning to break down.

Macron said that the Paris summit was taking place 15 years to the day after the Fukushima-Daichi nuclear accident in Japan. He said the lessons of Fukushima had been drawn, safety standards had been reinforced, and that nuclear energy today was a “deeply safe source of power.”
Macron said Europe had spent years methodically constructing rules that prevented banks and insurers from financing nuclear. Image couretsy NES2026.

title: Von Der Leyen Sets Out EU SMR Strategy With €200M Guarantee At Paris Nuclear Summit
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Retreat from nuclear power was ‘strategic mistake’ says Commission head

European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen used a speech at the Nuclear Energy Summit in Paris to announce a new European strategy for small modular reactors (SMRs), backed by a proposed €200m ($232m) investment guarantee funded through the European Unions’s emissions trading system.

Von der Leyen said the goal was to have SMR technology operational in Europe by the early 2030s, where it could play a role alongside traditional nuclear reactors in a flexible and efficient energy system.

She proposed three main pillars: simplified regulation through cross-border regulatory sandboxes, mobilisation of private investment through the new guarantee, and coordinated cooperation between member states on permitting, skills and supply chains.
The Commission president said Europe's share of nuclear in its electricity mix had fallen from one-third in 1990 to around 15% today, and called that decline a strategic mistake.
"I believe that it was a strategic mistake for Europe to turn its back on a reliable, affordable source of low-emissions power," she said.

"Europe's has been a pioneer in nuclear technology and could once again lead the world in it," Von der Leyen said, adding: "A next generation nuclear reactor could become a European high-tech high-value export and this is what brings us to Paris today. Over the last years we see a global revival of nuclear energy and Europe wants to be part of it."

Von der Leyen said that nuclear and renewables were not alternatives but complements. Renewables produce the lowest-cost electricity but are dependent on weather conditions, she said, while nuclear provides reliable round-the-clock generation.
"The most efficient system combines nuclear and renewables, underpinned by storage, flexibility, and grids," she said.

She said Europe's high electricity prices were a structural problem with direct consequences for industrial competitiveness, warning that the industries and technologies of the future, including robotics and artificial intelligence, would be built on affordable electricity.

Von der Leyen said the EU had already moved to update state aid rules to expand support for nuclear, launched the world's first industrial alliance for small modular reactors, and proposed more than €5bn in its next budget for fusion research including ITER. She said the new SMR strategy was the next step in that effort.

The EU emissions trading system is the bloc’s carbon market that sets a cap on greenhouse gas emissions from power plants, industry and aviation and allows companies to buy and sell emission allowances to meet those limits.

Nuclear energy has gained greater recognition in recent EU policy frameworks. The EU sustainable finance taxonomy included nuclear under certain conditions as a low-carbon investment, and revised EU state aid rules allow governments to support nuclear power and nuclear fuel projects.

However, nuclear has been largely absent from some recent EU industrial and energy initiatives, including the REPowerEU plan and the Net-Zero Industry Act, which have focused mainly on renewables and clean technology manufacturing. Decisions on nuclear deployment remain the responsibility of individual member states.

The EU has recently reformed its electricity market design to promote long-term contracts such as contracts for difference and power purchase agreements and continues to rely on the EU emissions trading system as the core carbon pricing instrument under its Fit for 55 climate package, targeting of at least a 55 % reduction in greenhouse gas emissions by 2030.

The European Commission’s 2025 nuclear illustrative programme (Pinc) estimates that Europe requires €241bn in nuclear investment by 2050 to meet net-zero targets. The Pinc report warned that without long-term operation of existing nuclear plants, the EU’s nuclear capacity would be close to nothing by 2050, making the energy transition significantly more difficult.
The European nuclear industry has been calling on Brussels for years to apply the principle of technological neutrality to all low-carbon sources when it comes to policy support.

SMR plants have not been commercially deployed in the Western world, with first demonstration plants expected online in North America at the turn of the decade. Europe has a number of companies developing SMR technologies eyeing the 2030s for pilot deployment.
All of Europe's nuclear-powered electricity comes from a fleet of about 100 large-scale conventional reactors.

"I believe that it was a strategic mistake for Europe to turn its back on a reliable, affordable source of low-emissions power," EU Commission president Ursula von der Leyen told a Paris leadership summit. Image courtesy European Commission.

title: Oklo, Centrus Plan Joint Venture To Boost US Advanced Nuclear Fuel Supply
author: Nigel Davies
text: Plans focused on developing cooperation at Piketon site in Ohio

Advanced nuclear technology company Oklo and nuclear fuel supplier Centrus Energy will study the formation of a joint venture focused on deconversion services for high-assay low enriched uranium (Haleu) and bolstering the US nuclear fuel supply chain.
Oklo said that activities under the joint venture are proposed for Centrus’ Piketon site in southern Ohio, which would be next to its planned site for a 1.2 GW power campus.

The company said that the potential joint venture would aim to provide “an integrated and efficient” coupling of uranium enrichment and deconversion to lower costs on one site, while in turn expanding US nuclear fuel capacity.
Uranium deconversion is the process of converting uranium hexafluoride gas into a stable uranium oxide or metal form that can be used to manufacture nuclear fuel.
“Advanced nuclear energy development requires not only reactors but also reliable fuel cycle capabilities that support these reactors,” said Jacob DeWitte, chief executive of Oklo.
Speaking on Bloomberg, Amir Vexler, CEO of Centrus, also said that it was the right moment for such a joint venture to happen.
“It makes all the sense in the world to co-locate that deconversion process together with enrichment for cost efficiencies and for security issues.”
He added that a surge in fuel contracts signed by advanced manufacturers aided the case for such a joint venture.

“In the last six months or so we have seen a huge acceleration in these advanced reactors and their ability to lock in fuel contracts. In other words, things are getting really serious and now is the time to completely close that fuel supply chain.”
Similarly, DeWitte added on Bloomberg that the main constraint facing manufacturers was fuel supply.
“The biggest bottleneck fundamentally is fuel, and so we’re working together to change the paradigm.”

In a statement, Oklo said that a central site could end the need for individual fuel facilities around the country to have their own deconversion line, which could lower the transportation costs of Haleu and improve competitiveness across the industry.

The companies said that they would also explore potential coordination of regulatory and research activities, including working together with federal agencies to propose solutions for the co-location of deconversion and enrichment services.
Oklo is developing its 75-MW Aurora nuclear powerhouse project slated for deployment at Idaho National Laboratory in Tennessee.

The Aurora consists of a small fast neutron fission reactor with integrated solar panels. It uses liquid metal as a coolant and is designed to operate on fresh fuel like high-assay low-enriched uranium (Haleu) or recycled used nuclear fuel of the type that could be manufactured at the new facility.
Centrus has announced plans for a major expansion of its uranium enrichment facility in Piketon, expected to increase production capacity for low-enriched uranium (Leu) and Haleu.
Centrus Energy's main uranium enrichment facility is located at Piketon in southern Ohio. Image courtesy Centrus.

title: Nuclear And Onshore Wind Most Cost-Effective For Meeting Sweden’s Power Demand, Says Report
author: Nigel Davies
text: Stockholm has ambitious plans to scale nuclear power

A mix of nuclear energy and onshore wind is the most cost-effective way of meeting Sweden’s rising electricity needs and net-zero ambitions, a report from the OECD’s Nuclear Energy Agency has concluded.

The report said that under its base case scenario for 2050, Sweden would have 13 GW of installed nuclear capacity, up from 7 GW today. Meanwhile, onshore wind would rise from 17 GW at present to 30 GW in 2050. Sweden aims to achieve net zero emissions by 2045.
Under the scenario for nuclear, 10 GW would come from new plants to be built, while three of the country’s six current reactors would continue to run in the long-term.

The annual system costs of this base case would be $18bn (€15.5bn). The report said that onshore remained the cheapest to build at around $1,500 per kilowatt (€1,295), while nuclear costs were $7,000 (€6,044). However, system costs were reduced using both together, given nuclear produces electricity at all hours with no weather intermittency.
Offshore wind was not seen as a viable alternative at present, with costs to build of $3,000 per kilowatt (€2,590).

“While it is reasonable to disagree on the precise nature of the optimal capacity mix in 2050, it is incontrovertible that both nuclear energy, including long-term operations and new build, and onshore wind will play the leading roles in any future least-cost capacity mix when considering a large increase in electrical demand,” the report said.

However, the report cautioned that nuclear new build would need to begin shortly given construction times of around seven years. If nuclear expansion targets were not met, then more onshore wind could be used given construction times of around two years.

“Regarding the deployment of new generation capacity, the time until 2050 is short. In particular, nuclear new build with a construction time of seven years, will need to start soon to be able to contribute to increasing demand.”

Indeed, under its base case scenario, the report said electricity demand was forecast to grow to 264 TWh by 2050, a 95% increase from 2023 levels of 135 TWh, particularly to meet increasing electrification of industry. A lower demand scenario would be 224 TWh, and a higher demand scenario of 349 TWh.

The report also said that flexibility provision including electrolysers, storage, load shedding and shifting, as well as hydrogen storage capacity, and interconnections would prove a key a determinant as to the precise share of nuclear and onshore wind power the system would require.
Sweden plans to develop two new large-scale reactors by 2035, and up to 10 new reactors, including small modular reactors (SMRs) by 2045.

At present, country has six reactor units in commercial operation at three sites: Forsmark, Oskarshamn and Ringhals. According to International Atomic Energy Agency data, nuclear energy provided 29% of the country’s electricity generation in 2024.
Sweden has been pushing for several years for a revival of its nuclear sector in an effort to boost supply security and predictability. Image courtesy Creative Commons.

title: Swedish Government Proposes Legislation To Ease Rules For Building New Nuclear Plants
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Bills submitted to parliament to allow more coastal locations and streamline licensing
The Swedish government has approved three draft laws aimed at making it easier to build new nuclear power plants and expand nuclear generation in the country, a statement said.
The proposals, which will now be submitted to parliament for approval, include changes to environmental legislation that would allow nuclear plants to be considered in more coastal locations.
The statement said the changes are intended to allow more companies, both established and new, to invest in nuclear power across a wider range of locations.
Acting minister of climate and environment Johan Britz said the decision opens the way for more players, large and small, to invest in nuclear power.
"When more companies are given the opportunity to build new nuclear power, we strengthen competition and innovation in the energy sector, which is good for both the climate and jobs," he said.
The government also introduced measures to make the permitting process more efficient, including a new law that allows for earlier decisions from the government and local municipalities.
Another proposal would enable developers to seek binding advance decisions on specific technical issues to provide greater regulatory certainty during the assessment phase.

The legislative package also includes provisions enabling the restart of shut-down reactors. Sweden has six large-scale reactors that have been permanently taken offline, and previous restrictions had made it illegal to restart them.
The bills will also propose that a facility for the extraction and processing of nuclear materials would no longer be classified as a nuclear facility under Swedish law.

Minister of energy Ebba Busch said the legislative changes would create better conditions for new nuclear power, provide simpler permit processes and enable nuclear development in more locations across Sweden.

The new approval law will apply to applications for new nuclear power submitted after 10 March 2026. Legislative amendments relating to the permit review process are proposed to enter into force on 17 June 2026, with the remaining changes taking effect on 15 July 2026.
Sweden's Nuclear 'Revival'
The legislative package follows a broader government push to revive nuclear power in Sweden since 2022.

Last month the government said
it would increase support to SEK 20 million (€1.9m, $2.1bn) from SEK 15 million for municipalities wishing to carry out feasibility studies into new nuclear. Thirteen municipalities carried out such pilot projects during 2024-2025, with several showing conditions suitable for new nuclear power.

In May 2025, Sweden passed a law establishing
a state aid framework including government-backed loans and two-way contracts for difference for companies planning to build nuclear reactors, covering projects with a total capacity of up to 5,000 MW.

The government has proposed a financial framework of up to SEK 220 billion over 12 years to support new reactor construction, with annual price guarantee allocations of SEK 1-3 billion for up to 40 years after new units begin operation.

State-controlled utility Vattenfall has requested state financing to build new reactors at its Ringhals plant, with plans for small modular reactors on the Varo peninsula in southwest Sweden through its subsidiary Videberg Kraft.

Sweden has six reactor units in commercial operation at three sites: Forsmark, Oskarshamn and Ringhals. According to International Atomic Energy Agency data, nuclear energy provided 29% of the country’s electricity generation in 2024.
Sweden has been pushing for several years for a revival of its nuclear sector in an effort to boost supply security and predictability. Image courtesy Creative Commons.

title: Regulator To Review Standard Design For South Korean Small Modular Reactor
author: Nigel Davies
text: Country keen to develop domestic SMR flagship

South Korea’s Nuclear Safety and Security Commission (NSCC) will begin a design review for a proposed Innovative Small Modular Reactor (i-SMR) submitted by the country’s SMR Technology Development Project Group.

The NSCC said a meeting was held between the country’s nuclear regulators and developers including Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power (KHNP) and Korea Electric Power Engineering & Construction (Kepco) to kick off the review process.
Developed with the Korea Atomic Energy Research Institute (Kaeri), the i-SMR is a 170-MW pressurised water reactor, with foreseen applications in electricity generation.
The NSCC said that this standard design approval would be valid for a ten-year period and allow for repeat construction of the same nuclear power plant design.
The regulatory body also said that it would form a ‘nuclear regulatory issues working group’ to discuss pending issues and schedules related to future licensing of plants.
The project team, including developers, also said that it would subsequently submit outstanding safety testing and verification reports to advance on the design approval application.
In February, South Korea passed an SMR development act as the country looks to quickly develop in the industry having solely developed, until now, large-scale reactors.

At present, the country has 26 nuclear units in commercial operation, according to the International Atomic Energy Agency, as well as two, Saeul-3 and -4 listed as under construction. Together they provide 31.7% of the country’s electricity production.

KHNP is looking to rapidly advance in SMR development, including in overseas projects. Recently, the company signed an agreement with Singapore to assess the capacity of SMRs to help the nation meet its rising energy needs.
The smaller design of SMRs means lower upfront costs and flexibility in construction, and they can also be deployed in remote regions or to provide energy to heavy industry.

title: Czech Consortium Wins Contract To Modernise I&C Systems At Dukovany Nuclear Plant
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Project is part of a wider programme to ensure long-term operation.

A consortium of Czech companies ZAT and I&C Energo has won a contract to refurbish the instrumentation and control systems (I&C) at all four units of the Dukovany nuclear power station in the Czech Republic, operator ČEZ said.
The state-controlled company said the project will involve replacing major parts of the block control systems for both the primary and secondary circuits at the plant.
The work will be carried out over about 10 years and is part of a wider programme aimed at ensuring the safe long-term operation of the station.
ČEZ said the work must be carried out without affecting the safety or stable operation of the units.

Bohdan Zronek, a member of the ČEZ board and head of the company’s nuclear division, said the utility invests about CZK 7 billion (€290m, €336m) annually in its nuclear power plants to improve efficiency, safety and long-term reliability.
ZAT will supply its proprietary SandRA control system platform and is responsible for the project’s technical concept. The company said it has been working on the concept since 2020.
I&C Energo will carry out installation, commissioning and part of the engineering work. The company has been involved in maintenance of instrumentation and control systems at Dukovany since 1993.

The Dukovany nuclear power station is the Czech Republic’s first nuclear plant. Construction began in the late 1970s and the four Soviet-designed VVER-440 reactors entered commercial operation between 1985 and 1987.
ČEZ has implemented several modernisation programmes in recent years to extend the operating lifetime of the Dukovany units beyond their original 30-year design life.
The four-unit Dukovany is one of two nuclear power stations in the Czech Republic. Nuclear energy provides about 40% of national electricity production. Image courtesy ČEZ.

title: First Segment Of Inner Steel Containment Installed At China’s Ningde-6 Nuclear Plant
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Fujian province site has four operational reactor units
The first segment of the inner steel containment has been installed for Unit 6 of the Ningde nuclear power station in Fujian province in the southeast of China, local reports said.

According to the official China National Nuclear Power News Network (CNNPN), the component, placed on the concrete baseplate of the nuclear island, has a diametre of about 43 metres and a weight of about 112 tonnes.
Construction of Ningde-6, a 1,200-MW Hualong One pressurised water reactor unit, began in December 2025 with pouring of first concrete.
The Ningde station currently has four 1,018-MW CPR-1000 PWR units, which began commercial operation between April 2013 and July 2016.
The CPR-1000 was designed by CGN based on a French 900 MW design imported in the 1980s.
Units 5 and 6 will both be indigenous HPR1000 PWRs, or Hualong Ones, which combine features from China National Nuclear Corporation’s ACP1000 and China General Nuclear’s ACPR1000+ designs.
The International Atomic Energy Agency’s (IAEA) database of nuclear plants in China says China has 58 plants in commercial operation and 33 under construction.
However, construction has begun of another three units that are not listed by the IAEA, bringing the number to 36. About half of those are domestic Hualong One units.

China is aiming for 200 GW of nuclear capacity by 2035, up from around 57 GW today. Nuclear is expected to contribute about 10% of power generation in the country by 2035 – up from around 4.5 today – and 18% by 2060, the China Nuclear Energy Association has said.
A crane is lifting into place the 112-tonne first inner steel containment segment at Ningde-6. Image courtesy CNNPN.

title: Japanese Courts Reject Lawsuits Seeking To Block Shika Restart And Ikata Operation
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Local utilities have restarted 15 of 33 operable nuclear units

Courts in Japan have rejected two lawsuits seeking to block the restart or operation of nuclear reactors, ruling that the plaintiffs failed to demonstrate a clear safety risk, local media reports said.
The Toyama district court dismissed a lawsuit seeking to prevent Hokuriku Electric Power from restarting Units 1 and 2 at the Shika nuclear power station in the central Ishikawa prefecture.

Six plaintiffs, including company shareholders, argued that restarting the reactors could cause irreparable damage to the company because safety investigations and analyses had not been adequately carried out, the Japan Times reported.

The court said it the restart did not pose a risk of immediate damage and said that by implementing safety measures required under the Japan’s Nuclear Regulation Authority’s post-Fukushima regulatory standards, the company’s management was “fulfilling its duty to prevent serious accidents.”
The plaintiffs said they plan to appeal the ruling, according to the reports.

In a separate case, a branch of the Yamaguchi District Court rejected a request by residents of neighbouring Yamaguchi prefecture to stop the operation of the Ikata-3 pressurised water reactor unit operated by Shikoku Electric Power.

The Mainichi daily said about 160 residents argued that the reactor in southwestern Ehime prefecture posed safety risks due to potential earthquakes and the possibility of a large volcanic eruption at Mount Aso in Kyushu, about 130 kilometres from the site.

According to the reports, the court said Shikoku Electric’s geological surveys were thorough and found no evidence suggesting that nearby faults were active. The court also ruled that the company’s conclusion that Mount Aso was not at imminent risk of a major eruption was reasonable.

Ikata-3 is the only reactor operating at the Ikata nuclear station after units 1 and 2 were shut down for decommissioning in 2016 and 2018. The unit resumed operation in 2016 after passing Japan’s post-Fukushima safety screening.

Previous provisional injunctions issued by the Hiroshima High Court in 2017 and 2020 to halt the reactor were later overturned. Courts have also rejected other lawsuits seeking to stop the unit’s operation, the Mainichi said.

Hokuriku Electric is seeking to restart the 1,108-MW Shika-2 boiling water reactor unit, which has been offline since the Fukushima accident Japan-wide shutdowns. The utility said in 2023 it aimed to resume operation in fiscal year 2026*, after Japan’s nuclear regulator concluded in that no active seismic fault runs beneath the site. The restart plan has faced renewed scrutiny following the powerful Noto Peninsula earthquake in January 2024.
Japan has 33 commercially available units, 15 of which have now resumed operation under stringent post-Fukushima rules. Restarts face high regulatory hurdles and need local government support.
The most resent restart was that of Tepco’s Kashiwazaki Kariwa-6 in Niigata Prefecture, western Japan.

The 15 reactor units that have restarted are: Kashiwazaki Kariwa-6 (Tepco), Onagawa-2 (Tohoku Electric Power), Shimane-2 (Chugoku Electric Power), Mihama-3, Takahama-1, -2, -3, -4, and Ohi-3, -4 (Kansai Electric Power), Ikata-3 (Shikoku Electric Power), Genkai-3, -4, and Sendai-1 -2 (Kyushu Electric Power).
Before the 2011 Fukushima disaster Japan’s fleet of 54 nuclear plants generated about 30% of the country’s electricity, but were all shut down for safety checks following the accident.
According to the International Atomic Energy Agency, nuclear power provided nearly 10% of Japan’s electricity production in 2024.
Japan’s new prime minister Sanae Takaichi has said she will push for the accelerated revival of nuclear power in the country.

title: Newcleo Subsidiary SRS Wins €36M Contract To Build Lead-Cooled Reactor Facilities In Romania
author: Nigel Davies
text: Efforts part of EU-funded Alfred project
Advanced nuclear reactor developer Newcleo subsidiary Servizi di Ricerche e Sviluppo (SRS) has been awarded a €36m ($42m) contract to build lead-cooled fast reactor research facilities in Romania.
The project is being led by Romanian nuclear research company Raten and forms part of Newcleo’s work to build the ‘Alfred’ lead-cooled fast reactor demonstrator, a statement said.

Under the contract, SRS will design, supply and commission a liquid lead loop-type facility called Helena-2, a liquid pool-type facility called E, and confined modules to study the interactions between liquid lead and irradiated and non-irradiated fuels during accidents called Meltin’Pot.
The facilities will be built at Raten’s Mioveni site in Romania around 120km from capital Bucharest.

France-based Newcleo said in a statement that SRS would deliver the work by the end of 2028 working alongside the Italian National Agency for new technologies, Energy and Sustainable Economic Development (Enea).

Newcleo said that Raten would use the facilities to investigate thermal-hydraulic behaviour, materials performance and component qualification in liquid lead systems. In turn, it would support Romania’s roadmap to develop next-generation nuclear facilities.
In February, newcleo also signed an agreement with a nuclear industry consortium called the European Eagles to build a lead-cooled fast reactor demonstrator in Belgium.
Newcleo also said that SRS was currently working on the installation of a 10MW pool-type non-nuclear test system in Bologna, Italy due for completion in 2026.
Newcleo is developing its own lead-cooled fast reactor design, the LFR-AS-200. The company hopes to deploy its first commercial units in the mid-2030s.
The Alfred project in Romania is a demonstration initiative to build an advanced lead-cooled fast reactor under the EU’s Generation IV nuclear technology roadmap.

It was launched in 2013 with a consortium of Romanian and European partners and is funded through a mix of European funds, national Romanian research and infrastructure budgets, and industry contributions.
Alfred (Advanced Lead-cooled Fast Reactor European Demonstrator) is a 300-MWt and 125-MWe lead-cooled fast reactor designed by Italy's Ansaldo Energia. Image courtesy Creative Commons.

title: Singapore Energy Authority And KHNP Sign SMR Cooperation Agreement
author: Kamen Kraev
text: MoU to support joint studies on possible small modular reactor deployment

South Korea’s KHNP (Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power) and the Energy Market Authority of Singapore and have signed a memorandum of understanding on civil nuclear energy cooperation focused on small modular reactors (SMRs), a statement said.

The agreement was signed on during a bilateral summit in Singapore. It is the first MoU on civil nuclear cooperation between a South Korean nuclear power company and a Singapore government agency, the statement said.

Under the agreement, the two sides will conduct joint studies on the potential application of SMRs in Singapore. The cooperation will also include collaboration on human resource development and training, as well as sharing of technical information and best practices in advanced nuclear technologies.
EMA said the partnership is part of its efforts to explore pathways to decarbonise Singapore’s power system while maintaining reliability and energy security.
Singapore has no domestic energy resources and currently relies mainly on natural gas and electricity imports.

A Singapore a government report in 2025 said the country does not have the natural attributes, resources or land to deploy renewable energy solutions such as hydropower or wind energy at scale. Even covering all possible spaces with solar panels would only meet up to 10% of the island state’s needs.

In 2012, the Singapore government conducted a pre-feasibility study on nuclear energy. While the study concluded that nuclear power plants of the time were not suited for a small and densely populated city-state, it recommended that Singapore continue to monitor the progress of new nuclear energy technologies.

Tan See Leng, Singapore’s minister of energy, science, and technology, told a parliament session recently that the country is “seriously studying” the potential deployment of advanced nuclear energy technologies.
He said nuclear energy “has the potential to be safe, reliable, and cost-completive option” with high fuel density which is a “especially attractive for land-scarce” Singapore.

Leng said Singapore is building its capabilities using the International Atomic Energy Agency’s milestone approach for newcomer countries and is open to cooperation with partners from the US, France, and South Korea.

The South Asian he city-state is studying the potential role of advanced nuclear technologies, including small modular reactors, as part of its long-term energy strategy. Image courtesy Creative Commons.

title: India Pours First Concrete For Kaiga Nuclear Plant Units 5 And 6
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Country follows ambitious programme for deployment of domestic reactor technology

The Nuclear Power Corporation of India (NPCIL) has begun construction of Units 5 and 6 of the Kaiga nuclear power project in the Karnataka state, west India, with the pouring of first concrete for the nuclear island foundation slabs.
The operation took place on 1 March 2026, marking the formal start of construction of the two 700-MW pressurised heavy water reactors at the site, a statement said.
India’s Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB) granted approval for the first concrete pouring last week.
The AERB said the approval follows a regulatory review of NPCIL’s application and supporting safety submissions.
NPCIL said Kaiga-5 is expected to achieve first criticality about five years from the first concrete milestone, meaning a target deadline in 2031.
Kaiga-5 and -6 will be 700-MW PHWRs based on the reference design of Kakrapar nuclear power station Units 3 and 4.

Excavation works for Kaiga-5 and -6 began in May 2022. The units will be part of a series of 10 Indian-designed PHWRs to be built in “fleet mode”, designed to bring economies of scale and maximise efficiency.

The units belong to the IPHWR-700 reactor class, a Generation III+ evolution of India’s earlier 220-MW and 540-MW PHWR designs. These designs use natural uranium oxide fuel and heavy water as both coolant and neutron moderator.
