The 10 plants are Kaiga-5 and Kaiga-6 in Karnataka state, Mahi Banswara 1-4 in Rajasthan state Gorakhpur-3 and -4 in Haryana state, and Chutka-1 and -2 in Madhya Pradesh state.
There are currently four smaller 202-MW PHWR units in commercial operation at Kaiga. Kaiga-1 and -2 began operation in 2000, while Kaiga-3 and -4 started in 2007 and 2011.
According to the International Atomic Energy Agency’s (IAEA) reactor database, India has 21 commercial plants in operation and six under construction, excluding Kaiga-5 and -6.
Pouring of first concrete is considered a milestone marking the start of nuclear island construction at nuclear power plants. Image courtesy NPCIL.

title: US Advanced Nuclear Company Deep Fission Signs Fuel Agreement With Urenco
author: Nigel Davies
text: Experimental borehole reactor to use low-enriched uranium

California-based advanced nuclear developer Deep Fission has signed a fuel purchase agreement for low-enriched uranium (LEU) with enrichment services provider Urenco USA to support its testing and demonstration activities.
Deep Fission, which aims to place small modular reactors (SMRs) in boreholes one mile beneath the Earth’s surface, also said the fuel would help with development efforts.
Deep Fission’s Gravity reactor will use fuel sourced from Urenco’s enrichment plant in New Mexico, a statement said.
The company’s reactor design was previously referred to as the Deep Fission Borehole Reactor-1, or DFBR-1, but was recently renamed by the company to the Gravity Nuclear Reactor, or simply Gravity.

“Securing fuel is one of the most important steps for any nuclear project,” said Liz Muller, chief executive and co-founder of Deep Fission. “This agreement with Urenco enables us to move quickly towards commercialisation and scaling our technology with a high-quality fuel.”
Recently, the company also raised $80m (€67m) in new financing and has formed a partnership with alternative asset manager Blue Owl.
Deep Fission’s design combines pressurized water reactor technology with drilling techniques used in the oil and gas industry, alongside heat transfer methods from geothermal sources.
The company says that by using already established methods and supply chains from other industries that it can reduce construction costs by 70-80% versus traditional nuclear plants.

The company was selected for the DOE’s Reactor Pilot Program in 2025 and later that same year broke ground on its pilot project in Parsons, Kansas. The company has also announced a development pipeline representing 12.5 GW of future planned deployments.
The DOE’s pilot programme aims to deploy an advanced reactor on US home soil by 4 July 2026.
Photo courtesy Deep Fission.

title: IAEA Reports No Radiation Increase After Strikes In Iran
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Agency says Bushehr nuclear plant and other facilities show no signs of damage

The International Atomic Energy Agency said it has detected no increase in radiation levels in countries bordering Iran following recent military attacks in the Islamic Republic and the wider Middle East.

Director-general Rafael Grossi said the agency’s incident and emergency centre had been activated to assess potential radiological consequences of the strikes. He said the IAEA’s regional safety monitoring network had been placed on alert and was in continuous contact with the agency.
“So far, no elevation of radiation levels above the usual background levels has been detected in countries bordering Iran,” Grossi said.

He said there was currently no indication that nuclear installations in Iran had been damaged or hit. These include the Bushehr nuclear power plant, the Tehran research reactor and other fuel cycle facilities.
Efforts to contact Iran’s nuclear regulatory authorities through the IAEA’s emergency communication channels were continuing, but no response had yet been received, Grossi said.
At a press conference after the meeting Grossi said that communication with Iranian representatives at the IAEA was "until last Thursday [26 February] very intense" but is now "limited".

He warned that the presence of operational nuclear power plants, research reactors and fuel storage facilities in Iran and other countries in the region increases the risk to nuclear safety in the event of further escalation. The United Arab Emirates operates four nuclear reactors, while Jordan and Syria have research reactors. Other states in the region use nuclear applications in medicine, industry and research.

Grossi said that armed attacks on nuclear facilities should never take place and could lead to radioactive releases with serious consequences beyond national borders. He said the situation remains “very concerning” and that a radiological release cannot be ruled out.
The IAEA said it would continue to monitor developments and stands ready to hlep if nuclear safety or security is compromised.
Grossi also called for a return to diplomacy, saying a negotiated solution is essential to ensure that Iran does not acquire nuclear weapons and to preserve the global non-proliferation regime.

Reuters reported that Iran's ambassador to the IAEA, Reza Najafi, told reporters outside the IAEA meeting that the Natanz enrichment complex had been attacked. However, no further confirmation or details have been provided.
Iran has one commercial nuclear plant in operation and a second and third under construction at Bushehr, about 1,000 km south of Tehran on the Persian Gulf.

Iran’s other main declared nuclear sites include enrichment plants at Natanz and Fordow, the conversion and fuel plants at Isfahan, the unfinished Arak heavy water reactor project, and Tehran’s research reactor complex.

Rafael Grossi, IAEA director general, delivers his statement at the opening of the Board of Governors meeting held at the agency headquarters in Vienna, Austria on 2 March 2026, Image courtesy Dean Calma / IAEA Images.

title: ASP Isotopes Advances Haleu Plans With South Africa’s Necsa
author: Kamen Kraev
text: ‘Pre-implementation’ agreement supports potential enrichment plant at Pelindaba.

A South African subsidiary of Quantum Leap Energy has signed a pre-implementation services contract with the South African Nuclear Energy Corporation (Necsa) aimed at advancing plans for a high-assay low-enriched uranium enrichment (Haleu) facility at the Pelindaba nuclear research site.

Quantum Leap Energy, a wholly owned subsidiary of US-based ASP Isotopes, said the agreement covers siting, design, construction, commissioning and operation support for a proposed enrichment plant at Necsa’s facilities west of Pretoria.
A statement said that under the agreement, Necsa will provide access to infrastructure, utilities and related services at Pelindaba. A joint coordination committee will oversee implementation.
The project remains subject to site regulations and approvals from South Africa’s nuclear Regulator and other authorities.
Quantum Leap Energy said its objective is to achieve commercial readiness for production of Haleu, fuel enriched to between 5% and 20% uranium-235 and required by many advanced reactor designs.

Chief executive officer Ryno Pretorius said access to Necsa’s facilities would help move the project from planning to implementation, while Necsa group chief executive officer Loyiso Tyabashe said the collaboration aligns with Necsa’s strategy to expand its nuclear fuel capabilities.

Necsa is a state-owned company established under South Africa’s nuclear energy act and operates nuclear research and isotope production facilities at Pelindaba centre, which houses the Safari-1 research reactor.

In 2024, ASP Isotopes said it is in discussions with government authorities in three countries regarding the establishment of (Haleu) enrichment facilities, with priority interest in South Africa under a memorandum of understand in with Necsa.

ASP Isotopes also entered into a non-binding agreement with TerraPower, the nuclear innovation company founded by Bill Gates, related to the construction of a uranium enrichment facility capable of producing Haleu and the future supply of Haleu for TerraPower’s Natrium advanced reactors.

The startup company has said it is developing a proprietary aerodynamic separation process (ASP), which uses high-speed gas flow dynamics for isotope separation, and a laser-based quantum enrichment technique. It subsidiary Quantum Leap Energy aims to apply these methods to advanced nuclear fuels including Haleu.
Global demand for Haleu is expected to grow as small modular reactors and other advanced nuclear technologies move toward deployment.

The US is seeking to reduce its dependence on Russian enrichment services, which historically supplied a significant share of global Haleu capacity. The Department of Energy (DOE) has identified the fuel availability as a priority for deployment of advanced reactors later this decade.

Efforts to establish domestic Haleu supply are also being led by established enrichment companies. Centrus Energy is producing limited quantities of Haleu under a DOE contract using centrifuge technology in Ohio and is working on capacity expansion, while Urenco USA has announced plans to expand enrichment capabilities in New Mexico to support future Haleu demand.
Pelindaba is South Africa's main nuclear research centre, run by the South African Nuclear Energy Corporation (Necsa). Courtesy Wikipedia.

title: Refurbishment Construction Phase Completed At Canada’s Bruce-3 Nuclear Power Plant
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Second of six planned life-extension outages completed under long-term programme.
Canada’s Bruce Power has completed the construction phase of the major component replacement project at Unit 3 of its Bruce nuclear power station in Ontario, the company said.
Bruce Power said the refurbishment of the Candu heavy water reactor unit remains on budget and ahead of schedule, with the focus now shifting to returning the unit to service in the coming months.
Unit 3 was taken offline in March 2023. The work included replacement of 480 fuel channels, 960 end fittings and eight steam generators as part of the life-extension programme.
Refuelling with 5,760 fuel bundles is expected to begin later this month, followed by final inspections and regulatory approvals.
Bruce Power said the refurbishment will extend Bruce-3’s operating life by 30 to 35 years.
The project is the second of six planned major component replacement outages between 2020 and 2033 covering Units 3 to 8 and aiming to extend the Bruce station’s life by 40 years.
Unit 4 entered refurbishment in February 2025, with Unit 5 scheduled to follow in November. In September 2023 Unit 6 at Bruce returned to commercial operation after refurbishment.
According to earlier reports, the refurbishment project is expected to cost CAD13 billion ($9.4bn, €8bn).
Canada’s Independent Electricity System Operator has projected that Ontario’s electricity demand could grow by as much as 75% in the coming decades.
Bruce Power said the life-extension programme will support long-term electricity supply and maintain production of medical isotopes.

Bruce Power operates eight Candu heavy water reactor units at the Bruce site, which is one of the largest operating nuclear stations in the world. The eight units began commercial operation between September 1977 and May 1987.
Bruce Power is using Canada's homegrown Candu technology at the eight-unit Bruce nuclear station on the shores of Lake Huron in Ontario. Courtesy Bruce Power.

title: Sweden’s Nuclear Coordinator Proposes Creation Of Nordic Research Reactor
author: Nigel Davies
text: Report puts forward ‘skills supply council’ to bolster workforce

Sweden’s Nuclear Coordinator said the country should build a Nordic research reactor and develop a skills council to bolster the nuclear workforce as the country ramps up its investment in the energy source.

Carl Berglöf, the government’s nuclear new-build coordinator, proposed that a feasibility study was carried out by the Swedish Energy Agency jointly with innovation group Vinnova into the possibility of building a new research reactor in Sweden.

Writing in an interim report to the government, he said that there were no longer any research reactors in Sweden, Norway, Denmark or Finland and that they were dependent on irradiation services and radioisotope production from other regions.

“Given Sweden's extensive investment in new nuclear power, the increasing need for expertise for existing nuclear power, and the government's expressed ambition to once again become a leading nuclear power nation, it is reasonable to investigate the conditions for Sweden to host a Nordic research reactor,” Berglöf said.

He also said that the Swedish state should be involved from the start to clarify the state’s role, but that investment should also come in such a reactor from the various industries that could benefit, including medicine, defense, energy and space technology.

Berglöf said that while the country currently had a workforce that largely met the needs of its nuclear power plants, that it would need to be developed to meet new nuclear set to be built in the country and lifetime extensions of certain plants.

He proposed that the Swedish Energy Agency establish a skills supply council. He suggested that over 2026 a council could investigate the skills and training that the industry will require in coming years, before it presented a detailed plan of action in 2027.

Berglöf said that the nuclear industry should continue to play a key part in the training of personnel as it does at present. However, he said there was a challenge within the national education system to finance capital-intensive training facilities.
Investment support might also be needed to build specific facilities such as full-scale copies of small modular reactors (SMRs) or safety systems.

Making investments such as these would prove their worth in the long-term, he said. “Such facilities contribute more benefits than just skills development. The training facilities also strengthen the possibility of developing innovative companies in the nuclear power sector.”
Sweden’s centre-right government has pledged to quickly develop the country’s nuclear energy industry, reversing a decades-long policy of shutting down ageing reactors.
Recently, the country announced a streamlining of its licensing process for new nuclear plants and said it would open up more of its coastline to build more capacity.

Sweden has six reactor units in commercial operation at three sites: Forsmark, Oskarshamn and Ringhals. According to International Atomic Energy Agency data, nuclear energy provided 29% of the country’s electricity generation in 2024.

Sweden’s last operating research reactor R2 at Studsvik was shut down in 2005. R2 was a materials testing and neutron research reactor, which supported fuel development, reactor physics experiments, isotope production, and qualification of materials for Sweden’s commercial nuclear fleet.

title: Europe Needs To End ‘Energy Dogmas’ And Back Nuclear, Says EESC Vice-President
author: David Dalton
text: Alena Mastantuono calls for bloc to urgently rebuild its own energy sovereignty

The European Union can no longer afford “energy dogmas” and needs to back nuclear with streamlined state aid procedures, faster licensing, access to EU funding, and a financing framework that treats nuclear and renewables equally, said Alena Mastantuono, vice-president of the European Economic and Social Committee (EESC). *

Mastantuono said in an opinion column that as the European Commission works on plan for a nuclear strategy, it has the chance to pivot from “hesitation to enablement” and choose “enablers, not bottlenecks.
The long promised and rarely practiced technological neutrality must finally become a guiding principle, she said.

According to Mastantuono, Europe's geopolitical reality only makes the need clearer. With Russian gas being phased out and LNG supply chains under strain due to shaky transatlantic relations, the EU must urgently rebuild its own sovereignty.

She said that thanks to European energy market and interconnection, consumers across the European continent can benefit from the nuclear electricity coming from more than 100 nuclear reactors in 13 member states.

“Europe has set itself an ambitious 2050 climate neutrality target,” Mastantuono said. “Reaching it while preserving strategic autonomy and economic strength will require every credible low‑carbon option on the table.”

* The European Economic and Social Committee is a consultative body of the European Union established in 1958. It is an advisory assembly composed of representatives from employers' associations, workers' unions and civil society organisations.

title: US Nuclear Regulator Accepts Partial Construction Permit Application For Holtec's Palisades SMRs
author: Nigel Davies
text: Timeline presented for environmental report and limited work authorisation

The US Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) has accepted the first part of a construction permit application for review from US-based Holtec International for two SMR-300 small modular reactor (SMR) units in the state of Michigan.
The NRC also said that its final safety evaluation report and final environmental impact report for the project would be available in March 2027.

A decision on a limited work authorisation would then be made by June 2027. The NRC also said that an exemption decision would be taken by August 2026, which would allow Holtec to proceed with the construction of permanent retaining walls.
Texas-based Holtec aims to build two SMR-300 units, called Pioneer Unit 1 and Unit 2, each with a capacity of around 340 MWe at the Palisades nuclear site.
The NRC has also advanced the project from its pre-applicant list to a short-list of official reactor applicants, which Holtec said was a “meaningful step forward in the regulatory process.”
A limited work authorisation would allow Holtec to move forward with early construction activities, including soil compaction, backfilling and foundation installation.
Holtec would still need to meet further safety requirements before receiving an operating licence.
The company aims to have the SMRs running by the early 2030s.

Before that time, Holtec plans to restart the existing single-unit 805-MW pressurised water reactor at Palisades in early 2026. This would be the first nuclear plant in the US to restart after entering into decomissioning.
The Holtec-designed SMR-300 is a pressurised light-water reactor design with an output of 300-340 MWe and 1,050 MWt of thermal power for process applications such as reactor heat for industry.
A computer-generated image of two SMR-300 units at the Palisades site in Michigan. Courtesy Holtec.

title: Steel Dome Installed For China’s Xudapu-1 CAP1000 Nuclear Plant
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Liaoning province site will eventually have six reactor units.
The inner steel containment dome has been hoisted into place for Unit 1 of the Xudapu* nuclear power station being built in Liaoning province in northeast China.
Developer China National Nuclear Corporation (CNNC) said the operation will allow the project to transition from the civil engineering to the equipment installation phase.
The dome, a steel component that weighs about 780 tonnes, was installed earlier this month, CNNC said.
Xudapu-1 is of the CAP1000 PWR design, a domestic version of the Westinghouse AP1000 design. Construction started in November 2023.
The steel containment is an important part of the Generation III plant’s nuclear island reactor building and a key safety barrier to prevent the leakage of radioactive materials.
CNNC said the Xudapu nuclear station is designed to have six units in total.
Units 1 and 2 are of the CAP1000 design, while Units 3 and 4 are of the Russia-supplied VVER-1200 PWR design. The technology for the fifth and sixth unit has not been disclosed.

According to the latest data, China has 36 reactor units under construction. Of those, 12 CAP1000 units are under construction: two each at Haiyang, Lianjiang, Sanmen, Xudapu, Lufeng, and Guangxi Bailong.
* Xudapu is also written in English as Xudabao or Xudabu. The IAEA reactor database uses the official ‘Xudapu’ transcription.
Workers installed the 780-tonne steel dome at Xudapu-1 earlier in February. Image courtesy CNNC.

title: Enusa And GNF Secure New Fuel Contract For Sweden’s Forsmark Nuclear Plant
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Joint venture to supply fuel assemblies from 2028
US-based Global Nuclear Fuel and Spanish nuclear fuel company Enusa have been awarded a contract to supply fuel reloads to Sweden’s Forsmark nuclear power station, the companies said.
The contract was awarded to Genusa, a joint venture owned by GNF and Enusa. It will begin in 2028 and covers several reloads of GNF2 fuel assemblies.
The three-unit Forsmark is owned and operated by Swedish utility Vattenfall.
GNF2 is a boiling water reactor fuel design developed to support higher performance and improved operating efficiency, said GE Vernova, which owns GNF.
The fuel for Forsmark will be fabricated at Enusa’s nuclear fuel manufacturing plant in Juzbado, Spain, using components supplied by GNF.
Craig Ranson, chief executive officer of GNF, said Enusa has manufactured more than 3,500 GNF-designed fuel assemblies for Forsmark since 1993.
Mariano Moreno, president and chief executive officer of Enusa, said the new agreement extends a collaboration with Vattenfall that began more than 30 years ago.
Forsmark-1, -2, and -3, all of the boiling water reactor design, began commercial operation respectively in 1980, 1981, and 1985. The units represent a half of Sweden’s commercial reactor fleet.
GNF2 Fuel Bundle cutaway. Image credit courtesy GE Vernova.

title: Clayco Joins Consortium Aiming To Develop Nuclear-Powered Data Centre Campuses
author: David Dalton
text: Group led by Deep Atomic planning including facility at Idaho National Laboratory

US-based Clayco, a design-build firm specialising in complex mission-critical facilities, has joined a consortium led by Swiss American energy company Deep Atomic that is planning to develop next generation nuclear-powered AI data centre and energy infrastructure campuses.
The consortium is aiming to file submissions to the US Department of Energy (DOE) to develop campuses, including a proposed facility at the Idaho National Laboratory (INL).
Clayco said that pending DOE approval, the INL facility could represent the first fully integrated nuclear-powered AI data centre in the US.
Clayco said it will provide early-stage delivery planning, constructability analysis, and integrated design-build expertise.
The consortium brings together organisations with expertise spanning advanced nuclear technology, energy systems, cost and risk modelling, regulatory strategy, and large-scale computing.
Deep Atomic is advancing an approach that pairs advanced nuclear energy with AI data centre infrastructure to support power needs for next-generation computing.

Deep Atomic is developing the MK60, a 60 MW, Generation III+ SMR designed specifically for onsite, zero-carbon power and cooling for data centres. It uses passive safety systems, proven light water reactor technology, and is designed to provide both electrical energy and 60 MW of cooling capacity.
Deep Atomic says the MK60 is a Generation III+ pressurised light water reactor built on decades of proven nuclear technology. Courtesy Deep Atomic.

title: UK Ready To Begin Generic Design Assessment For TerraPower’s Natrium Reactor
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Acceptance marks company’s first international regulatory filing

The UK has announced its readiness to begin the pre-licensing generic design assessment (GDA) process for TerraPower’s Natrium reactor after the company’s application was accepted for review, a statement said.

The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ) asked the Office for Nuclear Regulation (ONR), the Environment Agency (EA) and Natural Resources Wales to start the process following a readiness review. The review concluded that the design is ready to begin GDA.
A statement said the assessment will begin once necessary arrangements around timescales and resources have been put in place.

TerraPower, which was founded by Bill Gates and other backers, submitted
its GDA application in October 2025. The company said this is its first regulatory filing for the Natrium plant in an international market.
TerraPower chief executive officer Chris Levesque said the company was pleased that its application had been accepted into the UK’s GDA process.

He said TerraPower would bring its regulatory experience and technical expertise to support the review and would work with DESNZ, ONR and the EA in the coming months with the aim of advancing deployment of a Natrium reactor in the UK.

The Natrium technology features a 345 MW sodium-cooled fast reactor with a molten salt-based energy storage system. The storage technology can boost the system’s output to 500 MW for more than five and a half hours when needed.

TerraPower says this innovative addition allows a Natrium plant to integrate seamlessly with renewable resources and leads to faster, more cost-effective decarbonisation of the electric grid while producing dispatchable carbon-free energy.

The company’s first Natrium project is under development in the US as part of a public-private partnership with the US Department of Energy. The company began construction of non-nuclear facilities at a former coal site in Kemmerer, Wyoming, in June 2024.
When completed, the project is expected to be among the first utility-scale advanced nuclear power plant in the US.

In the UK, the GDA process is used by nuclear regulators to assess the new nuclear power station designs. It allows the regulators to assess the safety, security and environmental implications of new reactor designs, separately from applications to build them at specific sites.
TerraPower is building the first Natrium nuclear power plant at a former coal site in Kemmerer, Wyoming. Rendering courtesy TerraPower.

title: Medical Radioisotope Production At Belgium’s BR2 Reactor Sets Record
author: David Dalton
text: Facility met needs of 13 million patients, says nuclear research centre SCK CEN
Production of medical radioisotopes at the Belgian nuclear research centre SCK CEN’s BR2 research reactor met the needs of 13 million patients in 2025, a new record.

SCK CEN said it had increased the number of operating days from 160 to 210 a year in 2020.  This led to a record during of 12 million patients who received diagnosis or treatment thanks to that production. This was five million more than the previous average.
By 2025, 13 million patients were relying on BR2’s production for diagnosis or treatment, SCK CEN said.

Doctors use medical radioisotopes to detect cancers, heart diseases and other illnesses and, in recent years, even treat cancer. However, hospitals cannot stockpile radioisotopes due to radioactive decay.

This decay means that after a certain period – called the half-life – only half the radioactivity remains. That half-life can range from several days to hours. “This means that every minute between production and injection in a hospital counts,” said BR2 director at SCK CEN Steven Van Dyck.
The BR2 research reactor was originally built to test materials and nuclear fuels. It continues to do so but its main job for decades has been the production of medical radioisotopes.

BR2 typically produces 10 to 15 different radioisotopes per operating cycle. This total production figure involves two radioisotopes that account for most of the production: molybdenm-99 (Mo-99) and lutetium-177 (Lu-177).

Mo-99 is the source of the major diagnostic radioisotope technetium-99m, which is used to detect cancer, heart diseases and other illnesses. Lu-177 is a radioisotope used in the fight against prostate cancer and neuroendocrine tumours.
The BR2 research reactor at the SCK CEN nuclear research centre in Belgium. Courtesy SCK CEN.

title: Croatia Sets Goal Of 30% Electricity From Nuclear By 2040 Under New Draft Law
author: Nigel Davies
text: Plans underway for separate legislation to decide location of first plant
Croatia has set a target of producing 30% of its electricity demand from nuclear sources by 2040 under a new draft law covering the development of nuclear energy in the country.

The draft law also stated that within six months an “activity programme” would be developed covering all necessary studies and analyses, and a year later a Plan for the Development of Nuclear Energy for Civilian Purposes would be presented.
A separate law would then be enacted deciding the final location of any potential nuclear power plant once all regulatory procedures had been carried out.

The draft law was presented by Croatian economy minster Ante Šušnjar, who said it represented a strategic step forward in strengthening the country’s energy security, the competitiveness of its economy, and sustainability of its electricity system.

“At a time when electricity consumption is growing and climate goals are becoming ever more demanding, nuclear energy represents a stable, low-carbon, and long-term cost-effective source of energy,” said Šušnjar.
“With this law, Croatia chooses a new energy source and makes a strategic decision that confirms its commitment to energy security, climate responsibility, and technological progress.”
Croatia does not have any nuclear power plants on its own territory, but it co-owns the single-unit Krško nuclear power plant in neighbouring Slovenia.
The draft law said the government would continue to consider additional units at Krško and look at further nuclear capacities including small modular reactors (SMRs).

The Krško pressurised water reactor plant supplies around 20% of Slovenia’s electricity needs, and 16% of Croatia’s. The 696-MW plant, which began commercial operation in January 1983, was granted a lifetime extension until 2043 in 2016.
Slovenia is also preparing feasibility studies to research the potential of adding a second reactor at the plant through partnerships with France’s EDF and US-based Westinghouse.
Croatia does not have any nuclear power plants, but co-owns the single-unit Krško in neighbouring Slovenia. Courtesy Katja143/Creative Commons Licence.

title: Unit 1 At China’s Sanao Nuclear Station Reaches First Criticality
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Facility will eventually consist of six Hualong One units
Unit 1 of the Sanao nuclear power station in the eastern Chinese province of Zhejiang reached first criticality on 14 February, according to local sources.
Sanao-1 is a 1,117-MW domestic Hualong One, or HPR1000, pressurised water reactor (PWR) unit.
First criticality at a PWR is the moment when the reactor core achieves a self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction for the first time.
Construction of Sanao-1 began in December 2020. The unit completed hot functional testing in June 2025.
Fuel was loaded into the reactor core in late December 2025 after the unit received an operating licence earlier that month.
The Sanao nuclear power station will eventually consist of six Hualong One units, with Sanao-1 now under commissioning and another two, Sanao-2 and -3, being under construction.
The Hualong One is an indigenous pressurised water reactor unit that incorporates elements of China National Nuclear Corporation’s ACP1000 and China General Nuclear’s ACPR1000+ reactor designs.
China is moving forward with its indigenous reactor technology. About a half of the county’s 36 reactor units under construction are of the Hualong One design.
Sanao-1 in the eastern Chinese province of Zhejiang has reached first criticality. Courtesy CNNPN.

title: Netherlands Establishes State-Run Nuclear Energy Organisation To Oversee New Reactor Deployment
author: Nigel Davies
text: Federal body will be responsible for every aspect of delivery, says government

The Netherlands has created a new body called the Nuclear Energy Organisation Netherlands (NEO NL) under its Ministry of Climate and Green Growth that will serve to prepare, deliver and operate new nuclear power reactors in the country.

According to the government, NEO NL’s main task will be to build two new nuclear reactors both at the same location and each with at least 1,000 MW* capacity, which would provide the equivalent of electricity to around two million homes.
NEO NL would be responsible for every aspect of the delivery of the power plants from preparation and selection of constructors and suppliers, through to the operation of the plants.
The Ministry of Climate and Green Growth said that a preliminary decision on the reactors’ location would be made after the summer of 2026.

“The establishment of NEO NL is an important step in the construction of new nuclear power plants in the Netherlands and contributes to a stable and future-proof energy supply, making us less dependent on foreign countries,” said Sophie Hermans, caretaker minister at the Ministry of Climate and Green Growth.

NEO NL is in the process of selecting a constructor for the site, and will take over the planning and organisation of the location from the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Climate Policy once a decision over the location was finalised.

A new coalition government recently unveiled a policy document including the development of the nuclear industry and construction of four new reactors in the country, be it large-scale plants or small modular reactors (SMRs).

While the ministry said a location would be unveiled after the summer, in December 2022 the previous Dutch government chose the Borrsele
site as its preferred location for two new nuclear units.

Borssele, in the south of the Netherlands, is the country’s only commercial nuclear plant. The single 482-MW pressurised water reactor unit began commercial operation in 1973. According to the International Atomic Energy Agency, in 2024 it provided a 2.8% share of the country’s electricity production.

The Netherlands recently established a consortium led by US-based engineering and technology company Amentum that will work with NEO NL to provide management and technical solutions to build the country’s nuclear development.
As well as large-scale plants, the Netherlands also plans to develop SMRs in the country, and support maritime nuclear innovations.
*The article was corrected on 2 March 2026 to reflect the fact that 1,000 MW is the lower end of reviewed reactor capacity by the Netherlands and avoid any implication of specific technology.
Borssele, in the south of the Netherlands, is the country’s only commercial nuclear plant. Courtesy Amentum.

title: French Nuclear Startup Blue Capsule Starts Construction Of Key Test Rig
author: David Dalton
text: ‘Elise’ facility will replicate conditions of company’s high-temperature reactor
France-based advanced nuclear reactor startup Blue Capsule Technology has announced the start of construction of “Elise”, a new test rig for sodium at high temperatures.
The company said construction began this week at Peyrolles-en-Provence, outhern France, in collaboration with France-based industrial group CSTI Groupe.
Blue Capsule said Elise is the first installation on its development roadmap and is set to run for several years.

High-temperature sodium test rigs are specialised facilities designed to study material compatibility, thermal hydraulics and component performance in liquid sodium. They are critical for the development of HTRs that use sodium as a coolant.
“Elise will replicate the conditions of the Blue Capsule high-temperature reactor (HTR), with temperatures reaching 750°C,” said the company’s technical director, Domnin Erard.

“This full-size installation will stand at nine metres high when completed, and provide valuable data on thermo-hydraulics and the natural circulation of liquid sodium at high temperatures,” he added.
Blue Capsule president Edouard Hourcade, said the Elise installation will be the “first of its kind" in France, and will be opened to other players in the field, “either institutional or commercial”.
“It is important that the broader nuclear energy sector can benefit from Elise,” he said. “But it’s also a milestone for our company and a sign of steady progress.”
The ELISE project is funded by fresh investment by the company’s historical investors, as well as CSTI Groupe, Robatel, which provides custom radiation protection systems, and Helionix.
Blue Capsule Technology is developing a HTR technology for energy-intensive industries such as cement and metal refining, hydrogen production, and chemical sites.
These vital industries increasingly need a reliable source of fossil-free heat, steam and electricity.
Blue Capsule said its HTR will provide all three: heat to 700°C, steam/vapour to 650°C, and 50 MW of electricity as needed by the customer.
The sodium-cooled reactor will use Triso fuel.  Last November, Blue Capsule announced an agreement with Framatome to advance cooperation on Triso fuel.

“We aim to deploy low-enriched Triso fuel at less than 5% in our reactors, given the wide use of low-enriched uranium in the industry, and the export potential of reactors that use LEU,” a statement said.

Triso (TRi-structural ISOtropic) nuclear fuel is a highly robust, advanced fuel form for high-temperature gas-cooled reactors. It consists of a uranium-based fuel kernel surrounded by three distinct layers of ceramic and carbon materials, which form an individual containment system for each particle.

This tri-structural design is said to provide exceptional resistance to corrosion, high temperatures, and irradiation, making it impossible to melt under extreme conditions and containing radioactive fission products effectively.
The first-of-a-kind Blue Capsule reactor is scheduled for deployment at the beginning of next decade.
A computer-generated image of a cross-section of a Blue Capsule nuclear opower plant. Courtesy Blue Capsule.

title: US Grants Funding To Boost Deployment Of Advanced Nuclear Technologies In Philippines
author: David Dalton
text: Power utility in Asian nation will develop shortlist of reactor technology suppliers

The US is accelerating the deployment of advanced nuclear technologies to the Philippines with funding for the Asian nation’s major power utility to evaluate US small modular reactor (SMR) designs and develop a roadmap for Manila’s first SMR nuclear power plant.

The US Trade and Development Agency (USTDA), which announced the funding, said the project will help address the Philippines’ rising energy demand and position US industry as a long-term partner for nuclear power development in the country.

USTDA’s assistance will provide MGEN, a subsidiary of the Philippines’ largest private electric distribution utility Manila Electric Company (Meralco), with a comprehensive technical review of advanced US-made SMR reactor designs.

The findings will enable MGEN to develop a shortlist of US technology providers for its future procurement needs. The assistance will also deliver a roadmap that incorporates international best practices for project structuring and financing.

USTDA, which backs the development of critical infrastructure projects in emerging markets, said its funding will create opportunities for US industry to be “a preferred partner for building the Philippines’ energy future”.

To complement the technical assistance and further support the Philippines’ SMR goals, USTDA announced it will bring a delegation of Philippine energy decision-makers to the US through a reverse trade mission to observe novel US SMR solutions.
Meralco chairman and chief executive officer Manuel Pangilinan said Meralco sees the USTDA grant as the beginning of a long but necessary journey.

“It simply is right for the country to think nuclear and Meralco is prepared to act as though leader in that regard. We look forward to the progress this collaboration will bring – and to a secure energy future we will build together.”

The Philippines is keen to push ahead with a nuclear power programme and late last year published a comprehensive framework for the integration of nuclear energy into its power generation mix while moving ahead with plans to consider financing options.
In September Philippine president Ferdinand Marcos Jr signed a new law creating an independent regulator to oversee the use of nuclear energy and radiation sources in the country.

The law, known as the Philippine national nuclear energy safety act, establishes the Philippine Atomic Energy Regulatory Authority (PhilATOM) as a quasi-judicial body with exclusive jurisdiction over nuclear and radiation safety.

In June, the Philippine Senate approved a bill to establish the PhilATOM, marking a major step toward developing a legal and regulatory framework for the country’s planned introduction of nuclear power.
In early 2024, the Philippines Department of Energy unveiled plans to deploy 2,400 MW of nuclear power capacity by 2032.
Marcos Jr has repeatedly voiced strong support for nuclear power, stressing the need to reassess the Philippines’ strategy and policies on its use.
In November 2023, the country advanced its nuclear ambitions by signing a so-called 123 Agreement with Washington, opening the door to US nuclear technology, fuel and equipment.
The Philippines built a Westinghouse-supplied 621-MW pressurised water reactor at Bataan, northwest of Manila, which was completed in 1984, but never commissioned.

It was mothballed due to safety concerns in the wake of the Chernobyl disaster in 1986 and issues regarding corruption under the government of Marcos’s late dictator father, Ferdinand Marcos Sr. The site is under consideration for the construction of a small modular reactor.

The Philippines, an archipelago nation of more than 7,000 islands, has been exploring clean and sustainable options to generate power, as the country regularly suffers power outages and faces high power tariffs. Coal remains the main source of electricity, accounting for over half of its power generation.
The Bataan nuclear power plant, north of Manila, was never commissioned. Courtesy Jiru27/Wikipedia Creative Commons Licence.

title: China Announces Progress At Three Nuclear Construction Sites
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Beijing has ambitious plan for 200 GW of reactor capacity by 2035
China has announced further progress at three nuclear construction sites, with containment building components installed at sites in Shandong and Guangdong provinces, said local reports.
At the Haiyang-4 nuclear power unit in Shandong, eastern China, the steel dome of the external containment was hoisted into position on 9 February.
Haiyang-4 is a 1,161-MW CAP1000 pressurised water reactor, China’s Generation III indigenous version of US-based Westinghouse’s AP1000 design. Construction of Haiyang-4 began in April 2023.
In the southern province of Guangdong, workers completed the installation of the inner containment building dome for Unit 1 of the Lianjiang nuclear power station on 10 February.
Lianjiang-1 is the first of two CAP1000 pressurised water reactor units planned as the initial phase of the station, which will eventually house six such reactors.
Construction of Lianjiang-1 began in September 2023, while all main nuclear island equipment installation was in October 2025.
At a third site, the second segment of the inner steel containment for Unit 1 at the Zhaoyuan nuclear power project in Shandong province was successfully hoisted into place on 8 February.
The 245-tonne module was lifted into place by a 2,000-ton crawler crane.
Zhaoyuan-1 will be a domestically developed Hualong One pressurised water reactor unit. First concrete was poured for the nuclear island slab in November 2025.

A total of six reactor units are planned for each of the Zhaoyuan, Haiyang, and Lianjiang sites. Two Westinghouse AP1000 PWR units are already operating at Haiyang since 2018, while Zhaoyuan and Lianjiang are new sites.

The International Atomic Energy Agency’s database of nuclear plants in China says the country has 58 plants in commercial operation. However, recent construction starts have brought the total number of units under construction to 36.

China is aiming for 200 GW of nuclear capacity by 2035, up from around 57 GW today. Nuclear is expected to contribute about 10% of power generation in the country by 2035 – up from around 4.5 today – and 18% by 2060, with a total generation capacity of 400 GW by 2060, the China Nuclear Energy Association has said.

Top photo: Workers completed installation of the external containment building dome for Lianjiang-1. Bottom: the second segment of the inner steel containment for Zhaoyuan-1 was hoisted into place. Courtesy CNNPN.
The steel dome of the external containment i hoisted into position at Haiyang-4. Courtesy CNNPN

title: US Military Airlifts Next-Generation Nuclear Microreactor In Historic First Operation
author: David Dalton
text: Trump administration expects three small reactors to be critical – or running smoothly – by 4 July

The US on 15 February conducted its first air transport of a nuclear microreactor, flying the unit aboard a C-17 Globemaster III aircraft from California to Utah in a move designed to demonstrate how advanced nuclear power could be rapidly deployed for military and civilian use.

The next-generation Ward 250 nuclear reactor was loaded aboard a C-17 Globemaster III aircraft at March Air Reserve Base, California, for transport to Hill Air Force Base, Utah. The reactor will eventually head to the Utah San Rafael Energy Lab for testing and evaluation.
The reactor, developed by California-based Valar Atomics, was transported without nuclear fuel.

The Ward unit, slightly larger than a minivan, is designed to generate up to 5 MW of electricity – theoretically enough to power around 5,000 homes. According to Valar Atomics, the reactor is expected to begin operating in July at 100 kW, rising to 250 kW later this year before eventually reaching full output.
The Ward 250 uses high-temperature gas reactor (HTGR) design principles. Valar Atomics said this architecture has an unmatched safety profile and proliferation resistance when paired with Triso fuel.

A HTGR uses uranium fuel and graphite moderation to produce very high reactor core output temperatures. According to the International Atomic Energy Agency, interest in HTGRs is increasing because they can provide efficient and cost-effective electricity and produce high-temperature process heat usable for various industrial applications.
The US military wants to deploy mobile nuclear microreactors to ensure, resilient, carbon-free and independent power for remote bases and critical infrastructure.

US energy secretary Chris Wright and under-secretary of defense for acquisition and sustainment Michael Duffey accompanied the flight, describing the operation as a milestone for nuclear logistics and base energy resilience.
Wright said the American nuclear renaissance is to “get that ball moving again, fast, carefully, but with private capital, American innovation and determination”
Part of that effort, he said, will mean that by 4 July, the administration expects three small reactors will be critical – or running smoothly.

In August 2025 the US Department of Energy (DOE) officially kicked off a nuclear reactor pilot programme that will see it initially work with 11 advanced reactor projects with the goal of building, operating and achieving criticality of at least three test reactors by 4 July 2026.

The DOE said it had initially chosen 10 companies for the programme. They were: Aalo Atomics, Antares Nuclear, Atomic Alchemy, Deep Fission, Last Energy, Oklo, Natura Resources, Radiant Industries, Terrestrial Energy and Valar Atomics.
In November 2025 Valar Atomics said it had achieved cold criticality – an essential nuclear milestone – with the help of one of the country’s top nuclear laboratories.
The company, which last year secured a $130m (€112m) funding round, claimed that it was the first nuclear startup to create a critical fission reaction.

Valar Atomics said approach-to-criticality operations began at Los Alamos National Laboratory’s National Criticality Experiments Research Center at the Nevada National Security Site on 12 November and zero-power criticality was achieved at 11:45 local time on 17 November.

Zero-power criticality, or “cold criticality”, is the foundational milestone which precedes nuclear operation with power. It is a self-sustaining chain reaction of uranium-235 within a nuclear core, but without reaching full operating temperatures or actively removing heat with a working fluid.
The C-17 Globemaster III aircraft with the reactor on board at March Air Reserve Base, California. Courtesy US Department of War.
The Ward 250 microreactor is loaded into the back of a C-17 Globemaster III aircraft on 15 February 2026, at March Air Reserve Base, California. Courtesy US Department of War.

title: South Korea Passes ‘SMR Special Act’ With Aim Of Becoming Global Leader In Technology
author: Nigel Davies
text: New committee to decide on key matters governing rapid rollout of additional nuclear capacity

South Korea’s Ministry of Science and Information and Communication Technology has passed a special small modular reactor (SMR) development act in the National Assembly as the country aims to catch up with others in the SMR race.

The ministry confirmed the news on its website. It said that until now South Korea had focused on developing large-scale nuclear plants, while other countries such as the US and UK had already enacted laws to support the growth of SMRs.

Under the new legislation, the ministry said it would establish an SMR development plan and implementation plan, which it would update every five years and which would cover SMR development goals, R&D and promotion strategies and financing.
The government said the plan would be established within one year following cabinet and presidential approval.
In addition, it said it would pursue new large-scale projects to accelerate the completion of SMR core technology development and design alongside private companies to prepare for commercialisation.

“The nuclear community has continuously called for the enactment of special legislation to ensure policy consistency for SMRs and accelerate research and development, and this long-standing wish of the nuclear community has been fulfilled through the passage of the SMR Special Act in the National Assembly,” the ministry said in a statement.
An SMR system development promotion committee would also be created that would decide on key matters governing a rapid rollout of SMR capacity.

The ministry said it would support the creation of public-private companies and research institutes to successfully develop SMR technology, as well as training facilities to secure professionals to operate them.

Deputy prime minister Bae Kyung-hoon welcomed the news. “The National Assembly’s passage of the SMR Special Act is an achievement that embodies the will of the National Assembly and the government to accelerate the development of SMRs, a core energy source in the AI era, and a leap forward as a global SMR leader,” he said.

The statement said that the ministry expected the act to serve as a key foundation for accelerating R&D, proving SMRs as a stable carbon-free energy source and “for Korea to take the lead in the global SMR market”.
The ministry also said that it would implement policies to increase understanding and acceptance of SMRs among the general public.

South Korea has 26 nuclear units in commercial operation, according to the International Atomic Energy Agency, as well as two, Saeul-3 and -4 listed as under construction. Together the 26 units provide 31.7% of the country’s electricity production.

Global interest in SMRs, meanwhile, is gathering pace, as their smaller design means lower upfront costs and flexibility in construction, and they can also be deployed in remote regions or to provide energy to heavy industry.
South Korea has 26 nuclear units in commercial operation and two, Saeul-3 and Saeul-4, under construction. Courtesy KHNP.

title: Nuclearelectrica Shareholders Approve Plans For Small Modular Reactor Project At Former Romania Coal Site
author: David Dalton
text: Doicesti could have up to six modules supplied by US company NuScale

Nuclearelectrica, the operator of Romania’s only nuclear power station at Cernavodă, said on 12 January that its shareholders have approved the final investment decision for a 462 MW small modular reactor (SMR) project in the southern commune of Doicesti, around 90 km northwest of the capital Bucharest, which will use technology developed by US-based NuScale Power.

The company's shareholders, including the energy ministry, approved a credit line of up to $243m (€205m) to RoPower Nuclear, with $6m earmarked for immediate pre-engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) activities, Nuclearelectrica said in a statement.

The pre-EPC budget for the project is estimated at around $600m. Pre-EPC activities will begin in May and include geotechnical investigations, continuing the licensing process, finalising pre-EPC contract negotiations and negotiating contracts for long-lead items.
The proposed site for the Doicesti SMR is on a former coal power plant. NuScale confirmed last year that infrastructure had been removed at the site to allow construction to begin.

Under the approved plan, RoPower Nuclear, a project company equally owned by Nuclearelectrica and partner Nova Power & Gas, will initially pay NuScale for one 77-MW SMR module, out of the six planned for Doicesti.
RoPower will pay for the other five SMRs only after the first reactor is proven to be fully functional, moving part of the risk on the project to NuScale.
Alternatively, RoPower could choose to pay for all six SMRs from the start, but would be allowed to ask for a refund on the final five SMRs if the first one does not function as intended.

The first SMR module is scheduled to become operational in July 2033, while the entire facility is expected to be completed in December 2034, depending on commercial agreements for the acquisition of the remaining five SMR modules.
Nuclearelectrica and NuScale had initially announced that the SMR would be deployed by 2030.

Energy minister Bogdan Ivan said the final investment decision for the SMR project in Doicesti marks the transition from the analysis phase to the implementation phase, consolidating Romania’s position at the forefront of the new European nuclear industry.

“We are replacing 600 MW from a former thermal power plant with 462 MW of clean, stable, and predictable energy. Approximately 4,000 jobs will be generated in the development phase, in construction, production, and component assembly, and in the long term, we are talking about stable, well-paid jobs and the development of a horizontal Romanian industry.”

Bogdan said that over the next six months, the project will “enter a phase of financial structuring and partnership consolidation”, during which financing mechanisms will be defined and discussions with potential investors for the execution phase will be advanced.
Cernavodă has two 650-MW Canada-designed Candu-6 reactors which generate an almost 20% share of electricity production. Bucharest is planning to add two new reactors at the site.
RoPower Nuclear is planning to deploy six 77-MW NuScale SMR modules at Doicesti. Courtesy NuScale.

title: France Publishes Energy Roadmap That Confirms Plans For Six New Nuclear Power Plants
author: David Dalton
text: Strategy also includes option for eight more advanced EPR2 plants as part of major commitment to nuclear
France has published a key energy roadmap, aiming for 60% electricity consumption by 2030, with six new nuclear reactors and a mix of renewable energies.

At the heart of the strategy, officially labelled the third multi-year energy programme, or PPE3, is the major objective of increasing electricity’s share of France’s total energy consumption to 60% by 2030, up from around 30% today.
Reports in France said the PPE3 had been finalised after years of wrangling. It calls for cuts in wind and solar power targets and drops a mandate for state-run firm EDF to shutter nuclear plants.
Six new-generation EPR2 nuclear reactors are included in the roadmap, with eight additional reactors listed as an option.

State-owned power company EDF said it was committed to the PPE3 with the construction programme for six EPR2 nuclear reactors and an option for eight more, extending the operating life of existing nuclear reactors, and revitalising investments in hydropower while maintaining expertise in renewable energy, particularly offshore wind projects.
“EDF teams are mobilised to carry out these projects in compliance with the requirements set in terms of safety, security, quality, deadlines and costs,” a statement said.

EDF chairman and chief executive officer Bernard Fontana said: “The publication of the multi-year energy programme allows EDF to move forward towards its objectives: to provide the French people, today and for future generations, with competitive, sovereign and low-carbon electricity.”

France’s state-owned multinational fuel cycle company Orano said the opportunities presented by the PPE3 represent significant ongoing and future investments across the entire fuel cycle. This includes the challenge of ensuring mining supplies and increasing industrial uranium enrichment capacity.

The PPE3 would also mean the continuation of France’s treatment and recycling strategy, including the “renewal” of the La Hague nuclear fuel treatment and recycling plant in Normandy, northern France, and the Melox recycling plant in Gard, southern France, Orano said.
It said this translates into a programme representing significant investments over several decades.
EDF has already submitted an application for authorisation to build two EPR2 plants at Penly in Normandy. A second pair of EPR plants is being planned for Gravelines, about 170 km northeast of Penly.
EDF said in October that it was planning to submit an application for an environmental permit and begin preparatory work as early as 2027 for a two EPR2s at the Bugey site, in southeastern France.
Bugey would be the third project in a major French plan to deploy new EPR2 units.

The construction plans align with the new energy roadmap. They were originally announced by president Emmanuel Macron during a speech in 2022. He said the new units would be part of a programme for a “rebirth” of France’s nuclear industry with the possible construction of 14 EPR2 units and operating extensions for older nuclear plants from 40 years to 50 years or more.
In addition to the six EPR2 units at Penly, Gravelines and Bugey, another eight could also be built on existing sites, Macron said at the time.
Macron is bullish on nuclear. His government has asked state nuclear operator EDF to accelerate efforts to finalise its plans to build the six new EPR2 plants.

France’s share of generation from its fleet of 56 nuclear plants last year was about 62% – the highest in the world. However, it only has one commercial plant under construction, the Flamanville-3 EPR plant, a project which has been hit by cost overruns and delays. Flamanville-3 was connected to the grid in December 2024, but has not yet begun full commercial operation.

Eleven pro-nuclear European governments led by France have said nuclear should be part of the EU’s energy policies and the European Commission should facilitate the development of the technology in Europe.
EDF has already submitted an application for authorisation to build two EPR2 plants at Penly in Normandy. Courtesy Sfen.
Flamanville-3 is the only nuclear plant under construction in France. It was connected to the grid in December 2024, but has not yet begun full commercial operation. Courtesy EDF.

title: US Pledges $9 Billion Investment In Armenia Nuclear Power
author: David Dalton
text: Aim is for country to reduce energy reliance on Russia
US vice-president JD Vance signed a civil nuclear cooperation agreement with Armenia, pledging as much as $9bn (€7.5bn) in potential investment.

The accord, known as a Section 123 agreement, establishes the legal framework for US companies to export nuclear technology, fuel and services to Armenia and opens the door for US firms to compete for a deal to replace the Soviet-era Armenian nuclear power station.

“It’ll pave the way for American and Armenian companies to strike deals on civil nuclear projects. That means up to $5 billion in initial US exports, plus an additional $4 billion in long-term support through fuel and maintenance contracts,” Vance said at a briefing in Yerevan.

“This is a classic win-win for both Armenia and the United States of America. It means stronger energy security for my own country, stronger energy security for Armenia, and it’s also going to create a lot of new jobs.”

Armenia has relied on Moscow for both energy and security since independence from Russia in 1991. The Armenian nuclear facility is operated by Russia’s state-owned nuclear corporation Rosatom and nuclear fuel for the plant is imported from Russia.

The Armenian nuclear power station, also known as Metsamor, has a 416-MW (net) pressurised-water reactor, Armenian-2, that went into commercial operation in 1980. Another unit, Armanian-1, was permanently shut down in 1989. Both units were supplied by Russia.
Last year the Armenian government established a company that will evaluate options for new reactor construction in the country.

The company will look into technology vendors’ proposals on the possible design and cost of a new nuclear unit in Armenia, with the goal of having a development plan for the new capacity by the middle of 2026.
Cooling towers at the Armenian nuclear power station. Courtesy Adam Jones/Flickr.

title: Experience Gained From Pallas ‘Could Save Billions’ For Netherlands New Build
author: David Dalton
text: Government considering construction of up to four nuclear reactors

The experience gained from development and construction of the new Pallas research reactor in the Netherlands could lead to a time saving of around one to three years in construction and financial benefits from between €1bn ($1.1bn) and €6bn when the country comes to build new commercial plants, a report has shown.
The report say the Pallas project is of great added value for the construction of new nuclear power plants in the Netherlands.
It shows that the knowledge gained from Pallas could result in risk reduction due to a lower chance of redesigns and fewer issues with suppliers or regulators, thereby reducing the risk of delays.

Pallas also contributes to strengthening the nuclear ecosystem by enabling a new generation of professionals to gain experience and suppliers to invest in knowledge in order to meet nuclear quality standards.

Maurits Wolleswinkel, chief executive officer of NRG Pallas, the company in charge of the Pallas project, said: “With Pallas, the Netherlands has been able to gain unique knowledge about what realisation of a large-scale nuclear project practically entails.
“Research agency SEO was asked whether it would be worthwhile to proactively retain this knowledge and manpower once the programme has completed all the various project phases.”

The Dutch government is preparing to build
two new nuclear power plants and is exploring the possibility of building two more. NRG Pallas said this task is taking place in an international context in which large-scale nuclear power plant construction projects often face delays and cost overruns.
Delays usually occur in the phase prior to the start of construction –permitting, design, contracting and planning – because that is when the design principles are established.
Against this backdrop, SEO looked at the value of the Pallas programme for the construction of future Dutch nuclear power plants.
Pallas, which will replace the High Flux Reactor (HFR) in Petten, is the first major nuclear project in the Netherlands since the 1970s. Construction officially began in September 2025.

NRG Pallas has said that, unlike the older HFR, which was primarily designed for research, the Pallas reactor is being purpose-built to focus on both radioisotope production and research applications.
Pallas is expected to play a central role in ensuring a reliable European supply of radioisotopes for medical, industrial, and research use.
File photo from 2025 shows work on the reactor pit at the new Pallas research reactor in the Netherlands. Courtesy NRG Pallas.

title: Polish Research Network And OSGE Join Forces On Development Of SMRs
author: David Dalton
text: Plans for centre to train staff for operation of BWRX-300 nuclear reactor fleet
The Lukasiewicz Research Network and Orlen Synthos Green Energy (OSGE) have launched a collaboration to advance the development of small modular reactors (SMRs) in Poland.

Plans include the establishment and joint operation of a nuclear energy training centre. The agreement was signed at the Lukasiewicz–Electrotechnical Institute in Warsaw, where the facility is planned to be located.
The training centre will support the development of personnel to operate a fleet of SMRs. It will also serve as a hub for information, training and educational programmes.
The cooperation will encompass R&D work and the commercialisation of technologies related to SMRs.
OSGE is planning to build BWRX-300 reactors designed by GE Vernova Hitachi Nuclear Energy.

The statement said SMRs will play a pivotal role in Poland’s energy transition by filling the gap in low-emission, stable energy production that will be left by the closure of coal-fired power plants in the 2030s and 2040s.

“Building a fleet of BWRX-300 reactors in Poland is an unprecedented undertaking,” said Bartosz Fijalkowski, vice-president of OSGE. “This process requires the highest technological and safety standards, as well as competent personnel.”

The Lukasiewicz Research Network is an organisation comprised of 22 institutes. It was established in 2019 as a state entity designed to bridge the gap between science and business, operating under the supervision of the Polish government.

OSGE is a joint venture established by state energy company Orlen and privately owned SGE (formerly Synthos Green Energy), which is part of the MS Galleon Group holding, the largest private industrial group in Poland, owned by Polish billionaire and investor Michal Sołowow. The Galleon Group is also owner of chemical firm Synthos, one the group's largest industrial subsidiaries.
In December 2023, joint venture OSGE received a decision-in-principle for the construction of up to 24 SMRs at six potential sites across the country.
OSGE is planning to build BWRX-300 reactors designed by GE Vernova Hitachi Nuclear Energy. Courtesy GVH.

title: US Job Cuts At DOE And NRC Are Hurting Goal Of Energy Leadership, Says Thinktank
author: Nigel Davies
text: Nuclear Innovation Alliance president tells hearing more staff needed as industry activity grows

Job cuts at both the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) and the Department of Energy (DOE) could risk hurting the country’s goal of accelerating energy leadership, according to thinktank the Nuclear Innovation Alliance (NIA).

In testimony to the US House Committee on Energy and Commerce’s Subcommittee on Energy in January, NIA president Judi Greenwald, said that many offices in the DOE were short of staff and may face further cuts to their budgets and staffing.

She said that while the DOE had taken on a rapidly expanding portfolio of nuclear energy programmes and public-private partnerships, that the number of staff had dramatically declined. Citing reports, she said that close to 3,500 DOE staff had left the agency.
“These reductions in staff run counter to the vision of US energy leadership laid out by the Trump administration and supported by Congress,” she said in the written testimony.
In particular, she said that since 2012 the DOE’s Office of Nuclear Energy (NE) had seen its budget increase by 133%, but funding had fallen by 3%.

Greenwald said in order for the NE “to build and sustain effective public-private partnerships, accelerate the commercialisation of next-generation nuclear technologies…it needs adequate funding and staffing to match its expanding mission”.

She also said that the DOE’s Office of Energy Dominance Financing (EDF) had seen staffing levels reduced by 60% over the past year, and could not keep pace with the need to issue new loan guarantees needed to finance energy and manufacturing investments.

“It is in Congress’s interest to ensure that the EDF has the personnel and funding necessary to responsibly distribute these loan guarantees, conduct rigorous due diligence, and maximise the public value of every dollar invested.”
Similarly, Greenwald said that the NRC was suffering from staffing shortages. She said that 400 staff had left the agency in 2025 and many leadership positions had been vacated, with only 63 joining.
“The exodus of these experienced personnel is highly concerning,” she said.

Greenwald argued that the NRC’s role in re-establishing US nuclear energy leadership, meant that it required “a bipartisan set of independent commissioners, experienced civil service leaders, and a dedicated, accountable, and empowered staff are the essential conditions for successful nuclear technology regulation”.

She said that the functioning of executive agencies, and of the NRC in particular, had become a hot topic. Greenwald said that some recent actions “are undermining NRC’s transparency and independence”, while indicating that it was not too late to be corrected.
Greenwald said the firing of chairman Chris Hanson was “against both law and precedent” and that NRC rule-making procedures had reduced its transparency.

She added that “a trusted and competent safety regular is required to achieve the ambitious nuclear power expansion goals set forth by presidents from both parties and supported by bipartisan majorities in Congress.”

During the testimony, Greenwald called for the DOE to accelerate the distribution of the $3.4 billion (€2.9bn) Haleu Availability Program, which aims to end US dependance on Russia for the high-assay low-enriched uranium needed for many advanced reactor designs.
She said that while the DOE had selected the final candidates for the enrichment programme, it so far had awarded them $2.7bn (€2.3bn) and that the remaining funds must be distributed without delay.
“Any additional delay in distributing the remaining funding would be detrimental to the United States’ ability to secure our nuclear fuel supply chain, specifically, our deconversion capacity.”
Greenwald said that the US’ “secret sauce for successful energy innovation and commercialisation” had always been a cross-societal effort with private sector leadership and government enabling.
She urged Congress to ensure that the government had the people, resources and public trust needed to enable nuclear energy to play a major role in an affordable, reliable and clean US energy system.

title: Eagles Consortium And Newcleo Join Forces To Develop Lead-Cooled Fast Reactor Demonstrator In Belgium
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Facility at Mol expected to be completed by 2034

The European Eagles* consortium and French advanced reactor developer newcleo have agreed to work together on the development of a lead-cooled fast reactor demonstrator in Belgium, a joint statement said.

The statement said the partners will cooperate on Leandrea, a low-power lead-cooled reactor to be built at the site of the Belgian nuclear research centre SCK-CEN near Mol, in Flanders, northern Belgium.
The facility is expected to be completed by 2034 and will serve as both a technology demonstrator and a test reactor for fuels and materials.

The Eagles consortium includes Italy-based nuclear company Ansaldo Nucleare, ENEA (the Italian National Agency for New Technologies, Energy and Sustainable Economic Development), Romania’s state nuclear research company Raten and SCK-CEN.
The statement said Leandrea will provide the irradiation capacity needed to support the development of lead-cooled fast reactor technology in Europe.
Under the agreement, Eagles and newcleo will share engineering work and coordinate research activities to avoid duplication.
The partners said the cooperation will help speed up progress toward commercial deployment of their respective reactor designs.
Newcleo is developing its own lead-cooled fast reactor design, the LFR-AS-200. The company hopes to deploy its first commercial units in the mid-2030s.

Belgian energy minister Mathieu Bihet announced the deal during an event in Brussels. He said that “the fast-neutron reactor sector represents an essential path forward” for energy sovereignty in Europe.

Roberto Adinolfi, chief executive of Ansaldo Nucleare, said the partnership allows the groups to “reduce duplication, optimise resources, and shorten timelines” to market readiness. Newcleo chief executive officer Stefano Buono said the agreement “redefines the lead-cooled fast reactor as Europe’s reference advanced reactor technology”.
SCK-CEN, which will operate the Leandrea facility, said the design will use "proven technology" where possible to make sure construction stays on schedule for 2034.

According to the announcement, Leandrea will be part of the Eagles roadmap, which will use a "step-by-step" approach. After the demonstrator is completed in Belgium, the group plans to build a larger demonstrator called Alfred in Romania.
Their companies’ goal is to have their Eagles-300, a 300-MW commercial lead-cooled fast small modular reactor, ready for the market by 2039.

Earlier reports said the Eagles-300 plant will include high power output and grid flexibility, making it suitable for electricity production, industrial heat supply and hydrogen production. Its modular design will mean less investment in construction compared to previous generations, faster construction and flexible deployment.

Lead-cooled fast reactors are considered Generation IV technology. Because they use fast neutrons, they can also use nuclear fuel more effectively and reduce the amount of long-lived radioactive waste.
Both the Eagles-300 and Newcleo's LFR-AS-200 design have been included in a shortlist of projects of interest for deployment by the European industrial alliance on small modular reactors.
*European Advanced Generation IV Lead-Cooled Energy System
The signing of the agreement between the European Eagles consortium and advanced reactor developer newcleo. Courtesy Eagles Consortium/newcleo.

title: Tepco Restarts Unit 6 At Japan’s Kashiwazaki Kariwa Nuclear Power Station
author: David Dalton
text: Move follows delay last month after problem related to control rods
Tokyo Electric Power Company (Tepco) has restarted a unit at its Kashiwazaki Kariwa nuclear power station after operations were suspended in January shortly after the initial restart.

Press reports in Japan, quoting a Tepco spokesperson, said Unit 6 at the facility in Niigata Prefecture, western Japan, was restarted at 14:00 local time on 9 February. The unit’s power output will be gradually increased, with the goal of full commercial operation on 18 March. The utility which owns and operates the Kashiwazaki Kariwa facility, was initially aiming for Feb. 26 before the hiccup.
The restart of Kashiwazaki Kariwa-6 was initially suspended last month a day after the process began.

Workers at the plant, which had been offline since the 2011 Fukushima disaster, originally began restarting the unit on 21 January. But the process had to be suspended hours later due to a malfunction related to control rods, which are essential to starting up and shutting down reactors, Tepco said. The Japan Times said the fault was caused by an electrical problem inside the panel used to operate and monitor the unit’s control rods.

Tepco said there was no safety issue from the glitch and it was checking the situation while suspending the restart operation. The utility later said it was putting the reactor back into shutdown for a fuller examination.
Unit 6 is a 1,315-MW boiling water reactor unit that originally began commercial operation in 1996. Fuel loading for its restart was completed in June.
The plant’s restart would mean Japan has returned 15 units to service since the Fukushima disaster.

Kashiwazaki Kariwa is the world’s largest nuclear power station by capacity. According to the International Atomic Energy Agency, its seven boiling water reactor units have a combined net capacity of 7,965 MW.
The facility served as an important energy source to supply electricity to the Tokyo metropolitan area before the 2011 earthquake, tsunami and nuclear accident at Fukushima-Daiichi.
Tepco wants to bring the station back online and said in 2020 it was concentrating its resources on restarting the newer Units 6 and 7.
Units 6 and 7 at Kashiwazaki Kariwa have been offline since March 2012 and August 2011 respectively.

Japan has 33 commercially available units, 15 of which, including Kashiwazaki Kariwa, have now resumed operation under stringent post-Fukushima rules. Restarts face high regulatory hurdles and need local government support.

The 15 that have restarted are: Kashiwazaki Kariwa-6 (Tepco), Onagawa-2 (Tohoku Electric Power), Shimane-2 (Chugoku Electric Power), Mihama-3, Takahama-1, -2, -3, -4, and Ohi-3, -4 (Kansai Electric Power), Ikata-3 (Shikoku Electric Power), Genkai-3, -4, and Sendai-1 -2 (Kyushu Electric Power).
Before the 2011 Fukushima disaster Japan’s fleet of 54 nuclear plants generated about 30% of the country’s electricity, but were all shut down for safety checks following the accident.
According to the International Atomic Energy Agency, the figure for 2023, was 5.5%, but the government want to see this climb to 20%.
Japan’s new prime minister Sanae Takaichi has said she will push for the accelerated revival of nuclear power with reactor restarts key to reducing costly fuel imports.
Kashiwazaki Kariwa is the world’s largest nuclear power station by capacity. Courtesy Tepco.
The central control room at the Kashiwazaki Kariwa nuclear power plant. Courtesy Tepco.

title: Inner Steel Dome Lifted Into Place At China’s Zhangzhou-3 Nuclear Plant
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Facility will have six Hualong One reactor units in total

The inner steel dome of the containment building has been installed for the Zhangzhou-3 nuclear reactor unit under construction in Fujian province, eastern China, the China Nuclear Energy Association (CNEA) reported.
The dome forms part of the reactor’s containment building, which consists of an inner steel shell and an outer concrete shell.
The containment is designed to protect the reactor from external effects and withstand high external and internal pressures and protect against radiation release.
According to the CNEA, the single-piece Zhangzhou-3 inner steel dome weighs 370 tonnes.
Last month, workers completed the installation of all three steam generators for the 1,126-MW domestic Hualong One, or HPR1000, pressurised water reactor unit.
Construction of Zhangzhou-3 began in February 2024.
The Zhangzhou nuclear station will have six Hualong One reactor units in total.
In January 2025, Zhangzhou-1 became the first Hualong One unit to start commercial operation at the site. Zhangzhou-2 started commercial operation in January 2026.
The Hualong One, also known as the HPR1000, is a domestically developed PWR that combines features from China National Nuclear Corporation’s ACP1000 and China General Nuclear’s ACPR1000+ designs.
