The International Atomic Energy Agency’s (IAEA) database of nuclear plants in China says China has 58 plants in commercial operation and 29 under construction.
However, construction has begun of another seven units that are not listed by the IAEA, bringing the number to 36. About half of those are of the domestic Hualong One design.
Installation of the inner steel dome of the containment building at Zhangzhou-3 in China. Courtesy CNEA.

title: Electricity Production At Armenian Nuclear Power Plant Shows 2025 Increase
author: David Dalton
text: Country still considering options for possible new-build
The Armenian nuclear power plant produced 2.7 billion kWh net of electricity in 2025, an increase of 2.7% over 2024, operator Armenia Nuclear Power Plant (ANPP) said.
The nuclear share in the country’s overall national electricity production was 30.62% net and the average load factor of the plant was 74.83%.

In May, the plant’s only operating unit, Unit-2, was shut down for its annual outage for 60 days, which is longer than the plant’s standard outage time of the plant. This was due to the addition of several new projects to existing ones, including replacing the automation in the turbine shop and upgrading the generator and transformer protection systems.

The World Association of Nuclear Operators (WANO) conducted a number of missions to the plant in 2025. The first was a support mission on integrated risk management systems. A preliminary corporate peer review was held in June and in August there was an expert mission from the WANO Moscow Centre. That visit was a part of WANO’s enhanced monitoring programme.
In October an International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) team completed a review of long-term operational safety of the Armenian nuclear power plant.
The review mission was for Unit 2, a 412-MW (net) pressurised-water reactor that went into commercial operation in 1980. Unit 1 was permanently shut down in 1989.

In October 2021, the Armenian Nuclear Regulatory Authority (ANRA) issued a permit for Unit 2 to operate until September 2026. ANPP has requested permission from ANRA to operate for an additional 10 years until September 2036.
Last year the Armenian government established a company that will evaluate options for new reactor construction in the country.

The company will look into technology vendors’ proposals on the possible design and cost of a new nuclear unit in Armenia, with the goal of having a development plan for the new capacity by the middle of 2026.

title: Core Power Tells US To Act Now On Using Nuclear Technologies In Shipbuilding
author: David Dalton
text: Comments come against backdrop of global race to deploy maritime reactor systems

Core Power, a developer of maritime nuclear technologies for both grid-scale energy generation and commercial shipping, has said the US has the opportunity to use nuclear technologies to shape the future of its shipbuilding industry, but must act now to protect its “first mover advantage”.

At a summit in Washington which brought together senior leaders from the administration and Congress, delegates heard how competitor nations are moving with intent because they recognise what leadership in maritime nuclear confers: market access, influence over global rules, and long-term dependency through fuel, service and certification conventions.

The summit explored how advanced nuclear technologies can drive a revival of US shipbuilding while strengthening national energy security and adding resilience to global shipping and the trade that depends on it.

Core Power said the summit took place against the backdrop of a global race to develop and deploy maritime nuclear systems for coastal energy and commercial shipping, with major strategic, industrial, and standards-setting consequences.

The company, which is headquartered in London with offices in Washington and Tokyo, said it maintains that the US has the strongest starting position to compete in this race with a deep civilian nuclear technology base, unmatched naval nuclear experience, world-class regulators, and a maritime heritage that is primed for reindustrialisation.

But with international competitors biting at its heels, the US must do all it can to protect its first mover advantage to secure not only its own maritime industry, but the standards which will govern the future of international shipping.

Core Power chief executive officer Mikal Bøe said: “We believe that home-grown construction of floating nuclear power ships and, subsequently, civil nuclear propelled vessels is critical to revitalising shipbuilding in the US.

“However, several competitor nations have also recognised the opportunities from maritime nuclear, for energy generation and shipping, and the US cannot afford to let others define safety expectations, operating norms, training pathways, liability conventions, and port access requirements as these standards may not align with American interests.”

Core Power said it industrialises proven reactor designs into fully modular nuclear energy systems that are manufactured and integrated in US shipyards – delivering factory-built floating nuclear power plants for reliable, relocatable electricity and nuclear-propelled vessels.
Mikal Bøe said home-grown construction of floating nuclear power ships and civil nuclear propelled vessels is critical to revitalising shipbuilding in the US. Courtesy Core Power.

title: US NRC Launches ‘Significant Reorganisation’ In Bid For Streamlining
author: David Dalton
text: Move follows executive orders issued by Donald Trump

The US Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) is launching what it called a “significant reorganisation” to streamline decision making, consolidate functions and align with national goals for more efficient licensing and deployment of innovative nuclear technology.
The regulatory agency said in a statement that it will reorganise around core business lines of new reactors, operating reactors, and nuclear materials and waste.

Licensing and inspection functions will be integrated within each business line to create a single point of accountability and improve coordination between licensing and inspection teams from the onset of projects.

In addition, functions carried out under the corporate support business line will be consolidated to improve efficiency.  The corporate support business line provides essential administrative and infrastructure support for the NRC’ nuclear safety and regulatory programmes.

“We are in one of the most consequential periods in the NRC’s history, and this reorganisation enables us to meet the moment with more efficient and timely decision making,” said NRC chairman Ho Nieh, who was sworn in as an NRC commisioner in December 2025 and designated chairman by president Donald Trump in January 2026.

“This reorganisation focuses the NRC’s structure around national priorities aimed at accelerating the safe deployment of nuclear technologies. This reorganisation is also aimed at achieving greater consistency in the implementation of agency safety programs across the NRC regional offices.”

The NRC said the changes meet requirements in Trump’s Executive Orders (EO) 14300, “Ordering Reform of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission,” and EO 14210, “Implementing the Department of Government Efficiency Workforce Optimization Initiative.”
“Moving carefully but expeditiously to carry out this reorganization is imperative to provide much-needed stability and certainty for our staff,” said executive director for operations Mike King.
Ho Nieh (left) being sworn in as an NRC commisioner in December 2025. Courtesy NRC.

title: Kazakhstan Approves Construction Of Second Nuclear Power Station
author: Nigel Davies
text: Facility will be built next to first plant on shores of Lake Balkhash

Kazakhstan has approved construction of its second nuclear power station on a site alongside the one already chosen for its first nuclear plant near Lake Balkhash, in the southwest of the country, about 400 km north of the former capital Almaty.

The news was confirmed in a brief resolution signed at the end of January by prime minister Oljas Bektenov. The resolution was published online, but gave no further details of plans for the second plant.

Kazakhstan plans to build its first nuclear power station, called Balkhash, on the shores of Lake Balkhash. The facility is expected to deploy two Russian Generation III+ WER-1200 pressurised water reactor units.

Press reports in Kazakhstan said the second station is expected to use technology from the China National Nuclear Corporation. In time, a third station is also expected to be built in Kazakhastan using the same Chinese technology.

In January, the country’s president Kassym-Jomart Tokayev said Kazakhastan must build nuclear power stations to meet growing electricity demand and fix the “historical absurdity” of being a large uranium producer and yet having no nuclear power capacity.
Kazakhstan holds around 40% of the global supply of uranium and is the world’s largest producer.
The country aims for nuclear power to represent around 5% of its energy mix by 2035.

Tokayev said in his state of the nation address in September that the construction of Kazakhstan’s first commercial nuclear power station will not be enough to ensure stable economic growth and the country must begin planning the construction of a second and even a third facility.

The US is also looking to build up its presence in the country. Washington announced recently that it would establish a small modular reactor (SMR) classroom simulator at Kazakhstan’s Institute of Nuclear Physics in Almaty to accelerate deployment of US SMRs in the country.

Kazakhstan is advancing its nuclear power programme to diversify its energy mix and reduce reliance on coal, which make up roughly 50% of the total energy supply, with substantial use in the industrial and residential sectors.

title: Europe Must Show Stronger Policy Support Towards Nuclear To Attract Private Investment, Says Thinktank
author: Nigel Davies
text: Centre for European Policy Studies says Sweden and Poland may provide pathway

Financing for nuclear projects within the European Union remains the central bottleneck for a real nuclear renaissance and clearer public policies are required to stimulate private investment, Brussels-based thinktank the Centre for European Policy Studies (CEPS) says.
CEPS said that while the advent of small modular reactors (SMRs) might eventually alter the dynamic, strong public backing, as well as funding, remained indispensable.

“This doesn’t diminish the role of private investment,” CEPS said. “Strong political and policy support, including de-risking options such as state-backed guarantees, are essential for underpinning private investment and lowering financing costs.”
CEPS added that private investors would only commit to financing projects if EU states provide “robust, transparent risk-sharing to kickstart deployment”.
It said that EU funding and de-risking tools also matter, with the European Investment Bank’s (EIB) “cautious re-engagement” with nuclear being welcomed.
The EIB finances some nuclear power projects, but is particularly focused on those that are seen as “technically, environmentally and economically justified”.

CEPS said that currently perhaps only Sweden met the conditions of providing a clear policy outlook. It said its government loans, political guarantees, and two-way contracts for difference were useful case studies.
Sweden has since 2022 looked to bring back nuclear power to the table having recognised the limitations of creating a system principally led by renewables.

According to the CEPS, Poland also provided a good example having committed state aid to finance its first nuclear power station. The project was signed off in a record time of under 12 months by the European Commission.

Poland committed an estimated PLN 60 billion (€14.2b, $16.8bn) for a power station that will use three Westinghouse AP1000 reactor units. Having provided such support, the country also said in December that it had received 26 preliminary offers from banks to support the debt financing for the project.

CEPS said that more EU states were beginning to turn to nuclear in recognition of its system-level benefits, its contribution to meeting climate goals, and its role as a core component of the energy system transformation.
“At EU level, pragmatism appears to be gaining ground, even as existing frameworks still fall short of fully leveraging nuclear’s strengths,” CEPS said.

It cautioned, however, that the prospects of nuclear still hinged on the industry’s ability to deliver projects on time and within budget, and most importantly on states’ willingness to provide financial and political backing.

CEPS said that all eyes would be on the ability of Korea Hydro & Nuclear (KHNP) to replicate its on-time and on-budget Barakah nuclear project in the United Arab Emirates with its $18bn (€15.7bn) project in the Czech Republic.

CEPS also said that challenges over storage for renewables reopened the space for nuclear. Nuclear’s low-carbon firmness, inertia and stability were making the case for the power more relevant within the EU.

Revenues from nuclear generation must also be considered by EU states, too, said CEPS. It said nuclear was designed to provide baseload energy, but as renewables began to run for more hours nuclear was beginning to be pushed towards load-follow, which in turn eroded revenues.
CEPS said that while 2022-24 electricity market reforms offered solutions for greater revenue predictability, the problem of zero or low marginal cost generation was unresolved.

Electricity market reforms, driven by the energy crisis following Russia's invasion of Ukraine, focused on reducing dependency on volatile gas prices, incentivising long-term investments in renewables, and increasing consumer protection.
Strong political and policy support are essential for underpinning private investment and lowering financing costs for new nuclear, the report says. Courtesy PEJ.

title: Britain Launches Framework To Accelerate Advanced Nuclear Reactor Projects For AI Boom
author: David Dalton
text: Gov’t says it will provide clear route to market and support for credible proposals

Britain has unveiled a framework to accelerate development of advanced nuclear power plants, aiming to become a global leader in pioneering reactor technology to power the AI boom and grow the country’s economy with clean energy.

The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DENZ) said on 4 February that the government will recognise the most credible advanced nuclear projects as part of plans to help unlock private investment and get projects off the ground.

The government said it would be publishing a framework which aims to stimulate private investment in innovative nuclear technologies, providing a clear route to market and support for credible projects.
DENZ said Britain could see some of the world’s first advanced nuclear power stations powering factories and AI data centres.
It said Britain is one of the first to champion the development of cutting-edge nuclear projects driven by the private sector, recently announcing major commercial deals between UK and US companies.

This includes plans for X-Energy and Centrica to build 12 advanced modular reactors in Hartlepool, supporting 2,500 jobs, as well as plans for Holtec, EDF and Tritax to build small modular reactors (SMRs) at the former coal-fired power station Cottam in Nottinghamshire. Meanwhile TerraPower, the US nuclear technology company co-founded by Bill Gates, is working with engineering firm KBR to explore the potential deployment of its Natrium advanced reactor technology in the UK and beyond.

To speed up deployment of advanced nuclear and attract private investment, the government is launching a “pipeline” of projects that meet essential readiness criteria. A new service will help developers understand requirements around UK planning, regulation and fuel, and enable them to source private investment.

Advanced nuclear technologies – including advanced, small and micro modular reactors – are manufactured in factories meaning they could be built quicker and at a lower cost, with jobs across multiple regions. The government says these reactors can provide energy to the grid or directly to private industrial consumers to meet growing clean energy demand and help decarbonise industry.
Developers are aiming for their first advanced modular reactors to be operational in the UK by the mid-2030s.

The plans follow the biggest government investment in nuclear power for a generation, greenlighting Sizewell C in Suffolk and choosing Wylfa in North Wales to host the country’s first small modular reactors. Last year Rolls-Royce SMR was chosen as the preferred technology provider
in the UK’s SMR competition.

Developers will be able to use the new framework to submit proposals to join the pipeline from March this year. Proposals will then be assessed by experts in government and Great British Energy-Nuclear (GBE-N) according to key criteria such as technology status, developer capability, and financing plans. GBE-N is the government body responsible for delivering the national nuclear programme.
Successful applicants would receive in principle government endorsement.

Projects will need to secure private financing, but will also be able to discuss government support and can seek investment from Britain’s National Wealth Fund, which was set up in 2024 to drive economic growth and support the country’s net zero transition. Government support could include revenue support once projects are operational and risk protections for “extremely rare events”, allowing developers to develop projects with little risk for the taxpayer.

The government said the Nuclear Decommissioning Authority – the body that manages the decommissioning of former nuclear stations and owns 17 nuclear sites – is releasing surplus land for clean energy projects including at Chapelcross in Scotland, Pioneer Park in Cumbria and Trawsfynydd in Wales.

Chapelcross and Trawsfynydd are both existing nuclear sites, but all reactors have been permanently shut down. Pioneer Park is government-backed clean energy development site at Moorside in West Cumbria, next to the Sellafield nuclear facility.
The government will also be publishing a statement on civil nuclear fuel use which sets out the requirements for uranium-based fuels used in civil nuclear reactors, providing clarity for the sector.
Minister for nuclear Patrick Vallance said: “Advanced nuclear technology could revolutionise how we power industry and propel the AI data centre boom – delivering more clean energy and jobs.
“We are seizing the opportunity to become a frontrunner in this space as part of our golden age of nuclear, creating the conditions for the industry to flourish.”

Neil Cooper, chief financial officer at GBE-N said today’s announcement is hugely positive for the nuclear industry in the UK and “signals the start of a disciplined and transparent partnership between government and the private sector, built on evidence, not optimism”.
Tom Greatrex, chief executive of the London-based Nuclear Industry Association, said the government’s plans provide welcome clarity and momentum for advanced nuclear projects in the UK.

He said: “A clear process by which projects can get an in-principle government endorsement is vital to unlocking private investment and giving developers the confidence to move from ambition to delivery.”

Since 2000, the UK has seen permanent reactor shutdowns at Hinkley Point A, Bradwell, Calder Hall, Hunterston, Oldbury, Sizewell, Chapelcross, Dungeness and Wylfa, leaving nine units in commercial operation and only Hinkley Point C’s two France-supplied EPRs under construction and plans confirmed for a further two EPRs at Sizewell C.
Hinkley Point C in southwest England is the only commercial nuclear plant project under construction in Britain. Courtesy EDF Energy.
Rolls-Royce SMR has been chosen as the preferred technology provider in the UK’s SMR competition. Courtesy Rolls-Royce SMR.

title: Westinghouse And Tetra Tech Sign MOU On Nuclear Reactor Deployment In Ontario
author: David Dalton
text: Company says its reactors can be ‘leading solutions for Canada’

Westinghouse Electric Company and engineering services company Tetra Tech Canada have signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) aimed at supporting the development and deployment of Westinghouse’s AP1000 and AP300 reactor projects in Ontario.
Westinghouse said the partnership aims to strengthen domestic project development capabilities and position its technologies as leading solutions for Canada.
The announcement is the latest in a series of agreements with Canadian firms to support Westinghouse’s AP1000 and AP300 projects globally.
Westinghouse says that for each AP1000 unit built outside of Canada, it could generate approximately CAD1bn (€620m, $731m) in gross domestic product (GDP) through local suppliers.

Westinghouse, owned by Canadian energy companies Brookfield and Cameco, says it is the only nuclear vendor with an advanced, proven and fully operational Generation III+ reactor technology that is ready to be deployed in Canada and generate electricity by as early as 2035.
A four-unit AP1000 facility in Canada could power at least three million homes while supporting CAD28.7bn Canadian dollars in GDP during construction.
The four-unit plant would also generate $8.1 billion in GDP and support 12,000 high-quality full-time Canadian jobs annually during its 60-plus year lifespan.

Westinghouse and Tetra Tech have signed an agreement to collaborate on AP1000 and AP300 projects in Ontario. From left: Brian Schmidt, Canada project procurement senior manager, Westinghouse; David Tanel, Westinghouse regional vice-president, global markets; Sanjay Krishnan, unit president, nuclear services, Tetra Tech; and Marwan Zayouna, director, business strategy, Tetra Tech. Courtesy Westinghouse.

title: NRC Agrees To Review Early Site Permit Renewal For Grand Gulf Nuclear Plant
author: David Dalton
text: US regulator has issued six ESPs for various reactor sites across the country
The US Nuclear Regulatory Commission has agreed to review an early site permit (ESP) renewal application submitted by Entergy in September for its Grand Gulf site in Mississippi.

The initial ESP for the site had been issued in 2007, following a 2003 application submittal. The site is currently home to a single 1,401-MW boiling water reactor unit that began commercial operation in 1985.

The NRC said in a statement that the 2007 ESP resolved many site-related safety and environmental issues, and concluded the site is suitable for possible future construction and operation of a nuclear power plant.
It said Entergy, or any other potential applicant interested in the site, must still seek NRC approval for a construction permit or combined licence before any significant construction could occur.

An ESP is an approval from the NRC that authorises a specific site for potential nuclear power plant construction, independent of a specific reactor design or application for a construction permit. It confirms the suitability of a location regarding environmental, safety and emergency planning concerns, with a lifespan of 10 to 20 years.
In its original ESP application, Entergy said the site selected for evaluation is co-located with the existing Grand Gulf Nuclear Station near Port Gibson, Mississippi.
It said: “Entergy Corporation has not yet selected a specific reactor design for any future plant that may be built at this proposed site.”
A renewed ESP would allow a construction permit or combined licence application to reference the ESP for 20 years beyond the current permit’s expiration date of 5 April 2027.
A notice of the NRC’s decision was published in the Federal Register on 27 January.

To date, the NRC has issued six ESPs. The other recipients are Constellation Energy, for the Clinton nuclear site (2007); Dominion Energy, for North Anna (2007, amended 2013); Southern Nuclear, for Vogtle (2009); PSEG Nuclear, for Salem County (2016); and, most recently, the Tennessee Valley Authority, for its Clinch River site (2019).
Grand Gulf has a single 1,401-MW boiling water reactor unit that began commercial operation in 1985. Courtesy Entergy Corporation.

title: MEPs Call For Europe To Unlock Potential Of Nuclear Fusion
author: David Dalton
text: Bloc needs ‘clear political backing and mechanisms to attract private capital’

Members of the European Parliament have called for the EU to unlock the potential of nuclear fusion by making it a key part of a robust fusion action plan with clear milestones towards first-of-a-kind demonstration plants.

The ‘Call to Action’ published by MEPs from the centre-right European People’s Party also called for predictable and proportionate regulation distinct from fission, and mechanisms that enable first movers through strong public-private partnerships.

The declaration followed a public event in Brussels this week of policymakers, industry leaders and investors. The event, organised by the non-profit Fusion Industry Association (FIA), heard that fusion has reached a turning point and Europe must “move decisively from ambition to implementation”.

“European fusion companies are scaling, private investment is mobilising, and industrial capabilities are aligning toward deployment,” the FIA said. “What is now required is clear political prioritisation and delivery-focused policy frameworks.”
The Call to Action published by the MEPs says Europe’s competitiveness, resilience and climate leadership depend on its ability to urgently translate ambition into industrial reality.
The plea comes as the European Commission prepares to present a fusion strategy in the near future, a spokesperson confirmed, without revealing specific timelines.

The MEPs said European industrial capability and private investments are converging toward deployment. “What is now required is clear political backing, effective mechanisms to attract private capital, and a delivery-focused European framework that positions fusion as an industrial asset for the EU’s long-term prosperity, decarbonisation, and autonomy.”

They said: “We call for urgent European action to ensure the EU Fusion Strategy delivers measurable outcomes, meaningfully integrates the private sector and accelerates commercial fusion energy deployment in Europe.”

Nuclear fusion is the process by which two light atomic nuclei combine to form a single heavier one while releasing massive amounts of energy. It is the same process that powers the sun and the stars and could potentially provide limitless amounts of energy.

The International Atomic Energy Agency says nuclear fusion research is being carried out in more than 50 countries, but how long it will take for fusion energy to be successfully rolled out will depend on mobilising resources through global partnerships and collaboration – and on how fast the industry will be able to develop, validate and qualify emerging fusion technologies.
The biggest fusion project is the €20bn ($23.8bn) International Thermonuclear Experimental Reactor (Iter) plant in southern France
The €20 billion Iter nuclear fusion project is under construction in southern France. Courtesy Iter Organisation.

title: China Completes Welding Of Main Circulation Pipeline For Lianjiang-1 Nuclear Plant
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Construction of indigenous CAP1000 unit began in 2023
Welding has been completed of the main circulation pipeline for Unit 1 of the Lianjiang nuclear power station under construction in Guangdong province, southern China, local reports said.
The official China National Nuclear Power News Network (CNNPN) said the successful operation means that workers can now prepare for main system flushing and col hydraulic testing.

The main circulation pipeline at a nuclear power plant carries coolant, usually water, through the reactor core to absorb heat generated by nuclear fission. It connects the reactor pressure vessel with the steam generators and the reactor coolant pumps and is an integral part of a pressurised water reactor system.
Lianjiang-1 is the first of two CAP1000 pressurised water reactor units planned as the initial phase of the station, which will eventually house six such reactors.
The CAP1000 is China’s indigenous version of the Westinghouse AP1000 PWR nuclear plant.
Construction of Lianjiang-1 began in September 2023, while all main nuclear island equipment installation was completed in October 2025.
China has nine CAP1000 units under construction: two each at Haiyang, Lianjiang, Sanmen, and Xudapu (also known as Xudabao), along with one unit at Lufeng (Lufeng-1).
File photo from November 2025 of construction at Lianjiang-1. Courtesy CNEA.

title: 71% Of Estonians Support Preparation For New-Generation Nuclear Plant, Survey Shows
author: David Dalton
text: Backing for reactor rollout at highest level since 2019
Seventy one percent of respondents support continuing preparations for the construction of a new-generation nuclear power plant in Estonia, according to a survey.

Compared to the previous survey carried out in April 2025, support for the introduction of nuclear energy has increased and is now at its highest level across the entire survey period since 2019. At the same time, the share of opponents of nuclear energy has continued to decline.

According to the latest survey, 17% of respondents oppose the development of nuclear energy, split almost evenly between “strong” opponents (8%) and those who are “rather” opposed (9%). A clear position could not be determined for 12% of respondents.
The survey, conducted by Kantar Emor in January, was commissioned by nuclear energy company Fermi Energia, which is planning to deploy small modular reactors in Estonia.
The survey showed that nuclear energy continues to be viewed by Estonian residents as the most preferred direction for developing electricity generation.

When asked, “Which type of electricity generation should be developed in Estonia, considering the reduction of electricity production from oil shale?”, 58% of respondents said that, in their view, a new-generation small nuclear power plant deserves to be developed in Estonia as oil-shale-based production is reduced.

Compared to the previous year, the popularity of both wind and solar energy has declined noticeably. Wind energy development is supported by 30% of respondents and solar energy by 29%, both significantly lower than a year ago. In contrast, support has increased for electricity generation from oil shale alongside oil production, which 32% of respondents consider worthy of development.
Fermi Energia is working towards the deployment of BWRX-300 SMRs in Estonia. Courtesy Fermi Energia.

title: EU Nuclear Energy Production Increased By 4.8% In 2024, Says Eurostat
author: David Dalton
text: Latest data shows rise for second consecutive year

In 2024, 12 EU countries with nuclear electricity production generated 649,524 GWh of electricity, an increase of 4.8% compared with 2023, according to the latest data from the bloc’s statistical office Eurostat.
This was the second consecutive year with a rise since a decrease in 2022 to 609,255 GWh. Nuclear power plants accounted for 23.3% of the total electricity production in the EU.

The EU’s largest nuclear producer, France, generated 58.6% of the EU’s nuclear power (380,451 GWh). Spain followed with 54,510 GWh (8.4%), ahead of Sweden (50,665 GWh; 7.8%) and Finland (32,599 GWh; 5.0%).

Compared with 2023, nuclear electricity production increased the most in France (+12.5%), followed by Sweden (4.5%) and Slovenia (+4.2%). The other producers of nuclear electricity registered an average decrease of 4%, varying between -0.6% in Slovakia and -10.3% in the Netherlands.
Germany was the second-largest producer in the EU up until 2021, having ended nuclear production completely in April 2023 after shutting down all its commercial nuclear plants.

The EU countries most reliant on nuclear electricity in 2024 were France (67.3% of all electricity generated) and Slovakia (61.6%). In Hungary, Bulgaria, Belgium, Finland and Czechia, around 40% of all electricity generated was nuclear.
By contrast, only 2.9% of electricity produced in the Netherlands came from nuclear power.
The EU’s largest nuclear producer, France, generated 58.6% of the EU’s nuclear power. Creative Commons Licence.

title: Slovakia Ready To Roll Out SMRs In Next 10-15 Years, Concludes US-Backed Study
author: Nigel Davies
text: Washington’s Project Phoenix aims to help partner countries move away from coal

A feasibility study into the rollout of small modular reactors (SMRs) in Slovakia has confirmed that the country has the right sites and expertise to be able to deploy this technology over the next 10 to 15 years.

The Project Phoenix feasibility study evaluated 100 parameters from the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) covering external risks, geological conditions, environmental and safety concerns, as well as site suitabilty.

The study was developed by engineering company Sargent & Lundy, the Ministry of Economy of the Slovak Republic and Slovakia’s electricity company Slovenské elektrárne. It had the support of a US Department of State programme known as First (Foundational Infrastructure for Responsible Use of Small Modular Reactor Technology), which aims to build capacity in US partner countries that are establishing nuclear energy programmes to meet climate and energy security goals.

Four potential locations were assessed: the country’s two existing commercial nuclear power station sites at Bohunice and Mochovce, the shutdown Vojany thermal power station site in the east of the country and US Steel Košice, a steel works site in eastern Slovakia that is run by a subsidiary of Pittsburgh-based United States Steel Corporation.
All four sites met the criteria required for SMR deployment. Assessments at the sites also covered seismic stability, water availability, grid connectivity and environmental impact.
The study confirmed the compatability of several SMR designs from global manufacturers for the sites that would meet international standards.

Slovenské elektrárne  said: “The study marks a significant milestone in shaping Slovakia’s energy future. Within the next 10 to 15 years, SMRs could become a safe, clean, and economically viable addition to the country’s energy mix.”

SMRs are generally categorised as reactors with a capacity of up to 300 MW. Slovenské elektrárne said they would help the country to reduce its emissions to meet EU and national climate goals, create new jobs and strengthen grid resilience.

Project Phoenix was launched by the US in 2022 with the aim of helping reduce reliance on coal. Project Phoenix funding to assess the potential for SMRs has been granted for Poland, the Czech Republic, Slovenia and Slovakia.

The study was welcomed by Szabolcs Hodosy, first secretary of Slovakia’s Ministry of Economy. He said: “Nuclear energy is experiencing its renaissance, and we must take timely steps – both in education and in preparing infrastructure, as well as in promoting support for nuclear energy across all platforms, so that we can share the benefits of nuclear energy production at both the national and regional levels.”
The US said it stood ready to support Slovakia’s efforts to strengthen energy resilience.

“Project Phoenix demonstrates Slovakia’s robust nuclear energy experience, infrastructure, regulatory framework, and industrial base provide a strong platform for early deployment of small modular reactor technologies under the highest international safety and security standards,” US deputy chief of mission Heather Rogers said.

Slovakia recently signed an agreement with the US to develop a large-scale nuclear power unit at the Bohunice power station. This will likely be a Westinghouse AP1000 unit, which would be one of the largest infrastructure investments in Slovakia and have a capacity of around 1,200 MW with a target operational date of 2040.
The country has two nuclear power stations at Bohunice and Mochovce, with both using Russian technology. Bohunice has two units and and Mochovce three, with one under construction.
According to the International Energy Agency, Slovakia derives around 29% of its energy from nuclear, with coal around 11%, and oil and gas around 46%.
The SMR study recommended now developing a regulatory framework, conducting detailed site investigations, and continuing to explore the right technology. Public involvement would also be key.
The Mochovce nuclear power station site is one option for the deployment of SMRs in Slovakia. Courtesy Slovenské elektrárne.

title: Spain’s Nuclear Regulator Gives Almaraz Operators February Deadline For Information On Plant Extension
author: Nigel Davies
text: CSN wants to submit final document to government by summer

Spain’s nuclear regulator, the Consejo de Seguridad Nuclear (CSN), has given the operators of the Almaraz nuclear plant in the South-West of the country until 18 February to provide additional information it has requested before it can submit a report on the plant’s extension.

Local media reports in Spain said the CSN’s chairman, Juan Carlos Lentijo, had set that date for the plant’s owners – Iberdrola, Endesa and Naturgy – to submit information pertinent to the request made to extend the life of the plant until 2030.
Lentijo said the CSN would then submit its report to the Spanish government by the summer, which would then decide on the plant’s fate – a decision expected in early 2027.
Lentijo also said that the process to delay the plant’s closure would be simpler given that it was a relatively short lifetime extension that was being requested.

A request to extend the plant’s operational lifetime by three years until June 2030 was made in November 2025 by the operators. The move by the three companies was seen as a possible first step by Spain to reconsider its plan to shut down the country’s nuclear power plants.

Almaraz is the country’s largest nuclear power station and its reactors are due to shut down in 2027 and 2028. The plant uses two Westinghouse pressurised water reactor units that according to the International Atomic Energy Agency have a combined net capacity of 2,017 MW.
Almaraz-1 began commercial operations in 1983 and Almaraz-2 in 1984.
Spain has a total net capacity from its seven nuclear plants of 7,123 MW, providing around 20% of the country’s electricity demand.
Almaraz is the country’s largest nuclear power station and its reactors are due to shut down in 2027 and 2028. Courtesy CSN.

title: US Startup Raises $140 Million To Boost Production Of Advanced Nuclear Reactor Fuel
author: David Dalton
text: Standard Nuclear to use funding for additional facilities

US nuclear fuel startup Standard Nuclear has raised $140m (€117m) to boost production of fuel for advanced reactors in an effort to expand the US energy supply chain amid surging interest in fission power.

The Series A round was led by venture capital firm Decisive Point and included new investors Chevron Technology Ventures and StepStone Group, with existing backers Andreessen Horowitz, according to a statement.

The Tennessee-based company, founded one year ago, began fabricating Triso fuel this month at its facility in Oak Ridge, Tennessee using high-assay low-enriched uranium (Haleu), a more potent form of uranium that will be used for many advanced reactors. Triso – or “tristructural-isotropic” – is an advanced, highly robust nuclear fuel designed to withstand extreme temperatures without melting.
Standard Nuclear said it plans to use the funding to start production at additional facilities, without giving further details.
The company is one of a few makers of Triso, demand for which is expected to grow as more companies begin deploying advanced nuclear power reactor to meet surging demand for electricity.

Dozens of companies, both in the US and around the world, are developing advanced nuclear designs, but there has been concern about whether there would be enough fuel available as they start testing and building systems.

Russia has been the world’s primary commercial supplier of Haleu, with state-owned Tenex dominating the market. The US is developing domestic capacity through companies like Centrus and General Matter.

Standard Nuclear can make about 500 kg of Triso a year at its Tennessee site. It is developing a second facility there and another one at Idaho National Laboratory, which are both expected to go into service by mid-2026. Each will be able to deliver about one metric tonne annually.

Kurt Terrani, chief executive officer of Standard Nuclear, said: “With this funding, we are positioned to accelerate our roadmap, scale operations, and deliver on the promise to fuel the next generation of reactors powering industry, defense, and space.”
Standard Nuclear said earlier this month that it had received a critical shipment of Haleu feedstock at its facility in Oak Ridge, Tennessee.
Standard Nuclear said it was the first company to both receive authorisation by the US Department of Energy (DOE) and physically receive Haleu for production of advanced Triso fuel.
A cross-section of a Triso nuclear fuel pellet. Courtesy Idaho National Laboratory.

title: Amentum Expands UK Nuclear Services Portfolio with $730 Million Major Contracts Win
author: David Dalton
text: Scope includes projects at Hinkley Point C and continued operation of existing fleet

US-based engineering and technology company Amentum has won a suite of new contracts from EDF worth up to $730m (€614m), expanding the critical solutions it provides for the UK’s existing nuclear reactors as well as the construction of the new Hinkley Point C nuclear power station.

The newly awarded contracts include 10-year professional services agreement frameworks with Hinkley Point C and a five-year project management resources framework to support existing station operations, life extensions and preparation for decommissioning.

Loren Jones, Amentum senior vice-president, said: “Amentum’s expertise in gigawatt reactor operational support and life extension makes it the ideal partner for EDF, one of the world’s largest nuclear utilities.
“This award advances our strategy to accelerate the growth of our nuclear energy business in line with the opportunities being created by the worldwide nuclear resurgence.”

Amentum said in a statement that it will deploy the skills and experience of more than 1,000 UK-based specialists to provide the full breadth of nuclear skills, solutions, and products essential to the continued operation and life extension of the UK’s existing nuclear fleet.

Since 2000, the UK has seen permanent reactor shutdowns at Hinkley Point A, Bradwell, Calder Hall, Hunterston, Oldbury, Sizewell, Chapelcross, Dungeness and Wylfa, leaving nine units in commercial operation and only Hinkley Point C’s two EPRs under construction and plans confirmed for a further two EPRs at Sizewell C.

Last week a consortium led by Amentum said it had won a new contract valued at up to $207m to provide programme management and technical solutions for planning and development of nuclear new build in the Netherlands.
UK small modular reactor developer Rolls-Royce SMR has appointed Amentum as its programme delivery partner, a pivotal role in enabling the delivery of it first reactors.
The UK plans to have its first SMR on the island of Angelsey off the Welsh coast, employing technology from Rolls Royce SMR.
The Heysham nuclear power station in northwest England. Courtesy EDF.

title: New York Extends Zero Emissions Credit Programme Covering Financing For Nuclear Fleet To 2049
author: Nigel Davies
text: Move will allow state’s four nuclear reactors to remain operational

The New York State Public Service Commission has extended a 2025 zero-emissions credit (ZEC) programme until 2049, which will provide the financing necessary for its nuclear plants to continue operating until that time.

In a statement, New York’s Department of Public Services said that the ZEC programme was one of the most cost-effective ways to retain energy resources with low emissions and ensure that its nuclear power stations continue to operate safely in to the future. ZEC programme are designed to compensate certain nuclear power units for production of zero carbon electricity.
The commission said the programme provides the plants with sufficient funding beyond what they can earn in the markets and from federal tax credits.
It also said that it would provide the nuclear plant operator Constellation with the financial support necessary for it to begin the licence renewal process with the Nuclear Regulatory Commission.

Constellation owns four nuclear reactors at three sites in New York State – Fitzpatrick, Ginna, and Nine Mile Point, which has two units. The company has applied to federal authorities to relicence the facilities, which began commercial operation from 1969 to 1988.  It is also evaluating adding new, large, or small modular reactors (SMRs) at its existing sites to meet the need for additional nuclear capacity.

Rory Christian, chair of the commission, said that failing to extend the ZEC programme would have a significant impact on reliability, resource adequacy, and in achieving the state’s clean energy goals.
The commission said that Constellation’s four reactors, the only ones in the state, provide around 21% of New York’s power and over 40% of its zero emission power.
It also said that in granting the ZEC extension, it recognised the need for new investments in those plants to reduce age-related risks.

The financing also includes safeguards including a contract performance requirement, a mechanism for reducing ZEC payments should other financial support become available, and a review process to ensure funding is just and reasonable.

The state recently unveiled a ‘Nuclear Reliability Backbone’ initiative that would add a further 4 GW of new nuclear energy to existing capacity in the state, in addition to plans for a new 1 GW plant, leaving a total of 8.4 GW of power.

Governor Kathy Hochul has launched an initiative to catalyse new, advanced nuclear energy development in New York. In June, Hochul directed the New York Power Authority (NYPA) to develop and construct an advanced nuclear power plant in upstate New York.

Plans for the new 1 GW plant are progressing. A total of 23 developers and partners have expressed interest in collaborating with the NYPA plans. In addition, eight communities in the state have stated their interest in hosting the plant.
In December 2025, the NYPA signed a memorandum of understanding with Ontario Power Generation to collaborate on the development of both large-scale and small modular reactors in New York.
Governor Kathy Hochul has launched an initiative to catalyse new, advanced nuclear energy development in New York. Courtesy Kathy Hochul.
The single-unit Ginna nuclear power station in the US state of New York. Courtesy Constellation.

title: South Korea Announces Plans For Two New Large-Scale Nuclear Plants
author: David Dalton
text: State-owned KHNP to begin search for suitable sites with first SMR also in pipeline
South Korea has said it will build two large-scale nuclear power plants by 2038 with work expected to begin soon on finding a site.

Reports in South Korea said state-owned Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power (KHNP) plans to open bidding for sites for the new reactors, followed by an evaluation and site selection process expected to take five to six months.
The company is targeting construction permits in the early 2030s and completion of the reactors in 2037 and 2038.

Climate minister Kim Sung-whan said on 26 January that the government would continue the construction of the new nuclear power plants as scheduled under the 11th Basic Plan for Electricity Supply and Demand.

The plan, devised by the previous government and finalised in February 2025, outlined national electricity supply policy for 2024-2038. It included the construction of two new large-scale reactors between 2037 and 2038 and deployment of the country’s first commercial small modular reactor (SMR) in 2035.
South Korean media said the construction of the two new large-scale plants had been put on hold for a “public consensus process” when Lee Jae Myung became president in June last year.

The English-language Korea JoonAng Daily said public opinion polls commissioned by the government have since showed that an average of 80% of respondents said nuclear power is needed, with 60% supporting the additional construction plan.
Lee had originally pressed for a focus on renewable energy, reversing course from the more pro-nuclear stance of his predecessor, Yoon Suk Yeol.

He said in September that building more nuclear power plants is not realistic because it takes more than 15 years to construct a new facility from scratch. However, he had been supportive of using reactors that are already online or have started construction.
Moon Jae-in, who served as president from 2017 to 2022, oversaw a nuclear phaseout policy that drew fierce resistance from industry and labour unions.
Yoon, who served from 2022 until he was impeached and removed from office in 2025, reversed that policy, resuming construction of nuclear reactors and planning to expand nuclear output.
When Lee was elected president in June 2025, his administration said it would re-examine the role of nuclear energy.

According to the International Atomic Energy Agency, South Korea has 26 nuclear units in commercial operation and two, Saeul-3 and -4, listed as under construction. The 26 plants provided 31.7% of the country’s electricity production share in 2024, the IAEA said.
In December South Korea’s nuclear regulator approved the start of operations at the Saeul-3 nuclear power plant near Busan in the south of the country.

Construction of the indigenous 1,340-MW APR1400 pressurised water reactor unit at the Saeul nuclear station, formerly known as Shin-Kori, began in April 2017, but has been delayed by changes in government policy.
South Korea’sHanbit nuclear power station which has six units in commercial operation. Courtesy Yonggwang NPP/Creative Commosn Licence.

title: Japan Suspends Kashiwazaki Kariwa Nuclear Plant Restart Due To Control Rod Problem
author: David Dalton
text: Operator Tepco says reactor is stable and there is no radioactive impact
The restart of Unit 6 at Kashiwazaki Kariwa nuclear power station in western Japan has been suspended, a day after the process began, operator Tokyo Electric Power Company (Tepco) said.
Workers at Kashiwazaki Kariwa-6, which has been offline since the 2011 Fukushima disaster, began restarting the unit on 21 January.

But the process had to be suspended hours later due to a malfunction related to control rods, which are essential to safely starting up and shutting down reactors, Tepco said. The duration of the shutdown was still unknown.

Tepco said there was no safety issue from the glitch and it was checking the situation while suspending the restart operation. The utility later said it was putting the reactor back into shutdown for a fuller examination.
“We were investigating the malfunctioning electrical equipment,” spokesperson Takashi Kobayashi told the AFP news agency.
The reactor “is stable and there is no radioactive impact outside”, he said.
Unit 6 is a 1,315-MW boiling water reactor unit that originally began commercial operation in 1996. Fuel loading for its restart was completed in June.
The plant’s restart would mean Japan has returned 15 units to service since the Fukushima disaster.

Kashiwazaki Kariwa is the world’s largest nuclear power station by capacity. According to the International Atomic Energy Agency, its seven boiling water reactor units have a combined net capacity of 7,965 MW.
The facility served as an important energy source to supply electricity to the Tokyo metropolitan area before the 2011 earthquake, tsunami and nuclear accident at Fukushima-Daiichi.
Tepco wants to bring the station back online and said in 2020 it was concentrating its resources on restarting the newer Units 6 and 7.
Units 6 and 7 at Kashiwazaki Kariwa have been offline since March 2012 and August 2011 respectively.
The seven-unit Kashiwazaki Kariwa nuclear power station in Niigata Prefecture, western Japan. Courtesy Tepco.

title: Consortium Wins $207 Million Contract For Development Of Netherlands New Build Programme
author: David Dalton
text: European nation has identified nuclear energy as a key element of climate policy

A consortium led by US-based engineering and technology company Amentum has won a new contract valued at up to $207m (€180m) to provide programme management and technical solutions for planning and development of nuclear new build in the Netherlands.

The Nexus-NL consortium comprises of Amentum, Netherlands-based design, engineering and management consulting company Arcadis, Belgian engineering company Tractebel, and NRG Pallas, the Dutch nuclear research and production company that operates the High Flux Reactor at Petten and is building the new Pallas research reactor on the same site.

The consortium will work on the development of up to two new gigawatt-scale power plants to support the nation’s strategies for decarbonisation and energy security and will support the Nuclear Energy Organisation Netherlands (NEO NL), which will be established next month.

The two-year agreement, with options for three additional one-year extensions, was awarded by the Ministry of Climate Policy and Green Growth. In the initial phase, the consortium will oversee site characterisation, technology selection, and planning work scope for site enabling, utility connections and transportation links.

In a statement, the ministry said: “We are confident that the Nexus-NL consortium can perform the role as technical support organisation excellently due to its extensive expertise and experience, both in the international nuclear domain and in the Dutch context.”

Amentum will contribute its expertise in managing large nuclear new-build programmes, including setting up a project management office, technology selection, design and engineering expertise and commercial and procurement strategies.
Arcadis will focus on siting studies, conventional licensing, and permitting.
Tractebel will bring its engineering experience to define technical requirements for technology selection and will lead front-end engineering design studies.
NRG Pallas will offer specialised Dutch nuclear expertise from the Pallas reactor programme, particularly on key interfaces between nuclear and conventional licensing.
The Dutch government has identified nuclear energy as a key enabler of its policy to achieve climate neutrality in the energy supply by 2040.
In December 2022 the Dutch government chose the Borssele site as its preferred location for the proposed construction of two new nuclear units.
The government said the units should be deployed by 2035, each have a capacity of between 1,000 MW and 1,650 MW, and use Generation III+ reactor technology.

Borssele, in the south of the Netherlands, is the country’s only commercial nuclear plant. The single 482-MW pressurised water reactor unit began commercial operation in 1973. According to the International Atomic Energy Agency, in 2024 it provided a 2.8% share of the country’s electricity production.
In October the Dutch government confirmed plans to extend the lifespan of Borssele beyond 2033 and to invest €20m in the development of small modular reactors.
The Netherlands is planning two new large-scale reactors at the Borssele site. Courtesy EPZ.

title: Laramide To Abandon Kazakhstan Greenfield Uranium Project Due To Newly Enacted Policy Changes
author: David Dalton
text: Canada company says Astana government may have scored ‘spectacular own goal’

Laramide Resources has pulled out of a greenfield uranium exploration venture in Kazakhstan, citing policy changes that it says have effectively shut the door on economically viable foreign investment in the country’s uranium sector.

The Toronto, Canada-based company announced on 20 January it has terminated its option agreement with privately held Aral Resources for the Chu-Sarysu Basin project, ending its involvement in what it had previously described as one of the world’s most prospective under explored uranium regions.

The option agreement, which was signed in September 2024, gave Laramide access to 22 exploration licences covering more than 5,500 sq km in the Chu-Sarysu Basin in central Kazakhstan. The region hosts several of Kazatomprom’s largest producing mines and is known for geology suitable for low-cost, in-situ recovery uranium deposits.
Laramide had been funding early-stage exploration work since late 2024 and was preparing a major drilling programme that was scheduled to begin in the second half of 2025.
Laramide said delays in securing drilling permits from regional authorities meant no drilling took place as planned in the fourth quarter of 2025.

Although the final permits were granted on 24 December, the regulatory landscape shifted almost immediately afterwards when, two days later, Kazakhstan’s president signed into law amendments to the Subsoil Use Code that materially alter the economics of uranium exploration for new entrants.

Under the revised framework, Kazatomprom is granted priority rights over prospective uranium areas, stricter minimum ownership thresholds in new production agreements, and enhanced control over extensions, reserve increases, and additional exploration at producing deposits.

Laramide said those changes, combined with higher holding costs following an earlier increase in annual property taxes, undermine the investment rationale for continuing exploration in the country. The company has ceased all funding related to the project with immediate effect.

The company said it believes an economic case for foreign direct investment in uranium exploration no longer exists in Kazakhstan. Marc Henderson, Laramide’s president and chief executive, said in a statement that motivated by an effort to address, and ideally reverse, the obvious and severe decline in the resource base of Kazatomprom, their national uranium company, it appears Kazakhstan may have scored “a spectacular own goal” with their de facto nationalisation of future uranium exploration in country.

In a statement outlining the amendments, the company highlighted new provisions that raise the minimum ownership stake required in new uranium production agreements to more than 75%, up from 50% previously, and impose additional conditions tied to technology transfer for extensions and reserve increases.
Laramide said it will now focus entirely on advancing its two development-stage uranium assets: the Churchrock-Crownpoint project in New Mexico and the Westmoreland project in Queensland, Australia.
Kazakhstan holds the world’s largest uranium reserves, with estimates exceeding 2 million tonnes, and is the leading global producer, supplying over 40% of the world's uranium.
A uranium mine in Kazakhstan. Courtesy Kazatomprom.
Kazakhstan holds the world’s largest uranium reserves and is the leading global producer. Courtsy Kazatomprom

title: South Korea’s KHNP Takes Stake In Bill Gates Nuclear Company TerraPower
author: Nigel Davies
text: State company joins three-way alliance with SK Innovation

State-run Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power (KHNP) has taken a stake in the Bill Gates-founded US nuclear technology company TerraPower, joining fellow South Korean energy company SK Innovation as an investor.

TerraPower said that KHNP joined as an investor to help support the construction of its Natrium advanced nuclear site in the US state of Wyoming, and would help with its plans to build other plants in the US and abroad, including in South Korea.

SK Innovation said this week that it had transferred part of its 10% stake in TerraPower to KHNP to form a three-way alliance. Reports in South Korea estimated KHNP’s investment at $40m (€34m). SK Innovation’s original investment in TerraPower was $250m.

“We have strong relationships with multiple Korean entities across the nuclear energy supply chain, and today’s announcement is one more step to realising the Natrium technology’s promise to deliver next generation nuclear power not just in the United States, but around the world,” said Chris Levesque, TerraPower president and chief executive officer.

Park In-sik, executive vice-president and head of the export business division at KHNP, said that the three companies would sign definitive commercialisation agreements this year to establish a foundation for global projects.

“This investment is a major milestone for KHNP in supporting the global deployment of next-generation nuclear energy,” Park aid. “By combining our 50 years of experience in nuclear plant construction and operation with SK Innovation’s competitiveness in energy and TerraPower’s technology, we will play a leading role in expanding the advanced nuclear market.”

TerraPower is developing the Natrium technology at a former coal site in The Natrium combines a 345-MW sodium-cooled fast reactor with a molten salt-based storage system, capable of increasing output to 500 MW during peak demand.

In December, the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission gave the green light for TerraPower’s safety evaluation allowing the company to proceed with the development of the Kemmerer Power Station Unit 1, which will be built near an existing coal plant. TerraPower is also looking to expand fast overseas.
In December, Turkey said it was holding talks with the company to install small modular reactors (SMRs) as it aims to construct 5,000 MW of SMR capacity by 2050.
TerraPower is building it first Natrium plant in Wyoming. Courtesy TerraPower.

title: EDF In Negotiations With UK Government Over Sizewell B Lifetime Extension to 2055
author: Nigel Davies
text: Talks focus on long-term price for power to enable £800m investment in Suffolk nuclear plant

French state power company EDF says it is in negotiations with the UK government to extend the lifetime of the Sizewell B nuclear plant in the eastern region of Suffolk to at least 2055, which would require an £800m investment (€916m, $1.07bn).
The 1,198-MW plant at Sizewell B reached an anniversary of 30 years in operation in 2025 and is now the only pressurised water reactor (PWR) left up and running in the UK.
However, EDF said that alongside partner Centrica, which has a 20% stake in the UK’s nuclear fleet, they stood ready to invest to extend the lifetime of the plant.

“Operating the power station beyond 2035 to at least 2055 is technically feasible, has been achieved at similar power stations worldwide, and would provide a reliable source of power as new nuclear and renewable projects are brought online,” EDF said in a nuclear fleet update.
“Negotiations are ongoing with the UK government to agree a long-term price for the power that will enable the required investment to make this extension happen.”
The company said that in 2025, Sizewell B produced 10.4 TWh of electricity, the second highest output in its 30-year history, and had a load factor 99% for the calendar year.

EDF said that in 2025, nuclear output in the UK was 32.9 TWh, which was a 12% decrease on the previous year, due to unspecified “operational challenges”, particularly at the Hartlepool nuclear power station in northern England. The generation produced last year was equivalent to 12% of the UK’s electricity consumption. The objective in 2026 is to produce around 36 TWh.
The company said that it had also extended the lifetime of its advanced gas-coooled reactor (AGR) plants by 38 years since it took them over in 2009.
EDF said it aimed to generate electricty from its AGR fleet until at least 2030, which would require investment of £1.2bn from 2026 to 2028.

“In November, the UK government said that the retirement of the AGRs risks leaving a dangerous gap in Britain’s low-carbon energy supply,” said Mark Hartley, managing director of EDF’s nuclear operations.
He said the lifetime of the AGRs would remain under review to assess whether further extensions can be achieved.

The UK has around 5.8 GW of nuclear capacity, and could reach 21.6 GW by 2050 if it rolls out new nuclear operations, according to the National Energy System Operator (Neso), the independent body that plans the country’s electricity and gas networks.

To reach such levels, the UK would need to invest in a new generation of nuclear plants to replace retiring capacity, including the extension of existing plants and new projects such as small modular reactors (SMRs).
The UK plans to have its first SMR on the island of Angelsey off the Welsh coast, employing technology from Rolls Royce SMR.

Since 2000, the UK has seen permanent reactor shutdowns at Hinkley Point A, Bradwell, Calder Hall, Hunterston, Oldbury, Sizewell, Chapelcross, Dungeness and Wylfa, leaving nine units in commercial operation and only Hinkley Point C’s two EPRs under construction and plans confirmed for a further two EPRs at Sizewell C.
Sizewell B is now the only pressurised water reactor left up and running in the UK. Courtesy EDF Energy.

title: Czech Republic’s ČEZ To Invest €180 Million This Year To Upgrade Dukovany Nuclear Power Plant
author: Nigel Davies
text: Move follows recent announcement of €156m modernisation of Temelín facility

Czech state power company ČEZ has announced that it will spend 4.4 billion crowns (€180m, $209m) on modernisation projects at its Dukovany power station this year including on  turbines, pumps and other key equipment.

The announcment of works to be carried out at Dukovany follows ČEZ’s recent announcement that it would invest 3.1 billion crowns (€156m, $182m) at its two-unit Temelín power station to extend its lifetime to at least 60 years.

In the case of Dukovany, the company said the investment comes as some low-pressure parts of the turbogenerator reach their end of life and with ongoing preparations to transfer heat from the nuclear station to the hot water pipeline to Brno as part of a project to supply district heating to the nearby city.

ČEZ said that in addition to steam turbine upgrades, specialists would focus on generators, steam separators, low and high pressure regeneration systems, as well as condensers and equipment used to transfer electrical power.
The upgrades would be carried out gradually during planned maintenance shutdowns of individual units, and the company said could lead to a small increase in output due to increased efficiency.

Dukovany has four Russian designed VVER-440 units that began commercial operation from 1985 to 1987. There are also plans to build two new South Korea-supplied APR1000 nuclear units with a generation capacity of up to 976 MW each.

In December the European Commission opened an in-depth investigation to assess whether public support that the Czech Republic plans to grant for the construction and operation of the two new nuclear units in Dukovany is in line with European Union state aid rules.

“The project is a series of investment actions that we must coordinate so that the renovation of the facility not only makes sense technically, but also brings an additional effect in the form of savings or increased production,” said Bohdan Zronek, member of the ČEZ board and director of its nuclear division.
He added that alongside this work, the plant was also investing in modern maintenance, diagnostic and control methods and technologies to help optimise costs and limit downtime.
The company said it was carrying out calculations and analyses of individual equipment and circuits, with a final technical and budget for the project due by the end of the year.

Roman Havlín, director of the plant, said: “According to assumptions, the modernisation of the engine room equipment could bring an increase in the unit’s electrical output by up to several megawatts.”

The company said a “generational change” at the plant was now almost complete, with the majority of those who worked at the plant when it was launched in 1985 now retired. This had brought down the average age at the plant to 42 years.
A turbine hall at the Dukovany nuclear power station in the Czech Republic. Courtesy ČEZ.

title: In Bullish Uranium Outlook, Sprott Points To Policy Certainty And Tight Supply
author: David Dalton
text: Canada asset management company says US has ‘made its intentions clear’ on nuclear

Uranium is well-positioned to build on its longer-term bull market in 2026 as tightening fundamentals, improving policy clarity and a re-accelerating contracting cycle begin to align, Sprott said in an outlook for the year ahead.

The Canada-based precious metals asset management company, whose physical uranium fund holds more than 75 million pounds of U3O8, said the spot uranium price gained 11.43% in 2025. It now stands at around $82/lb.
According to Sprott, the term price has risen to $86/lb, which signals utilities are beginning to accept higher long-term prices.

Tight supply is driving the bullish outlook. Sprott said supply growth is failing to keep pace with the increasing demand from reactors. Production is concentrated and slow-moving; new projects face long lead times, and geopolitical and jurisdictional risks persist as a significant part of the price formation process.

“In a deglobalising world, supply concentration increasingly carries a security premium, especially as much of the current supply is outside the West,” Sprott said. “Producer discipline reinforces this dynamic.”

Large producers have shown no willingness to expand output without higher prices, and the market continues to face the practical reality that meaningful greenfield supply is difficult to deliver quickly and efficiently.

According to Sprott, uranium’s outlook is strengthening for reasons that are “observable and structural”: improving policy clarity, expanding AI-linked and utility-led demand visibility, a constrained supply response and a contracting cycle that has room to re-accelerate.

Sprott said policy uncertainty that sidelined utilities earlier in 2025 has lifted. The US has made its intentions clear by providing up to $80bn of funding support to build new reactors. Big Tech is reinforcing the demand side with Microsoft, Amazon, Google and Meta making multi-year, multi-billion-dollar commitments to secure nuclear power for the growth of AI and data centres.

This is occurring alongside continued progress on reactor restarts and life extensions, reinforcing that nuclear is increasingly treated as essential, reliable baseload capacity while electricity demand rises and grid constraints become more visible, Sprott said.

“In a commodity where procurement is ultimately non-discretionary, and supply is slow to adjust, these conditions support a bullish bias for uranium prices and uranium equities as 2026 unfolds,” Sprott said.
A tunnel at Cameco’s Cigar Lake uranium mine in Caada. Courtesy Cameco.

title: China Pours First Concrete For ‘Hybrid’ Nuclear Power Station Project
author: David Dalton
text: Innovative Xuwei facility will supply both industrial heat and electricity

First concrete has been poured for the nuclear island of Unit 1 at Phase I of China’s Xuwei nuclear power project – a “hybrid” facility that will supply both industrial heat and electricity by coupling a high-temperature gas-cooled reactor (HTGR) with two Hualong One pressurised water reactors (PWRs).
Xuwei Phase I, in Jiangsu province, eastern China, was among 11 reactor projects approved by China’s State Council in August 2024.

China National Nuclear Corporation (CNNC) said it plans to build two 1,208 MW Hualong One units and one 660 MW high-temperature gas-cooled reactor (HTGR) unit at the site. The Hualong One, also known as the HPR1000, combines features from CNNC’s ACP1000 and CGN’s ACPR1000+ designs.
The project will be equipped with a steam heat exchange station, which will use “heat-to-electricity” technology for the first time.

Demineralised water will be heated by primary steam from the Hualong One units to produce saturated steam, and the primary steam of the HTGR will be used to heat the saturated steam for the second time, producing “superheated” steam, thus producing the high-temperature process heat needed for and produce high-temperature process heat usable for various industrial applications industrial applications, such as oil refining, desalination, and steel production.

CNNC described the project, known as the Jiangsu Xuwei Nuclear Heating and Power Plant, as the “world’s first dual-coupling demonstration project combining a third-generation nuclear PWR and a fourth-generation nuclear HTGR”.
It said the project is designed primarily for industrial heat supply while also providing electricity.

CNNC said that once the project is in operation, it will supply 32.5 million tonnes of industrial steam annually, with a maximum power generation of more than 11.5 billion KWh. This could reduce the use of standard coal by 7.26 million tonnes and reduce carbon dioxide emissions by 19.6 million tonnes each year, CNNC said.

The International Atomic Energy Agency’s database of nuclear power plants says China has 29 units under construction, but this does not include Xuwei or recent concrete pouring at Guangxi Bailong and Lufeng, both in the south of the country.
China’s Jiangsu Xuwei nuclear power project will be a “hybrid” facility to supply both industrial heat and electricity. Image courtesy CNNC.

title: Russia Extends Leningrad-4 Nuclear Plant Operating Licence For Five Years
author: Kamen Kraev
text: RBMK plant could now remain online until 2030

Russia’s nuclear regulator has extended the operating life of Unit 4 at the Leningrad nuclear power station in northwest Russia until 2030, allowing the RBMK-1000 reactor to operate for up to 50 years.

State nuclear corporation Rosatom said Rostechnadzor extended the 925-MW unit’s operating licence after a comprehensive safety review covering equipment condition, documentation, modernisation work and replacement of life-expired components.
Rostechnadzor also issued a licence allowing continued production, transport and storage of radioactive materials at the unit, enabling isotope production until 2030.
Rosatom said the unit produces medical isotopes including molybdenum-99, iodine-125, iodine-131, samarium-153 and lutetium-177, used in diagnosis and treatment, and cobalt-60 used for sterilization,
The Leningrad site, about 100 km west of St Petersburg on the Gulf of Finland, has four units in operation, two that are permanently shut down, and two under construction.

The operational units are Leningrad-3 and Leningrad-4, Leningrad 2-1 and Leningrad 2-2. Leningrad-1 and Leningrad-2, both Soviet-era RBMK-1000 light-water graphite units, were permanently shut down in 2018 and 2020 respectively.
Leningrad-3, also an RBMK-1000, received a lifetime extension until 2030 in February 2025.
The commercial Leningrad 2-1 and Leningrad 2-2 are of the VVER-1200 pressurised water reactor design.
Rosatom is also building two additional VVER-1200 PWR units at the site. Construction of Leningrad 2-3 began in March 2024 and of Leningrad 2-4 in March 2025.
According to Rosatom, the latest two units are set to replace Leningrad-3 and Leningrad-4 once they retire from commercial operation.
Russia is the only country to still operate the RBMK reactor technology. It has seven such units in its fleet of 36 commercial reactors.
The RBMK is a Soviet-designed, graphite-moderated, water-cooled nuclear reactor featuring individual pressure tubes for fuel and the capability for onload refuelling.
The design was involved in the 1986 Chernobyl accident in Ukraine, but has since undergone significant refurbishment and safety upgrades for all remaining units.
The Leningrad nuclear site, about 100 km west of St Petersburg on the Gulf of Finland, has four units in operation. Courtesy Rosatom.

title: Germany’s State Of Bavaria Outlines Plans To Develop Three Nuclear Fusion Projects
author: David Dalton
text: First commercial reactor could be deployed at Gundremmingen site
The state of Bavaria in southeast Germany has announced plans to develop three fusion projects spanning both demonstration and commercial-scale machines.
The proposed rollout includes three distinct reactor projects, each with a unique focus and location:
Garching: A magnet-based fusion demonstration device is planned at Garching near Munich under the Alpha project, led by Proxima Fusion, targeting net-positive energy output.

Gundremmingen: The site of a former commercial nuclear power station has been selected for Bavaria’s first commercial-scale fusion reactor plant, known as ‘Stellaris’. The project is also led by Proxima Fusion, backed by private investment and expected to operate within around 15 years,

Southern Bavaria: Preliminary plans are in place for a commercial reactor using laser-based fusion technology. Details of this facility remain limited, but officials have indicated it could help diversify technology approaches.
The state said it is working closely with federal authorities and aims to reuse existing grid and nuclear infrastructure.
Proxima was founded in April 2023 as a spin-out from the Max Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Germany.

The company recently revealed a concept design for Stellaris, which it said is the world’s most viable commercial nuclear fusion power plant. The company said Stellaris is “the world’s first integrated concept for a commercial fusion power plant designed to operate reliably and continuously”.

Stellaris will use high-temperature superconducting magnets in a stellarator. A stellarator is a doughnut-shaped ring of precisely positioned magnets that can contain the plasma from which fusion energy is born.

Most fusion experiments today are tokamaks because they are better understood and are closer to achieving ignition conditions. However, there has been renewed interest in stellarators since the 1990s.
According to the International Atomic Energy Agency, both reactor types have certain advantages. While tokamaks are better at keeping plasmas hot, stellarators are better at keeping them stable.
The latest funding came three months after Proxima announced what it said was Europe’s largest-ever private fusion funding round.

Proxima is finalising a site for Alpha, its demonstration stellarator. Alpha is scheduled to begin operations in 2031 and is a critical step to demonstrating net energy gain and moving towards a first-of-a-kind fusion power plant.

UK-based fusion energy analyst Buddy Alcock said the plans signal strong public-private collaboration in Bavaria, as the state incorporates existing regional progress within its plans for a diverse fusion landscape.

“This is a forward-thinking move,” Alcock said. “We are going to need more than one fusion power plant, and Bavaria is deciding early to build plans for that reality. It’s also positive to see support for a diverse range of fusion concepts.”
Last year the German federal German government set out a “high tech agenda” explaining how it intends to build a nuclear fusion reactor as part of efforts to become climate neutral by 2045.

Germany has shut down its commercial nuclear power plants, but chancellor Friedrich Merz is an enthusiastic supporter of fusion research and has said the country should host the world’s first fusion reactor to be connected to the energy grid.
