The Bicycle initiative is related to investment announced in November of more than £18m (€20.4m, $23.6m) in plans to recycle spent nuclear fuel to create an “evergreen” supply of new precision cancer medicines, offering hope for patients with previously untreatable cancers.

The programme, run by the UK’s national innovation agency, Innovate UK, is to invest £9.9m in the “unique” project to develop cutting-edge new treatments for cancer, backed by a further £8.9m from industry, for a total of £18.8m.

The government said it is determined to unleash a golden era of nuclear technology and innovation, and today’s announcement comes hot on the heels of government backing for Sizewell C on the Suffolk coast and small modular reactors at Wylfa in North Wales.
Radiopharmaceuticals work by delivering radiotherapy directly to cancer cells. Courtesy Nuclear Energy Agency.

title: Poland’s SGE Signs Small Modular Reactor MOU With South Korea’s Samsung C&T
author: David Dalton
text: Focus is on deployment of BWRX-300 technology in Central and Eastern Europe

Poland-based small modular reactor (SMR) project developer Synthos Green Energy (SGE) and South Korea’s Samsung C&T have signed an MOU to collaborate on the deployment of SMRs, marking what they said was a significant step towards advancing clean, reliable and affordable energy solutions.
The partnership aims to accelerate the rollout of SMRs as a cornerstone of sustainable energy, energy security and carbon-neutral goals worldwide.

The partnership will initially outline the framework for future cooperation, focused the potential development of SMR projects using GE Vernova Hitachi Nuclear Energy’s BWRX-300 technology in the Central and Eastern Europe region.
To accelerate and expand the rate of SMR deployments in Europe, Samsung is considering a strategic investment into SGE’s development platform.
As part of the collaboration, the parties will share information such as feasibility studies, site data, environmental assessments and evaluation reports.

Michal Solowow, the billionaire owner and founder of SGE said: “Samsung C&T is the world’s leader in energy infrastructure construction. SGE is proud to deepen and align our relationship with Samsung as a potential equity partner.”

SGE is a co-investor in the standard design for the BWRX-300, designed by GE Vernova Hitachi Nuclear Energy. SGE is establishing partnerships and projects in more than a half-dozen European countries.

The company’s flagship project is in Poland, where, in cooperation with state-controlled energy company Orlen, SGE has been preparing for development at three separate sites – Wloclawek, central Poland, Ostroleka, northeastern Poland, and Stawy Monowskie, in the south of the country. It is expecting to complete the first unit near Wloclawek by 2032.
In December 2023, joint venture OSGE received a decision-in-principle for the construction of up to 24 SMRs at six potential sites across the country.
Michal Solowow, owner and founder of SGE, and Oh Sechul, president and chief executive officer of Samsung C&T, sign the MOU in Seoul, South Korea.

title: Canada Moves Deep Geological Repository Into Multi-Year Regulatory Process
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Construction of facility for spent nuclear fuel could begin in mid-2030s

Canada’s plan for a deep geological repository for used nuclear fuel has moved into a multi-year federal regulatory process after the Nuclear Waste Management Organisation (NWMO) confirmed the selection of the Revell area in northwestern Ontario and said the host communities of Ignace and Wabigoon Lake Ojibway Nation had demonstrated willingness to proceed.

The NWMO said the Revell siting decision, taken in November 2024, followed technical studies and community engagement carried out over more than a decade. The Revell area lies within the 2.7-billion-year-old Revell batholith, a crystalline rock formation where boreholes to about 1 km indicate the geological stability and depth required for a repository.

According to a spokesperson, both Ignace and Wabigoon Lake Ojibway Nation completed “community-driven willingness processes”. The organisation said this met its criteria for informed and voluntary participation.

The spokesperson said: “In the interim, the NWMO will be taking part in the federal government’s regulatory decision-making process and Wabigoon Lake Ojibway Nation’s regulatory assessment and approval process and beginning to transition our operations to the site”.

The federal regulatory review will be led by the Impact Assessment Agency of Canada and involve licence applications to the Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission (CNSC). These assessments are expected to continue into the 2030s. In parallel, the project will be examined under the sovereign Regulatory Assessment and Approval Process of Wabigoon Lake Ojibway Nation.

Construction of the repository is expected to begin in the mid-2030s, but only after all regulatory reviews have been completed. The NWMO said near-term work will focus on preparing submissions for both regulatory processes, beginning the transition of operations to the selected site and progressing design and planning.

The siting decision has drawn criticism and legal challenge from some Indigenous groups. In late December 2024, Eagle Lake First Nation applied for a judicial review, arguing that it was unjustifiably excluded as a potential host community and that the chosen site lies on its traditional territory. The NWMO has said it will review the filing and continue discussions.

In 2021, the NWMO estimated the cost of the project, including the repository, surface facilities and used-fuel transportation system, at about CAD 26bn (18.5bn US$, €15.9bn)* over an approximately 175-year lifecycle, based on a reference inventory of up to 5.5 million used fuel bundles from Canada’s existing reactor fleet. The estimate is reviewed and updated at least every five years.
According to earlier reports, construction of the facility itself is expected to cost at least CAD 4.5bn, although detailed costs will likely depend on licensing and design decisions.

The planned repository would be constructed 650-800 metres underground in crystalline rock and would use a system of engineered and natural barriers. Plans include the construction of a demonstration facility first once a construction permit is granted. The demonstration is expected to confirm facility parameters before actual construction begins. Once built, the main repository facility will be operated for about 40-50 years while receiving actual waste after which a monitoring programme will begin.

The repository is intended for Canada’s used nuclear fuel – a high-level, long-lived waste – and not for low- and intermediate-level radioactive waste, which is managed under separate programmes. Canada’s used nuclear fuel is currently safely managed in facilities licensed for interim storage.

The NWMO has cooperation agreements with a number of radioactive waste management organisations around the world, including Australia, Belgium, France, Japan, South Korea, Sweden, Switzerland, the UK and the US. In Finland it has worked with Posiva, which is overseeing development of what could be the world’s first deep geological repository for spent nuclear fuel.

Commercial nuclear power in Canada is based on domestically designed Candu pressurised heavy-water reactors, which began entering service in the early 1970s. Today 17 nuclear reactor units are operating commercially at four sites. Another eight reactor units have been permanently shut down.

Refurbishment programmes are extending the operating lifetimes of reactors by 20 or 30 years, meaning many units are expected to operate into the late 2030s and 2050s. Canada is also pioneering the deployment of small modular reactors, with a pilot project at the existing Darlington nuclear site in Ontario.
*2020 CAD value, currency conversion at current rates for orientation
Surveying work for a potential repository being carried out in the Wabigoon Lake Ojibway Nation in Ontario. Courtesy NWMO.
Canada’s used nuclear fuel is currently safely managed in facilities licensed for interim storage. Courtesy NWMO.

title: Talks On Small Modular Reactors Continuing Between Turkey And Bill Gates’ TerraPower
author: David Dalton
text: Ankara wants 5,000 MW of SMR capacity by 2050

Discussions are continuing between Turkey and US-based nuclear reactor company TerraPower, founded by Bill Gates, to incorporate small modular reactors (SMRs) in Ankara’s broader 2050 nuclear energy target of 20,000 MW of installed capacity, Turkish energy and natural resources minister Alparslan Bayraktar said.
Speaking at the 15th Turkey Energy Summit in Istanbul, Bayraktar said Turkey plans to reach at least 5,000 MW of SMR capacity as part of its long-term plan.
That plan includes 12 large-scale reactors, including four already under construction at Akkuyu and an additional eight units at Sinop and and Igneada.

Akkuyu is on the Mediterranean coast on the southern province of Mersin, Sinop is on the Black Sea in northern Turkey and Igneada is in Thrace, also on the Black Sea, not far from the Bulgarian border.

Akkuyu will have four Russia-supplied VVER-1200 pressurised water reactor units. Unit 1 was originally expected to enter commercial operation by the end of 2025 with the remaining units coming online by 2028. Bayraktar said recently that the first unit at Akkuyu is scheduled to begin commercial operation next year.
TerraPower confirmed last year that it had held informal talks with countries in Europe, including Turkey.
TerraPower is developing the Natrium technology, which combines a 345-MW sodium-cooled fast reactor with a molten salt-based storage system, capable of increasing output to 500 MW during peak demand.
The company is building its first plant at a former coal site in Kemmerer, Wyoming. TerraPower began non-nuclear construction activities at the site in 2024.

title: Funding For Fusion Energy Jumped By 30% From June-Sept, With US And China Dominating
author: Nigel Davies
text: Report shows that together, US and China account for 87% of global backing

Cumulative investment in fusion energy jumped by 30% between June and September to €13bn ($15.1bn) from €9.9bn, with the US and China dominating the landscape, according to a report by the European Union’s F4E Fusion Observatory.

Data from the Observatory showed the US as clear leader in the fusion energy space, taking 53% of global funding, or €6.9bn, with China holding a 34% share of investments at €4.4bn. Some way behind, lies the EU with a global share of roughly 5% of global funding, with Germany accounting for 85% of that capital.

This divergence was also creating a rise of “fusion unicorns”, the report said, with four companies in the US and China – Commonwealth Fusion Systems, China Fusion Energy Co, NEO Fusion and TAE Technologies – all exceeding €1bn in global private investment.

The Observatory, part of the EU’s Fusion for Energy organisation supporting the development of fusion energy in the EU, also noted in the report that there are now 77 companies globally investing in the technology, with 42 based in the US, eight in China and a further eight in the EU.
The report said key developments had helped drive US dominance in recent months, including Commonwealth Fusion Systems raising $863m in additional funding as it seeks to commercialise fusion power.

The report also highlighted a sharp split between private and public sector investment in fusion energy. The US model was led by a 94.5% private capital investment, whereas a growing industry in China was led by a 71.2% state-led approach. A hybrid model was seen in the EU of 33.9% public, 64% private and 2.1% public-private funding.

A split among technologies was also becoming more apparent, the report showed. Indeed, private investment of €10.1bn was concentrated in magnetic confinement fusion (MCF), particularly in China and the US.

However, investment in the EU was divided between inertial confinement fusion (ICF) and MCF. The Observatory said this may be the result of the availability of stable public funding for MCF in the EU.

MCF uses magnetic fields to confine and control hot plasma until fusion occurs. ICF uses powerful laser or particle beams to rapidly compress and heat a tiny fuel pellet very rapidly for it to fuse before it can expand.
Commonwealth Fusion Systems recently raised $863m in additional funding to commercialise fusion power. Courtesy CFS.

title: BWRX-300 Small Modular Reactor Passes Step 2 Of UK’s Generic Design Assessment
author: David Dalton
text: GVH says momentum around plant continuing to build globally
The GE Vernova Hitachi Nuclear Energy (GVH) BWRX-300 small modular reactor (SMR) has completed Step 2 of the generic design assessment (GDA) process in the UK.
The BWRX-300 completed Step 1 of the GDA process in December 2024 and GVH has now received formal notification about completion of Step 2.

The Office for Nuclear Regulation (ONR), the Environment Agency (EA) and Natural Resources Wales use the GDA process to ensure that new reactor designs meet safety, security and environmental protection standards.
The ONR and EA said their Step 2 assessment has not identified any fundamental safety, security safeguard or environmental protection shortfalls with the design of the BWRX-300.

The first BWRX-300 SMR is under construction at utility Ontario Power Generation’s (OPG) Darlington nuclear site in Canada, with completion expected by the end of the decade. That would make it the first SMR in the Western World.

Orlen Synthos Green Energy (OSGE), which is working to deploy the BWRX-300 in Poland and Eastern Europe, coinvested in the GDA for the BWRX-300 as part of a project to benefit from regulatory lessons learned.

GVH said momentum around the BWRX-300 is continuing to build globally. Four units are planned for the Darlington site and the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission has accepted and is reviewing Tennessee Valley Authority’s (TVA) application to construct the first BWRX-300 in the US at the utility’s Clinch River site in Oak Ridge, Tennessee.
OPG, TVA, Duke Energy and Synthos Green Energy in Poland are investing in the standard design of the BWRX-300.

The BWRX-300 is a 300-MW simplified, next-generation boiling water reactor. It relies on established BWR technology but incorporates significant design simplifications. It uses existing fuel and could potentially power up to 300,000 homes or provide process heat for industry.
Work has already begun on construction of a BWRX-300 plant at Darlington in Canada. Courtesy OPG.

title: UK Nuclear Capacity Could Hit Almost 22 GW By 2050 With Long-Term Gov’t Support, Report Says
author: David Dalton
text: Independent body suggests significant portion of capacity could be represented by SMRs

Nuclear capacity in the UK could reach 21.6 GW in 2050, up from around 5.8 GW today, under a scenario that requires the rollout of high reactor and renewable capacities, according to the country’s energy system operator.

The National Energy System Operator (Neso), the new independent body that plans the country’s electricity and gas networks, released cost estimates
on 11 December covering a series of scenarios for how the UK can meet its 2050 net zero target – as well as the costs of falling short.

It said nuclear power will play an important role in achieving a clean power system in Britain by 2030 and beyond, through a new generation of nuclear plants that will replace retiring capacity and meet growing demand as the economy electrifies.

This would require the extension of existing plants and long-term government support to build the supply chain out for new infrastructure, including large-scale nuclear projects and more novel projects such as small modular reactors (SMRs).
In the various pathways to net zero outlined by Neso, 39-59% of the installed nuclear capacity is represented by SMRs.

Neso warns, however, that in a “falling behind” scenario, nuclear might only hit 10.4 GW by 2050. This scenario considers a world where some decarbonisation progress is made against today, but at a pace not sufficient to meet net zero.
Neso noted that most of Britain’s existing nuclear plants are due to retire before 2030 – some before new plants come online – creating a transition challenge.
Because of this, select plants are currently being considered for life extension, subject to approval from the Office for Nuclear Regulation.

Since 2000, the UK has seen permanent reactor shutdowns at Hinkley Point A, Bradwell, Calder Hall, Hunterston, Oldbury, Sizewell, Chapelcross, Dungeness and Wylfa, leaving nine units in commercial operation and only Hinkley Point C’s two EPRs under construction and plans confirmed for a further two EPRs at Sizewell C.

The government said recently it has chosen the island of Anglesey off the Welsh coast to host Britain’s first small modular reactors, designed by Rolls-Royce SMR, in a significant step forward for the industry.

It also announced that Great British Energy-Nuclear (GBE-N), the body overseeing new nuclear in the UK, has been tasked with identifying suitable sites that could potentially host new large-scale reactors.

Energy stakeholder consulted for the report acknowledged the role of nuclear to ensure energy security and meet decarbonisation targets. Despite this, many pointed out the challenges in the sector, such as long lead times for building large nuclear power plants, public perception and planning issues.
According to the report, Britain’s energy costs are set to halve over the next 25 years as the shift to renewables cuts the multibillion-pound bill for imported oil and gas.
Neso said total system costs, which are currently about 10% of national income, decline to roughly 5-6% by 2050 despite growing energy demand.

It said the reduction reflects a structural shift towards electrification: greater investment in renewable generation, grid infrastructure and electric vehicles steadily reduces the UK’s reliance on imported fossil fuels.
A view of the Hinkley Point C nuclear power station under construction in England. Courtesy EDF Energy.

title: Turkish Defence Company Prepares To Enter Nuclear Energy Sector
author: David Dalton
text: Baykar, which manufactures drones, aiming to develop small modular reactor

Turkish defence company Baykar, best known for the production of drones, is preparing to step into the nuclear energy sector with the development of a small modular reactor (SMR), according to energy and natural resources minister Alparslan Bayraktar.
Baykar is reported to be working on a 40-MW SMR unit, which would have the capacity to power more than 100,000 households on its own, Bayraktar told local media.
The move comes as Ankara prepares a comprehensive legislative package to regulate the nuclear energy industry. Turkey aims to reach 7.2 GW of nuclear capacity by 2035 and 20 GW by 2050.
It plans to build three conventional large-scale nuclear power stations and complement them with SMRs.
The first of the large-scale stations is already under construction at Akkuyu, on the Mediterranean coast in the southern province of Mersin.

Ankara has previously said it was in talks with Russia, China, Canada and South Korea on the second and third stations it plans to build at Sinop and Igneada. Sinop is on the Black Sea in northern Turkey and Igneada is in Thrace, also on the Black Sea, not far from the Bulgarian border.

Reports in Turkey said Baykar’s initiative is expected to form the technological foundation of the country’s plan to have 5,000 MW of SMR capacity, an amount officials say could eventually cover around 10% of electricity demand.
Officials said localising part of the production would help create a new supply chain, support employment and enable Turkey to enter export markets for SMR components and technologies.

A new draft law governing SMRs is expected to be submitted to parliament in the coming days. A planned framework for SMR development and deployment is set to include incentives similar to those already put in place for wind and solar investments.

Regulations would aim to attract both domestic and international investors, encourage private-sector partnerships, and open access to long-term financing tools. Turkish authorities are also exploring opportunities to leverage green-energy funding from international financial institutions.
Ankara has already signed cooperation agreements with the US and South Korea to advance SMR development and technology transfer.
Construction of Turkey’s first nuclear power station continues at Akkuyu. Courtesy Rosatom.
Baykar, best known for the production of drones, is reported to be working on a 40-MW small modular reactor. Courtesy Baykar.

title: INL Chooses Five Teams To Develop Marvel Test Microreactor
author: David Dalton
text: Plant will be connected to microgrid and used for demonstration

Idaho National Laboratory (INL) has chosen five teams for its Marvel project to develop a sodium-potassium-cooled microreactor designed to test microreactor applications, create regulatory processes and explore electrical and nonelectrical uses.
The Marvel reactor is planned to generate 85 kW (0.085 MW) of thermal energy and as much as 20 kW (0.02 MW) of electricity.

The unit will be at the INL’s transient reactor test facility, where it will serve as an operational microreactor for demonstration purposes. INL intends to connect Marvel to a nuclear microgrid and have the reactor operating by late 2027.

INL’s initial five teams for Marvel are Amazon Web Services; DCX USA and Arizona State University; General Electric Vernova; Radiation Detection Technologies; and Shepherd Power, NOV and ConocoPhillips.

Researchers from these teams propose to demonstrate several test cases, including those involving desalination, remote operations, advanced sensors and viability of powering data centres with advanced nuclear technologies.
The unit will be built at the INL’s transient reactor test facility. Courtesy INL.

title: Deep Fission To Break Ground On Underground Advanced Reactor Pilot Project In Kansas
author: David Dalton
text: 15-MW nuclear plant scheduled to go critical by 4 July 2026

Deep Fission, the nuclear energy company placing small modular pressurised water reactors in boreholes one mile underground, has selected the Great Plains Industrial Park in Kansas as the site of its advanced reactor pilot project.

The California-headquartered company, founded in 2023, said it will hold a groundbreaking ceremony on 9 December, marking a significant milestone in its first demonstration of the Gravity nuclear plant.

Deep Fission plans to deploy 15-MW pressurised water reactors one mile underground via 30-inch boreholes. Its reactor was previously referred to as the Deep Fission Borehole Reactor-1, or DFBR-1, but was recently renamed by the company to the Gravity Nuclear Reactor, or simply Gravity.

Deep Fission is participating in the US Department of Energy’s new reactor pilot programme, an initiative designed to accelerate the deployment of advanced nuclear technologies through a streamlined regulatory pathway under the Atomic Energy Act.

The company aims to complete construction of its first reactor and achieve criticality by 4 July 2026, at the Kansas location. Deep Fission and the Great Plains Development Authority have signed a letter of intent outlining their collaboration on the pilot and their intention to develop a full-scale commercial project at the same site.

The Great Plains Industrial Park, in Labette County, Kansas, is an established site for industrial and energy development. It offers Deep Fission the unique opportunity to scale onsite and potentially grow with the park “for decades to come”, Deep Fission said.
Deep Fission’s proprietary Gravity reactor design uses methods from the nuclear, oil and gas, and geothermal industries.

The company said that by placing reactors one mile underground, the surrounding geology provides billions of tons of passive shielding and natural containment – improving safety and security while significantly reducing cost, surface footprint, and visual impact.
Photo courtesy Deep Fission.

title: Czech Public Continues To Show Strong Support For Nuclear, Says Poll
author: Nigel Davies
text: Planned Dukovany expansion resulting in ‘positive media coverage’
The Czech public continues to back the growth of nuclear power generation in the country as a way to help maintain energy independence, an Ipsos poll showed.

The poll, commissioned by state utility company ČEZ, showed 77% of the country’s citizens supported its development, and that 93% agreed that the Czech Republic should aspire to be self-sufficient in terms of electricity production.
The poll showed the principal reasons behind the public’s support of nuclear development were economic savings, environmental issues and strengthening the country’s energy independence.
Ipsos said the results in part reflected positive media coverage of nuclear in the country, in particular due to the planned expansion of the Dukovany nuclear power plant.
In October, the Czech Republic applied to the European Commission for the approval of state aid to back the construction of two new reactor units at Dukovany.
The government plans to build two new large-scale APR1000 pressurised water reactor units at Dukovany, in the south of the country about 50 km from the border with Austria.
The reactors will be supplied by South Korea’s Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power under a contract signed earlier this year.

The poll also showed that over half of Czechs backed the use of nuclear power for its electricity production over renewables, although the majority also saw the combination of nuclear and renewable sources as being ideal.
“Demand for energy self-sufficiency has been very strong in the Czech Republic for a long time,” said Michal Straka, Ipsos consultant for energy research.

“This opinion strengthened after the start of the war in Ukraine and the subsequent energy crisis. The public recognises that nuclear power plants play an irreplaceable role in energy self-sufficiency.”
The Czech Republic has six commercially operational reactor units: four Russia-designed VVER-440 units at Dukovany and two larger VVER-1000 units at Temelín.
The Czech Republic is planning to build two new large-scale APR1000 pressurised water reactor units at Dukovany. Courtesy ČEZ.

title: IAEA Says Chernobyl Shelter Lost Primary Safety Functions Following Drone Strike
author: David Dalton
text: February incident caused major fire in outer cladding of massive steel structure

A comprehensive safety assessment of the New Safe Confinement (NSC) at the Chernobyl nuclear site in Ukraine has shown it had lost its primary safety functions, including the confinement capability, following a drone strike in February, the International Atomic Energy Agency said.
The agency said a team completed the assessment of the NSC last week.

The drone strike on 14 February pierced a large hole through the roof of the €1.5bn ($1.7bn) NSC, which was built to prevent any radioactive release from the destroyed Unit 4 reactor and protect it from external hazards.
The event also caused a major fire in the outer cladding of the massive steel structure built to prevent any radioactive release from the reactor destroyed in the 1986 accident.

The IAEA assessment confirmed that the NSC had lost its primary safety functions, including the confinement capability, but also found that there was no permanent damage to its load-bearing structures or monitoring systems.

“Limited temporary repairs have been carried out on the roof, but timely and comprehensive restoration remains essential to prevent further degradation and ensure long-term nuclear safety,” IAEA director-general Rafael Grossi said.

Based on the mission findings, the IAEA has recommended further restoration and protective work of the NSC structure, including humidity control measures and an updated corrosion monitoring programme, as well as an upgrade of an integrated automatic monitoring system for the shelter object structure built on top of the reactor immediately after the accident.

In 2026, with support from the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD), the Chernobyl site will undertake additional temporary repairs to support the re-establishment of the NSC’s confinement function, paving the way for full restoration once the conflict ends.
“The IAEA – which has a team permanently at the site – will continue to do everything it can to support efforts to fully restore nuclear safety and security at the Chernobyl site,” Grossi said.

The IAEA also said an agency team is criss-crossing Ukraine this month to assess the status of electrical substations critical for nuclear safety and security, following recent military attacks targeting energy infrastructure.

The 1-12 December is focussing on more than 10 substations – essential nodes in the electrical grid related to the nuclear power plants – to assess the damage, review repair efforts, and identify practical steps to strengthen the resilience of offsite power supplies to the country’s nuclear stations, three of which – Khmelnitski, Rivne and South  Ukraine – are still operating to generate electricity.
The drone strike in February pierced a large hole through the roof of the €1.5bn ($1.7bn) structure known as the New Safe Confinement. Courtesy IAEA.

title: US DOE Announces $800 Million In Grants To Accelerate Advanced Reactor Deployment
author: David Dalton
text: Funding aims to help deliver new nuclear generation in early 2030s
The US Department of Energy (DOE) has announced $800m (€884m) in grants to accelerate the early deployment of advanced light-water small modular reactors (SMRs) in the US.

Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA) will receive $400m in cost-shared funding for a GE Vernova Hitachi BWRX-300 nuclear plant and Holtec Government Services will receive $400m, also cost-shared, for SMR-300 deployment.

Federally owned utility TVA is planning to advance deployment of a BWRX-300 at the Clinch River nuclear site in Tennessee, as well as accelerate the deployment of additional units with utility Indiana Michigan Power and project developer Elementl Power.
Holtec plans to deploy two SMR-300 reactors at the Palisades nuclear station site in Covert, Michigan, demonstrating viability for additional orders both domestically and abroad.

The DOE said Holtec is pursuing an innovative one-stop-shop approach to SMR deployment by fulfilling the roles of technology vendor, supply chain vendor, nuclear plant constructor and electricity merchant selling the power to nearby utilities and end-users.

The DOE said the funding will help deliver new nuclear generation in the early 2030s, strengthen domestic supply chains, and advancing president Donald Trump’s executive orders to usher in a nuclear renaissance.

“As the nation prepares for continued growth in electricity demand, President Trump has charged DOE with adding new, affordable and reliable energy to keep America energy secure,” a DOE statement said.

“Small modular reactors offer flexible deployment, proven technology, and the ability to leverage existing supply chains, making them one of the fastest and most scalable pathways to new nuclear capacity.”

In March 2025, the DOE issued a $900m solicitation to de-risk the deployment of Gen III+ SMRs. The remaining $100m will be awarded later this year to support additional deployments and address key barriers in design, licensing, supply chain and site readiness.
The TVA SMR is targeted for commercial operation in the early 2030s. If that target is met, it would become the nation’s first commercial SMR.

TVA, which runs the Browns Ferry, Sequoyah and Watts Bar nuclear plants, led a coalition of utility and industry partners, including GE Vernova Hitachi, in applying for funding through the DOE’s Generation III+ SMR programme.

GE Vernova Hitachi said the coalition involved in the funding application reflects the industry’s confidence in the BWRX-300 and the role its accelerated deployment through this grant will play in strengthening the US nuclear supply chain.

In May of this year TVA submitted a construction permit application to the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) to build the first BWRX-300 in the US at Clinch River, originally the site of the Clinch River Breeder Reactor Project in the 1970s, funding for which was terminated in 1983. The NRC is reviewing the application.

In May the province of Ontario and OPG approved a CAD20.9bn (€13bn, $15.2bn) plan to build the first of four BWRX-300 SMRs at OPG’s Darlington site in Canada with commercial operation expected by the end of 2029.
Only a handful of SMRs have been completed and only in Russia and China. The Darlington project is expected to be the first to be deployed in the developed Group of Seven countries.
Early site preparation work at Darlington, on a site next to an existing nuclear station with four operational large-scale nuclear plants, has been completed.
TVA anticipates preliminary site preparation work at Clinch River could begin as early as next year while the NRC reviews the company’s construction permit application.

The BWRX-300 is a 300 MW advanced light-water system and a smaller, simplified version of GE Vernova Hitachi licensed Economic Simplified Boiling Water Reactor. According to TVA the plant will make use of established supply chains that could accelerate deployment.
Holtec’s SMR-300 is a pressurised water reactor producing around 300 MW of electrical power or 1,050 MW of thermal power for process applications.
Holtec’s SMR-300 could be deployed at the Palisades nuclear power station site. Courtesy Holtec.
The BWRX-300 SMR, to be deployed at Clinch River site in Tennessee, is targeted for commercial operation in the early 2030s. Courtesy GE Verona.

title: Environmental Group Files Lawsuit Opposing Restart Of Palisades Plant
author: Nigel Davies
text: Beyond Nuclear says exemption granted to restart reactor was unlawful
Environmental group Beyond Nuclear has filed a federal lawsuit in the US state of Michigan opposing the restart of the single-unit Palisades nuclear power station by Holtec.

The lawsuit says that “the exemption granted by the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission from the requirements of the Atomic Energy Act of 1954… which would allow the owner of a permanently shut down commercial nuclear power plant to be restored to commercial generation is unlawful.”
It says that Holtec should be forced to pursue a new licence application.

US energy company Holtec bought the Palisades plant on the shore of Lake Michigan in 2022 with the original intent to decommission it, but in 2023 applied to the US Department of Energy to return the plant to commercial operation. The plant had begun commercial operation in 1972, but ceased operations in May 2022.
The lawsuit alleges that when certifications were given for the decommissioning of the reactor they legally prohibited any further operation of the Palisades reactor or replacement of fuel.

The lawsuit, filed by Maryland-based Beyond Nuclear alongside other environmental groups Don’t Waste Michigan and Michigan Safe Energy Future, alleges the Palisades plant was poorly maintained and has suffered age related degradation, which it says could impact health, safety, security, property and the environment.
In October, the plant received new nuclear fuel – 68 assemblies in total – as part of the restart plans. The plant returned to operational status in August following three years in decommissioning.

As yet, the 805-MW pressurised water reactor is not generating electricity, but its change in status meant it could proceed to acquire new fuel to power the plant once final inspections and reassembly are finished.
When the plant is running again, Holtec also plans the construction and commissioning of small modular reactors at Palisades to be brought on line by the beginning of the next decade.
The single-unit Palisades nuclear power station in the US state of Michigan. Courtesy Holtec.

title: North American Trio Selected For Engineering Contract At Bulgaria’s Kozloduy Project
author: Nigel Davies
text: Final investment decision on two new Westinghouse reactor units expected next year

North American companies BWX Technologies, Laurentis Energy Partners and Canadian Nuclear Partners have been selected as a consortium to provide consultancy engineering services for the project to build two new nuclear plants at the Kozloduy nuclear power station in Bulgaria.
The companies said the 10-year owner’s engineer (OE) services contract for Units 7 and 8 at Kozloduy was valued in the “hundreds of millions of euros”.

The announcement came after Alex Nestor, chairman of the board of Kozloduy NPP-New Build, the state-owned company in charge of the project, said recently that he expected a final investment decision for its expansion to come in the second half of next year.
The consortium said over the first 12 months of the OE that they will help Kozloduy with services such as engineering, procurement and construction contract negotiations.
Following a final investment decision, the second phase of the contract would cover engineering services over the execution of the plant.

“Our country has secured leading international partners with proven experience across the full nuclear lifecycle, from design through to commissioning,” said Zhecho Stankov, Bulgaria’s minister of energy.
He confirmed that 30% of specialists working on the project, that will use two Westinghouse AP1000 pressurised water reactors, would be local.
Nestor said last week that 36 Bulgarian companies have signed memoranda of understanding with Westinghouse, with that number expected to grow.

A statement from Bulgaria’s ministry of energy expressed confidence that the agreement would help the country on its path to achieving its long-term clean energy goals and strengthening its energy security.
Bulgaria forecasts Unit 7 to be operational in 2035, with Unit 8 coming on line by 2037. In total, the two plants will produce an estimated 2,300 MW of electricity.
That would add to the 2,000 MW already in operation at Kozloduy from its two 1,000-MW Russia-designed VVER units. The site also has four older VVER-440 PWRs that are being decommissioned.
Kozloduy is the country’s sole nuclear power plant and provides around a third of Bulgaria’s electricity.
A rendering of two new planned AP1000 nuclear power plants at Kozloduy in Bulgaria. Courtesy Westinghouse.

title: Reactor Company Publishes Comprehensive Mapping Study For European Nuclear Fusion Plants
author: David Dalton
text: Future units must be ‘woven into the fabric of existing industrial base’

Germany-based nuclear fusion company Gauss Fusion and the Technical University of Munich have completed a comprehensive mapping study to pinpoint where fusion power plants could be located across Europe.

The study identifies 150 industrial clusters and 900 potential sites in countries including Germany, France, Italy, Spain, Switzerland, Denmark, the Netherlands, Austria and the Czech Republic, typically located in high-energy-demand industrial centres or conurbations.

Assessment was carried out against a consistent set of technical, environmental, and infrastructure criteria, including grid connectivity, access to cooling and heat recovery systems, and the ability to repurpose existing energy infrastructure.
Gauss Fusion recently unveiled what it claimed to be Europe’s first full design for a commercial nuclear fusion power plant, marking what it called “the shift from research to reality”.
Gauss Fusion chief executive officer Milena Roveda said: “Future fusion power plants should not exist in isolation but instead be woven into the fabric of Europe’s existing industrial base.

“This site mapping study brings that future a step closer, demonstrating that across Europe the infrastructure, industry and energy networks already exist to make fusion a practical, scalable and sovereign energy source.”

Gauss Fusion, based in Berlin and founded in 2022 by an alliance of five private companies from Germany, Italy, Spain and France,  said the results of the site mapping study will now be discussed with European governments, industry partners, and regulators across the continent.

Gauss Fusion’s strategy is to develop a nuclear fusion plant based on high-field magnetic confinement fusion, an approach that uses very strong magnetic fields to contain and compress a superheated plasma, enabling fusion reactions.
Gauss Fusion is aiming to develop a nuclear fusion plant based on high-field magnetic confinement fusion. Courtesy Gauss Fusion.

title: Studsvik To Provide Key Reactor Design and Verification System For Romania SMR Project
author: David Dalton
text: Software will verify core and operational safety of NuScale reactor
Studsvik has announced its first sale of design evaluation and verification software to a small modular reactor (SMR) utility customer.

Sweden-based Studsvik, which offers technical services to the nuclear power industry, said RoPower Nuclear SA in Romania has selected Studsvik’s Core Management System 5 (CMS5) as its methodology to support the country’s first SMR project.
Romania is planning to build what could be the first European SMR power station using six, 77 MW reactor modules deigned by US-based NuScale.

RoPower Nuclear, the joint venture established for the SMR project, intends to use NuScale’s technology for the facility at a former coal site in Doicesti, about 90 km northwest of the capital Bucharest.
With CMS5, RoPower will be equipped to perform the design evaluation and verification of the SMR plant’s core and operational safety. Studsvik said.
“This new collaboration with RoPower extends the use of Studsvik’s proven technology from the reactor designer to the first utility deploying an SMR fleet,” a statement said.
The final investment decision for a 462 MW small modular reactor (SMR) at Doicesti could be delayed to early 2027, Nucale chief executive officer John Hopkins said recently.
RoPower and US-based NuScale want to build a small modular reactor nuclear plant at a former coal plant in Doicesti. Mockup courtesy NuScale.

title: Hokkaido Governor Announces Backing For Restart Of Tomari-3 Nuclear Plant
author: David Dalton
text: Japan pushing for operation of reactors that were shut down after Fukushima disaster
The governor of Hokkaido prefecture in northern Japan announced on 28 November his support for the planned restart of Unit 3 at Hokkaido Electric Power Company’s Tomari nuclear power station.
“The use of nuclear power is a realistic option that can be taken for now,” Naomichi Suzuki told the Hokkaido assembly.
Suzuki said he plans to make a final decision early next month based on discussions in the assembly and the opinions of other related local governments.

In remarks at the assembly, the governor said the region needed a stable supply of electricity amid an expected surge in demand. He said he expected to see a drop in electricity rates due to the Tomari-3 restart and the carbon-free nature of nuclear power.
In August, the federal government asked for support for the restart from Hokkaido and four local municipalities, including the village of Tomari, which hosts the power plant.

Tomari-3 is a 866-MW pressurised water reactor unit which began commercial operation in 2009. There are two other units at the site, both of which were taken offline after the 2011 Fukushima disaster.
Earlier this year Japan’s Nuclear Regulation Authority approved a safety screening report that said Tomari-3 met safety standards introduced after Fukushima.
Japan has 33 commercially available units, 14 of which have resumed operation under stringent post-Fukushima rules. Restarts face high regulatory hurdles and need local government support.
Before the 2011 Fukushima disaster Japan’s fleet of 54 nuclear plants generated about 30% of the country’s electricity, but were all shut down for safety checks following the accident.
According to the International Atomic Energy Agency, the figure for 2023, was 5.5%, but the government want to see this climb to 20%.
Japan’s new prime minister Sanae Takaichi has said she will push for the accelerated revival of nuclear power with reactor restarts key to reducing costly fuel imports.
Mugu-shisai/Creative Commons Licence.

title: US Utilities Should Join Forces In ‘Consortium Approach’ As Momentum For Nuclear Renaissance Grows
author: Nigel Davies
text: Thinktank head says what is missing from equation are ‘firm orders’

The chances of a “nuclear renaissance” in the US are building, but could be better assured if utility companies form a consortium to help increase the orders needed for the industry to scale up, Adam Stein, a nuclear analyst at the California-based Breakthrough Institute environmental thinktank said.

Speaking in a recorded interview on a Platts podcast analysing the state of the nuclear industry, Stein said that what is missing from the equation towards seeing a real nuclear renaissance was firm orders.

He said orders could not solely come from technology companies building data centres or industrial companies like Dow, which is planning to deploy X-energy small modular reactors (SMRs) at its chemical plant in Seadrift, Texas, but must come through utility companies, which provide the bulk of electricity generation in the US.
Given there were over 300 utility companies in the US with the majority lacking the capacity or need to buy a large offtake from nuclear power, then they must find a way to band together.

“The next challenge to overcome, above the regulatory challenges that are still being worked out, is how to build a consortium of buyers than can share cost risk and each have a small offtake,” Stein said.
“Getting to a consortium approach will help to build orders and that’s how we would get to a real renaissance as we saw a decade or a decade and a half ago.”

He added that over the next five years he expected to see the most progress within nuclear coming from advanced reactors, with one or two, or perhaps more if there was additional support, of large reactors under construction in the US.

However, he cautioned that the challenge would be to obtain orders for second, third, and fourth plants, while the first-of-a-kind plants are being constructed, to carry momentum through and continue to scale up.

Speaking in a separate recorded interview on the Platts podcast, Drew Marsh, chief executive officer of power utility Entergy and new chair of the Washington-based Nuclear Energy Institute, also backed the argument for a nuclear renaissance.
“That term has been used before, but this time I think it’s fundamentally different as it’s demand driven, and the unique profile of nuclear to serve data centre demand.”
He said companies such as Google, Microsoft, Amazon and Meta, all have a massive appetite for clean energy.
“That’s what’s going to be driving this new build out of nuclear, and I don’t expect that to slow down any time soon.”
According to Platts analysts on the podcast, SMRs could a be a $1-2tn (€862m-1.73tn) market with 343 GW by 2050 driven primarily by data centre demand.
Stein said that he saw technology companies in the US willing to pay higher costs for new projects or restarts of reactors in the near term.

Marsh gave a timescale of how he saw the nuclear industry developing. He said over the next five years we would see a lot of restarts of reactors, such as the Palisades plant in Michigan as well as upgrades.
“We will also see a lot of upgrades and capacity improvements. If we can get 50 MW, 100 MW from an existing unit, spread across 100 units, that’s a lot of extra nuclear capacity.”
And then real growth would be a little further down the line. In five to 10 years, he said we would see some of the new reactors come on, and in 15 years the industry would be really rolling.

“So, if we’re thinking about meeting the objectives of quadrupling the nuclear capacity out there by 25 years, by the time you get to 15 years out there should be a lot of projects coming to fruition by that time.”

Despite Marsh’s optimism over prospects for the industry, he said they must narrow down the uncertainty associated with construction. If they were able to do this, then “you would see the utilities come in in a very big way”.
He said the challenge was not that the industry was risk averse, but that customers were risk averse. When costs over run, he said, they were assigned to shareholders, and the rest to customers.

“At that point the company does not have the opportunity to earn its return or earn back its money, it’s locked in forever at the lower price. It’s really important to get the costs well understood and get that uncertainty reduced.”
The Palisades nuclear plant in the US state of Michigan is one of a number that could be restarted. Courtesy Holtec International.
Utility companies should form a consortium to help increase the orders needed for the nuclear industry to scale up, analyst Adam Stein said. Courtesy Georgia Power.

title: Orano Condemns ‘Illegal’ Shipment Of Uranium From Somair Mine In Niger
author: David Dalton
text: French company lost control of mines following military coup in African nation
French nuclear materials company Orano has condemned what it called and “illegal” shipment of uranium that had been stored at the Somair mining site in Niger.
The company said in a statement it had learned from media reports that a shipment of uranium had left the site in Arlit, northern Niger.
Orano said it is “not the initiator of this shipment and strongly condemns it”.

Orano lost operational control of its Niger mines in December 2024 and has no official information on the quantity of uranium transported, its final destination, or the conditions under which the transport was undertaken in terms of safety and security.

The company said the shipment is in breach of the decision handed down in favour of Orano on 23 September by the Washington, US-based International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes (ICSID) arbitration tribunal in the dispute between Orano and the State of Niger concerning the Somair uranium mine.
The court of arbitration had ordered the Niger “not to sell, transfer, or even facilitate the transfer to third parties of uranium produced by Somair” held in violation of Orano's rights.

“Orano will continue to steadfastly defend its interests and reserves the right to take any additional action necessary, in particular criminal proceedings, including against third parties, in the event of preemption of the material in violation of its offtake rights, the statement said.
The ICSID case was part of wider tensions over control of Niger’s uranium resources following political upheaval in the country.
Somair (Société des Mines de l’Aïr) is majority-owned by Orano and has been one of the country’s largest uranium producers for decades.
In January 2025, Orano filed an arbitration procedure against Niger following the loss of operational control of the Somair uranium mine.
The move followed an initial proceeding against Niger over the Imouraren uranium deposit in December 2024.

Orano had said the West African country’s obstruction of the commercialisation of production, and the suppression of Orano's offtake rights, had “only aggravated Somair’s financial situation and the prejudice suffered by Orano”.
Orano announced in October 2024 it would be halting its uranium production in Niger, citing a “highly deteriorated” situation and its inability to operate.
A July 2023 coup in Niger led to a halt in imports of critical materials necessary for uranium exploitation at Somair, such as soda ash, carbonate, nitrates, and sulphur.
According to Orano, Somair is the only uranium mine in commercial operation in Niger.
The company said earlier this year that 1,500 tonnes of uranium were still stockpiled at the site and threatened to pursue criminal charges if any of it was sold without permission.
According to Reuters, a source at the mine said at the time that Niger had not yet sold any uranium but “potential buyers include Iranians, Russians and Turkey”.
In July 2025, Niger's government said it planned to nationalise the Somair mine.
Uranium is a cornerstone of Niger’s economy, despite declining output in recent years.
The Somair open pit mine in Niger. Image courtesy Maurice Ascani / Orano.

title: UK Nuclear Industry Welcomes Chancellor’s Budget Plans to Cut Red Tape And Boost Financing
author: David Dalton
text: Gov’t will ‘go further’ to make nuclear power cheaper and to accelerate its deployment

The UK-based Nuclear Industry Association has welcomed chancellor Rachel Reeves’ endorsement of a recent nuclear regulatory review in her budget speech, in which she described the report as “an ambitious plan to cut the red tape that has tied our nuclear industry in knots for decades.”
The government confirmed that it accepts the principle of all the recommendations and will publish a full implementation plan within three months.

The report, published earlier this week
by a task force set up by prime minister Keir Starmer, warned that the UK has become the most expensive country in the world to build a nuclear power station because of overly complex and misunderstood environmental, safety and bureaucratic processes, according to a government review.
The report outlined 47 recommendations for the government to speed up building new nuclear projects at a lower cost and on time.
Reeves made her budget announcements on 26 November, detailing the government’s plans to “go further to make nuclear power cheaper and to accelerate its deployment”.

Earlier this month, the government announced that Wylfa in Anglesey, North Wales, will host the UK’s first small modular reactor project. The government also plans to continue identifying potential sites for large-scale nuclear power.

These plans include setting out pathways for investment in the nuclear sector where updates to the Green Financing Framework will add nuclear energy for power generation to the list of policies eligible to be funded by green gilts and retail Green Savings Bonds.

The NIA said the move was “another major win for the industry”, ensuring it can access the same investment incentives as other clean energy technologies and helping to reduce the cost of capital for new projects.
NIA chief executive Tom Greatrex said: “We welcome the chancellor’s support for the Nuclear Regulatory Review and her commitment to publish a plan within the next three months.

“It’s now crucial that the government sticks to this timeline and adopts the task force’s recommendations with urgency, so we can maintain momentum and turn these proposals into reality – strengthening our energy security and ensuring reliable, clean power for decades to come.”

Greatrex said the announcement that nuclear will be included within the UK’s Green Financing Framework is a vital step that will help reduce the cost of financing, unlock investment at scale and put nuclear on a level footing with other clean energy technologies.
Chancellor Rachel Reeves has laid out plans to boost nuclear deploymentm in the UK. Courtesy UK Govt/X.

title: Broad Support For Thorizon Reactor Project As Site Assessment Begins In Netherlands
author: David Dalton
text: Nuclear demonstrator is part of plans to industrialise molten salt technology

There is broad industrial and regional support for plans to deploy the first demonstration and research Thorizon Pioneer nuclear power plant in the Netherlands, with work already underway on the assessment of potential sites, the company developing the technology said.
Amsterdam-based Thorizon said at the Made for Nuclear event in Hilversum, southeast of Amsterdam, that it had signed an “ambition agreement” with a coalition of partners to accelerate the project.

The coalition brings together leading Dutch industrial companies including VDL Groep, nuclear operator EPZ and engineering and construction firm Haskoning, supported by a strong ecosystem of universities, knowledge institutes, manufacturing, energy and high-tech service providers.

Thorizon, originally a spin-off from the Dutch nuclear research institute NRG, said several Dutch provinces have confirmed their engagement and are now assessing potential sites for the demonstrator, as well as opportunities to establish an innovation hub around the facility with testing capabilities for materials and components.

The nuclear demonstrator, known as Thorizon Pioneer, is part of Thorizon’s plans to industrialise the technology. The facility will be a smaller, non-commercial version of the Thorizon Pioneer reactor focused on validating the reactor core without electricity production.

The Thorizon Pioneer could be the first molten salt nuclear installation running in Europe, providing unique opportunities for research and development, Thorizon said. It is designed to demonstrate Thorizon’s ability to design, licence and build a nuclear installation. The Pioneer will also enable the qualification of supply-chain partners, and testing of key materials and components.

According to Thorizon, molten salt reactors (MSRs) are recognised as one of the most promising advanced nuclear technologies from both a safety and economic perspective. Their liquid fuel-salt mixture allows operation at low pressure and creates a self-stabilising core that increases intrinsic safety. The design eliminates much of the complexity and cost of high-pressure systems found in conventional reactor types and enables simpler, more modular construction.

MSRs can dramatically increase the energy extracted from uranium resources by recycling long-lived waste from spent nuclear fuel and enabling future use of thorium. “MSRs offer a pathway to reliable and affordable industrial heat and electricity, particularly for off-grid or hard-to-decarbonie industrial clusters where stable, low-cost heat is essential,” Thorizon said.

To prepare for European licensing, Thorizon is engaged in a joint preparatory safety review with the Dutch, French and Belgium nuclear safety authorities. The next major milestone will be securing a suitable site.

The project will be supported through a combination of private investment and public funding. Thorizon is backed by Positron Ventures, Invest-NL and the regional development agencies of Zeeland and North Holland, and has secured grants from the French government, the European Commission’s Joint Transition Fund in Zeeland and the Province of Brabant.
Thorizon chief executive officer Kiki Lauwers (sitting) speaks at the Made in Nuclear event where the company announced an ‘ambition agreement’ with a coalition of partners. Courtesy Thorizon.

title: X-energy Gets $700 Million Backing As Investors Bet On Advanced Nuclear Deployment
author: David Dalton
text: US company working on major projects to roll out Xe-100 small modular reactor

X-energy, a company backed by technology giant Amazon, has closed one of the largest fundraisings by an advanced nuclear reactor developer with a $700m (€607m) funding round led by US investor Jane Street with participation from more than 10 other institutional investors.

The deal brings the total funds raised by Maryland-based X-energy in the past 13 months to $1.4bn as it aims to deliver major contracts with Amazon, Dow Inc and Centrica to build a fleet of small modular reactors (SMRs) in the US and UK.
X-energy is planning deployment of the first Xe-100 SMR at Dow Inc’s UCC Seadrift Operations in Texas.

In May 2025, the proposed four-reactor project reached a critical milestone when its construction permit application was accepted for review by the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission. The plant, known as Long Mott, could become first advanced nuclear facility at a US industrial site.
X-energy and UK energy company Centrica plan to build up to 12 SMRs in Hartlepool in northeast England, with a follow-on UK-wide programme targeting a fleet of 6 GW of power.
The company is also advancing Xe-100 deployment with Energy Northwest in Washington state in collaboration with Amazon.
The project, known as the Cascade Advanced Energy Facility, is for 12 reactors producing a maximum of 960 MW of electricity.
Amazon took two seats on X-energy’s board when it invested in the SMR developer last year in a deal aimed at bringing the Washington state reactors online by 2039.
The facility will supply Energy Northwest with power and augment the single-unit Columbia nuclear power station, the Pacific Northwest’s only existing commercial nuclear facility.
As part of the deal, Amazon will finance the construction of the project and the power will flow to Energy Northwest – which in turn supplies power for Amazon’s nearby data centres.

The Xe-100 is a Generation IV high-temperature gas-cooled reactor (HTGR). According to the International Atomic Energy Agency, interest in HTGRs is increasing because they can provide efficient and cost-effective electricity and produce high-temperature process heat usable for various industrial applications.

Each Xe-100 reactor is designed to produce 80 MW of electricity or 200 MW of process heat using Triso particle fuel, known for its high safety performance. The reactors are expected to operate for up to 60 years.
X-energy recently announced the start of vertical construction for its TX-1 fuel fabrication facility in Oak Ridge, Tennessee.
The company said the facility will be the first of its kind in the US and will manufacture the company’s proprietary Triso fuel for its commercial reactors.
The Cascade Advanced Energy Facility will be constructed in three phases, each with four of X-energy’s 80-MW, high-temperature gas-cooled reactors. Courtesy X-energy.

title: Enec And Framatome Fabricate First Lead Test Fuel Assemblies For Barakah Nuclear Station
author: David Dalton
text: UAE welcomes step in diversification of supplies

The Emirates Nuclear Energy Company (Enec) and French nuclear company Framatome have announced the successful fabrication by Framatome of the first lead fuel assemblies in Richland, US, for the Barakah nuclear power station in the United Arab Emirates (UAE).

Enec, the state entity established to oversee nuclear power projects in the UAE, said in a statement that the achievement marks a significant milestone in the implementation of the fuel supply agreement announced by the two companies in July 2025, which aims to strengthen the UAE’s national energy security through the diversification of nuclear fuel supplies.

“The agreement between Enec and Framatome is a key development in Enec’s long-term strategy to diversify its fuel supply chain, enhancing energy security by ensuring an uninterrupted source of carbon-free power from the Barakah Plant to businesses, industries and homes across the UAE,” the statement said.
The lead fuel assemblies were manufactured at Framatome’s facility in Richland, Washington State and will now be delivered as complete nuclear fuel assemblies for testing at the Barakah Plant.

Barakah consists of four South Korea -supplied APR-1400 pressurised water reactor (PWR) units generating a total of 40 TWh of electricity annually. Enec says it is the largest source of clean energy in the region, supplying around 25% of the UAE’s electricity.

Construction of Barakah, the first commercial nuclear power station to operate in the Arab World, began in 2012. The first of its four South Korea-supplied APR1400 plants began commercial operation in April 2021. The fourth and final unit began commercial operation in September 2024.
Framatome’s facility in Richland, Washington State. Courtesy Framatome.
The fuel assemblies were manufactured at Framatome’s facility in Richland, US. Courtesy Framatome/Enec.

title: RPV Delivered To Akkuyu-4 Nuclear Power Plant In Turkey
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Russia supplying four PWRs for project on Mediterranean coast
The reactor pressure vessel (RPV) for Unit 4 of Turkey’s Akkuyu nuclear power station has been delivered to the construction site in Mersin province, project company Akkuyu Nuclear said.

The 320-tonne vessel, manufactured by Rosatom’s Atommash plant in Volgodonsk, was shipped by combined road and sea transport in early October and arrived at Akkuyu’s eastern cargo terminal on 12 November.
The shipment also included the equipment lock for Unit 3 and the pressuriser for Unit 4, Akkuyu Nuclear said.

The company chief executive Sergei Butskikh said delivery of the Unit 4 RPV means all four reactors for the plant have now arrived on site. He said the RPVs for Units 1, 2 and 3 have already been installed.
Russia is supplying four VVER-1200 pressurised water reactor units for Akkuyu, on the Mediterranean coast in the southern province of Mersin.
Construction of the four units started consecutively in 2018, 2020, 2021, and 2022.
The first Akkuyu unit was initially expected to come online in 2023, but possible in-service dates have been pushed back to 2026.
The RPV has been delivered for Unit 4 at the Akkuyu nuclear power station in Turkey. Courtesy Rosatom.

title: Sweden’s Nuclear Power Coordinator Says Interest In Using Financing Exceeds 2035 Goals
author: Nigel Davies
text: Nordic nation’s plans for reactors are advanced, but clear vision and ambition needed

Sweden’s national nuclear power coordinator has said that interest in tapping the financing established in the government’s 2026 budget to meet the country’s goal of having 2,500 MW of new nuclear capacity by 2035 already outstrips the target.

Writing in an interim report published earlier this month, Carl Berglöf said the country’s budget for 2026 had presented the financial frameworks for an expansion roughly in line with the government’s goal of 2,500 MW of new nuclear power capacity by 2035.
“The nuclear power coordinator has through stakeholder dialogues noted a collective interest in accessing this financing that exceeds 2,500 MW,” Berglöf said in the report.
By 2045 the government’s target is to have expansion of up to 1,000 MW.
Sweden’s budget for 2026 includes financing frameworks of SEK220bn (about €20.3bn, $23.4bn) in the form of loans for companies to use towards the construction of new reactors.

The frameworks are based on lending over a 12-year period and future annual expenditures for hedging agreements worth around SEK1-3bn (€90m-€272, $104m-$314m) annually over 40 years once the reactors are commissioned.

Berglöf went on to caution in the report that the commissioning of this capacity by that timeframe would depend on several aspects such as the type of technology chosen, the capacity of the industry to deliver, as well as other countries’ timelines for nuclear power expansion.

The report also called for Sweden to present a full strategy. “The totality of political decisions and a more detailed path forward should be formulated by the government in a national nuclear power strategy.” Berglöf added that it was his intention to contribute to such a strategy.

The report said that preparations were well advanced for the country to develop new nuclear power, including its financing model, licensing processes, and that a system for nuclear waste management was being worked on.
However, the report added that it would be increasingly important to establish a clear vision and ambition in certain areas.

Berglöf highlighted several areas Sweden needed to work further on, including goals for a domestic industrial supply chain, international cooperation and nuclear technology research. He said there was the potential need for a research reactor to help develop new technology.

The report also asked if Sweden should go further than its recent decision to lift its ban on the mining of uranium by allowing the development of other parts of the nuclear fuel supply such as conversion and enrichment.
Berglöf urged the government to use its decision to become a co-owner in Vattenfall's nuclear power project at Ringhals to learn how to further progress the industry.

“In addition to providing financial stability to the project, the government has the opportunity to use the ownership to build its own competence through the experiences gained. This will be an important factor in reducing costs in future projects.”

The report highlighted work to assess how many skilled workers would be needed to develop new nuclear power, with discussions taking place through universities, vocational training centres and research institutes.

Sweden’s centre-right government made new nuclear power one of its key election pledges. The move reverses a decades-long policy to shut down the country’s ageing reactors and replacing them with renewable energy.

The country has six reactor units in commercial operation at three sites: Forsmark, Oskarshamn and Ringhals. According to International Atomic Energy Agency data, nuclear energy provided 29% of the country’s electricity generation in 2024.
Sweden has six reactor units in commercial operation at three sites: Forsmark, Oskarshamn and Ringhals (pictured). Courtesy Vattenfall.

title: China’s Zhangzhou-2 Nuclear Power Plant Connected To Grid
author: David Dalton
text: Beijing aiming for mass deployment of indigenous Hualong One technology

Unit 2 of the Zhangzhou nuclear power station in Fujian Province, eastern China, has been successfully connected to the grid for the first time, state media outlets and the Chinea Nuclear Energy Association (CNEA) reported.
CNEA said the move is a major step forward in the mass deployment of China’s indigenous Hualong One reactor technology.
After the initial grid-connection test on Saturday, onsite checks confirmed that the unit was operating stably and that all technical indicators met design standards, CNEA said.
The reactor will now undergo a series of scheduled tests to further verify its performance and ensure it meets all conditions for commercial operation,
Zhangzhou-2 is a 1,126-MW domestic Hualong One, or HPR1000, pressurised water reactor (PWR) unit. Construction began in September 2020.
CNEA said the Zhangzhou nuclear station will eventually have six Hualong One reactor units.
In January 2025, Zhangzhou-1 became the first and only unit so far to start commercial operation at the site.
Construction of Zhangzhou-3 began in February 2024 and of Zhangzhou-4 in September 2024.
The Zhangzhou project is owned by CNNC-Guodian Zhangzhou Energy Company, a joint venture between CNNC (51%) and China Guodian Corporation (49%).
The Hualong One, also known as the HPR1000, is a domestically developed PWR that combines features from China National Nuclear Corporation’s ACP1000 and China General Nuclear’s ACPR1000+ designs.
According to International Atomic Energy Agency data, China has 29 reactors under construction, 14 of which are of the Hualong One design.
Two additional Hualong One units are reportedly under construction at Jinqimen and one CAP1000 at Lufeng, but these three units are not listed by the IAEA.
If these units are taken into account, the number of reactors under construction in China – including Zhaoyuan-1 and Sanao-3 – is now 34, with 18 being Hualong One designs.
An aerial view of the Zhangzhou nuclear power station site in eastern China. Courtesy CNEA/CNNC.

title: Anfield Energy Applies For State Approval To Restart JD-8 Uranium Mine
author: David Dalton
text: Application comes as Washington attempts to bolster supply
Anfield Energy has applied for state approval to restart its past-producing JD-8 uranium and vanadium mine in Colorado, positioning the company to restart production in the second half of 2026.
The JD-8 uranium and vanadium project has been inactive due to poor market conditions, which made production uneconomic.

The application by the Canada-based company comes as the Trump administration intensifies efforts to bolster US energy security by cutting reliance on imported uranium and revitalising the nuclear sector.
Federal support for restarting reactors and accelerating permits for new uranium projects has increased amid rising power demand linked to AI-related data centres and other infrastructure.
“This permitting milestone for JD-8 is a pivotal step in Anfield's strategy to help restore US uranium production capacity,” said Anfield chief executive officer Corey Dias.
The high-grade site is backed by the Shootaring Canyon Mill, one of only three licensed conventional uranium mills in the US.

In May, the Trump administration approved Anfield’s proposed Velvet-Wood uranium mine project in Utah, after a rapid 14-day environmental review as part of a new process to fast-track permitting of energy and mining projects.

On Tuesday, the Trump administration said it had lent Constellation Energy
$1bn (€862m) to restart a nuclear reactor at the Pennsylvania plant formerly known as Three Mile Island, now renamed as the Crane Clean Energy Center. In 1979 Three Mile Island was the site of the most serious commercial nuclear power accident in US history.
Anfield Energy’s Shootaring Canyon Mill is one of three licensed, permitted and constructed conventional uranium mills in the country. Courtesy Anfield Energy.

title: US Nuclear Company Becomes ‘First Ever Startup’ To Achieve Cold Criticality
author: David Dalton
text: Valar Atomics part of federal programme to deploy advanced reactor by 4 July 2026
Startup Valar Atomics said it has achieved cold criticality – an essential nuclear milestone – with the help of one of the country’s top nuclear laboratories.
The California-based company, which recently announced it had secured a $130m (€112m) funding round, claims that it is the first nuclear startup to create a critical fission reaction.

Valar Atomics said approach-to-criticality operations began at Los Alamos National Laboratory’s National Criticality Experiments Research Center at the Nevada National Security Site on 12 November and zero-power criticality was achieved at 11:45 local time on 17 November.

Zero-power criticality, or “cold criticality”, is the foundational milestone which precedes nuclear operation with power. It is a self-sustaining chain reaction of uranium-235 within a nuclear core, but without reaching full operating temperatures or actively removing heat with a working fluid.

Zero-power criticality allows Valar to gain a greater understanding of the neutronic characteristics of the core and verify assumptions about fuel, moderators, active reactivity control and burnable poisons.
Project Nova (Nuclear Observations of Valar Atomics), a collaboration between LANL and Valar Atomics, is a series of criticality experiments on a Haleu Triso-fuelled core.
Haleu-Triso is a type of advanced nuclear fuel for high-temperature reactors that combines Haleu (high-assay low-enriched uranium) with Triso (tristructural-isotropic) particle fuel technology.

The campaign builds on earlier work with LANL, including the Deimos critical assembly in 2024, which established the core test geometry and instrumentation approach used as the foundation for Nova. The central portion of the Nova core was built by Valar Atomics.
Experiments will continue over the coming weeks to evaluate the neutronic behaviour and key performance characteristics of Valar Atomic’s Ward 250 High-Temperature Gas Reactor (HTGR) design.

HTGRs are a type of gas-cooled nuclear reactor which use uranium fuel and graphite moderation to produce very high reactor core output temperatures. According to the International Atomic Energy Agency, interest in HTGRs is increasing because they can provide efficient and cost-effective electricity and produce high-temperature process heat usable for various industrial applications.

Valar Atomics was one of 11 companies chosen in August for a federally backed nuclear reactor pilot programme that will see the US Department of Energy initially work with 11 advanced reactor projects to move their technologies towards deployment.
The goal is to build, operate and achieve criticality of at least three test reactors using the DOE authorisation process by 4 July 2026.
In October it was one of four nuclear technology companies chosen by the DOE to take part in a new pilot programme to develop advanced nuclear fuel production lines.
Los Alamos National Laboratory’s National Criticality Experiments Research Center in Nevada. Courtesy LANL.

title: X-energy Begins Vertical Construction for First-In-US Advanced Nuclear Fuel Fabrication Facility
author: David Dalton
text: Tennessee plant will produce around 700,000 Triso fuel pebbles each year
X-energy announced the start of vertical construction for its TX-1 fuel fabrication facility in Oak Ridge, Tennessee.
The Maryland, US-based company said the facility will be the first of its kind in the US and will manufacture the company’s proprietary Triso fuel for its commercial reactors.

X-energy subsidiary Triso-X recently selected Clark Construction Group for a $48.2m (€41.8m) award as part of the US Department of Energy’s Advanced Reactor Demonstration Program (ARDP) to complete vertical construction. ARDP funding provides up to 50% cost sharing with X-energy for their Xe-100 Advanced Reactor Demonstration Project, including construction of the TX-1 fuel fabrication facility.

The group will start building the shell of the 214,812 sq ft (19,900 sq m) facility that will be used to fabricate around 700,000 Triso fuel pebbles each year, which is enough fuel for 11 Xe-100 small modular reactors.

TX-1 will be the first of two facilities planned for the site to fabricate the company’s ceramic fuel designed to withstand extreme temperatures and retain fission products under all reactor conditions.
In addition to ARDP funding, the US Department of Energy also awarded X-energy $9m in 2018 to support the initial design of the company's fuel fabrication facility that later evolved into TX-1.

Triso-X anticipates regulatory approval by May 2026 and recently received approval from the DOE to spend an additional $30m to secure long-lead procurement items to adhere to the overall project schedule.

Operations are projected to start the following year with the initial fuel production supporting X-energy’s first commercial reactor, a proposed four-unit plant in partnership with Dow Chemical Company at their chemical plant in Seadrift, Texas.
The proposed Long Mott Generating Station at Seadrift would be the first advanced nuclear facility to power an industrial site in the US.
The facility will be the first of its kind in the US and will manufacture X-energy’s proprietary Triso fuel. Courtesy X-energy.

title: Washington Reaches Initial Deal With Saudi Arabia on Nuclear Sharing
author: David Dalton
text: Agreement could open kingdom to US companies
US negotiations with Saudi Arabia on a nuclear technology-sharing deal have been completed, potentially opening the door for US companies to build power reactors in the kingdom.

Energy secretary Chris Wright and his Saudi Arabian counterpart signed a joint declaration signifying the talks were finished, the Trump administration said on 18 November, following a White House visit by the kingdom’s Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.

The White House said the deal builds the legal foundation for a decades-long, multi-billion-dollar nuclear energy partnership with Saudi Arabia and confirms that “the United States and American companies will be the Kingdom’s civil nuclear cooperation partners of choice”.
A formal 123 agreement, which customarily includes non-proliferation requirements, has yet to be signed, a US Department of Energy said.
