A 123 agreement refers to Section 123 of the US Atomic Energy Act of 1954 and is required to permit the US government and US companies to work with entities in the kingdom to develop a civil nuclear industry.
The act specifies nine non-proliferation criteria a state must meet to keep it from using the technology to develop nuclear arms or transfer sensitive materials to others.

Progress on the discussions had previously been difficult because Saudi Arabia did not want to sign a deal that would rule out the possibility of enriching uranium or reprocessing spent fuel – both potential paths to a bomb.
Bin Salman has long said that if Iran developed a nuclear weapon, Saudi Arabia would follow suit.

Saudi Arabia, the world’s largest oil exporter, is seeking to generate substantial renewable energy and reduce emissions, under the crown prince’s Vision 2030 reform plan. At least some of this is expected to come from nuclear energy.
The White House said the deal builds the legal foundation for a decades-long, multi-billion-dollar nuclear energy partnership with Saudi Arabia. Courtesy US Government.

title: Governor ‘Ready To Give Approval’ For Kashiwazaki Kariwa Restart
author: David Dalton
text: According to reports, Unit 6 at facility could be first to go back online
The governor of Niigata Prefecture in western Japan is set to give approval as early as this week for the restart of the Kashiwazaki Kariwa nuclear power station, local media reported on 19 November.
The approval will clear the final hurdle in Tokyo Electric Power Company’s (Tepco) bid to bring the facility back online, more than a decade after the Fukushima disaster led to its shutdown.
Earlier reports said Tepco would focus on restarting Unit 6 at the seven-unit facility. Fuel loading at Unit 6 was completed in June.
Press reports have also said Tepco will bring forward a decision on the fate of other units at Kashiwazaki Kariwa after restarting Unit 6.

Kashiwazaki Kariwa is one of the world’s largest nuclear power stations. According to the International Atomic Energy Agency, its seven boiling water reactor units have a combined net capacity of 7,965 MW.
Kashiwazaki Kariwa served as an important energy source to supply electricity to the Tokyo metropolitan area before the 2011 earthquake and nuclear accident at Fukushima-Daiichi.
Tepco wants to bring the station back online and said in 2020 it was concentrating its resources on restarting the newer Units 6 and 7, which originally began commercial operation in 1996 and 1997.
Units 6 and 7, both 1,315-MW boiling water reactor units, have been offline since March 2012 and August 2011 respectively.
Kashiwazaki Kariwa is one of the world’s largest nuclear power stations. Courtesy Tepco.

title: US Introduces Bill To Boost Nuclear Manufacturing Through Tax Credits
author: Nigel Davies
text: Bipartisan bill would apply to components for fusion reactors

Democrat and Republican senators have joined forces in the US to introduce the Fusion Advanced Manufacturing Parity Act, which would give nuclear fusion energy manufacturers access to tax credits of 25%.

The bill would extend the federal advanced manufacturing credit to US manufacturers of fusion components including superconducting magnets, high-voltage capacitors, fusion heating systems and plasma vacuum vessels.
Components manufactured domestically would be eligible for the 25% tax credit until 2031, after which time credits would be gradually cut until 2034.
The bill also updates the federal critical minerals list to include those required for fusion manufacturing, including deuterium, tritium, helium-3, lithium compounds, tungsten and vanadium.

The bipartisan bill was introduced by Democrat senator for Washington Maria Cantwell, a senior member of the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources, and Republican senator John Curtis. Accompanying legislation has also been introduced in the House.

“Fusion energy represents the kind of bold, American innovation that built the West and can power our future,” said Cantwell. “This bill ensures we’re not just competing in the fusion race, we’re winning it by manufacturing these critical components here at home, creating good-paying jobs and securing our energy independence for the next century."

The manufacturing credit was originally introduced under the Biden administration aimed at spurring growth in the renewables industry for components such as solar panels and wind turbines, which was terminated by president Trump. However, the credit remains active for other components.

A recent report said China is rapidly advancing its fusion energy capabilities through massive state investments and aggressive technological development and without decisive action the US risks falling behind.
The report said US leadership in fusion is not just a matter of scientific progress – it is a geopolitical necessity to maintain technological supremacy and ensure national security.
Trump signed a raft of executive orders in May 2025 aimed at expediting reactor approvals, boosting US uranium production and enrichment capacity, and boosting nuclear technologies.
Under those orders, the Department of Energy was instructed to build 10 large reactors by 2030 as well as upgrade existing facilities.
A nuclear fusion facility at the Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory in California. Courtesy LLNL.

title: Belarus To Build Third Nuclear Unit At Existing Site And Start Surveys For Second Station
author: David Dalton
text: Mogilev Oblast in east of country a potential location for new capacity

Belarus has decided to build a third nuclear unit at the Belarusian nuclear power station site and will also start surveys for a second station, state news agency BelTA reported deputy prime minister Viktar Karankevich as saying.
BelTA said Karankevich made the announcement following a meeting with president Alexander Lukashenko on the development of nuclear energy.

The government aid Belarus need for new capacity and studies had been carried out to decide whether that would be in the form of a new unit at the Belarusian power station, near Ostrovets in northwest Belarus, or at a new site in the east of the country.

Lukashenko, according to an account of the meeting on the president’s website, said the option of building a third unit at the existing site had the benefits of an already approved site as well as a skilled workforce and the necessary social infrastructure.
“The ground conditions there have already been thoroughly studied. There is no need for any additional surveys,” he was reported as saying.

Vice-premier Viktor Karankevich said the decision to go ahead with the third unit at the Belarusian site would also be matched by work to survey potential locations in Mogilev Oblast, in the east of the country, with the possibility of more new capacity in that region if energy demand supports it.
During the meeting, the performance of the existing nuclear power plant was reviewed, more than four years after the first unit came online.

Lukashenko said: “The construction of the nuclear power plant not only strengthened our energy security, but also determined the further development of Belarus as a high-tech state… we have provided ourselves with a source of affordable, environmentally friendly energy for decades to come, and have achieved an economic and environmental effect.”
Belarusian-1 became the country’s first nuclear power plant to begin commercial operation in June 2021 after being connected to the grid in November 2020.
Unit 2 of the Russia-backed project began commercial operation in November 2023.

The two pressurised water reactor units at Belarusian are both Russia-supplied 1,110-MW VVER V-491 plants. According to the International Atomic Energy Agency, the two plants provided a 36.4% share of Belarus’s electricity generation in 2024.

Belarus's energy mix is dominated by natural gas, which is the primary fuel for electricity generation, accounting for over 64% of total generation in 2023. Nuclear energy is the second-largest source.
There are two Russia-supplied nuclear units in operation at the Belarusian station. Courtesy Rosatom.

title: Clean Core’s Export Licence ‘A Milestone’ In Development Of Thorium As Alternative To Uranium
author: Rachel Rigby
text: US company says nuclear fuel is on ‘fast track to realisation’

The recent granting of a Part 810 export licence for US-based Clean Core Thorium Energy (CCTE) is a major step towards closer cooperation with India on nuclear energy and marks a milestone in the development of thorium as an alternative to uranium for fuelling nuclear reactors, CCTE’s chief operating officer told NucNet.
Milan Shah said thorium as a fuel for nuclear power plants has made huge progress and is on “a fast track to realisation”.

He said the Part 810 licence for exports to India marks a turning point, not just for Clean Core but for the US-India civil nuclear partnership. “It places thorium at the centre of the global energy transformation,” he said.
A Part 810 licence is issued by the US Department of Energy and controls the export of nuclear technical data and assistance.

The licence means CCTE can transfer its thorium fuel to end users in India including the Department of Atomic Energy, Nuclear Power Corporation of India Limited, and the Atomic Energy Regulatory Board.

Thorium has long been seen as a good alternative to uranium because it is more abundant, produces both smaller amounts of long-lived radioactive waste and reduces the risk that materials from the fuel cycle will be diverted into weapons manufacturing.

Pressurised heavy-water reactors (PHWRs) are particularly well-suited for thorium because heavy water absorbs very few neutrons, preserving a high neutron economy. This allows more neutrons to be available for the conversion of thorium-232 into uranium-233, improving the efficiency of a thorium fuel cycle.

According to data from the International Atomic Energy Agency, there are 46 PHWRs operating worldwide: 17 in Canada, 19 in India, three each in Argentina and South Korea, and two each in China and Romania.
India is bullish on thorium reactors and has set out a three-stage development plan for nuclear power that involves eventually phasing thorium into the fuel cycle for its fleet.

CCTE has ambitions to go beyond PHWRs. Within two years, it plans to design a version of its fuel that could work in the light-water reactors that make up most of the world’s fleet, including the entire US fleet of 94 reactors.

CCTE’s nuclear fuel is called as ANEEL, a patented thorium-based fuel that combines thorium with high-assay low-enriched uranium (Haleu). It is designed to produce less waste, improve safety, and be resistant to proliferation.
In February, the privately-held, Chicago-based company raised a $15.5m (€13.3m) Series Seed round of financing to advance Aneel fuel.
Before ANEEL fuel can enter the marketplace, CCTE must prove its performance and safety to industry and regulators.
The company has been testing the fuel at the Idaho National Laboratory, one of the few places with the expertise and capabilities to properly qualify their design at an accelerated rate.

In August CCTE said the fuel continues to surpass burnup rate records, surpassing the capabilities of conventional nuclear fuels used in PHWRs. The burnup rate is a measure of how much energy is extracted from nuclear fuel, indicating how much of it has been used in a reactor. A higher burnup rate signifies that more energy has been produced from a given amount of fuel.
Clean Core’s ANEEL nuclear fuel pellets. ANEEL is a patented thorium-based fuel that combines thorium with high-assay low-enriched uranium. Courtesy Clean Core.

title: Westinghouse Signs Pilot Contract To Supply Nuclear Fuel For Hungary’s Paks
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Move part of European nation’s plans to diversify sources
US-based Westinghouse Electric Company has signed a pilot contract with Hungary’s state-owned MVM Group for the supply of nuclear fuel for the Paks nuclear power station, a statement said.
Under the contract, Westinghouse will provide fuel for the Russia-designed VVER-440 pressurised water reactor units at Paks.
Westinghouse said deliveries are scheduled to begin in 2028 following completion of the necessary licensing procedures. The company said the fuel will be manufactured in its Europe-based facilities.
MVM Group chief executive Karoly Matrai said the contract with Westinghouse is “is a clear response to today's energy challenges” and called it a “strategically important step.”
“The diversified fuel procurement reduces external exposures, provides predictability and affordable energy for families and corporate customers,” he said.

Westinghouse has already supplied its VVER-440 fuel to Ukraine’s Rivne nuclear power plant, Finland’s Loviisa plant, and the Czech Republic’s Dukovany facility. The company also provides VVER-1000 fuel to units in Bulgaria, Ukraine, and the Czech Republic.

The Paks fuel contract with Westinghouse comes after a meeting last week between US president Donald Trump and Hungarian prime minister Viktor Orban, which included discussion around Budapest’s dependence on Russian oil and its use of Russian nuclear fuel.
According to a statement by the US Department of State, Hungary had agreed to buy fuel for Unit 1 of the Paks nuclear station under a contract valued at about $114m (€98m)
Hungary’s four VVER-440 reactors at Paks, which provide about half of the country’s electricity generation, are currently fuelled by Russia’s Tvel under a long-term supply contract.
Budapest has been among the last European Union member states to take steps to diversify nuclear fuel sources in line with the bloc’s REPowerEU roadmap target set for the end of 2027.
The reactor hall at the Paks nucear power station in Hungary. Courtesy Paks NPP.

title: South Korea’s Regulator Approves Continued Operation Of Kori-2 Nuclear Plant
author: David Dalton
text: Asian nation says nuclear will help it meet AI ambitions
South Korea's Nuclear Safety and Security Commission (NSSC) has approved the continued operation of Unit 2 at the Kori nuclear power station until 2033, reports in the Asian nation said.
The 640-MW pressurised water reactor unit, near Busan in the southeast of the country, has been offline since April 2023, when its original 40-year operating permit expired.
Owner and operator Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power (KHNP) submitted a safety assessment report and applied for a permit for the plant’s continued operation in April 2022.
The Chosun Daily said the NSSC voted on the proposal at a meeting on the 13 November, passing it with five votes in favour and one against.
KHNP said it plans to restart Kori-2 in February 2026 after completing facility improvements and confirming safety through regular inspections by regulatory agencies.

South Korea’s environment minister said recently that nuclear power will remain part of the country’s energy mix while the government works to rapidly reduce coal, oil and natural gas as part of its efforts to tackle climate change.
Moon Jae-in, who served as president from 2017 to 2022, oversaw a nuclear phaseout policy that drew fierce resistance from industry and labour unions.
Yoon Suk Yeol, who served from 2022 until he was impeached and removed from office in 2025, reversed that policy, resuming construction of nuclear reactors and planning to expand nuclear output.
When Lee Jae-myung was elected president in June 2025, his administration said it would re-examine the role of nuclear energy.

Data from majority state-owned Korea Electric Power Corporation (Kepco) showed that generation from the nation’s 26 commercial nuclear power plants grew 8.7% year-on-year in the first half of 2025, three times the forecast annual growth of 2.9%. Over the same period, coal-fired output fell by 16%.
The 1,340-MW Shin-Hanul-2 nuclear plant southeast of Seoul came online in April 2024. A twin unit, Shin-Hanul-1, began commercial operation in December 2022.
South Korea has two APR-1400 plants under construction at the Saeul nuclear station, formerly known as Shin-Kori.
The previous government also wanted to complete construction of two additional delayed plants – Units 3 and 4 – at Shin-Hanul.

The Chosun Daily said the government, which has set a goal of becoming one of the world’s top three AI powers, has judged that extending the operation of existing nuclear reactors is essential to meet rapidly increasing electricity demand.
The Kori nuclear power station. Image courtesy Creative Commons (CC BY-SA 2.0)

title: Vattenfall Signs €36 Million Investment And Collaboration Agreement On New Nuclear In Sweden
author: David Dalton
text: Up to five small modular reactors being planned for existing Ringhals site

Swedish state-owned power company Vattenfall and the industrial consortium Industrikraft have signed an agreement for joint investment and collaboration that will enable the next steps in a project to deploy new nuclear power in Sweden.
Vattenfall said in a statement that Industrikraft will become a 20% shareholder in the nuclear project company Videberg Kraft and invest SEK400m (€36m, $42m) in the project.

Vattenfall and Industrikraft, formed in June 2024 to support the expansion of Swedish non-fossil fuel electricity supply, will work on the deployment of small modular reactors (SMRs) at Vattenfall’s existing Ringhals nuclear site on the Värö Peninsula, southwest Sweden.
The agreement covers areas such as responsibilities and financing. Industrikraft will contribute resources, expertise in project management and selection of technologies.
Other companies involved in the project include  ABB, Alfa Laval, Boliden, Hitachi Energy, Höganäs AB, SSAB, Saab, Stora Enso and the Volvo Group.
Vattenfall said Swedish technology has a role to play in driving the development of a strong supplier cluster in Europe.
In August Vattenfall said it will proceed with US-based GE Vernova (GEV) and British company Rolls-Royce SMR as it looks to choose a potential supplier for new nuclear power plants next to Ringhals.
Vattenfall said at the time final investment decisions will be made “later in the process”.

It said both companies offer SMRs with proven technology and simplified designs that have integrated learnings from previous nuclear projects worldwide. Both use fuel for which Vattenfall has established supply chains.
GEV’s technology is the 300-MW BWRX-300. Construction of the first BWRX-300 unit is underway at Ontario Power Generation’s Darlington nuclear site near Toronto in Canada.
Rolls-Royce SMR is developing a 470-MW unit. The company has been selected by the British government as the preferred bidder to develop SMRs for the UK.
Vattenfall is planning a project with either five BWRX-300 plants for a total capacity of 1,500 MW or three Rolls-Royce SMR plants for 1,410 MW.

The company also said it is already looking at the next step to build an additional 1,000 MW of SMR capacity at the Ringhals site, where two large-scale reactors are in operation and two have been permanently shut down.

The company said building a series of smaller units as opposed to single, large-scale reactors, brings clear cost advantages. SMRs require less space, need significantly fewer personnel, and lead to more manageable logistics.
The Ringhals site, where two large-scale reactors are in operation and two have been permanently shut down. Courtesy Vattenfall/Annika Ornborg.
Anna Borg, president and chief executive officer of Vattenfall, and Tom Erixon, chairman of Industrikraft. Courtesy Vattenfall.

title: Greece Sees Significant Increase In Public Support For Nuclear Energy
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Prime minister has signalled potential shift in policy

Public support for nuclear energy in Greece has increased significantly over the past seven years, according to a survey published by Athens-based Athlos Energy in collaboration with research company MARC S.A.
The survey, conducted in October, found that 30% of respondents are in favour of using nuclear energy in Greece, compared with only 18% in 2018.
Opposition has dropped from 75% to 42.8%, while 21.2% of respondents remain undecided, according to the survey.

The results could indicate a gradual softening of public attitudes toward nuclear energy, which has never been part of Greece’s electricity generation mix. Greeks have traditionally maintained an anti-nuclear attitude because of by public concern following the 1986 Chernobyl accident and by its geographic proximity to nuclear plants in neighbouring Balkan countries.

Athlos Energy, the first Greek startup specialising in the nuclear sector, said the findings point to “mature conditions for an evidence-based public dialogue” on the role of nuclear in meeting climate and energy goals.
The results of the survey showed that climate concerns are particularly high, with 85% of respondents expressing worry about global warming.
However, nearly half (47.5%) incorrectly believe nuclear power plants emit carbon dioxide, and only a quarter classify nuclear as a “green” form of energy.
About half said they would back the use of nuclear technologies in shipping or floating plants, reflecting interest in non-electric applications of nuclear power.
The bulk of Greece’s electricity is generated from natural gas, followed by renewables, but the country also traditionally imports electricity from Bulgaria, a nuclear power operator.
In 2022, Greece was among countries that dropped their opposition to the inclusion of nuclear energy in the EU’s sustainable finance taxonomy and its delegated acts.

In June, Greek prime minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis opened the door to a shift in policy that could see the country develop nuclear energy for the first time as part of its energy transition strategy, the Greek daily Kathimerini reported.
Athens has hinted it is interested nuclear technology in its search for low-carbon baseload power. Courtesy Greek National Tourism Organisation.

title: Ohio Launches $100 Million Energy Fund To Help Boost Nuclear Power Projects
author: Nigel Davies
text: Fund will support small modular reactor generation and creation of nuclear centre of excellence

The US state of Ohio has launched a $100m (€86m) five-year JobsOhio Energy Opportunity Initiative providing companies with grants and low-interest loans for the development of natural gas and nuclear power production projects in the state.

The initiative was announced by Ohio governor Mike DeWine at a business conference and will in part be used to attract supply chain companies for the growth of small modular reactor (SMRs) manufacturing and for the creation of a nuclear energy centre of excellence.

“To continue Ohio’s growth and to create jobs, we must focus on energy,” said DeWine. “Ohio must have an energy policy that ensures we have the supply we need for current and future demand, which will help keep costs reasonable.”
JobsOhio, a non-profit economic development corporation for the state, said the initiative was based on four pillars:
DeWine also said at the announcement of the Initiative that the funding fits with ongoing legislative work to accelerate natural gas and nuclear power capacities in the state.

In September, Centrus Energy
laid out plans for a ‘multi-billion-dollar’ expansion of its uranium enrichment plant in Piketon, Ohio, boosting production of low-enriched uranium and high-assay, low-enriched uranium (Haleu) – a higher-enriched fuel needed for many advanced reactor designs.
The company said the project would create around 1,000 construction jobs, and 300 permanent operations jobs.
The Statehouse in Columbus, capital of Ohio. Courtesy MJ/Creative Commons Licence.

title: Nuclear Energy Seeing ‘Revival In Fortunes’ That Could See Reactor Capacity Grow By 70%
author: David Dalton
text: Technology sector supporting emergence of new business models, says IEA

Nuclear energy is experiencing a revival in fortunes with investment rising in both traditional large-scale plants and new designs, including small modular reactors (SMRs), and capacity set to increase by at least one-third to 2035 – and potentially by as much as 70%, according to a new report.
The International Energy Agency’s (IEA) World Energy Outlook 2025 says more than 40 countries now include nuclear energy in their strategies and are taking steps to develop new projects.

The report says that after more than two decades of stagnation, installed nuclear capacity could expand by as such as 70% by 2035 in its Net Zero Emissions by 2050 scenario, which maps out a pathway to achieve specific energy and climate-related goals. Under less ambitious scenarios nuclear capacity is forecast to increase by one third.
In addition to reactors that are restarting operation, notably in Japan, there are more than 70 GW of new capacity under construction, one of the highest levels in 30 years.
Technology companies are supporting the emergence of new business models, with agreements and expressions of interest for 30 GW of SMRs, mainly to power data centres.

In recent months, technology companies and utilities have announced deals to extend the lifetime of existing nuclear plants. Google and US reactor developer Kairos Power have signed the first power purchase agreement for a demonstration small modular reactor to power a data centre.
In the report’s “stated policies scenario”, or Steps, nuclear power provides 190 TWh of additional electricity for data centres by 2035.

The report warns that nuclear power experienced significant delays and cost overruns in recent years for largescale reactors in Europe and the US, which on average have been completed eight years later than planned and cost 2.5-times as much as originally estimated. However, some nuclear projects have been completed closer to original timelines and cost estimates in other countries, including China, Russia and South Korea.

The IEA said countries around the world are contending with pressing energy security threats and growing longer-term risks across an unprecedented range of fuels and technologies, thrusting energy into the heart of geopolitical tensions and elevating it as a core issue of economic and national security.

It said a group of emerging economies – led by India and Southeast Asia and joined by countries in the Middle East, Africa and Latin America – comes to increasingly shape energy market dynamics in the years ahead.

Collectively, they take up the baton from China, which accounted for half of global oil and gas demand growth and 60% of electricity demand growth since 2010, although no country or group of countries comes close to replicating China’s energy-intensive rise.
The Barakah nuclear power station in the United Arab Emirates. Courtesy Enec.

title: Turkey Acknowledges Concern Over Reliance On Russia For Akkuyu Nuclear Fuel
author: David Dalton
text: Ankara in discussions on new reactor projects with alternative suppliers
The Turkish government has acknowledged its dependence on Russia for uranium fuel at the Akkuyu nuclear power station, reports said.
According to Nordic Monitor the admission reflects both growing discomfort in Ankara and a wider effort to rebalance relations toward the West.

Energy minister Alparslan Bayraktar told parliament’s budget committee on 7 November that Turkey relies entirely on Russia’s state-owned nuclear corporation Rosatom for the uranium that will power Akkuyu, its first commercial nuclear power.
According to Nordic Monitor Bayraktar’s remarks marked the first official recognition that Moscow, already Turkey’s main natural gas supplier, also controls the country’s nuclear fuel chain.

“Will there be uranium dependence? Yes,” Bayraktar said. “To overcome this dependence, we are talking about fuel cooperation both with the country we are currently working with and with others we are discussing new projects with.”
Russia is supplying four VVER-1200 pressurised water reactor units for Akkuyu, on the Mediterranean coast in the southern province of Mersin.

Ankara has previously said it was in talks with Russia, China, Canada and South Korea on the second and third stations it plans to build at Sinop and Igneada. Sinop is on the Black Sea in northern Turkey and Igneada is in Thrace, also on the Black Sea, not far from the Bulgarian border.
Turkey’s president Recep Tayyip Erdoğan has discussed cooperation on both small and large reactors with the US, Canada and France, Bayraktar recently told broadcaster CNN Türk.
The Akkuyu nuclear station contruction site in Turkey. Courtesy Akkuyu NPP.

title: Fluor And NuScale Announce Agreement Regarding Stake Monetisation
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Texas-based Fluor has been largest shareholder in reactor company during Voygr SMR design

US engineering group Fluor Corporation has reached an agreement with NuScale Power Corporation to convert and monetise its remaining ownership stake in the US-based small modular reactor (SMR) developer, a joint statement said.

Under the deal, Fluor aims to fully monetise its stake in NuScale by the end of the second quarter of 2026, converting its remaining Class B units in NuScale into Class A shares and then beginning a structured monetisation of shares, guided by mutually agreed volume restrictions to maintain the value of NuScale’s equity.

According to NuScale past filings with the US Securities and Exchange Commission, Class B units represent non-public ownership interests that carry limited voting but no economic rights within the limited-liability company NuScale Power, which preceded NuScale Power Corporation. Class A common stock is publicly traded equity listed on the stock exchange.
Converting the shares allows Fluor to sell its holdings on the open market, a process known as monetisation, meaning it will gradually realise cash value from its investment.

Fluor has also agreed to support NuScale’s planned share-count increase, reduce its economic rights under a tax receivable agreement, and waive certain commercial claims between the two firms. In return, NuScale committed to temporary limits on new equity issuances until February 2026 to maintain market stability.
The transaction follows months of negotiations between Fluor and NuScale’s board, including a special committee established to oversee the discussions, the companies said.
Texas-based Fluor first invested in NuScale in 2011 and has been its largest shareholder and engineering partner during the development of the company’s 77-MW Voygr SMR modular design.
Last month, Fluor said it had sold 15 million converted Class A shares in NuScale, which generated net proceeds of about $605m (€523m). The shares were converted in August 2025.

Fluor said it used most of the proceeds to support its share repurchase programme and continued to hold about 111 million Class B units and associated Class B shares, representing roughly 39% of NuScale’s equity.
In August NuScale chief executive officer John Hopkins said the company aimed to have “hard contracts” with “two or three major customers” by the end of 2025.

Hopkins’ comments came as the company reported a significant jump in expenses in its Q2 2025 earnings update. It attributed the change to “higher business development costs associated with NuScale’s transition from a research and development-based company to a commercial company”.
NuScale has been developing the 77-MW Voygr small modular reactor design. Courtesy NuScale.

title: South Africa’s Koeberg-2 Gets Green Light To Operate For Additional 20 Years
author: David Dalton
text: Nation recently announced plans for additional nuclear capacity, including SMRs

South Africa’s nuclear regulator has approved operation of the 930-MW Koeberg-2 unit near Cape Town for a further 20 years of operation until 9 November 2045, state power company and nuclear operator Eskom said.

Eskom said the National Nuclear Regulator (NNR) approved the licence extension following detailed safety assessments, technical reviews and infrastructure upgrades as part of the station’s long-term operation (LTO) programme.

“The approval marks a significant step in strengthening South Africa’s long-term energy security and reflects Eskom’s commitment to maintaining world-class nuclear safety standards,” a statement said.

NNR board chairperson Protas Phili said: “This licence approval was granted after a rigorous safety assessment which confirmed that all regulatory requirements for the period of long-term operation have been met for Unit 2 and relevant public representations were considered in the decision-making process.”

The two-unit Koeberg is the only operating commercial nuclear power plant on the African continent, although units are under construction at El Dabaa in Egypt and a number of other African nations have expressed an interest in reactor deployment.
Unit 1 at Koeberg began commercial operation in July 1984 and Unit 2 in November 1985. Both units have undergone extensive maintenance and upgrades to enable their long-term operation.
Unit 2 was reconnected to the grid on 30 December 2024 after the completion of extensive maintenance to extend its operational lifespan by an additional 20 years.
In July 2024 the NNR gave Eskom permission to operate the 924-MW Unit 1 for an additional 20 years until July 2044.
South Africa has said it plans to revive its small modular nuclear reactor project and increase nuclear generation.
The two-unit Koeberg is the only commercially operating nuclear station in Africa. Courtesy Eskom.

title: Hungary To Buy US Nuclear Fuel And Move Forward On Plans For Small Modular Reactors
author: David Dalton
text: Washington pushing Budapest to reduce reliance on Russia for supplies to Paks reactors
Hungary is to sign a nuclear cooperation agreement with Washington including the purchase of US nuclear fuel and a deal on plans to deploy small modular reactors (SMRs) in the European country.

The deal will be signed when US president Donald Trump meets Hungarian prime minister Viktor Orban on 7 November. The two leaders are expected to discuss Hungarian dependence on Russian oil and its use of Russian nuclear fuel.

“We will sign an important intergovernmental agreement on nuclear energy cooperation with my fellow foreign minister, Marco Rubio,” said Hungarian foreign minister Péter Szijjártó, adding he had told International Atomic Energy Agency director-general Rafael Grossi about the upcoming discussions.
Hungary is one of the few European Union countries to maintain close ties with Moscow since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and is reluctant to reduce its dependence on Russian energy.
Trump is a supporter of the right-wing leader Orban, but has called on European countries to reduce energy ties with Moscow and buy more energy from the US.

Hungary is diversifying its nuclear fuel supply to supplement its reliance on Russian fuel. Starting in 2027, French company Framatome will supply fuel for the reactors at Paks, and Hungary has also signed contracts with Westinghouse for future supplies.
Szijjártó said that as part of a “major economic and energy cooperation package” Hungary would buy US nuclear fuel for Paks.
“In addition to maintaining existing supplier relations, for the first time in Hungarian energy history, we will also buy American nuclear fuel,” said Szijjártó.
Paks, near the town of Paks, about 100 km south of Budapest, is Hungary’s only commercial nuclear facility and has four Russia-supplied reactors that came online in the 1980s.
Hungary will also buy US technology for the storage of used nuclear fuel at Paks, Szijjártó said, without giving details.
The agreement will include plans to deploy SMRs in Hungary, he said.
Szijjártó said earlier this year that Hungary would begin preliminary work to prepare for the introduction of US SMR technology.

Those comments came as Poland-based nuclear project developer Synthos Green Energy and Hungary’s nuclear technology company Hunatom signed a letter of intent to assess the deployment of GE Vernova Hitachi Nuclear Energy BWRX-300 SMRs in Hungary.
Hungary is also working with Moscow to build two new Generation III+ VVER-1200 pressurised water reactor units at the Paks site.
The project, led by Hungary’s Russian partner, the state nuclear corporation Rosatom, has seen a number of legal challenges and significant delays in recent years.

This week the Hungarian Atomic Energy Authority said it had issued a partial permit for soil stabilisation works on the nuclear island for the first of two new reactor units at Paks, potentially paving the way for the pouring of first concrete early next year.
The reactor hall at the Paks nuclear power station in Hungary. Courtesy Paks NPP.

Hungarian foreign minister Péter Szijjártó (second right) told International Atomic Energy Agency director-general Rafael Grossi (second left) about the upcoming discussions. Courtesy Péter Szijjártó/X.

title: World Nuclear Exhibition 2025 Roundup: Urenco Announces Multi-Billion-Euro Uranium Enrichment  Deal For Nuclear Plants In France And UK
author: David Dalton
text: Company says contract is enormous step for energy security in Europe
Multinational enrichment company Urenco signed an agreement with French state-backed power company EDF to supply uranium enrichment services for nuclear power stations across France and the UK.
The chief executives of both companies, Boris Schucht and Bernard Fontana, put pen to paper on 6 November – the final day of the World Nuclear Exhibition (WNE) 2025 in Paris.
The multi-billion-euro contract will enable Urenco to support EDF’s nuclear fleet into the 2040s, contributing to the reliable and sustainable generation of electricity.

Urenco chief executive officer Boris Schucht said: “This deal represents an enormous step forward for energy security in Europe at a time when it has never been so important in the geopolitical landscape.”

Italian companies Ansaldo Energia and Ansaldo Nucleare have signed a joint declaration of intent with EDF subsidiary Nuward, marking a further step in Nuward’s programme to develop and deploy a small modular reactor (SMR). A statement said the declaration – signed at the World Nuclear Exhibition (WNE) 2025 in Paris together with Arabelle Solutions, Framatome and Tractebel – reinforces a coordinated path to accelerate Nuward’s SMR programme. The declaration follows the first collaboration agreement between Ansaldo Energia, Ansaldo Nucleare, EDF and Nuward signed in July 2023. Nuward is developing a new generation of water-cooled SMRs that will provide both electricity and heat for multiple applications such as industrial applications and district heating.

Naarea, a French startup developing a Generation IV molten salt fast neutron nuclear microreactor, signed a partnership agreement with Fluid Wire Robotics (FWR), an Italian startup specialising in the design of electric robotic systems for remote and unmanned inspection, maintenance, repair and assembly in extreme environments such as radiation, heat, underwater and vacuum. Naarea said the aim of the partnership is to provide it with safe and reliable robotic handling capabilities for its fuel production facility, and for its XAMR microreactors, in particularly during maintenance operations or dismantling.

France’s Orano group signed engineering partnerships with Ametra, Assystem and Vulcain as part of its effort to renew its nuclear fuel processing and recycling plants. The work is part of a programme known as Aval du future, which includes a fuel unloading facility and a new mixed-oxide fuel fabrication plant at the La Hague site in northern France, with commissioning scheduled for the early 2040s, and a new used fuel processing plant planned for the mid-century, as well as keeping existing facilities in operational condition. Orano director of engineering Guillaume Dureau said the company is undergoing a complete transformation to be ready to handle a project workload estimated to rise to over 10 million hours by 2030. “To rise to this challenge, we are leveraging all the resources at our disposal: recruitment, regional and local development, and, above all, stronger partnerships with recognised industry players,” Dureau said.

More than 30 European companies from the international nuclear and maritime sectors have formally signed the ‘Declaration of Cooperation for Accelerating Nuclear for Maritime Applications to meet Climate Ambitions’. One of the signatories, the testing, inspection and certification body Bureau Veritas, said the signing represents a landmark initiative uniting international stakeholders across the nuclear, maritime, research, financial and regulatory communities in a shared commitment to promote a European initiative to advance the safe and sustainable use of nuclear technologies for maritime decarbonisation. The declaration recognises the critical role of the maritime sector in achieving global climate goals and the need to transition to low-carbon energy systems. It highlights the potential of small modular reactors (SMRs) to become a safe, reliable and sustainable solution for maritime and port energy systems. Together, the signatories reaffirmed their commitment to advancing innovation in line with the France 2030 Investment Plan, which allocates €1bn ($1.15bn) to the development of innovative nuclear technologies, including SMRs.

Italy-based engineering group Maire and subsidiary Nextchem signed a memorandum of understanding with EDF and subsidiary Nuward to jointly explore opportunities for cooperation in the development and deployment of the Nuward small modular reactor (SMR) programme. Maire said the initiative aligns with its objective to collaborate with nuclear technology providers developing small and advanced modular nuclear technologies and supports Nextchem’s vision for creating low-carbon chemical production and data centre “e-factories” by integrating them with a clean, reliable energy source. Nextchem recently launched Next-N, a joint venture dedicated to developing new intellectual property for the conventional island of next-generation nuclear power plants.
The World Nuclear Exhibition in Paris, France, attracts hundreds of exhibitors. Courtesy WNE.

title: Hungary Issues Paks 2 Partial Permit As Nuclear Project Moves Towards First Concrete In Early 2026
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Approval is for soil stabilisation works at first of two planned units

The Hungarian Atomic Energy Authority (OAH) has issued a partial permit to Paks II Nuclear Power Plant for soil stabilisation works on the nuclear island for the first of two new reactor units at Paks, potentially paving the way for the pouring of first concrete early next year.

According to the OAH decision, the “partial occupancy and use permit” covers the deep soil works carried out beneath the future Paks 2-1 nuclear unit, which will be the first unit of the new Paks 2 project, but the fifth unit at the site.
The stabilised soil mass is designed to prevent soil collapse during seismic events and to improve the mechanical properties of the natural foundation.

OAH said the permit is conditional on technical and safety requirements, including the continuous operation of the site’s dewatering system, the monitoring of pore-water pressure and frost effects and the submission of updated engineering documentation before the pouring of first concrete.
The Paks II project company said OAH has also issued civil construction licences for the control building, auxiliary building and technological service building for Paks 2-1.

Under a 2014 agreement, Russian state-owned nuclear corporation Rosatom is building two VVER-1200 pressurised water reactor units next to the existing four-unit Paks station on the Danube River, about 100 km south of Budapest.

Preparatory works including pit excavations and the construction of a stabilisation groundwater cutoff wall began at Paks 2 in the summer of 2023. The main construction licence for Paks 2 was issued by OAH in August 2022.
Rosatom said in a statement that the Hungarian regulator’s permit decision can pave the way towards first concrete pouring in 2026, adding that “active preparation” for the move can begin.
Paks II said first concrete pouring, seen as the formal start of nuclear island works, is expected to take place in February 2026.

The OAH permit does not authorise the start of nuclear island concreting, but is a prerequisite for the actual construction phase. A separate permit overing the base slab pouring would still be needed once regulatory conditions are met.

In September 2025, the European Court of Justice struck down EU approval for Russia to build Paks 2, arguing that it was unclear whether the Hungarian government followed EU procurement rules when awarding Rosatom the contract without a public tender.

Judges at the Luxembourg-based court ruled on 11 September that the European Commission should have taken into consideration EU public procurement rules when it approved Budapest’s plans to subsidise the construction.
Hungary’s government has said it would continue the project as planned, but was ready to cooperate with the commission to demonstrate it had met public procurement and state aid requirements.
Concrete pouring for the first new unit could take place early in 2026. Courtesy Paks II.
Russia’s Rosatom has been contracted to build two VVER-1200 units next to the existing four-unit Paks station, about 100 km south of Budapest. Courtesy Paks II.

title: Path Cleared For Full-Scale Construction As All Financing Confirmed For Sizewell C
author: David Dalton
text: Backing demonstrates depth of support for pioneering financing model, says project company
Full-scale construction of the planned Sizewell C nuclear project in the UK is set to begin with all necessary financing now finalised and available for the two-unit facility in southeast England.

Project company Sizewell C said the planned nuclear station, which has an estimated cost of £38bn (€43bn, $49.5bn), reached financial close on 4 November, indicating that all funding will now be able to flow into the major infrastructure project.
Sizewell C concluded an equity raise this summer and has now confirmed it has secured a further £5.5bn through debt and loan arrangements.

In July Sizewell C announced the successful conclusion of a £38bn equity raise and a final investment decision. The company has now confirmed £5bn of debt raised through the BpifranceAE export credit facility and a £500m working capital facility, both sitting alongside a term loan from the National Wealth Fund, a public investment institution.
Thirteen banks have supported the £5bn debt raise and a subset of these are providing the working capital facility.
Sizewell C the backing demonstrated the depth of support for its pioneering financing model.
Sizewell C is the first nuclear power project to be financed using the UK’s Regulated Asset Base (RAB) model.

RAB is a financing mechanism for large-scale infrastructure projects that provides a guaranteed, regulated return on investment for developers during the construction and operational phases of a project.

By attracting private investment through this model, it aims to lower the cost of capital and reduce costs for consumers. Funding is secured through a levy on electricity bills, which allows consumers to contribute to the project during construction, helping to manage costs and interest on loans.

For its most recent nuclear project at Hinkley Point C the UK used a contracts for difference (CfD) model. CfD sees developers finance the entire construction cost up front, and only began receiving revenue when the station starts generating electricity.
This model led to the cancellation of potential projects, such as Hitachi’s project at Wylfa Newydd in Wales and Toshiba’s at Moorside in Cumbria.
Under the RAB scheme, private investors receive greater certainty through a lower and more reliable rate of return in the early stages of a project.

“This landmark moment sees funding for the project beginning to flow, unlocking full-scale construction of the Suffolk-based plant, which, once operational, could create savings of £2 billion a year across the future low-carbon electricity system – leading to cheaper power for consumers,” Sizewell C said.

The company, the first British-majority owned nuclear power station in decades, is backed by major investors including the UK government, La Caisse, Centrica, EDF and funds advised or managed by Amber Infrastructure Group, including International Public Partnerships and the Nuclear Liabilities Fund.

Once operational, the station’s two France-supplied EPR units will power six million homes for at least 60 years and according to the government could save the electricity system £2bn a year by cutting dependence on imported gas.
The project, majority-owned by British investors, is also expected to generate more than 10,000 skilled jobs and 1,500 apprenticeships, with 70% of contract value going to UK businesses.

The UK nuclear industry welcomed the development. Tom Greatrex, chief executive of the London-based Nuclear Industry Association, said reaching financial close for Sizewell C is a landmark moment for the UK’s clean energy future.
“It proves that new nuclear can attract significant investment – a vital step towards energy security, skilled jobs, and achieving net zero,” he said.

“The financing model used for Sizewell C is crucial to unlocking further private investment in new nuclear projects, cutting our reliance on fossil fuels, and driving an industrial revival across Britain.”

Since 2000, the UK has seen permanent reactor shutdowns at Hinkley Point A, Bradwell, Calder Hall, Hunterston, Oldbury, Sizewell, Chapelcross, Dungeness and Wylfa, leaving only nine units in commercial operation and only Hinkley Point C’s two EPRs under construction.
The UK already has two EPR units under construction at Hinkley Point C. Courtesy EDF Energy.
Once operational, Sizewell C’s two France-supplied EPR units will power six million homes for at least 60 years. Courtesy Sizewell C.

title: UK Regulator Approves Decommissioning Of Hinkley Point B Nuclear Station
author: David Dalton
text: Commercial operation at Somerset site ended in August 2022
The UK’s Office for Nuclear Regulation (ONR) has granted formal consent to EDF Energy’s project to decommission Hinkley Point B nuclear power station in Somerset, southwest England.
The decision comes after a public consultation and a detailed assessment by ONR specialist inspectors of EDF’s environmental statement and habitats regulations assessment.

The environmental statement included a detailed environmental impact assessment for the proposed decommissioning project at the site, along with mitigation measures designed to prevent or reduce any significant adverse environmental impacts.

ONR said it is satisfied that the environmental statement proposes adequate mitigation measures to address the adverse environmental impacts of the decommissioning project and considers the statement to be “complete, of the right quality, and in line with relevant good practice”.
In August 2022, Hinkley Point B reached the end of its operating life after nearly 46 years of generating electricity and moved into its defuelling phase.
The facility has two units, Hinkley Point B-1 and B-2, both advanced gas-cooled reactor units that began commercial operation in 1978 and 1976 respectively.
Both reactors have been defuelled in advance of the site moving into its decommissioning phase.

The nuclear site will later transfer from EDF to Nuclear Restoration Services (NR), a subsidiary of the Nuclear Decommissioning Authority. NRS will decommission the site, which will involve dismantling and demolishing the plant and buildings as well site clearance and restoration.
NRS is responsible for decommissioning 13 sites across the country, including the first generation of nuclear and research sites.
Hinkley Point B reached the end of its operating life in August 2022after nearly 46 years of generating electricity. Courtesy EDF Energy.

title: Illinois Passes Legislation That Will End Moratorium On New Nuclear Power Plants
author: David Dalton
text: Bill also includes provisions to encourage deployment of small modular reactors
The Illinois General Assembly has passed a clean energy bill that would, in part, lift a 30-year moratorium on new large-scale nuclear power plants in the state.

The legislation now heads to governor J B Pritzker, who is scheduled to sign it into law on 6 November. He said he looked forward to “signing this bill into law and help Illinoisans keep costs lower and keep the lights on.”
The bill passed the state Senate 37-22, and the state House 70-37.

The bill lifts the ban on new large-scale nuclear reactors starting on 1 January 2026. It follows a law that Pritzker signed in 2023 lifting the moratorium on small modular reactor (SMRs) builds in the state.
The American Nuclear Society (ANS) said the bill would encourage the building of new SMRs. It would also, however, increase fees on nuclear plant operators.

In addition, the bill includes provisions for increased battery storage, expanded energy efficiency programmes, and new planning tools to better manage energy demand and supply. The goal of the legislation is to lower electricity costs by improving grid reliability and promoting clean energy, ANS said.
Illinois boasts the highest number of utility-scale nuclear reactors in the US with 11 across six sites at Braidwood, Byron, Clinton, Dresden, LaSalle and Quad Cities.
Illinois already gets 54% of its electricity from those 11 reactors, making it one of the most nuclear reliant states in the nation.
There has been increasing interest in nuclear energy in recent years with the development of artificial intelligence and the power-hungry data centres needed to power big tech.
In June, utility Constellation and social networking company Meta signed an agreement that will support the continued operation of the Clinton nuclear power station in Illinois for another 20 years.
Constellation said the power purchase agreement will support Meta’s clean energy goals and operations in the region with 1,121 MW of nuclear energy from Clinton’s single boiling water reactor unit.

Meta’s deal with Constellation was the company’s first with a nuclear power plant. Other large tech companies are looking to secure electricity as US power demand rises significantly in part due to the needs of AI and data centres.
Constellation and Meta have signed an agreement that will support the continued operation of the Clinton nuclear power station for another 20 years. Courtesy Constellation.

title: The Haleu Race: Why The US Needs Advanced Nuclear Fuel And The Hurdles That Remain
author: NucNet Staff Writer
text: Russia dominates market, and stakes are high as Washington plays catch-up

The world’s next-generation nuclear plants depend on new technologies that are revolutionising the way reactors operate and the fuel that goes inside them. Haleu – or high-assay low-enriched uranium – is emerging into the spotlight of the US’s nuclear revival.

Earlier this year, the US Department of Energy (DOE) announced its first wave of conditional Haleu allocations. In August it followed up with a second round of commitments to three more US companies. With each announcement, the message has grown clearer: Haleu is now a strategic linchpin for advanced reactors, microreactors and small modular reactors (SMRs).

Regular uranium fuel, used by today’s light-water reactors, is enriched to about 3-5% Uranium-235 (U-235), an isotope of uranium that makes up about 0.72% of natural uranium and is important because it is fissile, meaning its nucleus can be split to release a large amount of energy. This fission process, when initiated by a neutron and allowed to create a chain reaction, is used in nuclear power plants to generate electricity and in nuclear weapons.

Haleu, by contrast, boosts that enrichment, offering reactor designers the ability to shrink reactor size, extend operating cycles, reduce refuelling frequency and unlock more compact, flexible formats.
Yet despite its importance, the US lacks a commercial Haleu-supply chain and for years most capacity has been tied to foreign sources, notably from Russia.

Recognising the need to boost the fuel supply chain in the US, the DOE launched a Haleu availability programme under the Energy Act of 2020. It aims to catalyse supply and pave the way for a commercially viable domestic fuel chain.

With the need further exacerbated by geopolitical developments – Russia is the only country currently able to supply Haleu on a commercially viable scale – the programme then began accepting requests from advanced-reactor developers and fuel-fabrication companies for Haleu allocations to meet near-term fuel needs.

The DOE allocated its first amounts of Haleu to five companies  in April, with three of them requiring fuel delivery in 2025. Three additional companies were selected for conditional commitments in August.
The DOE said the programme is ongoing and these conditional commitments mark a step toward its objective of enabling a domestic commercial Haleu capability by around 2030.
For companies designing fuel and reactors around Haleu, the allocations provide validation, but also underscore the risk of falling behind.

For example, Kairos Power’s Hermes demonstration reactor in Oak Ridge, Tennessee, is built with Haleu in mind. Kairos told NucNet that: “The US DOE Office of Nuclear Energy has conditionally agreed to commit Haleu… for the startup and operation of Kairos Power’s Hermes Low-Power Demonstration Reactor”.
Kairos has also signed a non-binding memorandum of understanding to collaborate with Urenco, a global enrichment company, to provide Haleu for its future commercial reactors.

But the company has a fallback strategy. “We are exploring alternate solutions for the interim until Haleu is more widely available,” it said, noting that its innovative reactor design can also use low-enriched uranium.

While Haleu is the ideal fuel, Kairos is pragmatic enough to plan for what comes if Haleu supply lags behind demand. The company told NucNet: “We believe multiple options exist for us to demonstrate the technology’s viability, which will send a strong customer demand signal to spur new Haleu enrichment capacity.
“We are exploring alternate solutions for the interim until Haleu is more widely available.”

US advanced reactor and fuel company X‑energy told NucNet that through its participation in the DOE’s Advanced Reactor Demonstration Program, its project at Dow’s Seadrift facility in Texas
was awarded the first allocation of Haleu. X-energy said this was “a critical step toward commercialising its Xe-100 SMR.
In contrast to Kairos Power, X-energy’s view on Haleu allocations shows that it is an imperative for development and operation. Without these allocations, the technology roadmap could stall.
An advanced reactor developer taking a different route is Oklo, a company in which OpenAI chief executive officer Sam Altman is a major investor.

The plans for Oklo’s Aurora reactor show that it will use recycled fuel. An Oklo spokesperson told NucNet: “The first core for the Aurora powerhouse at [Idaho National Laboratory] will use recovered fuel from the historic EBR-II program … and that has already been allocated”.
The EBR-II, or Experimental Breeder Reactor-II, was a sodium-cooled fast reactor designed built and operated by Argonne National Laboratory that operated from 1964 to 1994.

Oklo also plans a Haleu-capable fuel-fabrication centre. In August the company announced plans to design, build, and operate a used nuclear fuel recycling facility in Tennessee as the first phase of an advanced fuel centre. The facility will fabricate fuel for future Aurora powerhouses, which are able to run on fuel fabricated from used nuclear fuel as well as fresh Haleu.
Oklo’s dual strategy highlights a subtle but important point: domestic Haleu supply will support new reactor startups and help close the fuel-cycle loop by recycling existing used nuclear fuel.

Even with the recent Haleu allocations, industry engagement and plans for development, the path ahead is far from smooth. The scale of Haleu production is still small, planned fabrication facilities have to go through licensing processes, and regulatory frameworks must adapt.

Licensing remains particularly uncertain. Haleu’s higher enrichment bracket triggers stricter safeguards and expanded transport and storage regimes, and the US commercial industry has yet to prove full-scale Haleu-fabrication workflows.

This creates time pressures. Reactor developers may expect Haleu-based fuel in the late 2020s, but according to the DOE’s timeline domestic supply lines may only reach commercial-scale around 2030. That leaves a narrow window where the project risks outpacing fuel readiness.
In 2022, TerraPower, another advanced reactor developer which was founded by Bill Gates and is building a demonstration Natrium nuclear plant in Wyoming, but has warned about the lack of Haleu fuel.
TerraPower said last year that the supply of Haleu for fuel is the greatest uncertainty when planning for deployment.
TerraPower has signed a non-binding agreement with ASP Isotopes related to the construction of a uranium enrichment facility in South Africa capable of producing Haleu for its reactors.
“This serves as one of many investments TerraPower has made to secure access to the fuel for the Natrium reactor and energy storage system being developed in Kemmerer, Wyoming,” the company said.
The future of advanced nuclear energy may depend less on reactor design and more on the fuel beneath it.
The DOE’s allocations are part of a deliberate effort to reboot the US’s nuclear fuel sovereignty, but the real test will be whether the supply chain can keep pace with ambition.
The stakes are high. The US may gain cleaner power and a new industrial platform if it succeeds. If it doesn’t, the next-generation nuclear wave could stall.
A Triso fuel particle cross-section. Triso is part of the advanced nuclear fuels the US is working to commercialise for next-generation reactors. Image courtesy DOE.

title: Data Centre Firm Crusoe Signs Agreement With Blue Energy To Develop Nuclear-Powered Campus In Texas
author: David Dalton
text: Company says it could deploy up to 1.5 GW of reactor capacity
US-based AI data centre developer Crusoe has partnered with US nuclear energy firm Blue Energy to develop a nuclear-powered data centre campus in the Port of Victoria, Texas.

Under the agreement, Blue Energy secured a site to design, develop and operate an advanced nuclear power plant of up to 1.5 GW, delivering “affordable, reliable power” to Crusoe-developed artificial intelligence (AI) factories on a nearby site.
Blue Energy said it will deliver power to the planned site as early as 2028.
Blue Energy will initially provide energy through gas-powered generation, which will subsequently be converted into nuclear energy by 2031.
According to Blue Energy, the site was chosen for its location, existing infrastructure, and available energy resources to support a gigawatt-scale AI factory.
It is close to existing and planned transmission lines and fibre-optic networks, and offers access to one of the US’s largest natural gas pipeline systems.

Unlike most other advanced nuclear firms, Blue Energy is not a reactor manufacturer. Instead, it focuses on the design of modular nuclear power plants, which will be manufactured offsite at shipyards and then transported to the site.
The company claims to be reactor agnostic, instead designing the “plant architecture” around the reactor, enabling different reactor vendors to plug in.
It said it will focus on deploying mature light-water reactors and submerging the reactors in a pool of water to improve their safety.

“This partnership with AI infrastructure leader Crusoe marks a key milestone for Blue Energy as we work to meet rising global energy demand and, for the first time in the nuclear industry's history, build a plant with cost and schedule certainty,” said Jake Jurewicz, Blue Energy co-founder and chief executive officer.

The Port of Victoria, about 130 miles (209 km) southwest of Houston, serves the city of Victoria and the nearby regional area. It is a centre for the chemical, construction and steel fabrication industries, and agribusiness.
The Port of Victoria is southwest of Houston in the US state of Texas. Courtesty Port of Victoria.

title: Agreement Lays Groundwork For Kazakhstan Uranium Exports To Finland
author: David Dalton
text: Countries plan ‘practical negotiations’ on supply volumes
Kazakhstan’s Atomic Energy Agency and Finland’s Radiation and Nuclear Safety Authority (Stuk) have signed an agreement that lays the groundwork for potential uranium supplies to Finland.
According to Almasadam Satkaliev, head of the Kazakh agency, the agreement establishes a legal framework for future deliveries of Kazakh uranium to Finnish nuclear power plants.

“The possibility of supplying Kazakh uranium to Finnish nuclear power plants is currently under discussion,” Satkaliev told reporters. “We’ve made such offers before, and the Finnish side has shown serious interest. This visit is an opportunity to move toward practical negotiations on supply volumes.”
The agreement, signed during Finnish president Alexander Stubb’s official visit to Kazakhstan this week, also includes provisions for sharing expertise and experience in the nuclear energy sector.
Satkaliev praised Finland’s regulatory framework, describing it as a model recognised by the International Atomic Energy Agency.

Kazakhstan, the world’s largest uranium producer through state company Kazatomprom, is also advancing its own nuclear power ambitions. The country plans to commission its first nuclear power plant by 2035.
In 2024, a nationwide referendum showed over 71% support for nuclear energy development.

In June 2025, Russia’s state nuclear corporation Rosatom was chosen to build the first plant near the village of Ulken, on the western shore of Lake Balkhash, approximately 400 km northwest of the city of Almaty.

Two additional nuclear projects are planned in cooperation with China’s state-owned China National Nuclear Corporation (CNNC). Satkaliev said CNNC is assessing potential sites in the Almaty and Zhambyl regions.
Kazakhstan’s state company Kazatomprom is the world’s largest uranium producer. Courtesy Kazatomprom.

title: NRG Pallas Signs Expanded Radium-224 Supply Agreement With TAG1
author: David Dalton
text: Partnership will help address growing demand for isotopes and support development of cancer therapies

Netherlands-based nuclear solutions company NRG Pallas and US medical isotope supplier TAG1 have expanded their partnership to include a multi-year agreement supporting radium-224 supply – a key step in producing lead-212 (Pb-212) and helping targeted alpha therapy for cancer continue to grow worldwide.

The agreement enables the further development and deployment of TAG1’s proprietary Pb-212 generator platform in Europe and unlocks new opportunities for radiopharmaceutical developers and research institutions across the continent, a statement said.

The TAG1 generator is a proprietary generator designed to unlock the supply of Pb-212 for pre-clinical and clinical trials of targeted alpha therapies using this vital radioisotope. A generator is a device that produces radioactive Pb-212 for use in medical treatments, particularly in targeted alpha therapies for cancer. Alpha therapies are an emerging class of cancer treatments that use alpha particles to destroy cancer cells while minimising damage to healthy tissue.

By establishing a regional supply of radium-224, a key precursor to Pb-212, the partnership will help address the growing demand for isotopes and support the development of alpha therapies in oncology, the statement said.

“This partnership marks a major step forward in TAG1’s mission to expand clinical access to Pb-212,” said Sumit Verma, chief executive officer and founder of TAG1. “With access to radium-224 from NRG Pallas for both US and European generator development, we are not only enabling a new market but also strengthening the infrastructure required to bring innovative radiotherapeutics closer to the patients who need them.”

NRG Pallas chief executive officer Maurits Wolleswinkel said making high-quality radium-224 available is a key step in producing Pb-212 at scale and helping targeted alpha therapy continue to grow worldwide.

At the High Flux Reactor at Petten in the Netherlands, NRG Pallas produces medical isotopes for diagnosis and therapeutic treatment of life-threatening diseases. Every day, more than 30,000 patients rely on medical isotopes from Petten.
To ensure future security of the supply, NRG Pallas has started the construction of the Pallas reactor to replace the HFR.
The High Flux Reactor at Petten in the Netherlands. Courtesy NRG Pallas.
TAG1 chief executive officer and founder Sumit Verma (left) and NRG Pallas chief executive officer Maurits Wolleswinkel sign the agreement. Courtesy NRG Pallas/TAG1.

title: European Investment Bank Lends €90 Million For Upgrade Of Olkiluoto Nuclear Reactors
author: David Dalton
text: Operation of two units in Finland could be extended by as much as 20 years
The European Investment Bank (EIB) is lending Finnish energy supplier Teollisuuden Voima Oyj (TVO) €90m ($104m) to upgrade the Olkiluoto-1 and -2 nuclear power plants in Finland.

The EIB – the long-term lending institution of the European Union, owned by its member states – said in a statement that TVO plans to update automation and control systems and replace components known as steam separators in the two units.

The upgrades, which will be implemented progressively over a number of years, are essential for maintaining high safety standards and operational reliability at the Olkiluoto plant, which has a total of three units, the EIB said.

The planned improvements are required under Finnish and EU nuclear-safety legislation. They are part of TVO’s long-term investment programme to ensure operation of the Olkiluoto plant and follow other EIB-backed enhancements at the site in 2016.

TVO has said plans for Olkiluoto’s long-term operation includes extending the licences for Units 1 and 2, which are currently set to operate until 2038, by up to 20 more years, and potentially increasing their power output.

TVO said in a statement that the operation of the two units contributes to the EU’s objective of having competitive, emissions-free and secure energy. It also aligns with the EU’s Energy Roadmap 2050, which foresees nuclear energy continuing to play a role in the bloc’s energy mix.
“TVO is systematically modernising all three Olkiluoto plant units through annual maintenance and modernisation projects throughout their operational lifetimes,” TVO said.
“The Olkiluoto nuclear power plant is Finland’s most significant electricity producer. Last year, approximately 28% of all electricity consumed in Finland was generated at Olkiluoto.”
The EIB finances nuclear power, but has not financed greenfield nuclear power generation in more than three decades.

Instead, it has taken a cautious approach focused on projects that are “technically, environmentally and economically justified”. Recent financing has included loans for uranium enrichment, upgrades to existing plants and waste management facilities.
The bank recently said nuclear energy projects including the development of small modular reactors could be eligible if they are “bankable” under strict economic assessment criteria.
In April TVO signed an investment loan agreement for €75m with the Nordic Investment Bank for the financing of projects that could lead to extended operation for Olkiluoto-1 and -2.

NIB said in a statement that the 10-year loan would finance key investments aimed at maintaining and improving safety measures and ensuring the possible extended operational lifetime of the two nuclear units.

Olkiluoto-1 is an 890-MW boiling water reactor unit that began commercial operation in 1979. The identical Olkiluoto-2 began commercial operation in 1982. The main contractor for both units was ASEA-Atom, now a part of Westinghouse Electric Sweden.
The third unit at the site, Olkiluoto-3, is a France-supplied 1,575-MW EPR unit that began commercial operation in 2023.
Finland has two other units at Loviisa, owned and operated by Fortum.
In 2024 the five units produced a 39.1% share of Finland’s electricity production, according to International Atomic Energy Agency data.
The Olkiluoto nuclear power station has three power reactors. Courtesy TVO.

title: Nuclear Process Heat Gains Traction While EU Debates Industrial Decarbonisation
author: Mathieu Carey
text: France’s Blue Capsule Technology is designing a reactor that could help meet demand for industrial heat

The European Union is rolling out its first €1 billion auction to decarbonise industrial heat, but the exclusion of nuclear technologies isn’t stopping some ambitious atomic projects across the continent.
On 10 October 2025, the European Commission launched its first pilot auction for industrial heat decarbonisation under the Innovation Fund, geared towards renewable and electrified heat projects.

The initiative, part of the broader Clean Industrial Deal, marks the first time Brussels has treated process heat emissions as a standalone policy priority, ahead of the planned €100 billion Industrial Decarbonisation Bank in 2030.

The International Energy Agency, among others, has repeatedly flagged process heat as “the missing piece” in Europe’s decarbonisation puzzle. It notes that few low-carbon technologies can reliably (or competitively) deliver heat above 400°C – a threshold that’s critical for energy-intensive industries.

In terms of carbon emissions, this is a problem. According to the IEA, industrial heat accounts for 20% of global primary energy demand each year, with up to 89% of high-temperature demand (e.g., steel, cement, chemicals) still met by fossil fuels.
In Europe, more than 1,400 TWh/year of heat is consumed by industry, with at least 75% still sourced from imported gas, coal and oil.

For processes above 400°C, innovators are working on low-carbon solutions to address this growing market. But stable, on-site options are limited. Industry players are increasingly asking about nuclear.
One of the few European companies developing an option for this segment is France’s Blue Capsule Technology, the start-up designing a modular, high-temperature reactor (“HTR”).
Designed to produce high-grade heat, steam, and electricity if needed, Blue Capsule is the only European technology to offer all three “vectors” for high-temperature processes.
The company is targeting heat to 700°C, steam to 650°C, and 50 megawatts of electricity, all co-located with industry clusters, or “inside-the-fence" industrial users.
That includes industries such as alumina, cement, the soda ash and ammonia sectors, and even the production of hydrogen or synthetic fuels.

For that to happen, Blue Capsule must meet its objective of providing cost-competitive heat at €50 per megawatt hour for European markets – something the EU Emissions Trading Scheme (EU ETS) will make possible, says the company.
“Both natural gas and coal will carry additional carbon costs by 2035, which is when we intend to launch our first reactor,” says Blue Capsule president Edouard Hourcade.
“Industries can no longer cope with volatile fossil fuel prices and insecurity of supply. They need reliable solutions that run for decades.”
The company says it wants to see “European industry flourish again” and has been quietly boosting its partnerships.
“The French and European supply chains are crucial to the success of our project,” says the company’s chief technology officer Alexey Lokhov.
“Whether it’s a pilot line for TRISO fuel in France, or tie-ups with industrial end users, Blue Capsule is doing everything we can to anchor our project in Europe's industrial fabric.”
But the company also says its reactor could target markets outside the EU.
Reactor architect at Blue Capsule, Domnin Erard, says the choice of TRISO fuel at under 5% enrichment could be crucial for the company.

“It was a very deliberate choice for us. Low-enriched uranium (LEU) is used in the vast majority of the world’s nuclear power plants. Obviously, we hope that could facilitate licensing and export. But it’s not just about making the reactor exportable; we want everything in place for our first-of-a-kind unit. We’re not sure that would be possible if we chose HALEU.”
The company says that using robust TRISO fuel will enhance the safety of the reactor, which is even air-cooled and suited for arid sites with no water resources.
At its heart, however, the project is a European one.

But while France has gained decades of advancements in sodium-cooled technologies, and Europe (Germany in particular) has pioneered high-temperature reactors, it is countries like China, Japan and the United States that are developing both.
Blue Capsule says it wants to build a European solution that’s suited for industrial applications. One that combines the best of both technologies.

“We know that sodium coolant at atmospheric pressure takes away the need for pressurisation in the reactor. That's a plus point for safety, economics, and a supply chain that’s independent from water reactors,” explains president Edouard Hourcade.

“Allied with a good fuel choice and a clear target market, this makes for a safe, efficient nuclear system that’s competitive. That’s the point of our innovation. That’s why we think nuclear heat can be part of Europe’s decarbonisation drive.”
Concept rendering of Blue Capsule’s modular high-temperature reactor system, designed to supply carbon-free process heat, steam and electricity for industrial end users.
Cross-section rendering of Blue Capsule’s modular high-temperature reactor facility, showing the reactor hall.

title: Eight Companies Confirmed On UK’s £8.7 Million Nuclear Advisory Framework
author: David Dalton
text: Appointments come as UK prepares for deployment of new reactors

Eight companies have been awarded places on the UK government’s £8.7m (€9.8m, $11.5m) Nuclear Energy Regulatory Justification Services Framework, which will help the government as it prepares to deploy new nuclear power plants.

The appointment to the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) framework mean the companies are all approved suppliers to provide technical advice and expertise in support of the UK’s nuclear programme.
The eight companies are Egis, Frazer Nash, Assystem, Afry, PA Consulting Services, TUV SUD, Energy, Safety and Risk Consultants and RSK Environment.

The appointments come as the UK looks to maximise the benefits of new nuclear technologies ranging from gigawatt-scale reactors to small modular reactors, advanced modular reactors and future fusion energy facilities.

Starting this month, the new government framework will run for five years. The eight companies will support the licensing activities for UK nuclear new build innovation across a range of different nuclear technical disciplines.
They join a small pool of suppliers appointed by Defra to provide access to expert technical advice which supports “nuclear energy regulatory justification”.

This mandatory process formally requires demonstrating that the societal benefits of introducing a class or type of nuclear practice outweigh the potential health detriments. A positive decision must be made before any new nuclear energy technology can be adopted in the UK.
