Earlier this week, the team conducted a check to observe the status of the emergency diesel generators that were in standby mode at the time. The team also confirmed that the essential service sprinkler ponds – which provide cooling to the reactors and the spent fuel pools – were operating as usual. Radiation levels at the site remain normal, the team reported.

The team has continued to report military activities at various distances from the site. On Tuesday evening, the team members heard five explosions one after the other, occurring close to the site and shaking windows in their building.
The IAEA teams based at the other nuclear sites in Ukraine – Khmelnitski, Rivne, South Ukraine and Chernobyl – also report military activities on most days.
All six units at the Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant in Ukraine have been shut down. Courtesy IAEA.

title: Regional Countries Need To Explore Long-Term Collaboration On Nuclear, Says US Thinktank
author: David Dalton
text: Paper calls for states to focus on ‘broader agenda’ and work with groups such as IAEA and WANO

Regional groupings of countries should explore long-term collaboration in areas of nuclear energy such as fuel fabrication or waste management in an effort to share costs, distribute risks and reassure their neighbours and the broader international community that the deployment of reactors can contribute to energy security and economic development, according to a Carnegie Endowment for International Peace paper.

The US-based thinktank’s paper, Beyond the Gigawatts: A Broader Agenda for Nuclear Energy Deployment, says countries could codevelop and perform joint regulatory reviews to facilitate the deployment and export of advanced nuclear systems, technologies and components in their regions.
Regional partners, particularly those with limited resources, could see benefits from joint workforce development and supply chain management.

And neighbouring countries could partner with the International Atomic Energy Agency in establishing new regional technical support roles to provide technical advice and to perform onsite inspections.

“These mechanisms could enable the IAEA to gain efficiency and strengthen its core competencies in performing assessments and implementing safeguards as part of its ‘trust but verify’ philosophy,” the paper says.

It calls for states to work with the IAEA, the Nuclear Energy Agency, the World Association of Nuclear Operators and other international entities to promulgate high standards and practices for nuclear use while also seeking efficiency and effectiveness.
Focusing exclusively on near-term challenges does not guarantee that a significant expansion of nuclear energy will deliver all the claimed benefits for its users, the paper warns.

Those near-term challenges include “up-front requirements” such as initiatives for shortening the time to market for new reactors, streamlining regulations, producing adequate quantities of specialised fuels, securing financing, mitigating supply chain constraints, and developing the needed workforce.

Resolving these issues is integral to achieving ambitious objectives for nuclear power, but governments and industry also need to address a broader agenda of requirements, including building support among the general public and especially intended host communities for nuclear plants.
The paper says nuclear power is an increasingly sought after option for meeting energy demand at scale and around the clock.
Despite significant up-front investment, once built, nuclear plants promise consistent and reliable energy at low operating costs.
They are widely perceived as important contributors to energy security, economic development, and carbon emission reduction.

title: Slovakia’s Prime Minister Says Deal With US For New Nuclear Plant ‘Signed And Approved’
author: David Dalton
text: Reactor at existing Bohunice site could be supplied by Westinghouse
Slovakia’s prime minister Robert Fico said his government has signed an agreement with the US to build an additional nuclear reactor at the existing Bohunice site in the west of the country.

Fico announced on 10 September during a speech at the annual European Nuclear Energy Forum (Enef) in the Slovak capital of Bratislava that a deal was “signed and approved”. He did not disclose any more details on the deal.
He said that the new reactor will be have an output of over 1,000 MW and be fully owned by the state.
Fico said earlier this year that Slovakia was preparing to sign an intergovernmental agreement with the US that would pave the way for Westinghouse Electric Company to provide a unit for Bohunice.

“As long as this goes through, we can move toward the signing of an intergovernmental agreement that would be aimed at having American company Westinghouse build a new nuclear power unit at the Jaslovske Bohunice nuclear power plant,” Fico was reported as saying at a press conference.
He also referred at the time to a pending US final proposal on the agreement.
Bohunice is one of Slovakia’s two nuclear power station sites and has two Russia-designed VVER-440 pressurised water reactor units operated by Slovenske Elektrarne.
The other site is Mochovce, which has three Russia-supplied operational plants and one, also supplied by Russia, under construction.
In 2024, the Slovak government approved plans to develop a new unit at Bohunice with a capacity of around 1,200 MW and a target operational date of 2040.
“It is a huge investment. We are talking about a new unit with output of 1,250 MW,” said Fico, according to Reuters, without disclosing a value for the potential deal.
In 2023, Westinghouse signed two agreements with Slovak state-owned nuclear company Javys for the potential deployment of AP1000 reactors and AP300 small modular reactors.
Slovak prime minister Robert Fico at the Bratislava European Nuclear Energy Forum 2025.

title: Cavendish Nuclear Wins Monju Prototype Fast Reactor Decommissioning Contract
author: Kamen Kraev
text: JV with Amentum will build UK treatment facility for sodium coolant

UK-based Cavendish Nuclear and its US-based partner Amentum have been awarded the next phase of work by the Japan Atomic Energy Agency (JAEA) to support the decommissioning of the Monju prototype fast reactor in Fukui Prefecture, western Japan.
A statement said their joint venture, Alkali Metal Processing, will build a UK facility to treat the reactor’s sodium coolant, converting it into sodium hydroxide for industrial reuse.
The contract follows a design and engineering phase and draws on experience from decommissioning the UK’s Dounreay prototype fast reactor, which shares design similarities with Monju.
Cavendish was first awarded work on the Monju decommissioning project in 2019, drawing on its UK expertise in dismantling fast reactors.
Japan’s regulator approved a 30-year decommissioning roadmap in March 2018.
Monju, a 246-MW sodium-cooled fast breeder reactor, was designed to run on uranium-plutonium mixed fuel and generate more fissile material than it used.
Although it achieved first criticality in 1994, it has been largely idle since a 1995 accident involving a sodium leak and fire.
The government decided in 2016 to shut the facility for good, with dismantling costs put at about $3.2bn (€2.7bn) by Japanese media.
The  Monju prototype fast reactor site in Fukui Prefecture, western Japan. Courtesy Nife/Wikipedia Creative Commons Licence.

title: GVH Forms Alliance With Samsung C&T For BWRX-300 Nuclear Plant Deployment
author: David Dalton
text: Companies aim to roll out units outside North America, including in Sweden

GE Vernova Hitachi Nuclear Energy (GVH) and South Korea-based construction and engineering company Samsung C&T have announced an alliance to advance the deployment of the BWRX-300 small modular reactor
(SMR) in global markets outside North America.
The two companies said they will focus their efforts on developing the supply chain and project delivery solutions for GVH’s SMR.
They will also work together on the potential deployment of five BWRX-300s in Sweden.

“With the first unit of our BWRX-300 under construction in Canada, we are well positioned to lead the deployment and scale of the SMR industry,” said Maví Zingoni, chief executive officer of the power division at GE Vernova.

Zingoni said the collaboration with Samsung C&T, which has a solid track-record of helping to deliver nuclear projects, will further strengthen the BWRX-300 position among “the most advanced, deployment ready, and lowest risk SMR technology available today”.
Se-chul Oh, chief executive officer of Samsung C&T, said the agreement marks a collaboration where Samsung C&T and GVH aim to become global leaders in the nuclear power segment.

The first BWRX-300 SMR is under construction at utility Ontario Power Generation’s Darlington nuclear site in Canada, with completion expected by the end of the decade. That would make it the first SMR in the Western World.
Key components like the reactor pressure vessel are being manufactured, and site construction is progressing according to plan, GVH said.

Additionally, the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission has accepted and is reviewing Tennessee Valley Authority’s application to construct the first BWRX-300 in the US, at the federal utility’s Clinch River site in Oak Ridge, Tennessee.

Poland-based nuclear project company Orlen Synthos Green Energy has selected Wloclawek as the site for Poland’s first SMR. In Sweden, state utility Vattenfall is considering the BWRX-300 as it evaluates the construction of new reactors adjacent to its Ringhals nuclear plant site.

So far, only China and Russia operate SMRs, which are defined by the International Atomic Energy Agency as nuclear plants with a power capacity of 300 MW or less that are designed with modular construction, allowing for factory fabrication and streamlined installation.

According to GVH, each BWRX-300 can provide approximately 300 MW of electricity, enough to produce the equivalent electricity needed to power 300,000 homes while significantly reducing the complexity and cost associated with traditional nuclear reactors.

Samsung C&T’s landmark projects include Burj Khalifa in Dubai – the world’s tallest building.  In the nuclear energy sector, the company has delivered 12 GW across 10 units, including the Barakah nuclear power plant in the United Arab Emirates.
Maví Zingoni, CEO Power at GE Vernova, and Se-chul Oh, Samsung C&T CEO. Courtesy GVH.

title: GNF Introduces Next-Generation Nuclear Fuel For Boiling Water Reactors
author: David Dalton
text: First assemblies contracted for deployment in 2026
US-based Global Nuclear Fuel (GNF) has announced the introduction of GNF4, a next generation nuclear fuel product for boiling water reactor (BWR) units.

The company, a GE Vernova-led alliance with Hitachi, said the 11x11 GNF4 product builds upon the operating history of GNF2 and GNF3 and features two advanced components that are licensed by the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission: Ziron cladding and aluminosilicate doped uranium dioxide pellets.
fuel costs per megawatt hour through increased performance and reliability,” said Crai

Ziron cladding was developed to better resist corrosion, ensuring that fuel remains safe and reliable and is an enhancement to the Zircaloy 2 cladding that has been ued in more than 175,000 GNF fuel assemblies worldwide. Aluminosilicate doped uranium dioxide pellets add an extra layer of reliability. GNF4 will also use GNF’s proprietary NSF channel material and Defender+ debris filter.
NSF channel material is a distortion-resistant zirconium alloy primarily composed of zirconium, niobium, tin and iron. It is designed to reduce fuel channel distortion in BWRs.

“GNF4 is engineered to provide plant operators with lower fuel costs per megawatt hour through increased performance and reliability,” said Craig Ranson, installed base chief executive officer at GE Vernova Hitachi Nuclear Energy.

GNF4 is being fabricated at GNF’s manufacturing facility in Wilmington, North Carolina. The first lead use assemblies of GNF4 are contracted for deployment in 2026 and full reload quantities are expected to be available in 2030.
GNF4 is being fabricated at GNF's manufacturing facility in Wilmington, North Carolina. Courtesy GNF.

title: Kazatomprom Eyes Fuel Cycle Expansion Beyond Mining Under 2034 Strategy, Says Expert
author: Rachel Rigby
text: Conversion and fuel fabrication described as ‘low-hanging’ fruit for Kazakh state champion
Kazakh state uranium mining company Kazatomprom is to look to explore other parts of the nuclear fuel cycle beyond its traditional area of uranium mining, an analyst said.

Vadim Merkulov, director, capital markets research, at the Kazakhstan-based Freedom Broker brokerage, told NucNet that the company’s 2025-34 strategy "explicitly allows expanding its footprint in the nuclear fuel cycle where it’s economically justified, while maintaining mining as its core."

Merkulov said that this "includes the Ulba-FA plant, which reached full capacity in 2024, producing 200 tonnes of low-enriched uranium fuel annually using French Framatome technology alongside China's CGN."

Kazatomprom is the world’s largest natural uranium producer, providing 40% of the uranium on the global market. Kazatomprom in 2024 had total uranium output of 23,270 tonnes, a 10% increase compared to the 21,112 tonnes of uranium that it produced in 2023.
In August, Kazatomprom said that its guidance for 2025 uranium production had not changed from its previous range, released earlier, of between 25,000 tonnes and 26,500 tonnes.
However, Kazatomprom also said that its 2025 production would likely turn out to be "closer to the lower limit of the current guidance."

Merkulov said that there were two areas of "low-hanging fruit" in the nuclear fuel cycle in which Kazatomprom can collaborate with other entities to further its expansion: uranium conversion and nuclear fuel fabrication.

Kazatomprom’s "updated strategy also includes developing segments for rare and rare-earth metals as part of its critical minerals agenda," Merkulov said, adding: "This diversification leverages existing mining expertise and infrastructure, addressing the growing demand for renewable energy."

"For example, the Ulba Metallurgical Plant (UMP) is the only CIS facility with a complete production cycle for tantalum, niobium, and beryllium, ranking second globally in beryllium products and fourth globally in tantalum products," he added.

According to Merkulov, Kazakhstan’s top five uranium players are Russia’s Rosatom, France’s Orano, Canada’s Cameco, China General Nuclear Power Corp (CGN), and the China National Nuclear Corporation (CNNC).
Orano owns the majority stake in a Katco mining joint venture (JV) with Kazatomprom in the South Tortkuduk region, while Cameco is a minority owner in the Inkai JV mine.
China’s presence in Kazakshtan’s uranium sector includes the Ulba-FA fuel plant, the Semizbay-U and Ortalyk JV mines with CGN.
CNNC is also a major buyer of Kazah uranium, said Merkulov. "Last year, CNNC secured contracts representing over 50% of Kazatomprom’s booked assets."
The analyst also said that he still observed a "significant strategic relationship between" Russia and Kazakhstan, despite some changes in ownership in uranium mining assets in Kazakhstan.
"Russia is the leading importer of unenriched uranium, making its presence significant," Merkulov said.

In December 2024, Rosatom’s subsidiary, Uranium One Group, sold stakes in several mines to Chinese companies, including a 49.9% stake of the Zarechnoye mine and a 30% stake in both the Khorasan-U and Kyzylkum joint ventures, Merkulov said.

"However, in 2023 Rosatom offset this divestment by acquiring via its Uranium One subsidiary a 49% stake in the Budenovskoye joint venture, which is set to become the world’s largest uranium mine, expected to account for about 10% of global output," the analyst added.
Merkulov noted that this production is "exclusively designated for Russia’s civil nuclear industry until 2027."

Kazatomprom's production will be lower than previously planned for 2026, with full expected output now being lowered by around 10%, or some 3,000 tonnes of uranium, following start-up issues at new mines and sluggish demand, the company said during an August trading update.

Statistical data shows that between 20% and 25% of the uranium feeding Europe’s reactor fleets comes has come from Kazakhstan in recent years. The situation is similar on the US market, according to data by the Energy Information Administration.
Canada is the number two supplier for Europe and the US with a supply share just slightly under that of Kazakhstan.

title: US Regulator Allows Urenco To Produce 10% Enriched Uranium At New Mexico Site
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Pilot manufacturing expected to start by the end of 2025

Urenco’s US-based subsidiary Urenco USA (UUSA) has received authorisation from the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) to enrich uranium up to 10% U-235 (uranium-235), a statement by the company said on Thursday.
Urenco said the permit means its Eunice site in New Mexico has become the first commercial uranium enrichment facility in the US to produce so-called low-enriched uranium plus (LEU+).

The NRC issued its approval on 30 September after UUSA completed an operational readiness review, implemented system upgrades and safety modifications, and made extensive changes to its plant procedures.
The company said initial production of LEU+ will begin this year, with the first deliveries to a fuel manufacturer expected in 2026.

In December 2024, the NRC approve an amendment to UUSA’s existing Eunice licence towards increasing enrichment levels up to 10% U-235. The commission said at the time it had to still review the implementation of the amendment’s requirements.
The license allows UUSA to produce enrichment levels of up to 10% U-235 across all cascades at its Eunice facility.

UUSA managing director John Kirkpatrick said the new product would “support the long-term success of the US nuclear industry” by helping operators extend reactor cycles and reduce refuelling outages, potentially cutting costs, and improving performance.
LEU+ can also fuel many of the advanced reactor designs now under development in the US.
The company also said that LEU+ could serve as an important feedstock for a future US facility to produce high-assay low-enriched uranium (Haleu), needed for majority of next-generation reactors.
In 2023, Urenco announced a 15% capacity expansion of its Eunice site, which is expected to bring an additional 700,000 SWU* per year in 2027. The project began in October 2024.
Low-enriched uranium was already produced at two new cascades, first in May 2025 and then in September 2025.
Traditional LEU is limited to enrichment levels of about 5% of U-235, while LEU+ refers to nuclear fuel enriched to between 5% and 10% U-235.
Fuels containing LEU+ can improve the efficiency of existing reactors by providing higher burnups, longer fuel cycles of from 18 to 24 months and by producing less spent fuel waste.

Haleu, for comparison, has an enrichment level of 10% to 20% U-235. The US has mounted an effort to reach commercial scale Haleu production by the end of the decade to coincide with expected advanced reactor deployments.
The US is expected to be the first major market for LEU+, with demand driven by its existing reactor fleet operators and advanced reactor fuel testing and deployment plans.

Magnus Mori, head of technical sales at Urenco, told NucNet in late 2024 that Urenco had not supplied LEU+ for fuel fabrication to clients at the time, but the company had several contracts signed with utilities in North America for potential deliveries targeted for 2026 or early 2027.
He said the commercial delivery of LEU+ would depend on the licensing progress of advanced, or accident-tolerant fuels, which are being tested at several US nuclear plants.

* SWUs are the standard measure of the effort required in a uranium enrichment facility to separate uranium-235 (U-235) from uranium-238 (U-238), thereby increasing the concentration of U-235, the isotope that can split to produce energy.
Urenco's National Enrichment Facility at Eunice, New Mexico, is operated by subsidiary Louisiana Energy Services. Image courtesy Urenco USA.

title: New Mexico Chosen For $1 Billion Pacific Fusion Campus
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Site will host demonstration system aimed at proving commercial-scale fusion.
Pacific Fusion has chosen Albuquerque, New Mexico, as the site of its first research and manufacturing campus, where it will build a $1bn (€850m) facility to house its demonstration fusion system.
The system is designed to achieve net energy gain, producing more energy from fusion than consumed by the facility, by 2030, a statement said.
Governor Michelle Lujan Grisham said the investment positions New Mexico at the forefront of the emerging fusion energy industry.
The project will create more than 200 long-term jobs, hundreds of construction jobs, and wider economic benefits for the state, according to the statement.

Pacific Fusion, headquartered in California, said the demonstration is intended to deliver 100 times higher energy gain at 10 times lower cost than the National Ignition Facility at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, which achieved a demonstration of 4 times gain
in April 2025.
Construction of the campus at the Mesa del Sol site is expected to begin in 2026.
The governor’s office said the facility will not produce any power but focus on manufacturing operations, expected to kick off by the end of 2025.

The office said Pacific Fusion’s expansion into New Mexico is supported by state and local performance-based incentives, which the company will receive only as it fulfills its commitments to create new jobs and make significant capital investments.
Pacific Fusion, founded in 2023, has raised more than $900m from investors including General Catalyst, Breakthrough Energy Ventures, Lowercarbon Capital, and Lightspeed Venture Partners.

Pacific Fusion said it remains on track to deliver the first commercial fusion system in the US by the mid-2030s, with the Albuquerque facility serving as a foundation for scaled deployment of affordable fusion power.

The company is pursuing a pulsed magnetic path to inertial fusion, that is, using fast-rising, high-current pulses to magnetically squeeze and heat small containers of deuterium-tritium fuel, driving the fuel to fusion conditions.
An artist's rendering of the Pacific Fusion proposed New Mexico research and manufacturing campus. Image courtesy Pacific fusion.

title: Orano Wins Key Ruling In Niger Uranium Mine Dispute
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Arbitration tribunal orders Niger not to sell uranium from Somair site.

The Washington-based International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes (ICSID) has issued a ruling in favour of French nuclear group Orano in its ongoing dispute with Niger over the Somair uranium mine.
The arbitration tribunal last week ordered Niger not to sell, transfer, or facilitate the transfer of uranium produced at Somair that was withheld in violation of Orano’s rights.

The tribunal also requested the release of Orano representative Ibrahim Courmo, who has been detained in Niger since May 2025 despite a Niamey Court of Appeal decision in July calling for his release.
The case is part of wider tensions over control of Niger’s uranium resources following political upheaval in the country.
Somair (Société des Mines de l’Aïr), based in Arlit in northern Niger, is majority-owned by Orano and has been one of the country’s largest uranium producers for decades.
Uranium is a cornerstone of Niger’s economy despite declining output in recent years.
In January 2025, Orano filed an arbitration procedure against Niger following the loss of operational control of the Somair uranium mine.
The move followed an initial proceeding against Niger over the Imouraren uranium deposit in December 2024.

Orano had said the West African country’s obstruction of the commercialisation of production, and the suppression of Orano's offtake rights, have “only aggravated Somair’s financial situation and the prejudice suffered by Orano”.
Orano announced in October 2024 it would be halting its uranium production in Niger, citing a “highly deteriorated” situation and its inability to operate.
A July 2023 coup in Niger led to a halt in imports of critical materials necessary for uranium exploitation at Somair, such as soda ash, carbonate, nitrates, and sulphur.
According to Orano, Somair is the only uranium mine in commercial operation in Niger.
The company said 1,500 tonnes of uranium are still stockpiled at the site and threatened to pursue criminal charges if any of it is sold without permission.
According to Reuters, a source at the mine said Niger had not yet sold any uranium but "potential buyers include Iranians, Russians and Turkey".
In July 2025, Niger's government said it plans to nationalise the Somair mine.
The Somair open pit mine in Niger. Image courtesy Maurice Ascani / Orano.

title: Russia Ships RPVs For Turkey’s Akkuyu-4 And Egypt’s El Dabaa-1 Nuclear Plants
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Both countries building VVER-1200 reactor units at pilot sites

Russia’s state nuclear corporation Rosatom has begun shipping two VVER-1200 reactor pressure vessels, one for Unit 4 of Turkey’s Akkuyu nuclear power station and the other for Unit 1 of Egypt’s El-Dabaa plant.
The RPV is one of the largest reactor components at a nuclear plant, weighing about 320 tonnes. It is a vessel containing the nuclear reactor coolant, core shroud, and the reactor core and fuel.

Rosatom said the components will be shipped from two factories: Atommash in Volgodonsk, where the Akkuyu vessel was produced, and the Izhora plant in St. Petersburg, where the El-Dabaa vessel was manufactured.
Rosatom said it was the first time in the history of the Russian nuclear industry that two reactors were shipped simultaneously from different locations.
The Akkuyu shipment will take about three weeks by rail and sea, while the El-Dabaa vessel will arrive at its site in about one month.
According to Rosatom, its factories are currently working on 22 sets of nuclear equipment for projects in Russia and abroad.

Turkey’s Akkuyu nuclear station, under construction by Rosatom in the southern province of Mersin on the Mediterranean coast, will have four VVER‑1200 1200 pressurised water reactors. Construction of the four units started consecutively in 2018, 2020, 2021, and 2022.
El Dabaa, Egypt’s first commercial nuclear station, will have also four VVER-1200 PWR units, with the first unit expected to be online in 2026. Construction of El Dabaa-1 began in July 2022.
The Akkyu-4 RPV shipping from an Atommash factory in Volgodonsk with an industrial anniversary ceremony. Image courtesy Akkuyu Nuclear.

title: Uzbekistan Extends Agreements With Russia On Construction Of First Nuclear Power Plant
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Central Asian country to host SMRs and large-scale nuclear at ‘integrated’ plant
Uzbekistan and Russia have signed two agreements earlier this week taking another step toward building nuclear power plants in the Central Asian country, a statement said.

The country's nuclear energy agency (Uzatom) said the move builds on an agreement signed in June 2025 with Russia’s state nuclear corporation Rosatom to study the possibility of deploying nuclear reactors.

Uzatom said the first agreement sets out the main conditions for project implementation, focusing on an “integrated” nuclear power station combining both large and small-scale reactors on a single site in the Jizzakh region.
The project would include the construction of two Generation III+ VVER-1000 pressurised water reactors and two RITM-200N small modular reactors.
The second agreement covers nuclear fuel supply and related equipment for both types of reactors, Uzatom said.
Uzatom director Azim Akhmedkhadjaev said the project combines “the proven reliability of large-scale nuclear with the innovation of small modular reactors.”
Rosatom chief executive Alexei Likhachev said Uzbekistan will be the first country in the world to have an integrated nuclear station where both large and small reactors operate on the same site.
In June, Uzatom and Rosatom agreed to explore the possibility of deploying two to four VVER-1000 PWR units in Uzbekistan.

In 2024, the two sides signed a protocol for the start of work on a project to build a nuclear station that would house six 55-MW RITM-200N small modular reactor units. The RITM-200N technology is an adaptation of marine technology for land-based deployment.
Uzbekistan, a Central Asian country of 33 million people, is looking to nuclear power as a low-carbon energy source to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and boost electricity generating capacity.
Neighbouring Kazakhstan has also formally begun a nuclear power programme, recently selecting Rosatom as its initial development partner.

title: NRC Renews Point Beach Nuclear Station Licences For Another 20 Years
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Two Wisconsin reactors cleared to run until 2050 and 2053
The US Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) has renewed for a second time the operating licences of the Point Beach nuclear power station’s two pressurised water reactor units in Wisconsin.
The NRC said both units can operate for an additional 20 years after a final environmental impact statement in August 2025 and a safety evaluation in May 2022.
The renewal allows Point Beach-1 to operate until October 2050 and Point Beach-2 until March 2053, extending the facility’s lifetime to up to 80 years of operation.
Owner NextEra Energy submitted a subsequent licence application to the NRC in November 2020.
Both Point Beach plants are 591-MW Westinghouse pressurised water reactor units. Pont Beach-1 began commercial operation in December 1970 and Point Beach-2 in October 1972.
The NRC approved the initial licence renewal in December 2005, with Unit 1 currently licensed to operate until 5 October 2030 and Unit 2 until 8 March 2033.
The NRC is reviewing applications for initial licence extensions for three reactor units at two sites: Diablo Canyon and Clinton.
Another 10 reactor units at five sites are being reviewed for subsequent licence extensions: St. Lucie, Browns Ferry, Dresden, Hatch, and Robinson.
Aerial view of the Point Beach nuclear power plant on the shore of Lake Michigan near Two Rivers, Wisconsin. Image courtesy Wikipedia.

title: Construction Officially Launched For Pallas Research Reactor In Petten
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Facility to replace High Flux Reactor and secure isotope supply for Europe
Construction has officially begun of the Netherlands’ new Pallas research reactor, which will replace the High Flux Reactor (HFR) in Petten, developer NRG Pallas said.

In July 2025, the reactor-related section received the green light from the Dutch ministry of health, welfare, and sport after preparatory works, including site preparation and delivery of the construction pit, were completed.
On 29 September, Anita van den Ende, the ministry’s secretary-general, formally launched the start of construction, a statement said.
In May 2025, workers completed the construction pit and its concrete foundation. Work on the pit began in 2023. Next construction stage would include work on the lower section of the reactor.

Every day, more than 30,000 patients rely on the production of medical radioisotopes from the existing High-Flux Reactor (HFR) at Petten. This number is expected to increase with the introduction of new treatments using medical isotopes from reactors and the growth of patients with cancer and cardiovascular diseases worldwide.
In 2012, the Dutch government and the province of Noord-Holland decided that the HFR should be replaced to ensure the supply of medical radioisotopes and the continuation of nuclear research.
Last year, the European Commission approved the Dutch government’s €2bn ($2.3bn) measure to provide public support for the construction of the Pallas reactor.
Programme director Peter Dijk said the move into the construction phase followed years of careful preparation, state support, and financing agreements.
“We are proud of what we have achieved together and what we are yet to achieve: building a reactor in the construction pit,” he said.

The 25-MWt Pallas reactor is of the pool-type design, with its core placed in a large water pool that naturally provides neutron moderation and shielding. The reactor will offer improved neutron flux for medical isotope production.

Anita van den Ende, secretary-general of the ministry of health, welfare and sport, Peter Dijk, Pallas programme director, and Maurits Wolleswinkel, CEO NRG Pallas, mark the official start of construction of the Pallas reactor in September 2025. Image courtesy NRG Pallas.

An artist’s rendering of what will be the new Pallas complex at Petten. The future Pallas reactor building is in the centre, with the existing High Flux Reactor visible at the bottom. Image courtesy of NRG Pallas.

title: Oklo And Blykalla Form Partnership On Liquid Metal Fast Reactors
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Companies eye joint supply chain cooperation and $5m investment to accelerate commercialisation

US-based Oklo and Sweden’s Blykalla have announced a strategic partnership to cooperate on technology, supply chains, and regulatory approaches as both companies work to commercialise advanced nuclear reactors.
Blykalla said in a statement that the agreement includes Oklo committing to take a $5m (€4.2m) stake in the Swedish company ‘leading’ the next funding round.
The statement said the two companies have agreed to share insights on materials, component sourcing, and licensing best practices across the US and Europe.
The companies will examine the options for shared suppliers for reactor-neutral equipment with the aim of improving availability, lowering costs, and reducing schedule risks.
Both companies are working on developing liquid metal fast reactor designs.
Oklo is developing sodium-cooled fast reactors of up to 75 MWe, while Blykalla is advancing its 55 MWe lead-cooled Sealer design.
According to the statement, the partnership, one of the first of its kind between US and European fast reactor developers.
Oklo chief executive Jacob DeWitte said the cooperation would “shorten critical paths to deployment” and strengthen the growing advanced reactor ecosystem in response to rising global power demand.
Blykalla chief executive Jacob Stedman said joint efforts could “unlock efficiencies for both companies and help suppliers plan for scale.”

In February 2025, Blykalla broke ground on its advanced reactor testing facility at the Oskarshamn nuclear site to the south of Stockholm. The facility will house the electrical Sealer-E prototype reactor and aims to validate critical components and safety systems for a future reactor.

Last week, Oklo broke ground on the non-nuclear part its first Aurora powerhouse project at Idaho National Laboratory, where it will build the pilot Aurora-INL facility based on sodium-cooled fast reactor technology.
Artists' renderings of the plants proposed by Blykalla (top) and Oklo.

title: Iran Signs $25 Billion Deal With Russia For Four New Nuclear Units, Reports Say
author: Kamen Kraev
text: New units near Sirik to use large-scale 'Gen III technology'
Iran and Russia have signed a $25bn (€21bn) deal to build four nuclear power units in Iran’s southern Hormozgan province, Iran’s state news agency IRNA reported.

IRNA said Russian state-owned nuclear corporation Rosatom and the Iran-Hormoz company signed an “implementation agreement,” that covers the construction of four Generation III reactor units near the city of Sirik.
The reactors are expected to have a capacity of about 5,000 MW, meaning they will be of the large-scale type, most likely Russia’s VVER-1200 pressurised water reactor design.
Russian official sources have not confirmed the deal.
The announcement follows a memorandum of understanding signed last week between Rosatom and Iran’s Atomic Energy Organisation (AEOI) on cooperation for small nuclear power plants.
According to Rosatom, that document outlined specific steps aimed at developing small-scale nuclear facilities in Iran, though no further details were provided.
AEOI chief Mohammad Eslami had said Iran wants Russia’s help to build up to eight new nuclear reactor units.

In February 2024, officials in Iran reportedly inaugurated the construction of a four-unit nuclear power station with a capacity of about 5,000 MW in the southern coastal province of Hormozgan, but details on the development were scarce.

IRNA said at the time the nuclear station would be known as Iran-Hormoz and be located near Sirik, however, it remained unclear which company would be the supplier of reactor technology for the new-build projects.

Over the last couple of years Iran has claimed it is developing domestic reactor technology a site being prepared at Darkhovin, but no recent progress has been announced publicly or indicated to the IAEA.
Iran operates one Russia-supplied commercial nuclear plant, Bushehr-1, which began operation in 2013.
Iran and Russia signed an agreement to build two new units at Bushehr in November 2014. This was followed in June 2019 by the signing of a final contract for construction.
Construction Bushehr-2 began in 2019. First concrete for Bushehr-3 was planned for the end of 2024, but no recent updates have been released.
The Bushehr nuclear power station, where Iran has a single operating VVER reactor unit, with two more to be deployed. Image courtesy AEOI.

title: IAEA, CAF Sign Agreement To Support Nuclear In Latin America And Caribbean
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Agreement follows World Bank policy shift on financing energy source in developing nations

The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) and the Development Bank of Latin America and the Caribbean (CAF) have signed a memorandum of understanding to improve cooperation on nuclear energy and technology across the region.

The three-year agreement, signed in New York during the recent United Nations general assembly, sets a framework for collaboration in areas such as nuclear energy for decarbonisation and energy security, water resource management, waste management, food production under changing climate conditions, and the promotion of a circular economy.

CAF executive president Sergio Diaz-Granados said the agreement is a milestone for sustainable development in Latin America and the Caribbean, describing nuclear as “a fundamental alternative to diversify our regional energy matrix and achieve decarbonisation goals.”
The IAEA said it will provide technical assistance to CAF in areas including energy planning, development of infrastructure, innovation, and the safe management of radioactive waste.
The agency’s director-general Rafael Grossi said nuclear energy is becoming “an increasingly attractive option” for countries in the region seeking clean, reliable baseload power.
The cooperations aims to boost institutional capacity, improve regulatory frameworks, and ensure that nuclear technologies are deployed safely and peacefully to support regional development.
The signing comes amid growing international financial support for nuclear energy.

In June, the World Bank lifted
its long-standing ban on financing nuclear projects and later signed
a separate agreement with the IAEA to cooperate on the development and financing of nuclear power for developing countries.

The two institutions said at the time they would work together to extend the lifespan of existing nuclear power plants as a cost-effective source of low-carbon power and accelerate the development of small modular reactors, saying that they have potential for widespread adoption in developing countries.
CAF executive president Sergio Diaz-Granados and IAEA director-general Rafael Mariano Grossi. Image courtesy IAEA.

title: Sweden Needs Thousands Of Workers For Nuclear Expansion, Report Warns
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Calls for ‘urgent’ efforts to avoid skills shortages

Sweden will need to train and recruit thousands of skilled workers to build at least 2,500 MW of new nuclear capacity by 2035, according to a final report prepared for the country’s National Nuclear Coordinator’s office.

The study, prepared by the RISE research institute, warns that without urgent national action to expand education, training, and validation of skills, a shortage of qualified staff could delay or derail new-build projects.

The report said Sweden’s nuclear workforce has shrunk in recent decades, with many senior experts close to retirement. Educational capacity is “far too low” across vocational schools, universities, and the regulator. At the same time, there is no system for validating the skills of foreign professionals, despite the likelihood that Sweden will need to rely on international recruitment.
The report also warned of a lack of so-called a “buyer-side” capacity to plan and manage large, complex projects, which it said increases risks for new construction.
Sweden has announced plans to deploy new nuclear in the mid and late 2030s with a capacity of up to 5,000 MW from both large and small nuclear reactor units.

The government has recently proposed
a €19.9bn ($23.4bn) over 12 years in a loan package to support the policy.
The report called for nuclear workforce planning to be treated as critical national infrastructure.

Among its main recommendations is the founding of a national nuclear college by 2026, expanded university and vocational programmes by 2027–29, and a new system to validate foreign professionals’ skills.

Recommendations also included the creation of a competence council, expanded education and training programmes, stronger industry-academia partnerships, and regional hubs near existing nuclear sites. It also calls for communication campaigns to attract young people, better inclusion of underrepresented groups, and long-term financing to ensure sustainable workforce development.
A full-scale mobilisation of workers could then be in place for ramping-up construction in the early 2030s, the report said.

According to the report, international experience has shown the scale of the challenge. The UK has set up a Nuclear Skills Taskforce aiming for 40,000 jobs by 2030, while France has established a national nuclear skills school. Finland’s Olkiluoto-3 project highlighted the delays and costs that can result when a country lacks enough nuclear competence.

Sweden has six reactor units in commercial operation at three sites: Forsmark, Oskarshamn and Ringhals. According to International Atomic Energy Agency data, nuclear energy provided 29% of the country’s electricity generation in 2024.

title: Zaporizhzhia Plant Suffers Fresh Blackout, Emergency Generators Activated
author: Kamen Kraev
text: IAEA confirms backup onsite power sufficient for 20 days

Ukraine’s Russia-occupied Zaporizhzhia nuclear power station lost all off-site power yesterday, the tenth such incident since the start of the conflict in February 2022, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) said.

The plant, Europe’s largest, was disconnected from its last remaining 750 kV external power line at 16:56 local time on 23 September. The disconnection was confirmed by both the Zaporizhzhia plant operators and Ukraine’s regulatory authority.
The IAEA said emergency diesel generators started automatically to supply power, and the plant later confirmed that all available generator units had been activated.

The agency said Zaporizhzhia has been dependent on a single external line for nearly five months after losing its last 330 kV back-up. The plant last suffered a complete loss of off-site power on 4 July 2025, when it ran on diesel for almost four hours.

IAEA director-general Rafael Grossi described the situation as “deeply concerning,” warning that repeated power losses “pose a real risk to nuclear safety and increase the likelihood of a nuclear accident.”

The IAEA said fuel tanks for the generators had recently been replenished with supplies sufficient for about 20 days of operation in case of further losses. The agency’s onsite team is assessing the cause of the latest outage.
The six-unit Zaporizhzhia station fell under Russian military occupation in March 2022, days after the start of Russia’s incursion into Ukraine on 24 February.
All six units have been in cold shutdown mode since September 2022, but they still require a constant supply of electricity to cool residual reactor core activity and spent fuel pools.
The IAEA has repeatedly warned that the loss of off-site power lines remains one of the most serious risks to nuclear safety at the station.
Grossi has visited the facility several times and established a permanent IAEA support and assistance mission at the site in September 2022.

The agency continues to call for the establishment of a nuclear safety and security protection zone around the facility, warning that repeated shelling, loss of external power, and restrictions on staff access increase the risk of a nuclear accident.
IAEA director-general Rafael Grossi tours the Zaporizhzhia nuclear station and its surrounding area during his second official visit to Ukraine on 29 March 2023. Image courtesy Fredrik Dahl/IAEA.

title: Belgium Begins Building Long-Planned Repository For Radioactive Waste
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Dessel facility designed to serve for a period of at least 300 years
Belgium has started construction of its first surface repository for low-and intermediate-level short-lived radioactive waste at Dessel, the national waste agency Ondraf/Niras announced.

A foundation stone ceremony was held on 18 September, led by prime minister Bart De Wever. Ondraf/Niras director-general Marc Demarche said the milestone marks “a unique moment for our country,” adding that the project follows years of preparation, including a 25,000-page safety dossier to demonstrate safety for at least 300 years.
The repository will consist of 34 modules containing almost 29,000 concrete compartments, which will encapsulate the waste in mortar.
A statement said disposal will continue for around 50 years, after which the site will be covered with natural and artificial layers, forming two hills about 20 metres high.

The facility and its surroundings will be monitored for three centuries after closure. A control phase will begin around the first 100 years of operation, when no new waste will be added, with monitoring to 300 years and beyond.
The construction is being carried out by a consortium led by Belgian companies BESIX and Vanhout, who are managing the civil works for the repository project under a joint venture.
BESIX said construction of the first 20 concrete modules will take about five years. Each module will be measuring 25 by 27 metres and 11 metres high, with walls up to 80 centimetres thick.
Ondraf/Niras applied for a licence to build the Dessel repository in 2019. Authorities granted the permit in May 2023.

Dessel, near Antwerp, in Flanders, already hosts Belgium’s centralised interim surface storage facility for radioactive waste, known as Belgoprocess, where conditioned low-and intermediate-level waste is stored pending final disposal.

According to Ondraf/Niras, the total estimated cost for the construction, operation, and closure of the Dessel surface repository, including supporting infrastructure, is approximately €2.6bn ($3.05bn). The figure reflects the overnight capital cost and covers the full lifecycle of the facility.
Mock-up of Belgium’s first near-surface repository for low-and intermediate-level short-lived radioactive waste, under construction at Dessel. Image courtesy Ondraf/Niras.
A mockup of the Dessel repository after its final encapsulaiton, scheduled after the first 100 years of operation. Imace courtesy Ondraf/Niras.

title: SMRs Have Potential To Replace 450 GW Of Coal Generation By 2050, Says NEA Report
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Most near-term opportunity lies in North America

Small modular reactors (SMRs) could replace up to 450 GW of coal-fired generation capacity worldwide by 2050, equivalent to more than today’s entire operating nuclear fleet, according to a new report by the Paris-based OECD Nuclear Energy Agency (NEA).

The study, SMRs for Replacing Coal: Opportunities and Challenges for Small Modular Reactors, identified an immediate global replacement potential of 143 GW by 2035, increasing to 238 GW by 2040 and a further 68 GW after 2040. About 75% of this market could be realised before 2040, the report said.

The NEA said that about 65% of the near-term opportunity lies in North America, driven largely by the US, with Europe accounting for 16% and Asia 12%. Beyond 2040, growth potential shifts towards Asia and Eastern Europe as new nuclear nations join the market.

The report also said that coal-to-nuclear transitions would bring multiple benefits, including significant reductions in CO2 emissions and air pollution, the ability to reuse existing infrastructure and grid connections, and the preservation of skilled jobs in communities where coal plants are closing.

Repurposing former coal sites offers advantages for SMR deployment, including the potential to reuse transmission infrastructure, cooling water resources, and site permits and licensing, compared with building on new sites, the report added.

However, the NEA warned that challenges remain. High upfront investment requirements, regulatory uncertainties, and siting constraints could slow progress. Utilities are often reluctant to act as “first-movers” without policy incentives, government support, or risk-sharing frameworks in place, said the report.

The NEA said that public-private partnerships will be essential, alongside clear regulatory pathways and early community engagement to build social acceptance. Financing frameworks tailored to SMRs are also seen as a priority to bridge the gap between commercial potential and actual deployment.

According to the report, the successful deployment of SMRs at former coal sites could become a cornerstone of the global energy transition. With more than 2,400 GW of coal capacity in operation today, replacing even a fraction of it with SMRs would have a major impact on emissions reduction targets.

The study concluded that while SMRs face significant challenges, they represent a major decarbonisation opportunity if governments and industry act quickly to capture the window of opportunity before 2040.
The Sherburne County (Sherco) generating station, a coal-fired power plant, near Becker, Minnesota. Image courtesy Wikipedia Commons/Tony Webster.

title: Japan Utility Finds ‘Technically Feasible’ Site For Interim Spent Fuel Storage
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Facility needed as nuclear plants are running out of space

Japanese utility Chugoku Electric Power has found a site in Kaminoseki Town, Yamaguchi Prefecture, southern Japan, to be technically feasible for the construction of an interim spent fuel storage facility, following the results of a year-long feasibility study.

According to the Tokyo-based Japan Atomic Industry Forum (Jaif) industry group, the utility said that “there are no technical issues that cannot be addressed”. It has submitted its report to Kaminoseki local authorities, Jaif said.
The study began in response to a February 2023 request from the mayor’s office to consider regional development measures.

Chugoku Electric, which owns and operates the Shimane nuclear power station in Shimane Prefecture, southwestern Japan, has carried out investigations into the possibility of developing a dry storage interim facility on its premises in Nagashima, Kaminoseki, with a key focus on ground conditions.

The company said that while three major active land faults were confirmed within about 30 km and 35 in the surrounding sea area, the site could remain viable through appropriate seismic design measures. Bedrock beneath the proposed site was also judged suitable.
Additional studies of weather, volcanic activity, hydrology, ecosystems, industrial activity and traffic concluded that the facility would not adversely affect the natural or social environment.
Chugoku Electric said it will now prepare a business plan defining the scale of the project and timing of construction.
If built, the Kaminoseki facility would be Japan’s second interim spent fuel storage facility. There is an existing facility at Mutsu, in Aomori Prefecture, northern Japan.
According to Jaif, the project is planned as a joint venture with Kansai Electric Power, owner and operator of the Mihama, Takahama, and Ohi nuclear power stations.
Chugoku Electric announced plans in the late 1990s to build new nuclear plants at Kaminoseki. Preparatory work began in 2009, but was suspended following the 2011 Fukushima disaster.
Japan has been looking for interim spent fuel options as its nuclear plants are running out of pool space to store spent fuel, raising concerns about the ability to keep reactors operating.
The problem originates from delays to the Rokkasho reprocessing plant and the decommissioning of the Monju fast breeder reactor, which derailed plans to recycle plutonium.

Japan’s strategy since the 1970s has been to reprocess spent fuel to recover plutonium and uranium, then reuse the plutonium as MOX fuel in its reactors, but the failure of the Rokkasho and Monju projects meant Japan is increasingly faced with increasing stocks of spent fuel and separated plutonium.
Kaminoseki in southern Japan was hoping to be the site of a new nuclear power plant. Courtesy Kaminoseki Tourism.

title: European Nuclear Society Celebrates 50th Anniversary With Vienna Event
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Guests highlight ‘critical role’ in shaping the future of the industry.

The Brussels-based European Nuclear Society (ENS) celebrated its 50th anniversary on 15 September with a special event bringing together members from across generations, international partners and guests from the global nuclear community.

The celebration was hosted by the Austrian Nuclear Society at the Technical University of Vienna (TU Wien) and included keynote speakers such as William Magwood, director-general of the OECD Nuclear Energy Agency, Aline des Cloizeaux, director of the IAEA’s nuclear power division, Sama Bilbao y León, head of the World Nuclear Association, Jan Panek from the European Commission energy directorate, and Ulla Engelmann, director at the JRC in Germany.
A highlight of the event was an online address by Casimir-Pierre Zaleski, ENS president from 1981 to 1983 and one of the society’s founding members.

ENS was created in 1975 out of the need for closer cooperation across Europe’s nuclear sector. Established initially by 11 organisations, the society has grown to represent 22 national nuclear societies from Europe and beyond, representing 13,500 professionals.

Over five decades, ENS has acted as a hub for knowledge exchange and collaboration. It launched Nuclear Europe, once one of the largest print magazines in the field, supported the creation of organisations such as NucNet (1990), Women in Nuclear (1992), and established internal networks including the ENS Young Generation Network (1995) and the High Scientific Council (2002).

ENS has also organised more than 100 scientific conferences across nuclear disciplines, providing a platform for innovation, dialogue, and policy engagement, and has been instrumental in the Nuclear4Climate initiative focused on nuclear power as one of the tools to tackle climate change.
Speaking at the event, Bilbao y León underlined the critical role of nuclear societies in shaping the future of the industry.
“I cannot overstate how important the role of nuclear societies is, as associations of individual nuclear experts, in moving forward the next generation of nuclear leaders,” she said.

“There is a role that each and every one of the members of the nuclear sector should embrace: to inspire youngsters to consider a career in science and technology… even… in nuclear science and technology.”

Reflecting on the 50-year milestone, ENS leaders emphasised the society’s role as both a bridge between generations and a catalyst for international cooperation, underlining the continuing importance of its mission for the decades ahead.

At a time when nuclear energy may be once again increasingly at the centre of global attention, many see ENS as having a vital role to play in supporting what could become a new renaissance for the sector.

title: First Tier Of Inner Steel Containment Installed At Leningrad 2-3 Nuclear Plant
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Russia site on Gulf of Finland already has four units in operation
The first tier of the inner steel containment has been installed for Unit 3 of the Leningrad 2 nuclear power station on the Gulf of Finland in Russia, state nuclear corporation Rosatom said.
The unit, Leningrad 2-3, will be a VVER-1200 pressurised water reactor with a net capacity of 1,150 MW. Construction began in March 2024.
The inner containment is designed to preserve hermetic conditions during reactor operation and prevent radioactive leakage into the environment in the event of an emergency.
Rosatom said the first tier weighs 227 tonnes, has a height of 10 metres and a diameter of 44 metres.

A VVER-1200 inner steel containment has seven cylindrical tiers. The fifth tier is a transition section between the main cylinder portion and the dome. The dome itself is composed of a lower and upper tier
The Leningrad site has four units in operation and two that are permanently shut down. The operational units are Leningrad-3 and Leningrad-4, Leningrad 2-1 and Leningrad 2-2.
Leningrad-1 and Leningrad-2, both Soviet-era RBMK-1000 light-water graphite units, were permanently shut down in 2018 and 2020 respectively.
Leningrad-3 and Leningrad-4, also Soviet-era RBMK-1000 light-water graphite units, are scheduled for closure.
Concrete was poured in March 2025 for an eight unit, Leningrad 2-4.
Leningrad 2-3 will be a VVER-1200 pressurised water reactor with a net capacity of 1,150 MW. Courtesy Rosatom.

title: Nano Announces Plans To Sell Odin Microreactor Design To UK’s Cambridge Atom Works
author: David Dalton
text: US company plans to focus on Kronos MMR as flagship project

US-based nuclear reactor technology company Nano Nuclear Energy has signed a letter of intent to sell its Odin low-pressure coolant microreactor design to UK company Cambridge Atom Works for $6.2m (€5.2m).

This company said the move will allow it to concentrate on its gas-cooled microreactor portfolio, including the Kronos micro-modular reactor (MMR), the Loki MMR, which is designed for space applications, and the Zeus solid core battery reactor.

“The sale is seen as a way to enhance developmental and regulatory efficiencies and to capitalise on the recent US-UK Atlantic Partnership for Advanced Nuclear Energy, which aims to expedite nuclear power advancements,” Nano said in a statement.

The company plans to focus resources on the Kronos MMR as its flagship project, which is in the licensing process with the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission, while using synergies with the Loki and Zeus reactors for further efficiencies.
The Kronos MMR is a high-temperature gas-cooled reactor, or HTGR, a type of nuclear reactor which uses uranium fuel and graphite moderation to produce very high reactor core output temperatures.
Nano said it expects to receive $5.95m in 2026 and potential future royalties from Odin’s commercialisation.
In April Nano signed an agreement with the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign to build the first research Kronos MMR on the university’s campus.
Rendering of a planned Kronos nuclear microreactor at the University of Illinois in the US. Courtesy Nano Nuclear.

title: Hungary And Russia Agree To Speed Up Paks Nuclear Expansion Project
author: David Dalton
text: Move, announced after high-level meeting, follows recent setback at European Court of Justice

Hungarian foreign minister Péter Szijjártó and Alexey Likhachev, director-general of Russia’s state nuclear corporation Rosatom, have agreed at a meeting to speed up the Paks nuclear power station expansion project.

Hungarian prime minister Viktor Orbán and Russian president Vladimir Putin signed an agreement in 2014 to build two new VVER-1200 nuclear reactor units at the Paks site, about 120 km south of the capital Budapest in central Hungary.

However, earlier this month the European Court of Justice struck down EU approval for Russia to build the new plants, arguing that it was unclear whether Orbán’s government followed EU procurement rules when awarding Rosatom the contract without a public tender.

Judges at the Luxembourg-based court ruled on 11 September that the European Commission should have taken into consideration EU public procurement rules when it approved Budapest’s plans to subsidise the construction.

Hungary’s government said it would continue the project, known as Paks 2, as planned, but was ready to cooperate with the commission to demonstrate it had met public procurement and state aid requirements.
“The court did not say the project failed to meet public procurement rules, only that its reasoning was not satisfactory,” EU affairs minister János Bóka said.
“There is no legal reason not to continue the Paks investment at its current pace.”
Originally scheduled for commissioning in 2023, the project has seen some progress but remains in its early stages, with completion not now realistically expected by the mid-2030s.
In December 2024 Szijjártó announced that the Hungarian nuclear regulator had approved a preliminary safety report for the project, paving the way for the pouring of first concrete.
In August 2024, the core catcher components, part of the first large nuclear island system, were delivered for Unit 1 at Paks 2.

Preparatory works including pit excavations and the construction of a stabilisation groundwater cutoff wall began at Paks II in the summer of 2023. The main construction licence for Paks 2 was issued by the Hungarian regulator in August 2022.

There are already four smaller earlier-generation Russia supplied VVER units at the site, which in 2023 supplied 48.8% of the country’s electricity production, according to International Atomic Energy Agency data.
Hungary’s energy ministry also announced this week it had signed an agreement with China to increase cooperation in nuclear energy.
A rendering of the Paks 2 expanson project in Hungary. Courtesy Paks.

title: European SMR Alliance Adopts Ambitious 10-Point Plan To Address Challenges Of Nuclear Deployment
author: David Dalton
text: Support crucial because reactor development is part of “global technological race”

The European Industrial Alliance on Small Modular Reactors (SMRs) has adopted an ambitious five-year action plan calling for industry and government to address challenges that could help the development, demonstration and deployment of a new generation of reactors in Europe by the early 2030s.

The plan outlines 10 specific and targeted actions to deliver over the next five years, focusing on key challenges to SMR deployment such as market demand for SMRs beyond electricity production, revitalising the supply chain, promoting R&D and skills development, unlocking financial opportunities, and simplifying regulatory frameworks.
The plan also emphasises activities aimed at financing, public engagement, fuel and waste management, as well as the issues related to safety and security.

The plan says the deployment of SMRs is crucial for maintaining the competitiveness of European industry, driving the transition towards a carbon-neutral future by 2050, and improving the EU’s autonomy in the energy sector.

By June 2026 the alliance aims to establish a framework for SMR demonstration pilot projects in applications such as data centres, energy-intensive industry and district heating. This could be achieved through possible tripartite agreements between the public sector, SMR developers, and energy-consuming industries.
By December 2026 the aim is to identify, assess and prioritise experimentation and testing facilities for key R&D needs for SMRs.

The plan says strong market demand and business cases need to be developed for SMRs to attract public and private investments. The process of attracting state aid for nuclear energy needs to be “simplified and accelerated”.

Research and development need to be strengthened and codes and standards for SMRs developed and deployed. These code and standards would be used for R&D and design development, equipment manufacturing and fuel supply.

The plan says regulations need to be simplified to encourage the exchange technology and data between EU member states and a “robust and reliable” European supply chain needs to be established that includes “a dynamic ecosystem” of well-established firms, innovative SMEs and specialised startups.
This support is particularly critical as the development of SMRs is part of “a global technological race”, the plan says.

It warns that a European workforce will need to be equipped with the right skills, public trust will need to be built and further harmonisation of regulatory frameworks and practices in the EU will be essential, both on nuclear and non-nuclear aspects.

“Coordinated progress across multiple areas is essential to enable the effective rollout and sustained impact of SMR projects in Europe over the coming decades,” the plan says. “This integrated approach is critical for ensuring regulatory alignment, infrastructure readiness, public acceptance, and investment mobilisation.”

Amidst a renewed interest in nuclear energy and technologies, many EU member states that use nuclear energy, including France, Slovakia, the Czech Republic, the Netherlands, Sweden, Romania and Bulgaria, as well as newcomers such as Poland and Estonia, have decided to launch ambitious programmes to support new nuclear build. Most of them are also considering the integration of SMRs into their future nuclear fleet.

The European Industrial Alliance on SMRs was established in February 2024 by the European Commission to accelerate the development and deployment of the first SMR projects in Europe in the early 2030s. It brings together more than 350 SMR stakeholders, including industry leaders, researchers and policymakers.

According to the alliance, SMRs and other advanced reactors can provide grid services to accommodate the intermittency of renewables or help decarbonise specific industrial processes, such as hydrogen production or desalination.
Many EU member states are considering the integration of SMRs into their future nuclear fleet. Courtesy GVE.

title: European SMR Consortium Signs Agreement With Three Regulators To Begin Pre-Licensing Initiative
author: David Dalton
text: Companies want to improve standardisation and harmonisation for Eagles-300 nuclear plant

A European consortium whose goal is to develop Eagles-300, a next-generation lead-cooled small modular reactor (SMR) that could be commercialised and deployed globally in 2039, has signed an agreement with three regulators to officially begin an international pre-licensing initiative.
The Eagles consortium signed the agreement the nuclear regulators of Belgium (Fanc), Italy (Isin), and Romania (CNCAN).

The project is the first pilot project under the International Atomic Energy Agency’s Nuclear Harmonisation and Standardisation Initiative, which aims to advance the harmonisation and standardisation of SMR design, construction, regulatory and industrial approaches.

The Eagles-300 consortium comprises Italian construction engineering company Ansaldo Nucleare, Italian research and development agency Enea, Romanian nuclear research and development company Raten, and SCK CEN, the Belgian nuclear research centre.

The consortium said SMRs are designed for global deployment and to become available more quickly through serial production. Yet each country still applies its own nuclear safety rules and licensing procedures.
These different national rules and procedures could require developers to go through separate licensing processes in every country, making it harder to benefit from the scalability of SMRs.

“And that is precisely where international harmonisation can make the difference,” the consortium said. “The Eagles-300 pre-licensing project is a first-of-a-kind initiative. Never before have national regulators collaborated so early in the development process of an advanced small modular reactor.”

By aligning safety standards and regulatory expectations early, the Eagles pre-licensing project aims to reduce duplication, clarify requirements and accelerate the worldwide deployment of advanced SMRs.

The consortium, officially established in June, says it is committed to reinforcing Europe’s leadership in next-generation nuclear reactors, aligning with European Union energy policies and the need for reliable, low-carbon energy sources.
It said: “The Eagles-300 reactor will be designed to offer reliable, affordable and decarbonised energy, setting a new standard for small modular reactors.”

According to the consortium, key features of the Eagles-300 plant will include high power output and grid flexibility, making it suitable for electricity production, industrial heat supply and hydrogen production. Its modular design will mean less investment in construction compared to previous generations, faster construction and flexible deployment.
The Eagles-300 will use mixed-oxide nuclear fuel, including recycled materials, reducing radioactive waste and improving sustainability, the consortium said.
Lead-cooled nuclear plants are not yet operating, but are being developed as next-generation, or Generation IV, reactors.

Lead has a very high boiling temperature of 1,749°C which means the problem of coolant boiling is for all practical purposes eliminated. This brings with it important safety advantages that also result in design simplification and improved economic performance.
International Atomic Energy Agency director-general Rafael Grossi (centre) at the signing of the Eagles-300 agreement in Vienna. Courtesy SCK CEN.

title: Southeast Asia Will Need $208 Billion By 2050 For Nuclear Ambitions, Analysis Shows
author: David Dalton
text: Small modular reactors will emerge as referred technology, says Wood Mackenzie

Southeast Asia’s nuclear ambitions will require $208bn (€176bn) of investments to develop 25 GW of capacity by 2050, with small modular reactors (SMRs) emerging as the preferred technology despite significantly higher costs, according to new analysis.
Currently, Southeast Asia has no operational nuclear capacity, relying heavily on coal and gas for baseload power.
However, growing pressure to decarbonise and concerns over energy security are driving renewed interest in nuclear technology across the region.

A report by UK-based research and analysis firm Wood Mackenzie, ‘What if Southeast Asia goes nuclear?’, analyses the impact on the region if countries dramatically accelerate nuclear power deployment.
The report marks a significant shift from Wood Mackenzie’s current base-case outlook, which projected no nuclear capacity additions in the region before 2050.

According to Wood Mackenzie, SMR technology emerges as the preferred nuclear option in the region, despite a higher generation cost of $220/MWh by 2050, which is more than double the $101/MWh for large conventional nuclear power plants.

Among Southeast Asia countries, only Vietnam and the Philippines have announced plans for large nuclear facilities so far. The Philippines built a nuclear plant with Westinghouse reactors which was completed in 1984, but it was never fuelled and commissioned. The facility, at Battaan, was mothballed due to safety concerns in the wake of the Chernobyl disaster in 1986, nuclear sentiment and issues regarding alleged corruption under the regime of dictator Ferdinand Marcos.

Wood Mackenzie’s nuclear scenario predicts that only Vietnam is likely to deploy a pressurised water reactor (PWR) nuclear power plant. This limited adoption highlights the substantial financial and technical challenges associated with large-scale nuclear development in emerging markets.

According to Wood Mackenzie, Vietnam will be at the forefront of nuclear development in the region, with plans to expand its capacity as early as 2030. Vietnam’s government country is aggressively aiming for its nuclear installations to reach between 10.5 and 14.0 GW by 2050.

“Nuclear power offers Southeast Asian governments an interesting proposition: emissions-free baseload power that can be deployed without major grid upgrades,” said Robert Liew, a director at Wood Mackenzie.
“Yet the region’s limited operational experience raises significant risks around political opposition, cost overruns and long-term uranium fuel security.”
The Philippines built a nuclear plant at Bataan which was completed in 1984, but never fuelled and commissioned. Courtesy Wikipedia/Creative Commons Licence.

title: UK Nuclear Jobs Surge Near 100,000 From Record Government Investment
author: David Dalton
text: NIA report shows boost for England, but calls for action in Scotland and Wales

The UK’s nuclear industry has reached a record high in terms of jobs, with 98,173 people now employed across the sector, according to the London-based Nuclear Industry Association’s (NIA) annual Jobs Map, the sector’s major jobs report.

The figure represents an 11,000 increase on last year’s total and a 55% surge over the past decade, driven by £14.2bn (€16.3bn, $19.3bn) of additional government investment in Sizewell C, £2.5bn for small modular reactors, and major ongoing decommissioning programmes.

Hinkley Point C, where two France-supplied EPR nuclear units are under construction, has tripled the southwest region’s nuclear workforce – from 8,200 in 2015 to over 31,000 today – making it the country’s largest nuclear hub. The project has also brought £5.3bn of investment into the region, with the benefits soon to be replicated by Sizewell C in Suffolk, which will support 70,000 jobs across the country.

Decommissioning continues to generate high-quality jobs and investment in communities from Dounreay at the northern tip of Scotland to Dungeness and Winfrith on the south coast, the NIA said the northwest is the centre of this work, with 12,000 employees at the Sellafield nuclear site, as well as wider work in the fuel cycle, reactor design, and research.

NIA chief executive Tom Greatrex said the industry is pushing for a change of policy in Scotland, which saw the slowest growth in nuclear employment of any part of the country. The devolved Scottish government has said it does not want to build new nuclear plants.
“Scotland has a good site for new nuclear in Torness and an urgent need for industrial employment after decades of brutal decline,” Greatrex said.
“Similarly, we want to see a clear future laid out for Wylfa in Wales, which again has lagged behind England in nuclear job creation.
“This is and should be a British programme, and we want to see the opportunities brought to every part of the country.”

The jobs figures were released as the UK and US announced a landmark deal to boost the building of nuclear plants in both countries, clearing the way for a major expansion of new nuclear projects and the speeding up of approvals for new reactors.

The deal – known as the Atlantic Partnership for Advanced Nuclear Energy – is expected to be signed during US president Donald Trump’s state visit to the UK this week and could see multiple leading US nuclear companies build projects in the UK.
The nuclear jobs figure represents an 11,000 increase on last year’s total. Courtesy EDF Energy.

title: China State Group Puts Forward Plans For ‘Coal To Nuclear’ Revolution
author: David Dalton
text: Retiring plants could be given a new lease of life and help Beijing reach decarbonisation goals
A Chinese state-owned energy infrastructure group has proposed a decarbonisation plan that would increase the country’s use of nuclear power by deploying new reactors at coal sites.
China Energy Engineering Group (CEEC) is studying ways to convert retiring coal-fired facilities into nuclear power plants, according to the Hong Kong-based South China Morning Post.

CEEC has said its “Coal to Nuclear,” or C2N, strategy would enable new reactors to take advantage of the existing land, grid, and water access of coal-fired plants, which would enable faster construction of new nuclear power reactors.

Government data shows China has about 1.2 TW of coal-fired power generation capacity, with about 100 GW slated for retirement in the next five years. The South China Morning Post said China’s existing coal capacity is “enough to run the entire United States”.

It said that by repurposing coal plants’ established grid links, cooling systems and land, China hopes to cut costs, save time, and ease the challenge of finding suitable new sites for nuclear projects.

Globally, coal-fired plants are responsible for 30% of energy-related carbon dioxide emissions. In China, coal still generates over half of the country’s electricity, making it the single largest source of greenhouse gases. China produced 4.71 billion tonnes of coal in 2023, accounting for over half of global production.

According to the South China Morning Post, China could be the only country capable of a major coal to nuclear programme because its Generation IV reactors can generate much hotter steam than ordinary reactors to power the coal-fired gas turbines with high efficiency, are already up and running.
China is home to what it says is the world’s first operational Generation IV nuclear power plant, Shidao Bay-1, which began commercial operation in December 2023.
This high-temperature gas-cooled reactor-pebble-bed module, or HTR-PM, uses helium for cooling, boasts passive safety features, and is a significant advancement in nuclear technology.
China is not the only country planning to use existing coal plant infrastructure for new nuclear.

In the US, TerraPower, a company founded by Bill Gates, is building its first Natrium reactor at a former coal site in Wyoming.  Just this week, energy technology company Holtec, EDF and Tritax said they are planning to develop advanced data centres powered by small modular reactors at the former Cottam coal-fired power station in Nottinghamshire, eastern England. That announcement was part of a string of potential deals planned by the UK and the U and announced in the runup to president Donald Trump’ state visit to the UK.
The US Department of Energy has identified more than 400 coal sites that could potentially be home to new nuclear power generation.
​According to the US Energy Information Administration, China has the fastest nuclear growth rate in the world with 57 reactors commissioned since 1991.
According to International Atomic Energy Agency data, China has 57 nuclear plants in commercial operation and another 29 with a combined capacity of more than 30 GW under construction.
In China, coal still generates over half of the country’s electricity. Courtesy Tobixen/Wikipedia Creative Commons Licence.

title: Europe’s Top Court Rejects Approval Of Russia-Backed Paks II Nuclear Project In Hungary
author: David Dalton
text: Budapest ‘willing to cooperate’, but vows to continue with new reactors as planned
