“Unlike previous attempts, our method is massively scalable, pragmatically achievable, and economically irresistible,” Marathon said.
It said that in deuterium-tritium fusion, high-energy neutrons drive “multiplication” reactions by producing the tritium needed to sustain operation.

Marathon said its approach makes use of those neutrons to drive a multiplication reaction on mercury-198 to produce mercury-197, which then decays in a few days to gold-197, the only stable isotope of gold.

One potential complication is that the presence of other types of mercury is likely to result in the production of unstable gold isotopes alongside gold-197, meaning the metal could be partially radioactive. Marathon estimates this could mean the gold has to be stored for 14 to 18 years for it to be labelled completely safe.

“The technology described could have a major impact on the economics of fusion energy if it’s able to be fully realised and integrated into upcoming power plants,” said Dan Brunner, former chief technology officer of Commonwealth Fusion Systems, a spinout from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, and scientific advisor to Marathon.

“Improved economics could further relax some engineering and scientific requirements, accelerating the path to commercial deployment. This is potentially highly impactful, and I'll be paying close attention to the results of rigorous peer review.”

Marathon was founded in 2023 by chief executive Kyle Schiller and chief technology officer Adam Rutkowski as an engineering company aiming to solve some of the technical challenges of building fusion power plants.
The startup, which has 12 full-time employees, has raised $5.9m in investment and about $4m in US government grants to date.

Initially the team worked on challenges such as how to make the fuel burning system in a fusion power plant more efficient and started thinking about the possibilities of nuclear transmutation earlier this year.
A prototype nuclear fusion reactor. Courtesy UKAEA.

title: Advanced Reactor Developer Kairos Installs RPV At Nuclear Test Unit
author: David Dalton
text: Company aims to deploy Generation IV KP-FHR technology

US advanced nuclear reactor developer Kairos Power has successfully installed the reactor pressure vessel (RPV) for its third Engineering Test Unit (ETU 3.0) at the company’s campus in Oak Ridge, Tennessee.
The four-metre vessel is the central component in Kairos’ non-nuclear ETU 3.0 reactor mockup and its installation marks a significant milestone for the company in the construction of the facility.

Kairos is using its ETU programme to validate a safe, cost-effective pathway for the future deployment of its Generation IV fluoride salt-cooled high-temperature reactor (KP-FHR) technology in the US.

The ETU 3.0 facility will serve as a vital proving ground to refine civil construction methods and quality assurance procedures for Kairos’s Hermes Low-Power Demonstration Reactor, and will ultimately support the Hermes reactor as an operator training centre and test platform for remote handling and maintenance equipment.
The RPV for the ETU 3.0 was fabricated in partnership with the UK’s University of Sheffield and Cambridge, England-based mechanical engineering company Cambridge Vacuum Engineering.
In May, Kairos completed the first installation of nuclear safety-related concrete for the Hermes Low-Power Demonstration Reactor, marking the start of “nuclear construction” on the project.
Hermes is a scaled demonstration of the KP-FHR technology and the first advanced nuclear reactor to receive a construction permit from the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission.

In October tech company Google announced it would back the construction of seven SMRs from Kairos Power, becoming the first tech company to commission new nuclear power plants to provide low-carbon electricity for its energy-hungry data centres.
The RPV is the central component in Kairos’ non-nuclear ETU 3.0 reactor mockup. Courtesy Kairos Power.

title: WNTI And Nemo Join Forces To ‘Help Shape Future’ Of Maritime Nuclear Power
author: David Dalton
text: UK-based organisations to champion development of international standards

The World Nuclear Transport Institute (WNTI) and the Nuclear Energy Maritime Organisation (Nemo) have signed a memorandum of understanding to jointly help shape the future of nuclear-powered shipping and transportable nuclear power plants.

The partnership aims to champion the development of international standards for both the transport of nuclear and radioactive materials and the use of nuclear energy at sea or in remote deployment locations.

Under the MoU, WNTI will focus on the transport of nuclear materials and transportable nuclear power plants. Nemo will lead on issues related to nuclear-powered and propelled ships, including regulation, design, and operations.
For floating nuclear power plants, both organisations will work side by side.

The two organisations, both based in London, England, said the partnership comes at a pivotal moment, as the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) looks to launch the Atlas programme later this year, designed to help countries develop regulations and guidance for the transport of small modular reactors (SMRs) and use of nuclear energy at sea.

According to the International Maritime Organisation (IMO), the maritime shipping industry is responsible for approximately 2.9% of global carbon emissions, and reducing this to meet net zero targets is a priority.

WNTI and Nemo said civil nuclear propulsion offers a pathway to eliminate greenhouse gas emissions from shipping by replacing fossil-fuelled engines with compact, emission-free nuclear propulsion systems.

Meanwhile, transportable nuclear power plants (TNPPs) can be delivered by sea or land to regions that lack reliable grid infrastructure or face energy security challenges. Once deployed, these reactors generate clean electricity – and in some cases, high-temperature steam or heat on site. In addition to electricity, TNPPs can support power-hungry applications like hydrogen generation or seawater desalination.
Nuclear propulsion offers a pathway to eliminate greenhouse gas emissions from shipping by replacing fossil-fuelled engines with compact reactor systems. Courtesy HD KSOE.

title: French Startup Raises €23 Million In Bid To Develop Fast Neutron Molten Salt Reactor
author: David Dalton
text: Stellaria wants first production unit ready for commercial deployment by 2035
French startup Stellaria has raised €23m ($26m) to develop its fast neutron molten salt nuclear reactor by 2035.
The new round of funding comes two years after a successful first round in 2023.

The round was co-led by US impact fund At One Ventures and Supernova Invest, alongside Stellaria’s historical investors, including CEA Investissements, Schneider Electric, Exergon, and Technip Energies.

Stellaria, which was founded by the French Alternative Energies and Atomic Energy Commission (CEA) and France-based technology company Schneider Electric, said the funding will be used to finance all the technical and regulatory studies necessary to establish a first molten-salt facility capable of sustaining a fission reaction, scheduled for 2029.
Stellaria aims to double its workforce to accelerate R&D around its reactor and finalise the development of a liquid-core fast-neutron reactor demonstrator.
It also plans to invest in its research laboratory in Grenoble and submit an application to the safety authorities for the construction of its prototype.
Founded in 2023, Stellaria is developing the Stellarium, a Generation IV molten-salt nuclear reactor capable of fully “regenerating” its fuel during operation.
This means the plant will be self-sufficient for more than 20 years, while reducing long-lived nuclear waste.
The Stellarium can be fuelled by uranium, plutonium or thorium depending on the chosen specification.
The first production unit is expected to be offered for commercial deployment by 2035.
The Stellarium reactor can be fuelled by uranium, plutonium or thorium. Courtesy Stellaria.

title: US Announces Start Of Pilot Programme To Accelerate Advanced Reactors And Strengthen Fuel Supply
author: David Dalton
text: DOE wants at least three designs that have potential to achieve criticality by 4 July 2026
The US Department of Energy (DOE) has announced the start of a new pilot programme to accelerate the development of advanced nuclear reactors and strengthen domestic supply chains for nuclear fuel.
The DOE said it had issued a request for application and is seeking qualified US companies to build and operate nuclear fuel production lines.

It said the initiative will help end the US’s reliance on foreign sources of enriched uranium and critical materials, while opening the door for private sector investment in the country’s nuclear renaissance.
The move supports president Donald Trump’s recent executive orders to reform nuclear reactor testing at the DOE and deploy nuclear reactor technologies for national security.
Trump directed the government to fast-track construction of nuclear reactors and reform the “risk averse” culture of regulation in a bid to quadruple the US’s nuclear energy capacity by 2050.
The programme will establish a domestic nuclear fuel supply chain for testing new reactors, the DOE said.

“America has the resources and the expertise to lead the world in nuclear energy development, but we need secure domestic supply chains to fuel this rapidly growing energy source and achieve a true nuclear energy renaissance,” said energy secretary Chris Wright.

Last month the DOE launched a new reactor pilot programme to speed up the testing of advanced reactor designs that will be authorised at sites outside of the nation’s network of federal National Laboratories.
The pilot programme builds on current efforts to demonstrate advanced reactors on DOE sites through microreactor testbeds and other projects led by the Department of Defense and private industry.
The DOE said it is reviewing potential applicants and anticipates selecting at least three advanced reactor designs later this summer that have the potential to achieve criticality by 4 July 2026.
Advanced reactors aim to be cleaner, safer, and more efficient than previous generations, offering potential for power generation, process heat and other industrial uses.
However, the US currently lacks the sufficient domestic nuclear fuel resources to meet projected demand, the DOE said.
The DOE wants to choose at least three advanced reactor designs later this summer that have the potential to achieve criticality by 4 July 2026. Courtesy INL.

title: Framatome Signs Agreement For Supply Of Nuclear Fuel Assemblies To Barakah Nuclear Station
author: David Dalton
text: Deal is part of UAE’s plans to diversify supplies

French nuclear company Framatome and Emirates Nuclear Energy Corporation (Enec) have signed an agreement for the supply of nuclear fuel assemblies and engineering services for the Barakah nuclear power station in the United Arab Emirates.

Enec, the state entity established to oversee nuclear power projects in the UAE, said the agreement is a key step in its long-term strategy to diversify its fuel supply chain and ensure an uninterrupted supply of 24/7 power from the four-unit Barakah.
Under the agreement, Framatome will supply complete nuclear fuel assemblies for use at Barakah.
Framatome said the fuel assemblies will be fabricated at its fabrication facility in the US, which is licenced by the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission.
Framatome will provide engineering support services from its US headquarters in Lynchburg, Virginia.

Mohamed Al Hammadi, managing director and chief executive officer of Enec, said: “Our agreement with Framatome advances our strategy to strengthen the security and reliability of our nuclear fuel supply chain.
“Diversification is key to ensuring that we continue to deliver safe, clean, and reliable electricity – powering the sustainable growth of the UAE’s economy.”

Construction of Barakah, the first commercial nuclear power station to operate in the Arab World, began in 2012. The first of its four South Korea-supplied APR1400 plants began commercial operation in April 2021. The fourth and final unit began commercial operation in September 2024.
Barakah is the first commercial nuclear power station to operate in the Arab World. Courtesy Enec.

title: Orano And Denison Resume Uranium Operations At McClean Lake Using Sabre Method
author: David Dalton
text: Operations at Canada site suspended in 2008 in response to weak prices

Joint venture partners Orano Canada and Denison Mines have restarted uranium operations at McClean Lake in Canada, now using a patented mining method known surface access borehole resource extraction, or Sabre.

Orano Canada owns a 77.5% interest and is the operator of the McClean Lake joint venture and Denison owns a 22.5% interest. The McClean Lake property is within the eastern part of the Athabasca Basin in northern Saskatchewan.
Orano and Denison announced last year that they planned to restart uranium mining operations at McClean Lake.
Operations were suspended in 2008 in response to weak uranium prices.
The property consists of four mineral leases covering an area of 1,147 hectares and 13 mineral claims over an area of 3,111 hectares.
Orano said Sabre mining of the McClean North uranium deposit began in June with approximately 250 tonnes of high-grade ore recovered from the first mining cavity.

Orano Canada also reported that it had successfully backfilled the first cavity, advanced the Sabre rig to the planned second mining cavity, and begun processing of the recovered ore at the McClean Lake mill.

Xavier Saint Martin Tillet, president of Orano Mining said: “The first commercial production of uranium with the Sabre technique marks a new chapter, allowing us to access and explore new territories.”
According to Orano, Sabre is a non-entry, surface-based mining method that uses a high-pressure water jet placed at the bottom of a drill hole to excavate a mining cavity.

Orano said Sabre has the potential to allow for access to relatively small high-grade orebodies in Canada’s Athabasca Basin that are either too small or too deep to be mined economically by conventional open-pit and underground mining methods.
The McClean Lake uranium mill in Canada’s Athabasca Basin. Courtesy: Denison Mines Corp.

title: Rolls-Royce SMR And ČEZ Sign Agreement To Begin Site-Specific Work For Reactor At Temelín
author: David Dalton
text: Nuclear plant supplied by UK company could be built in Czech Republic in mid-2030s

UK-based nuclear plant developer Rolls-Royce SMR and Czech utility ČEZ have signed an early works agreement enabling site-specific work to begin for a new small modular reactor (SMR) at the Temelín site.

Under the agreement, a joint team will begin site-specific activities, initially focused on the Temelín site – home to the existing Temelín nuclear power station, operated by ČEZ, in the southern Czech Republic. Additional deployment opportunities are also being explored at Tusimice in the northwest of the country.
The first SMR is expected to be built at Temelín in the mid-2030s, a statement said.
The agreement builds on the signing this week by UK prime minister Keir Starmer and Czech prime minister Petr Fiala of a commitment to work together to seize SMR opportunities in both countries.
ČEZ has already chosen Rolls-Royce SMR as its preferred SMR technology partner to provide up to 3,000 MW of energy for the Czech Republic.

Rolls-Royce SMR chief executive officer Chris Cholerton, said: “This agreement is an important step forward in our partnership with ČEZ, demonstrating our shared ambition to move at pace to deliver reliable, clean nuclear power in the Czech Republic.”

Tomas Pleskac, a member of the board and director of the new energy division at ČEZ, said SMRs represent a significant opportunity for the Czech economy and are an essential part of the ongoing energy transformation.
The early works at Temelín will include regulatory approvals and licensing, environmental assessments and preparatory site work.
Each Rolls-Royce SMR will generate 470 MW of clean, affordable electricity – enough to power one million homes – and is designed to operate for at least 60 years.
Each Rolls-Royce SMR will generate 470 MW of clean, affordable electricity – enough to power one million homes. Courtesy Rolls-Royce SMR.

title: Westinghouse And Google Collaborate On AI To ‘Transform’ Construction Of Nuclear Power Plants
author: David Dalton
text: Tools will also optimise performance of current reactor fleet

Westinghouse Electric Company and Google Cloud are collaborating to use artificial intelligence (AI) tools to transform the construction of advanced Westinghouse nuclear reactors into an “efficient, repeatable process”.

Together, the two companies will pair Westinghouse’s powerful Hive and Bertha nuclear AI solutions with Google Cloud technologies and expertise to streamline construction of new nuclear plants. AI tools will also improve the current nuclear fleet with data-driven AI insights.

Westinghouse interim chief executive officer Dan Sumner said that by partnering with Google Cloud to enhance the Hive and Bertha technology, the company can accelerate the deployment of new AP1000 units while implementing powerful AI technologies that will optimise the construction and operations of nuclear power plants.
Kyle Jessen, managing director, commercial industries at Google Cloud, said AI can give companies a “critical competitive advantage”.

As part of the collaboration, Westinghouse and Google Cloud have already achieved a first-of-a-kind proof of concept using Westinghouse’s WNEXUS digital plant design platform and Hive AI to autonomously generate and optimise modular construction work packages for Westinghouse’s AP1000 nuclear plant.

Westinghouse introduced Hive and Bertha in September 2024. These nuclear-specific AI solutions are intended to optimise the deployment of the company’s large-scale AP1000 reactor, AP300 small modular reactor and eVinci microreactor technologies.

Westinghouse said Hive will be a game-changing capability that will drive improved cost and schedule through the entire reactor lifecycle from design, licensing, manufacturing, construction and operations.

Hive features the Bertha nuclear large language model (LLM) AI system, named after Bertha Lamme, the first woman in the US to receive a mechanical engineering degree – in 1893 – and who then became the first female engineer hired by Westinghouse.
LLMs are machine learning models that can comprehend and generate human language text. They work by analysing massive data sets of language.
Vogtle-3 and Vogtle-4 in the US state of Georgia were the last two Westinghouse AP1000 nuclear plants to begin commercial operation. Courtesy Georgia Power.

title: Nuclear Energy Maritime Organisation Strengthens Global Role With NGO Status At IMO And IAEA
author: David Dalton
text: Nemo welcomes ‘major milestone’ for role of reactors

The Nuclear Energy Maritime Organisation (Nemo) has officially been granted non-governmental organisation consultative status at the International Maritime Organisation (IMO) and has been formally invited to regularly attend the sessions of the general conference of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA).
Nemo said it will now actively contribute to global discussions and policy development at the highest levels of international governance at the IAEA and IMO.

This status enables Nemo to provide expert insights, technical guidance, and recommendations on the integration of nuclear technologies in shipping, offshore energy systems and floating nuclear power plants, a statement said.

Nemo is expected to participate in the IAEA’s Atomic Technologies Licensed for Applications at Sea (Atlas) initiative, which is due to launch later in 2025 and is the agency’s international programme supporting the development of regulatory frameworks for nuclear energy at sea.

“This major milestone reflects the growing importance of nuclear innovation in the maritime sphere for achieving global decarbonisation and energy security goals,” said Nemo chairman Mamdouh El-Shanawany.

Nemo was founded in London last year to establish global standards and regulations for the deployment, operation and decommissioning of nuclear power in the maritime environment and promote the commercialisation of nuclear power at sea.

Founding members include Asian shipbuilding giant HD Korea Shipbuilding & Offshore Engineering, TerraPower, a leading US small modular reactor (SMR) company founded by Bill Gates, Westinghouse EC, class society Lloyd’s Register, and Denmark’s Seaborg, an innovator in molten salt reactors.
Nemo, founded last year in London, is promoting the commercialisation of nuclear power at sea. Courtesy Hapag Lloyd.

title: UK-Czech Small Modular Reactor Agreement Will Kickstart ‘Golden Age Of Nuclear’
author: David Dalton
text: Countries ‘can be frontrunners’ in global race to build and export new technology

A “landmark” agreement between the UK and the Czech Republic will see the two countries work closer together on small modular reactors (SMRs) and kickstart what London called “the golden age of nuclear”.

The agreement, signed by UK prime minister Keir Starmer and Czech prime minister Petr Fiala at Downing Street, London, will unlock new opportunities for industrial collaboration and the potential for the UK and the Czech Republic to export SMRs to other countries in Europe, a statement said.

The signing follows UK government backing for new nuclear in its recent spending review, including the selection of Rolls-Royce SMR as preferred bidder to build the UK’s first SMRs and a £14.2bn (16.3bn $19bn) investment
to build two new large-scale EPR nuclear units at Sizewell C in Suffolk, southeast England.

Last week, during French president Emmanuel Macron’s state visit to the UK, French energy giant EDF confirmed it will take a 12.5% stake
in Sizewell C, taking the project one step closer to being given the green light.

The agreement between London and Prague will support the delivery of up to six new reactors in the Czech Republic by Rolls-Royce SMR, a subsidiary of engineering company Rolls-Royce, potentially worth billions of pounds.
It comes after Rolls Royce SMR and the Czech Republic’s largest public company, ČEZ, agreed last year to partner on SMR deployment, with ČEZ acquiring a 20% stake in the British company.

According to the International Energy Agency, the global SMR market is projected to reach up to nearly £500bn by 2050, with the agreement potentially giving the UK and the Czech Republic the competitive advantage as frontrunners in the global race to build and export new nuclear technology.

The UK government said building more nuclear will help drive the country’s energy security by replacing the country’s dependency on fossil fuel markets controlled by dictators with clean power controlled by the UK.

The government said it has pledged over £2.5bn for the overall SMR programme – with this project potentially supporting up to 3,000 new skilled jobs and powering the equivalent of around three million homes.

“Small modular reactors are also smaller and quicker to build than traditional nuclear plants, with costs likely to come down as units are rolled out, helping to delivering clean, homegrown energy for British billpayers,” the government said.

Starmer said that by working with Czech partners on SMRs, “we’re backing British engineering, strengthening our industrial base, and putting the UK in a leading position to export the technologies of the future”.
Fiala said that nuclear energy holds significant potential for the coming years, as the sector is undergoing “a true renaissance”.

“That is why I am especially pleased that ČEZ and Rolls-Royce will cooperate on the development and production of small modular reactors. This collaboration will bring tangible benefits to both Czech and British economies, including job creation,” he said.

In a separate statement on social media Fiala said: “We are working to make sure one of the production facilities is located in the Czech Republic. It’s an important move for our energy security and a major opportunity for Czech industry.”

Rolls-Royce SMR welcomed the agreement. Chief executive Chris Cholerton, said: “Political cooperation is a cornerstone of the civil nuclear industry and today’s meeting between the UK and Czech prime ministers highlights the significant partnership that has been secured between Rolls-Royce SMR and Czech state utility, ČEZ.
“We welcome the desire from both governments to accelerate the development of SMR technology and will work with them to optimise opportunities for supply chain localisation.”
The agreement will support the delivery of up to six new reactors in the Czech Republic by Rolls-Royce SMR. Courtesy Rolls-Royce SMR.
The agreement was signed by UK prime minister Keir Starmer (right) and Czech prime minister Petr Fiala at Downing Street, London. Courtesy Government of Czech Republic.

title: Japan’s Tepco Says No Plans To Build New Nuclear Plants, With Focus On Restarts
author: NucNet Staff Writer
text: Company now seeking to continue construction of unit at Higashi Dori

Tokyo Electric Power Company (Tepco) has confirmed it has no plans to build new nuclear power plants in Japan, but is instead focused on restarting idled reactors, particularly at the world’s largest nuclear power station at Kashiwazaki Kariwa and at Higashi Dori.

Since the 2011 shutdown of 54 reactors following the Fukushima earthquake and tsunami, Japan’s energy mix has relied on fossil fuel imports for about 90% of its energy. Fourteen reactors have been returned to service since 2011, producing less than 10% of national electricity, compared to almost 30% from a fleet of 54 units before 2011.

Tepco told NucNet that new-build projects are not on the company’s radar. Instead Tepco is directing resources towards reactivating reactors with existing permissions, a response to national policy shifts and rising electricity demand.

In February 2025, Japan’s Cabinet approved a revised energy plan, signalling a shift in language from reducing nuclear dependence to the “maximum utilisation of nuclear power generation” alongside renewables.
In the first update to the plan in about three years, the government vowed to work towards the restart of idled nuclear reactors and the refurbishment of aging reactors.
Restarting Kashiwazaki Kariwa is vital not just for capacity, but for energy security and economics, Tepco has said. Tepco could gain about $700m (€598m) in annual profits, according to Reuters.

A Tepco spokesperson told NucNet: “We currently have no concrete plans to develop or construct a next-generation nuclear power plant,” but will instead “work toward restarting Kashiwazaki Kariwa nuclear power station and realising the construction of Unit 1 of the Higashi Dori nuclear power station”.

Tepco has implemented extensive post-Fukushima retrofits to two of the seven units Kashiwazaki Kariwa. Unit 7 was “technically ready” to restart operation in March 2025 and Unit 6 is expected to follow in summer 2025, but Tepco said it will first gain the support and understanding of the local community.
The Tepco spokesperson told NucNet: “At Kashiwazaki-Kariwa… we will continue our activities… to answer [local] questions and concerns… and to provide thorough explanations to the local people.”

The Higashi Dori nuclear station is in Aomori Prefecture, northern Japan. The site comprises two adjacent reactor areas with Tepco owning two units which are under construction, while Tohoku Electric owns two other units – one started operation in 2005 but was shut down in 2011 and the second never officially started construction. Tepco is now seeking to continue construction of one of its units.
Tepco said it remains aware of next-generation technology, noting that small modular reactors and other innovative reactor types are being monitored, but with no immediate commercialisation plans.
“We recognise that momentum for research and development of next-generation innovative reactors, including small reactors, is increasing,” the spokesperson said.

Masanori Tsuruda, deputy commissioner for international affairs at the Ministry of Economy and Trade and Industry of Japan, recently told a conference that Japan’s nuclear policy focus is on restating nuclear plants and making maximum use of existing reactors.
However, he said next-generation nuclear technologies and advanced reactors remain in Tokyo’s scope.
Tsuruda said Japan is focusing its effort to establish “a robust” nuclear supply chain.
Tepco has implemented extensive post-Fukushima retrofits to two of the seven units Kashiwazaki Kariwa. Courtesy Tepco.

title: Kazakhstan Signs MOU To Supply Uranium For Slovakia’s Nuclear Plants
author: David Dalton
text: European country wants to diversify sources away from Russia

Kazakhstan’s national nuclear company Kazatomprom has signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with Slovakia that includes plans to establish supplies of natural uranium concentrate* and potential deliveries of uranium dioxide (UO2)** for Slovak nuclear power plants.
The MOU, signed with Slovakian power company Slovenske Elektrarne, also includes proposals to explore “additional areas of future cooperation”, Kazatomprom said in a statement on 14 July.
Slovenske Elektrarne is Slovakia’s largest electricity producer. It generates over 70% of Slovakia’s total electricity supply and operates two nuclear power stations – Bohunice and Mochovce.
Bohunice has two Russia-supplied VVER units and Mochovce has three units, also Russia-suppled VVERs. Another VVER is under construction at Mochovce.
“By signing this memorandum, we are taking an important step towards strengthening cooperation with our European partners,” said Kazatomprom chief executive officer Meirzhan Yussupov.
Branislav Strycek, chief executive officer and chairman of Slovenske Elektrarne, emphasised the strategic importance of diversifying nuclear fuel supply sources.
Slovakia primarily sources its nuclear fuel from Russia, through the company Tvel, a subsidiary of state nuclear corporation Rosatom.

However, Bratislava is working to diversify its nuclear fuel supply and reduce its dependence on Russia, particularly following the invasion of Ukraine. It is in the process of securing fuel from other sources, including US-based Westinghouse and France’s Framatome.

Slovakia’s prime minister Robert Fico said recently that Slovakia was preparing to sign an intergovernmental agreement with the US that would pave the way for Westinghouse to build a new nuclear reactor unit at the existing Bohunice site.
Slovakia’s five nuclear reactors units generated about 60% of electric power in 2023, according to data by the International Atomic Energy Agency.

* Natural uranium concentrate, often referred to as yellowcake, is a concentrated form of uranium extracted from uranium ore. It’s a crucial intermediate product in the nuclear fuel cycle, used to produce fuel for nuclear reactors.
** Uranium dioxide is a crystalline powder and a primary fuel material used in nuclear reactors.

title: Hitachi Announces ‘Metaverse’ Platform That Can Improve Nuclear Plant Construction And Maintenance
author: David Dalton
text: Technology allows virtual access to facilities through sharing of digital twin

Japan-based Hitachi has announced the development of a new virtual reality “metaverse” platform for nuclear power plants that uses metaverse and AI technology to streamline operations and help with construction, maintenance and decommissioning.

The platform recreates nuclear power plants in a metaverse and can improve information sharing, schedule coordination and asset management by being shared with partners such as electric utilities and contractors, Hitachi said.

The platform streamlines operations such as design, onsite construction, maintenance and asset management by sharing a digital twin of a nuclear plant with electric utilities and partners such as contractors.
When new equipment is installed or modifications are made to nuclear power plants, precise planning and reliable execution are essential to complete onsite work to schedule.
However, access to nuclear power plants is often restricted by regulations, limiting the opportunities to prepare for construction and maintenance work.
In some cases, controlled zones are not accessible during operation, restricting onsite surveys.
“These constraints require extensive coordination among stakeholders, with electric utilities playing a central role in sharing information and revising work plans,” Hitachi said.

According to Hitachi, the metaverse platform can improve productivity by allowing for the sharing of site conditions among stakeholders, real-time schedule coordination and reductions to the amount of rework.

The company also said the platform would help address the skills shortage that arose when Japan’s nuclear power plants were shut down for extended periods following the 2011 Fukushima earthquake and tsunami.

“During this time, the industry experienced a wave of retirements among highly skilled and knowledgeable personnel, a decline in onsite training opportunities for new plant construction, and a shrinking labour force due to demographic changes such as an aging population and declining birthrate,” Hitachi said.
“These factors have made knowledge transfer and productivity enhancement pressing challenges across the nuclear sector.”
The platform was developed with GlobalLogic, the Hitachi-owned digital engineering company based in Silicon Valley, California.
Access to nuclear power plants is often restricted by regulations, limiting the opportunities to prepare for construction and maintenance work.

title: Nano Nuclear And UrAmerica To Cooperate On Developing Argentina’s Uranium Industry
author: David Dalton
text: Buenos Aires looking to reform nuclear sector to attract international investment

Nano Nuclear Energy, a US company specialised in advanced nuclear technologies, has signed a memorandum of understanding with UrAmerica to help modernise and develop Argentina’s nuclear fuel supply chain.
UrAmerica is a private critical metals exploration company holding exploration licences for resources, including uranium, primarily located in Chubut Province in southern Argentina.
UrAmerica’s extensive land package, within the San Jorge Basin in Chubut, contains one of Latin America’s most prolific uranium deposits, the company said.

The MOU formalises negotiations between the two companies around opportunities related to uranium mining and conversion of uranium ore into uranium hexafluoride (UF6), a critical compound for nuclear fuel production.
Discussions could lead to definitive contracts on specific projects, notably in extraction, processing and nuclear fuel supply sectors, Nano Nuclear said.
Both companies are considering uranium purchase agreements and potential investments in mining infrastructure and nuclear fuel cycle facilities.

Other plans include possible joint partnerships and various industrial collaborations aimed at modernising Argentina’s nuclear sector while ensuring a reliable source of critical materials for the US.

Argentina holds some of the most significant uranium reserves globally. The Argentine government is studying partial privatisation of its nuclear sector to attract international investments and reinforce its industrial and technological capabilities.

According to the Paris-based Nuclear Energy Agency, Argentina’s uranium resources total only about 11,000 tonnes uranium (tU), although Buenos Aires estimates that there is some 80,000 tU as exploration targets.

“Through this MOU, Nano Nuclear and UrAmerica aim to build the mining and milling capacities of the uranium supply chain in Argentina with the intention to be a part of the uranium fuel cycle exports into the US,” a statement said.
“Argentina holds substantial deposits of strategic metals, like uranium, that could be a strategic supplier to us in the future,” said James Walker, chief executive officer of Nano Nuclear.

“The timing is also favourable, as the Argentine government is actively looking to reform its nuclear sector to attract international investment. We look forward to advancing our discussions and exploring future opportunities in South America.”
Argentina’s president Javier Milei has said he wants the country to build nuclear reactors to power technology sectors such as artificial intelligence.
Argentina has three operating commercial power reactors – a Candu unit at the Embalse nuclear station and two Siemens KWU-designed PHWR units at Atucha.
It is building the Carem25 small modular reactor and is planning to build a third unit at Atucha.
UrAmerica holds exploration licences for resources, including uranium, primarily located in Chubut Province in southern Argentina. Courtesy UrAmerica.

title: Canada’s ARC Completes Key Design Review In Bid To Licence SMR
author: David Dalton
text: Sodium-cooled plant ‘ready for next stages’ of development

Canada-based nuclear power plant developer ARC Clean Technology announced on 9 July that it has achieved a major milestone with the successful completion of Phase 2 of the Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission (CNSC) vendor design review for its advanced small modular reactor, the ARC-100.
In its report, the CNSC concluded that no fundamental barriers to licensing have been identified, marking a pivotal step toward the commercial deployment of the ARC-100.
The ARC-100 is a 100 MW sodium-cooled fast neutron reactor designed for both on-grid electricity production and industrial heat applications.
ARC said the plant builds upon proven technology and can provides clean, reliable power to support grid stability and industrial applications.
The ARC-100 is the first advanced, sodium-cooled fast neutron reactor to complete a review of this type with the CNSC, ARC said.
With the conclusion of this CNSC review, ARC is well-positioned to proceed with the next stages of licensing and deployment, ARC said.

A sodium-cooled nuclear reactor is one that uses liquid sodium to dissipate heat. The use of sodium as a cooling agent distinguishes this type of reactor from conventional reactors, which rely on water as a cooling solution.

Sodium-cooled reactors are said to offer two key advantages over water-cooled plants: greater efficiency, because sodium remains an effective cooling medium at higher temperatures than water; and a lower risk of explosion caused by high pressure, since sodium coolants operate at lower pressures than water.

ARC said the Phase 2 vendor design review provides feedback to the vendor on matters related to CNSC regulatory requirements and expectations. As part of the multi-year review, which began in 2022, ARC submitted hundreds of technical documents covering 19 focus areas defined by the CNSC and of importance to future licensing applications.
The submissions included information related to safety systems, safety analyses, reactor and process system design, regulatory compliance and quality assurance.

ARC and Swiss-American company data centre project company Deep Atomic recently signed a memorandum of understanding to explore the deployment of ARC-100 SMRs to power next-generation data centres and AI infrastructure.
New Brunswick Power has chosen the ARC-100 for potential deployment at its Point Lepreau nuclear site, where a single Candu 6 plant has been in commercial operation since 1983.
Canada’s Belledune Port Authority is also working on plans to use ARC-100 plants as part of a future expansion at the northern New Brunswick port, eastern Canada.
The ARC-100 is a 100 MW sodium-cooled fast neutron reactor designed for both on-grid electricity production and industrial heat applications. Courtesy ARC.

title: Poland Working Group To Examine Potential Of SMRs For Country’s Booming Data Centre Industry
author: David Dalton
text: Investment by big tech companies in eastern European nation could see sector require more than 1,000 MW of capacity by 2034

Orlen Synthos Green Energy (OSGE) and the Polish Data Center Association have formed a working group dedicated to using small modular reactors (SMRs) to supply the huge amounts of power needed for Poland’s booming data centre industry.

OSGE said the primary objective of the working group is to develop a white paper outlining the potential for cooperation between the data centre sector and SMR developers, along with possible challenges.

The paper will include an analysis of the technological aspects of both sectors, identify areas of synergy and recommend the potential legislative and regulatory changes needed to accelerate collaboration between the two industries.

OSGE is a joint venture between Poland’s state-controlled energy company Orlen and privately owned Synthos Green Energy, which has sought to build GE Hitachi’s BWRX-300 SMRs developed by GE Vernova Hitachi Nuclear Energy in Poland.

Earlier this year Orlen laid out plans for deploying 600 MW of nuclear power capacity from SMRs by 2035. In 2023, OSGE was granted a decision-in-principle for the construction of up to 24 SMRs at six potential sites across Poland.
OSGE said the Polish data centre sector is expanding at a remarkable pace, currently reaching nearly 200 MW of operational capacity and maintaining an annual growth rate of almost 20% since 2020.
Major global cloud service providers – including Google Cloud, Amazon Web Services and Microsoft Azure – are expanding their presence in Poland.

The local data centre ecosystem is growing as well. OSGE said that in Warsaw, Microsoft has launched the first data processing region in Central and Eastern Europe and the company continues to invest in infrastructure, positioning Poland as a key technology hub in that part of Europe.

According to forecasts by PMR Market Experts and power transmission system operator PSE, the power demand of Polish data centres could reach 500 MW – enough to power up to 500,000 homes – by 2030 and the sector could require as much as 1,063 MW by 2034. The advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) is intensifying these requirements.
This dynamic growth brings significant challenges, OSGE said. The Polish data centre sector must secure sources of stable electricity and at the same time meet sustainability requirements.
Earlier this year, OSGE signed a pledge to triple nuclear capacity by 2050.  The declaration was also joined by major data centre market players such as Amazon, Google and Meta.
OSGE’s chief executive officer, Rafal Kasprow, said: “We see a strong synergy between data centres, artificial intelligence, and small modular reactors.
“Technology giants are investing billions of dollars in these technologies to secure delivery of clean, safe electricity which is essential for the sector’s development.
“We are ready to answer to these demands and deliver based on the fleet of the GE Vernova Hitachi BWRX-300 reactors,” Kasprow said.

OSGE said another area of synergy between SMRs and data centres is district heating. The integration of BWRX-300 reactors with data centres can provide significant heat supplies and support the decarbonisation of Poland’s district heating sector — the largest in Europe.

District heating systems take energy released as heat from a range of energy sources – in this case a nuclear power reactor – and connect it to energy consumers through a system of highly insulated pipes.
OSGE wants to integrate BWRX-300 reactors with data centres in Poland. Courtesy GVE.

title: US NRC Approves Vistra’s Application To Operate Perry-1 Nuclear Plant For 60 Years
author: David Dalton
text: Single boiling water reactor unit in Ohio began commercial operation in 1987

Texas-based power utility Vistra has received approval from the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) to extend the operation of its Perry-1 nuclear power plant in Ohio until 2046, an additional 20 years beyond its original licence.
The single 1,240-MW General Electric boiling water reactor unit began commercial operation in 1987 and is currently operating under its initial 40-year licence.
Vistra, which owns and operates the plant, submitted its application for the licence renewal to the NRC in 2023.
Perry is the last of Vistra’s six nuclear power reactors to apply for and receive a licence extension to 2046. Each of Vistra’s reactors is now licensed to operate for 60 years.
The reactors are Perry-1 (Ohio), Beaver Valley-1 and Beaver Valley-2 (Pennsylvania), Comanche Peak-1 and Comanche Peak-2 (Texas), and Davis-Besse-1 (Ohio).

The Beaver Valley, Davis-Besse and Perry nuclear power plants came from Vistra’s acquisition of Energy Harbor, which was approved by Federal Energy Regulatory Commission in February last year. Vistra originally announced the $3.4bn (€2.9bn) purchase in March 2023.
The single-unit Perry nuclear power station in Ohio. Courtesy Cards84664 (Creative Commons Licence).

title: Scotland Globally Isolated On Nuclear Over Ideological Opposition To Reactors, Minister Says
author: David Dalton
text: Country ‘missing out’ on skilled jobs and economic growth, as well as clean affordable energy

Scotland is becoming globally isolated on nuclear power and missing out on much needed skilled jobs and economic growth because of the Scottish government’s ideological stance on nuclear power, a British minister has said.

Secretary of state for Scotland Ian Murray said nuclear energy could create thousands of new, highly-skilled jobs in Scotland, while delivering clean, secure and more affordable energy for working people. Reliable, cheap nuclear power can support critical modern infrastructure in Scotland, such as supercomputers.

Speaking ahead of a visit to Torness nuclear power station to the east of Edinburgh in East Lothian on 3 July, Murray cited new research which shows that Scotland risks becoming one of few areas in Europe where the devolved government is publicly against new nuclear development.

The research by the Nuclear Industry Association (NIA) and World Nuclear Association shows that 87% of the world economy is pursuing new nuclear power, including France, Sweden, Finland and the Netherlands.

According to the research, many previously anti-nuclear European countries are abandoning their positions, including Italy, Denmark, and Belgium, while Germany has dropped its opposition to EU-level initiatives on nuclear energy.
“In other parts of the UK, the UK government is driving forward nuclear power, as are countries across Europe and indeed the world,” Murray said.
“But in Scotland the Scottish government clings to its ideological objection to new nuclear sites.
“That means that Scotland is being left behind, missing out on thousands of skilled jobs and economic growth, as well as clean affordable energy.
“I urge the Scottish Government to put Scotland’s interests first.”

Tom Greatrex, chief executive of the NIA said: “The Scottish government’s refusal to countenance replacing Torness when it retires in a few years is indicative of a fundamental lack of seriousness of policy.”
Until 2021 Scotland had four commercial nuclear reactors at two sites – Hunterston B and Torness. It now has two units in operation, both at Torness.
The two Hunterston B units were shut down in November 2021 and January 2022. The remaining two units at Torness are due to close in 2028, two years earlier than originally planned.
Two older units at Hunterston were permanently shut down in 1989 and 1990.
The UK government said it has committed to building Sizewell C in southeast England and small modular reactors as part of its drive to deliver cleaner, more affordable energy.
Two new large-scale units are under construction at Hinkley Point C in southwest England.

Earlier this year a major trade union urged politicians in Scotland to reconsider the country’s ban on nuclear power plants, saying new reactors at the existing Hunterston site would result in a £1bn economic boom for the area of North Ayrshire.
GMB Scotland, a general trade union, warned that ministers’ opposition to new reactors in Scotland not only risks net zero targets but a massive economic windfall.
Scotland’s only commercial nuclear power station is Torness, which has two units. Courtesy EDF.

title: Concreting of Containment Dome Complete At China’s Changjiang-3 Nuclear Plant
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Construction of Hualong One unit began in March 2021
Workers have finished concreting the containment building dome for Unit 3 of the Changjiang nuclear power station in Hainan province, southern China, the China Nuclear Energy Association (CNEA) said.
The association said the milestone means the plant is now ready for hot functional testing, which will verify the operation of reactor components and systems before fuel loading.
Changjiang-3 is a domestic Hualong One, or HPR1000, pressurised water reactor (PWR) unit with a gross design capacity of 1,200 MW. Construction began in March 2021.
In April 2025, the unit underwent cold hydraulic testing of pressure tightness for key systems such as welds, joints, pipes and components in the primary circuit.

In 2023, the steel dome for Changjiang-3’s inner containment was raised by crane and placed on top of the walls of the double containment structure. The outer steel dome was lifted into place in October 2024.
Two CNP-600 PWRs have been in operation at the Changjiang site since 2015 and 2016.
A fourth unit, the Changjiang-4 Hualong One, has been under construction since December 2021.
China is moving forward with its indigenous reactor technology, with 19 Hualong One reactor units now either operational or under construction.
According to data by the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), China has 29* reactors under construction, 14 of which are of the Hualong One design.

* Five Hualong One units are in commercial operation and 14 under construction, according to IAEA data. Two additional Hualong One units are reportedly under construction at Jinqimen and one CAP1000 at Lufeng, but these three units are not listed by the IAEA. If these units are taken into account, the number of reactors under construction in China is 32.
Workers have finished concreting the containment building dome for Changjiang-3. Courtesy CNEA.

title: Commissioning Phase Begins For First Unit At Turkey’s Akkuyu Nuclear Power Station
author: David Dalton
text: Russian official calls for continued cooperation on new-build projects
The commissioning phase has begun for the first unit of the four-unit Akkuyu nuclear power station under construction in Turkey, Anton Dedusenko, chairman of project company Akkuyu Nuclear, has said.

Dedusenko, who is also chief executive officer of Rusatom Energy International, a subsidiary of Russia’s state nuclear corporation Rosatom, confirmed the completion of general construction and the beginning of testing operations for the station’s first unit.
Akkuyu, near Mersin on the southern Mediterranean coast, is being built by Rosatom under a contract signed in 2010.
“This is a very important phase for a nuclear power unit. Despite some challenges we’ve encountered, everything is progressing on schedule,” Dedusenko told Turkey’s state-run Anadolu news agency.
“We plan to carry out preparations this year to connect the switchyard of Unit 1 to the power transmission system,” he added.
Dedusenko highlighted the potential for broader cooperation between Russia and Turkey, particularly in light of negotiations over a possible second nuclear project at Sinop:

“We have made significant progress with our Turkish partners in recent years,” he said. We are ready to present technical and economic feasibility studies this year, though the final decision rests with the Turkish side.
“We are open to exploring opportunities to expand our cooperation and are very positive about Turkey’s initiative to build new NPPs.”

He added that selecting local suppliers for future projects would be key. The Nuclear Energy Association of Türkiye told NucNet recently
that for future projects, Ankara is aiming for majority local participation and shared ownership models.

Salih Sari, acting head of the Turkish energy ministry’s nuclear projects unit, said recently that Ankara aims to sign international deals
for two new nuclear power stations by the end of the year if it receives competitively priced offers that meet its localisation goals.
The two planned nuclear stations are Sinop, on the Black Sea in northern Turkey, and Igneada is in Thrace, also on the Black Sea, not far from the Bulgarian border.

All four VVER-1200 pressurised water reactor units at Akkuyu are now under construction, with Unit 1 expected to enter commercial operation by the end of 2025. The remaining units are scheduled to come online by 2028.
Once fully operational, the plant will supply 10% of Turkey’s electricity demand.
The facility has a planned 60-year operational lifespan, extendable by another 20 years.
There are four Russia-supplied VVER-1200 pressurised water reactor units under construction at Akkuyu. Courtesy Rosatom.

title: New Consortium To Evaluate Floating Nuclear Power Plants For Mediterranean
author: David Dalton
text: Facilities could meet energy demands of islands, ports and coastal communities

Shipping nuclear propulsion startup Core Power has formed a consortium with the American Bureau of Shipping (ABS) and Greece-based Athlos Energy to evaluate the potential of floating nuclear power plants (FNPPs) to meet the energy demands of islands, ports and coastal communities in the Mediterranean Sea.

The consortium will research how FNPPs can unlock a wide range of applications including the provision of grid scale electricity to remote locations, decarbonising ports by providing emission free energy and providing reliable clean energy to desalination plants that will provide potable water to drought-affected coastal communities.

“FNPPs can revolutionise the way we deliver reliable and affordable nuclear energy to provide vital carbon-free energy security to islands and coastal infrastructure in the Mediterranean,” said Core Power chief executive officer said Mikal Boe.
“By constructing and mass-assembling a fleet of FNPPs in shipyards, we can deliver clean nuclear energy on time and budget, solving many of the largest energy challenges we face.”

Core Power said that as global efforts to decarbonise energy systems and strengthen energy security accelerate, the use of small modular reactors (SMRs) on floating platforms could offer a viable alternative.
It said the new consortium will develop original FNPP concepts of operations and publish a visual display of their prospective locations.
The consortium will also study the feasibility of using nuclear to supply power and other benefits in the Aegean Sea.

“As Greece reconsiders its energy future, the role of nuclear power is increasingly back on the agenda. This study marks an important first step in assessing the feasibility of deploying floating nuclear reactors in the Aegean Sea,” said Dionysios Chionis, co-founder of Athlos Energy.
In October 2024, ABS unveiled the industry’s first comprehensive requirements for floating nuclear power plants.
The consortium said FNPPs can unlock a wide range of applications including the provision of grid scale electricity to remote locations. Courtesy Core Power.

title: Framatome Wins Key Contracts As Belgium Prepares For Nuclear Extensions
author: David Dalton
text: Two reactors scheduled to remain online for additional 10 years
French nuclear company Framatome has been selected by Electrabel for two major projects at nuclear power plants whose operational lifetimes are being extended in Belgium.

The majority state-owned company said it had won contracts for modernisation of the flux monitoring system of the Tihange-3 nuclear plant, and the modernisation, maintenance, and operational support of the motors and stators of the reactor coolant pumps at Doel-4 and Tihange-3.
The contracts follow the agreement signed in 2023 between French energy group Engie and the Belgian government to extend the operational lifetime of the two reactors.
The two plants are majority-owned by Engie’s Belgian unit Electrabel while Luminus, a subsidiary of French power company EDF, holds a minority stake.

Framatome said the modernisation of the flux monitoring system at Tihange-3, planned over several years, aims to fully replace the existing system. It includes every phase, from engineering studies to the supply of all necessary electrical, electronic, and mechanical components. Onsite installation and ongoing maintenance operations are also part of the project scope.

The flux monitoring system plays a critical role in reactor control, providing precise measurements of neutron power distribution within the reactor core and ensuring that the core’s behaviour aligns with both design and operational expectations.
The modernisation, maintenance and operational support of the motors and stators of the reactor coolant pumps at Tihange-3 and Doel-4 includes the supply of spare parts.

The reactor coolant pumps are crucial for the safety and efficiency of nuclear power plants. They circulate coolant at high temperature and pressure to remove heat generated by nuclear fission within the reactor core.
In March Engie formalised a 10-year extension of the Tihange-3 and Doel-4 nuclear power plants in partnership with the Belgian state.

In March 2022, in light of concerns about security of supply in the context of the energy crisis and the Russian war against Ukraine, the Belgian federal government decided to keep the two newest Belgian nuclear power plants – Tihange-3 near Liege and Doel-4 near Antwerp – in operation for an additional 10 years.

In February the Doel-1 nuclear power plant was permanently shut down, bringing the number of commercial reactors in operation in the country to four. Doel-3 and Tihange-2 had already been shut down in 2022 and 2023.
The Doel nuclear power station in Belgium. Courtesy Engie.

title: UK Nuclear Body Identifies New Sites For Nuclear Power Plants
author: David Dalton
text: Study a ‘significant step’ towards deploying reactors in English Midlands
A UK nuclear body has taken a significant step towards integrating nuclear power into the country’s low-carbon energy mix by examining and assessing potential sites for new power stations.

Midlands Nuclear said the siting study assesses where and how nuclear energy could supply low-carbon electricity, hydrogen, and sustainable fuels for industry, transport and homes in the English Midlands.

It said the project has identified a range of brownfield and greenfield locations that have the potential to pass the relevant criteria and therefore, subject to further investigations, could be “technically suitable for deploying new nuclear power stations subject to approvals, the presence of a willing developer, investor(s) and ability to overcome any challenges that the sites may pose during development”.

It did not name the sites. In a Q&A released to the media Midlands Nuclear said “it is generally ill-advised in any infrastructure development project to publicly share locations prior to any potential project being initiated”.

Midlands Nuclear, which brings together the nuclear supply chain, developers, generators, researchers and skills providers, said the UK government outlined its commitment to clean energy in a strategy published on 23 June.
The strategy focuses on clean energy, industrial decarbonisation and lowering energy costs, pledging to double investment in clean energy to over £30bn (€34bn, $41bn) by 2035.
Alongside this, up to 24 GW of new nuclear capacity is planned by 2050, backed by £20bn of investment in Sizewell C and small modular reactor development.
Midlands Nuclear believes the Midlands could attract similar investment, strengthening energy security, advancing net zero goals and establishing the region as a key player in the energy transition.

Projects would support regional jobs and industrial growth, enabling the Midlands to capture more of the potential 3,000 jobs at peak construction for a single SMR and £500-£660m increase in economic output from a two-unit deployment delivering almost 1GW of clean electricity.
Restoring the Midlands’ role in energy generation could revitalise local economies, bring energy production closer to where it is used, and help reduce energy bills nationwide, Midlands Nuclear said.
Midlands Nuclear believes the Midlands region of the UK could attract investment for new reactors. Courtesy Midlands Nuclear.

title: NRC Renews Summer-1 Nuclear Plant Operating Licence For Another 20 Years
author: Kamen Kraev
text: South Carolina reactor can now operate until 2062
The US Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) has renewed the operating licence for the Summer-1 nuclear power plant in South Carolina for an additional 20 years, a 30 June statement said.
This marks the second licence renewal for the 973-MW pressurised water reactor unit, which can now operate until August 2062.

The NRC said it had reviewed operator Dominion Energy’s application along two separate tracks: a safety evaluation report, issued in February, and a final supplemental environmental impact statement released in May.
The commission said both assessments supported the decision to extend the reactor’s operating life from 60 to 80 years.
Summer-1, near in Jenkinsville, South Carolina, began commercial operation in January 1984.
The plant received its first 20-year licence renewal in 2004, about 20 years before the expiry of the initial licence.
Dominion Energy applied for a second licence renewal in 2023.
The NRC is reviewing applications for initial licence extensions for four reactor units at three sites, including Perry, Diablo Canyon and Clinton.
Another 12 reactor units at six sites are being reviewed for subsequent licence extensions: Point Beach, St. Lucie, Browns Ferry, Dresden, Hatch and Robinson.
Summer-1, near in Jenkinsville, South Carolina, began commercial operation in January 1984. Courtesy DJSlawSlaw/Wikipedia Creative Commons Licence.

title: Google Signs Deal to Buy Fusion Energy From Bill Gates-Backed Nuclear Startup
author: David Dalton
text: US-based Commonwealth Fusion Systems hopes to have first Arc nuclear plant online in early 2030s

Google has agreed to purchase power from a planned nuclear fusion plant in the 2030s as it seeks to lock in the massive electricity supplies needed for the boom in data centres and artificial intelligence.

The technology group has committed to buying 200 MW of electricity from Commonwealth Fusion Systems’ (CFS) planned power station in Virginia under a multiyear power purchase agreement, the companies said in a statement.
Google has been an investor in CFS since 2021 and also is increasing its investment stake in the Massachusetts-based company, the statement said.
CFS did not provide the exact dollar figure for the Google deal, but said that it was in the multibillions.

The deal for 200 MW of energy – about enough to power 75,000 homes – from CFS’s first commercial Arc plant in Chesterfield County, Virginia, marks the first direct deal between a customer and a fusion energy company, and the largest deal of this scale in terms of energy provided.
The deal accounts for roughly half of the expected energy production from the plant, with an option to purchase more energy from future plants.

In 2023, Microsoft signed a deal with Helion Energy for 50 MW of fusion energy, to be provided through Constellation Energy as the power marketer. That deal included a commitment to start producing by 2028.
CFS, which raised a record $1.8bn (€1.5bn) from investors including Google in 2021, hopes the proposed 400 MW Arc facility will be the first fusion power station to be connected to the grid.

CFS, which is backed by Bill Gates’s technology fund Breakthrough Energy Ventures, is currently building a demonstration plant in Massachusetts which it aims to operate in 2027. It hopes the plant that would supply Google will be ready by the early 2030s.
The deal comes as technology companies including Google, owned by Alphabet, compete to lock in access to electricity to supply the rollout of data centres required to power AI systems.

In 2023 Microsoft signed a power purchase agreement
with OpenAI founder Sam Altman’s fusion company Helion, agreeing to offtake electricity from a proposed 50 MW facility that the companies said would be online by 2028.

Fusion is the process of generating energy by melding atoms. Current nuclear power plants create energy through nuclear fission, or splitting atoms. Fusion has the potential to create nearly limitless energy using common elements such as hydrogen, and has the added benefit of generating little to no long-lived nuclear waste.
So far, no company has created commercial fusion energy, though a number of startups are trying to commercialise what could be a holy grail of clean-energy production.

CFS, which was spun out of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology’s (MIT) Plasma Science and Fusion Center, aims to produce energy through a tokamak fusion process using high-temperature superconducting magnets developed in collaboration with MIT.

The company is working to build the Sparc prototype fusion machine at its headquarters in Devens, Massachusetts. Sparc is a compact, high-field, net fusion energy device that would be the size of existing mid-sized fusion devices, but with a much stronger magnetic field. It is predicted to produce 50-100 MW of fusion power.
Sparc is expected to produce its first plasma in 2026 and net fusion energy shortly after, demonstrating for the first time a commercially relevant design that will produce more power than consumed.
Sparc will pave the way for a first commercially viable Arc fusion power plant, which will generate about 400 MW – enough to power large industrial sites or about 150,000 homes.

“It’s a pretty big signal to the market that fusion’s coming,” CFS co-founder and chief executive Bob Mumgaard said about the Google deal. “It’s desirable, and that people are gonna work together to make it happen,”.

Mumgaard added that this could help mobilise the industry more generally, attracting more buyers for the future technology. “This puts fusion into this category of ‘this is not like someday future stuff.’ This is concrete,” he said.
Michael Terrell, head of advanced energy at Google, said: “By entering into this agreement with CFS, we hope to help prove out and scale a promising pathway toward commercial fusion power.

“We’re excited to make this longer-term bet on a technology with transformative potential to meet the world’s future energy demand, and support CFS in their efforts to reach the scientific and engineering milestones needed to get there.”

US president Donald Trump is looking to push nuclear energy. In May he signed four executive orders
that aim to quadruple nuclear-power generation in the next 25 years, though this will mostly rely on fission power.
The planned Arc fusion power plant will generate about 400 MW – enough to power large industrial sites or about 150,000 homes. Courtesy CFS.

title: UKAEA Signs 20-Year Nuclear Fusion Skills Agreement With Local Authority
author: David Dalton
text: Aim is to provide workers for country’s Step demonstration reactor
The UK Atomic Energy Authority (UKAEA) and a local government authority have announced a new 20-year collaboration to advance fusion energy training and skills development.

The UKAEA’s collaboration with the East Midlands Combined County Authority (EMCCA) will focus on developing and delivering fusion related skills, including apprenticeships and wider vocational training programmes, to support the Spherical Tokamak for Energy Production (Step) project – the UK’s first prototype fusion energy power plant that will be built on a former coal power station site in West Burton, Nottinghamshire.
A statement said the collaboration will provide crucial skills for Step and support a growing fusion industry across the region.

An assessment commissioned by local authorities has calculated that by the time it is fully operational the West Burton site is anticipated to accommodate 6,500 full-time jobs across Step and the surrounding business park.
The statement said nuclear fusion has the potential to provide abundant, clean power, and deliver energy security.

“Bolstered by the government’s record £2.5 billion (€2.9bn, $3.4bn) investment, the sector promises to create thousands of jobs and empower the UK to export its world-leading technology to a global market, expected to be worth trillions of pounds in the future,” the statement said.
The government said the £2.5bn investment is part of its effort to help progress the Step programme, which aims to see a prototype plant built at West Burton by 2040.
The collaboration will support the Spherical Tokamak for Energy Production (Step) project – the UK’s first prototype fusion energy power plant. Courtesy UKAEA,

title: Fortum Advances Nuclear Plans With Early Works Agreement For Small Modular Reactor Deployment
author: David Dalton
text: Latest move with GVH follows signing of similar agreement with Westinghouse for AP1000 nuclear plants

Nordic power company Fortum and US-based reactor developer GE Vernova Hitachi Nuclear Energy (GVH) and have entered into an early works agreement to advance potential deployment of the BWRX-300 small modular reactor (SMR) in Finland and Sweden.
Fortum completed a new nuclear feasibility study in March and announced that it had selected the BWRX-300 as one of the technologies it is considering for potential deployment in both nations.

The early works agreement will see GVH and Fortum work on pre-licensing and engineering activities for site adaption in Finland and Sweden with potential BWRX-300 deployment in the second half of the 2030s.

In June the Ontario government approved construction of the first of four BWRX-300 SMR nuclear plants at the Darlington site in Canada, making Ontario the first jurisdiction in the G7 to approve construction of a grid-scale SMR.
Construction of the first unit is scheduled to be completed by the end of the decade.
GVH said momentum continues to build around the global deployment of the BWRX-300.

Tennessee Valley Authority recently announced that it had submitted an application to the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission to construct the first BWRX-300 in the US, at the utility’s Clinch River site in Oak Ridge, Tennessee.

The agreement with GVH follows Fortum’s recent signing of an early works agreement with US-based Westinghouse Electric Company for the possible deployment of Westinghouse’s advanced large-scale AP1000 reactor in the Nordics.

Fortum, which owns and operates the two-unit Loviisa nuclear station in Finland, had said it plans to develop new nuclear as a long-term option to meet projected customer demand growth and with view to replacing existing assets at the end of their lifetime.

The company’s feasibility study, concluded earlier this year, said new nuclear can play an important role in a resilient and competitive low-carbon Nordic power system, but an economically viable new-build project will require visibility on income, a solid financing framework and technology-neutral treatment in regulation.
The feasibility study covered both SMRs and conventional large reactors, and involved discussions with several technology vendors, potential partners and customers, and societal stakeholders.
Fortum also has a minority interest in the three-unit Olkiluoto nuclear station in Finland and in four units – Oskarshamn-3, Forsmark-1, Forsmark-2 and Forsmark-3 – in Sweden.
Fortum has chosen the BWRX-300 as one of the technologies it is considering for potential deployment in Finland and Sweden. Courtesy GVH.

title: Finland’s Regulator Completes Preliminary Assessment Of Steady Energy Reactor
author: Kamen Kraev
text: SMR nuclear plant intended for installation underground

Finnish small modular reactor (SMR) startup Steady Energy has announced an early-stage regulatory milestone as the country’s radiation authority concluded that the company’s LDR-50 design concept can be developed to meet national nuclear safety requirements.

The Radiation and Nuclear Safety Authority (Stuk) completed its preliminary assessment of the LDR-50 design earlier in June, saying there are no technical or organisational barriers that would prevent the project from complying with Finland’s nuclear standards.
The review was not mandatory under current law and was conducted at the request of Steady Energy, the company said.

“This assessment reinforces our belief that we are on the right path — both technologically and in terms of our organisational development,” said Juho Vierimaa, head of licensing and quality at Steady Energy.
The LDR-50, which has a thermal output of 50 MWt, has been under development at Finland’s VTT technical research centre since 2020. Steady Energy was spun out from VTT in 2023.
Steady Energy intends to deploy its plant to serve Finland’s district heating needs.
The design is a simplified pressurised light-water reactor (PWR) that functions at much lower pressures compared to traditional PWRs.
Steady Energy plans to build a full-scale pilot at the site of a former coal plant in Helsinki operated by energy firm Helen.

The company has said that the LDR-50 reactor, roughly the size of a standard shipping container, is intended for underground installation, improving safety while freeing up surface space in densely populated areas.
The next phase in the regulatory process will include an international assessment involving nuclear regulators from multiple countries building on Stuk’s findings, said Steady Energy.
A computer-generated image of a Steady Energy LDR-50 nuclear plant installed undergroud. Courtesy Steady Energy.

title: US Companies To Develop AI Software To Speed Up Construction And Reduce Cost Of Nuclear Plants
author: David Dalton
text: Country needs to increase pace of reactor rollout to compete with China, says Palantir
US software giant Palantir Technologies is teaming up with a nuclear deployment company to develop an AI-driven software system built for the construction of nuclear reactors.
Palantir and The Nuclear Company, also US-based, will jointly create the nuclear operating system, which will simplify construction, allowing nuclear plants to be built faster and at lower cost.
Palantir said the AI software will help build plants cheaper, safer and faster, with the goal of outpacing China.

The US has not built a new nuclear plant in 30 years, but the Nuclear Company, with Palantir’s software, aims to deliver electricity by the 2030s and meet president Donald Trump’s goal of 400 GW of nuclear power by 2050, up from around 97 GW today.
The US needs to increase its nuclear power to compete with China, according to Mike Gallagher, head of defense at Palantir Technologies Inc.
The collaboration aims to transform nuclear construction into a data-driven, predictable process, addressing the industry’s persistent challenges of cost overruns and scheduling delays.
The Nuclear Company will pay approximately $100m (€85m) over five years for the development of the platform, according to a Palantir spokesperson.
The partnership will involve a dedicated engineering team working alongside The Nuclear Company’s construction and engineering staff.

“The future of energy security and sovereignty will be shaped by our ability to deploy advanced technologies at scale,” said Mike Gallagher, head of defence at Palantir Technologies. “This partnership marks the first time Palantir's software will be used to help power the next generation of nuclear energy infrastructure.”

The nuclear operating system will provide schedule certainty, cost savings via comprehensive supply chain tracking, problem prevention using sensors and digital twin technology, and regulatory confidence through AI-powered document review and validation.
According to International Atomic Energy Agency data, of 62 nuclear plants under construction around the world, 29 are in China.

In the last 30 years, the US has built only two plants, the Vogtle-3 and -4 unts in Georgia, both of which saw cost overruns and delays for reasons including supply chain issues, shortages of skilled workers, startup problems and the Covid-19 pandemic.

When Georgia approved the Vogtle project in 2009, the two reactors were expected to cost about $14bn and enter service in 2016 and 2017. However, along with the delays, the costs ballooned to $30bn and the units eventually began commercial operation in 2023 and 2024.

In May, Trump signed executive orders calling for 10 large-scale nuclear reactors to be under construction by 2030 and 400 GW of total nuclear power by 2050, over four times the country’s current capacity.
Earlier this week New York governor Kathy Hochul announced plans to build a nuclear-power plant in New York.

Subscribe
Vogtle-4 was the last commercial nuclear power plant to begin operation in the US in 2024. Courtesy Georgia Power.

title: IAEA And World Bank Announce Landmark Agreement To Cooperate On Nuclear Power Development
author: David Dalton
text: MOU is ‘sign of world’s return to realism’ and crucial first step for financing reactors

The International Atomic Energy Agency and the World Bank have announced a new agreement to cooperate on the development and financing of nuclear power for developing countries, including extending the life of existing reactors and speeding up deployment of small modular reactors (SMRs).
IAEA director-general Rafael Grossi and World Bank president Ajay Banga signed on 26 June the memorandum of understanding in Paris that is part of the bank’s return to nuclear energy financing.

The IAEA and the World Bank said in a statement that they agreed to work together to build knowledge in the nuclear field, including expanding the World Bank Group’s understanding of nuclear safety, security, energy planning, and waste management.

The two institutions also said they would work together to extend the lifespan of existing nuclear power plants as a cost-effective source of low-carbon power and accelerate the development of SMRs, saying that they have potential for widespread adoption in developing countries.

Grossi said that the “landmark” agreement was “a sign of the world’s return to realism on nuclear power” and would open the door for other multilateral development banks and private investors to consider nuclear power as a viable tool for energy security.
He called the partnership a “crucial first step” to clearing the financing path for SMR technology, which has the potential to cleanly power developing economies.

In a later social media post, Grossi said the agreement was “a much-needed and timely turning point for nuclear power”. He said the partnership will allow nuclear energy to support development, reduce poverty and help meet soaring global electricity demand.”
Banga said that reliable baseload power provided by nuclear energy was essential for job-generating sectors such as infrastructure, agribusiness, health care, tourism and manufacturing.

“Jobs need electricity. So do factories, hospitals, schools, and water systems. And as demand surges – with AI and development alike – we must help countries deliver reliable, affordable power,” Banga said.
“That’s why we’re embracing nuclear energy as part of the solution — and re-embracing it as part of the mix the World Bank Group can offer developing countries to achieve their ambitions.”
