Supply chain spending in the nuclear fusion sector almost doubled in 2024, with several companies eyeing pilot plants, according to a report from the Fusion Industry Association.
Based on a survey of 22 private fusion companies and 57 fusion suppliers, the report found that supply chain spending grew by 73% to $434m (€380m) in 2024, up from around $250m in 2023.
The FIA predicts that spending in 2025 will increase again by 25%, as fusion gradually moves from the lab to become a commercial technology.

According to the report, companies including Commonwealth Fusion Systems, Focused Energy, Helion, and Type One Energy have already announced sites for pilot plants that will deliver energy to the grid.
However, optimism is tempered by doubts around the supply chain’s ability to meet demand.

Nearly a third of fusion companies (31%) expressed concern about the availability of precision engineering and manufacturing suppliers to meet current commercial needs, rising to 63% for future needs.

“Our report shows significant cause for optimism, with the fusion industry supporting a thriving network of suppliers, proactively investing in the capabilities to deliver commercial fusion,” said FIA chief executive Andrew Holland.

“However, with such a broad range of approaches to fusion in development, the sector still faces roadblocks in developing and sourcing the highly specialised components required to meet their timelines.
“There is a danger this could slow progress towards commercial fusion. For many suppliers, the core risk remains in investing in specialised development when long-term viability isn’t guaranteed.”

According to the FIA, this “chicken and egg” scenario remains one of fusion’s biggest hurdles: suppliers need to know that there will be a market to invest in, but fusion companies struggle to commit long-term in advance of hitting timeline milestones.
The report proposes several solutions for overcoming these scaling challenges, with a focus on de-risking capacity building, supporting long-term planning and broadening the industry workforce.

Nuclear fusion is a process where two or more atomic nuclei combine to form one or more different nuclei, releasing massive amounts of energy. It is the opposite of nuclear fission, where heavy atoms split into lighter ones. This process is what powers the sun and other stars and is seen as a potential source of unlimited energy on Earth.
Courtesy Nasa.

title: Poland Unveils Initiatives In Bid To Boost Nuclear Energy Industry
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Warsaw already pushing ahead with its first reactors in Pomerania province
Poland has announced a set of initiatives aimed at strengthening its nuclear energy sector, including the formation of two government advisory bodies and the launch of a nuclear competence centre.

At a press conference in Warsaw, industry minister Marzena Czarnecka and deputy minister Wojciech Wrochna, who is also government plenipotentiary for strategic energy infrastructure, outlined the government’s strategy to boost local participation and regulatory preparedness as it prepares its first commercial nuclear power station project.

The first of the two newly established advisory teams will focus on ensuring the participation of domestic firms in the construction of the first nuclear station, a three-unit facility near the villages of Lubiatowo and Kopalino on the country’s Baltic coast. The team will include representatives from industry bodies, financial institutions and the public sector, and will be chaired by Wrochna.

Its mission will include preparing strategies to integrate Polish companies into the nuclear project supply chain, supporting them in meeting quality standards and fostering coordination between stakeholders.

“This topic has not been treated with due seriousness before,” Wrochna said. “Participation in the nuclear programme requires meeting appropriate quality standards, building competences and staff, as well as better coordination of work between various programme stakeholders.”
“As the ministry of industry, we want the funds invested in the implementation of nuclear energy to remain in Poland to the maximum extent possible,” he said.

The second advisory team will address the regulatory framework for strategic energy infrastructure. It will include representatives from transmission system operators Polskie Sieci Elektroenergetyczne (PSE), Poland’s gas and oil pipeline operators GAZ-SYSTEM and PERN, and legal and analytical institutions.
The group will examine legal and administrative barriers and propose changes to facilitate the energy sector’s transformation.

The government also announced the establishment of a Nuclear Competence Centre, which will serve as a national hub for education, training, and certification in nuclear energy. It will aim to address shortages of skilled workers and promote long-term domestic involvement in the sector.
The planned centre will also coordinate access to key research infrastructure such as the Maria research reactor near Warsaw.

As Poland aims to diversify its energy sources and reduce dependence on fossil fuels and coal in particular, nuclear power is seen as a cornerstone of its long-term energy security and climate policy.

In 2022, Warsaw chose Westinghouse to supply its AP1000 pressurised water reactor technology for the Lubiatowo-Kopalingo project on the Baltic Sea coast, northwest of Gdansk in the province of Pomerania.
Poland has said it expects to pour first concrete for the first AP1000 unit in 2028, with commercial operation scheduled for 2036.
While full financing for the project is still pending, Warsaw is moving ahead with plans for a second plant, with locations considered in central Poland.
In March, Polish outgoing president Andrzej Duda signed a law allocating 60 billion zloty (€14.4bn, $15.5bn) for the Lubiatowo-Kopalingo project, expected to cost between 150-200 billion zloty.
Poland has begun preparatory site work for its first commercial nuclear power station in the province of Pomerania. Courtesy PEJ.

title: Presidential Favourite Puts South Korea’s Nuclear Renaissance In Doubt
author: David Dalton
text: Frontrunner in 3 June election could reverse plans for use of reactors

South Korea’s presidential front-runner Lee Jae-myung has pledged to keep nuclear power “for the time being,” but plans a long-term shift to renewables if elected on 3 June – a stance that could undermine the Asian nation’s nuclear energy expansion plans at home and abroad.
Press reports said Lee, a member of the opposition Democratic Party, unveiled an “energy expressway” policy framework that relies on renewables, such as offshore wind, to supply industrial hubs.
His strategy calls for phasing out coal by 2040, curbing consumption of natural gas, and forming a ministry tasked with meeting South Korea’s 2050 net zero goal.
Lee supports extending the life of existing nuclear plants, but opposes new reactors, citing land constraints and waste management issues.
Last month Lee said nuclear power is “inherently dangerous” and there are “sustainability issues”. He said: “Let’s utilise it, but not too much. And we should transition to renewable energy.”

South Korea’s president is head of state and has significant powers including appointment of the prime minister and cabinet members, potentially heralding a change in civilian nuclear energy policy if Lee is elected.

Former president Yoon Suk Yeol, who has been impeached and removed from office after declaring martial law in December 2024 in a bid to crack down on dissent, enacted a pro-nuclear policy when he was elected in 2022 that reversed previous president Moon Jae-in’s policy of phasing out nuclear power.
Yoon’s policy saw reactors as a long-term means to boost energy security and curb emissions. He also sought to accelerate the export of South Korea’s nuclear technology in a bid to boost industry.

Kim Moon-soo, the nominee for the conservative People Power Party and Lee’s main rival, had previously vowed to eventually raise nuclear energy’s share to 60% of the mix – up from about 30% in 2024 – but later walked it back after criticism. Kim currently supports the addition of six new reactors, a policy that mirrors Yoon’s.

In February the energy and industry ministry said South Korea had approved a long-term electricity supply and demand plan outlining an expansion of nuclear power with the construction of two new large-scale reactor units and a small modular reactor (SMR) plant by 2038.
South Korea has 26 nuclear plants in commercial operation and two large-scale APR1400 pressurised water reactor units under construction at the Saeul nuclear station in the southeast of the country.
In April, the Shin-Hanul-2 APR1400 nuclear power plant in the east of the country became the latest unit to begin commercial operation.

In 2024, Seoul approved the completion of two APR1400s at Shin-Hanul-3 and Shin-Hanul-4. Work on both units was halted in 2017 under the nuclear phaseout policy of the previous government, but in 2022 a decision was made to resume construction in 2025.
In April, Shin-Hanul-2 in the east of the country became the latest nuclear plant to begin commercial operation. Courtesy IAEA.

title: Progress For Palisades Restart As Regulator Says ‘No Significant Environmental Impact’
author: David Dalton
text: Holtec planning to bring Michigan nuclear plant back online to produce power until at least 2051

The US Nuclear Regulatory Commission has said there is no significant environmental impact from the planned restart of the Palisades nuclear power station – the first restart of a commercial nuclear reactor in the US that had been shut down.
The NRC said in a statement it has issued the final environmental assessment for US-based Holtec International’s request to return the single-unit Palisades to an operational status.
The report contains the NRC staff’s evaluation and conclusion that there is no significant environmental impact from restarting Palisades, in Covert, Michigan.
The NRC conducted an environmental review with the Department of Energy’s (DOE) Loan Programs Office.

Palisades, which began commercial operation in 1972, permanently ceased operations in May 2022. Starting in late 2023, Holtec filed several licensing requests that, if approved, could return the plant to operational status.
The environmental review covered the scope of those licensing requests, considering new and significant information developed since an earlier October 2006 NRC review for Palisades’ licence renewal.
The DOE recently made a third loan disbursement to Holtec International to help with the company’s plan to restart the plant.
The Biden administration finalised an up to $1.52bn (€1.34bn) loan guarantee for the project in September 2024.
New Jersey-based Holtec has said it is on track to restart operations at Palisades in October and the NRC expects to issue a final decision on the required licensing actions by 31 July.

Holtec bought Palisades to decommission the facility, which had struggled to compete with natural gas-fired plants and renewable energy. But in early 2023, Holtec applied to the DOE for federal loan funding to repower the plant.
The single-unit 805-MW pressurised water reactor unit will be brought back online and upgraded to produce power until at least 2051.

In addition to the main 805 MW reactor, Holtec intends to use the Palisades site as the location for its first two small modular reactor units, which would potentially add an additional 800 MW of generation capacity.
The Palisades nuclear plant in Michigan permanently ceased operations in May 2022, but is being brought back online. Courtesy Holtec International.

title: Radiant Raises $165 Million For Development Of ‘World’s First’ Mass Produced Nuclear Reactor
author: David Dalton
text: US company planning to test Kaleidos microreactor in 2026
Radiant Industries, a US nuclear startup, announced it has raised $165m (€145m) in funding to complete what it says could be the world’s first mass-produced portable microreactor design.

The Series C funding round was led by California-based venture capital firm DCVC Management, and also included London, UK-based investment firm Giant Ventures Global and US investment company StepStone Group, according to a statement.
The El Segundo, California-based company said it now has raised $225m to develop its 1-MW Kaleidos microreactor system.
The Kaleidos microreactor is aimed at replacing diesel generators at military sites, remote villages or disaster relief efforts, and can operate for several years without refuelling.
It can be delivered in a single standardised shipping container and installed in a day, according to Radiant’s chief operating officer Tori Shivanandan.
The funding announcement follows the news that the US Department of Energy has selected Radiant as one of just five companies in the country to receive high-assay low-enriched uranium (Haleu) fuel.
Radiant will be using Haleu fuel for the first test of Kaleidos. The test is planned for 2026 at the Idaho National Laboratory.
The Kaleidos microreactor is aimed at replacing diesel generators at military sites, remote villages or disaster relief efforts. Courtesy Radiant Industries.

title: Holtec Backs SMR Deployment In Britain With Site For New Factory
author: David Dalton
text: Planned nuclear facility is centrepiece of company’s UK investment plans

Small modular reactor (SMR) developer Holtec Britain, one of three companies in the running to deploy SMRs in the UK, has chosen a site next to Doncaster-Sheffield Airport in northern England as the preferred location for its planned new UK factory.
The company said it is now entering detailed negotiations with the developer, Peel Land.
Holtec’s decision also comes weeks after the prime minister, Keir Starmer, confirmed £30m (€35m, $40.5m) to fund the reopening of the airport.
Since it closed in 2022, local politicians and businesses have campaigned to reopen it to drive growth across the region.
Holtec Britain, a subsidiary of US-based Holtec International, said it had chosen the site after evaluating 13 regions across the UK.

The company said the planned factory is the centrepiece of its UK investment plans. Crucially, the new hub will give the UK “first mover advantage” at the helm of a new export market for SMR components worth billions.
The factory will produce two SMR units annually, with half of the output slated for exports.

Holtec’s SMR-300 plant is a pressurised water reactor – the most common type in the world and a scaled-down version of the type under construction at Hinkley Point C, helping to standardise supply chains and develop an experienced UK workforce.
In February the government body Great British Nuclear announced that it had entered the final stage of its SMR selection process.
Holtec, GE-Hitachi, Rolls Royce and Westinghouse Electric were all invited to submit a final tender for the competition.
Three of those companies – Holtec, GE-Hitachi and Rolls Royce – have since confirmed they have submitted final tenders.

Holtec has chosen a site next to Doncaster-Sheffield Airport in northern England as the preferred location for its planned new UK factory. L-R: Stephen Wild managing director, Peel Land; Ros Jones, mayor of Doncaster; Holtec Britain’s director, Gareth Thomas; Dame Julia King, Holtec’s senior advisor; Damian Allen, chief executive of Doncaster Council; Julian Stott, director, Peel Land. Courtesy Holtec.

title: Oklo To Collaborate With South Korea’s KHNP On Global Reactor Deployment
author: David Dalton
text: California company aiming to build first Aurora nuclear powerhouse in Idaho

Advanced nuclear technology company Oklo has signed a memorandum of understanding with Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power (KHNP) outlining plans to collaborate on the development and global deployment of Oklo’s reactors.
Under the MOU, Oklo and KHNP intend to explore opportunities to jointly advance the standard design development and verification of Oklo’s planned Aurora powerhouse.

They also plan to cooperate on early-stage project development efforts, including manufacturability assessments and planning of major equipment, supply chain development for balance of plant systems, and constructability assessments and planning.

California, US-based Oklo, which is backed by OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman, an early-stage investor in the company, plans to deploy its 75 MW Aurora nuclear powerhouse at the Idaho National Laboratory (INL) site and is advancing through the licensing process.
The company is engaged with the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission in a pre-application readiness assessment and intends to submit a formal combined licence application, or Cola, later this year.
Oklo also plans to file follow-on applications to support its growing order pipeline, which exceeds 14 GW.
Unlike the traditional approach, which requires separate construction and operating licences, the Cola allows both to be granted simultaneously, streamlining the overall licensing process, Oklo said.

Jacob DeWitte, co-founder and chief executive officer of Oklo, said the company recently completed site characterisation borehole drilling for its first commercial powerhouse at INL and is preparing for construction, with commercialisation as a top priority.
He said partnering with KHNP, an accomplished nuclear builder, offers opportunities to cooperate on “key execution factors” such as manufacturability, constructability, and supply chain development.
Oklo co-founder and chief executive officer Jacob DeWitte and KHNP chief executive officer Whang Joo-ho following the virtual signing of the MOU. Courtesy Oklo.

title: Nuclear Supply Chain Needs More Capacity And Capability, Says WNA Head
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Sama Bilbao y León points to investment opportunity of about $2tn over next 15 years

A significant increase in nuclear supply chain capacity and capability will be needed to deliver a 500-GW projected expansion of nuclear power globally by 2050, Sama Bilbao y León, director-general of the World Nuclear Association (WNA), told an event in Warsaw, Poland.
Bilbao y León said at the World Nuclear Supply Chain conference that governments should work to align energy and industrial policies with the goal of speeding up supply chain and skills development.
She said new nuclear deployment should move from current individual reactor projects to a “programmatic approach” of continuous government programmes for new reactor buildouts.

According to Bilbao y León, WNA analysis has shown there will be an investment opportunity for the global supply chain valued at about $2tn (€1.76tn) over the next 15 years as demand for nuclear power is expected to grow.
She said the supply chain will need to see more government support and a boost in engagement between businesses and industrial players.
“The supply chain is central to delivery, and a healthy supply chain requires government support and an environment that enables business and draws investment," Bilbao y León said.
“We need to learn by doing, not just talking about it,” she warned.
Data by the International Atomic Energy Agency shows that as of 2025, 416 reactors are in operation worldwide, with another 61 under construction at various stages.
The WNA has said about 100 additional have been planned and about 300 proposed.

At the Cop28 climate summit in Dubai in late 2023, the international nuclear industry and 22 governments signed pledges committing to at least a tripling of global nuclear energy capacity by 2050 to help meet net-zero climate ambitions.
WNA director-general Sama Bilbao y León (right) and Poland’s Marzena Czarnecka, minister of industry. Courtesy Poland Ministry of Industry.

title: US Nuclear Industry Has Unlimited Potential, But Facing Headwinds, Says Korsnick
author: David Dalton
text: Head of NEI lobby group says sector needs to be ‘hyper-focused’ on protecting crucial federal policies

The US nuclear industry has a future of unlimited potential as demand rises to meet the needs of manufacturing and artificial intelligence (AI), but it is also facing headwinds and the actions it takes today will “define what that future looks like”, the president and chief executive officer of the Nuclear Energy Institute (NEI) lobby group has said.

In a “state of the industry” address at the Nuclear Energy Policy Forum in Washington, Maria Korsnick said demand from AI and data centres is bringing big tech to the nuclear table and private capital is pouring into nuclear.
But she said the industry needs to be “hyper-focused” on protecting federal policies and programmes that preserve and expand nuclear generation.
“I’m talking about programs like the Advanced Reactor Demonstration Program and the Loan Programs Office, and policies like the nuclear tax credits,” Korsnick said.
She said the NEI recently joined more than 120 of its member companies to send a letter to congressional leadership, urging them to retain the credits.

She said before tax credits were introduced “we were prematurely shutting down nuclear plants”. But after those tax credits were passed, “we started to see power uprates, plant restarts, and decades-long reactor extensions”.

Korsnick said: “All of that progress, the technological boom it’s fuelling, the financial boon it’s fostering…all of that could slow down or turn around completely if Congress fails to preserve the nuclear credits.
“The current language we’ve seen from the House phases out much-needed support. But we are not giving up. And we will be out there pounding the pavement every step of the way.”

The US nuclear industry is said to be intensifying its lobbying to save the credits, which it says are vital for meeting energy demand being fuelled by the development of AI and the need for data centres.

Lawmakers from the House ways and means committee, which is responsible for writing tax law, recently released draft legislation that would phase out nuclear energy subsidies starting in 2029, three years earlier than written in the Inflation Reduction Act, in a move that caught the sector by surprise.

According to the UK-based Financial Times (subscription required), lobbyists are racing to persuade lawmakers to rescind or moderate cuts to nuclear industry subsidies, which until recently had more bipartisan support than other low-carbon energy technologies such as wind and solar.
The Inflation Reduction Act was introduced by the Biden administration and became law in 2022.
Its aims included offering finance for struggling nuclear reactors in a bid to save reactors from being shut down early.
The legislation was welcomed by the US nuclear energy industry at the time as “sending a clear signal that nuclear is essential to the transition toward a carbon-free economy”.

Included in the legislation was a “zero-emission nuclear power production credit” that provides up to 0.3 cents per kWh for energy produced from a zero-emission nuclear power facility, starting in 2024 and ending in 2032.

Korsnick delivered her speech days before president Donald Trump signed four executive orders aimed at speeding up reactor approvals, boosting domestic uranium production and enrichment capacity, and accelerating deployment of advanced nuclear technologies.
Trump directed the government to fast-track construction of nuclear reactors and reform the “risk averse” culture of regulation in a bid to quadruple the US’s nuclear energy capacity by 2050.

Korsnick attended the signing ceremony at the White House. An NEI spokesman later said: “We appreciate the administration’s ongoing actions to preserve existing nuclear plants and usher in the deployment of next generation nuclear.
“Policies to strengthen nuclear are essential to bolstering our national security and meeting our energy goals.”
Korsnick said demand from AI and data centres is bringing big tech to the nuclear table and private capital is pouring into the industry. Courtesy NEI.

title: Westinghouse Signs SMR Agreement With Canada First Nations Communities
author: David Dalton
text: US company eyeing AP300 reactor deployment in New Brunswick

Westinghouse Electric Company has signed a memorandum of understanding with the Pabineau and Eel River Bar First Nations Indigenous communities to promote Westinghouse technology for nuclear new build projects at the Port of Belledune in the province of New Brunswick, Canada.

The US company said the initial focus of the agreement explores AP300 small modular reactor (SMR) opportunities with local developers, including the Belledune Port Authority and New Brunswick Power, as well as industrial and data centre customers.
The Port of Belledune is a special development district on Canada’s Atlantic Coast.
Pabineau First Nation chief Terry Richardson said the SMR partnership with Westinghouse will benefit First Nations and the whole province of New Brunswick.
“The Port of Belledune offers a great opportunity with land and a deep-water port that gives access to world markets,” Richardson said.
Pabineau First Nation and Eel River Bar First Nation are both Mi’kmaq communities located in northern New Brunswick.
Pabineau First Nation is situated along the Nepisiguit River near the city of Bathurst, and Eel River Bar First Nation is located along the Eel River and Chaleur Bay near the town of Dalhousie.
As Indigenous rightsholders at the Port of Belledune, both communities work with the port to support regional economic development, Westinghouse said.
Westinghouse said the initial focus of the agreement explores AP300 small modular reactor opportunities. Courtesy Westinghouse.

title: Enec And GVH Announce Plans To Cooperate On ‘Global Deployment’ Of SMRs
author: David Dalton
text: Emirati company says collaboration will drive next-generation nuclear innovation
Emirates Nuclear Energy Company (Enec) and GE Vernova Hitachi (GVH) have signed an agreement to work together to begin exploring the global deployment of small modular reactors (SMRs).

Enec, the state company that led the project to build four South Korea-supplied APR-1400 reactor units at the Barakah nuclear power station in the United Arab Emirates, said the agreement builds on the companies’ earlier agreement signed at Cop28 and will enable collaboration to drive next-generation nuclear innovation as part of our Advance programme.
Enec launched Advance in 2023 to work with a network of international technology suppliers of advanced reactors, to drive decarbonisation of energy intensive and heavy industry.
Enec said at the time that advanced reactors will be pivotal in delivering the UAE’s strategy to reach net zero by 2050.

Heavy industry such as steel, aluminium, oil, gas, cement, chemicals and transport contribute about 50% of the UAE’s total carbon emissions. These sectors are challenging to decarbonise as they require vast amounts of energy continuously and a significant portion of the emissions arises from activities conducted off-grid.

Advanced reactors and SMRs offer an “innovative decarbonisation solution” for these sectors, Enec said. These reactors can be co-located with critical infrastructure and provide a reliable supply of clean electricity, as well as clean steam, heat and hydrogen. SMRs are easier to manufacture, thereby contributing greater economies of scale, in addition to being flexible, safe and efficient to deploy.

GVH is developing its BWRX-300 SMR, a 300-MW water-cooled, natural circulation nuclear plant with passive safety systems. It is based on an existing boiling water reactor design – the ESBWR – that is licensed in the US. It also uses an existing, licensed fuel design.

In Canada, federally owned utility Tennessee Valley Authority recently submitted an application to the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission to construct a BWRX-300 SMR at the Clinch River site in Oak Ridge, Tennessee – the first construction permit application for a BWRX-300 in the US.

TVA has invested in the design of the BWRX-300 as part of a technical collaboration agreement with GVH, Canadian power company Ontario Power Generation (OPG) and Poland-based nuclear developer Synthos Green Energy.

Synthos plans to deploy a fleet of SMRs in Poland and other central and eastern European countries. In 2023 Poland’s Ministry of Climate and Environment issued decisions-in-principle for the construction of BWRX-300 SMRs at six locations. A total of 24 BWRX-300 reactors are planned at the sites.
Advanced reactors and SMRs such as the BWRX-300 offer an ‘innovative decarbonisation solution’. Enec said. Courtesy GVH.

title: NuScale ‘In Advanced Discussions’ And Could Deliver Operating SMR By 2030
author: David Dalton
text: Early customers could include data centres, heavy industry and utilities

US nuclear reactor company NuScale Power is in advanced discussions with several potential customers for its small modular reactor (SMR) technology and could deliver an operating power plant in 2030, chief executive officer John Hopkins said during a first-quarter earnings call.
NuScale remains on track for an expected July approval from the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) for its uprated 77-MW electric design, the company said.

Manufacturing partner Doosan has 12 NuScale modules in production now and could deliver 20 per year as orders materialise, Hopkins said. NuScale envisions four-, six- and 12-module deployments, with plant outputs ranging from 308 MW to 924 MW.

“Our focus right now is to get closure on near-term contracts. We are no longer chasing or announcing [memoranda of understanding],” Hopkins said. “We’re actually in the process of submitting and negotiating term sheets. We’ve got customers that [want] to… touch steel.”
Possible early power customers include large data centre operators, other heavy industrial customers and utilities, NuScale said.

The company said last year that it had experienced a surge in interest in its SMR technology from data centres and manufacturers, driven by the Advance Act and Department of Energy funding for SMR deployment.
The rapid growth of data centres in support of artificial intelligence is the “most exciting source of new demand” for clean, firm electricity, Hopkins said.
NuScale’s technology remains the only SMR to receive design certification from the US NRC.

That January 2023 certification was based on an earlier 50-MW version of NuScale’s Voygr reactor, but the company’s application for NRC approval of a 77-MW version is on track to conclude by mid-2025, Hopkins said.

Following the November 2023 cancellation of the 462-MW Carbon Free Power Project in Idaho, NuScale’s most advanced project is an effort to build a 462-MW nuclear generation facility on the site of a former coal-fired power plant in Romania, Hopkins said.
The Carbon Free Power Project was for the construction of a demonstration NuScale Voygr SMR power plant at the Idaho National Laboratory that was scheduled to be online in 2029.
A digital mockup of a potential NuScale small modular reactor nuclear plant. Courtesy NuScale.

title: Estonia Begins Planning Process For Small Modular Reactor Nuclear Plant
author: David Dalton
text: Baltic country could deploy 600 MW of capacity using GE Hitachi BWRX-300 technology

Estonia has formally decided to begin a national planning process and environmental impact assessment for a 600 MW small modular reactor (SMR) nuclear power plant based on a proposal put forward in January by nuclear development company Fermi Energia.
Fermi Energia, which is based in Estonia, said in a statement that submission of the construction permit application for the project is planned for 2029.

The company is planning to deploy GE Hitachi’s BWRX-300 SMR technology. It said the government’s plans to move ahead with the planning process and environmental assessment “underscore a collective commitment to Estonia’s energy security and climate goals”.

Fermi Energia chief executive officer Kalev Kallemets said that while planning and environmental impact assessments have historically been contentious issues in Estonia, Fermi Energia’s extensive community outreach and the trust established with local municipalities “provides reason for confidence that the planning process will proceed successfully”.
Fermi Energia said that over the past six years, continuous communication and cooperation with local communities have been central to the project.
Polling indicates that the local population is generally open to the idea of potentially hosting a nuclear power plant – around 50% are in support and roughly one-third are opposed.
At the national level, public backing for the introduction of nuclear energy into Estonia’s energy mix is even stronger, with 69% of respondents expressing support as of January 2025.

The planning process is structured into three decisive phases. Between 2025 and 2027, a site pre-selection phase will focus on promising areas near Kunda in Viru-Nigula County and the village of Aa in Luganuse County. Both areas are in the north of the country.
This phase will evaluate each location’s access to existing infrastructure, alongside environmental impact assessments, to identify the most viable and sustainable options for development.

To support this effort, Fermi Energia has successfully closed a €2.3m (€2.6m) funding round with participation from both existing and new investors. The capital will be used to finance the initial phase of Estonia’s national special planning process, specifically the site pre-selection studies.

In 2027, the process will advance to detailed site confirmation. During this phase, in-depth studies – covering geology, hydrology, environmental monitoring, and grid connectivity – will be conducted to ensure the selected site meets the stringent safety and performance standards required for deploying the BWRX-300 reactor.

Fermi Energia recently signed a teaming agreement with South Korean construction and engineering company Samsung C&T, which is being considered as a prospective engineering, procurement and construction contractor for the project.
Estonia has no nuclear power plants, but its climate strategy includes plans for up to four SMRs with the first to be operational around 2035.
Fermi Energia is working to deploy GE Hitachi’s BWRX-300 SMR technology. Courtesy Fermi Energia.

title: US Nuclear Industry Intensifies Lobbying In Bid To Save Tax Credits Introduced By Biden
author: David Dalton
text: Draft legislation says subsidies could be phased out in 2029

The US nuclear industry is intensifying its lobbying to save the Inflation Reduction Act tax credits it says are vital for meeting energy demand being fuelled by the development of artificial intelligence and the need for data centres.

Lawmakers from the House ways and means committee, which is responsible for writing tax law, this week released draft legislation that would phase out nuclear energy subsidies starting in 2029, three years earlier than written in the Inflation Reduction Act, in a move that caught the sector by surprise.

According to the UK-based Financial Times
(subscription required), lobbyists are now racing to persuade lawmakers to rescind or moderate cuts to nuclear industry subsidies, which until recently had more bipartisan support than other low-carbon energy technologies such as wind and solar.
According to the FT, in the first quarter of 2025 nuclear companies and industry bodies have increased spending on lobbying.
Oklo, the nuclear technology company backed by OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman, spent $424,000 (€377,468) – an increase of more than 500% year-on-year.
Nuclear reactor developers NuScale Power and the Bill Gates-founded TerraPower, as well as the Nuclear Energy Institute, also increased their spending, the FT said.

Constellation Energy, which has partnered with Microsoft to restart the Three Mile Island plant in Pennsylvania, spent more than $1.7m in the first quarter on lobbying across its portfolio – a 16% increase.
The Inflation Reduction Act was introduced by the Biden administration and became law in 2022.
Its aims included offering finance for struggling nuclear reactors in a bid to save reactors from being shut down early.
The legislation was welcomed by the US nuclear energy industry at the time as “sending a clear signal that nuclear is essential to the transition toward a carbon-free economy”.

Included in the legislation was a “zero-emission nuclear power production credit” that provides up to 0.3 cents per kWh for energy produced from a zero-emission nuclear power facility, starting in 2024 and ending in 2032.
Constellation Energy has partnered with Microsoft to restart the Three Mile Island plant in Pennsylvania. Courtesy Constellation Energy.

title: Canada’s Candu Energy Signs Agreement With Argentina To Boost Heavy Water Production
author: David Dalton
text: Deal will support operation of existing units and planned rollout of new reactors

Canada-based Candu Energy has signed a memorandum of understanding with the National Atomic Energy Commission (CNEA) of Argentina to produce heavy water* for existing Candu nuclear power plants and potential new units.

The company, a subsidiary of AtkinsRéalis, the original equipment manufacturer of the government of Canada-owned Candu nuclear reactor technology, said the MOU provides for the restart of an industrial heavy water plant in Neuquén, Argentina, along with the long-term acquisition of its heavy water output.

The Neuquén plant, in western Argentina, is owned by CNEA. It was originally commissioned around 30 years ago and has supplied Argentina’s Candu 6 plant at the Embalse nuclear station, as well as exported heavy water to various countries.
The facility is expected to resume operation as early as 2027. Following basic refurbishment work supported by AtkinsRéalis, it will provide an immediate near-term supply for Candu reactor needs.
CNEA is the Argentinean government agency devoted to research and development in nuclear energy.
The MOU also provides for planning related to the establishment of one or more similar heavy water production facilities in Canada.

“These developments will support the ongoing operation of existing Candu reactors in Canada and around the world, as well as the commissioning of new Candu units globally,” Candu Energy said in a statement.
Joe St. Julian, president, nuclear at AtkinsRéalis, said: “This MOU is a significant investment for Canada in the global heavy water market during this renaissance period for the nuclear industry.

“Following commitments at Cop28, a growing market for 1,000 new reactors and demand for Candu technology, including refurbishment projects and a fleet of reactors like the Candu Monark and Enhanced Candu 6, investing in heavy water capacity supports the expansion of Candu reactor infrastructure domestically and internationally.”

The Candu reactor is a Canadian-designed, heavy-water moderated and cooled nuclear reactor that uses natural uranium as fuel and is known for its ability to be refuelled while operating, helping it maintaining high load factors.

Argentina has a fleet of three nuclear reactor units at two sites – Atucha-1 and -2, and Embalse. Embalse is a Candu 6 unit. Atucha-1 and -2 are a different type of pressurised heavy water plant developed by Siemens.

Canada operates a fleet of 17 commercial reactor units that are all Candu plants. Overseas, Candus are operated in Argentina, Romania, South Korea, China and India, with some Indian reactors being Candu derivatives.

* Heavy water (D2O) is water where the hydrogen atoms are replaced by deuterium, a heavier isotope of hydrogen. It is also known as deuterium oxide. While physically and chemically similar to ordinary water (H2O), heavy water has different nuclear properties, making it useful in nuclear reactors as a moderator and coolant.
The Embalse nuckear power plant in Argentina is a Canada-supplied Candu 6 unit. Courtesy Nuclearelectrica.

title: Taiwan Parliament Passes Proposal For Referendum On Nuclear Power
author: David Dalton
text: Move comes just days after Asian nation shut down its last commercial reactor

Taiwan’s legislative yuan has passed an opposition-backed proposal to hold a referendum on restarting the Maanshan nuclear power station where the island nation’s last commercially operating reactor was shut down on 17 May.
Reperts in Taiwan said the referendum proposal was passed in a 58-49 vote, supported by the main opposition Kuomintang (KMT) and the smaller Taiwan People/s Party (TPP).

First put forward by the TPP on 18 April, the referendum question read: “Do you agree that the third nuclear power plant [Maanshan] should continue operation upon approval by the competent authority and confirmation that there are no safety concerns?”
The referendum proposal was passed just three days after Maanshan-2 was shut down, fulfilling the government’s promise to make Taiwan “nuclear-free”.
Maanshan-2, a 938-MW pressurised water reactor unit in Pingtung County, southern Taiwan, began commercial operation in 1985.
Taipower shut down the Maanshan-1 nuclear power plant, a 936-MW PWR that began commercial operation in 1984, in July 2024.
The phasing out of nuclear power has been a goal of the ruling Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) even before it took power in May 2016.

Soaring energy demand driven by the island’s semiconductor industry is rekindling the debate about nuclear energy. The country’s electricity needs are expected to rise by 12-13% by 2030, largely driven by the boom in artificial intelligence (AI), according to the Ministry of Economic Affairs.

Environmental group Greenpeace has estimated that the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, the world’s largest contract chipmaker, will by itself consume as much electricity as roughly one-quarter of the island’s 23 million people by 2030.

The island’s appetite for power complicates Taipei’s pledge to reach net-zero emissions by 2050, a pledge which is heavily dependent on raising renewable energy production to about 60-70% of the total from about 12% at present.
Nuclear power advocates argue that the energy source is the most feasible way for Taiwan to reach its competing industrial and environmental goals.
In 2023, nuclear accounted for about 6.9% of Taiwan’s electricity production, which is dominated by coal and liquified natural gas.
Taipower said that with the closure of Maanshan-1, the share of power generated by nuclear sources would fall to 2.8%.
At one point, nuclear energy from six reactors in Taiwan provided more than half of heavily industrialised island’s electricity.
Late last year Taiwan’s premier Cho Jung-tai said the country was “very open” to using new nuclear technology to meet rising demand from chipmakers using electricity to provide power for the AI boom.

“As long as there is a consensus within Taiwan on nuclear safety and a good direction and guarantees for handling nuclear waste, with this strong consensus, we can have a public discussion,” Cho said in an interview with Bloomberg News.
His comments were one of the strongest signs yet that the government has been rethinking its opposition to commercial power reactors.
Cho appeared to be referring to advanced reactors, potentially including small modular reactors (SMRs) that are being developed in a number of countries.
Taiwan’s National Atomic Research Institute this week said it had launched a $3.3m (€2.9m) SMR research project that could pave the way for the introduction of advanced nuclear reactors.
Maanshan-2, a 938-MW pressurised water reactor unit in Pingtung County, southern Taiwan, was permanently shut down on 17 May. Courtesy Wikipedia/Creative Commons Licence.

title: Urenco USA Begins Enriched Uranium Production At New Cascade
author: David Dalton
text: Planned expansion in New Mexico will increase domestic capacity by about 15%
Urenco USA has begun production of enriched uranium in its newest gas centrifuge cascade, marking the next phase of expansion at its enrichment facility in New Mexico.
The new cascade is the first of several planned to come online at the National Enrichment Facility by early 2027.
Once completed, this expansion of the facility will provide an approximately 15% increase in domestic enrichment capacity.
Urenco USA said its new supply will strengthen the US nuclear fuel supply chain and will support “a transition away from reliance on Russian supply”.

Urenco USA is the US’s only commercial producer of enriched uranium and has been enriching uranium in the US since 2010. The company operates the National Enrichment Facility, which it says is an essential part of the US nuclear fuel supply chain.
The facility represents a commercial investment to date of more than $5bn (€4.4bn) in US manufacturing.
Urenco USA currently has the capacity to meet approximately one-third of the enrichment needs of US commercial nuclear power plants.
The company is evaluating potential additional expansion subject to market demand and underpinned by contracts.

“As the only commercial scale uranium enrichment facility in North America, Urenco USA plays an essential role in the nuclear fuel supply chain, which ends with the generation of reliable, secure, and sustainable energy for US consumers,” the company said.
Urenco USA is owned by Urenco, which is in turn owned by the governments of the UK, Netherlands, and two German utilities E.ON and RWE.
The new cascade is the first of several planned to come online at the National Enrichment Facility by early 2027. Courtesy Urenco USA.

title: ČEZ Confirms Possible Location For New Nuclear Power Station In Czech Republic
author: Kamen Kraev
text: State utility notifies ministry of plans for small modular reactors at Tušimice in North Bohemia
Czech state-controlled utility ČEZ has notified the country’s environment ministry of a proposed location for a third nuclear power station, at Tušimice in North Bohemia in the north of the country.
A set of documents submitted to an official governmental portal indicate the move is a first step in the process of obtaining an environmental impact assessment for the proposed location.

According to earlier reports, Tušimice was already one of the locations considered by ČEZ for the potential deployment of Rolls-Royce’s 470-MW small modular reactor (SMR) plants. With the submission of plans to the environment ministry this has now been confirmed.
The first location is the existing Temelín nuclear site, with proposed deployment earmarked for the early 2030s.

In 2023, ČEZ unveiled two further possible sites for additional SMR plants after Temelín – the coal-fired generation sites at Detmarovice in the east of the country close to the border with Poland, and Tušimice in the northwest, close to the border with Germany.
The Czech government approved an SMR deployment roadmap in 2023.
The Detmarovice and Tušimice power plant sites will undergo “further intensive exploration and monitoring works” before it is clear whether they are suitable locations for SMRs, ČEZ said at the time.

The selection of the Tušimice site takes into account existing infrastructure and legislative requirements for the location of nuclear power facilities, said ČEZ in the notification to Czech authorities submitted on 7 May.
The notification said developing an SMR project at the Tušimice site “represents a technically, ecologically and socially optimal solution”.
The document said the site is “optimal” from the special planning and infrastructure points of view.
According to the notification, the project foresees the deployment of one to six SMR units, with a maximum capacity of 1,500 MW.

The document said none of the possible SMR designs will be excluded in advance.  List of potential designs includes Rolls-Royce SMR, GEH’s BWRX-300, France’s Nuward and Westinghouse’s AP300, all of which are reference designs for the Temelín SMR project.
According to ČEZ, the Tušimice coal power plant will be retired in 2030 and the possible start of construction of SMRs can be in 2034.
The documents said 2038 could be the earliest deployment target date, with more units following by 2042.
ČEZ recently concluded an deal with UK-based reactor developer Rolls-Royce SMR, taking a 20% in its reactor business as part of a project to deploy its SMR plants at Temelín.
The 1,500 MW limit set in the Tušimice notification means the deployment of up to three Rolls-Royce SMR units, but the notification remains design-neutral.
The Czech Republic has six commercially operational reactor units: four Russia-designed VVER-440 units at Dukovany and two larger VVER-1000 units at Temelín.

Prague has awarded a contract to Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power (KHNP), a subsidiary of state-run Kepco, for two new large-scale APR1000 units at Dukovany, but that decision has been challenged by France’s state-owned EDF, which along with US Westinghouse was also a bidder.
The government is also considering new large- or small-scale reactors at Temelín in the 2030s.
According to the International Atomic Energy Agency, the six units provide about 36.7% of the country’s electricity production.
In January 2025, a national energy plan submitted to the European Commission saw an end to coal use by 2033 and an increase in the share of nuclear power in the energy mix to 68% by 2040.
The Tušimice coal power plant will be retired in 2030 and the possible start of construction of SMRs can be in 2034. Courtesy ČEZ.

title: Trump Draft Executive Orders Aim To Speed Construction Of Nuclear Plants
author: David Dalton
text: Administration aims to set goal of quadrupling size of the nation’s reactor fleet
The Trump administration is considering several executive orders aimed at speeding up the construction of nuclear power plants to help meet rising electricity demand, according to media reports.

Draft orders say the US has fallen behind China in expanding nuclear power and call for a “wholesale revision” of federal safety regulations to make it easier to build new plants. They envision the Department of Defense taking a prominent role in ordering reactors and installing them on military bases, the reports said.
They would also set a goal of quadrupling the size of the nation’s fleet of nuclear power plants, from about 96.5 GW of net electric capacity today to 400 GW by 2050.

“As American development of new nuclear reactor designs has waned, 87% of nuclear reactors installed worldwide since 2017 are based on Russian and Chinese designs,” reads one draft order, titled ‘Ushering In a Nuclear Renaissance.’
“These trends cannot continue,” the order reads, according to the New York Times. “Swift and decisive action is required to jump-start America’s nuclear renaissance.”

The four draft orders are marked “pre-decisional” and “deliberative”. They are among several potential executive orders on nuclear power that have been circulating but it is not clear which, if any, might be issued.

In one of his first acts in office, president Donald Trump declared a “national energy emergency”, saying the US had inadequate supplies of electricity to meet the country’s growing needs, particularly for data centres that run artificial intelligence systems.
While most of Trump’s actions have focused on boosting fossil fuels like coal, oil and natural gas, administration officials have also supported nuclear power.

“Our goal is to bring in tens of billions of dollars during this administration in private capital to get reactors built, and I’m highly confident we will achieve that goal,” Chris Wright, the energy secretary, said at a hearing before a House appropriations subcommittee last week.
Donald Trump is said to be considering several executive orders aimed at speeding up the construction of nuclear power plants. Courtesy The White House/Facebook.

title: Germany Drops Long-Held Opposition To Nuclear In ‘Rapprochement’ With France
author: David Dalton
text: ‘All the biases against nuclear’ in EU legislation will be removed, says German official

Germany has dropped its long-held opposition to nuclear power, potentially resolving a major dispute between the two countries that has delayed decisions on EU energy policy, including during the crisis that followed Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.
Berlin has signalled to Paris it will no longer block French efforts to ensure nuclear power is treated on par with renewable energy in EU legislation, according to French and German officials.
The move is being seen as a concrete sign of rapprochement with France by Berlin’s new government led by conservative chancellor Friedrich Merz.
“The Germans are telling us: we will be very pragmatic on the issue of nuclear power,” said a senior French diplomat involved in the talks.

This meant that “all the biases against nuclear power, which still remain here and there in EU legislation, will be removed.” “This will be a sea-change policy shift,” said a German official, as reported by the UK daily Financial Times (subscription required).
Berlin’s reversal on nuclear power is part of efforts by Merz to revive Franco-German co-operation, a precondition for major decisions at EU level that stalled under former chancellor Olaf Scholz.

Germany under Scholz was against the EU treating nuclear on an equal footing as solar and wind in the bloc’s policies to achieve net-zero by 2050. The anti-nuclear camp was led by Germany and Austria and said nuclear was not a “green” power source.

Until March 2011, when Germany’s older reactors were shut down immediately after the Fukushima disaster in Japan, Germany generated one-quarter of its electricity from nuclear energy with 17 reactors.
Shutdown plans began in 2002 under the Social Democrats and Green party government, led by then-chancellor Gerhard Schröder, who enacted a law to phase out nuclear energy.

Former chancellor Angela Merkel’s government announced plans to reverse the law in 2010, but the March 2011 Fukushima disaster in Japan resulted a major shift in Germany’s attitude towards nuclear power and Merkel did a complete U-turn.

Germany’s last three nuclear power plants – Isar-2, Neckarwestheim-2 and Emsland – were permanently shut down in April 2023, making good on the country’s delayed nuclear phaseout even amid Europe’s energy crisis caused by Russia’s war in Ukraine.
French president Emmanuel Macron is bullish on nuclear. His government recently asked state nuclear operator EDF to accelerate efforts to finalise its plans to build six new nuclear reactors.
France’s share of generation from its fleet of 56 nuclear plants last year was about 62% – the highest in the world.

Eleven pro-nuclear European governments led by France have said nuclear should be part of the EU’s energy policies and the European Commission should facilitate the development of the technology in Europe.
The Brussels-based nuclear group Nucleareurope has said all fossil-free and net zero energy sources must be treated on an equal footing.
Germany’s last three nuclear power plants – Isar-2 (pictured), Neckarwestheim-2 and Emsland – were permanently shut down in April 2023. Courtesy PreussenElektra.

title: Kazatomprom Concludes Loan Deal In Bid To Finance Key Sulphuric Acid Plant
author: David Dalton
text: Major uranium producer has seen shortages of crucial chemical

Kazakhstan’s national nuclear company Kazatomprom has concluded an agreement on opening a credit line to finance the construction of a sulphuric acid plant – less than a year after it said shortages of the chemical were partly to blame for a cut its 2025 production target.
The credit agreement was signed with the Development Bank of Kazakhstan JSC and Taiqonyr Qyshqyl Zauyty, the partnership company formed to oversee the construction project.
Kazatomprom said the plant, in the Turkestan region in the south of the country, will have a capacity of about 800,000 tonnes per year.
Total investment in the project, which is scheduled for completion in early 2027, will be about $220m (€196m) with loan financing from the Development Bank of Kazakhstan of about $167m.

Last year Kazatomprom, which generates a fifth of global uranium supply, cut its production target for 2025 by 17% to a range of 25,000 to 26,500 tonnes of yellowcake, or triuranium octoxide (U3O8), a type of uranium concentrate powder used to produce fuel for nuclear power reactors.

Kazatomprom said at the time that “the uncertainty around the sulphuric acid supplies for 2025 needs and delays in the construction works at the newly developed deposits resulted in a need to re-evaluate our 2025 plans”.

Sulphuric acid, essential to extracting uranium from deposits, has been in short supply in Kazakhstan because of delays in building new acid plants, competition with the fertiliser industry and trade restrictions.

title: As Taiwan Prepares To Shut Down Last Nuclear Plant, Parliament Approves Law Change
author: David Dalton
text: Measure aims to open way for ‘reintroduction’ of reactors as energy demand soars on Asian island nation

Taiwan’s parliament has approved an amendment to nuclear power legislation, allowing operators to apply for an extension of their operating licence by an additional 20 years, beyond the current limit of 40, potentially increasing the lifespan of a reactor to 60 years.

The state-owned Central News Agency said the amendment, supported by the opposition Kuomintang and Taiwan People’s Party, passed with 60 votes in favour against 51 against the ruling Democratic Progressive Party.

According to its proponents, the measure aims to reintroduce nuclear energy into the island nation’s energy strategy. The Nuclear Safety Council said any renewal requests must meet international standards and be subject to thorough technical and legal assessments.

The move comes as the government is scheduled this weekend to permanently shut down the Maanshan-2 nuclear power plant in Pingtung County, southern Taiwan, fulfilling its promise to make Taiwan nuclear free.

Economy minister Kuo Jyh-huei confirmed that any extension for Maanshan-2 would take up to 18 months to approve and implement. The government said the amendment does not change plans to shut down Maanshan-2.
In July 2024, state-owned nuclear plant owner and operator Taipower shut down the Maanshan-1 nuclear power plant, leaving the country with just one reactor unit, Maanshan-2, in commercial operation.

Soaring energy demand driven by the island’s semiconductor industry is rekindling the debate about nuclear energy. The country’s electricity needs are expected to rise by 12-13% by 2030, largely driven by the boom in artificial intelligence (AI), according to the Ministry of Economic Affairs.

Environmental group Greenpeace has estimated that the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company, the world’s largest contract chipmaker, will by itself consume as much electricity as roughly one-quarter of the island’s 23 million people by 2030.

The island’s appetite for power complicates Taipei’s pledge to reach net-zero emissions by 2050, a pledge which is heavily dependent on raising renewable energy production to about 60-70% of the total from about 12% at present.
Nuclear power advocates argue that the energy source is the most feasible way for Taiwan to reach its competing industrial and environmental goals.
In 2023, nuclear accounted for about 6.9% of Taiwan’s electricity production, which is dominated by coal and liquified natural gas.
Taipower said that with the closure of Maanshan-1, the share of power generated by nuclear sources would fall to 2.8%.
At one point, nuclear energy from six reactors in Taiwan provided more than half of heavily industrialised island’s electricity.
Late last year Taiwan’s premier Cho Jung-tai said the country was “very open” to using new nuclear technology to meet rising demand from chipmakers using electricity to provide power for the AI boom.

“As long as there is a consensus within Taiwan on nuclear safety and a good direction and guarantees for handling nuclear waste, with this strong consensus, we can have a public discussion,” Cho said in an interview with Bloomberg News.
His comments were one of the strongest signs yet that the government has been rethinking its opposition to commercial power reactors.
Cho appeared to be referring to advanced reactors, potentially including small modular reactors (SMRs) that are being developed in a number of countries.
Taiwan’s National Atomic Research Institute this week said it had launched a $3.3m (€2.9m) SMR research project that could pave the way for the introduction of advanced nuclear reactors
The Maanshan-2 nuclear power plant in Pingtung County, southern Taiwan, is scheduled to be permanently shut down this weekend. Courtesy Wikipedia/Creative Commons Licence.

title: US Fast-Tracks Utah Uranium Project As Trump Bids To Solve ‘Energy Crisis’
author: David Dalton
text: Environmental review for Velvet-Wood will be completed in just 14 days

The US Interior Department has announced it will fast-track environmental permitting for Anfield Energy’s proposed Velvet-Wood uranium mine project in Utah to boost president Donald Trump’s efforts to increase domestic energy production.
As a result, the project’s environmental review will be completed in just 14 days, the department said in a statement.
Such studies typically take years because of the potential environmental effects of uranium mining.

Canada-based Anfield Energy said Velvet-Wood is the first uranium project fast-tracked by the US government under Trump’s emergency declaration to restore American energy independence. It said the move was “a decisive shift in federal support for domestic nuclear fuel supply”.
Secretary of the interior Doug Burgum said America is facing an alarming energy emergency because of the prior administration’s climate extremist policies.
“President Trump and his administration are responding with speed and strength to solve this crisis, he said.
“The expedited mining project review represents exactly the kind of decisive action we need to secure our energy future.”

If approved, the Velvet-Wood mine project in San Juan County would produce uranium, used in both nuclear energy and nuclear weapons production, as well as vanadium, a metal than can be used in batteries or to strengthen steel and other alloys.
The Interior Department said the project would be at the site of a previous mining operation and lead to only three acres (1.2 hectares) of new surface disturbance.
Anfield also owns the Shootaring Canyon uranium mill in Utah, which it intends to restart. That mill would convert uranium ore into uranium concentrate that could be used as a nuclear fuel.

Anfield acquired the Velvet-Wood mine – which is currently in care and maintenance – from Uranium One in 2015. Between 1979 and 1984, Atlas Minerals mined approximately 400,000 tonnes of ore from the Velvet Deposit, recovering approximately four million pounds of triuranium octoxide (U3O8).
U3O8, also known as yellowcake, is a type of uranium concentrate powder used to produce fuel for nuclear power reactors.
The Velvet-Wood mine in Utah is currently in care and maintenance. Courtesy Anfield Energy.

title: Denmark Considers Lifting 40-Year Ban On Nuclear Power
author: David Dalton
text: Copenhagen says it will examine pros and cons of using small modular reactors to balance renewables

Denmark is considering lifting a 40-year-old ban on nuclear power as part of a bid to improve its energy security and avoid blackout of the kind that hit Spain and Portugal last month, its energy minister said.
Lars Aagaard told Danish newspaper Politiken on 13 May that the centrist coalition in Copenhagen would take a year to analyse the pros and cons of reviving nuclear power.
“We can see that there is a development underway with new nuclear power technologies – small modular reactors [SMRs],” Aagaard said.
“But it’s not enough that they have potential. We also need to know what it means for Danish society if we are to enable these technologies,” he said.
On 14 May Aagaard was due to appear at a public hearing in parliament and answer questions from opposition parties favouring the revival of nuclear power.
A lifting of its ban from 1985 would put Denmark in a growing group of countries looking at nuclear energy to help balance renewable sources in their electricity mix.

Neighbouring Sweden’s right-wing government is trying to revive nuclear power in the country, which still has three plants in operation, after big debates over closing them ever since the Three Mile Island accident in the US in 1979.
Norway, meanwhile, has set up a commission to consider nuclear power and companies are emerging that plan to deploy SMRs.
Anders Fogh Rasmussen, Denmark’s former prime minister and an ex-secretary general of Nato, told UK daily the Financial Times he was in favour of lifting the “ridiculous” ban.
Denmark has one of the highest shares of renewable energy in its electricity mix in Europe thanks to vast offshore wind farms along its coast.

Denmark has never had commercial nuclear power plants, but had three nuclear research reactors, which were brought online between 1957 and 1960. They have all been shut down and are being decommissioned.

Last month, a fund backed by Danish billionaire Joachim Ante announced plans to raise €350m ($397m) to back the advanced nuclear industry and its supply chain. 92 Capital is betting on a nuclear power renaissance because of a broader rise in concerns over energy security.
Ante, who founded video game software company Unity, has so far put in €50m of his own funds.
An earlier version of the fund, 92 Ventures, invested in Sweden’s Blykalla and Finland’s Steady Energy, both developers of SMRs.
Denmark’s Seaborg Technologies is exploring the potential deployment of its compact molten salt reactor floating “power barge” technology in a number of countries.
Lars Aagaard was due to appear at a public hearing to answer questions from opposition parties favouring the revival of nuclear power. Courtesy Lars Aagaard/X.

title: Testing Programme Demonstrates Robustness Of Transportable Nuclear Plants, Says Prodigy
author: David Dalton
text: Reactors could supply remote communities, mines, defence installations and arctic data centres

A first-of-its-kind test programme is demonstrating the robustness of transportable nuclear power plants (TNPPs) to resist accidental and threat scenarios – and generating critical data needed to support licensing for commercialisation of the plants by 2030.

Canada-based Prodigy Clean Energy and Serco said the testing had been funded in part by a CAD2.7m ($1.9m, €1.7m) award from the Canadian federal government as part of a programme to develop small modular reactors (SMRs).
Prodigy said its TNPPs will be fabricated at a maritime facility then transported to site, offering rapid deployment solutions to bring new nuclear power online sooner and at competitive costs.

The company essentially aims to “package” SMRs and microreactors into prefabricated and relocatable power plant structures. Units can be combined to provide capacities ranging from about 5 MW to 1,000 MW.
“TNPPs require a very small shoreline footprint and are customisable by reactor type and size,” the company said.

It said the partnership with UK-headquartered Serco is testing TNPP resilience and structural performance under “the most challenging conditions”, including against aircraft impact and ship collision; seismic, ice, and other severe weather and ocean events; fire and flooding; and for robustness to withstand internal missile impact.
“Prodigy is completing the real work needed to bring TNPPs to market in North America on schedule,” said Mathias Trojer, the company’s president and chief executive officer.
He said Prodigy’s reactor technologies are now at a suitable level of readiness to engage sophisticated partners on detailed engineering exercises.
Prodigy said its TNPPs can be used to supply carbon-free baseload to remote mines, communities, defence installations and arctic data centres.
Prodigy said its transportable nuclear power plants will be fabricated at a maritime facility then transported to site. Courtesy Prodigy.

title: UK Group Warns Nuclear Workforce Will Need To Grow ‘Considerably’
author: Rachel Rigby
text: Long-term demand remains challenging, with 120,000 needed in industry by 2030

A national organisation set up in partnership with the UK government and nuclear sector organisations is succeeding in attracting the critical workers needed for the country to meet its ambitious nuclear rollout plans, but has warned that the workforce will need to grow “considerably”.
Destination Nuclear was launched by the government’s National Skills Task Force in partnership with industry and educational institutions to drive recruitment in the nuclear sector.

Lynne Matthews, former programme lead at Destination Nuclear who was seconded to the organisation from France-based state power utility and nuclear plant operator EDF, told NucNet that collaboration is taking place at a national level to start to address the UK’s growing need for nuclear workers.

The London-based Nuclear Industry Association (NIA) has said that while the current workforce has grown to 96,000 – an increase of about 7,000 in the year ending in April 2024 – the long-term demand figures remain challenging, with 120,000 people needed in nuclear by 2030.
This represents a requirement for approximately 24,000 additional skilled personnel over the next six years.
The NIA said that to enable the sector to meet this demand, cross-sector collaboration to attract and retain skills is key, alongside making the diversity of the future workforce a priority.

Matthews, who has helped address workforce challenges for major nuclear projects such as Hinkley Point C and Sizewell C, helped to develop Destination Nuclear as part of the UK government’s national skills plan.

The programme spans the civil and defence nuclear sectors and seeks to attract a broad range of roles including critical skills areas such as welding, safety case engineers, project planning and controls, and radiation protection.  Matthews heralded Destination Nuclear as “a game changer” and the first cross sector national nuclear campaign.
“In February 2024, we were given three months to launch the programme something that ordinarily would take at least 10 months,” Matthews said.
“It was a challenge, but the pace was essential if at a national level we were going to partner organisations and their supply chain to reduce the skills gap.”

The campaign initially targeted mid-career switchers. Research suggests that nearly 80% of people have transferable skills that can be used in nuclear, but many are not aware of the range of roles available.
Using channels such as digital advertising, on demand TV including Netflix and the online educational gaming platform Minecraft, enabled Destination Nuclear to reach further and wider, Matthews said.
Early indications show a 52% increase in mid-career workers that had never considered nuclear but now are.
The team also worked with regional hubs and the government’s Department of Work and Pensions to start to target unemployed people and others who would normally be difficult to reach.
Matthews, who has now returned to EDF, said: “We are understanding more about the demand and supply of skills however the skills landscape is dynamic.
“We have already seen 2024 as a game changer with announcements from the likes of Amazon, Google and Microsoft around their increased demand for energy for data centres to drive AI.
“Their need for always-on power could create further opportunities for nuclear and in turn the development and deployment of skills and jobs.”
The nuclear sector already supports tens of thousands of jobs across the UK and could contribute over £70bn (€82bn, $93bn) to the economy by 2050.
Collaborations on skills and recruitment programmes are a positive step forward towards this, Matthews said.
About 120,000 additional workers will be needed in the nuclear industry in the UK by 2030. Courtesy UK Government.

title: Newcleo Teams Up With Italian Companies To Unveil Generation IV Reactor Design For Ships
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Company says LT-40 nuclear plant can use reprocessed waste as fuel
France-based nuclear developer Newcleo, Italian design company Pininfarina and Italian shipbuilder Fincantieri have unveiled a full-scale model of a next-generation nuclear reactor for maritime use.
The TL-40 reactor, developed by Newcleo, is a Generation IV, lead-cooled small modular reactor (SMR) intended to power large vessels.

The company, which unveiled the model at the 19th International Architecture Exhibition of the Venice Biennale, said the lead-cooling system incorporates passive safety mechanisms that eliminate the risk of nuclear incidents through the laws of physics that govern the reactor's operation.
The design can use reprocessed nuclear waste as fuel, addressing both energy generation and nuclear waste reduction.
Pininfarina contributed its design vision to the project, while Fincantieri contributed its shipbuilding experience, a statement said.
Newcleo and Fincantieri have been working together since 2023 on potential maritime uses for the reactor.
Pininfarina is also collaborating with Newcleo on the design of a nuclear fuel research and development centre in Chusclan, France.
Newcleo, which is based in France and has offices in the UK, Italy and Switzerland, says it is aiming to deliver a first demonstration reactor by 2031 and a commercial reactor by 2033.
The company has begun the process to acquire land for its first land-based lead-cooled LFR-AS-30 reactor in the Chinon Vienne et Loire region of western France.
The LFR design was included in a shortlist for support from the European industrial alliance on SMRs in October 2024.
Newcleo has not given a target date for deployment of the TL-40 design.
The TL-40  is a Generation IV, lead-cooled small modular reactor intended to power large vessels. Courtesy Newcleo.

title: Spain’s Nuclear Generation ‘Essential In Current Geopolitical Context’, Says Foro Nuclear
author: David Dalton
text: ‘Logical response’ to recent blackout would be to abandon planned reactor phaseout

Spain’s fleet of seven commercial nuclear power plants generated almost 20% of the country’s total net electricity production in 2024, guaranteeing the supply and energy independence that are essential in the current geopolitical context, Madrid-based industry group Foro Nuclear said.
In the latest edition of its annual report Foro Nuclear said Spain’s nuclear fleet generated almost 52.4 TWh net in 2024, slightly down from the 54.4 TWh generated in 2023.

As of 31 December, the total installed net capacity of the electricity generation fleet in Spain was 128,987 MW, of which nuclear accounted for 7,117 MW (net), or 5.52% of the total installed net capacity.
Nuclear was the second largest source of electricity production, behind renewables.

According to figures from Spain’s transmission system operator, Red Eléctrica, renewables accounted for 66% of the country’s total installed capacity and 56.8% of Spain’s electricity generation in 2024, up 10.3% compared with 2023.
“The seven operating reactors continued to guarantee supply and energy independence, as they produce baseload power constantly and reliably," said Foro Nuclear president Ignacio Araluce.
“These aspects are essential in the current geopolitical context, in which Europe is striving to achieve energy sovereignty.”

Araluce had said earlier that nuclear power is needed to stabilise Spain’s electrical system and the country should rethink its planned phaseout following the unprecedented blackout that recently affected the Iberian Peninsula.
The outage has reignited the debate over the plan to decommission all of Spain’s commercial nuclear power reactors by 2035.
Araluce said the logical response would be to keep the nuclear energy Spain has.

Four nuclear units at three nuclear stations were in operation when the outage struck and immediately went offline, but diesel generators kept them in “safe condition”, the country’s nuclear regulator CSN said.
The four units were Almaraz-2, Asco-1, Asco-2 and Vandellos-2.
A minister suggested recently that the government might be open to reconsidering the planned nuclear shutdown amid a global revival of nuclear energy.
Nuclear was the second largest source of electricity production in Spain in 2024, behind renewables. Courtesy CSN.

title: South Korea And Czech Republic ‘Remain Committed’ To Signing $18 Billion Dukovany Nuclear Deal
author: David Dalton
text: Contract for two new reactors delayed after appeal by losing bidder EDF

South Korea and the Czech Republic have reaffirmed their commitment to signing an $18bn (€16bn) nuclear power plant construction deal, despite a court ruling that temporarily delayed the contract signing.

According to press reports, at a cabinet meeting on 7 May the Czech government said Elektrarna Dukovany II, a subsidiary of Czech state utility ČEZ, would proceed with the contract to build two nuclear reactors with Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power (KHNP) at the “earliest possible timing”.
The two new large-scale APR1000 plants, supplied by KHNP, will be built at the existing Dukovany nuclear power station site in the Czech Republic.

The deal, originally planned to be signed on 7 May, was postponed after a court injunction was granted in response to a legal challenge by French energy company EDF, an unsuccessful bidder in the tender.

Czech prime minister Petr Fiala said the government would “avoid any delay of even a single day”, expressing his willingness to complete all related procedures as soon as the legal obstacles are cleared.

“KHNP’s proposal is the best in every respect and has been selected as the supplier,” Fiala said during a press conference following a meeting with South Korean industry minister Ahn Duk-geun and a South Korean delegation that had travelled to Prague for the planned signing.

Ahn expressed confidence that the contract would be signed. “While today’s unforeseen circumstances prevented us from finalising the main contract, I feel confident that – like the saying ‘the ground hardens after rain’ – this shared challenge has only strengthened the trust between our two countries,” he said.
According to a statement released by the Czech government, finance minister Zbynek Stanjura affirmed the integrity of the bid evaluation process.

“We are convinced that the bid evaluation process was carried out correctly and in accordance with applicable laws,” Stanjura said. “I believe the court will rule quickly so that we can continue preparing for the construction of new nuclear units and the state does not suffer any damage due to the delay.”
ČEZ chief executive officer Daniel Benes said 7 May the company would appeal the court injunction.
EDF welcomed the postponement, saying it “provides the necessary time for a thorough assessment of any potential infringement of its rights”.

The signing of the contract with KHNP – the biggest procurement deal in Czech history – would mark South Korea’s first overseas nuclear power station project since 2009, when it won a contract to build four APR1000 plants at Barakah in the United Arab Emirates.
The first new unit at Dukovany had been expected to become operational by 2036 and the second about two years later.
The two new nuclear plants, supplied by KHNP, will be built at the existing Dukovany nuclear power station site in the Czech Republic. Courtesy ČEZ.

title: Kairos Power Pours First Concrete For Demonstration Advanced Reactor In Tennessee
author: David Dalton
text: Hermes is scaled version of Generation IV fluoride salt-cooled nuclear plant
