title: All Nuclear Power Plants Belong To People Of Ukraine, Says Zelenskyy
author: David Dalton
text: Kyiv confirms discussions with Trump about occupied Zaporizhzhia facility

Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy has insisted that “all nuclear power plants belong to the people of Ukraine” after reports that his US counterpart Donald Trump said a US takeover of the country’s nuclear power would offer the “best protection” for it.
US president Donald Trump reportedly proposed that the US take over Ukraine’s nuclear power plants in a telephone call with Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy on 19 March.
But Kyiv said the discussions referred only to the Zaporizhzhia nuclear power station, which is under Russian occupation.
All nuclear power plants in Ukraine are state-owned and belong to Kyiv, Zelenskyy said.
“The temporarily occupied Zaporizhzhia [nuclear power station] belongs to Ukraine, everybody acknowledges it and recognises it,” he said.

Zelenskyy denied discussing with Trump the possibility of US ownership of Zaporizhzhia, but said they did discuss “how to find the solution from the situation and… take the station from the Russians”.
They also talked about potential US investment in the plant, the Ukrainian leader said.
But he added: “The issue with property we definitely did not discuss with Mr Trump.”

Zelenskyy’s comments followed a call earlier this week with Trump, after which US secretary of state Marco Rubio and national security adviser Mike Waltz said the two leaders had discussed Ukraine’s electrical supply and nuclear power plants.

“He [Trump] said that the United States could be very helpful in running those plants with its electricity and utility expertise,” a summary of the call issued by The White House said, with US ownership offering “the best protection” for Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
The six-unit Zaporizhzhia nuclear station is the largest in Europe with a net capacity of 5,700 MW when all units are fully operational.
Zaporizhzhia, near the city of Enerhodar, close to the frontline of fighting in southern Ukraine, has been under Russian occupation since 2022.

All six units are in a state of cold shutdown, defined by nuclear regulators as meaning the reactor coolant system is at atmospheric pressure and at a temperature below about 90°C following a reactor cooldown.

Cold shutdown reduces the need for cooling and lessens the risk of an accident. In a cold shutdown, the reactor is in a subcritical state, meaning no nuclear fission is taking place, and the fuel and control rods can be safely removed and replaced.

Ukraine and its allies have repeatedly urged Russia to withdraw its troops from the Zaporizhzhia plant. Throughout its occupation, the facility has been repeatedly disconnected from the Ukrainian power grid due to Russian attacks on the country’s energy infrastructure.

International Atomic Energy Agency director-general Rafael Grossi has on numerous occasions sounded the alarm about the continued risk of nuclear accidents as a result of Russia’s attacks on Zaporizhzhia and Ukraine’s power grid.
The Zaporizhzhia nuclear power station is near the city of Enerhodar, close to the frontline of fighting in southern Ukraine. Courtesy Energoatom.
Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy during a telephone call this week with António Costa, president of the European Council. Courtesy Gov’t of Ukraine/X.

title: Finland University To Build Two Facilities For Small Modular Reactor Safety Testing
author: David Dalton
text: Tests on Finnish and French nuclear technology to take place from 2026 to 2027

LUT University in Finland has announced plans to build two test facilities at its campus in Lappeenranta, in the southeast of the country, for research into the safety of small modular reactors (SMRs).
The university said in a statement on 20 March that one of the test facilities is based on Finnish technology and the other one on French technology.
One of the facilities will model passive decay heat removal of the LDR-50 district heating reactor developed by the Finnish company Steady Energy.

Passive decay heat removal systems rely on natural processes like convection and gravity to remove residual heat from a nuclear reactor core after shutdown, ensuring safe cooling without external power or operator intervention. Passive safety systems that do not require operator actions form an important part of the safety of new reactor types.
The tests will take place from 2026 to 2027 and the results will be reported in 2027 to 2028.
The tests based the French technology – which was not named – will focus on the functionality of the SMR’s emergency core cooling tank.

The university said SMRs could be used for district heating, reducing carbon dioxide emissions and reducing the need for fossil and wood fuels. They would improve the supply security of electricity and heating.
District heating is a system for distributing heat generated by a power station through a network of insulated pipes for residential and commercial heating.

Steady Energy has signed letters of intent on small district heating reactors with the energy companies Helen, Kuopion Energiav and Keravan Energia. Steady Energy is also marketing its solution to other European countries, such as Poland.
In Central Europe, district heating is still largely based on fossil fuels, which means nuclear heat would reduce emissions considerably.

“The research kicking off at LUT University will significantly advance the development of nuclear technology and our ongoing district heating projects,” said Lauri Muranen, head of public affairs at Steady Energy.

“The commercial breakthrough of small modular reactors is closer in heating than in electricity production, because small nuclear power plants producing district heating do not need public financing.”

The university said: “Nuclear power can ensure the availability of electricity independent of weather conditions, unlike wind or solar power. The less electricity is used for heating, the more electricity is available for other functions, such as transportation and industry.”

According to the university, the breakthrough of SMRs in Finland will require amendments to legislation and collaboration between authorities. The first SMRs are estimated to be operational in the early 2030s.
LUT University’s campus in Lappeenranta, in the southeast of Finland. Courtesy LUT University.

title: Westinghouse And Urenco Sign Long-Term Haleu Enrichment Agreement For eVinci Microreactor
author: Kamen Kraev
text: US company welcomes key step in building advanced fuel capability

Westinghouse Electric Company and Urenco have signed a long-term fuel enrichment agreement to supply high-assay low-enriched uranium (Haleu) for Westinghouse’s eVinci microreactor, the companies said.
A statement said that under the deal, Urenco will provide Haleu for a five-year deployment period, marking a step towards securing fuel supply chains for next-generation nuclear technologies.
“This is a key step in building our capabilities to supply advanced nuclear fuels,” said Tarik Choho, president of nuclear fuel at Westinghouse.

Westinghouse has said that the compact design of the eVinci microreactor, with a capacity of up to 5 MWe, enables easy transportation and fast onsite deployment. The reactor operates with minimal moving parts, functioning much like a nuclear battery.
It is intended for off-grid applications, including remote communities, disaster relief, industrial sites, defence infrastructure, marine propulsion, hydrogen production, and water purification.

Urenco, the Anglo-German-Dutch uranium enrichment company, has previously announced it has embarked on an effort to develop its Haleu production capacities, aiming for a future market for advanced reactors.
The company expects to be able to supply Haleu to its advanced reactor customers in the early 2030s.
In May 2024, the UK government announced it will provide funding to Urenco to build a dedicated Haleu enrichment facility at its Capenhurst site in northern England.
Urenco was also among four companies to receive a 10-year contract in October by the US Department of Energy for the eventual production of Haleu in the US.
According to earlier reports, Westinghouse’s eVinci is slated for scaled commercial deployment in the early 2030s.
Tarik Choho, president of nuclear fuel, Westinghouse, Laurent Odeh, chief commercial officer, Urenco, and Kallie Metzger, eVinci fuel director, Westinghouse, at the signing event in London.

title: Restart Preparations Complete At Japan’s Kashiwazaki Kariwa-7 Nuclear Power Plant
author: David Dalton
text: Tepco also hoping to start fuel loading at Unit 6 this summer

Restart preparations for Unit 7 at the Kashiwazaki Kariwa nuclear power station in Japan have been completed and a final decision on restarting the plant will be made once owner and operator Tokyo Electric Power Company (Tepco) has gained the understanding of the local community, NucNet has been told.

Tepco also said it plans to begin fuel loading at Unit 6 in June. By this summer, Unit 6 is expected to reach the same state as Unit 7, being “technically ready” for operation. Fuel loading at Unit 7 was completed in April 2024.
Tepco said press reports that it had changed the timeline for the completion of restart preparations at the facility, in Niigata Prefecture, western Japan, were not correct.

It said that although only about six months remain until an October 2025 deadline for installing a special safety facility at Kashiwazaki Kariwa, the main reactor facility has already passed the Nuclear Regulation Authority’s (NRA) regulatory review under new regulatory standards and is technically ready for restart.

Kashiwazaki Kariwa is one of the world’s largest nuclear power stations. According to the International Atomic Energy Agency, its seven boiling water reactor units have a combined net capacity of 7,965 MW.
Kashiwazaki Kariwa served as an important energy source to supply electricity to the Tokyo metropolitan area before the 2011 earthquake and nuclear accident at Fukushima-Daiichi.

Tepco wants to bring the station back online and said in 2020 it was concentrating its resources on restarting the newer Units 6 and 7, which originally began commercial operation in 1996 and 1997 respectively.
Before the Fukushima disaster Japan’s fleet of 54 nuclear plants generated about 30% of the country’s electricity, but were all shut down for safety checks following the accident.

Among the 33 operable nuclear reactors in Japan, 12 have now resumed operations after meeting post-Fukushima safety standards. The restarted plants are: Sendai-1 and -2, Genkai-3 and -4, Ikata-3, Mihama-3, Ohi-3 and -4 and Takahama-1, -2, -3 and -4.
Economy minister Yoji Muto said recently that Japan will need to maximise the use of existing nuclear power plants as AI and data centres are expected to boost electricity demand.
Kashiwazaki Kariwa has been offline since 2012 pending safety checks after the Fukushima disaster in 2011.

title: Tepco Brings Forward Planned Date For Restart Of Kashiwazaki Kariwa Nuclear Reactor
author: David Dalton
text: Uncertainty remains over when approval will be granted by Japan’s regulator

Tokyo Electric Power Company Holdings (Tepco) said it now aims to restart a reactor at its Kashiwazaki Kariwa nuclear power station in Niigata Prefecture, western Japan, in the fiscal year 2025, which starts next month.
The plan means the restart has been brought forward from a schedule announced recently of 2029.

Press reports in Japan said that according to changes made to the power utility’s business plan, approved by the government on 17 March, the restart of the reactor is expected to boost its earnings by around $672m (€615m) per year.
The Japan Times said Tepco’s changes to its business plan are provisional because it is still unclear when the company will be able to gain approval to bring the Kashiwazaki Kariwa plant back online.

Earlier this month Tepco said it had delayed the restart of Units 7 and 6 at Kashiwazaki Kariwa to 2029 and 2031 respectively, citing setbacks in completing required anti-terrorism measures due to struggles with the scale of construction and labour shortages.
The two units were originally scheduled to resume operations in October 2025 and September 2026, a schedule that now appears to have been reinstated.

Taking steps against terrorist threats and implementing additional safety and security measures became mandatory under stricter safety standards implemented after the 2011 nuclear accident at Fukushima-Daiichi – also owned and operated by Tepco – triggered by a massive earthquake and tsunami disaster.

Kashiwazaki Kariwa is one of the world’s largest nuclear power stations. According to the International Atomic Energy Agency, its seven boiling water reactor units have a combined net capacity of 7,965 MW.
Kashiwazaki Kariwa served as an important energy source to supply electricity to the Tokyo metropolitan area before the 2011 earthquake and nuclear disaster at Fukushima-Daiichi.

Tepco wants to bring the station back online and said in 2020 it was concentrating its resources on restarting the newer Units 6 and 7, which originally began commercial operation in 1996 and 1997 respectively.
Before the Fukushima disaster Japan’s fleet of 54 nuclear plants generated about 30% of the country’s electricity, but were all shut down for safety checks following the accident.

Among the 33 operable nuclear reactors in Japan, 12 have now resumed operations after meeting post-Fukushima safety standards. The restarted plants are: Sendai-1 and -2, Genkai-3 and -4, Ikata-3, Mihama-3, Ohi-3 and -4 and Takahama-1, -2, -3 and -4.
Economy minister Yoji Muto said recently that Japan will need to maximise the use of existing nuclear power plants as AI and data centres are expected to boost electricity demand.
Kashiwazaki Kariwa is one of the world’s largest nuclear power stations. Courtesy Tepco.

title: India’s Rajasthan-7 Nuclear Power Plant Connected To Grid
author: David Dalton
text: Unit is one in planned fleet of indigenous PHWR units

Unit 7 at the Rajasthan nuclear power station in Rajasthan state, northern India, was connected to the national grid on 17 March at 02.37 local time, state nuclear operator Nuclear Power Corporation of India Ltd (NPCIL) said.

The 630-MW Rajasthan-7 is the third in a series of 16 indigenous pressurised heavy water reactor units (PHWRs) which India has said it plans to build. The first two units, Kakarapar-3 and Kakrapar-4 in Gujurat state, western India, began commercial operation in 2023 and 2024.
NPCIL said the unit’s power level will now be increased in steps to full power, “in line with the regulatory clearances”.
A twin unit at the site, Rajasthan-8, is expected to be operational in 2025 or 2026, NPCIL said.

According to International Atomic Energy Agency data, India has 20 nuclear units in commercial operation, but this total does not include Rajasthan-7. The IAEA says India has seven units under construction, including Rajasthan-7. The nuclear fleet provided 3.1% of the country’s electricity generation in 2023.

Site works have begun for the construction of two PHWR units at Gorakhpur in Haryana state. Ten further 700 MW PHWRs have received administrative approval and financial sanction. They are: Kaiga-5 and Kaiga-6 in Karnataka state; Gorakhpur-3 and -4 in Haryana state; Chutka-1 and -2 in Madhya Pradesh state and Mahi Banswara-1, -2, -3 and -4 in Rajasthan.
The NPCIL-designed Generation III PHWR was developed from earlier 220 MW and 540 MW Canadian Candu designs.

New Delhi is bullish on nuclear. NPCIL said recently that India plans to add 18 more nuclear reactors to its national energy mix by 2031-32, bringing the total nuclear power capacity of the country to 22.4 GW.
NPCIL did not say whether the 22.4 GW would be net or gross, but either way it represents a significant increase from around 6.9 GW net today.
Unit 7 at the Rajasthan nuclear power station in Rajasthan state, northern India, was connected to the national grid on 17 March. Courtesy Govt of Rawatbhata.

title: Second Tier Installed At El Daaba-2 Inner Containment
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Egypt nuclear station will have four Russia-supplied VVER-1200 reactor units

The second tier has been installed of the inner steel containment shell for the second unit of the El Dabaa nuclear power station under construction in Egypt, Russia’s state nuclear corporation Rosatom said.

El Dabaa, Egypt’s first commercial nuclear station, will have four Russia-supplied Generation III+ VVER-1200 pressurised water reactors, with the first unit expected to be online in 2026. Construction of El Dabaa-2 began in November 2022.
At a nuclear power reactor, the inner containment acts as a hermetic protection system, designed to withstand high external and internal pressures and protect against radiation release.
The first tier for El Dabaa-2 was installed in October 2024 at the site, about 300 km northwest of the Egyptian capital Cairo on the country’s Mediterranean coast.
Rosatom said that after installation of the second tier, the reactor building became the tallest structure onsite, reaching slightly above 20 metres.

VVER-1200 plants have a total of seven cylindrical tiers for the inner steel containment, with the fifth one serving as a transition between the main part of the containment and its dome structure. The dome itself consists of a lower and upper tier.
According to earlier reports, Russia would lend Egypt $25bn (€23bn) for the construction of the El Dabaa station, which would constitute about 85% of the total cost of the project.
El Dabaa, Egypt’s first commercial nuclear station, will have four Russia-supplied Generation pressurised water reactors. Courtesy Rosatom.

title: Future Of Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Station Part Of Ukraine Peace Deal, Trump Suggests
author: David Dalton
text: Six-unit facility near frontline has been under Russian occupation since invasion in 2022
Washington has discussed with Ukraine the control of the Russian-occupied Zaporizhzhia nuclear power station as part of a potential peace deal, US president Donald Trump has suggested.
Trump did not mention Zaporizhzhia, but speaking in the Oval Office said that Ukraine and the US had discussed a lot of details of the final deal, including “concepts of land”.
“We have been discussing with Ukraine land and pieces of land that would be kept and lost and all of the other elements of a final agreement,” Trump said.

“There’s a power plant involved, a very big power plant involved,” Trump said. “Who is going to get the power plant, and who is going to get this and that, and so you know it’s not an easy process. But phase one is the ceasefire,” he added, referring to Kyiv’s agreement to a 30-day ceasefire proposed by Washington provided that Russia also agrees.
Press reports have suggested Trump was referring to the six-unit Zaporizhzhia nuclear station, the largest in Europe with a net capacity of 5,700 MW when all units are fully operational.
Zaporizhzhia, near the city of Enerhodar, near the frontline of fighting in southern Ukraine, has been under Russian occupation since 2022.

All six units are in a state of cold shutdown, defined by nuclear regulators as meaning the reactor coolant system is at atmospheric pressure and at a temperature below about 90°C following a reactor cooldown. Cold shutdown reduces the need for cooling and lessens the risk of an accident. In a cold shutdown, the reactor is in a subcritical state, meaning no nuclear fission is taking place, and the fuel and control rods can be safely removed and replaced.

Ukraine and its allies have repeatedly urged Russia to withdraw its troops from the plant. Throughout its occupation, the plant has been repeatedly disconnected from the Ukrainian power grid due to Russian attacks on the country’s energy infrastructure.

International Atomic Energy Agency director-general Rafael Grossi has on numerous occasions sounded the alarm about the continued risk of nuclear accidents as a result of Russia’s attacks on Zaporizhzhia and Ukraine’s power grid.

Three years of Russian strikes on its power grid have left Ukraine reliant on nuclear power for more than half of its electricity generation. That nuclear power is generated by three functioning stations – Khmelnitski, Rivne and South Ukraine.
Ukraine’s state nuclear company Energoatom is planning to complete Units 3 and 4 at Khmelnitski, in western Ukraine, construction of which is suspended.
The plan is to buy reactor equipment that was produced by Russia for the abandoned Belene nuclear power station project in Bulgaria.
Construction of two VVER-1000 units at Khmelnitski-3 and -4 was abandoned in 1990 in the aftermath of the 1986 Chernobyl accident in Soviet Ukraine and because of financial shortages.
The Zaporizhzhia nuclear power station has been the target of a number of military strikes. Courtesy IAEA.
Donald Trump: ‘There’s a power plant involved, a very big power plant involved.’ Courtesy The White House.

title: Negotiations On Czech Nuclear Project To Be Finalised ‘Later This Month’
author: David Dalton
text: South Korea won contract for two new reactors at Dukovany

Negotiations with the Czech Republic on a project to build two new nuclear plants at the Dukovany nuclear site are expected to be finalised later this month, South Korea’s state-run Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power (KHNP) said
“We are in the final stage of the negotiations with the Czech client and are now fine-tuning details at a reasonable level,” KHNP told Yonhap News Agency.
“We are planning to conclude the talks within March and set the date for signing after considering other factors, including internal procedures and government reporting.”

Press reports in South Korea said that while the two sides have reportedly reached an agreement on key points, such as the total project cost, they are still discussing specific issues, including the percentage of localization throughout the construction process.

If finalised, the deal, estimated at $16.7bn (€14.6bn) according to press reports, would mark South Korea's first overseas nuclear power plant project since 2009, when KHNP won the Barakah Nuclear Power Plant contract in the United Arab Emirates.
In July, KHNP was chosen as preferred bidder in a lucrative public tender to build two nuclear plants at Dukovany with the first unit scheduled to be online by 2036.

Two companies that lost out in the bidding, France’s state power company EDF and Westinghouse of the US, both filed complaints against Czech energy company ČEZ’s decision to award the contract to KHNP.
On 31 October the Czech anti-monopoly office UOHS preliminarily rejected both complaints.
KHNP settled an intellectual property dispute with Westinghouse in January, removing a major hurdle to the signing of the Czech project.
Westinghouse had previously claimed KHNP had infringed on its intellectual property.
KHNP has been chosen as preferred bidder in a lucrative public tender to build two nuclear plants at Dukovany. Courtesy ČEZ.

title: UK Prepares For Government Decisions On Sizewell C And Small Modular Reactors
author: Rachel Rigby
text: Financial review follows decision to increase defence spending and could impact nuclear

The UK nuclear power industry is facing two key financial events that could have a major impact on new nuclear construction including the planned Sizewell C nuclear station and the deployment of small modular reactors, industry sources have said.

The country’s Labour government will unveil its budget for the 2024-25 financial year on 26 March, followed in the second half of June by a spending review for the next three financial years covering the period from 2025 to 2027.

“The two big items for expenditure are the Sizewell C final investment decision [FID] and the SMR [small modular reactor] competition,” said Stephen Thomas, a professor of energy policy at the University of Greenwich in London.

An executive at a UK reactor development company said the UK government of prime minister Keir Starmer was “undertaking a financial review right across all departments, energy and nuclear power will of course be included in that”. The executive spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss financial information that was potentially sensitive to his company.

The executive noted that an increase in government defence spending had set the review in motion, but emphasised that the review did not assume any spending cuts in particular areas. The increase in defence spending from 2.3% to 2.5% follows efforts to increase support for Ukraine and to respond to US president Donald Trump’s Trump call for NATO countries to all spend 5% on defence.

The executive added that he believed that nuclear power would be “to a large degree protected from the review because this is an area that is very important to the government and clearly very directly linked to the net zero agenda”.

A second industry source added that it was “pretty clear that Sizewell C and the small modular reactor deployment are going to go ahead in the country. Clearly, there will be some form of funding for that in the strategic review, and quite likely in the budget this month as well”.

Sizewell C is a planned nuclear project in Suffolk in eastern England. The project is 76.1% owned by the UK government, with EDF Energy, the UK subsidiary of French nuclear power company EDF, holding 23.9%. Sizewell C will have two EPR units supplied by France.

A final investment decision on Sizewell C had been scheduled to take place during the second half of 2024, but was delayed until the first half of 2005 – after the completion of the government’s strategic spending review.

Sizewell C will be the sister plant of Hinkley Point C, which is under construction near the city of Bristol in southwestern England. The delayed project is expected to be completed by the end of 2029, but may be delayed until the early 2030s, according to the most recent schedule published by EDF Energy.

The UK government is running a competition to deploy a first SMR in the UK in the early 2030s and has shortlisted four reactor designs for this purpose. The four designs are from GE-Hitachi Nuclear Energy International, Holtec Britain, Rolls-Royce SMR and Westinghouse Electric Company UK.
Thomas said: “If we assume that the Sizewell C cost estimate at the time of the FID is £40bn (€47bn, $51bn), that commits government to £20 billion-plus over the next 15 or more years.”
We “cannot assume EDF will take any stake so it could be more and if the cost estimate is more, the government spend could be more,” Thomas added.
The UK is planning to buuld two France-supplied EPR nuclear units at Sizewell C in eastern England. Courtesy EDF.

title: Nuclear Fusion: Global Investment Increases, But Challenges Remain In Race For Commercialisation
author: NucNet Staff Writer
text: Private sector is throwing its weight behind the new technology, but must have access to government funding programmes

Fusion energy has long been touted as the future of clean power. By replicating on Earth the processes that energise the stars, including our own Sun, fusion offers the promise of a virtually limitless, carbon-free energy source.

Amid growing interest in nuclear energy driven by rising power demand –especially from major technology companies – recent breakthroughs, substantial investment and emerging industry leaders are moving fusion energy towards commercialisation.

Fusion works by joining light atomic nuclei, such as hydrogen isotopes, to form a heavier nucleus, releasing tremendous energy. To achieve fusion on Earth, scientists heat the fuel to millions of degrees, creating a plasma in which these atoms can collide and fuse. The main fuels for nuclear fusion are deuterium and tritium, which are isotopes of hydrogen.

One of the main fusion reactor designs is the tokamak – a donut-shaped device that uses strong magnetic fields to hold the hot plasma in place These magnetic “walls” prevent the plasma from contacting reactor walls and losing energy. This method is one of the most studied and is employed in major projects like the International Thermonuclear Experimental Reactor (Iter) in France.

Another fusion reactor design is known as inertial confinement fusion (ICF), which employs powerful lasers or ion beams to rapidly compress a small pellet of fusion fuel, heating it to the extreme temperatures and pressures required for fusion – albeit briefly before the fuel disperses. Essentially, it triggers a tiny, controlled explosion.
Hybrid systems can combine aspects of magnetic and inertial confinement for greater efficiency.

Each method has its own challenges and advantages and researchers are exploring all these techniques to find the most efficient and reliable way to harness fusion energy as a clean, virtually limitless power source.

In January 2025, scientists at the Experimental Advanced Superconducting Tokamak (East) in China produced a “steady-state, high-confinement” plasma for 1,066 seconds, breaking their previous record of 403 seconds set in 2023. “Steady-state, high-confinement” refers to creating a plasma state that's maintained for a sustained period of time in a tokamak and is a significant step toward developing a fusion reactor.
In February, the ‘West’ nuclear fusion machine in southern France set a new record for plasma duration, beating the East machine.

These achievements highlight the speed at which tokomak designs are developing. In December 2022, the Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory in the US achieved “net energy gain” by generating more energy from a fusion reaction than was used to initiate it. This breakthrough marked a critical step towards a self-sustaining and commercially viable fusion reaction.

ICF technology has also made progress. Ryan Ramsey, chief operating officer of First Light Fusion, a UK-based fusion company developing ICF technology, told NucNet that the company has achieved net energy gain and is now focusing on addressing challenges such as repeatability rates and consistency.

Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning have had a positive effect on the speed and reliability of exploring new materials and techniques. Ramsey said First Light has been using machine learning for simulations for over a decade and now AI is speeding up the process further.

“Because of the speed of AI technology, we run as many as 30,000 simulations on creating an amplifier [the projectile that is used to impact the fuel] before we actually precision manufacture it and test it in reality. This speeds up iterations during the testing process,” he said.

Andrew Holland, chief executive officer of the Fusion Industry Association (FIA), told NucNet that, for a long time, public programmes focused on plasma physics, with little attention paid to the science of building fusion power plants.

He said: “It’s really important that private fusion companies – the ones who are going to commercialise fusion and the ones that will build power plants – have access to and partnership with government programmes which have been working on fusion for over 60 years”.
Fusion energy’s development has been bolstered by significant global investment from governments and the private sector.
Holland told NucNet that public-private partnerships have accelerated fusion’s development as governments and private companies come together to advance the commercialisation of fusion energy plants.

In 2024, the US government allocated $790m (€725m) to the Department of Energy’s Office of Fusion Energy Sciences and an additional $690m for ICF research, bringing total public funding close to $1.5bn.
Such public funding supports long-term research and the creation of robust regulatory frameworks. Private sector interest in fusion energy is equally impressive.

Holland said: “We see more strategic investors getting involved, such as oil companies, utilities and energy firms. We think that that’s the obvious next step and we have the data that there’s well over $8 billion invested into private fusion companies right now around the world. Most of that has come in the last five years”.

Ramsey told NucNet that, while First Light Fusion has raised $100 million so far, there is very little government funding in the UK, predominately as they are focused on a national Magnetic Confinement Fusion (MCF) programme.
“I think that’s going to change,” Ramsey said. “Other countries, for example the US, are supporting a more balanced portfolio, and the UK will need to address this to stay in the race”.

Demonstrating this point, in January 2025, Washington, US-based Helion Energy announced it had raised $425m in Series F funding to accelerate the manufacturing of components and construction of its first fusion plant, scheduled for completion in 2028. This brought the total invested in the company to over $1bn and follows a 2023 agreement between Helion and Microsoft –facilitated by Constellation Energy – to supply electricity from the new plant.
This influx of capital not only accelerates technological development but also fuels the growth of startups and private enterprises dedicated to overcoming remaining technical challenges.
Despite promising advances and investments, several challenges remain on the path to commercial fusion energy.

Achieving and maintaining sustained net-positive energy output is one of the greatest technical hurdles. Managing the extreme conditions – high temperatures, pressures, and intense neutron fluxes – is no small feat.

Even if these technical challenges are overcome, establishing comprehensive regulatory frameworks and building a robust safety case is essential for the safe operation of fusion reactors. Regulators must balance safety with the need to avoid stifling innovation.

Holland said: “It may be tempting for many governments treat fusion as the next generation of nuclear and simply adapt the nuclear fission regulations. However, they are completely different, and in many ways, the opposite. So, we need a right sized regulatory regime that is completely separate from nuclear fission.”
“We are on the verge of completing this here in the United States, with the NRC rulemaking underway right now that regulate fusion as a particle accelerator”, he added.
For fusion to compete with traditional power sources, reactor designs must be cost-effective, and fusion-generated electricity needs to be competitively priced.

Helion told NucNet: “We do see our fusion power becoming economically viable and competitive with other energy sources. In fact, we estimate that Helion’s fusion power will be one of the lowest cost sources of electricity”.
The ‘pit’ being prepared to hold the tokamak at the Iter nuclear fusion plant in southern France. Courtesy Iter.
To achieve fusion on Earth, scientists heat the fuel to millions of degrees, creating a plasma in which these atoms can collide and fuse. Courtesy LLNL.

title: Poland ‘58% Ready’ For Nuclear Construction, As Negotiations Continue On Key EPC Contract
author: David Dalton
text: Analysis also shows work needed on securing qualified personnel

Poland is “58% ready” to start the construction of its first large-scale nuclear power project, but needs to make progress on technological, investment, and systemic preparations, particularly in securing qualified personnel and signing the engineering, procurement and construction contract, according to analysis published on 12 March.
The analysis, from UK-based law firm Baker McKenzie and Polish analysis company Polityka Insight, presents a “nuclear readiness index” developed around six key criteria.
The highest rating was given to the political aspect (nine out of 10 points in the index), while the regulatory and social areas each received eight points.

The lowest score, of three points, was given to the technological area. Investment and systemic issues, which include finances, personnel, ancillary investments, and the preparation of public administration, received only four points each.

Agnieszka Skorupinska, the partner leading the sustainability and energy transition team at Baker McKenzie in Warsaw, said Polish regulations reduce the overall level of risk associated with the construction and operation of nuclear power plants, which is significant from the perspective of planning and obtaining financing for these projects.

However, there are still issues that may require legislative solutions, such as the functioning of insurance pools, strengthening local content requirements at the ordering stage, or determining the method of calculating local content.
These issues are particularly important because the construction and operation of a nuclear power plant represent an opportunity for the development of the Polish economy and technology transfer.

Skorupinska said the signing of the engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) contract for the planned nuclear station in northern Poland might only take place after the current preliminary design work is completed.

She said the contract itself will be subject to lengthy negotiations, given the need to properly address the interests of both parties and minimise risks related to the investment’s timely completion.

In 2022, Warsaw chose US-based Westinghouse to supply its AP1000 pressurised water reactor technology for a three-unit nuclear station near the villages of Lubiatowo and Kopalino on its northern Baltic Sea coast in the province of Pomerania.
In 2023, Westinghouse and Bechtel, the US engineering, procurement, construction, and project management company, signed a formal agreement to partner on the design and construction of the station.

Polskie Elektrownie Jądrowe (PEJ), the state company set up to oversee the project, said recently discussions are continuing regarding the engineering, procurement and construction contract. It has already signed an engineering services contract with Westinghouse and Bechtel that includes finalising a site-specific design for three AP1000 nuclear islands.

“A longer time frame should also be assumed for obtaining the European Commission’s approval for granting state aid in connection with the investment,” Skorupinska said. “Although the European Commission is obliged to respond within 18 months of notification, the process usually takes longer for such complex projects.”

In December 2024, the commission announced an investigation into whether the nuclear power project, expected to cost in total between €35bn and €45bn ($36.4bn-$46.8bn), is in line with European Union’s competition rules.
Some initial work has been carried out preparing the site for Poland’s first commercial nuclear power station. Courtesy PEJ.

title: Westinghouse And Data4 Sign MOU To Explore AP300 Reactor Deployment For European Data Centres
author: David Dalton
text: Agreement comes amid significant interest in nuclear plants for powering big tech

US nuclear reactor supplier Westinghouse Electric Company and European data centre developer and operator Data4 have signed a memorandum of understanding to explore the use of Westinghouse AP300 small modular reactors (SMR) to power future data centres in Europe.
Under the agreement, Data4 has chosen the AP300 SMR as its technology of choice to evaluate deployment at one of its future data centres to reduce reliance on fossil fuels.
Data4’s chief executive officer Olivier Micheli said the data centre industry is undergoing a profound transformation. With the rise of AI, energy supply is evolving rapidly, he said.

“In the past, data centres relied solely on traditional power utilities,” Micheli said. “Today, we are entering an era where the campuses of the future will be powered by multiple intelligent sources, seamlessly integrating onsite generation, traditional grid supply and energy storage.”

Micheli said that by integrating the Westinghouse AP300 SMR, these campuses will gain greater energy autonomy, reducing their reliance on traditional grids and helping to alleviate pressure on public power networks.

Westinghouse president and chief executive officer Patrick Fragman said that as technology centres and cloud providers expand data infrastructure to meet increasing demand, SMRs offer a promising solution for powering the next generation of energy-intensive computing.
“Our AP300 modular reactor can provide data centres with a dedicated, on-site power source for reliable and carbon-free energy,” Fragman said.

The Data4 agreement with Westinghouse comes amid significant interest in nuclear plants for powering big tech, with several companies including Amazon, Google, Meta and Microsoft all looking at nuclear reactors to power their energy-intensive data centres and AI initiatives.

Data centres consume a substantial and growing share of the world’s electricity with International Energy Agency estimates ranging between 240 and 340 TWh in 2022. Data centre capacity is expected to double by 2030.
Westinghouse president and chief executive officer Patrick Fragman (left) and Data4 CEO Olivier Micheli signing the memorandum of understanding in Paris, France. Courtesy Business Wire.

title: Major Energy Users Sign Pledge To Support Goal Of Tripling Nuclear Capacity By 2050
author: David Dalton
text: Big tech turns to reactors with more companies expected to back target in coming months
A cross-industry group of large energy users including big tech companies Amazon, Google and Meta have signed a pledge supporting the goal of at least tripling global nuclear capacity by 2050.

The pledge, signed at the CERAWeek energy conference, in Houston, Texas, marks the first time major businesses beyond the nuclear sector have come together to publicly back an extensive and concerted expansion of nuclear power to meet increasing global energy demand, the London-based nuclear industry group the World Nuclear Association said.
The companies that signed the pledge urged other energy users to support the goal to triple nuclear energy.
The companies said they acknowledge government support and advocate for equal access to finance for nuclear energy.

Signatories at CERAWeek included Amazon, Google, Meta, Dow, Occidental Petroleum, Netherlands-based offshore energy contractor Allseas, Poland’s Orlen Synthos Green Energy and Japan-based industrial group IHI.
The WNA said the pledge is expected to gain more support over the coming months, reflecting growing interest in nuclear power from industries as diverse as maritime, aviation and oil and gas.

The goal to triple nuclear energy capacity by 2050 has earned support from 31 countries through a declaration initially signed by 25 countries at Cop28 and then by six more at Cop29, and more than 140 nuclear industry companies through an accompanying industry pledge. Fourteen of the world’s largest financial institutions backed the goal in September 2024.
According to the WNA, nuclear energy generates 9% of the world’s electricity from 439 commercial power reactors.
The pledge is expected to gain more support, reflecting growing interest in nuclear power from industries as diverse as maritime, aviation and oil and gas. Courtesy ČEZ Group.

title: UKAEA And Italy’s Eni To Build ‘World-Class’ Tritium Fuel Cycle Facility For Fusion Reactors
author: David Dalton
text: Plant in central England vital to deployment of future nuclear plants

The United Kingdom Atomic Energy Authority (UKAEA) and Italy-based energy company Eni have signed an agreement to jointly conduct research and development in fusion energy, starting with the construction of the world’s largest and most advanced tritium fuel cycle facility, which will produce a vital fuel for future fusion power stations.

UKAEA, the UK’s national organisation responsible for the research and delivery of fusion energy, said the UKAEA-Eni H3AT (pronounced “heat”) tritium loop facility will be bult at its Culham Campus in Oxfordshire, central England, and will be complete in 2028.

UKAEA said tritium recovery and re-use will play a fundamental role in the supply and generation of the fuel in future fusion power plants and will be crucial in making the technology increasingly efficient.
Tritium is a radioactive isotope of hydrogen that occurs naturally in the atmosphere and is also a byproduct of nuclear reactors. It is a potential fuel for future fusion power plants.
UKAEA said the new “world-class” facility is designed to provide industry and academia the opportunity to study how to process, store and recycle tritium.

Fusion is a form of energy whereby the power of the Sun is replicated on Earth. The fusion process sees two hydrogen isotopes fuse together under intense heat and pressure to form a helium atom, releasing large amounts of emissions-free energy through a safe, cleaner and virtually inexhaustible process.
Fusion energy could be transformational to contribute to energy security and decarbonisation.
UKAEA and Eni will collaborate to develop advanced technological solutions in fusion energy and related technologies, including skills transfer initiatives.
Eni will contribute to the H3AT project with its expertise in managing and developing large-scale projects.
UKAEA chief executive officer Sir Ian Chapman said the H3AT demonstration plant will set a new benchmark as the largest and most advanced tritium fuel cycle facility in the world.
UKAEA also announced it had signed a memorandum of cooperation with the Fukushima Institute for Research, Education and Innovation on joint research in robotics and autonomous systems.

The agreement covers key areas such as research into robotics and autonomous systems for nuclear decommissioning; sharing best practices in research facilities; and initiatives to drive partnerships and support talent and skills development.
The tritium fuel cycle facility will produce a vital fuel for future fusion power stations. Courtesy UKAEA.

title: US Researchers Develop Battery That Can Run On Spent Nuclear Fuel
author: David Dalton
text: Team used fission products to generate small amounts of power
Researchers at a US university have developed a battery capable of converting fission products from spent nuclear fuel into electricity through light emission, according to a study.

Using a combination of scintillator crystals, high-density materials that emit light when they absorb radiation, and solar cells, the team, led by researchers from The Ohio State University, demonstrated that ambient gamma radiation could be harvested to produce a strong enough electric output to power microelectronics, like microchips.

To test the battery, which is a prototype about four cubic centimetres small, researchers used two different radioactive sources, caesium-137 (Cs-137), and cobalt-60 (Co-60), some of the most significant fission products that come from spent nuclear fuel. The battery was tested at Ohio State’s Nuclear Reactor Laboratory.

Their results showed that when Cs-137 was used, the battery generated 288 nanowatts. Yet with the much stronger radioisotope Co-60, the battery produced 1.5 microwatts of power, about enough to switch on a tiny sensor.

Raymond Cao, lead author of the study and a professor in mechanical and aerospace engineering at Ohio State, said such devices could be scaled up to target applications “at or beyond the watts level”.

The researchers said these batteries, which are not designed for public use, would be used near where the spent nuclear fuel is produced, such as in nuclear waste storage pools or nuclear systems for space and deep-sea exploration.

Although the gamma radiation used in this work is about a hundred times more penetrating than a normal X-ray or CT scan, the battery itself does not incorporate radioactive materials, meaning it is still safe to touch.

Scaling up technology up could be costly unless these batteries could be reliably manufactured, said Cao. He said further research is needed to assess the batteries’ usefulness and limitations, including how long they might last.
The work was carried out by researchers from The Ohio State University. Courtesy Ohio State.

title: Simplified Nuclear Investment Laws Could Give ‘Major Boost’ To Poland’s First Reactor Project
author: Kamen Kraev
text: New rules being considered by government will ‘significantly reduce timelines’

An amendment to nuclear laws in Poland could simplify and accelerate the investment process in the sector, providing “a major boost” for the country’s first nuclear power project in the northern Pomerania province, according to Piotr Ciolkowski, partner and co-head of energy and natural resources at Warsaw-based consultancy Dentons.
In December 2024, the amendment to a 2011 law on the preparation and execution of investments in nuclear power and related facilities was published in the government’s official legal journal.

Ciolkowski said the proposal introduces the possibility of dividing the investment process into stages and obtaining permits for individual phases separately. The new regulations will allow preparatory works and administrative procedures to run in parallel, significantly reducing project timelines.

“For PEJ’s (Polskie Elektrownie Jądrowe) project in Lubiatowo-Kopalino, this means that the investor can start construction work earlier by obtaining permits for preparatory work before securing a full construction permit for the entire nuclear facility,” Ciolkowski said.

“It is a major milestone for Poland’s first nuclear power plant, especially given the project’s history of delays due to bureaucratic hurdles, financial uncertainties, and lengthy approval processes.”
Warsaw is looking to deploy between 6 GW and 9 GW of nuclear power in the 2030s and 2040s as a way to secure stable and carbon-free baseload power supply once its coal generation is phased out.

In 2022, Warsaw chose US-based Westinghouse to supply its AP1000 pressurised water reactor technology for the construction of three units near the villages of Lubiatowo and Kopalino, to the northwest of Gdansk on the Baltic coast in Pomerania.
The first plant is scheduled for commercial operation in 2036 with first concrete in 2028.
A revised timeframe was announced in December 2024 with a three-year delay to previous plans for the plant to be operational in 2033.

The outdated legal framework for nuclear projects in Poland has been in the sights of policymakers for several years, even before preparations for deployment began. Poland’s first modern nuclear programme dates from 2014 and was first updated in 2020, with a more recent update expected later this year.

The previous regulatory framework was outdated and lacked the flexibility needed to accommodate the complexities of modern nuclear energy development, said Ciolkowski. He said regulations required a full construction permit before any work could begin, which could cause significant delays.
“The recent amendments aim to address these gaps, providing a more streamlined and effective approach to planning and constructing nuclear facilities,” he said.

“This enables key construction activities to begin earlier. In practice, this parallel approach to preparatory works and administrative procedures could shorten the overall investment timeline by several months or even more than a year.”

Poland has so far earmarked about €14bn ($15bn) of funding to support deployment of the Pomerania nuclear station. The funding will cover about 30% of PEJ’s capitalisation, with the remaining 70% to be sourced from foreign borrowing, including from foreign export credit agencies in the US and Canada.

In December 2024, the European Commission announced an investigation into whether Poland's proposed plan to support its nuclear power project, expected to cost between €35bn and €45bn, is in line with European Union’s competition rules.

According to Wojciech Wrochna, Poland’s undersecretary of state for strategic energy infrastructure, time is “the biggest challenge” when it comes to going through the European Commission’s procedure because a decision could take between 18 and 24 months.
Wrochna told the Polish Press Agency that without a commission ruling, Warsaw will not be able to increase share capital on time, risking investment delays that could impact the project's timeline.
“Time is very crucial here. We will try to do everything to accelerate intensive talks with the European Commission, but this is a huge challenge,” he said.
PEJ said last week it is ready to begin preparatory work this year for the first plant at Lubiatowo-Kopalino.

Poland’s first nuclear project “is historically significant” as it marks the country’s shift away from coal dependence toward nuclear energy, aligning with broader European energy goals, Ciolkowski said.
However, he warned that the biggest challenges remain international procedures, EU approvals and logistical issues related to construction and supply chains, which could still cause delays.

title: Orano And Energoatom Sign ‘Major Agreement’ For Long-Term Supply Of Enrichment Services To Ukraine
author: David Dalton
text: French company has embarked on expansion to meet growing demand

French nuclear fuel cycle company Orano and Energoatom, the Ukrainian national nuclear operator, have signed a major long-term commercial agreement for the supply of enrichment services through to 2040.
The contract guarantees Energoatom a reliable and diversified supply of enrichment services to provide fuel for the Ukrainian nuclear power generation fleet, Orano said in a statement.

The contract was signed by Nicolas Maes, chief executive officer of Orano, and Petro Kotin, acting chief executive officer of Energoatom, during a ceremony in Vienna, Austria, the presence of chairman of Energoatom’s supervisory board Jarek Niewierowicz.

Kotin said Energoatom is continuing to strengthen Ukraine’s energy security and uranium enrichment is one of the important stages in the process of nuclear fuel production. The agreement allows Ukraine to plan a stable, bright future, relying on the operation of nuclear power plants, Kotin said, adding that “given Ukraine’s plans to expand nuclear capacity, Energoatom’s need for uranium enrichment services will only grow in the future”.
Orano said that to meet growing demand from its customers, in 2023, it embarked on a major project to extend the production capacity of its Georges Besse 2 uranium enrichment plant in France by 30%.

“This development will raise the maximum annual capacity of the plant to 11 million SWUs* between now and the start of the next decade, thus consolidating Orano's position as a key player in the global supply of enrichment services,” the company said.
Ukraine has a fleet of 15 commercial nuclear plants although six, at the Russia-controlled Zaporizhzhia nuclear station, are in cold shutdown.

Energoatom is planning to complete Units 3 and 4 at the Khmelnitski nuclear power station, about 300 km west of the capital Kyiv in western Ulraine. Both are Russia-designed VVER-1000 pressurised water reactor units, construction of which is suspended.
The plan is to buy reactor equipment that was produced by Russia for the abandoned Belene nuclear power station project in Bulgaria.

Three years of Russian strikes on its power grid have left Ukraine reliant on nuclear power for more than half of its electricity generation. That nuclear power is generated by three functioning stations – Khmelnitski, Rivne and South Ukraine.
* The separative work unit (SWU) is the unit of measure used as the international standard to quantify production from enrichment activity.
The contract was signed by Nicolas Maes (left), chief executive officer of Orano, and Petro Kotin, acting chief executive officer of Energoatom. Courtesy Orano.

title: Canada Announces CAD304 Million Backing For Development Of Monark Nuclear Power Plant
author: David Dalton
text: Ottawa says new reactor will reinforce commitment to domestically sourced and processed uranium

The Canadian government has signed a preliminary agreement worth more than CAD300m with nuclear engineering company AtkinsRéalis to support the development and modernisation of a new Canada-designed nuclear power reactor called Monark.
The government said in a statement that it intends to lend AtkinsRéalis a maximum of CAD304m ($211, €195m) over four years to finance half of the design project.
The agreement will see both sides co-finance up to half of the design costs, to a maximum of $304m each.

This work will also include Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, the country’s nuclear operators and the broader Canadian supply chain. AECL owns the intellectual property for Candu nuclear power plants and is working with AtkinsRéalis to use it for today’s energy markets.

AtkinsRéalis, part of Canada’s SNC-Lavalin Group, unveiled the Monark nuclear power plant at the World Nuclear Exhibition in Paris in 2023. The Monark, which uses Canada’s own Candu pressurised heavy water technology, is the most advanced reactor design with the highest output of any Candu plant at 1,000 MW.

Energy minister Jonathan Wilkinson said nuclear is an integral part of Canada’s resilient and independent energy future, and Candu technology is “helping us get there” while creating good domestic jobs and supporting international Canadian energy exports.

“By advancing innovative projects like Monark reactors, this government is reinforcing our commitment to domestically sourced and processed uranium, which is creating good-paying jobs in Ontario and throughout the country,” he said.

Wilkinson said that through investments in Ontario Power Generation’s project to deploy small modular reactors (SMRs) at Darlington and further SMR projects planned in Alberta, the government is providing a powerful example of how public and private sectors can work together to improve energy security and advance made-in-Canada nuclear technologies.

Wilkinson also announced CAD55m in funding to support the Darlington new nuclear project. The next phase of the project will focus on advancing the deployment of three GE Hitachi BWRX-300 SMRs. Each GE Hitachi BWRX-300 SMR produces about 300 MW of electricity and the three SMRs together could supply enough electricity needed to power about 900,000 homes.

Wilkinson said the government has increased funding from CAD24m to CAD80m to the Saskatchewan government in support of utility SaskPower’s SMR pre-development work. The funding will support pre-engineering work and technical studies, environmental assessments, regulatory studies and community and Indigenous engagement to help advance this important project.

Wilkinson highlighted a total investment of CAD52.4m for various projects supporting the development and deployment of SMRs and Candu reactors and decarbonisation efforts in Saskatchewan, Alberta and Ontario.

Candu technology was developed in Canada in the late 1950s and 1960s. AtkinsRéalis said there are 28 Candu plants globally: 19 in Canada, four in South Korea, two in Romania, one in Argentina and two in China.
AtkinsRéalis unveiled the Monark nuclear power plant at the World Nuclear Exhibition in Paris in 2023. Courtesy AtkinsRéalis.

title: Ansto Announces Start Of Decommissioning For Australia’s First Research Reactor
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Hifar reactor operated between 1958 and 2007

Decommissioning has begun for Australia’s first nuclear research reactor, the High Flux Australian Reactor (Hifar), in a project that "marks the end of an era" at the Australian Nuclear Science and Technology Organisation (Ansto), a statement said.

Hifar, commissioned in 1958 and operational for nearly five decades before being shut down in 2007, played a pivotal role in the country’s nuclear medicine production and scientific research, Ansto said.
The decommissioning project follows a license issued by the Australian Radiation Protection and Nuclear Safety Agency in late 2024, allowing initial works to proceed.
Ansto’s chief executive Shaun Jenkinson said the reactor, located at the Lucas Heights research facility in southern Sydney, laid the foundation for Australia’s nuclear capabilities.

“Hifar pioneered Australia’s nuclear medicine production and silicon irradiation capabilities and housed the first neutron beam research instruments,” Jenkinson said. “This project will be carried out in line with international best practices and guided by Ansto’s extensive expertise in radiation protection, safety, and engineering.”

According to Ansto, the first phase of decommissioning will involve dismantling neutron beam instruments, the control room, and other peripheral equipment. Later stages will focus on removing the reactor’s circuits and storage block contents. A second phase, which will require further licensing and a national waste disposal strategy, will involve dismantling the reactor core.

Senior project manager Brett Wheeler said decommissioning preparations have spanned a decade, with initial post-shutdown measures, including fuel removal and reactor cooling system drainage, completed in 2008.
The first phase of the project is expected to be completed by 2026. Hifar will be the second research reactor to be decommissioned by Ansto, following the dismantling of the Moata reactor in 2012.
Hifar is a 21-metre-tall, 10-MW research reactor, originally constructed for the purpose of testing materials for use in future nuclear power reactors

Construction began in 1955, with first criticality achieved in January 1958. Its purpose evolved into producing neutrons for nuclear medicine production, irradiating silicon for the global semiconductor industry, and for scientific use, said Ansto.
The organisation said the majority of the waste generated from the first decommissioning stage will be solid waste which can be safely recycled after its final characterisation.
The small quantity of radiological waste will be managed and stored onsite at Lucas Heights in purpose-built facilities.
Opal (Open Pool Australian Lightwater Reactor) is currently Ansto’s only operational research reactor at Lucas Heights.
Australia has never introduced nuclear power for electricity generation.
An aerial-view archival image of the Hifar reactor facility at the Lucas Heights research centre in southern Sydney. Image courtesy Ansto.
An archival photo of the Hifar reactor exterior. Courtesy Ansto.

title: Finland Completes Key Trial For World's First Deep Geological Nuclear Waste Repository
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Posiva concludes successful test of above-ground encapsulation process
Finland has made progress toward the permanent disposal of spent nuclear fuel, completing the first trial run at Posiva’s Onkalo final repository encapsulation plant, a statement said on Tuesday.

Posiva said five spent nuclear fuel canisters had been encapsulated during the trial. Those were subjected to inspections and transferred successfully to the underground storage at a depth of 430 metres.
According to Posiva’s production director Karri Osara, staff is now ready to begin the trial run phase for the repository facilities located underground.
A full-system trial run at Onkalo began on 30 August 2024 to test all equipment and related systems working together for the first time.
The first stage of the trial in September involved transferring an empty test cask for spent fuel from nuclear operator Teollisuuden Voima’s (TVO) interim storage to Posiva’s encapsulation plant.

In the final disposal facility, spent fuel assemblies will be encapsulated and placed in the bedrock at a depth of about 400 metres. The facility comprises two sections: the above-ground encapsulation plant for the encapsulation of the spent fuel in canisters, and the final repository deep in the bedrock, with tunnels in which the spent fuel will be placed.
Posiva said it has been using non-radioactive test elements instead of actual spent nuclear fuel during the trials.

According to the company, the trial run of final disposal is a final demonstration of the functionality of the final disposal process as a whole and of the readiness of the personnel for commercial operation.

Posiva has been working for several decades at the Onkalo site to develop a concept for final disposal and demonstrate long-term safety. In May 2021, excavation began of final disposal tunnels while Posiva has also built the above-ground encapsulation plant for used fuel at the Onkalo site.
Onkalo will become the first operational deep geological disposal facility in the world with full startup scheduled for the mid-2020s.
Four of the test spent fuel canisters used for the encapsulation plant trial run. Image courtesy Posiva.

title: Iter Launches Private Sector Engagement Project In Bid To Capitalise On Increased Interest In Nuclear Fusion
author: James West
text: ‘Help desk’ to coordinate requests to access documents, connections to experts and technical questions

The International Thermonuclear Experimental Reactor (Iter) has launched a project for private sector engagement as it bids to engage with private initiatives and capitalise on increased interest in fusion and its potential as a source of almost limitless energy.

Iter – the world’s most ambitious effort to replicate the power of the Sun on Earth – announced it had set up help desk to serve as a central coordination point for requests to access Iter documents, connections to Iter experts and technical questions.

“The driver has been a series of questions, asked and answered repeatedly: ‘How can Iter help?’, Iter said. “How can we effectively match the pace of private-sector demand, within resource constraints? And what are the structures, platforms and channels best suited to delivering?”

Other initiatives related to the project are progressing, Iter said. Iter-developed integrated modelling analysis suite (IMAS) software, which contains advanced tools to organise and manipulate fusion data, is ready for imminent open-sourced release, meeting a longstanding request of the private sector.

The Iter Design Handbook, a multi-year effort to systematically document the knowledge gained in the design, manufacturing, construction, installation, and assembly of the Iter facility, is well underway.

And discussions are progressing on how to enable private sector participation in the International Tokamak Physics Activity, a group which provides a framework for internationally coordinated fusion research.

“A marriage of the public and private sector, on any area of cutting-edge R&D, is a complex endeavour,” Iter said. “But the hoped-for results will be worth it: a whole that is greater than the sum of its parts.”

Iter’s collaboration with the private sector stems from increased interest in fusion and its potential as a source of almost limitless energy. The US-based Fusion Industry Association said in its latest annual report that total investment in the fusion industry now stands at over $7.1bn (€6.8bn) with government funding increasing 57% in 12 months to $426m and timelines on track for deployment in the 2030s.

As Iter advances, private-sector fusion companies are also moving ahead with ambitious timelines. Last month, US fusion startup Helion, whose backers include tech billionaires Sam Altman and Peter Thiel, raised $425m to keep it on track to achieve its target of producing electricity from nuclear fusion in 2028.

“Private companies bring billions in investment, agility, and faster iteration,” said Luke Thompson of UK-based First Light Fusion, which was spun out of the University of Oxford in 2011. The company is developing an approach that involves targeting a grain-sized capsule of atoms with colossal lasers, sparking instantaneous bursts of energy. This is different from the leading global approach of magnetic confinement fusion, which involves confining fusion fuel with magnetic fields.
Thompson emphasised collaboration over competition. “There are no competitors in fusion because we are all working to the same end. Iter and private initiatives are complementary efforts.”
He underscored, however, the need for balanced government support. “The UK must back fusion as boldly as it backs other renewables,” he said.

The UK government has promised a record £410m (€474m, $500m) investment in fusion which could help construct a world-leading fusion power project on the site of an old coal plant in Nottinghamshire, England.

Iter’s private sector fusion engagement project recognises this dynamic. Iter director-general Pietro Barabaschi told NucNet that “Iter can position itself as a hub for global fusion innovation and “the surge in private-sector activity increases Iter’s relevance”.

“The Iter project is a project of peace,” Barabaschi said. “Even amidst geopolitical tensions, including the war in Ukraine, Iter’s multi-nation alliance has endured,” he said, noting that Russian contributions, crucial to the project’s progress, continue under exemptions from European sanctions.

Meanwhile, national fusion programmes in countries including China and Germany – which has shut down all its commercial nuclear plants, but is backing nuclear fusion – are advancing. “China’s momentum, backed by the government, is impressive,” an Iter spokesperson said. “Germany has seen rapid growth in support for fusion.” These efforts highlight the competitive global landscape but also underscore Iter’s importance as a central knowledge base.

“Fusion is about pulling together resources and competencies,” said Ambrogio Fasoli, vice-president for academic affairs at École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne and former programme manager for Eurofusion, the EU-funded consortium of national fusion research institutes from the EU, the UK, Switzerland and Ukraine.

Iter, said Fasoli, sets the stage for the next step, a demonstration power plant known as Demo. With the transition from Iter to Demo, fusion will go from a science-driven, lab-based exercise to an industry-driven and technology-driven programme. A key target for Demo is the production of electricity, although not in the quantities produced by commercial power plants.

The Iter project, the most complex engineering endeavour in history, has faced challenges, but saw its most productive year in 2024 with key milestones met including the arrival of major components and the successful resumption of vacuum vessel assembly after defects were detected in 2022, resulting in the need for extensive re-engineering.

Iter director-general Pietro Barabaschi said Iter’s priorities remain clear. a “robust” reactor startup programme that will allow the project to make up for some of the delays it has accumulated and provide for better risk mitigation.

Announcing details of an updated Iter schedule last year, Barabaschi said that an earlier 2016 schedule had seen a “low-energy, low-current first plasma” startup as the first major milestone – to be immediately followed by a multiyear assembly period to install major in-vessel components.
Barabaschi said the new schedule replaces the 2016 schedule, which for some time had been publicly acknowledged to be no longer “feasible, practical or optimal”.

He said the major drivers of delay – the Covid pandemic that slowed factory work and inspections and caused delays in the supply chain, and repairs required on key machine components – also created new opportunities to reconsider Iter’s path to assembly and operation.
He said operations would now begin with “a more complete machine”.

Iter’s first operational phase, the start of research operations, is targeting deuterium-deuterium fusion operation in 2035, a level of operation that is designed for testing, but releases limited energy.
Europe is contributing almost half of the cost of Iter’s construction. The other members of the venture – China, India, Japan, South Korea, Russia and the US – are contributing the rest equally.

The cost of Iter has been estimated at €20bn, but this has not been confirmed. The Iter spokesperson told NucNet project costs cannot be determined precisely because most Iter members’ costs are not published. “But we are working on a new estimate and will provide that over time.”

title: Reactor Pressure Vessel Lifted Into Place At China’s Lianjiang-1
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Two CAP1000 nuclear units planned at Guangdong site

The reactor pressure vessel (RPV) has been lifted into place for Unit 1 of the Lianjiang nuclear power station under construction in Guangdong province, southern China, the China Nuclear Energy Association (CNEA) said.
The move marks the beginning of the nuclear island equipment installation phase at the plant, the CNEA said.
Lianjiang-1 is the first of two CAP1000 pressurised water reactor (PWR) units planned as the initial phase of the station, which will eventually house six such reactors.
The CAP1000 is China’s indigenous version of the Westinghouse AP1000 pressurised water reactor nuclear plant.
Construction of Lianjiang-1 began in September 2023.

The RPV is one of the largest reactor components at a nuclear plant containing the nuclear reactor coolant, core shroud, and the reactor core and fuel. According to the CNEA, the CAP100 RPV weighs about 270 tonnes.

China currently has nine CAP1000 units under construction including two at the Haiyang, two at the Sanmen, two at the Lianjiang, two at the Xudapu (Xudabao), and one at the Lufeng nuclear power stations.
According to earlier reports, four further CAP1000 reactor units are planned for the second phase of the Lianjiang project, but no additional details have been disclosed.
