title: Moltex Validates ‘Innovative Technology’ That Could Transform Nuclear Waste Management
author: David Dalton
text: Canada company says advancement is ‘pivotal moment’

Moltex Energy Canada has validated an innovative technology that could transform nuclear waste management by consuming most of the transuranic elements present in used fuel bundles from Canada’s Candu reactors and using them as fuel.

Moltex said it has validated its “waste to stable salt” (Watss) process on used fuel bundles from a commercial reactor in Canada through hot cell experiments, marking what it called a pivotal moment in closing the nuclear fuel cycle and advancing next-generation nuclear sustainability.
According to Moltex, the advancement vastly reduces nuclear waste volumes.
The transuranic elements, which are created during the fission process, are radioactive for thousands of years.
Unlike traditional reactors that accumulate these elements over time, Moltex’s Stable Salt Reactor – Wasteburner (SSR-W) is designed to consume them as fuel.
Moltex said validation of the Watss process supports its development of the SSR-W, which it claims can significantly reduce nuclear waste while producing clean energy.

Moltex has been chosen by utility NB Power to progress development of its reactor technology in New Brunswick, Canada, with the goal of deploying first-of-a-kind SSR-W, Watss and GridReserve units at the existing Point Lepreau nuclear power station site.
The GridReserve system stores heat in tanks of molten salt, allowing the energy to be used to cover peaks in demand.

With 66 reactors currently under construction and more than 80 small modular reactor designs being progressed across the world, Watss offers a financially attractive pathway to managing higher waste volumes more sustainably, Moltex said.
A computer-generated image of a Moltex SSR-W nuclear power facility. Courtesy Moltex,

title: Nuclear Industry Welcomes European Proposals That Pave Way For Advanced Reactors
author: David Dalton
text: Commission to assess red tape and consider ‘investment needs’ for new build

The European nuclear energy industry has welcomed European Commission proposals that pay significant attention to ensuring a technology neutral approach to low-carbon energy sources and pave the way for the rollout of advanced reactor technologies.

Publishing its clean industrial deal and action plan for affordable energy on 26 February, the commission said it had a plan to help polluting industries such as steel and cement make the switch to the net zero emissions future, as well as boosting clean tech companies such as firms making electric vehicle charging points.

The clean industrial deal includes a single reference to nuclear, saying that member states have the right to decide on their energy mix and the commission will assess state aid for nuclear supply chains and technologies “with respect to technological neutrality”.

But the action plan for affordable energy goes further, saying the commission will assess the possibility of streamlining red tape including current permitting and licensing practices for the deployment of new nuclear energy technologies such as small modular reactors.
It says the commission will assess investment needs in nuclear energy and foster investment in next-generation clean energy technologies such as nuclear fusion.
And it confirms plans for a new EU policy instrument on nuclear investment, a revision of the so-called Pinc (Nuclear Illustrative Programme of the Commission).
The Pinc, last issued in 2016, includes up-to-date forecasts and concrete recommendations to support European nuclear projects
According to the Brussels-based nuclear energy group Nucleareurope, the proposals focus on the goal of lowering energy bills and accelerating the roll-out of clean energy and electrification.
“The proposals published today show a much greater willingness from the commission to ensure technology neutrality in policy,” said Nucleareurope director-general, Yves Desbazeille.
“Indeed, many of the ideas outlined in the two documents apply to both nuclear and renewables.
“We look forward to engaging with policymakers over the coming months with the goal of ensuring that the EU puts in place the right tools to strengthen its competitiveness.”
Last week, 11 pro-nuclear European governments said nuclear should be part of the action plan for affordable energy and the commission should facilitate the development of the technology.

The countries, which form the EU Nuclear Alliance, called for commission to be ambitious and put forward a comprehensive strategy that integrates the need for renewables, baseload and dispatchable generation capacities, including nuclear.
The European Commission will assess the possibility of streamlining permitting and licensing practices for the deployment of new nuclear energy technologies.

title: Nuclear Companies Sign Manifesto As Momentum Grows For Spain To Reconsider Nuclear Phaseout
author: David Dalton
text: Move follows approval of recent parliamentary motion calling for lifetime extensions

Companies representing the Spanish nuclear industry have signed a manifesto calling for the long-term operation of the country’s nuclear power plants as momentum grows for a reconsideration of longstanding government policy that would see the reactor fleet shut down by 2035.
The manifesto, signed by 32 companies, calls for “dialogue and renegotiation” of the 2019 agreement on the phased shutdown of nuclear power plants.

The release of the manifesto follows approval of a motion by Spain’s lower house of parliament that calls on the government to extend the operating lifetimes of the country’s nuclear power plants. The motion was put forward by the right-leaning People’s Party.
The manifesto says: “This agreement was made under an industrial, geopolitical, social and economic context that is vastly different from today’s reality.

“Our industrial network must not see its competitiveness reduced due to the decision to shut down nuclear power plants starting in 2027, beginning with the Almaraz nuclear power plant, without first securing a viable alternative involving all CO2-free energy sources,” it says.
Legislation means Almaraz-1 is scheduled to shut down permanently in 2027 and Almaraz-2 in 2028.

The companies say that extending the operation of Spain’s nuclear plants would “ensure the sustainability of our increasingly demanding energy system without jeopardising security of supply or the expansion of renewable infrastructures. Additionally, it would reinforce geostrategic independence from other nations”.
But to achieve this “it is crucial to ensure the economic viability of nuclear power plants, with a special emphasis on the excessive tax burden imposed on the sector”.
Madrid-based nuclear group Foro Nuclear has repeatedly said that nuclear energy has endured an “asphyxiating” increase in fiscal pressure over the last five years.

It said the specific tax burden borne by the nuclear fleet has increased by 70% in this period, going from €16/MWh to €28/MWh. This discriminates against nuclear generation compared to other technologies and makes its economic viability unsustainable, Foro Nuclear said.

In October, the group confirmed it had filed a legal challenge with the country’s top court against a 30% increase of the nuclear waste levy, with the main operators of the country’s nuclear plants moving to join the fight.

Spain’s fleet of seven commercial nuclear power plants generated just over 52 TWh net of electricity in 2024, accounting for 19.57% of the country’s total net electricity production, Foro Nuclear said.
The Almaraz-1 nuclear plant is scheduled to shut down permanently in 2027 and Almaraz-2 in 2028. Courtesy Foro Nuclear.

title: Kazakhstan Commission Meets To Discuss Proposals For Reactor Technology
author: David Dalton
text: Country’s first commercial nuclear station planned for Zhambyl region

A Kazakhstan government commission has met to review proposals from potential suppliers for the country’s first nuclear power station, days after reports emerged that the country had chosen a potential site for the facility.

Local press reports said the interdepartmental nuclear development commission, consisting of representatives from state bodies and organisations within the nuclear and energy sectors. had met on 25 February to review the proposals.

Proposals have been received from China National Nuclear Corporation, Russia’s Rosatom, South Korea’s Korea Hydro and Nuclear Power and EDF of France. All the proposals are for large-scale pressurised water reactor units.
Kazakhstan has designated the Zhambyl district in the south of the country as the site for its first nuclear power station, according to a government decree, reported by local media.
Reports said the decision was announced by prime minister Olzhas Bektenov, who said an approved decree confirming Zhambyl as the site took effect on 30 December 2024.
Zhambyl, also spelled Jambyl, borders Kyrgyzstan. Its main administrative centre, Taraz, is almost 500 km west of the nation’s largest city of Almaty.
Press reports in Kazakhstan said the exact location for the planned nuclear station has not been announced, but it is expected to be near the village of Ulken.
Ulken is about 350 km northwest of Almaty on the shores of Lake Balkhash in southeastern Kazakhstan.

Ulken was established in the 1980s to house workers for a planned hydroelectric power plant. That project was unfinished when the Soviet Union collapsed and high-rise apartments are the only completed constructions from the period.
In October, voters in Kazakhstan backed the construction of a nuclear power station in a referendum.

According to the Central Election Commission, 71% of participants voted in favour of the project, while 26% voted against. Voter turnout in the nation of 19 million people was about 63.66%, the data showed.
Kazakhstan is the world’s largest uranium producer, but has no commercial nuclear power plant. It has four operational research reactors that are used for fuels and materials testing.

Plans to deploy large-scale nuclear power during the Soviet era were dropped due to the availability of other energy options, although the country operated a single fast neutron reactor at the Caspian Sea site of Aktau between 1972 and 1999.

According to the International Energy Agency, Kazakhstan is a significant producer of coal, crude oil and natural gas, and a major energy exporter. While coal dominates the country’s energy mix, renewable sources of energy are a small but growing share of Kazakhstan’s electricity generation.
Courtesy IAEA.

title: Biggest Holdup To New Reactors Is Regulatory, US Energy Secretary Tells Fox News
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Chris Wright says ‘unrealistic and bureaucratic system’ was created decades ago
The biggest holdup in building new reactor units in the US has been regulatory, according to new energy secretary Chris Wright.
“I think there is an unrealistic and bureaucratic system created decades ago that has simply been ineffective,” Wright told Fox News.

“We want to have safe, careful regulation of nuclear plants and we have the ability to do that,” he said adding that “so far it has been impossible to build anything new” and the new administration “needs to change that”.
Wright said that he thinks nuclear will grow rapidly in the coming years because the “technology is there, the businesses are there, the capital is there, and public support is there as well.”
The US needs more energy and should “absolutely” build more nuclear, Wright said.
Earlier this month, Wright signed his first secretarial order aiming to “kickstart the golden era of American energy dominance”.

He said a “long-awaited American nuclear renaissance” should start during president Trump’s administration and pledged the Department of Energy will work to enable the rapid deployment and export of next-generation nuclear technology.

Wright’s comments come at time when observers are raising questions about the future of the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) amid the Trump administration’s proposed efforts to revamp US government agencies.
Trump has established the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), which aims to streamline federal operations by requiring comprehensive reviews of existing regulations.
The NRC, which has historically operated as an independent authority responsible for nuclear safety, will now be subject to greater oversight from the White House.
This has raised concerns among critics about its autonomy and ability to maintain independent oversight of nuclear facilities.
Opponents warn that increased political influence could result in the loosening of vital operational and permitting safeguards established for decades.
Proponents have been saying that DOGE efforts could lead to a more cohesive regulatory environment, reducing redundancy and bureaucratic inertia.

In December 2024, Texas, Utah, and small modular reactors (SMR) developer Last Energy filed a lawsuit against the NRC challenging a long-standing 1956 utilisation facility rule, arguing that the rule enforces overly strict licensing standards on SMRs and microreactors, impeding their advancement.
The plaintiffs said that smaller reactors, which use limited nuclear material and present lower safety risks, should not be regulated under the same framework as large-scale nuclear plants.
New US energy secretary Chris Wright said he thinks nuclear will grow rapidly in the coming years. Courtesy Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee.

title: First Concrete Marks Start Of Construction For Lufeng-1 CAP1000 Nuclear Plant In China
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Country building nine units of domesticated Westinghouse PWR design

Pouring of first concrete has been completed for the foundation slab of the nuclear island at the Lufeng-1 reactor unit in eastern China marking a main milestone for the start of construction of the project.

The China Nuclear Energy Association (CNEA) said Lufeng-1, in Guangdong province, will be a 1,161-MW CAP1000 pressurised water reactor (PWR), China’s Generation III indigenous version of US-based Westinghouse’s AP1000 design.
Construction of two CAP1000 PWR units, Lufeng-1 and -2, was approved in August 2024, the CNEA said.
Six rector units will be deployed at the Lufeng nuclear station – four CAP1000 PWRs and two domestic Hualong One units, also known as HPR1000.
Construction of the Hualong One units, Lufeng-5 and -6, started in September 2022 and August 2023.

China currently has eight CAP1000 units under construction including two at the Haiyang, two at the Sanmen, two at the Lianjiang, and two at the Xudapu (Xudabao) nuclear power stations. First concrete for Lufeng-1 brings the number of projects to nine.
China also has four Westinghouse-supplied AP1000 PWRs in commercial operation since 2018, two units at each of the Sanmen and Haiyang sites in eastern China.
First concrete pouring is the industry standard for the start of a nuclear plant's construction. Image courtesy Lufeng plant owner China General Nuclear.

title: EU Approves State Aid To Extend Lifespan Of Two Belgian Nuclear Reactors
author: David Dalton
text: Doel-4 and Tihange-3 to remain online for further 10 years
EU competition regulators have approved Belgium’s plan to grant state aid to French energy company Engie’s Belgian business to extend the lifespan of two nuclear power reactors.
Under the Belgian nuclear phaseout law of 2003, all seven* nuclear reactors in Belgium had to be permanently shut down by 2025.

In March 2022, in light of concerns about security of supply in the context of the energy crisis and the Russian war against Ukraine, the Belgian federal government decided to keep the two newest Belgian nuclear power plants – Doel-4 near Antwerp and Tihange-3 near Liege – in operation for an additional 10 years.

In June 2024, Belgium notified the European Commission of its plan to support the lifetime extension of the two nuclear reactors, which together have a net electricity generation capacity of more than 2,000 MW.
Belgium and Engie had agreed a deal in December 2023 to extend the life of the two nuclear reactors to preserve the security of electricity supply in Belgium and neighbouring countries.
Under the deal, the Belgian State and Electrabel will issue shareholder loans and inject equity for a total of around €2bn ($2.09bn) to cover the capital cost of the extension.
The deal also includes Electrabel transferring liabilities, related to the long-term storage and final disposal of nuclear waste and spent fuel to the Belgian state for a lump sum payment of €15bn.
The reactors are majority-owned by Engie’s Belgian unit Electrabel while EDF subsidiary Luminus holds a minority stake.

When opening its investigation in July, the European Commission said it wanted to focus on the financial arrangements as well as on the proportionality of the amount of the transferred nuclear waste liabilities.

“The commission concluded that the aid is necessary and appropriate to achieve the objective pursued, as well as proportionate as it is limited to the minimum necessary, while competition distortions caused by the measure are minimised,” the commission said in a statement.
“On this basis, the commission approved the Belgian measure under EU state aid rules.”

Belgium’s new government has announced plans to secure the country’s reliance on nuclear energy, aiming for a 4 GW share in the country's electricity mix as part of efforts to secure a carbon-free baseload capacity. The four reactors now remaining in operation have a net capacity of around 3.4 GW
According to a coalition agreement, the aim to “restart” Belgium’s nuclear industry and see the operating life extension of existing nuclear plants and the construction of new reactors.

* Earlier this month the Doel-1 nuclear power station was permanently shut down, bringing the number of commercial reactors in operation in the country to four. Doel-3 and Tihange-2 had already been shut down in 2022 and 2023.
Units at Doel and Tihange (pictured) will remain online for a further 10 years.

title: French Generation IV Nuclear Reactor Startup Announces Collaboration With Belgium’s Tractebel
author: David Dalton
text: Move follows announcement of recent funding package
French nuclear startup Hexana is to collaborate with Belgian engineering company Tractebel on the development of Hexana’s small modular reactor technology.

Hexana, which was spun out the state-run Alternative Energies & Atomic Energy Commission (CEA) in March 2023, said the collaboration will see Tractebel involved in the design of the building and utility systems for the nuclear island, an essential step for the operation of the SMR platform.
The partnership also covers the handling and maintenance of components, and compliance with European safety regulations, a fundamental requirement for the development and operation of the plant.
Hexana’s Generation IV “energy platform” integrates two to six small modular fast neutron reactors designed to produce high-temperature heat and ultra-low carbon electricity.
In January Hexana announced it had secured €25m ($26m) to support the accelerated development of its modular sodium-cooled fast neutron reactor.
The funding comprises fundraising of €15m and a grant of €10m from Bpifrance Financement, awarded under the France 2030 initiative for innovative nuclear reactor projects.
Hexana said the funding was supported by investors such as Eren Industries, CEA Investissement and Région Sud Investissement.

The funding will enable Hexana to complete the conceptual design of the reactor, submit the safety options file to the French regulator, and progress to the basic design phase. Hexana added the funding would also play a pivotal role in securing its first industrial customers and sites across Europe.

title: South Korea Announces Plans For Two New Large-Scale Nuclear Plants And SMR
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Share of electricity generated by reactors could rise to 35% after U-turn on new build

South Korea has approved a long-term electricity supply and demand plan outlining an expansion of nuclear power with the construction of two new large-scale reactor units and a small modular reactor (SMR) plant by 2038, a statement by the ministry of energy and industry said.
According to the plan, nuclear power’s share of the national power mix is expected to be about 35% by 2038, aiming to support energy security and reduce carbon emissions.

Data by the International Atomic Energy Agency shows that a fleet of 26 commercial nuclear reactor units generated about 30% of South Korea’s electricity in 2023, or a total of 180.5 TWh of electricity.
The ministry’s plan foresees nuclear-powered electric generation to reach about 248 TWh in 2038.

Reports in local media said that the plan was initially expected to pass in 2024, but faced political hurdles, particularly over the scale of nuclear expansion. An agreement with opposition parties led to a compromise that reduced the number of large reactors by one, while increasing investments in solar energy and energy storage systems, said The Chosun Daily.

South Korea has 26 nuclear plants in commercial operation and two large-scale APR1400 pressurised water reactor units under construction at the Saeul nuclear station in the southeast of the country. In April, the Shin-Hanul-2 APR1400 nuclear power plant in the east of the country became the latest unit to begin commercial operation.

In 2024, Seoul approved the completion of two APR1400s at Shin-Hanul-3 and Shin-Hanul-4. Work on both units was halted in 2017 under the nuclear phaseout policy of the previous government, but in 2022 a decision was made to resume construction in 2025.

In July 2022, the South Korean government laid out a new energy policy which aimed to maintain nuclear’s share of the country’s energy mix at a minimum of 30% by 2030. It also set the goal of exporting 10 nuclear power plants by 2030, and the development of a South Korean SMR design.
Following his election 2022 president Yoon Suk Yeol* reversed previous president Moon Jae-in’s policy of phasing out nuclear power.
South Korea’s new electricity plan also outlines a major boost for renewables and energy storage systems.
The government plans to expand renewable energy generation capacity from about 39 GW in 2025 to about 122 GW in 2038, with 77 GW of solar power and 40.7 GW of wind power.

The energy plan also calls for significant growth in energy storage, adding 9 GWh of capacity to reach a total of 138 GWh by 2038. The expansion of energy storage systems is seen as critical for managing the intermittency of renewable sources like solar and wind, ensuring grid stability.

According to Business Korea, by 2036 all 28 coal-fired power plants will be phased out and converted for the use of liquified natural gas (LNG), while between 2036 and 2038, 12 coal and LNG plants reaching the end of their operating life will be refurbished to use carbon-free power sources like pumped storage and hydrogen.

Earlier this month, the industry ministry said South Korea will provide more than $100m (€96m) worth of financial support this year to businesses in the nuclear power plant industry to encourage development of the sector.
* Yoon was impeached in December 2024 over a failed attempt to impose martial law late last year and his powers are currently suspended.
South Korea has approved the completion of two APR1400 nuclear plants at Shin-Hanul in the east of the country. Courtesy IAEA.

title: India’s Vedanta Seeks ‘Globally Recognised’ Partner For 5 GW Of Nuclear Power Capacity
author: David Dalton
text: New Delhi wants to boost foreign and private investments in its civilian nuclear energy sector

The India-based Vedanta Group controlled by billionaire Anil Agarwal is seeking bids from global firms for building 5 GW of nuclear power capacity in India, which the mining conglomerate plans to use for meeting energy needs at its facilities.

The company is looking for a globally recognised firm with a track record of designing, building, and operating nuclear power plants, according to a document seeking expressions of interest, published on Vedanta Ltd’s website.
Initial bids are to be submitted within 30 days, the company said on 20 February.
“All the local permits and regulatory approvals, land, battery limit utilities and infrastructure support will be provided by Vedanta,” the document said.
Vedanta’s businesses ranged from crude oil extraction to aluminium and zinc production, with facilities spread across the country.
Vedanta’s current energy portfolio includes 9,000 MW of thermal and 4,000 MW of renewables under construction. It is aiming to expand the capacity to 20,000 MW in the next three years.
Earlier this month, Jindal Nuclear, a subsidiary of one of India’s major industrial groups, said it plans to build 18 GW of nuclear power generation capacity in India over the next two decades.

Jindal Nuclear, part of the Naveen Jindal steel and power group, and a 100% subsidiary of Jindal Renewables, said that the plan will include indigenously developed Bharat small modular reactors (SMRs), non-Bharat SMRs and Generation-IV reactors. The company plans to own and operate the plants.

Last month, Nuclear Power Corporation of India Ltd issued a request for proposals for the deployment of Bharat SMRs, opening the doors of the nuclear sector to Indian private companies for the first time.

Sitharaman said the development of at least 100 GW of nuclear energy by 2047 is essential for the country’s energy transition efforts. India currently has about 6.9 GW of nuclear capacity in operation with about 5.4 GW under construction.

India said earlier this month it wants to amend its liability law to boost foreign and private investments in its civilian nuclear energy sector and also aims to set up a Nuclear Energy Mission with an outlay $2.3bn (€2.2bn) to operate at least five Bharat SMRs by 2033.
According to the finance ministry, the mission will focus on research and development of SMRs.
Vedanta’s businesses ranged from crude oil extraction to aluminium and zinc production, with facilities spread across the country. Courtesy Vedanta.

title: Swiss Nuclear Utility Signs Uranium Contract With Kazakhstan In Move Away From Russia
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Agreement is for reactors at Beznau and Leibstadt and is first of kind between two countries

Swiss nuclear operating utility Axpo has signed new uranium supply contracts for its Beoznau and Leibstadt nuclear power stations in an effort to diversify its fuel supply chain away from Russia, the Swiss company said in a statement.

According to the statement, new natural uranium supply contracts have been signed with Kazakhstan because Russian companies will no longer supply uranium to Axpo. Contracts have  also been signed with Canada, Axpo said.
Axpo said that after the start of Russia’s war on Ukraine, the company decided not to enter into any new contracts with Russian suppliers and to terminate existing ones if possible.
The company’s nuclear fuel strategy was fundamentally revised with the aim of diversifying suppliers and eliminating Russian suppliers throughout the entire supply chain, Axpo said.

Kazakhstan’s national nuclear corporation Kazatomprom said in a separate statement that it had signed a contract for the supply of natural uranium concentrates for the Beznau and Leibstadt nuclear power stations.
Kazatomprom said this was the first-ever contract signed in the Alpine country.

Bruno Zimmermann, head of nuclear fuel at Axpo said: “The signing of a contract with Kazatomprom, the world’s largest uranium producer, is of strategic importance for Axpo as we continue to diversify and secure our fuel supplies.”
Axpo said uranium will be further processed into reactor fuel in France, Germany, the Netherlands, the UK and the US.

The company also said the first deliveries under the new contracts will take place from 2026. The fuel supply to Leibstadt and Beznau has not depended on Russian supply since 2022 thanks to fuel reserve stocks onsite.

There are two nuclear units at Beznau and one at Leibstadt. Switzerland has a fleet of four reactors that provide about 32% of its electricity generation. In December, Axpo announced plans to invest about $400m (€382m) to enable Beznau to operate until 2033.
The Beznau units are the oldest of Switzerland’s operating nuclear power plants. Unit 1 has been in commercial operation since 1969 and Unit 2 since 1972.
Axpo Power head of nuclear fuel Bruno Zimmermann (left) and Kazatomprom’s chief commercial officer Vladislav Baiguzhi at Axpo headquarters in Switzerland. Courtesy Kazatomprom.

title: Blykalla Gets €15 Million European Investment For Sealer Reactor Project
author: David Dalton
text: Sweden-based company says award also includes €2.5m grant

Sweden-based small modular reactor (SMR) developer Blykalla has been selected for funding under a European Union programme which will give the company €15m ($15.6m) equity investment and a €2.5m grant.

The funding has been awarded under the European Innovation Council’s (EIC) accelerator programme in what Blykalla said was “the most competitive funding round ever” with awards granted to only 5% of applicants.
According to the EIC, funding is awarded to “develop and scaleup innovations with the potential to create or disrupt markets”.
Blykalla chief executive officer Jacob Steadman said the funding validates the potential of the company’s Sealer reactor technology and accelerates its mission to develop Europe’s first advanced SMR.
The company said the funding would “significantly de-risk” its next phase of development.
Earlier this month Blykalla broke ground on its advanced reactor testing facility at the Oskarshamn nuclear site to the south of Stockholm.
The facility will house an electrical Sealer-E prototype reactor and aims to validate critical components and safety systems for a future nuclear plant. The pilot plant will not use nuclear fuel.
Blykalla is building an advanced reactor testing facility at the Oskarshamn nuclear site to the south of Stockholm. Courtesy Blykalla.

title: Japan Confirms Commitment To ‘Maximum Use Of Nuclear Power’
author: David Dalton
text: Revised energy plan says gov’t will aim to bring almost all of country’s reactors back online
The Japanese government said on 18 February that the country will make maximum use of nuclear power as it is preparing for a surge in electricity demand from data centres.

The commitment, made in a revised basic energy plan adopted at a cabinet meeting, represents a major policy shift after the government had sought to reduce dependence on nuclear power as much as possible after the 2011 Fukushima accident.

The basic plan sets the direction of the country’s medium- to long-term energy policy. In the first update to the plan in about three years, the government vowed to work towards the restart of idled nuclear reactors and the refurbishment of aging reactors.

The government said it will aim to bring almost all of the country’s nuclear reactors online and said nuclear power is expected to account for about 20% of its total electricity generation in fiscal 2040.

In the revised plan, the government said that it is necessary to take concerns over the safety of nuclear power seriously after it received as much as over 40,000 public comments about its energy policy.

“In many nations, including the United States, large-scale investments in decarbonized power sources are underway,” economy, trade and industry minister Yoji Muto said at a press conference, stressing the need for decarbonisation efforts.
Muto said nuclear power will account for about 20% of the country’s total energy output in fiscal 2040, around the same level as the fiscal 2030 target of 20% to 22% and up from 8.5% in fiscal 2023.
Before Fukushima, Japan’s fleet of 54 nuclear plants generated about 30% of the country’s electricity, but were all shut down for safety checks following the accident.

Among the 33 operable nuclear reactors in Japan, 14 have now resumed operations after meeting post-Fukushima safety standards. The restarted plants are: Sendai-1 and -2, Genkai-3 and -4, Ikata-3, Mihama-3, Ohi-3 and -4, Onagawa-2 (temporarily offline), Shimane-2 and Takahama-1, -2, -3 and -4.
In October, Japan’s new economy minister said the country will need to maximise the use of existing nuclear power plants because AI and data centres are expected to boost electricity demand.
Adding more emissions-free power such as nuclear is seen as crucial to allow Japan to attract more big tech operators and advanced manufacturing like semiconductor factories.

The revised energy strategy should also enable Japan, the fifth-largest carbon dioxide polluter, to boost decarbonisation efforts that have been criticised by scientists and climate groups as insufficient.
Japan is considering a new target to cut emissions by 60% by 2035 from 2013 levels, though that remains less ambitious than countries like the UK.
Before Fukushima, Japan’s fleet of 54 nuclear plants generated about 30% of the country’s electricity. Courtesy Jaif/Kyushu Electric Power.

title: Core Power Announces Programme To Bring Floating Nuclear Power To Market By Mid-2030s
author: David Dalton
text: US-based project will ‘lay foundation’ for use of reactors in maritime sector

UK-based maritime nuclear innovation company Core Power has launched a US-anchored maritime civil nuclear programme, titled Liberty, that aims to bring floating nuclear power to market by the mid-2030s.

The programme will lay the foundation for the use of nuclear power in the civil maritime sector, Core Power said, adding it will encompass modular construction of advanced fission technology and create the regulatory and supply chain frameworks necessary to enable this technology to be rolled out worldwide.

Core Power chief executive officer Mikal Boe said the Liberty programme will unlock a floating power market worth $2.6tn (€2.4tn), and shipyard construction of nuclear will deliver on time and on budget.
“Given that 65% of economic activity takes place on the coast, this will allow nuclear to reach new markets,” Boe said.
The first part of the programme will see the mass production of floating nuclear power plants (FNPPs), while the second part will involve developing nuclear propulsion for civil ships.

Core Power said: “A fleet of FNPPs can be mass produced and towed to customer locations without complex site preparations, while a central yard carries out commissioning, maintenance, refuelling, and waste management.
“This mass production is possible because the Liberty programme will employ advanced nuclear technologies, such as molten salt reactors.

“Unlike conventional nuclear technologies, these next-generation reactors are inherently and passively safe and operate at near atmospheric pressures – negating the need for a large emergency exclusion zone and vastly improving the insurability of FNPPs and nuclear-powered commercial ships.”
Earlier this month Core Power said it had partnered with naval architecture company Glosten for the design of a floating nuclear power plant for ports in the US.
Core Power chief executive officer Mikal Boe said the Liberty programme will unlock a floating power market worth $2.6tn. Courtesy Core Power.

title: Belgium Down To Four Nuclear Reactors After Shutdown Of Doel-1
author: David Dalton
text: Gov’t considering lifetime extensions and new build
Unit 1 of the Doel nuclear power station to the north of Antwerp in Belgium has been permanently shut down, bringing the number of commercial reactors in operation in the country to four.

Doel-1 operator Electrabel, the Belgian subsidiary of France’s Engie, said the 445-MW Westinghouse-supplied pressurised water reactor unit was taken offline for the final time at 21:37 local time on 14 February after 50 years of operation.
Belgium used to have a fleet of seven commercial reactors, but two of them – Doel-3 and Tihange-2 – had already been shut down in 2022 and 2023, with Doel-1 now following.

The closures are in line with Belgium’s 2003 nuclear phaseout policy. Under current regulations, Tihange-1 and Doel-2 will also shut down this year, while Doel-4 and Tihange-3 could receive operational extensions until around 2035.
However, the new Belgian government has said it is interested in additional life extensions for nuclear power plants and is also considering building new nuclear capacity.

Mathieu Bihet, the country’s new energy minister, said in an interview with La Libre that the government wants to validate a deal with owner Engie to extend operation of Doel-4 and Tihange-3 to 2035 “but also wants to extend other capacities”.
Additional agreements could lead to extensions for one or more of the two other remaining plants – Tihange-1 and Doel-2.

Earlier this month, the new government announced plans to secure the country’s reliance on nuclear energy, aiming for a 4 GW share in the country's electricity mix as part of efforts to secure a carbon-free baseload capacity. The four reactors now remaining in operation have a net capacity of around 3.4 GW
According to a coalition agreement, the aim to “restart” Belgium’s nuclear industry and see the operating life extension of existing nuclear plants and the construction of new reactors.
Stand Up for Nuclear, a global initiative in support of nuclear energy, said the closure of Doel-1 means the loss of 445 MW of clean energy.

The group called upon stakeholders to halt decommissioning, restart reactors and abolish the nuclear phaseout law. “Two more reactors are slated to close this year,” Stand Up for Nuclear said on social media. “We don’t have time to waste.”
Electrabel said that in the coming days, operators will cool down the reactor and lower the pressure in the primary cooling circuits to the level of the ambient air pressure.
It said: “As soon as the plant has cooled down sufficiently, the unloading of the nuclear reactor can begin.
“In this process, the fuel rods are lifted out of the reactor one by one and transferred to separate docks, where they will continue to cool under water for several years.”
Three of Doel’s four nuclear reactors have now been shut down. Courtesy Engie.

title: Bulgaria Minister Discusses Kozloduy Financing With Exim Officials
author: David Dalton
text: Sofia planning two Westinghouse AP1000 nuclear reactors at site

Officials from the US Export-Import Bank (Exim) have met Bulgaria’s energy minister Zhecho Stankov to discuss next steps following the $8.6bn (€8.2bn) letter of interest issued by Exim for the financing of two new reactors at the Kozloduy nuclear site in northern Bulgaria, Exim said in a statement.
During the meeting, Stankov discussed financing for the construction of two Westinghouse AP1000 nuclear reactors at Kozloduy, site of Bulgaria’s only two commercial nuclear plants.
The meeting was also attended by Petyo Ivanov, chief executive of Kozloduy NPP – New Build, the company set up to oversee Sofia’s plans for new reactors.
The meeting addressed Exim’s broad range of financing tools for nuclear projects, the statement said.

It said: “Exim is prepared to support American energy dominance, consistent with president Trump’s agenda by financing nuclear energy investments in Bulgaria which support American businesses, create jobs and prosperity for families and workers in America, and reduce the global influence of malign and adversarial states.”

US-based Westinghouse was selected in 2023 to provide its AP1000 PWR technology for Kozloduy-7 and -8. In early 2024, Sofia chose South Korea’s Hyundai E&C for the construction, delivery and eventual commissioning of the proposed plants.
According to earlier reports, officials in Bulgaria expect the two-unit Kozloduy expansion project to not exceed the price tag of $14bn.
The Bulgarian energy ministry said parliament has given a deadline of July 2025 for the completion of negotiations on securing external financing for the project.
Officials discussed financing for the construction of two Westinghouse AP1000 nuclear reactors at Kozloduy. Courtesy KNPP.

title: India And France To Work Together On SMRs And Advanced Nuclear Reactors
author: David Dalton
text: As Modi heads to meeting with Trump, New Delhi is opening up to greater international cooperation
India and France have signed a declaration of their intent to establish a partnership on advanced and small modular nuclear reactors (SMRs), the Indian foreign ministry said on 12 February.

During a meeting in Paris, Indian prime minister Narendra Modi and French president Emmanuel Macron emphasised the importance of nuclear energy for strengthening energy security and moving towards a low-carbon economy.
India’s foreign ministry said New Delhi and Paris would develop SMRs and advanced modular reactors for civil use.
Indian foreign secretary Vikram Misri said the aim was to initiate “cooperation” as modular reactor technology was “still in its initial stages”.

“We intend to be able to cooperate in co-designing the reactors, co-developing them and co-producing them, we feel this will allow us to tackle complications faced in other conventional projects,” Misri said.

The declaration comes days after India announced plans to change its strict nuclear liability law, which holds operators accountable for accidents or incidents and has been blamed for delays to previous nuclear projects.

Strict liabilities under the Civil Liability for Nuclear Damage Act, 2010, have hampered implementation of an India-US deal that would allow participation in India new-build projects of US reactor technology companies such as General Electric and Westinghouse.
The BBC said the proposed India-France partnership signals a shift in India’s nuclear energy policy.
Modi’s government, previously known for strict regulation of nuclear power, appears to be opening up to greater international cooperation and private sector participation.

Finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman unveiled ambitious nuclear energy targets earlier this month, setting a goal of generating 100 GW of nuclear energy by 2047. India currently has about 6.9 GW of nuclear capacity in operation with about 5.4 GW under construction.
The government has promised more than $2bn (€1.9bn) for nuclear research and development, most of which will be used with the aim of developing the indigenous Bharat SMR by 2033.
The focus on SMRs also represents a shift in India’s collaboration with France on nuclear power.

The countries had previously planned to build the world’s biggest nuclear station in the Maharashtra region of western India. In April 2021, French power company EDF said it had made a binding offer to build six 1,600-MW EPR units at the Jaitapur site in Maharashtra.
The project has, however, been held up, mainly because of clauses in India’s nuclear liability law.
Modi is currently in the US for a two-day visit where he will hold meetings with president Donald Trump and business leaders.
Earlier in the week, India’s oil minister Hardeep Puri hinted that nuclear energy would be on the agenda for the two leaders.

On Tuesday, US vice-president JD Vance met Modi on the sidelines of an AI summit in Paris and discussed ways in which Washington could help New Delhi diversify its energy sources by investing in US nuclear technology, news agencies reported quoting a White House statement.
Indian prime minister Narendra Modi and French president Emmanuel Macron emphasised the importance of nuclear energy when they met this week. Courtesy Government of France/X.

title: UK Moving ‘With Urgency’ On Delayed Investment Decision For Sizewell C Nuclear Power Station
author: Rachel Rigby
text: Gov’t ‘sensitive to accusation’ it is not enthusiastic about new reactors

The delayed final investment decision (FID) for the planned Sizewell C nuclear power station in eastern England will take place once the government completes its financial review for the next three years, a UK government nuclear power advisor told NucNet.

The FID for the station, the next large nuclear generating facility planned in the UK after Hinkley Point C, was delayed from 2024 because of a July general election and a lack of immediate interest on behalf of private sector investors in taking an equity stake in the facility from the UK government, according to multiple UK press reports.

Sizewell C is currently owned 77% by the UK government and 23% by EDF Energy, the UK subsidiary of French state nuclear power company EDF. The French company has long said that it does not want to own more than 20% of the Sizewell C plant.
The FID is now scheduled to be made as part of a government spending review due this spring.

The government advisor, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss potentially sensitive government thinking on the issue, said that while the FID had been delayed because of the election and to give the new Labour government time to outline spending for over the next three years, the government would look to “push forward with urgency to FID”.
The advisor said that the government was sensitive to the accusation that it was not enthusiastic about the development of nuclear power in the UK.
The source added that both EDF Energy and the government recognised that the project was already facing potential delays and so believed it should be developed urgently.
Hinkley Point C, which is 66.5% owned by China General Nuclear Corporation and 33.5% by EDF Energy, is scheduled to start operating in very late 2029 at the earliest, according to EDF.
The nuclear station, near Bristol in western England, has suffered a series of delays and is over budget in comparison to original cost estimates.
EDF has said that Sizewell C, the sister plant to Hinkley Point C, will cost around 20% less to build. Like Hinkley Point C, it will have two France-supplied EPR nuclear units of 1,630 MW (net) each.

A spokesperson for the UK’s Department of Energy Security and Net Zero, asked about the Sizewell C project, said: “New nuclear power stations such as Sizewell C will play an important role in helping the UK achieve energy security and net zero, while securing thousands of good, skilled jobs and supporting our energy independence beyond 2030.”
“It is expected to reduce the cost of the electricity system, boost our supply of secure homegrown power and generate major investment nationwide.
“The project is making good progress and a final investment decision on whether to proceed will be taken in the spending review.”

Earlier this month the government said it would ease the rules around where nuclear power plants can be built in a bid to revitalise the sector and put Britain “back in the global race for nuclear energy”.
Starmer’s Labour government, which came to power following a July 2024 general election, has backed nuclear energy.

In October it said it was making available an additional £2.7bn (€3.2bn, $3.3bn) of taxpayer money as efforts continue to try to secure the critical final investment decision for the planned Sizewell C nuclear power station in Suffolk, eastern England.

The government has also promised a record £410m investment in nuclear fusion which could help construct a world-leading fusion power project on the site of an old coal plant in Nottinghamshire, England.
Last month plans were announced for special data centre districts with dedicated nuclear power plants.

Meanwhile, Great British Nuclear (GBN), the public body set up to drive the delivery of new nuclear energy projects in the UK, has issued an “invitation to negotiate” to the four companies that were chosen for the shortlist of the government’s SMR selection process.
GBN said that after these negotiations are concluded, the companies will be invited to submit final tenders, which it will then evaluate.
The four companies remaining in the process are GE Hitachi Nuclear Energy International, Holtec Britain Ltd, Rolls Royce SMR Ltd and Westinghouse Electric Company UK.
The UK government is aiming to make a final investment decision this year on plans to build two new EPR units at Sizewell C. COurtesy EDF Energy.

title: Trade Union Urges Scotland’s Politicians To Reconsider Ban On Nuclear Plants
author: David Dalton
text: Region could see ‘£1 billion economic boom’ from new reactors at Hunterston

A major trade union has urged politicians in Scotland to reconsider the country’s ban on nuclear power plants, saying new reactors at the existing Hunterston site would result in a £1bn (€1.2bn, $1.2bn) economic boom for the area of North Ayrshire.
GMB Scotland, a general trade union, has warned that ministers’ opposition to new reactors in Scotland not only risks net zero targets but a massive economic windfall.

The nuclear industry already supports almost 3,700 jobs in Scotland, adding £400m to the economy, including at Hunterston, about 50 km west of Glasgow, where four reactors have been permanently shut down.
Louise Gilmour, GMB Scotland secretary, said that is only a fraction of the potential economic benefits if the Scottish government reverses its ban on new nuclear power.
She said industry estimates suggested four small modular reactors (SMRs) at Hunterston would create up to 800 jobs, generating £60m a year in wages.
And the GMB report said wages to contractors visiting the site could reach £15m with much of that bolstering the economies of surrounding communities.

Now GMB has urged ministers to review their opposition to nuclear – days after British prime minister Keir Starmer said the UK government would ease the rules around where nuclear power plants can be built in a bid to revitalise the sector and put Britain back in the global race for nuclear energy.
Gilmour said: “For every possible reason, the Scottish government must review and reverse its opposition to new nuclear.
“It makes no sense if ministers want to achieve net zero targets and it makes no sense if they want Scotland’s economy to grow again.
“Ministers say they want to produce safe, reliable and clean energy in Scotland. New nuclear is all of those things and, in addition, supports thousands of highly-skilled, well-paid jobs.”

Until 2021 Scotland had four commercial nuclear reactors at two sites – Hunterston B and Torness. The two Hunterston B units were shut down in November 2021 and January 2022, while the remaining two units at Torness are due to close in 2028, two years earlier than originally planned.
Two older units at Hunterston were permanently shut down in 1989 and 1990.
Four nuclear power reactors at Hunterston have been permanently shut down. Courtesy EDF Energy.

title: Thinktank Warns On US Enrichment Capacity, Calls For Public-Private Partnerships
author: David Dalton
text: Washington faces ‘critical challenge’ after years of reliance on Russia

The goal of building US domestic uranium enrichment capacity to safeguard from disruptions should remain a priority, but despite the optimistic outlook, the jury is still out on whether these efforts are sustainable in the long run, analysis published by the US Atlantic Council thinktank has said.
According to the analysis, investments in US domestic enrichment capacity will not have immediate results.

Additionally, the nuclear fuel cycle, by design, is hard to sustain competitively without close public-private collaboration. Public-private partnerships and long-term demand signals to suppliers are essential for building a resilient enriched uranium supply chain, the analysis concludes.
The sourcing of enriched uranium for commercial nuclear reactors is a critical challenge for the US, which has consistently depended on Russia for enrichment services, the analysis said.

At the same time, the US enrichment capacity, once thriving, has dwindled, giving way to foreign imports. Nearly 73% of enriched uranium in 2023 originated abroad, from countries including Kazakhstan and Russia.
“Such reliance on a handful of foreign sources, and especially adversarial countries, introduces severe supply vulnerabilities,” according to the analysis.

Russia has a consistent track record of weaponising energy dependence to coerce other countries. Approximately 27% of the enriched uranium used in the US comes from Russia, which is responsible for around 44% of global enrichment capacity.

Although the Biden administration banned Russian uranium imports in 2024, the legislation permits US firms to procure nuclear fuel from Russia’s state-run nuclear energy corporation Rosatom, under a waiver programme until alternative suppliers are secured. These waivers, however, can only be granted until 2028 and are designed to give US energy providers sufficient time to adjust to the new conditions.

In response, in November 2024, Moscow announced “tit-for-tat” restrictions on uranium exports to the US. According to the new rules, exemptions might be made under one-off licences issued by the Russian Federal Service for Technical and Export Control.
“While it is unclear whether such licences will be granted, this move yet again showcases the risks of relying on external fuel sources,” the analysis said.
Nearly 73% of US enriched uranium in 2023 originated abroad, from countries including Kazakhstan and Russia.

title: UK Making ‘Sensible Decisions’ On Nuclear, But Needs Decision On Sizewell And Technology For Small Modular Reactors
author: Rachel Rigby
text: Industry head tells NucNet ‘discussions must now end with proper decisions’

The UK’s Labour government is making some sensible decisions on nuclear energy but must make a final investment decision on Sizewell C and finish the process of technology selection for the country’s planned deployment of small modular reactors (SMRs), Tom Greatrex, chief executive of the London-based Nuclear Industry Association (NIA), said in an interview on 3 February.
Greatrex told NucNet that Labour has “the right nuclear policy”, but needs to ensure that by the midpoint of this year a financial structure is put in place for construction at Sizewell C.

“By the summer, it’s urgent that the final investment process [for Sizewell C] and the SMR selection is completed. They [the government] need to make conclusions as the ongoing discussions must now end with proper decisions, Greatrex said.

Greatrex said there was “a lot of engagement in parliament” during the recent Nuclear Week in Parliament event with interest from new MPs across all parties. He said prime minister Keir Starmer’s government is “supportive and keeps enabling nuclear to happen by meeting across all the [political] parties”.

But Greatrex said energy decisions “need to be taken now for 2050” because electricity use will increase because of the need for power for data centres and the fact that the UK “is moving away from carbon heavy energy”.

He said the Labour party is “making sensible statements and decisions”. It is supporting investment for the planned Sizewell C nuclear power station in England and now needs to finish the process of technology selection for SMR deployment in order to get the process of SMR construction in the UK started.

Sizewell C is a planned two-unit nuclear power station in Suffolk, eastern England, that will use French EPR nuclear plant technology. The project is a sister project to the Hinkley Point C nuclear station being built by EDF Energy in southwest England. Hinkley Point C is the only nuclear power station being built in the UK.
In October, the government made available an additional £2.7bn (€3.2bn, $3.5bn) of taxpayer money as efforts continue to try to secure the critical final investment decision for Sizewell C.

The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero and the public body Great British Nuclear (GBN) are running a project to award a contract for the deployment of at least one SMR in the UK by the early 2030s. There is at present a shortlist of four potential SMR providers into the competition.
GBN has entered the negotiation phase with shortlisted vendors. Final decisions will be taken in the spring.

Last year’s general election added “a bit of a delay”, but the incoming government was aware of the nuclear policies and there is no reason for further delay, Greatrex said. Sizewell C will go ahead, with the government as an 85% shareholder. They just need to make final investment structure decisions.”
Greatrex said: “Financing is not a problem, there are lots of private investors wanting to invest but for that to happen, the government needs to make it happen.”
Greatrex also welcomed plans to ease the rules around where nuclear power plants can be built in a bid to revitalise the sector and put Britain back in the global race for nuclear energy.

The government announced last week that more nuclear power plants will be approved across England and Wales as prime minister Keir Starmer cuts red tape to get Britain building – as part of his “plan for change”.

“This is the prime minister’s strongest signal yet that new nuclear is critical to the growth and clean power mission,” Greatrex said. “A more streamlined planning system will give certainty to investors, the supply chain and communities, and will enable us to get on with building new nuclear plants on more sites and at pace for a cleaner, more secure power system.”

Greatrex added: “We need to make Britain the best possible place to build new nuclear, both large-scale and SMRs, which means avoiding unnecessary stumbling blocks and ensuring regulations are proportionate to our urgent need for low carbon power, energy security and good jobs.”
Hinkley Point C is the only nuclear power station being built in the UK. Courtesy EDF Energy.
Tom Greatrex said energy decisions ‘need to be taken now for 2050’. Courtesy NIA.

title: Belgium Considering Additional Nuclear Extensions And New Build, Says Minister
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Incoming gov’t says investment will be needed but ‘we think it can be done’

The incoming Belgian government is interested in additional life extensions for nuclear power plants and is also considering building new nuclear capacity, according to Mathieu Bihet, the country’s new energy minister.
Bihet told a televised interview with La Libre that the government wants to validate a deal with owner Engie to extend operation of Doel-4 and Tihange-3 “but also wants to extend other capacities”.

The existing deal with Engie is to extend the operating lifetimes of Doel-4 and Tihange-3 until around 2035. Additional agreements could lead to extensions for one or more of the other plants. – Tihange-1, Doel-1 and Doel-2.
Bihet said the government will hold meetings with Engie and the Belgian nuclear regulator to discuss whether these reactors can be “brought up to standard” to maintain power generation.
Belgium has five commercial reactor units at two sites – Doel in the northern province of Antwerp and Tihange near the eastern city of Liege.
The country used to have a fleet of seven commercial reactors, but two of those – Doel-3 and Tihange-2 – were shut down in 2022 and 2023.
Under current regulations, Tihange-1, Doel-1 and Doel-2 will remain operational until 2025, while Doel-4 and Tihange-3 will receive operational extensions until around 2035.

Both units were scheduled to be shut down in 2025, but in December 2023 the previous Belgian government signed an agreement with French utility company Engie to extend the life of two of the two units in the aftermath of the war in Ukraine and ensuing energy security concerns.
Earlier this week, the new coalition government announced plans to secure the country’s reliance on nuclear energy, aiming for at least a 4 GW share in electricity generation.

The move signalled a reversal of previous policies aimed at a partial phasing out of nuclear power by 2025 pursued by consecutive governments which had drawn plans to cut down nuclear based on a 2003 law.
Bihet told the De Tijd newspaper that Belgium could secure 4 GW of capacity from existing reactors and potentially deploy new capacities for an additional 4 GW.
“We want to keep that existing capacity open. We know that a discussion with Engie will be necessary for that,” he said.
Bihet also told La Libre that keeping existing units online is “the first framework” in the government’s plans, while “the second framework is to work on creating new capacity”.
“Why do we do this? Because we know that nuclear energy provides abundant, low-carbon energy,” he said.

Asked about whether it is too late to begin preparations for life extensions at Tihange-1, and Doel-1 and -2, Bihet said the government will hold meetings with Engie and the Belgian nuclear regulator to discuss whether these reactors can be “brought up to standard” to maintain power generation.
“We believe it’s possible. It will require investments and upgrades, but we think it can be done,” Bihet added.

On the topic of new-build, the minister said he would not commit to set targets and dates, but the government needs to be “ambitious”. He said more investment is needed into research and development around small modular reactors (SMRs) but also there is a need to invest in large capacities “important for strategy”.
“We still have to evaluate which technology we will use. But it is clear that it will not be just SMRs,” Bihet also told De Tijd, adding that “small reactors alone will not be enough.”
“We want to reverse this tendency towards anti-nuclearism and return to an energy mix that treats all sources of energy production evenly,” Bihet said for La Libre.
“But above all we want to decarbonise. That’s the basis.”
Belgium has five commercial reactor units at two sites – Doel (pictured) in the northern province of Antwerp and Tihange near the eastern city of Liege. Courtesy Engie.

title: US Nuclear Industry Calls For Federal Support And Warns ‘China Is Running Circles Around Us’
author: David Dalton
text: Restoring commercial capabilities will be a long, hard, expensive road, society head tells new energy secretary

The US nuclear industry has called for federal support from new energy secretary Chris Wright, warning that the country’s supply chain has atrophied and “China is running circles around us in new builds”.

In an open letter to Wright, American Nuclear Society chief executive officer Craig Piercy said Russia has the best “zero money down” offer on nuclear reactors in the world “and they’ll even take back your used nuclear fuel”.
Piercy said: “Both nations have made civil nuclear exports a core pillar of their foreign policies. It’s time for the US to do the same.”

According to Piercy, the US is on track to have several first-of-a-kind advanced reactors operational in the 2030s, but nobody knows for sure if operating prototypes will be enough to kickstart a full-on commercial build-out.

“Many in the industry think additional government support will be needed to reach nth-of-a-kind nuclear plant construction costs, while others believe rising electricity demand alone will take care of that in time,” Piercy said.

He said restoring America’s commercial nuclear capabilities is a long, hard, expensive road and “we must learn again what we once knew well”. He added: “But it will be worth it, for jobs, economic growth, and national security.”

Piercy said: “Yes, it will likely require more funding and investment from the federal government, but I guarantee you – on your last day as secretary of energy, you will not regret a minute you spent fighting for it.”

The open letter was published as Wright took up office promising to “unleash American energy innovation” by prioritising affordable, reliable, and secure energy technologies, including advanced nuclear, fossil fuels, geothermal and hydropower.
Wright this week signed his first secretarial order this week to “kickstart the golden era of American energy dominance”, the Department of Energy (DOE) said.

The DOE must also prioritise true technological breakthroughs such as nuclear fusion, Wright said. To that end, the DOE will comprehensively review its R&D portfolio and “rigorously enforce project milestones” to ensure that taxpayer resources are allocated appropriately and cost-effectively.
Wright said: “The long-awaited American nuclear renaissance must launch during president Trump’s administration.
“As global energy demand continues to grow, America must lead the commercialisation of affordable and abundant nuclear energy.”
He said the DOE will work diligently and creatively to enable the rapid deployment and export of next-generation nuclear technology.
Wright is best known for his role as chief executive officer of Liberty Energy, a fracking company, but he has also served on the board of advanced reactor company Oklo.
In 2023, Wright signed a letter supporting nuclear energy in which oil and gas executives called for political parties to unite in the support of nuclear energy both in the US and abroad.

Wright said during his recent confirmation hearing that his priority was expanding domestic energy production, including nuclear power, and said the US should be the world’s leader in developing, deploying and exporting next-generation nuclear technology.
US energy secretary Chris Wright signed his first secretarial order this week to ‘kickstart the golden era of American energy dominance’. Courtesy DOE.

title: Tepco To Begin Water Tank Dismantling At Fukushima-Daiichi Nuclear Station
author: David Dalton
text: Step seen as milestone in decades-long decommissioning project

The operator of the crippled Fukushima-Daiichi nuclear power station will start dismantling treated water tanks next week to clear space needed to store nuclear fuel debris to be extracted from the reactors.

The step is a milestone of a sort as Tokyo Electric Power Company (Tepco) moves ahead with a decades-long project to dismantle the entire facility, which has been shut down since it was hit by a catastrophic tsunami in 2011, leading to the meltdown of three reactors.
“The company will start dismantling welded water tanks on February 13, if the weather allows,” a Tepco spokesman said.
Since the accident, Tepco has stored around 1.3 million tonnes of water – a combination of groundwater, seawater and rainwater – at the site along with water used for cooling the reactors.
The water is filtered to remove various radioactive materials, but has remained inside more than 1,000 tanks that occupy much of the facility’s ground.
After removing the tanks, Tepco plans to build facilities to store molten fuel debris to be extracted from inside the reactors.
Scrapping the water tanks became possible after Tepco began releasing the stored water from the plant into the Pacific Ocean in August 2023.
Japan has insisted that the water does not harm the environment, a position backed by the International Atomic Energy Agency.
The tanks have been used for storing contaminated water at the Fukushima site. Courtesy Dean Calma/IAEA.

title: Vietnam To Hold Talks With Reactor Suppliers As Plans Move Ahead To Revive Nuclear Programme
author: David Dalton
text: Hanoi wants to build two stations in central province of Ninh Thuan

Vietnam is planning hold talks with potential foreign partners this month about developing its first two nuclear power stations after the government formally approved a plan with the aim of having a reactor online in the next decade.

The Southeast Asian launched a regulatory framework, and plans to establish human resources and research infrastructure needed to develop nuclear energy by 2030, according to a statement on a government website.

According to the statement, the “plan for development and application of atomic energy for the period up to 2030, with a vision to 2050” was signed by Vietnam’s deputy prime minister and foreign minister Bui Thanh Son.

According to the statement, the “plan for development and application of atomic energy for the period up to 2030, with a vision to 2050” was signed by Vietnam’s deputy prime minister and foreign minister Bui Thanh Son.
State utility EVN and oil and gas firm PetroVietnam have been assigned as the investors for the first two stations, the government said in a statement.
It also said in a draft amendment to its energy plan that the first nuclear plant could be in operation “from 2035 at the earliest”.
Hanoi will discuss the projects with Russia, Japan, South Korea, France and the US, according to state media.
The country’s planned nuclear programme will involve building two nuclear power stations with a combined capacity of 4,000 MW in the central province of Ninh Thuan.
Vietnam had planned the two stations as far back as 2009, but the National Assembly rejected the proposal in 2016 on cost grounds.
The proposed plants were planned to be built by Russia’s state nuclear corporation Rosatom and Japan Atomic Power Company.
In December, lawmakers asked the government to resume the development of the nuclear power programme after a vote on 30 November, according to the official government news portal.
The central committee of the communist party of Vietnam had already agreed to restarting Hanoi’s nuclear programme.

The government estimates that power consumption will reach 1,200 TWh by 2045 compared to 1,000 TWh in the eight national power development plan, which provides targets for 2030 and “a vision” towards net-zero in 2050.

According to a report by accountancy company PwC, Vietnam’s expected economic growth over the next three decades means a need for 150 GW in installed capacity by 2030, and 500 GW by 2050, from about 80 GW today.
Hanoi is aiming to have its first commercial nuclear power plant online within a decade. Credit Wikimedia Creative Commons.

title: Russia’s Leningrad-3 Nuclear Plant Granted Operating Extension Until 2030
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Country still operates seven RBMK reactors at three sites
Unit 3 at the Leningrad nuclear power station in northwest Russia has received regulatory approval to operate until 2030, state-owned nuclear operator Rosenergoatom said.
Leningrad-3 is a 925-MW graphite-moderated RBMK-1000 reactor unit in commercial operation since 1980.
Rosenergoatom said the unit has generated more than 290 TWh of electricity since its launch.
The company said the until will now be able to operate for 50 years. It had previously received a 15-year lifetime extension by authorities.

The extension will help maintain and improve the reliability of Russia’s power system while minimising electricity price increases for consumers and preserving carbon-free energy sources in the country’s energy balance, statement said.

State nuclear corporation Rosatom also confirmed that licensing documents have been submitted to extend the operational life of a twin unit, Leningrad- 4, alongside similar initiatives for reactors at the Kursk, Smolensk and Kalinin nuclear stations.
If approved, the extensions could preserve up to 7 GW of power generation capacity.
Two older RBMK-1000 reactor units, Leningrad-1 and -2, were permanently shut down in 2020.
Russia is the only country to still operate the RBMK reactor technology. It has seven such units in its fleet of 36 commercial reactors.
The RBMK is a Soviet-designed, graphite-moderated, water-cooled nuclear reactor featuring individual pressure tubes for fuel and the capability for onload refuelling.
The design was involved in the 1986 Chernobyl accident in Ukraine, but has since undergone significant refurbishment and safety upgrades for all remaining units.
The reactor hall at one of the RBMK units at the Leningrad nuclear station. Courtesy RIA Novosti/Alexey Danichev (CC-BY-SA 3.0)

title: Belgium’s New Government Revives Nuclear Energy Plans, Aims for 4 GW Capacity
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Industry forum warns ‘we cannot afford to repeat the mistakes of the past’

Belgium’s new government announced plans to secure the country’s reliance on nuclear energy, aiming for a 4 GW share in the country's electricity mix as part of efforts to secure a carbon-free baseload capacity.

According to a coalition agreement, plans will aim to “restart” Belgium’s nuclear industry and see the operating life extension of existing nuclear plants and the construction of new reactors in the coming years.

The government plans to repeal 2003 legislation that mandated a nuclear phaseout in Belgium, enabling the continued operation and expansion of nuclear capacity. Consecutive governments had drawn up plans to reduce nuclear power based on the 2003 law and amendments in 2019 that planned for a partial nuclear phaseout in 2025.
Out of Belgium’s seven commercial reactors, two – Doel-3 and Tihange-2 – were shut down in 2022 and 2023. The country currently operates a fleet of five reactor units at Doel and Tihange.
Under current regulations, Tihange-1, Doel-1 and Doel-2 will remain operational until 2025, while Doel-4 and Tihange-3 will receive operational extensions until around 2035.

Both units were scheduled to be shut down in 2025, but in December 2023 the Belgian government signed an agreement with French utility company Engie to extend the life of two of the two units in the aftermath of the war in Ukraine and ensuing energy security concerns.
The coalition agreement confirmed the lifetime extensions of Doel-4 and Tihange-3 for at least 10 years.
It also said efforts will be made to “remove obstacles” and “facilitate and accelerate” the construction of new reactors.

The government wants “more prominence” for nuclear on the European Union agenda and said it will advocate for a European nuclear strategy, including an update to the Euratom treaty, which coordinates nuclear energy research, ensures a secure supply of nuclear fuel, and promote safety standards across EU member states.
The government also pledged to preserve Belgium’s nuclear expertise and intellectual property to “avoid the loss of a strategic asset for the country.”

The Belgian Nuclear Forum, a Brussels-based nuclear industry group, has called on the government to repeal the nuclear phaseout law “without further delay” as to remove any legal obstacle to the extension of existing reactors and the construction of new ones.

“There is no time to lose on the energy issue,” the forum warned in a statement and said it will invite all government and industry stakeholders to a newly formed task force which will aim to facilitate “this nuclear revival”.
“We cannot afford to repeat the mistakes of the past by working in silos,” the forum said.

In terms of new-build, the forum believes small modular reactors are a priority option to look at, while concerning the existing large-scale fleet, the forum sees a need to consider changing the current reactor operator if it “continues to adhere to its announced strategy and no longer sees a future for nuclear energy in Belgium.”

The forum said there must be clarity as soon as possible about the role that the current operator still wants to or can play. The Belgian reactor fleet is operated by Electrabel, subsidiary of France’s Engie.
Belgium’s new government has been formed after general elections in June 2024 followed by nearly eight months of multi-party negotiations.

The coalition, led by prime minister Bart De Wever of the New Flemish Alliance, comprises five parties leaning mostly towards the right or centre-right of the political spectrum. These are: the New Flemish Alliance (N-VA), Christian Democratic and Flemish (CD&V), Vooruit (Forward), the Reformist Movement (MR), and Les Engagés.

title: 7 Power For Big Tech, But ‘Beware Of The Hype’, Says Policy Expert
author: Rachel Rigby
text: Comments follow concerns that DeepSeek’s AI model could lead to lower demand and stall development of next-generation reactors

Nuclear appears to be a possible solution for providing power to the booming data centre sector because it is a round-the-clock source of electricity, but there has been “a bit too much hype” and government policy should not be based on unrealistic forecasts of demand and costs for untested nuclear technologies, a professor of energy policy at a London university told NucNet.
Stephen Thomas, of the University of Greenwich Business School, said UK nuclear expansion policies have always been based on an “over-forecast” of electricity demand.
He said: “In 2007 Tony Blair’s government made the assumption there would be 20% growth in electricity demand by 2025 and it’s actually fallen significantly and demand is lower than in 2005.”
“Had electricity demand grown as forecast, the delay completing Hinkley Point C and the failure to progress other projects would have resulted led to power shortages.”
Government electricity forecasts are always too high because they underestimate the impact of energy efficiency and overestimate economic growth, Thomas said.

His warnings come amid significant interest in nuclear plants for powering big tech, with several companies including Amazon, Google and Microsoft looking at nuclear reactors to power their energy-intensive data centres and AI initiatives.

Thomas said: “There will be improvements in the efficiency of electric vehicles and AI centres just as there was, for example, in lighting, where LED light bulbs use 10% of the amount of energy of the old light bulbs and modern TVs are now much more energy efficient.”

The UK’s Labour government announced last month it is planning special districts for constructing data centres and will explore dedicating nuclear energy to the sites as part of a project to boost technology growth and the ecosystem for AI.
The ‘AI Growth Zones’ will include improved access to electricity and easier planning approvals for data centres, the government said.

Thomas said stock markets tend to overreact to developments such as recent reports that China-based DeepSeek’s AI model could reduce the anticipated surge in electricity consumption and stall the development of next-generation reactors that are poised to accommodate growing electricity needs of AI technologies

DeepSeek released its powerful R1 AI program that it claims cost just $5.6m (€5.3m) to build, marking a possible shift from the massive levels of investment by technology industry giants in the energy – including nuclear – needed to power their data centres and AI initiatives.

Tom Greatrex, chief executive of the London-based Nuclear Industry Association, told NucNet the development of DeepSeek is not bad news for nuclear because tech companies will still need more power than is currently available.

He said short-terms falls in nuclear-related share prices do not reflect the reality because many shareholders or traders lack understanding of the energy market and “any recent drop is not an indication of a long-term trend”.
Data Centres will continue to try get power deals direct with nuclear suppliers because they do not want to depend on the national grid, Greatrex said.
He said one form of AI will not be so different from other forms. “Some forms might need less energy, but they will still need more than we have today,” Greatrex said.

Some nuclear stocks fell after the DeepSeek announcement. The sector had broadly gained ground after US president Donald Trump announced that Sam Altman’s OpenAI, SoftBank and Oracle were planning a joint venture called Stargate to build data centres and other AI infrastructure in the US, with investments of up to $500bn. Altman is one of the key investors in Oklo, a US company developing advanced nuclear reactors.
Demand for data is expected to grow massively by the end of the decade driven by AI R&D and deployment. Image courtesy Victor Grigas (CC BY-SA 3.0)

title: India Pushes Ahead With Plans To Open Up Nuclear Sector, Deploy More Reactors
author: David Dalton
text: New body will focus on research and development of SMRs
