India wants to amend its liability law to boost foreign and private investments in its civilian nuclear energy sector and also aims to set up a Nuclear Energy Mission with an outlay $2.3bn (€2.2bn) to operate at least five indigenously developed small modular reactors (SMRs) by 2033.
According to the finance ministry, the mission will focus on research and development of SMRs.

Finance and corporate affairs minister Nirmala Sitharaman said the development of at least 100 GW of nuclear energy by 2047 is essential for the country’s energy transition efforts. India currently has about 6.9 GW of nuclear capacity in operation with about 5.4 GW under construction.
The announcements were part of Sitharaman’s budget on 1 February and came ahead of prime minister Narendra Modi’s planned US visit from 12-14 February.

Strict liabilities under India’s Civil Liability for Nuclear Damage Act, 2010, have hampered implementation of an India-US deal that would allow participation in India new-build projects of US reactor technology companies such as General Electric and Westinghouse.

The US said last month, before Donald Trump was sworn in as president, that it was finalising steps to remove barriers to civil nuclear cooperation with India as it seeks to capitalise on the Asian nation’s ambition plans for reactor development and deployment.
Washington and New Delhi have been discussing the supply of US nuclear reactors to India since the mid-2000s.

But a longstanding obstacle has been the need to bring Indian liability rules in line with global norms, which require the costs of any accident to be channelled to the operator rather than the maker of a nuclear power plant.

The removal of US restrictions on civil nuclear cooperation is expected to bring a number of significant benefits for India’s domestic nuclear energy industry, including access to advanced technology, the transfer of knowledge and skills, greater investment in infrastructure and the strengthening of regulatory frameworks.

Last month, Nuclear Power Corporation of India Ltd (NPCIL) issued a request for proposals for the deployment of Bharat small modular reactors, opening the doors of the nuclear sector to Indian private companies for the first time.
Until now, only state-owned NPCIL has been allowed to build and deploy commercial nuclear power plants in India.

The proposal would allow private companies to build reactors under NPCIL’s control and supervision. On completion, plants would be operated by NPCIL under a long-term operation and maintenance agreement.
The deployment of the Bharat SMR – Bharat being the Hindi for “India” – forms part of the country’s plans under ‘Viksit Bharat’, which is Hindi for “Developed India”.

The details of the Bharat nuclear plant’s development remain unclear, but Sitharaman said in July the initiative would involve a joint venture between state power company National Thermal Power Corporation and state power generation equipment manufacturer Bharat Heavy Electricals Limited.

New Delhi is bullish on nuclear. NPCIL said recently that India plans to add 18 more nuclear reactors to its national energy mix by 2031-32, bringing the total nuclear power capacity of the country to 22.4 GW.
NPCIL did not say whether the 22.4 GW would be net or gross, but either way it represents a significant increase from around 6.9 GW net today.

According to the International Atomic Energy Agency, India has 20 reactors in commercial operation which provided about 3% of the country’s electricity generation in 2023. It has seven plants under construction.
India has 20 reactors in commercial operation which provided about 3% of the country’s electricity generation in 2023. Image courtesy Flickr/Afam Jones (CCBY2.0)

title: US Nuclear Generators Import Nearly All The Uranium Concentrate They Use, Data Shows
author: David Dalton
text: Origin of U3O8 could change after Biden administration legislation

US nuclear generators used 32 million pounds of imported uranium concentrate (U3O8) and only 0.05 million pounds of domestically produced U3O8 in 2023, according to latest data from the US Energy Information Administration (EIA).
Imports accounted for 99% of the U3O8 used in 2023 to make nuclear fuel in the US, according to the EIA, a federal agency responsible for energy data.
Foreign producers predominantly supply the US front-end nuclear fuel cycle, but federal policies have been implemented recently to improve the domestic US nuclear fuel supply chain.

In June 2024, the Biden administration issued a request for proposals to buy up to $2.7bn (€2.5bn) of enriched uranium from domestic sources in an effort to boost supplies of the nuclear reactor fuel and move the country away from buying it from Russia.

The Department of Energy said the move would help spur the build-out of uranium enrichment capacity in the US, promote diversity in the market and “provide a reliable supply of commercial nuclear fuel to support the energy security and resilience of the American people and domestic industries, free from Russian influence”.

According to the EIA, uranium production in the US peaked in 1980 and uranium purchases by US nuclear power plant operators from domestic suppliers peaked in 1981. Since 1992, most uranium purchased by US nuclear power plant operators was imported.

U3O8 is chemically extracted from uranium ore that has been mined and milled. The fine powder is packaged in steel drums and later enriched and processed further to prepare it for use as fuel in nuclear reactors.

US production of U3O8 in the third quarter of 2024 totalled 121,296 pounds, a 24% increase from production of 97,709 pounds in the second quarter. Production in the third quarter occurred at five US facilities: three in Wyoming (Nicholas Ranch, Lost Creek and Smith Ranch-Highland) and two in Texas (Alta Mesa and Rosita).
In 2023, the US imported U3O8 and equivalents primarily from Canada, Australia, Russia, Kazakhstan, and Uzbekistan.

The origin of U3O8 used in US nuclear reactors could change in the coming years, the EIA said. In May 2024, the Biden administration banned imports of uranium products from Russia beginning in August, although companies may apply for waivers until 1 January 2028.
The Alta Mesa uranium site in Texas was one of five US facilities that produced U3O8 in the third quarter of 2024. Courtesy enCore Energy

title: Canada Joint Venture Wins $2.4 Billion Pickering Nuclear Station Refurbishment Contract
author: Kamen Kraev
text: OPG planning to extend lifetime of four Candu heavy water reactor units

A contract won by a joint venture between Canadian reactor company Candu Energy and construction group Aecon for refurbishments at Ontario Power Generation’s (OPG) Pickering nuclear power station will be worth an estimated at CAD2.1bn ($1.46bn, €1.4bn), Candu Energy parent company AtkinsRéalis said.
According to AtkinsRéalis the contract includes CAD1.1bn for early works and roughly CAD1bn for the project’s definition phase.

The contract covers critical engineering, procurement and execution planning activities to extend the lifetime of the four commercial Candu heavy water reactor units at Pickering, about 45 km east of Toronto.

Once complete in the mid-2030s, the overhaul will allow Pickering Units 5, 6, 7, and 8 to operate into the mid-2060s, part of Ontario’s strategy to meet a projected 75% increase in electricity demand by 2050, AtkinsRéalis said.
“Refurbishing Pickering secures decades more of the low carbon reliable baseload electricity Ontario needs to meet forecasted soaring demand,” said Nicolle Butcher, OPG president and chief executive.
The contract comes after the Ontario government approved OPG’s plan to proceed with the refurbishing project to secure more power and create thousands of jobs across the province.
Pickering-5, -6, -7, and -8 are the only plants remaining in operation at the facility. The move marked a major turnaround for the station, which was scheduled to close by 2025.
Units 2 and 3 were permanently shut down in 2007 and 2008 and Units 1 and 4 were taken offline in 2024.
The four Pickering plants to be refurbished are newer and started commercial operation between 1983 and 1986.

Candu reactors are a domestically developed heavy water reactor designs which rely on natural uranium fuel and can be refuelled while online reducing outage time. Canada has a fleet of 17 commercial Candu reactor units, providing about 14% of the nation’s electricity generation.
The contract is for lifetime extension work at the four commercial Candu heavy water reactor units at Pickering. Courtesy OPG.

title: French Startup Hexana Raises €25m To Advance Generation IV Nuclear Plant
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Funds will be used to complete preliminary design
French nuclear startup Hexana has raised €25m ($26m) to advance its RNR Sodium advanced reactor technology with the aim of finalising the reactor’s preliminary design phase.

RNR Sodium is a Generation IV, sodium-cooled fast neutron reactor technology designed to produce high-temperature, carbon-free energy with improved fuel recycling and flexible output for heavy industries, Hexana has said.
According to a statement, the financing includes a €15m fundraising round and a €10m grant from Bpifrance Financement through the France 2030 programme for nuclear reactor innovation.

Hexana, which is also supported by investors such as Blast.Club, Eren Industries, CEA Investissement and Région Sud Investissement, said it plans to use the funds to complete the preliminary design of its reactor and submit a safety options file to French nuclear authorities, a pre-regulatory step.

Hexana also said the RNR Sodium technology builds on the expertise from past French projects like Phénix, Superphénix, and Astrid. The platform will consist of two 400 MWth modules and an energy storage system.
The French company expects to be able to commercialise the RNR Sodium technology by 2035.

Hexana president Sylvain Nizou said the financing demonstrates the credibility and relevance of the company’s low-carbon technology to replace fossil fuels. It will allow Hexana to continue to European commercial development and secure its first industrial sites.
Hexana co-founders Sylvain Nizou (left) and Paul Gauthé. Courtesy Hexana.

title: Generation IV Advanced Nuclear Reactor Forum Signs Agreement To Ensure Continued Collaboration
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Group is ‘bedrock of international research and development,’ says OECD head

An international forum dedicated to the development of a new generation of nuclear power plants has signed a framework agreement that will ensure collaboration continues beyond the expiration of the current agreement on 28 February 2025.

The Generation IV International Forum (GIF) said the new agreement, signed at Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) premises in Paris, France, marks the start of “a new chapter” for advanced reactor development.
GIF is an international organisation established in 2001 that coordinates the development of Generation IV reactors.

Canada, France, Japan and Switzerland signed the new agreement at this week’s ceremony. The UK and the US signed the agreement in the margins of Cop29 climate conference in Baku, Azerbaijan, in November 2024.

The OECD said other major nuclear energy countries are expected to sign the agreement, which will enter into force on 1 March 2025, increasing what is a collaborative effort on deployment of Generation IV nuclear energy systems “at a time when all options to deliver low-carbon energy are critically needed”.
No precise definition of a Generation IV reactor exists, but the term is used to refer to nuclear reactor technologies under development.

GIF provides a platform for collaborative research and development on six Generation IV reactor concepts: gas-cooled fast reactors; lead-cooled fast reactors; molten salt reactors; sodium-cooled fast reactors; supercritical-water-cooled reactors and very high-temperature reactors.

GIF also provides a forum for collaboration on general topics crucial to advancing nuclear systems such as safety and risk assessment, education and training, economic modelling, proliferation resistance and physical protection, advanced manufacturing, and non-electric applications such as hydrogen production and desalination.

OECD secretary general Mathias Cormann told ambassadors and delegates at the signing ceremony that this is GIF’s 24th year as the bedrock of international research and development on advanced reactor concepts with improved safety, performance, and proliferation-resistant features.

He said: “Work between national research laboratories, academia, and the private sector from GIF member countries under this framework continues to serve as among the world’s most important international initiatives in energy and science cooperation.”
The OECD’s Nuclear Energy Agency (NEA), which has supported GIF as the technical secretariat since its inception, will continue in this capacity under the new agreement.
NEA director-general William Magwood highlighted the importance of GIF’s work on new nuclear technologies.

“As someone who contributed to GIF’s launch in 2001, I have witnessed its growth and potential to support global progress in advanced nuclear energy systems,” he said. “This new agreement is not just a continuation; it will pave the way for GIF’s mission to support a new era for nuclear energy.”
Nuclear Energy Agency director-general William Magwood addresses the signing ceremony for the 2025 Generation IV International Forum framework agreement. Courtesy OECD.

title: US Nuclear Startup Backed By Tech Billionaires Secures $425m In Race For Fusion
author: David Dalton
text: Washington-based Helion has now raised more than $1bn and has a valuation of $5.4bn

A US startup whose backers include tech billionaires Sam Altman and Peter Thiel has raised $425m (€409m) to keep it on track to achieve its target of producing electricity from nuclear fusion in 2028.

A statement said the venture capital firm Lightspeed and SoftBank’s second Vision Fund are the investors joining OpenAI boss Altman, Thiel’s Mithril Capital and steel company Nucor in backing Helion. Altman is also a major backer – and chairman – of California-based nuclear reactor developer Oklo.
The privately owned Washington-based startup, founded in 2013, has now raised more than $1bn and has a valuation of $5.4bn, including the latest fundraising round.
Helion said the new investment will help it speed up the development of its next generation fusion reactor design.
It said the money would be spent on manufacturing pulse capacitors, an important component of its 7th generation prototype Polaris reactor in the US.

Helion founder and chief executive officer David Kirtley said: “The capacitor is where about a third of the cost of the whole system goes, and about 85% of Polaris’ capacitors were built overseas. We bought them and waited several years to get them in-house.”
He added: “We are now the first US manufacturer of large-scale pulse capacitors in decades, and we are going to expand that. So rather than waiting three years, we could get them in a year or less.”

Helion has a contract to start supplying Microsoft with electricity produced from its fusion system in 2028, and the new funds would put it “on course” to achieve the goal, said chief executive David Kirtley. The company also has an agreement to build a 500 MW power plant for Nucor.

Helion recently began operating Polaris, which is expected to demonstrate the first electricity produced from fusion. With its previous prototype, Trenta, Helion was the first private company to achieve a fuel temperature of 100 million °C, which is generally considered the required operating temperature for a commercial fusion power plant.
Helion said the new investment will help it speed up the development of its next generation fusion reactor design. Courtesy Helion.

title: Poland And Canada Sign ‘Landmark’ Cooperation Agreement On Nuclear Power
author: David Dalton
text: Warsaw preparing to start process of choosing a partner for a second nuclear station

Poland and Canada have signed what they called a “landmark” agreement that provides a legal framework for more intensive cooperation on nuclear power, Polish prime minister Donald Tusk and his Canadian counterpart Justin Trudeau announced after a meeting in Warsaw.

Trudeau said once in force, the agreement will deepen ties between Canadian and Polish energy sectors, enabling Canadian companies to apply their nuclear expertise to support Poland’s energy transition and enhance energy security for Poland and the region.
He added: “Canada will use our nuclear energy expertise to help Poland transition towards clean, reliable, and domestically sourced energy, phasing out coal from their national power grid.”

Poland, which is working to reduce its reliance on coal, has already chosen Westinghouse Electric to build its first nuclear station in the northern province of Pomerania on the Baltic Sea coast, but financing is still not fully agreed.
Warsaw is now preparing to start the process of choosing a partner for a second nuclear station.
At a press conference following the announcement of the agreement, Tusk said Canada’s small modular reactor (SMR) experience was part of the deal.

Canada expects to be the first G7 country to have the first operational SMR, the GE-Hitachi BWRX-300, by 2029. It is under development by Ontario Power Generation at its Darlington nuclear station, and Poland is watching developments at Darlington closely, as it plans to deploy the same SMR technology shortly thereafter, the Canadian government said in a statement.

In 2023, the Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission and the National Atomic Energy Agency of Poland signed a memorandum of understanding on SMRs, paving the way for increased exchanges on best practices and technical reviews related to SMR technology.
Poland does not yet generate nuclear power commercially, but it has ambitious plans to use both large-scale and SMR nuclear technology.

At the press conference, Tusk also referred to Westinghouse’s Canadian ownership. He said: “Canada is the main provider of technology for Poland’s first nuclear plant – Westinghouse is owned by Canadian companies.”

Westinghouse went bankrupt in 2017. It emerged from bankruptcy after being purchased by Brookfield Business Partners, a Canadian private equity fund. They sold it to a consortium of Canada-based Brookfield Renewable Partners and Cameco, the Canadian uranium and nuclear fuel company.
Polish prime minister Donald Tusk and his Canadian counterpart Justin Trudeau signed the agreement in Warsaw. Courtesy Chancellery of the Prime Minister of Poland.

title: Sweden Begins Work On Expansion Of Short-Lived Radioactive Waste Repository
author: David Dalton
text: SKB announces start of six-year project at Forsmark facility
Work to extend Sweden’s final repository for short-lived radioactive waste has begun with blasting 45 metres below ground, nuclear fuel management company SKB said.
The blasting marked the start of the six-year extension project at the at Forsmark facility, north of Stockholm in the east of the country.

The facility needs to be extended to accommodate decommissioning waste from Sweden’s six nuclear power plants, including three units at the nearby Forsmark station. The extension was approved by the government in December 2021.
The facility began operations in 1988. It has a final disposal capacity of about 63,000 cubic metres of waste, but SKB applied in December 2014 to triple that to about 200,000 cubic metres.
In 2019 the Swedish Radiation Safety Authority recommended approval of SKB’s application to extend the facility.

The Forsmark repository is part of SKB’s final repository system, which is one of Sweden’s most extensive environmental protection projects. It is used for short-lived operational waste from Swedish nuclear power plants and radioactive waste from medical care, industry and research.
SKB has also begun construction of a final repository for spent nuclear fuel at Forsmark and an encapsulation plant in Oskarshamn.
The construction of the repository, at Forsmark in Östhammar municipality, will take 10 years before deposition can begin, SKB said, after which the repository will be gradually expanded.
The facility needs to be extended to accommodate decommissioning waste from Sweden’s six nuclear power plants. Courtesy SKB.

title: High Cost Of Capital Remains Major Problem For Nuclear Industry, Says European Group
author: Rachel Rigby
text: Brussels-based Nucleareurope says financing a challenge, but bloc needs efficiency and stability of reactors

Despite low running costs once a reactor is built, the high cost of capital remains “a very big problem” for the European nuclear industry and for nuclear construction on the continent, according to Jessica Johnson, communications and advocacy director of Brussels-based nuclear industry trade association NuclearEurope.

Johnson told NucNet in an interview on 23 January that while the “financing of all large infrastructure projects is challenging”, this was particularly the case in new nuclear construction due to the “high upfront costs.”

The high initial costs of nuclear energy are particularly impacted not just by state funding, but by the rate of interest that nuclear operators borrow at from private investors, Johnson said. If reactor developers “have to borrow at high costs, that impacts profits”.
However, once new reactors are in operation, they tend to operate very efficiently, in contrast to renewable generation assets such as wind and solar, Jonson emphasised.
For instance, many nuclear power stations globally run at a capacity factor of over 90%, while solar and wind generation are in no way comparable in terms of reliability and efficiency, she said.

Johnson added that this efficiency is demonstrated by the large levels of nuclear electricity exports from France, a country in which nuclear power comprises around 75% of the electricity mix, to neighbouring countries, including Belgium, Germany and Luxembourg. France exported 35% of the extra energy it produced from nuclear power in 2024 to surrounding countries, Johnson said. Nuclear comprises around 25% of the European power mix at present, according to Johnson.

She noted that statistics from the Organisation of Economic Cooperation and Development’s Nuclear Energy Agency indicated that, as reactors are now able to operate for 60 to 80 years, and potentially even for 100 years, nuclear power was one of the lowest cost forms of power generation. The exceptionally long life expectancy for a nuclear reactor stands in contrast to an average life expectancy of around 25 years for a solar energy plant.

However, despite these efficiencies, cost of construction remains a challenge for the industry. For instance, the 1,650-MW Flamanville-3 EPR reactor now entering service in northern France is around 12 years behind its construction schedule and its €13bn ($13.6bn) cost is around four times more than the original estimate.

Similarly, the two EPR, 3,400-MW Hinkley Point C nuclear plant being bult in southwest England is over a decade behind schedule and at least three times over its initially planned budget. The first unit at that plant is now scheduled to begin commercial operation in late 2029, at the earliest, according to EDF.

Johnson said that in order to mitigate some of the costs of nuclear construction and the cost of money for such construction, nuclear generation has been recognised as a sustainable energy source in the European Union’s sustainable finance taxonomy.

While not providing funding directly to the industry, the taxonomy classifies various power sources as being sustainable energy sources, thus making them more likely to receive private green energy funding, such as green bonds, at lower rates of interest compared to the rates offered to other energy sources.
“In order to get lower interest rates, it was agreed that nuclear has to be seen as a sustainable renewable energy source in the taxonomy,” Johnson said.

There has been “too much focus” on the environmental benefits of renewable generation sources, Johnson said, adding: “If you look at the life cycle of nuclear and how much carbon dioxide is emitted per megawatt,” based on the life cycles of French reactors, only four grammes of carbon dioxide is emitted per megawatt hour and “production emissions from nuclear are zero”, according to Johnson.

She also emphasised that nuclear energy “brings stability to the power grid, especially when bringing renewables on board,” meaning that nuclear energy often serves as a low carbon source of baseload power to complement intermittent renewable generation assets such as wind turbines or solar farms, the effective operation of which is subject to weather conditions.
File photo of construction of Europe’s newest nuclear power plant, the Flamanville-3 EPR in France. Courtesy EDF.

title: General Atomics Completes ‘Significant Tests’ On Nuclear Fuel For Space Missions
author: David Dalton
text: Key work carried out in collaboration with Nasa

US-based General Atomics Electromagnetic Systems (GA-EMS) has successfully completed several significant tests to advance the development of nuclear thermal propulsion reactor technology for cislunar transportation and deep space missions, including human missions to Mars.
The company said the tests were at carried out at Nasa’s Marshall Space Flight Center in Alabama.

The tests were conducted in collaboration with Nasa to verify the ability of the GA-EMS nuclear fuel to meet the high-performance specifications required to withstand the extreme operational conditions expected in space.

GA-EMS said it executed several high-impact tests. The nuclear fuel was tested with hot hydrogen flow through the samples and subjected to six thermal cycles that rapidly ramped-up to a peak temperature of 2,600 Kelvin or 4,220° Fahrenheit (2,326° Celsius).
Each cycle included a 20-minute hold at peak performance to demonstrate the effectiveness of shielding the fuel material from erosion and degradation by the hot hydrogen.
Additional tests were performed with varying protective features to provide further data on how different material enhancements improve performance under reactor-like conditions.

Christina Back, vice-president of GA-EMS Nuclear Technologies and Materials, said: “We’ve also conducted tests in a non-hydrogen environment at our GA-EMS laboratory, which confirmed the fuel performed exceptionally well at temperatures up to 3,000 Kelvin, which would enable the nuclear thermal propulsion system to be two-to-three times more efficient than conventional chemical rocket engines.”
Tests on the nuclear thermal propulsion reactor technology were carried out in collaboration with Nasa. Courtesy General Atomics.

title: TVA Announces Plans For Initial Evaluation And Design Of Clinch River SMR
author: David Dalton
text: Company says it will use ‘integrated project delivery’ approach

Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA) will work with Bechtel and Sargent & Lundy to support initial planning and evaluation for the first GE Hitachi (GEH) small modular reactor (SMR) at TVA’s Clinch River nuclear site in Oak Ridge, Tennessee.

Bechtel and Sargent & Lundy will work with GEH and TVA to plan, design, and potentially procure, construct and commission the first GEH BWRX-300 SMR at Clinch River, with operation tentatively scheduled for 2033.
Clinch River is a 370-hectare site in Roane County for which TVA holds the nation’s only early site permit from the Nuclear Regulatory Commission.

During an initial validation phase the companies will work together develop the potential Clinch River SMR’s cost estimate and schedule. The validation phase is expected to be completed within one to two years.

TVA said the team will be using an “integrated project delivery” (IPD) approach for the Clinch River project. This is a delivery approach where all key stakeholders, including the owner, architect, engineer, and contractor, collaborate closely throughout the design and construction phases, sharing risks and rewards under a single contract. The aim is to optimise efficiency by maximising everyone’s expertise and involvement.
TVA said the aim of the IPD approach is to “align all parties in a unified plan”. It said the model “incentivises the parties involved to stay on budget and on time”.

According to TVA, the IPD approach has not been used for major nuclear projects, although OPG has used it for generation projects and is using it for its planned BWRX-300 SMR at Darlington in Ontario, Canada.
TVA is a federally owned power company which owns and operates the Sequoyah and Watts Bar nuclear stations in Tennessee and the Browns Ferry nuclear station in Alabama.

It announced earlier this week that it was leading a consortium of government and industry leaders that is applying for an $800m (€775m) US Department of Energy grant to accelerate the Clinch River project.
TVA is already working closely with GEH, OPG and Poland’s Synthos Green Energy through a technology collaboration agreement signed in 2023 that will develop the standard design for the BWRX-300.
TVA is planning to operate the first GEH BWRX-300 SMR at Clinch River around 2033. Courtesy GEH.

title: Ontario Gov’t Approves OPG Plan For Initial Phase Of Pickering Refurbishment
author: David Dalton
text: Contract worth €1.4 billion signed for early engineering and procurement

The Ontario government has approved Ontario Power Generation’s (OPG) plan to proceed with the project definition phase, the next step towards refurbishing four units at the Pickering nuclear power station to secure more power and create thousands of jobs across the province.

As part of the preparation for refurbishment, the government said it has authorised OPG to sign a CAD2.1bn ($1.46bn, €1.4bn) contract with CanAtom, a joint venture of Aecon and AtkinsRéalis, for early engineering and procurement to prepare for the execution of the retube feeder and boiler replacement programme.

Once refurbished, Pickering would produce more than 2,000 MW of electricity, equivalent to powering two million homes, to help meet increasing demand, driven by electrification and the province’s surging economic growth.
Based on OPG’s preliminary schedule, the refurbishment is anticipated to be completed by the mid-2030s.

The Conference Board of Canada, an independent research organisation, projects the full refurbishment project would create 11,000 jobs per year while contributing CAD19.4bn to Ontario’s GDP over 11 years.

OPG is planning to refurbish Units 5, 6, 7 and 8 at Pickering, the only plants remaining in operation at the facility. The move marks a major turnaround for the station, which was scheduled to close by 2025.
Units 2 and 3 were permanently shut down in 2007 and 2008 and Units 1 and 4 were taken offline in 2024.
OPG is planning to refurbish Units 5, 6, 7 and 8 at the Pickering nuclear station. Courtesy OPG.

title: Swedish Company To Break Ground On Non-Nuclear Test Reactor At Oskarshamn
author: David Dalton
text: Landmark ‘a major step for Swedish nuclear innovation’, says Blykalla
Sweden-based small modular reactor (SMR) developer Blykalla will break ground next month on its advanced reactor test facility at the Oskarshamn nuclear site to the south of Stockholm.
This test site will host a non-nuclear electrical reactor that is being developed by Blykalla and European energy giant Uniper in collaboration with engineering company ABB.
Blykalla said the landmark is a major step for Swedish nuclear innovation and “puts us at the forefront of advanced nuclear technology in Europe”.
Ground will formally be broken at a ceremony on 3 February by deputy prime minister and minister for energy, business, and industry Ebba Busch.

Busch has been a strong advocate of nuclear energy. The current government, which took office last year led by the conservative Moderate Party, in coalition with the Liberals and the Christian Democrats, has taken a number of measures to remove barriers and create better conditions for new nuclear power.
The SMR pilot facility, which will not use nuclear fuel, will test proof of concept before expanding to future plants.
Blykalla’s Sealer SMR plant uses liquid lead cooling and has what the company said are unique safety elements and proprietary innovations.
The company said the plant is “a perfect complement” to intermittent energy sources and can provide the baseload energy needed for a full transition to a fossil free future.
Lead-cooled nuclear plants are not yet operating, but are being developed as next-generation, or Generation IV, reactors.
Lead has a very high boiling temperature of 1,749°C which means the problem of coolant boiling is for all practical purposes eliminated.
This brings with it important safety advantages that also result in design simplification and improved economic performance.
Blykalla is developing the Sealer SMR plant, which uses liquid lead for cooling. Courtesy Blykalla.

title: New York Blueprint Says Advanced Nuclear Is Attractive, But ‘A Host Of Questions’ Remain To Be Answered
author: David Dalton
text: Document published as state governor unveils plans for responsible reactor masterplan

A blueprint for the deployment of advanced nuclear technologies in New York says nuclear offers attractive possibilities, but warns there are “a host of questions” to be answered regarding technological readiness, environmental and climate justice, waste, cost and cost risks.

The blueprint, published by the New York State Energy Research and Development Authority (Nyserda), says advanced nuclear power plants offer scalability, economic development, low land use, advanced operational and safety features, and potential applications for process heat for industry.

But it warns on cost, noting that nuclear plants in the US “have a long history of substantial cost overruns”. It says the most recent commercial reactors to be completed, the two AP1000 units at Vogtle in Georgia, were originally estimated to cost $13bn (€12bn), but eventually cost $32bn, with a seven-year delay.
According to the blueprint, an analysis of the cost overruns at Vogtle identified some best practices that were not followed, especially emphasising pre-project planning and project management.

Other factors were the bankruptcy of Vogtle’s initial engineering, procurement and construction contractor, Westinghouse, due to the fixed-price nature of its contract and increased accrual of interest during construction as delays mounted.

The blueprint says concerns about cost overruns have also affected newer technologies such as small modular reactors (SMRs). Utah Associated Municipal Power Systems withdrew from a deal with NuScale to construct six SMRs after overnight capital costs nearly quadrupled from an initial estimate of approximately $5,000/kW to over $20,000/kW.

The blueprint says the timing for development of advanced nuclear technologies will depend on the time for plant designs and construction capabilities to progress, the development of supply chains, and the successful demonstration of facilities to satisfy safety, performance, and scalability considerations.

It notes: “New York has the opportunity to participate in the national activities that are designed to lead to technology demonstrations and supply chain development, which may involve the cultivation of local labour forces and supply chain niches.”
The blueprint is part of proposals announced by New York state governor Kathy Hochul to develop a masterplan for “responsible advanced nuclear development” in New York.
New York also announced that it will help lead a multi-state consortium on nuclear energy focused on driving down costs and risk-sharing.

The blueprint was released as New York state and power company Constellation said they are working on a joint grant proposal to the US Department of Energy to support Constellation’s efforts to seek an early site permit from the Nuclear Regulatory Commission for one or more advanced nuclear reactors at the existing Nine Mile Point nuclear site in Oswego, New York.

The proposal will be filed by Constellation and Nyserda, a public-benefit corporation that offers information, technical expertise and funding aimed at helping New York increase energy efficiency, save money, use renewable energy, and reduce its reliance on fossil fuels.

If granted, the DOE funding would be used to pursue an early site permit at Nine Mile Point, which already has two operational large-scale boiling water reactor units that went online in 1969 and 1988. A decision on the funding is expected in early summer.

Constellation said an early site permit from the NRC approves a site for future development of a nuclear power plant. The permit is valid for 10 to 20 years, and the company can apply for a construction and operating license at any time during the permit period.
Baltimore, Maryland-based Constellation has the largest nuclear fleet in the US with 21 nuclear power plants at 15 sites*.
* Braidwood, Byron, Calvert Cliffs, Clinton, Crane (formerly Three Mile Island), Dresden, FitzPatrick, LaSalle, Limerick, Nine Mile Point, Peach Bottom, Quad Cities, Ginna, Salem and South Texas.
Constellation wants to build one or more advanced nuclear reactors at the existing Nine Mile Point nuclear site in Oswego, New York. Courtesy Constellation.

title: Primary System Flushing Begins At China’s Tianwan-7 Nuclear Plant
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Two Russia-designed VVER-1200 units under construction at site
Flushing of the primary cooling system has begun at the Tianwan-7 nuclear power plant under construction in Jiangsu province, eastern China, according to Russia’s state nuclear corporation Rosatom.

The operation involves pumping demineralised water through the circuits – including the active and passive safety system – to remove construction debris. It is the last step in installing the primary system.
Rosatom said the next stage will be assembly of the reactor system for the VVER-1200 pressurised water reactor (PWR) plant.
The reactor pressure vessel was hoisted into place in October 2023, while welding of the main circulation pipeline was completed in November 2024.
There are two Russia-designed VVER-1200 Generation III+ PWR units under construction at Tianwan. Construction of Tianwan-7 began in May 2021 and Tianwan-8 in February 2022.
According to Rosatom, after reactor assembly, other commissioning milestones will include cold and hot functional testing. However, the statement did not give an expected timeframe.
The Tianwan station has another six PWR units in commercial operation. Units 1 to 4 were built by Russia using its VVER-1000 PWR technology. Units 5 and 6 are China’s indigenous CNP-1000 PWR design.
There are two Russia-designed VVER-1200 units under construction at Tianwan. Courtesy Rosatom.

title: France’s Orano Files Second Arbitration Procedure Over Niger Uranium Crackdown
author: David Dalton
text: Litigation is company’s ‘last possible recourse’
French nuclear fuel cycle company Orano is lodging a second arbitration procedure against Niger following the loss of operational control of the Somair uranium mine.
Orano said it has filed its request for arbitration with the International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes.
“This litigation is now Orano’s last possible recourse, after several attempts at amicable resolution have gone unanswered,” Orano said in a statement on 21 January.

Orano said the West African country’s obstruction of the commercialisation of production, and the suppression of Orano's offtake rights, have “only aggravated Somair’s financial situation and the prejudice suffered by Orano”.
Orano announced in October it would be halting its uranium production in Niger, citing a “highly deteriorated” situation and its inability to operate.
Earlier this year, Orano said a July 2023 coup in Niger led to a halt in imports of critical materials necessary for uranium exploitation at Somair, such as soda ash, carbonate, nitrates and sulphur.
According to Orano, Somair is the only uranium mine in commercial operation in Niger.
Orano said in December it had begun arbitration proceedings against Niger after its licence to operate at the Imouraren uranium deposit was withdrawn in June.
The Nigerien government, whose leader Abdourahamane Tiani seized power in the coup, had previously made clear it would overhaul rules regulating the mining of raw materials by foreign companies.

The nation’s military rulers have turned their backs on Paris, Niger’s former colonial ruler, ordering French troops deployed there to leave and instead forging ties with fellow juntas in Burkina Faso and Mali – as well as Iran and Russia.
Orano’s Imouraren uranium mining site in Niger. Courtesy Orano.

title: Spanish Nuclear Group Warns Against Almaraz Shutdown, Calls For Dialogue With Ministry
author: David Dalton
text: Foro Nuclear says closure of two reactors will hit bills for households and businesses

The permanent closure of the Almaraz power station in central Spain would have a “very significant and direct negative impact” on the economy and employment in the region as well as resulting in higher electricity bills for households and businesses, industry group Foro Nuclear has warned.
Madrid-based Foro Nuclear said the planned closure would “negatively affect the entire energy sector in Spain”, reducing supply and worsening grid stability.
It called for a dialogue with the Ministry for Ecological Transition and the Demographic Challenge to “jointly analyse the situation”.
The group made the comments following demonstrations against the closure at the weekend.
Foro Nuclear said it is “aware of and fully understands the existing concern about the negative impact that the closure of the Almaraz nuclear power station would have”.
Legislation approved in 2020 means Almaraz-1 is scheduled to shut down permanently in 2027 and Almaraz-2 in 2028.

Foro Nuclear said that in the current global geopolitical context, and especially in Europe, where nuclear energy has been recognised in the green taxonomy, almost all industrialised countries are choosing to expand their nuclear fleets.

This is because of nuclear energy’s “enormous strategic value” as a firm, reliable energy source with no CO2 emissions, which increases the stability of the system and “contains the rise in electricity bills”, Foro Nucler said.

It said countries backing nuclear include the US, France, the UK, Sweden, Switzerland, the Netherlands and Belgium. Germany, which has phased out all nuclear generation, is experiencing “the negative effects” of its decision, Foro Nuclear said.
Foro Nuclear also repeated its position that nuclear energy has endured an asphyxiating increase in fiscal pressure over the last five years.

It said the specific tax burden borne by the nuclear fleet has increased by 70% in this period, going from €16/MWh to €28/MWh. This discriminates against nuclear generation compared to other technologies and makes its economic viability unsustainable, Foro Nuclear said.

In October, the group confirmed it had filed a legal challenge with the country’s top court against a 30% increase of the nuclear waste levy, with the main operators of the country’s nuclear plants moving to join the fight.
The Almaraz nuclear power station is about 200 km southwest of Madrid in the landlocked region of Extremadura.
Almaraz-1 is a 1,011 MW pressurised water reactor (PWR) unit that began commercial operation in 1983. Almaraz-2 is a 1,006-MW PWR that began commercial operation in 1984.

Foro Nuclear said recently that Spain’s fleet of seven commercial nuclear power plants generated just over 52 TWh net of electricity in 2024, accounting for 19.57% of the country’s total net electricity production.

The figure was down from 57.2 TWh in 2023. However, with a net installed capacity of 7,117 MW – significantly less than another other energy source and accounting for only 5.44% of the total – nuclear energy ranked as the second-largest source of electricity production in Spain, according to provisional data from Red Eléctrica analysed by Foro Nuclear.

In December, Spanish authorities said they had granted a lifetime extension to the single-unit Trillo nuclear power station, in the central Guadalajara region, allowing operations to continue for 10 more years. Trillo will now be able to operate commercially until 16 November 2034.
The Almaraz nuclear power station is about 200 km southwest of Madrid in the landlocked region of Extremadura. Courtesy Foro Nuclear.

title: Ukraine Committee Approves Plan To Buy Reactor Equipment From Bulgaria For Khmelnitski Completion
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Key components from Russia were for Belene nuclear project, which Sofia dropped in 2023

The energy committee of Ukraine’s parliament has voted in favour of a draft bill that will allow state-owned nuclear champion Energoatom to buy reactor equipment from Bulgaria for the potential completion of the Khmelnitski-3 and -4 nuclear plants, construction of which is currently suspended.

The bill, published on the parliament’s official portal, said Energoatom is granted “permission to conclude a contract” with Bulgaria’s state-owned energy company NEK for the purchase of reactor pressure vessels and related equipment necessary for the “future construction” of the two Khmelnitski units.
Energoatom will also be allowed to negotiate contract conditions, make payments in accordance with contractual terms and store the equipment, the bill said.
Bulgarian officials have said they would want no less than €600m ($618m) for the two-unit reactor equipment, which is stored at the planned Belene nuclear station site in northern Bulgaria.

Bulgaria received equipment for two VVER-1000 pressurised water reactor (PWR) units, including two reactor pressure vessel and steam generator sets, from Russia for the Belene project in 2018 after settling a Russian compensation claim to the International Court of Arbitration in 2016 for €620m resulting from the cancellation of the project in 2012.
In July 2023, Bulgaria’s parliament asked the country’s energy minister to begin negotiations on the proposed sale of the equipment to Ukraine.
Parliament said that the price from a possible sale should not be lower than €601.6m, which was the nominal compensation payment Bulgaria paid to Russia.

The Belene project was born at the end of Bulgaria’s socialist period, but abandoned in the early 1990s. The project was formally revived in 2008, then cancelled in 2012, only to be revived again in 2018. However, Bulgaria failed to find investors and the project was suspended again in 2021 and finally dropped in 2023.
Two VVER-1000 units at Khmelnitski-3 and -4 in western Ukraine were abandoned in 1990 in the aftermath of the 1986 Chernobyl accident in Soviet Ukraine and because of financial shortages.
According to Energoatom, Khmelnitski-3 is around 75% complete and Khmelnitski-4 about 28%.
There are already two Russia-supplied VVER plants at the site that began operation in 1988 and 2005.

The company had planned to complete the units and also build new Westinghouse-supplied plants at the site even before the war with Russia began in February 2022. There had been attempts to revive the project in the early 2010s.

Both Bulgaria and Ukraine are looking to refocus their nuclear new-build ambitions by considering the deployment of Westinghouse-made AP1000 PWR units. The proposed completion of Khmelnitski will probably see the last Russia-designed reactors to be deployed in Ukraine.

Sources have said that it is unclear what part of the equipment purchased from Bulgaria could actually be used and to what extent at Khmelnitski-3 and -4 given the current level of construction progress and the several decades of inactivity and suspension.
UKraine is plannung to complete two unifnished nuclear plants at the Khmelnitski site. Courtesy Energoatom.

title: France’s Orano Signs $1.6 Billion Agreement To Develop And Operate Mongolia Uranium Mine
author: David Dalton
text: Ulaanbaatar positioning itself as ‘strategic player and significant contributor in global climate effort’

France’s nuclear fuel cycle company Orano has signed a $1.6bn (€1.5bn) investment agreement for the development and operation of the Zuuvch-Ovoo uranium mine in Mongolia’s southeastern Dornogovi province.

The agreement, signed in the Mongolian capital Ulaanbaatar on 17 January, has been ratified by the government after being put before the Mongolian parliament. Orano said it marks 27 years of “presence and partnership” in Mongolia.

Under the terms of the agreement, Badrakh Energy, a joint venture between Orano and Mongolia’s state-owned MonAtom Group, will be responsible for the industrial operation of the major Zuuvch-Ovoo and Dulaan Uul/Umnut deposits, which have estimated uranium resources of close to 90,000 tonnes of uranium (tU).
With a 30-year estimated lifespan, the project represents an initial investment of around $500m before the deposit comes on stream, and a total of $1.6bn over the mine's lifetime, Orano said.
Development of the project is planned to take four years, after which the Zuuvch-Ovoo mine will go into production, with an estimated nominal capacity of around 2,500 tU per year.
With uranium demand set to be strong in the coming decades, Mongolia is positioning itself as a strategic player and a significant contributor in the global climate effort, Orano said.
In December Mongolia said it had reached a preliminary agreement with Orano to develop the Zuuvch-Ovoo uranium mine.
Orano is a major uranium producer with mines in Canada, Kazakhstan and Niger.
In October 2023 the company signed a protocol that it said paved the way for the mining of uranium in Mongolia.

France’s president Emmanuel Macron has said Mongolia would supply critical metals including uranium to France as Paris seeks to secure supplies for the country’s nuclear fleet and an ambitious programme of new-build.

France imports most of its uranium from Niger, Australia and Kazakhstan. Orano recently began arbitration proceedings against Niger after its licence to operate at the Imouraren uranium deposit was withdrawn by a ruling junta that took power in a July 2023 coup.
According to the Nuclear Energy Agency, Mongolia is not producing any uranium, but several mines are in the planning stage of development.

Uranium production in Mongolia started with the operation of the Dornod open-pit mine in the Mardai-gol district in the east of the country in 1989. Ore was transported by rail to Russia for processing, but because of political and economic changes in Mongolia and neighbouring areas of Russia, uranium production at Erdes was terminated in 1995.
Mongolia does not have nuclear generating capacity, but has signalled an interest in the use of small and medium-sized reactors, the agency said.
The Zuuvch-Ovoo uranium mine in Mongolia’s southeastern Dornogovi province. Courtesy Orano.

title: Share Of Deliveries To Western Nuclear Firms Via Trans-Caspian Route Over 60%, Says Kazatomprom
author: David Dalton
text: Company also announces increased uranium sales to Americas

The share of deliveries to western nuclear power facilities via the Trans-Caspian International Transport Route reached 64% in 2023, Kazakhstan’s state nuclear company Kazatomprom said in a 15 January statement outlining its development strategy for 2025-2034.
The share of deliveries via the route for the first half of 2023 was 58% and Kazatomprom had been hoping it would reach about 70% for the whole year.
The route, known as the TITR, offers an alternative through Azerbaijan and Georgia while Russian ports and transport routes are under sanctions due to the war in Ukraine.
It has been used as an alternative route since 2018 and “helps to mitigate the risk of the primary route being unavailable, for any reason”, according to Kazatomprom.

The primary route goes through the Russian port of St Petersburg. The TITR was developed before the Russian invasion of Ukraine because St Petersburg was temporarily unavailable to some nuclear material when the city was to host football matches as part of the 2018 FIFA World Cup competition.
Kazatomprom, the world’s largest producer of uranium with about 20% of global production, has since maintained the TITR and has used it for several shipments.

The company also said it had significantly expanded its geographical reach and sales portfolio, adding six new countries to its client base since 2018 – Brazil, Sweden, Spain, Argentina, Romania and the United Arab Emirates.
Its share of uranium sales to the Americas increased from 16% in 2018 to 26% in 2023.
Kazatomprom said it will increase its focus on uranium mining as its core business as it seeks to expand its footprint in the nuclear fuel cycle.
The company said efforts would be concentrated on “replenishment and efficient use of resource base”.
It said that in recent years it had transformed its uranium sales strategy by limiting sales to intermediaries and establishing its own trading arm.

“The growing importance of nuclear energy has become an integral part of global green energy policies, significantly strengthening fundamental dynamics of the uranium market, which are now stronger than ever,” Kazatomprom said.
In November 2024, Kazatomprom said its third-quarter pretax profit more than doubled as the result of significantly higher uranium spot prices and volumes sold.
It reported a pretax profit of 222.08 billion Kazakh tenge ($441m, €417m), compared with 99.25 billion tenge it booked in the same period last year. Revenue rose 78% to 437.73 billion tenge.

title: Spain’s Nuclear Fleet Generated Over 52 TWh Of Electricity In 2024
author: David Dalton
text: Output from reactors shows need for guarantee of supply

Spain’s fleet of seven commercial nuclear power plants generated just over 52 TWh net of electricity in 2024, accounting for 19.57% of the country’s total net electricity production, Madrid-based nuclear industry group Foro Nuclear said.

The figure was down from 57.2 TWh in 2023. However, with a net installed capacity of 7,117 MW – significantly less than another other energy source and accounting for only 5.44% of the total – nuclear energy ranked as the second-largest source of electricity production in Spain, according to provisional data from Red Eléctrica analysed by Foro Nuclear.
Wind was first in terms of generation, accounting for 22.89% of production, but with a 24% share of installed capacity.

Foro Nuclear said that once again, nuclear energy was the technology with the highest equivalent full-power operating hours with a load factor of 83.27%. In 2024, nuclear plants generated electricity for 7,314 hours out of the year’s 8,784 hours.
“This constant production reflects the guarantee of supply offered by nuclear energy day after day and year after year,” said Foro Nuclear president Ignacio Araluce.

“The electrical system needs stable baseload sources with consistent production, like nuclear, which provides stability, robustness, and firm capacity to the grid, regardless of external conditions,” Araluce added.

The Spanish government’s energy and climate plan specifies that installed nuclear capacity will remain at current levels until at least 2025, but will be reduced to just over 3,000 MW from 2030 onwards.
The Almaraz nuclear power station in Spain. The country has a fleet of seven commercial nuclear plants. Courtesy Foro Nuclear.

title: Sweden Begins Construction Of Final Repository For Spent Nuclear Fuel
author: David Dalton
text: Two years of surface work underway at Forsmark site
Sweden has begun construction of a final deep geologic repository for spent nuclear fuel, where highly radioactive waste will be stored for 100,000 years.

The construction of the repository, at Forsmark in Östhammar municipality, will take 10 years before deposition can begin, nuclear fuel management company SKB said, after which the repository will be gradually expanded.

Two years of surface work will now begin, including the construction of rock storage and water treatment facilities, a canister bridge over the cooling water canal and forest clearance. After that, rock work will begin down into the bedrock.
In October, SKB received an environmental permit to build and operate the repository at Forsmark and a related encapsulation facility at Oskarshamn.
The permit was issued by the Land and Environmental Court, which also granted SKB an order allowing initial work at both sites to start.
In January 2022, the Swedish government approved plans to build the repository and encapsulation facility.
That approval allowed SKB to take final steps and preparations for initial construction.

SKB’s plan is for spent nuclear fuel to be encapsulated in copper and nodular cast iron at the encapsulation facility in Oskarshamn before being transported to the final repository close to the Forsmark nuclear power station, about 140 km north of Stockholm.
When fully developed, some time in the 2080s, the repository will comprise around 60 km of tunnels with space for more than 6,000 canisters of spent fuel.
Sweden already operates a repository for shorter-lived radioactive waste at Forsmark, which opened in 1988 and extends to a depth of 50 metres below the seabed of the Baltic.

An application to extend this repository was submitted in 2014 and granted by the government in December 2021, following approval by nuclear regulator SSM and the Land and Environment Court, as well as the municipality of Ӧsthammar.
SKB has put the remaining costs for the country’s radioactive waste programme at around $11bn (€10bn).

The licensees of Swedish nuclear power plants take responsibility for all costs for programme, which includes decommissioning and demolition of the power plants, as well as the handling and final disposal of the nuclear waste and used nuclear fuel.

In 1980, Swedes voted to phase out nuclear power, but increased demand for energy and the need to address climate change led to a change of tack and in 2010 parliament agreed to the continued operation of existing reactors as well as leaving open the option of their eventual replacement.

Prime minister Ulf Kristersson has said Sweden will begin construction on a new nuclear power plant before the country’s next legislative election in 2026 as it pushes ahead with ambitious plans to increase nuclear capacity..
The government said in November 2023 it wanted to increase nuclear power production equivalent to two nuclear reactors by 2035, with a “massive expansion” to follow by 2045.

Sweden has six commercial reactors in operation at three nuclear stations: two at Ringhals, three at Forsmark and one at Oskarshamn. In January 2021, Ringhals-1 became the fourth commercial nuclear reactor to close in five years. The others were Ringhals-2, Oskarhamn-1 and Oskarhamn-2.
According to the International Atomic Energy Agency, nuclear generated 28.6% of the country’s electricity in 2023, down from 34% in 2019.
Sweden is one of only two countries to begin construction of a final repository. A similar facility for used fuel is being built at Olkiluoto in Finland.
The Finnish government granted a construction licence for that project in November 2015 and construction work on the repository started a year later.
When fully developed the repository will comprise around 60 km of tunnels with space for more than 6,000 canisters of spent fuel. Courtesy SKB.
Sweden’s environment minister Romina Pourmokhtari marks the start of construction at the repository at Forsmark. Courtesy Frida Karlsson/SKB.

title: Fermi Energia Begins Planning Process For Two BWRX-300 Nuclear Plants In Estonia
author: David Dalton
text: ‘Extensive evaluation’ of possible reactor sites to focus on two areas in north of country

Estonia-based nuclear development company Fermi Energia has submitted an application to begin a state planning process for a 600 MW nuclear power station, with the start of construction scheduled for 2031, potentially at one of two sites in the north of the country.

The company called the move “a significant step forward” in Estonia’s energy infrastructure development. It said the application was submitted to the Estonian Ministry of Economic Affairs and Communications.
Fermi Energia chief executive officer Kalev Kallemets said the process, known as a state spatial plan, is essential for identifying the best location for a nuclear plant.
“While initiating this planning process doesn’t guarantee construction, it establishes the foundation for future decision-making,” Kallemets said.
He said recent trends in electricity consumption underscore the Baltic state’s need for reliable, controllable energy capacity to ensure system stability and maintain competitive electricity prices.

The municipal councils of Viru-Nigula country and Luganuse county have formally agreed to participate in the spatial planning process with both areas possible sites. Viru-Nigula and Luganuse are near Estonia’s northern coast.
Fermi Energia said that over the past six years, it has demonstrated its commitment to community involvement by conducting more than 50 information sessions.
The company said its plan for nuclear is divided into three main phases: site pre-selection, site confirmation and construction.
Site pre-selection is scheduled to run from 2025-2027, site confirmation from 2027-2029 and construction from 2031-2035.
Site pre-selection will see a comprehensive evaluation of potential locations with the focus on areas near Kunda in Viru-Nigula county and Aa village in Luganuse county.
Fermi Energia said it plans to submit a construction permit application in 2029 with the start of construction targeted for 2031 and operation by the second half of 2035.
Fermi Energia plans to deploy two GE Hitachi BWRX-300 small modular reactors (SMRs), designed to meet Estonia's minimum baseload electricity requirements.
The company said this nuclear capacity will complement existing renewable energy sources, particularly during periods of low wind and solar generation.

It said the choice of the BWRX-300 technology choice has been further validated by the imminent construction start of a BWRX-300 SMR plant at the existing Darlington nuclear power station site Canada. Ontario Power Generation is planning for plants for the site.
Estonia has no nuclear power plants, but its climate strategy includes plans for up to four SMRs with the first to be operational around 2035.
Fermi Energia said it plans to submit a construction permit application for the two BWRX-300 plants in 2029. Courtesy Fermi Energia.
Fermi Energia plans to deploy two GE Hitachi BWRX-300 small modular reactors in Estonia. Courtesy Fermi Energia.

title: New York Company Completes Acquisition Of Major Assets Of Bankrupt Nuclear Startup
author: David Dalton
text: $8.5 million deal includes Ultra Safe’s patented micro modular reactor system

US nuclear company Nano Nuclear Energy has closed an $8m (€7.7m) deal to acquire the major assets of the bankrupt Ultra Safe Nuclear Corporation (USNC), a midsize startup that is developing microreactor technology and advanced nuclear fuel.
New York-based Nano, which is developing its Zeus and Odin microreactors, has acquired select nuclear energy technology assets from USNC and certain of its subsidiaries.
The acquired assets include USNC’s patented Micro Modular Reactor (MMR) system, along with all associated patents and other intellectual property rights.
Nano Nuclear said in a statement that the acquisition brings important demonstration project collaborations related to the MMR system, notably at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign.
Pending Canadian governmental approvals, the acquisition would also bring certain Canadian government relationships and support.

Some of the technology acquired by Nano Nuclear was being used by an affiliate of USNC to develop related technology in the UK. Nano Nuclear said it may be able to explore a potential future licence or acquisition of this technology in the UK, which could be accompanied by government support.
Oak Ridge, Tennessee-headquartered USNC filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy with estimated liabilities shown in court documents of $50m to $100m.
The company said at the time the move signalled a “restructuring phase” through which it would seek to secure new ownership while ensuring uninterrupted operations.
Chapter 11 is a court-supervised bankruptcy code chapter in the US that allows debtors to reorganize or liquidate their assets and liabilities.

The company’s filings in October at the US Bankruptcy Court for the District of Delaware included its key subsidiaries: USNC-Power Ltd, which develops the company’s flagship 5-MW Micro Modular Reactor (MMR) technology; Global First Power Limited (GFP), focused on nuclear project development within Canadian markets; and USNC-Technologies, which leads USNC’s nuclear technology research and development initiatives.

USNC said at the time it would maintain full operational continuity across its projects, including the deployment of its MMR systems in the US and Canada, large-scale production of Triso-based advanced nuclear fuels, and the fulfilment of space and defence projects for multiple US government agencies.

USNC is involved in two MMR high-temperature gas-cooled reactor (HTGR) projects, including the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign’s Grainger College of Engineering project, where USNC had been developing an MMR that would be built and operated by the university as a research and development facility.
The second MMR project is in Canada, where GFP had been spearheading a 15-MW MMR demonstration at Canadian Nuclear Laboratories’ Chalk River site in partnership with Ontario Power Generation.
In August 2022, USNC opened a pilot fuel manufacturing facility in Oak Ridge where it intends to produce the first fuel for testing and qualification for use in the MMR.
In 2023, USNC signed an agreement to study the potential deployment of one or MMR energy systems in the Philippines.

The company has also been collaborating with the US Department of Defense and Nasa on advanced radioisotope-based power production technology, nuclear thermal propulsion systems and advanced materials.
USNC has been involved in MMR high-temperature gas-cooled reactor projects in Canada and the US. Courtesy USNC.

title: Sweden’s Blykalla Announces Partnership To Produce Specialised Nuclear Pumps
author: David Dalton
text: Company is developing Generation IV lead-cooled reactor technology
Sweden-based small modular reactor (SMR) developer Blykalla and German multinational KSB have formed a partnership to develop specialised pumps for Blykalla’s Sealer nuclear power plant technology.

Blykalla said the partnership marks a significant step forward in the development of next-generation nuclear reactors because it contributes to a strong, strategic value chain for industrial development of key components.
Under the collaboration, Blykalla and KSB will design, develop, and manufacture pumps capable of operating in liquid lead environments.
Pumps are one of the most critical components in a liquid lead-cooled reactor, as their operational lifetime impacts the reactor's overall need for maintenance and hence cost-effectiveness.
Blykalla has said it is planning to build an electrical SMR pilot facility near the existing Oskarshamn nuclear power station south of Stockholm.
The SMR pilot facility, which will not use nuclear fuel, will test proof of concept before expanding to future plants.
Blykalla’s Sealer SMR plant uses liquid lead cooling and has what the company said are unique safety elements and proprietary innovations.
The company said the plant is “a perfect complement” to intermittent energy sources and can provide the baseload energy needed for a full transition to a fossil free future.
Lead-cooled nuclear plants are not yet operating, but are being developed as next-generation, or Generation IV, reactors.
Lead has a very high boiling temperature of 1,749°C which means the problem of coolant boiling is for all practical purposes eliminated.
This brings with it important safety advantages that also result in design simplification and improved economic performance.
Blykalla said its Sealer SMR nuclear plant is ‘a perfect complement’ to intermittent energy sources. Courtesy Blykalla.

title: UK Unveils Plans To Use Dedicated Nuclear Plants In Bid To Establish AI And Data Centres ‘Ecosystem’
author: David Dalton
text: First special growth zone will be at Culham, home of the UK Atomic Energy Authority

The UK is planning special districts for constructing data centres and will explore dedicating nuclear energy to the sites as part of a Labour government project to boost technology growth and the ecosystem for artificial intelligence.

The ‘AI Growth Zones’ will include improved access to electricity and easier planning approvals for data centres, the government said. It said the first such zone will be in Culham, home of the UK Atomic Energy Authority, with more to follow. Culham has been the site  of the UK’s fusion energy for over 40 years.
The government said in a statement on 13 January that these zones will also serve as “a testing ground to drive forward research on how sustainable energy like fusion can power our AI ambitions”.
“Artificial intelligence will be unleashed across the UK to deliver a decade of national renewal,” it said.
The AI Growth Zones will speed up planning permission and give companies the energy connections they need to power up AI, the statement added.
The government will form an AI energy council, composed of public and private officials, that will explore powering the data centres with small modular reactors.
The council will directly support the government’s mission to become a clean energy superpower by tapping into technologies like SMRs, the statement said.
The plan is part of a broader set of proposals to harness AI for public services, expand supercomputing projects and attract technical talent to the UK.
The idea of using nuclear reactors for the AI industry has already been discussed.

Last month a thinktank set up by former Labour prime minister Tony Blair said the UK should introduce new ‘AI growth zones’ around the country with simplified planning and environmental permitting applied to new nuclear plants for data centres.

The Tony Blair Institute for Global Change report, Revitalising Nuclear: The UK Can Power AI and Lead the Clean-Energy Transition, said the UK can harness innovative nuclear technologies to power its AI future, help decarbonise its industries and deliver low-cost electricity for its grids.

The UK’s nuclear industry welcomed the Blair report. Tom Greatrex, chief executive of the London-based Nuclear Industry Association, said at the time: “The Tony Blair Institute is right to say that Britain can become a global leader in nuclear energy with a huge opportunity to power the drive for AI, help decarbonise industries and provide clean electricity for the grid.
Several big tech companies, including Amazon, Google and Microsoft and are looking at nuclear plants to power their energy-intensive data centres and AI initiatives.
In December, Facebook parent company Meta said it wants to find developers that can provide nuclear reactors to support electricity demand from the tech company’s data centres and AI business.
Prime minster Keir Starmer said the AI industry “needs a government that is on their side, one that won’t sit back and let opportunities slip through its fingers”.
He said: “And in a world of fierce competition, we cannot stand by. We must move fast and take action to win the global race.”
The government said the first AI Growth Zone will be in Culham, home of the UK Atomic Energy Authority. Courtesy UKAEA.

title: Bill Gates’ Reactor Company Awards Major Contracts For Nuclear Enclosure System
author: David Dalton
text: TerraPower has already broken ground on demonstration plant in Wyoming

TerraPower, the US nuclear technology company founded by Bill Gates, has awarded the major manufacturing contracts for the first Natrium reactor enclosure system, calling the move a major milestone in establishing the advanced nuclear supply chain.

Washington-based TerraPower said the contracts advance the development and construction of the Natrium sodium-cooled fast reactor and represent a significant milestone in the deployment and commercialisation of the US’s first advanced reactor.

TerraPower said Spain-based nuclear equipment manufacturer Equipos Nucleares (Ensa) will produce the reactor head. South Korea’s Doosan Enerbility will supply the core barrel, guard vessel and internal supports for the Natrium reactor and HD Hyundai, also South Korea-based, will manufacture the reactor pressure vessel. Canada-based equipment manufacturer Marmen will build the rotating plug.
The enclosure system, also known as a reactor containment, is a gas-tight shell that contains radioactive material and protects the reactor from external hazards.
TerraPower, founded by Gates in 2008, broke ground in June 2024 for construction of its first commercial Natrium nuclear plant at Kemmerer, where a coal plant is shutting down.

The Natrium is a 345-MW electric sodium-cooled fast reactor with molten salt energy storage technology that can rapidly boost the system’s output to 500 MW for more than five and a half hours, allowing for integration with renewable energy and an overall increase in grid resiliency

A sodium-cooled nuclear reactor is one that uses liquid sodium to dissipate heat. The use of sodium as a cooling agent distinguishes this type of reactor from conventional reactors, which rely on water as a cooling solution.

Compared to water cooled units, sodium-cooled reactors offer two key advantages: greater efficiency, because sodium remains an effective cooling medium at higher temperatures than water; and a lower risk of explosion caused by high pressure, since sodium coolants operate at lower pressures than water.

“The Natrium design is a game-changing technology, and assembling the right team of vendors to construct the first reactor speaks to TerraPower’s commitment to commercialising this technology and ensuring advanced nuclear fulfils its role in addressing surging global energy demand,” said TerraPower president and chief executive officer Chris Levesque.
TerraPower said the Natrium project in Kemmerer is the only advanced reactor project “in the Western Hemisphere” to move from design into construction.
TerraPower is building its first commercial Natrium nuclear plant at Kemmerer, Wyoming, where a coal plant is shutting down. Courtesy TerraPower.
Courtesy TerraPower/Southern Company.

title: Nuclear Boost Sees France’s Electricity Exports Hit Highest Level In 22 Years
author: David Dalton
text: Main driver of success is recovery of reactor production after corrosion problems and maintenance

France’s net electricity exports were the highest in more than 20 years in 2024, boosted by a nuclear fleet that returned to high availability following years of maintenance and modernisation, nuclear society Sfen reported.
Sfen said net electricity exports in 2024 were 89 TWh, of which more than 90% was low-carbon. The 89 TWh surpassed the previous record of 77 TWh set in 2002.
“The French nuclear fleet, following years of maintenance and modernisation, has regained significant availability,” Sfen said.
“With a capacity forecasted to reach 50 gigawatts (GW) by January 2025, nuclear plants have strengthened their contribution to the electrical grid, meeting domestic demand while supporting exports.”
Sfen said: “The main driver of this success is undoubtedly the recovery of French nuclear production, which has returned to a near-optimal level after two years marked by stress corrosion problems.
“With nuclear production estimated at between 358 and 364 TWh in 2024, France has consolidated its leading position in the supply of decarbonised electricity in Europe.”
Sfen said this increase has been supplemented by an increase in renewable energies – wind, solar, and hydroelectric – which have helped to diversify and strengthen the energy supply.
Electricity exports were largely to Germany and Italy, along with the UK, Switzerland and Spain.
The “exceptional performance” can also be explained by a drop in domestic consumption, which was 6% lower than the average for the years 2014-2019, Sfen said.
This was due particularly to better energy efficiency and a slowdown in industrial activity, freeing up a significant share of national production for foreign markets.
Nuclear availability in France fell to a 30-year low in 2022 after stress corrosion problems near welds took a number of reactors offline.
The problems were first discovered at the Civaux nuclear power station December 2021.
In December 2024, France’s flagship nuclear power plant at Flamanville in Normandy was connected to the national grid after a dozen years of delay, state nuclear operator EDF said.

The 1,630-MW EPR unit is France’s 57th commercial nuclear power plant and its most powerful in terms of capacity. France’s share of generation before Flamanville-3 came online was already about 62% – the highest in the world.
France has ambitious plans for new nuclear power plants with EDF aiming to begin preparatory works for a new EPR2 nuclear plant at the existing Penly nuclear site in northern France.
In December 2024, France’s flagship nuclear power plant at Flamanville in Normandy was connected to the national grid. Courtesy EDF.

title: Westinghouse To Continue Development Of Space Microreactor For Nasa
author: David Dalton
text: US space agency aiming for lunar demonstration project within next decade
Nasa has chosen Westinghouse to continue the development of a space microreactor design for a fission reactor that could provide astronauts a reliable power supply for use on the Moon and beyond.

Westinghouse said the project, backed by the US Department of Energy through the federal Fission Surface Power (FSP) programme, will build on the successful design work Westinghouse has already completed on FSP systems.
The company said it aims to begin testing of critical technology elements.
“The continued progress under the FSP project can enable Nasa’s goal of a lunar demonstration within the next decade,” Westinghouse said in a statement.
Nasa’s FSP programme expands on the efforts of the its Kilopower project to develop affordable fission nuclear power technologies for long-duration stays on planetary surfaces.
Nasa is working with the DOE to design a fission power system that would provide up to 40 kW of power – enough to continuously run 30 households for 10 years.
A future lunar demonstration will pave the way for sustainable operations and base camps on the Moon and Mars.

Westinghouse said it is leveraging its eVinci microreactor technology to develop a resilient and mass efficient nuclear electric power and propulsion system for satellite, spacecraft and planetary surface power applications.

The eVinci, which has yet to be deployed, will generate reliable electricity and heating for remote communities, universities, mining operations, industrial centres, data centres, defence facilities, and soon the lunar surface and beyond, Westinghouse said.
Nasa is aiming for a lunar demonstration project for nuclear technology within the next decade. Courtesy Nasa.

title: Poland’s Cabinet Approves €14 Billion Funding For First Nuclear Power Station
author: Kamen Kraev
