Nuclear energy’s workforce in the US is trending older than other energy sources with 60% of the workers aged 30 to 54 – higher than both the wider energy workforce and national average.

According to the 2024 US Energy & Employment Report, which is based on data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics and supplementary surveys of tens of thousands of US energy sector employers, nuclear energy had 23% fewer workers under the age of 30 than the overall energy workforce.
That represents a shift from last year’s report, when the proportion of younger employees in nuclear was on par with other sectors.

The gap between early-career and late-career employment stats means that a significant chunk of the nuclear workforce is likely to retire over the next decade, creating plentiful job opportunities for younger workers who possess the necessary skills and training, the report said.
The report, published by the Department of Energy, warned that employers reported difficulty hiring workers across every industry in the nuclear energy sector.

Roughly 90% of professional and business services employers said they experienced at least some challenges finding qualified workers, despite leading the nuclear field in new hires. Even utilities, which employed three in five nuclear energy workers in 2023, reported hiring challenges.
A pipeline of young talent will be essential as the US nuclear industry seeks to commercialise and deploy next-generation advanced reactors in the coming decades.
Many of these jobs will not require a four-year advanced “Stem” (science, technology, engineering, or mathematics) degree, the report said.
It said the US nuclear energy sector employed 68,008 workers in 2023 across fuels and electric power generation, an increase of more than 1,800 jobs from the previous year.

Eighty-six percent of those jobs were in electric power generation. Jobs increased across five industries. Professional and business services accounted for two-thirds of all workers who entered the nuclear field last year. Utilities remained the largest employer in nuclear energy with 41,000 workers.
Employers reported difficulty hiring workers across every industry in the nuclear energy sector.

title: US Startup Last Energy Raises $40 Million For Ambitious Microreactor Project
author: David Dalton
text: Company wants to mass-manufacture 20 MW nuclear plants that can be built and shipped within 24 months
US nuclear company Last Energy has raised $40m (€36m) in Series B funding, bringing total capital raised to $64m since the company’s founding in 2019.

The Washington based company, which is developing a 20 MW micro-nuclear power plant, said the Series B funding will enable it to continue expanding its team and investing in project development as it works to deploy its first plant, targeting a 2026 online date.
Investors for the round include US-based venture capital firms Gigafund and Autodesk Foundation, and a series of family offices.

Last Energy also announced that it has reached commercial agreements for 80 units. The company said it has “incredibly ambitious” goals, aiming to build 10,000 units in the next 15 years, though to date it has not brought any online.

It said 39 of the 80 units will be built to serve data centre developers. Due to the uniquely intensive energy needs of services like AI and cloud computing, data centres have increasingly invested in nuclear development to ensure they have access to 24/7 clean baseload power, Last Energy said.

It said: “Microreactors offer a significantly higher energy capacity than renewables at a lower cost, with minimal land requirements, and without any of the necessary investments in storage capabilities.”

In April, Last Energy showcased a prototype of its nuclear reactor module at the Data Center World conference in Washington and hosted a demonstration event for industry executives and US policymakers.
The company has plans for two new prototypes, which will be revealed in 2025.

The startup claims that its microreactor is designed to be fabricated, transported, and built within 24 months, and is the right size to serve industrial clients. Under its business model, Last Energy aims to build, own, and operate its power plant at the customer’s site.
A Last Energy plant, referred to as the PWR-20, is comprised of a few dozen modules that snap together like a LEGO kit.
Like an independent power producer, Last Energy will not sell power plants. Instead, it will sell electricity to customers through long-term power-purchase contracts.

Bret Kugelmass, the company’s founder and chief executive officer, said that in the last eight months the company released a new prototype, demonstrated its fabrication and transport capabilities, nearly doubled its headcount, and accelerated commercial growth.
“Closing our Series B was the next step to unlocking key milestones as we continue down the path toward commercial operations.”
Last Energy said it is aiming to build 10,000 nuclear plants in the next 15 years. Courtesy Last Energy.

title: Pilot Fuel Elements For MBIR Research Reactor Pass Acceptance Tests
author: David Dalton
text: Generation IV nuclear unit scheduled for completion in 2026

Pilot fuel elements for the Generation IV MBIR multipurpose fast neutron research reactor under construction in Russia have passed acceptance tests, allowing state nuclear corporation Rosatom researchers to move on to production of fuel for the initial loading of the reactor core.
Rosatom said the pilot fuel elements had been manufactured by researchers in the fuel technology department of the Research Institute of Atomic Reactors (NIIAR), part of its scientific division.

The MBIR is being built at NIIAR, in Dimitrovgrad, southwest Russia, as part of a Russian government programme to develop nuclear science and technology. It is scheduled for completion in 2026 and physical startup for 2027.

The MBIR will primarily use sodium as a coolant and vibro-packed mixed-oxide (VMOX) fuel. VMOX is a Russian variant of MOX fuel in which blended uranium-plutonium oxide powders and fresh uranium-oxide powder are loaded directly into the cladding tube of the fuel assembly instead of first being manufactured into pellets.
The reactor will be used for the development of materials for Generation IV fast neutron reactors.
Scientists will use it for experiments on the operating parameters of core components under normal and emergency conditions when using sodium, lead, lead-bismuth, gaseous and molten salt coolants.
According to earlier reports, the total cost of the project could be up to $1.5bn (€1.35bn), but no recent figures have been made public.
The MBIR will be used for the development of materials for Generation IV fast neutron reactors. Courtesy Rosatom.

title: NRC Grants Second 20-Year Licence Renewal For North Anna Nuclear Station
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Two reactors at Virginia site can now operate until 2058 and 2060
The US Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) has awarded a 20-year licence renewal for the two commercial nuclear reactor units operating at the North Anna site in Virginia.
There are two Westinghouse-made 948-MW and 944-MW pressurised water reactor units at North Anna. Unit 1 began commercial operation in 1978 followed by Unit 2 in 1980.
North Anna-1 and -2 have already received initial 20-year licence renewals after the expiry of their 40-year design lifetime and could operate until April 2038 and August 2040.
The NRC said the subsequent 20-year licence renewal means the North Anna units can now operate unit April 2058 and August 2060.
Earlier this month, the NRC issued a final environmental impact report for the proposed lifetime extension of the two units.
The regulator said there were no adverse environmental impacts to bar the renewal of North Anna’s operating licences for an additional 20 years.

According to the NRC, with the renewal of the North Anna licences, eight commercial nuclear power reactors have received subsequent renewed licences which authorise operation extensions from 60 to 80 years.
Applications are under review for subsequent licence renewals at seven nuclear stations, the NRC said.

These are for: Point Beach-1 and -2 in Wisconsin; Oconee-1, -2, -3 in South Carolina; St. Lucie-1 and -2 in Florida; Monticello-1 in Minnesota; VC Summer-1 in South Carolina; Browns Ferry-1, -2, -3 in Alabama; Dresden-2 and -3 in Illinois.
There are two Westinghouse-made pressurised water reactor units at North Anna. Courtesy Dominion Energy.

title: PEJ Submits Permit Application For Nuclear Station Preparatory Works
author: David Dalton
text: Warsaw planning three Westinghouse rectors in Pomerania

Poland’s nuclear project company Polskie Elektrownie Jadrowe (PEJ) submitted an application on 28 August for a permit for starting preparatory works for the construction of the country’s first commercial nuclear power station.
PEJ said planned activities include securing the site for future construction and surveying.

It said it has submitted the permit application to the head of the province of Pomerania, the planned site for three Westinghouse AP1000 pressurised water reactor plants near the villages of Lubiatowo and Kopalino, to the northwest of Gdansk on the Baltic coast.

The announcement follows reports earlier this week that Poland plans to earmark 4.6 billion zloty (€1.08bn, $1.2bn) in the 2025 federal budget to begin preparations for building the nuclear power station.

According to the state-owned Polish Press Agency, finance minister Andrzej Domanski outlined the initial expenditure for what would be the country’s biggest-ever investment days before a cabinet meeting to approve next year’s draft budget.

PEJ president Leszek Juchniewicz said in a statement that PEJ has decided to divide the preparatory works into several stages in an effort to minimise “the potential nuisance associated with such activities”.
The permit application is for works such as surveying and the construction of fences.
PEJ said preparatory works are to be carried out on an area of about 300 hectares in two phases, first on about 45% of the site.
The company also said it has submitted a report on the project’s environmental impact reassessment for the first phase of the planned preparatory works.
US-based Bechtel is carrying out geological studies at the Lubiatowo-Kopalino site, which are expected to be completed by the end of 2024.
In late 2023, Westinghouse formed a consortium with Bechtel for the new-build project.
Poland is planning to build three nuclear plants at a site in the province of Pomerania. Courtesy PEJ.

title: Westinghouse Files Appeal Over Decision To Award Nuclear Contract To South Korea
author: David Dalton
text: US company says KHNP does not own underlying technology for its APR reactor units

US-based Westinghouse Electric Company has filed an appeal with the Czech anti-monopoly office to protest the decision by state power company ČEZ to choose Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power (KHNP) as the preferred bidder for the construction of two new nuclear reactors at the Dukovany nuclear power station.

The Czech government announced in July that KHNP had won the lucrative public tender – said to be worth about $18bn (€16bn) – to build at least two nuclear reactors with the first unit scheduled to be online by 2036.
KHNP beat France’s state power company EDF in the tender, which was launched in 2022. The Prague government said in January that a bid by Westinghouse did not meet its conditions.
Russia’s Rosatom and China’s China General Nuclear were excluded from the tender on security grounds.

Westinghouse said in a statement on 26 August that the tender required vendors to certify they possess the right to transfer and sublicense the nuclear technology offered in their bids to CEZ and local suppliers.
“KHNP’s APR-1000 and APR-1400 plant designs utilize Westinghouse-licensed Generation II System 80 technology,” Westinghouse said.
“KHNP neither owns the underlying technology nor has the right to sublicense it to a third party without Westinghouse consent.
“Further, only Westinghouse has the legal right to obtain the required approval from the US government to export its technology.”
Westinghouse filed a lawsuit in a US court in October 2022, alleging that KHNP infringed on its technology and claiming that KHNP must obtain US government approval to export the reactors.
The court dismissed the suit in September 2023, but did not rule on the issue of intellectual property infringement.

David Durham, president of energy systems at Westinghouse, said at the time that Westinghouse’s dispute with Kepco/KHNP crosses multiple jurisdictions and covers two issues: compliance with US nuclear technology export control requirements and Kepco/KHNP’s longstanding obligations to comply with Westinghouse’s intellectual property rights that they agreed to contractually.

“The use of Westinghouse intellectual property outside of Korea is the principal dispute between the parties. The decision by the US District Court merely holds that export control enforcement resides with the US government.”
Westinghouse said it intended to appeal the decision.
Westinghouse said it will continue to vigorously defend its intellectual property rights and compliance with US export control laws via international arbitration and US litigation.
The Korea Herald reported that South Korea is looking for a solution to end the dispute.

“The government is discussing with the US government through various channels to support the amicable resolution of the corporate dispute,” the newspaper quoted an official of the presidential office as saying.
“We will maintain close coordination with our US counterparts on the foundation of the ironclad Korea-US alliance, so that the dispute does not harm Seoul's nuclear exports.”
The Czech Republic has six commercially operational reactor units: four Russia-designed VVER-440 units at Dukovany and two larger VVER-1000 units at Temelín.
According to the International Atomic Energy Agency, in 2022 the six units provided 36.7% of the country’s electricity production.
The Czech Republic is planning to build two new nuclear reactors at the Dukovany nuclear power station. Courtesy ČEZ.

title: IAEA’s Grossi Confirms Plans To ‘Personally Lead Visit’ To Russian Nuclear Station
author: David Dalton
text: Agency head says he will evaluate safety and security conditions
International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) director-general Rafael Grossi has said he will personally lead a visit to Russia’s Kursk nuclear power station on Tuesday (27 August).
In a statement on 26 August Grossi said: “I am personally leading the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) mission to the Kursk Nuclear Power Plant (KNPP) in the Russian Federation.

“Since new developments and increased levels of military activity in the vicinity of the KNPP, I have been closely following developments on the ground, especially with respect to the plant,” Grossi said.
“I reiterate that the safety and security of nuclear facilities must, under no circumstances, be endangered.

“This is an evolving situation, and it is vital when I arrive at the plant tomorrow that I see first-hand the situation and discuss modalities for further activities as may be needed to evaluate the nuclear safety and security conditions of the KNPP.”

Grossi said last week he planned to visit the nuclear station in southwest Russia, saying he was taking “very seriously” the risk that the facility could be damaged during Ukraine’s incursion into the region.
Grossi told the Financial Times in an interview that the Kursk station was “technically within artillery range” of Ukrainian positions. “And since there is combat, I’m very concerned.”

Grossi said he would talk to Kursk’s managers and gather any evidence of whether it had already been targeted. He also wants to assess the state of external power supply and access routes to the plant, noting the recent Ukrainian destruction of bridges across the Seym river in the west of the region.
Kursk has two nuclear units in commercial operation, two under construction and two that have been permanently shut down.
Grossi’s plans to visit the facility were announced as the IAEA said it had been told by Russia on 22 August that the remains of a drone were found within the territory of the power plant.

The drone fragments were reported to have been found roughly 100 metres from the plant’s spent fuel nuclear storage facility. The IAEA was informed that the drone was “suppressed” in the early morning of 22 August.
August 2023 file photo of construction at the Kursk nuclear site in southwest Russia. Courtesy Rosatom.

title: Warsaw To Commit $1.2 Billion For First Nuclear Power Station
author: David Dalton
text: Finance minister confirms country’s ‘biggest ever investment’
Poland plans to earmark 4.6 billion zloty (€1.08bn, $1.2bn) in the 2025 federal budget to begin preparations for building the nation’s first commercial nuclear power station.

According to the state-owned Polish Press Agency, finance minister Andrzej Domanski outlined the initial expenditure for what would be the country’s biggest-ever investment days before a cabinet meeting to approve next year’s draft budget.

Earlier this month, the government assumed it would have to secure about $15bn for the project in 2025-2030 period, before it would get further financing from the US, which will supply the nuclear plant technology.
Domanski said the nuclear station is part of a strategic effort to diversify the country’s energy mix and reduce electricity costs.
Under a 2020 nuclear programme, Poland plans to build from 6,000 to 9,000 MW of installed nuclear capacity.

In November 2022, Warsaw chose Westinghouse to supply the AP1000 PWR technology for the first three-unit nuclear station near the villages of Lubiatowo and Kopalino, to the northwest of Gdansk on the Baltic coast in Pomerania.
The start of construction had been planned for 2026 with the first unit scheduled to be online in 2033.
Undersecretary of state for strategic energy infrastructure Maciej Bando said recently Poland expects to pour first concrete in 2028 for the first unit.
Bandos’ comment seemed to confirm earlier official indications that the construction schedule will need to be pushed back to allow for preparatory and licensing activities.
US-based Bechtel is carrying out geological studies at the Lubiatowo-Kopalino site, which are expected to be completed by the end of 2024.
In late 2023, Westinghouse formed a consortium with Bechtel for the new-build project.
Poland is planning to build from 6,000 to 9,000 MW of installed nuclear capacity.

title: Country Aiming To Deploy Up To 50 Indigenous Bharat Reactors, Says Executive
author: David Dalton
text: Engineering company working on redesign of existing PHWR nuclear power plant technology
An industry executive has suggested India is aiming to deploy 40-50 small modular reactors to replace captive thermal power plants* as it aims to achieve its goal of net-zero emissions by 2070.

Amit Sharma, managing director and chief executive officer of Tata Consulting Engineers, told Press Trust of India (PTI) that New Delhi is pushing ahead with plans to develop an indigenous SMR of about 220 MW based on its existing pressurised heavy water reactor (PHWR) technology, which was developed from earlier Canadian Candu designs.

The new plant will be known as the Bharat SMR. Finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman announced plans for the Bharat plant last month, saying the SMR initiative would involve a joint venture between state power company National Thermal Power Corporation and state power generation equipment manufacturer Bharat Heavy Electricals Limited.
She said the government plans to partner with the private sector to establish a company called Bharat Small Reactors and conduct research and development on SMRs and newer nuclear technologies.
Sharma said existing PHWR technology would be redesigned to achieve a high degree of standardisation that would allow easy deployment.
He said Tata Consulting Engineers is working on the redesign with the Department of Atomic Energy.
“We are going to take the old design of the PHWR and then reconfigure and redesign it to be modular, scalable and safety-aligned to post-Fukushima standards,” Sharma told PTI.

New Delhi is bullish on nuclear and recently said it aims to have an installed capacity of 100 GW of nuclear power by 2047, a massive increase from the current level of around 6.9 GW and on recent targets of 22.4 GW by 2032.

State nuclear operator Nuclear Power Corporation of India Limited (NPCIL) said recently that India plans to add 18 more nuclear reactors to its national energy mix by 2031-32, bringing the total nuclear power capacity of the country to 22.4 GW.
NPCIL did not say whether the 22.4 GW would be net or gross, but either way it represents a significant increase from around 6.9 GW net today.
NPCIL said 10 proposed new reactor units with combined capacity of 7 GW are undergoing “pre-project activities” in addition to eight reactor units already under construction.
According to the International Atomic Energy Agency, India officially has seven plants under construction with a total net capacity of about 5.3 GW.
It has 19 reactors in commercial operation which provided about 3% of the country’s electricity generation in 2022.
In December, India said it planned to build at least 10 more nuclear power units to increase the production of clean energy as the country is still largely dependent on coal.
The 10 plants are Kaiga-5 and Kaiga-6 in Karnataka state, Mahi Banswara 1-4 in Rajasthan state Gorakhpur-3 and -4 in Haryana state, and Chutka-1 and -2 in Madhya Pradesh state.
* A facility that provides a localised power source to an energy user, such as an industrial facility, large office, or data centre.
Construction at the Kudankulam nuclear power station site in India. Courtesyy IAEA.

title: World’s Largest Uranium Producer Cuts 2025 Production Target
author: David Dalton
text: Company cites uncertainty on crucial sulphuric acid supplies
Kazatomprom, the world’s largest uranium producer, has cut its production target for 2025 due to project delays and sulphuric acid shortages, potentially threatening supplies.

The Kazakh company, which generates a fifth of global uranium supply, cut its target for next year by 17% to a range of 25,000 to 26,500 tonnes of yellowcake, or triuranium octoxide (U3O8), a type of uranium concentrate powder used to produce fuel for nuclear power reactors.

The move is likely to put upward pressure on uranium prices, which have softened from a 16-year high above $100/lb this year but remain at historically elevated levels above $80/lb, according to UxC, a uranium pricing data provider.

Meirzhan Yussupov, chief executive of Kazatomprom, said that “the uncertainty around the sulphuric acid supplies for 2025 needs and delays in the construction works at the newly developed deposits resulted in a need to re-evaluate our 2025 plans”.

Sulphuric acid, essential to extracting uranium from deposits, has been in short supply in Kazakhstan because of delays in building new acid plants, competition with the fertiliser industry and trade restrictions.
Kazatomprom said it has a comfortable level of inventories to fulfil its existing contractual commitments in 2025.

“Taking into consideration high level of uncertainties related to the sulphuric acid supply and construction delay challenges, no decision has been taken regarding mine development activity and production volumes for 2026 and beyond,” the company said, adding that it expects to announce its 2026 production plans “not earlier than a year from now”.

title: Japco Says ‘Delay Of More Than Two Years’ To Safety Measures At Tokai-2
author: David Dalton
text: Work to build tsunami and storm surge barrier follows 2011 Fukushima disaster
The owner and operator of the Tokai-2 nuclear power plant northeast of Tokyo is expected to further delay the complete implementation of stricter safety measures, state broadcaster NHK reported.

NHK quoted sources as saying the Japan Atomic Power Company (Japco) has decided to reschedule the completion date for work that is being done to build a tsunami and storm surge barrier at the 1,060-MW boiling water reactor unit in Ibaraki Prefecture.
According to NHK, Japco planned to complete the work by September of this year, but it now expects the work to be finished by December 2026, a potential delay of more than two years
The move comes after defects were found in the foundation of the levee that the company has been constructing as part of safety measures against disasters, NHK said.

The plant, which began commercial operation in 1978, has been offline since a powerful earthquake and tsunami hit northeast Japan in 2011, crippling the Fukushima-Daiichi nuclear power station, which is about 118 km north of the Tokai station.

Japco told the Nuclear Regulation Authority earlier this month that it plans to carry out additional work on a large scale to reinforce internal parts of the structure and the grounds around it. But Japco noted that it will leave the foundation as it is, NHK said.
If the work is delayed, it will be the third time Japco has rescheduled the completion date since the nuclear regulator approved an assessment for the Tookai-2 in 2018.
The regulator’s approval is one of the preconditions set out for the plant to be put back online.
NHK said the Japanese government considers Tokai-2 to be one of the nuclear power plants that needs to be brought back online to meet electricity demands and ensure energy security.
Before Fukushima-Daiichi, Japan’s fleet of 54 nuclear plants generated about 30% of the country’s electricity, but were all shut down for safety checks following the accident.

Among the 33 operable nuclear reactors in Japan, 12 have resumed operations after meeting post-Fukushima safety standards. The restarted plants are: Sendai-1 and -2, Genkai-3 and -4, Ikata-3, Mihama-3, Ohi-3 and -4 and Takahama-1, -2, -3 and -4.

According to the International Atomic Energy Agency nuclear generated about 6.1% of the country’s electricity in 2022. The Tokyo-based Japan Atomic Industry Forum said recently that the fleet generated 81 TWh of electric power in 2023, about 50% higher than 2022.
Tokai-2 has been offline since a powerful earthquake and tsunami hit northeast Japan in 2011.

title: Nuclear ‘At A Crossroads’ As Agency Calls For Lifetime Extensions And  New Capacity
author: David Dalton
text: Growth centred on Asia, with China still the fastest expanding nuclear power producer in world

The global fleet of nuclear reactors continues to be a large and indispensable source of low-carbon electricity, but lifetime extensions and new reactor capacity will be needed if the world is to meet its climate change and energy security goals, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) has said.
The agency said newly released nuclear power data for 2023 paints a picture of a clean energy technology at a crossroads amid the emergence of a new global consensus to accelerate its deployment.
The data is in two newly released annual IAEA publications: Nuclear Power Reactors in the World (RDS-2) and Operating Experience with Nuclear Power Stations in Member States (OPEX).

Electricity production from nuclear power rose by 2.6% last year compared to 2022, according to operating data provided by IAEA member states to the Power Reactor Information System (PRIS) – the IAEA’s comprehensive and publicly available database on nuclear power.
Nuclear power continued to generate almost 10% of the world’s electricity and a quarter of all low-carbon electricity in 2023.

As of the end of December 2023, global operational nuclear power capacity was 371.5 GW(e), provided by 413 reactors in 31 countries. However, only 403 reactors, with a combined capacity of 364.5 GW(e), reported their electricity production to the IAEA.

Twenty-five reactors remained in suspended operations throughout the year, despite being licenced for operation. This includes four reactors in India with a combined net capacity of 639 MW(e) and 21 reactors in Japan with a combined net capacity of around 21 000 MW(e). Japan restarted two reactors in 2023, Takahama-1 and Takahama-2, which had been in suspended operation since 2011.
The IAEA said nuclear power capacity has remained at a consistent level over the past decade, with an additional 69.8 GW(e) nuclear capacity connected to the grid since the beginning of 2013.
Over 79% of this capacity growth occurred in Asia. China is still the fastest expanding nuclear power producer of the world.
The US remained the world’s top producer of nuclear electricity with 742.4 TWh, followed by China (406.5 TWh) and France (323.8 TWh).

In terms of nuclear share of electricity production, France was first with 65%, followed by Slovakia (61%) and Hungary (49%). The US, despite having the most reactors with a fleet of 94, was 17th with 19%, one percent behind the United Arab Emirates, which now has four reactors at Barakah.

China continued to lead in newbuilds, beginning construction on five reactors. Newcomer Egypt started building its second reactor. China has 56 nuclear power reactors in operation and a further 27 reactors under construction.
The data showed the global fleet operating at nearly full strength with a median capacity factor of 88%.
New grid connections were made at nuclear power plants in Belarus, China, South Korea, Slovakia and the US, but reactors were shut down in Belgium, China and Germany.
The IAEA said the 2023 data come against the backdrop of growing global ambitions for nuclear technology amid an aging reactor fleet. More than two-thirds of reactors are at least 30 years old.

In December 2023, at the United Nations Climate Change Conference (Cop28) in Dubai, the 198 signatory countries to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change called for accelerating the deployment of low-emission energy technologies
including nuclear power for deep and rapid decarbonisation, particularly in hard-to-abate sectors such as industry.

In addition, more than 20 countries at Cop28 pledged to work towards tripling global nuclear power capacity
to reach net zero by 2050.
“IAEA data shows the global fleet of nuclear reactors continues to be a large and indispensable source of low-carbon electricity,” said IAEA director-general Rafael Grossi.

“But it’s also clear that we will need to extend the lives of existing reactors, replace retiring facilities with new ones, and add a lot of new capacity so that global climate change and energy security goals can be reached.”
THe IAEA said China has 56 nuclear power reactors in operation and a further 27 reactors under construction.

title: Rosatom Ships RPV And Steam Generator For Xudabu-4 Nuclear Plant
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Four units under construction at site in northeast of country
Rosatom, has shipped the reactor pressure vessel (RPV) and one of the four steam generators for the Xudabu-4 nuclear power plant being built in Liaoning province in northeast China.
Construction of Xudabu-4 (also written in English as Xudabao and Xudapu) started in May 2022.
The plant will be a conventional pressurised water reactor unit using the Russian VVER-1200 technology.
The RPV is one of the largest reactor components at a nuclear plant. It is a vessel containing the nuclear reactor coolant, core shroud, and the reactor core and fuel.
The steam generators act as heat exchangers where water carrying heat generated from the nuclear reaction is used to turn demineralised water into steam for the plant turbines.
The Xudabu project was originally expected to comprise of six CAP1000 plants, with Units 1 and 2 in the first phase.
Site preparation began in November 2010, but plans changed with the construction of two VVER-1200 reactors for Units 3 and 4.
International Atomic Energy Agency data shows four units are currently under construction at Xudabu – Units 1 and 2 are CAP1000s, and Units 3 and 4 are VVER-1200s.
Russia has shipped the reactor pressure vessel  and one of the four steam generators for Xudabu-4 nuclear power plant in China. Courtesy Rosatom.

title: Gov’t Sets Up Company To Evaluate Options For New Nuclear
author: David Dalton
text: Yerevan ‘in negotiations’ with four potential reactor suppliers
The Armenian government has established a company that will evaluate options for new reactor construction in the country.

The entity will look into technology vendors’ proposals on the possible design and cost of a new nuclear unit in Armenia, with the goal of having a development plan for the new capacity by the middle of 2026, Armenian infrastructure minister Gnel Sanosian was reported as saying.
The new unit is planned to become operational by 2040 to replace the 416-MW Armenian-2, which is undergoing life extension work that will allow it to operate until 2036.
Sanosian said that Yerevan is in negotiations with Russian, US, French, and South Korean companies about building the new reactor.
Local press reports said the range of potential suppliers reflects a change in Armenian energy policy, which has historically dominated by Russian technology.
One of the main obstacles to the project is financing with the government considering state borrowing.
On a technical level, the integration of a new nuclear unit into a relatively modest national power grid, with an installed capacity of 4 GW, could also be challenging, website energynews.pro said.

The secretary of Armenia’s security council, Armen Grigoryan, was quoted as saying recently
that Armenia and the US had “entered a very substantive stage” of discussions about the possibility of building a new nuclear power station.

In May 2023, Armenian prime minister Nikol Pashinyan confirmed that his country’s single nuclear power plant, the Russia-supplied Armenian-2, will be shut down in 2036, but affirmed his support for negotiations to find a partner to build new nuclear units.

Armenian-2, at Metsamor, 30 km outside of the Armenian capital of Yerevan, began commercial operation in 1980. It was shut down after a major earthquake struck the region in 1988 and remained offline until 1995, when it was reopened in an independent Armenia then struggling to meet demand for electric power.

The VVER-440 pressurised water reactor unit had an initial operating lifetime of 30 years starting in 1996 and set to expire in 2026. In March 2023, Armenian authorities granted an extra 10 years of operation until 2036 subject to maintenance works.
The prime minister’s comments suggest there will be no more extensions to its working life with 2036 established as a hard deadline for its retirement.
The Armenian-2 nuclear power plant provides about 28% of the country’s electricity generation, but will be shut down in 2036.

title: Global Atomic Bullish On Dasa Uranium Project Following Letter Of Support
author: David Dalton
text: Company says letter confirms project is considered strategic investment for African nation
Global Atomic has received a letter from the government of Niger in which president Tiani and the Council of ministers confirm support for the company and development of its Dasa uranium project.

The Canada-based company said it continues to develop the Dasa Project and expects to be bringing the mine and the processing plant into production at the end of 2025 for delivery of yellowcake to utilities in the US and other countries in early 2026.

Global Atomic president and chief executive officer Stephen Roman said the letter confirms strong support from the government of Niger for the Dasa project and the company’s progress in its development to date.
Roman said the letter confirms Dasa is considered a strategic investment for Niger.
“The letter highlights that we have always complied with Niger’s regulations,” Roman said.

“The mines minister, during his site visit in May 2024, witnessed our commitment to predominately populate our local management and operating staff from Niger’s workforce and prioritise Niger companies for the supply of goods and services, where practical.
“We are pleased to see that the government recognises not only the socio-economic benefits that accrue to Niger from Dasa, but also the excellent ESG work we have been doing since 2008.”
The Dasa project lies within the Adrar Emoles III licence area, 105 km south of the established uranium mining town of Arlit.

It emerged recently that a US development bank postponed a scheduled July presentation about the Dasa project to its credit committee, with the company saying it will move to “finalise other financing discussions” if there are further delays.
Global Atomic said the unnamed development bank was moving a planned debt financing facility, previously reported to ben CAD295m ($215m, €195m), through its approval process.
The bank postponed its scheduled July presentation of the project to its credit committee, but Roman said the company remains confident that the bank will eventually approve the project.

In June, Niger’s ruling military junta, which came to power following a coup in July 2023, revoked the operating licence of French company Orano at the Imouraren mine, which sits on one of the biggest uranium deposits in the world.
Last month Canada-based GoviEx Uranium said the junta had withdrawn its licence for the Madaouela uranium mine, dealing a major blow to the development of one of the world’s largest uranium projects.
Global Atomic says the Dasa project is the highest-grade uranium project in Africa. Courtesy Global Atomic.

title: Vattenfall Calls For More Details On Nuclear New Build Risks
author: David Dalton
text: Company responds to gov’t commission report on reactor financing

Vattenfall has welcomed proposals for a financing model for new nuclear power in Sweden, but said it is “unclear to us” how construction risk and risks linked to the planning and implementation actual power plant construction will be handled.

State-owned Vattenfall, which owns and operates the Forsmark and Ringhals nuclear power stations in Sweden through local subsidiaries, said it is looking forward to a dialogue with the office being set up by the government to further develop the model, but will need to analyse it in more detail.
“We know for certain that the first reactors will be more expensive than the next ones and here the state needs to play an important role,” Vattenfall said in a statement.
“What we see missing at first glance is also how the state will guarantee that the entire programme of 4-6 GW proposed by the investigator is actually built.
“As the investigator mentioned, this is crucial if the costs of e.g. final repositories are to be reasonable.”

Vattenfall was responding to a government commission study released earlier this week that highlighted several features of the commission’s preferred financing model to provide certainty for investors in new nuclear.
Proposed funding instruments include government borrowing to support construction and 40 years of guaranteed revenues through a so-called contract-for-difference or CfD.
The CfD model has been used for both EDF’s Hinkley Point C project in the UK in the UK and is being considered for new units at Dukovany in the Czech Republic.

Under this mechanism, developers and the government agree a fixed price for electricity for a certain period of time, providing certainty of future revenue. If market prices fall too low, the generator receives a top-up from the state. On the flip side, the plant operator must pay back the difference if the market rate is higher.

The state should lend nuclear companies 75% of the cost of building power plants with the owners contributing 25%. The commission said the government should guarantee an electricity price of around 80 ore/Kwh to investors over 40 years.

The study said Sweden’s plans for a rapid expansion of its nuclear power capacity are likely to cost around 400 billion crowns ($38bn, €34bn) and should be financed by a mix of government loans and price guarantees, a government commission has recommended.

The commission proposed a programme of four or five new nuclear power plants with a total of 4,000-6,000 MW – or four large-scale reactors – of installed capacity in order to make the programme cost-effective.

“The risks that government investigator Mats Dillen points out are precisely those that need to be managed, i.e. the design risk, the market risk, the regulatory risks and the programme risk,” Vattenfall said.
“Guaranteeing revenues when a reactor is commissioned through Contracts for Difference, as proposed by the investigator, is a reasonable way to reduce market risk.
“The levels at which these contracts should be set will depend on the cost of the project. We therefore consider it a little premature to set exact levels.”

Late last year Sweden’s parliament approved a bill allowing more nuclear reactors to be built than planned, scrapping the previous cap of 10. New laws will also allow construction of nuclear reactors at sites other than existing ones.
Parliament also established a new energy policy goal of a completely fossil-free electricity system by 2040, which includes nuclear power.

The current government, which took office last year led by the conservative Moderate Party in coalition with the Liberals and the Christian Democrats, is calling for new nuclear power with a total output corresponding to at least two large-scale reactors to be in place by 2035. By 2045 it wants a further expansion that could correspond to at least 10 new large-scale reactors.

Vattenfall announced earlier this year that it had shortlisted Rolls-Royce SMR and GE Hitachi’s BWRX-300 SMR designs in an ongoing evaluation to potentially deploy new reactors at its existing Ringhals nuclear site in southwest Sweden.

Sweden’s six existing nuclear plants are at three sites: Forsmark, Oskarshamn and Ringhals. According to International Atomic Energy Agency data, nuclear energy provided 28.6% of the country’s electricity generation in 2023.
Vattenfall has already said it is considering new reactors at its existing Ringhals nuclear site. Courtesy Vattenfall.

title: Lloyds Register And Core Power Team Up On Regulatory Study For Nuclear-Propelled Shipping
author: David Dalton
text: Vessels could use Generation IV reactor technology

Lloyd’s Register and Core Power have begun a joint regulatory assessment study to conduct research on the regulatory feasibility and frameworks that need to be established for a nuclear container ship using a Generation IV nuclear power plant.

Lloyds Register, a technical and professional services organisation and a maritime classification society, said in a statement that the study will determine the safety and regulatory considerations for a next-generation nuclear-propelled feeder container ship to undertake cargo operations at a port in Europe. Feeders collect shipping containers from different ports and transport them to central container terminals where they are loaded to bigger vessels.

The joint study, which also involves Danish shipping and logistics company Maersk, will investigate the requirements for updated safety rules and the improved operational and regulatory understanding that is needed for the application of nuclear power in container shipping.

“In addition, this study will provide insight for members of the maritime value chain who are exploring the business case for nuclear power to help shape their fleet strategy towards achieving net zero greenhouse gas emissions,” Lloyds Register said.

Lloyd’s Register chief executive officer Nick Brown said the start of the joint study marks the beginning of an exciting journey towards “unlocking the potential of nuclear power in the maritime industry, paving the way for emissions-free operations, more agile service networks and greater efficiency through the supply chain”.

Core Power’s chief executive officer Mikal Boe said: “There’s no net-zero without nuclear”. He said one of the keys to unlocking the vast potential for nuclear energy to transform how the maritime sector is powered, is the standards framework for commercial insurability of floating nuclear power plants and nuclear-powered ships that would operate in nearshore environments, ports, and waterways.
CorePower, a UK-based maritime and technology innovation company, is looking to develop a molten salt reactor for ship propulsion.

A recent Lloyds Register report said nuclear power for the maritime industry would be a transformational technology leading to safer, more reliable, emissions free, longer-lived, and more productive ships.

International Atomic Energy Agency director-general Rafael Grossi has already called for a roadmap for nuclear energy to become a viable option to reduce commercial shipping’s global greenhouse gas emissions.
The maritime industry sees vast potential for nuclear energy to transform how the sector is powered.

title: Stockpiling For VVER Plants Sees 72% Increase In Uranium Imports From Russia
author: David Dalton
text: Over 91% of natural uranium supplied to EU came from four producing countries

Natural uranium supplies to nuclear utilities in the European Union continued to come from “diverse sources” in 2023 with 32.9% imported from Canada, an increase of 86.2% over 2022, and 23.4% from Russia, an increase of 72.6%, despite the need to diversify from Russian supply following Moscow’s February 2022 invasion of Ukraine.
According to the Euratom Supply Agency’s (ESA) latest annual report, deliveries of natural uranium from Russia increased in 2023 as utilities stockpiled fuel for Russia-designed VVER nuclear plants.

The ESA, which is responsible for maintaining a regular and equitable supply of nuclear materials in Europe, said EU utilities continue to diversify their sources of nuclear fuel, particularly for VVER reactors, in a bid to reduce dependency on “single suppliers and designs or reduce high-risk supplies”.
“Nearly all countries operating Russian-designed reactors are progressing in licensing alternative fuel designs, with promising developments expected in the near future,” the ESA said.

It said that since 2022, almost all EU operators of VVER nuclear reactors have contractually diversified their nuclear fuel supply. Some utilities operating VVER reactors have been building fresh fuel stocks to cover the period until alternative fuels – including related plant adaptations – are completed and licensed.
Other nuclear operators purchased higher quantities of enriched products as part of their security of supply measures.

This meant that deliveries of natural uranium and services at all stages of the nuclear fuel cycle increased in 2023, including deliveries from Russia, driven by VVER fuel stockpiling, where contracts are generally bundled with the supply of nuclear fuel-cycle services and material.
“At this stage, the increase should not be read as an indication of a trend or heightened EU dependency on Russian supplies,” the ESA said.

There are 19 VVER reactors in operation in the EU, including four VVER 1,000 MW reactors in Bulgaria and the Czech Republic, and 15 VVER 440 MW reactors in the Czech Republic, Finland, Hungary and Slovakia.
According to the ESA, the EU’s demand for natural uranium accounts for about 22% of global needs
Over 91% of natural uranium supplied to the EU came from four producing countries – Canada, Russia, Kazakhstan and Niger.
Canada supplied 4,801 tonnes of uranium (tU), while Russia supplied 3,419 tU and Kazaksthan was third with 3,061 tU.
Niger, where a ruling junta that came to power last year has cancelled permits for mines operated by France’s Orano and Canada’s GoviEx, supplied 2,089 tU, or 14.3%, a decline of almost 30%.
According to the ESA, no natural uranium supply for utilities came from within Europe.
ESA director-general Michael Hübel said the agency finds itself in “a complex and challenging environment”.

He said that in 2023, the nuclear supply market continued to face supply uncertainties linked to the impact of the war of aggression in Ukraine and the need to diversify from Russian supply and a changing geopolitical environment.

“At the same time, plans in some countries to extend or expand nuclear power generation, the emergence of innovative designs such as small and advanced modular reactors, but also the growing interest in the use of radioisotopes for medical purposes, are changing the supply landscape for nuclear material in Europe,” he said.
The ESA said that in 2023, nuclear power accounted for approximately 23% of the EU’s total electricity generation, with 103 operational reactor units.
There are 19 Russia-designed VVER nuclear plants in operation in Europe, including two at Temelín in the Czech Republic. Courtesy ČEZ.

title: Global Atomic Remains Confident On Dasa Financing, Despite Development Bank Delay
author: David Dalton
text: Ruling junta has already withdrawn licences for two major uranium projects

A US development bank postponed a scheduled July presentation about Global Atomic’s Dasa uranium project in Niger to its credit committee, with the Canada-based company saying it will move to “finalise other financing discussions” if there are further delays.
Global Atomic said the unnamed development bank is moving a planned debt financing facility, previously reported to ben CAD295m ($215m, €195m), through its approval process.

The bank postponed its scheduled July presentation of the project to its credit committee, but Global Atomic president and chief executive officer Stephen Roman said the company remains confident that the bank will eventually approve the project.
“Should the bank further delay their approval, we will move to finalise other financing discussions, which include minority joint venture partners and pre-payments tied to uranium offtake,” he said.

Roman said the company continues to make significant progress at Dasa, currently employing over 450 people at site and expecting to increase that number to 900 once plant construction is in full swing.
“We have an excellent relationship with the government and have the support of their entire cabinet, as they appreciate the jobs and economic benefit that Dasa will create for Niger,” Roman said.
He said a recent CAD20m private placement has allowed continued advancement of the project while the development bank considers financing.
Global Atomic says the Dasa project is the highest-grade uranium project in Africa and the only greenfield uranium project being actively developed today.

In June, Niger’s ruling military junta, which came to power following a  coup in July 2023, revoked the operating licence of French company Orano at the Imouraren mine, which sits on one of the biggest uranium deposits in the world.
Last month Canada-based GoviEx Uranium said the junta had withdrawn its licence for the Madaouela uranium mine, dealing a major blow to the development of one of the world’s largest uranium projects.
Global Atomic says the Dasa project is the highest-grade uranium project in Africa. Courtesy Global Atomic.

title: Marcos Wants To Work With UAE As Manila ‘Tries To Figure Out’ Next Steps On Nuclear
author: David Dalton
text: This has become a very high priority topic, president tells Enec delegation

Philippines president Ferdinand Marcos Jr is hopeful the country can work with Emirates Nuclear Energy Corporation (Enec) as the Southeast Asian nation explores the possible use of nuclear energy for power generation for the first time.
Marcos met Enec managing director and chief executive officer Mohammed Al-Hammadi at Malacanang Palace in Manila on Monday and discussed a potential partnership in nuclear energy.

“President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. is hopeful the Philippines could successfully partner with Emirates Nuclear Energy Corp. (ENEC) as the country explores the possible use of nuclear energy for power generation,” the Presidential Communications Office said in a statement.

Nuclear as an alternative energy option “is a subject that we have been talking about for a long time,” Marcos told Al-Hammadi at the meeting, adding that he has been trying to decide on the government’s next steps.
“And this had become a very high-priority topic. I hope we can find ways to help each other in this,” Marcos was quoted as saying.

“Thank you very much. I’m glad that we had this chance… for you to visit us. Because this is a subject that we have been talking about for a long time. And especially after the pandemic, I’m trying to figure out what are the needs of the government,” Marcos told Hammadi.

The Philippines, an archipelago nation of more than 7,000 islands, has been exploring clean and sustainable options to generate power, as the country regularly suffers power outages and faces high power tariffs. Coal remains the main source of electricity, accounting for over half of its power generation.
Enec is responsible for the implementation of the UAE’s nuclear energy programme, including the development and operation of the Barakah nuclear station in Abu Dhabi.

When Barakah-1 began commercial operation in 2021, the UAE became the first Arab state to operate a commercial nuclear power plant. There are four south Korea-supplied plants at Barakah. Barakah-4 was connected to the grid in March and is close to full operation.
Marcos’s communication office said 1,000 Filipinos are working at the Barakah station.

In November 2023, the Philippines took a significant step towards becoming a nuclear power nation with the signing of a 123 Agreement with Washington that will give it access to US material and equipment.
Marcos has been bullish on nuclear, saying “this is the right time” to reexamine the country’s approach and policy towards using nuclear energy.
The Philippines has a nuclear station at Bataan, north of the capital Manila in Luzon, but it has never operated and has been mothballed.
Work on the facility began during the presidency of Marcos’s father, also named Ferdinand, who imposed martial law and was deposed by a nonviolent revolution in 1986.
Philippines president Ferdinand Marcos meets Enec’s Mohammed Al-Hammadi (second right) at Malacanang Palace in Manila. Courtesy Presidential Communications Office.

title: African Charm Offensive Continues As Talks Held With Burkina Faso’s Junta
author: David Dalton
text: Nuclear power plant in landlocked West African country ‘will be tangible fact’, says energy minister

A delegation from Russia’s state nuclear corporation Rosatom has been visiting Burkina Faso to discuss a roadmap for the deployment of nuclear power plants in the West African country as Moscow continues its push to seal deals for new build across the continent.

Local press reports quoted Burkina Faso’s energy minister Yacouba Zabré Gouba as saying the purpose of the visit to the capital Ouagadougou was to make progress on a roadmap signed between the two parties in March 2024.

“We will be discussing much more technical aspects so that we can get rid of everything that needs to be done beforehand so that we can get on with the actual construction of this power plant,” said Gouba.
He said talks will focus on the implementation and impact of the project and will involve the ministries of environment, higher education, health and agriculture.
The nuclear power plant “will be a tangible fact… both parties will do their utmost to deliver the infrastructure within a reasonable timeframe,” said Gouba.
In October 2023, Burkina Faso and Russia signed a memorandum of understanding for the construction of a nuclear power plant in an effort to double the country’s electricity production by 2030.

According to press reports in Burkina Faso, the Russian visit is in line with the ambition of Ibrahim Traore, the military officer who has been the interim leader of Burkina Faso since a September 2022 coup, to equip the country with a nuclear power plant in order to reduce energy dependence.
The BBC reported last year that the agreements with Russia on nuclear energy are part of the junta’s plans to align itself with MOscow after falling out with most of its Western partners.
The junta has turned to Russia for economic and military support since it seized power, the BBC said.
Burkina Faso is one of the least electrified countries globally, with only 21% of people connected to power.
Burkina Faso gets most of its electricity from biofuels like charcoal and wood while oil products account for one-third of the total energy supply, according to the International Energy Agency.
According to the US development agency USAid, Burkina Faso also has one of the highest electricity costs in Africa.

South Africa is the only African state that produces nuclear power commercially from two units at Koeberg near Cape Town, but increasingly more nations on the continent are moving in the same direction.

Russia is helping Egypt to build a four-unit nuclear power station at Akkuyu at an estimated cost of $30bn (€27bn) following a deal signed by president Abdel Fattah al-Sisi and president Putin in 2017.
In recent years, Rosatom has signed agreements with about 20 African countries including Egypt, Nigeria, Ethiopia, Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, Congo, Rwanda, Mali, Sudan, Uganda and Zambia.
Last month Mali’s ruling military junta and Rosatom signed three cooperation deals and discussed projects including a Russian-designed low-power nuclear power plant.
Reuters said Rosatom has been on a charm offensive in Africa for years, seeking to drum up business by signing cooperation agreements with countries across the continent.
Koeberg in South Africa is the only operating nuclear power station on the African continent.
A delegation from Rosatom has been visiting Ouagadougou, the capital of Burkina Faso. Courtesy Jeff Attaway/Creative  Commons.

title: Operator Apologises After Guilty Plea Over String Of IT Security Failings At UK Site
author: David Dalton
text: Nuclear site awaits sentencing over breaches that it admitted could have threatened national security

The state-owned operator of the UK’s Sellafield nuclear waste site has apologised after pleading guilty to criminal charges relating to a string of cybersecurity failings at the UK’s most hazardous nuclear site, which it admitted could have threatened national security.
Among the failings at the site in Cumbria, northwest England, was the discovery that 75% of its computer servers were vulnerable to cyber-attacks, Westminster magistrates court in London heard.

Information that could threaten national security was left exposed for four years, the Office for Nuclear Regulation (ONR) revealed, and Sellafield said it had been performing critical IT health checks that were not, in fact, being carried out.
In a written witness statement referred to in court on 8 August Euan Hutton, chief executive of Sellafield, apologised for failures spanning years.
Hutton said: “I again apologise on behalf of the company for matters which led to these proceedings … I genuinely believe that the issues which led to this prosecution are in the past.”
In June Sellafield Ltd pleaded guilty to criminal charges brought by the ONR over IT security breaches.

Lawyers acting for Sellafield Ltd told a London court on 20 June that they accepted cyber security was “not sufficiently adhered to for a period”, although they insisted there had not been a successful cyberattack and that its systems were now secure.

One of the charges to which Sellafield Ltd pleaded guilty was that it failed in March last year to “ensure that there was adequate protection of sensitive nuclear information on its information technology network”.
The other two charges related to failures to arrange “annual health checks” for its systems.
Sellafield Ltd pleaded guilty to all three charges in the prosecution brought by the ONR under the Nuclear Industries Security Regulations 2003.

Sentencing had been scheduled to take place on August 8, but the ONR said in a statement: “We expect Sellafield Ltd to be sentenced in September, when further details will be provided on our website and social media channels.”
Sellafield Ltd is owned by the Nuclear Decommissioning Authority, a UK government body set up specifically to deal with the country’s nuclear legacy.
In March the ONR notified Sellafield Ltd that it would be prosecuted for alleged IT security offences during a four-year period between 2019 and early 2023.
The Sellafield site is one of the largest and most hazardous nuclear facilities in Europe.

It comprises of a range of nuclear facilities, including redundant facilities associated with early defence work, as well as operating facilities associated with the Magnox reprocessing programme, a mixed oxide fuel plant and a range of waste treatment plants.
It began life in the early 1950s making plutonium for nuclear weapons, and later that decade became the location of Calder Hall, the world’s first commercial nuclear power station.
The Sellafield site is one of the largest and most hazardous nuclear facilities in Europe.

title: US Production Increases In Q1 After Significant Fall In 2023
author: David Dalton
text: Signs point to revival of mining industry, says latest EIA data

Uranium miners in the US produced more than 82,000 pounds of uranium concentrate in the first quarter of 2024, more than in all of 2023, according to latest data from the Energy Information Administration (EIA).

The EIA, a federal statistical and analysis agency, said domestic uranium mines produced 50,000 pounds of triuranium octoxide (U3O8), also called uranium concentrate, in 2023, a significant decrease from the 194,000 pounds produced in 2022.

Production declined in 2023 because the US’s only operating conventional uranium mill, Energy Fuel Inc’s White Mesa Mill in Utah, did not produce. During 2023, uranium concentrate production occurred at five in-situ recovery facilities, four in Nebraska and one in Wyoming. In situ facilities use fluid to recover valuable minerals from the ground without digging.

Other signs point to increased uranium mining in the US, the EIA said. The number of exploration and development holes dug – a precursor to uranium production –jumped from 260 holes in 2021 to 1,008 holes in 2022 and to 1,930 holes in 2023.
The distance drilled per well, another precursor, increased from 123,000 feet in 2021 to 534,000 feet in 2022 and then to just over one million feet drilled in 2023.
The number of full-time employees engaged in uranium exploration activities also rose from 42 employees in 2021 to 110 employees in 2023.

In 2023, owners and operators of US civilian nuclear power reactors purchased 51.6 million pounds of uranium concentrate, a 27% increase from 2022. These purchases were made at a total weighted-average price of $43.80 per pound, an increase of 12% from a $39.08 per pound average price in 2022.

Uranium prices have generally risen over the last five years as a result of several factors, the EIA noted. Worldwide supply and demand have balanced following a supply surplus after the Fukushima-Daiichi accident in Japan in 2011. “Russia’s invasion of Ukraine has caused some countries to rethink a move away from nuclear energy, and we expect uranium consumption to increase from the nearly 60 reactors that are currently under construction around the world,” the EIA said.

Most uranium purchased in 2023 in the US was of foreign origin. More was from Canada than any other country at 27%. Uranium from Australia and Kazakhstan both accounted for 22% of purchases. Uranium from Russia accounted for 12%, and 10% was from Uzbekistan. Domestic supply accounted for 5% of total purchases in 2023, the same as in 2022.

The origin of uranium used in US reactors will likely change in the coming years. In May, the US banned imports of uranium products from Russia beginning in August, although companies may apply for waivers until 1 January 2028.

The passage of the ban on uranium imports from Russia also unlocked $2.72bn (€2.49bn) in funding to build out the domestic nuclear fuel supply chain and support new and existing nuclear power plant operators.
Production declined in 2023 because the US’s only operating conventional uranium mill, the White Mesa Mill (pictured) in Utah, did not produce. Courtesy Energy  Fuel Inc.

title: Greek MEP Says ‘Dynamic Legislative Framework’ Needed For New Nuclear
author: David Dalton
text: Reactors need ‘exceptionally high expenditure and a long-term strategy’
The European Union needs “a dynamic legislative framework” in a bid to overcome potential legal objections to the construction of new nuclear power plants, a Greek MEP has said.

Emmanouil Fragkos, a member of the European Parliament for the right-wing Greek Solution party, said the first cycle of investment for possible nuclear reactors in Greece will demand “exceptionally high expenditure and a long-term strategy”.
He warned of orchestrated “local reactions” against nuclear plans from NGOs that are “funded by energy competitors, energy exporters and local intermediaries of energy importers”.

The construction of a nuclear power plant near Akkuyu in Turkey, together with Turkey’s talks with Russia, the US, South Korea, China and Japan on the construction of additional plants, will result in “a huge, unacceptable energy imbalance” in the region, further increasing Turkey’s attractiveness for investments, Fragkos said. He added Europe urgently needs to create a supply chain for new nuclear.
In questions submitted to the European Commission, Fragkos asked if there is a usable European legislative framework in place to overcome the legal obstacles.

He asked the commission, which has not yet published a response to his questions, how Greece can apply for long-term targeted funding for “the earliest possible production of nuclear energy” and if Athens can contribute towards forming a coherent nuclear strategy.
Greece has no nuclear power plants and the 5 MW Greek Research Reactor-1 (GRR-1) at the National Centre of Scientific Research is currently licensed for extended shutdown.
In 2022 Bulgaria said it had begun negotiations with Greece for the potential construction of a new nuclear power station in Bulgaria which would supply electricity to both countries.
The bulk of Greece’s electricity is generated from natural gas, followed by renewables, but the country also traditionally imports electricity from Bulgaria.
The Paris-based Nuclear Energy Agency has said nuclear energy is not considered as an option for Greece “in the foreseeable future”.
Emmanouil Fragkos said Europe needs a usable legislative framework in place to overcome the legal obstacles.

title: Installation Of Reactor Enclosure Complete At Generation IV Nuclear Power Plant
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Brest-OD-300 lead-cooled reactor is part of pilot demonstration energy complex
Russia has installed the third and final tier of the enclosing structure in the reactor shaft the Brest-OD-300 pilot demonstration power plant in Seversk, southwest Siberia.

State nuclear corporation Rosatom said in a statement that the total weight of the three-tier enclosing structure is about 430 tonnes and it has a height of 17 metres. The final tier weighs 164 tonnes.
The statement said workers will next assemble the cooling system pipelines and an intermediate shell in the shaft. The newly formed cavity will be filled with heat-resistant concrete.

The 300-MW Brest-OD-300, under construction at the site of the Siberian Chemical Combine nuclear technology facility, is part of a pilot demonstration energy complex which comes under Russia’s “Breakthrough” project for the development of closed nuclear fuel cycle technology. It is a Generation IV* lead-cooled fast reactor design.

A closed nuclear fuel cycle means spent fuel is reprocessed and partly reused. Closing the nuclear fuel cycle would ease concerns over limited uranium resources and contribute towards making nuclear energy sustainable over the long term.

The reactor will use a mixed nitride uranium-plutonium fuel (MNUP) based on depleted uranium, which is a residual product of uranium enrichment for mainstream reactors, and plutonium extracted from irradiated spent nuclear fuel.

The facility, known as the Pilot Demonstration Energy Complex, will be a cluster of three main interconnected plants – a nuclear fuel production plant, the reactor unit itself and a facility for irradiated fuel reprocessing.
In 2021 Rosatom announced that the concrete base slab had been completed for the plant. Construction of the plant began with pouring of first concrete in June 2021.

According to earlier reports, Brest-OD-300 is expected to become operational in 2026. A fuel fabrication facility on the site is expected to be completed by the end of 2024, while construction of the irradiated fuel reprocessing plant is scheduled to start by 2024.
In December China said the Shidao Bay-1 nuclear plant had become the first Generation IV plant in the world to go online.

* No precise definition of a Generation IV reactor exists, but the term is used to refer to nuclear reactor technologies under development including gas-cooled fast reactors, lead-cooled fast reactors, molten salt reactors, sodium-cooled fast reactors, supercritical-water-cooled reactors and very high-temperature reactors. An international task force, the Generation IV International Forum (GIF), is sharing R&D to develop six Generation IV nuclear reactor technologies. GIF said goals of Generation IV reactor design include lower cost and financial risk, minimising nuclear waste and high levels of safety and reliability.
The Brest-OD-300 is under construction at the site of the Siberian Chemical Combine nuclear technology facility in Siberia. Courtesy Rosatom.
The third and final tier of the reactor enclosure weights 164 tonnes. Courtesy Rosatom.

title: Mining Companies And Opposition Leader Renew Calls For End To Uranium Ban
author: David Dalton
text: Nation ‘at risk of missing out on soaring global demand’ as world renews interest in nuclear

Uranium explorers are calling on Australian state governments to lift bans on mining the fuel, which analysts believes is likely to see a long-term increase in demand as decarbonisation spurs renewed interest in nuclear energy around the world.

“The bans in some states like Western Australia, which is known for its mining history, is nonsensical and leave the nation at risk of missing out on soaring global demand,” said Jonathan Fisher, chief executive officer of Cauldron Energy, a Sydney-listed explorer for the fuel.

“The time is now to remove these bans – there’s a real economic cost to not doing it,” he said in an interview with Bloomberg
before the annual Diggers & Dealers conference that started on Monday in Kalgoorlie, Australia.

Bloomberg said the gathering attracts hundreds of resources executives and financiers to the Outback town in Western Australia, which banned mining of the fuel in 2017, while exempting four previously approved projects yet to reach production.
Australia has nearly a third of known uranium ore deposits worldwide, but only two of the nation’s eight states and territories – South Australia and Northern Territory – allow the mining of it.

The country’s two operating uranium mines — BHP Group’s Olympic Dam project, where uranium is a byproduct of copper operations, and the Boss Energy-operated Honeywell – produce around 9% of the world’s disclosed output.

According to the Australia Strategic Policy Institute (ASPI), a Canberra-based thinktank, the four commercial uranium deposits in Western Australia that have in-place approvals to allow mine development are Mulga Rock, Wiluna, Yeelirrie and Kintyre.
Another 59 uranium exploration prospects have been identified: 14 in Western Australia, 24 in the Northern Territory, 14 in South Australia and seven in Queensland.

Ian Satchwell, an adjunct professor at the Sustainable Minerals Institute at the University of Queensland and a senior fellow at ASPI, said what is needed is for the Australian government to lead the states to adopt “nationally consistent, stable policies for uranium exploration and development that welcome investment while also setting out the conditions required for safe mining and supply chains to Australia’s energy partners”.
Mining approvals are decided at the state level in Australia, but the Labor-led federal government has so far not taken steps to encourage mining of the nuclear fuel.

Peter Dutton, who leads the federal government’s main rivals the Liberals and heads an opposition coalition, told reporters at the conference that the reluctance of Western Australia’s Labor government to remove the ban on uranium mining was costing the state.
He said Australia is the only one of the world’s top 20 economies that does not have or has not signed up to nuclear power.
Dutton told Mining.com.au that the demand is there, so “why would we be doing ourselves out of an export opportunity?”

He said: “Why would we be stopping ourselves from earning additional income for our country, creating extra jobs? We can do that through opening up uranium exports. I just don’t understand the government’s reluctance here.”
Dutton announced recently that his federal Coalition party wants to build seven large-scale nuclear power plants and two proposed small modular reactors.
At the Cop28 climate summit in Dubai last year, the Coalition said it would back a global pledge to triple nuclear energy if Dutton becomes prime minister.
BHP Group produces uranium ore at Olympic Dam as a byproduct of copper operations. Courtesy BHP.

title: US And Ghana Formally Launch Continent’s First Nuclear Training Hub
author: David Dalton
text: DOE wants additional $8m to help support new and emerging nuclear energy programmes around world

The US and Ghana have formally launched Africa’s first regional clean energy training centre to support the development of civil nuclear energy programmes as countries across the continent consider deploying nuclear power reactors.

The US Department of Energy said the centre will serve as a regional training hub for Ghana and other like-minded African countries considering nuclear energy as part of their economic development, energy security, and decarbonisation goals.

The DOE said the training centre builds upon previous work in the country, which included a training programme hosted by the US that covered the fundamentals of civilian nuclear power programmes ranging from project development and financing to nuclear security and national nuclear laws.

Through the training centre, the US will offer additional technical expertise and training with support from its nuclear industry, national laboratories, and academic institutions on topics such as workforce capacity building, reactor design and operation, and the management of spent nuclear fuel.

“This centre will be a critical resource for Ghana and other African countries working to deploy nuclear technology to address energy challenges while contributing to sustainable development,” said US deputy assistant secretary for international cooperation Aleshia Duncan.
The DOE established its first clean energy training centre earlier this year in Poland to help jump-start the country’s domestic civil nuclear energy programme.
US-based Westinghouse Electric Company is to provide its AP1000 reactor technology for Poland’s first nuclear power station, in Pomerania in the north of the country.

The DOE is requesting an additional $8m (€7.3m) in fiscal year 2025 funds to help establish similar hubs to support new and emerging nuclear energy programmes in Africa, Asia, and Central and Eastern Europe.
The DOE is looking to build upon the appetite for nuclear energy across Africa with a second US-Africa Nuclear Energy Summit in Kenya later this month focused on industry readiness.
The summit will be held in collaboration with Kenyan Nuclear Power and Energy Agency and the Ministry of Energy and Petroleum of Kenya.
In June the US and Ghana signed an agreement for the US to further support the West African nation’s use of nuclear power by advancing the deployment of a US small modular reactor in the country.

Earlier this year, Stephen Yamoah, executive director of state-owned project company Nuclear Power Ghana, told NucNet Ghana was aiming to choose a technology provider for a proposed first nuclear power station in 2024 and was already carrying out a series of studies at a preferred site, although financing remained a “major challenge”. He said plants might be large-scale units or SMRs.
US Department of Energy's Aleshia Duncan and Ghana Atomic Energy Commission's Samuel Boakye Dampare sign a statement of intent to launch the region's first Clean Energy Training Centre.

title: IAEA Issues Warning On Cooling Pond Water Levels At Zaporizhzhia
author: David Dalton
text: Availability ‘crucial for nuclear safety’, agency says

Dwindling water levels in the cooling pond at the Zaporizhzhia nuclear power station in Ukraine remains a potential source of concern, International Atomic Energy Agency director-general Rafael Grossi said on 2 August.

According to Grossi, the water level in the cooling pond is continuing to decrease and despite all six reactors at Zaporizhzhia remaining in a state of cold-shutdown, availability of this water is important for nuclear safety of the facility.
The IAEA said in a statement on 2 August that over the past weeks, staff at the site have observed a continuous decrease in the water level of the cooling pond.

“If this trend continues, ZNPP staff confirmed that it will soon become challenging to pump water from the pond,” the statement said. “Maintaining the level of the pond is made more difficult by the hot summer weather.”

Following the destruction of the Kakhovka dam last year, engineers at Zaporizhzhia drilled 11 wells at the site
as part of efforts to find new sources of cooling water.

These ponds supply sufficient water to cool all six reactor units in their current cold shutdown state. However, any compromise to the availability of water to the sprinkler ponds might necessitate using the cooling pond as a backup source.
Zaporizhzhia is near the frontline of fighting in southern Ukraine. It has been occupied by Russian forces since March 2022.
The IAEA said any compromise to the availability of water to the sprinkler ponds might necessitate using the cooling pond as a backup source. Courtesy IAEA.

title: First Large Nuclear Island System Delivered For Paks II Nuclear Construction
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Core catcher made journey from Russia via Black Sea and Danube River
The first large nuclear island system has been delivered for Unit 1 of the Paks II nuclear power station project in central Hungary, construction of which is expected to start early next year.
Project Developer Paks II Ltd said in a statement that the core catcher components were delivered via the Black Sea and the Danube River from Russia on 1 August.
“The Paks II project has reached a new milestone with the arrival of one of the most important long-lead items,” said Hungarian foreign minister Péter Szijjártó.

The core catcher – also known as a core melt localisation device or core trap – is designed to catch the molten core material, or corium, of a nuclear reactor in the event of a nuclear meltdown and to prevent it from escaping the containment.
The device is among the largest in a nuclear reactor system, with the steel casing weighing about 170 tonnes and having a height and diameter around six metres.
The total weight of an installed core catcher device under the reactor core exceeds 700 tonnes and has a diameter of about 11 metres and a height of 15 metres.
