But the report warns that to facilitate international movement of commercial nuclear-powered ships, and deployment of mobile floating nuclear power plants, both the International Maritime Organisation (IMO) and the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) need to revisit and adjust existing requirements.

Refuelling is an area where nuclear power presents the potential for significant operational changes for the maritime industry, but the high energy density of nuclear fuel creates the opportunity for reactors that will operate for multiple years before they need refuelling or replacing. Some designs may provide power for the entire lifespan of a ship.

Work is underway to create regulations and risk frameworks to enable nuclear-powered commercial vessels to call at commercial ports. While this work is ongoing, nuclear-powered naval vessels regularly receive permission to visit civilian ports and have done so for decades without incident.
Nuclear power generation has a strong track record in safety and an engaged set of regulatory bodies overseeing the safe development of new reactor technologies.

However, the introduction of nuclear-powered vessels to the maritime industry at any scale will require widespread updates to regulations, including the International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea (Solas), particularly related to regulations that cover reactor selection, radiation safety, surveys, certificates and special controls for nuclear ships.
Cooperation between the IMO and IAEA will be necessary to create a harmonised regulatory system for nuclear powered ships.

Interest in the use of nuclear power for shipping is driven by its emissions reductions, the report concludes. Nuclear power offers a path to the end goal of emissions reduction in shipping – zero emissions operation – and does so without the uncertainty of fuel and fuel infrastructure development at ports. The future availability of green fuel to operate a ship is no longer a concern once an agreement is in place for the lease of a reactor.

Interest in nuclear propulsion is split between those looking to have assets in the water in the shortest time frame using current technologies – around 2030 – and those working on a longer horizon for deployment of around 20 years who will have a wider range of technologies to consider.

The reports estimates the cost of a maritime reactor at $500m (€461m) for those delivered in the early 2030s, dropping off rapidly when production rates increase, is appropriate. But it warns that this is a simplistic example and does not include elements such as the regulatory journey for first-of-kind reactors.

Another option would be for a ship to use the power of a reactor owned by a third party, paying for “power by the hour” where megawatt hours are bought by the ship’s operator from the reactor owner on a contracted basis.
This would be a well-established cost as reactors are sealed units, hence total cost of life operation can be established with confidence before an asset is built.

Modelling the impact of introducing nuclear power into a typical Asia-Europe service, UK-based nuclear engineering company Core Power found that for a fleet of eight vessels, the average cost of each advanced reactor, along with its operation including insurance costs, cannot exceed $3.8bn over the course of 25 years to remain economically favourable compared to traditionally-fuelled vessels, a figure far above cost estimates for advanced reactors.
According to the report, nuclear power holds immense potential for revolutionising the maritime industry.

title: Junta Withdraws Licence For GoviEx Uranium’s Madaouela Project
author: David Dalton
text: Canada-based company says it reserves right to challenge decision

GoviEx Uranium no longer has rights over the perimeter of the Madaouela mining permit following the Niger government’s decision on Thursday (4 July 2024) to withdraw its licence, dealing a major blow to the development of one of the world’s largest uranium projects.

The Vancouver-based uranium miner said it had been informed by the Niger government, by way of a letter from the minister of mines, that it no longer has rights over the perimeter of the permit, which is now in the public domain.

GoviEx said the decision to withdraw the company’s mining rights “does not follow the withdrawal procedure prescribed under the applicable mining code” and it reserves the right to challenge the decision before the competent national or international jurisdictions.
The company had feared that its licence could be revoked if mining could not start by 3 July 2024, a deadline set by Niger’s military leaders, who came to power on 26 July 2023.

GoviEx said the government’s decision to withdraw the mining rights for the Madaouela uranium project, near Arlit in north-central Niger, will have a negative impact on the economic and social development of the region.

With a forecast initial capital expenditure of $343m (€316m), as well as considerable employment opportunities, the project was forecast to create up to 800 jobs over its projected 20-year mine life, with substantial royalty payments and taxes payable to the government.
The ruling government has a 20% stake in the Madaouela project.

Since the start of its operations in Niger in 2007, GoviEx said it has completed an unprecedented 650,000 metre drilling campaign to define Madaouela’s potential mineral resource, which is now amongst the largest known in the world.
GoviEx has advanced the Madaouela project from its initial exploration phase, through a period of historically low uranium prices, to the publication of its feasibility study in late 2022.
Production over the life of mine is forecast at 50.8 million pounds of uranium oxide (U3O8), or nearly 2.7 million pounds a year.

Over the past year, GoviEx has received expressions of interest in excess of $200 million for project-related debt finance, started social and environmental due diligence with a prospective lender, updated its environmental and social impact assessment, commenced front-end engineering designs and initial ground works, including the construction of an access road and started exploitation.
As recently as last month, the company received its radiological certificate, which is a regulatory requirement prior to starting mining operations.
Since January, Niger has temporarily suspended the granting of new mining licences and also ordered an audit of the sector.
Madaouela is the second high-profile uranium project that the self-appointed government has taken away.

In June, French miner Orano had its permit for the Imouraren project revoked. That project, also containing one of the world’s largest reserves, had its permit awarded in 2009 but has been put on hold by the company pending favourable market conditions.
The government had earlier warned in a statement that the Imouraren site, in the north of the country, would be nationalised if mining work did not begin there by 19 June.
GoviEx said it has completed a drilling campaign to define Madaouela’s potential mineral resource, which is amongst the largest known in the world.Courtesy GoviEx.

title: Russia Has Taken ‘Worrying Steps’ To Restart Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Reactors, Says Report
author: David Dalton
text: Moscow denies claims that plans are ‘well underway’ at occupied facility, where IAEA has reported more drone strikes

Russia has taken “worrying steps” towards restarting reactors at Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia nuclear power station, according to a report published by Bellona, a non-profit Environmental Foundation based in Norway.

The report, which analyses the technical and political aspects of a potential restart, says that restarting Zaporizhzhia’s six Soviet-built reactors would require a “colossal” effort, but suggests they are “well underway”.

Bellona said the station, seized by Russian forces in March of 2022, is the largest in Europe. It is also perilously close to the front lines of the war, and both sides have traded accusations that their opponent has attacked the plant.

The Bellona report was published as the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) said it had been informed that several drones struck locations in the vicinity of the Zaporizhzhia site on 3 July, injuring workers and causing forest fires.
“These repeated drone attacks are a threat to nuclear safety and people’s lives and must stop,” IAEA director-general Rafael Grossi said.

According to Bellona, since early in the invasion, all of Zaporizhzhia’s reactors have been placed in various states of shutdown. This was a critical safety measure, urged by the IAEA and agreed to by both Moscow and Kyiv, which would dampen the impact of a radiological disaster should any of the reactors suffer a catastrophic strike.

All six units are in cold shutdown mode. When a reactor is operating, it requires cooling to absorb the heat and keep the fuel rods from melting together, which would set off a catastrophic chain reaction. When a reactor is in cold shutdown, it no longer needs the same level of circulation.

Bellona said that despite the obvious risks, recent statements from Russian officials and, more concretely, the activities of Russia’s technical oversight agency within Ukraine, indicate that the station’s “Russian occupiers” could move to restart at least one of the reactor units sometime this year — thus removing this important assurance against disaster.

To restart a reactor, Russian technicians would first have to guarantee an ample and stable supply of cooling water. This task was made more difficult by the destruction of the nearby Khakovka Dam in June 2023, which compromised several reservoirs used for precisely that purpose.
But over the past year, the Russian side has announced plans to replenish the station’s damaged cooling ponds, which would then be capable of supplying up to three reactors, Bellona said
Bellona claimed Russian technicians have begun to rewire the power grid to divert the electricity produced by Zaporizhzhia towards Russia and the occupied territories of Ukraine.

It said satellite images of the Rosatom-controlled Zaporizhzhia terminal power plant, which connects the nuclear plant to the Ukrainian grid, show evidence of efforts to shift power lines away from Ukraine and into the occupied regions.
The official state Tass news agency reported in May that Russia is not planning to restart the reactors.
According to Tass, Rosatom chief Alexei Likhachev underlined the importance of the station’s safety and said restarting it was not on the agenda.
The environment group Greenpeace had claimed earlier in May that Rosatom had submitted plans to the IAEA to restart Zaporizhzhia.
Tass also said that the IAEA’s Grossi had held talks with a Rosatom delegation in the western Russian city of Kaliningrad, at which he said an understanding was reached on the safety of the station.
The Zaporizhzhia nuclear power station in Ukraine is perilously close to the front lines of the war, Bellona said. Courtesy IAEA.

title: Regulator Announces Action On ‘Improper Disposal’ Of Radioactive Waste
author: David Dalton
text: SSM issues injunctions to seven companies, including nuclear plants
Sweden’s Radiation Safety Authority (SSM) has ordered seven companies including the country’s three nuclear power stations to dispose of radioactive waste that may have been improperly disposed of.

SSM said in a statement that the waste comes from nuclear facilities and other activities and was placed in the final repository for short-lived low- and intermediate-level radioactive waste, known as the SFR, at Forsmark in Östhammar municipality, north of Stockholm, from the 1980s until 2001.
SSM said 75 containers containing 2,844 barrels are likely to contain low- and medium-level radioactive waste that has been stored incorrectly.
It said the waste could consist of radioactive substances, unknown liquids and “possibly also chemical and biological materials that are not permitted in the repository”.
According to SSM, the waste containers were originally intended for ocean disposal and were packed with concrete to make them sink.
SSM said the waste comes from various sources including the armed forces, research, non-nuclear operations and nuclear power plants.

The waste was packed by Studsvik Nuclear AB, which carries out nuclear research, and AB Svafo, a non-profit company with the purpose of decommissioning nuclear facilities from previous research and development activities in Sweden. The SFR is operated by Svensk Kärnbränslehantering AB.
SSM said it has issued injunctions against seven companies, including the country’s three nuclear power stations, Forsmark, Oskarshamn and Ringhals.

“The order means the companies must dispose of the waste for which they are responsible and, after analysis of the contents, ensure that it is finally stored or temporarily stored in a radiation-safe manner, by September 1, 2029 at the latest,” SSM said.
“Improperly deposited waste can in the long run have negative radiation safety consequences for people and the environment, and that is why the authority has taken the decisions on injunctions.”
The SFR facility with the Forsmark nuclear power station in the background. Courtesy SKB.

title: As Country Plans For First Nuclear Plant, IAEA Mission Says ‘Work To Be Done’ On Uranium
author: David Dalton
text: African nation aiming for reactors by 2031, but uncertainties remain over domestic fuel source

Uganda has a solid understanding of what is required to succeed in evaluating its uranium resources as it prepares for nuclear power, but significant work remains to be done, the International Atomic Energy Agency said.
Several areas in Uganda have been identified as potentially uranium-rich, though no proven resources are known to exist, the agency said.
Exploration practices to make a final determination will involve activities such as radiometric surveys and taking geochemical samples, it added.
The agency’s comments came as an IAEA-led team of international experts in Uganda concluded the agency’s inaugural review of a uranium production cycle.

The review was carried out at the request of the Ugandan government and assessed the East African country’s capabilities to develop its uranium exploration programme and eventually mine uranium for a domestic nuclear power programme.

The review team made recommendations to facilitate the success of the budding uranium exploration programme. These included that Uganda should ensure the development of skilled personnel for uranium exploration and that the discovery, assessment and development of potential uranium resources are accelerated by establishing a robust and well-funded exploration programme.
The IAEA said Uganda is looking to use nuclear power as part of its plan to meet its clean energy goals and increase access to electricity for its population of nearly 50 million people.
“For now, only about half of Ugandans have access to electricity, but its government has set a goal of achieving an electricity access rate of more than 99% by 2030,” it said.
“The country is aiming for nuclear power generation by 2031, with the help of domestically sourced uranium.”
According to Reuters, Uganda has signed a deal with China under which China National Nuclear Corporation would help Uganda build capacity in the use of nuclear energy.
The first nuclear project, Buyende Nuclear Power Plant, would be located at Buyende, about 150 km (93 miles) north of the capital Kampala, Reuters said.

It quoted a minister as saying preparation to evaluate the Buyende site is ongoing to pave the way for the first nuclear power project expected to generate 2,000 MW, with the first 1,000 MW to be connected to the national grid by 2031.
Press reports last year quoted president Yoweri Museveni as saying Uganda had chosen Russia and South Korea to build nuclear power plants.

Phiona Nyamutoro, Uganda’s minister of state for energy and mineral development, said recently that Uganda is reviewing its potential to produce uranium to support its plans for its first nuclear power plants as it moves to diversify its sources of electricity and accelerate its energy transition, a key part of its climate change response.
“To this effect, uranium exploration is ongoing in the country with the aim of discovering uranium deposits for sustainable nuclear fuel supply,” she said on social media.

She said the government plans to establish a centre for nuclear science and technology for nuclear education, training, and research. She said the centre will need uranium for the production of radioisotopes for industrial and medical applications.

The Paris-based Nuclear Energy Agency said Uganda does not report data on uranium but might do so in future because the IAEA has continued to support Uganda’s efforts to identify and evaluate uranium resources.

The Uganda Media Centre, the government’s official news outlet, has said Uganda is taking “firm steps” to integrate nuclear energy into the electricity generation mix to ensure energy security and provide sufficient electricity for industrialisation.
It said six other sub-Saharan African countries have committed to having nuclear as part of their energy mix between 2030 and 2037. They are Ghana, Nigeria, Sudan, Rwanda, Kenya and Zambia.
The only commercial power station in Africa is the two-unit Koeberg near Cape Town, South Africa. Russia is helping Egypt build a four-unit station at El-Dabaa.
Electricity demand in Uganda, a country of 43 million people, has increased significantly in recent years in line with its growing economy.

title: Installation Complete Of Steam Generators At Kudankulam-4
author: David Dalton
text: Four nuclear plants being built by Russia at site
The installation of the steam generators has been completed at Unit 4 of the Kudankulam nuclear power station in Tamil Nadu state, southern India, Russian state nuclear corporation Rosatom said.
All four steam generators – each about 14 metres long with a diameter of four metres and weighing 340 tonnes – were installed using the ‘open top’ method, first used at Kudankulam-3.

This method allows large equipment to be loaded into the reactor building using a heavy-duty crane before the reactor dome is closed. Rosatom said it can significantly cut the time taken to carry out the installation.
Construction of the Generation III Kudankulam-4, a 917-MW VVER pressurised water reactor unit supplied by Russia, began in October 2017.
There are three other units of the same design under construction at the site. Construction of Kudankulam-3 began in 2017 and of Kudankulam-5 and -6 in 2021.
Kudankulam-1 and -2, also both VVER V-412 units, have been in commercial operation since December 2014 and March 2017.
All four steam generators have been installed at the Kudankulam nuclear power station in India. Courtesy Rosatom.

title: Work To Begin In September On Six-Unit SMR Nuclear Power Station
author: David Dalton
text: Russia confirms signing of protocol for facility that will use RITM-200N reactors developed from icebreakers
Uzbekistan will start work in September on a nuclear station that will house six small modular reactors (SMRs), according local media reports and Russian state nuclear corporation Rosatom.
Uzatom, the country’s nuclear energy agency, signed a protocol with Rosatom at the site of the planned facility, in the Jizzakh region, near the border with Tajikistan in the east of the country

Rosatom said that during a visit to the site, a protocol was signed on “the procedure for the entry into force of the contract for the construction of the NPP”. That contract was signed on 27 May, Rosatom confirmed.
If the agreement is implemented, the SMR plant would become the first in Central Asia.

There are no nuclear power plants in any of the five ex-Soviet Central Asian republics, although Uzbekistan and its neighbour Kazakhstan, both uranium producers, have long said their growing economies needed them.
The plant will have a total capacity of 330 MW comprising of six reactors with a capacity of 55 MW each.
Rosatom will be the general contractor for the construction of the plant and local companies will be involved in the construction process, the statement said.
Russia will use its RITM-200N reactor technology, which is an adaptation of marine technology for land-based deployment.

RITM-200 reactors, on which the RITM-200N is based, have been used on Russian icebreakers. Since 2012, 10 RITM-200 reactors have been manufactured with the first three already in operation on vessels in the western Arctic.
Uzatom director Azim Akhmedkhadjaev said that according to forecasts, demand for energy resources in Uzbekistan will almost double by 2050.
“It is evident that for the stable operation of the energy system and economic development, our country must ensure a baseload power source in addition to renewable energy sources.
“We are witnessing a global increase in interest in new nuclear projects, both in large-capacity power plants and small modular reactors.”
Uzbekistan, a Central Asian country of 33 million people, is looking to nuclear power as a low-carbon energy source to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and boost electricity generating capacity.
A small nuclear plant based on the RITM-200N reactor is already under construction in the village of Ust-Kuyga, Yakutia, 4,000 km to the east of Moscow in the country’s Far East.

The first unit is expected to begin operation in 2028. The facility will provide electricity to industrial enterprises, including the development of the Kyuchus gold ore deposit and the Deputatskoye and Tirekhtyakh tin deposits.
Rosatom said small nuclear power plants offer advantages over larger plants including shorter construction times and the potential to increase capacity according to needs.
According to International Atomic Energy Agency, there are about 50 SMR projects and concepts at various stages of development worldwide.

Russia says it is the only country that has practical experience of SMR construction. In 2020, Russia was the first country to commission a floating nuclear power plant, the Akademik Lomonosov, which supplies energy to consumers in the remote city of Pevek in Chukotka.
Rosatom’s RITM-200N is a terrestrial version of marine reactors like this one. Courtesy Rosatom.

title: Copenhagen Atomics Signs Collaboration Agreement With Switzerland’s PSI
author: David Dalton
text: Danish company plans experiments to validate TMSR nuclear technology

Danish thorium molten salt reactor (TMSR) developer Copenhagen Atomics has signed an experimental collaboration agreement with Switzerland’s Paul Scherrer Institute (PSI), to validate the TMSR technology.
The partnership between Copenhagen Atomics and PSI aims to conduct a thorium molten salt critical experiment in 2026, a statement said.

Copenhagen Atomics said the experiment will provide valuable experience for the design, construction, licensing, operation and decommissioning of the new MSR technology and collect data for commercial deployment.
The collaboration agreement runs initially for four years and will position Europe at the forefront of advanced reactors, Copenhagen Atomics said.

It said TMSR technology has huge potential to become one of the world’s most abundant energy sources. To date, the bulk of TMSR experiments have taken place in China, so this represents “a major step forward for the tech in Europe”, Copenhagen Atomics said.

The company said the use of thorium over uranium has several advantages. Thorium, a naturally occurring radioactive metal that is found in soil, rock and water, is much more abundant than uranium and there is enough thorium in the Earth’s crust to “cover the entire lifetime of the human race”.
According to Copenhagen Atomics, thorium offers a lower price per kWh of energy generated and produces less long-lived nuclear waste than uranium.
In 2023 Copenhagen Atomics said it had raised €20m ($21.4m) to accelerate the development of its TMSR technology.
Co-founder Thomas Jam Pedersen said the funding would support plans to have the first commercial reactors online in 2028.
A rendering of a power plant based on Copenhagen Atomics thorium molten salt modular reactors. Courtesy Copenhagen Atomics.
The Copenhagen Atomics ‘onion core’ facility, with which critical experiments will be carried out in collaboration with PSI. Courtesy Copenhagen Atomics.

title: Country To Hold Nuclear Referendum This Autumn, Says President
author: David Dalton
text: Kassym-Jomart Tokayev says economic development impossible without stable energy supply
A referendum on the construction of a nuclear power station in Kazakhstan will be held this autumn, Kazakh president Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has said, according to local media reports.
“Indeed, the country has great opportunities for the development of nuclear energy,” Tokayev was quoted as saying.
“It is important to use them correctly and effectively. The people will make the final decision on this issue. The referendum will be held this fall. The government will determine the exact date.”
Tokayev said economic development will be impossible without a stable energy supply and he has instructed officials to begin work on plans for the construction of a nuclear power station.
“A broad discussion is currently underway,” he said. “Different points of view are being expressed.”

The site being considered for new nuclear is near Ulken village in the Almaty Region, although “this is subject to change”, an official at the National Nuclear Centre of Kazakhstan told NucNet last year.

Ulken is 330 km northwest of the city of Almaty on the shores of Lake Balkhash in southeastern Kazakhstan. The settlement was created in the 1980s to house workers for a planned hydroelectric power plant. That project was unfinished when the Soviet Union collapsed and high-rise apartments are the only completed constructions from the period.
The official said Kazakhstan faces a growing electrical power deficit, largely due to aging thermal power facilities from the Soviet era that desperately need replacement.
Kazakhstan president Kassym-Jomart Tokayev said a discussion on nuclear energy has begun.

title: Gov’t ‘Did Not Take Industry Objections Into Account’ On Nuclear Tax Rise
author: David Dalton
text: Levy on reactor operators goes to federal fund for radwaste management
Spain has approved legislation that increases the so-called Enresa tax on operators of nuclear power plants from €7.98/MWh to €10.36/MWh.
The new tax, representing an increase of almost 30%, goes to the federal fund for the management of radioactive waste, a task overseen by state nuclear waste agency Enresa.
The government said the increase was due to rising storage and disposal costs foreseen in its latest estimates.

But Madrid-based nuclear industry group Foro Nuclear said that in approving the new tax the government “has not taken into account any of the objections submitted in a timely manner by the Spanish nuclear industry last April”.

“At a time when numerous prestigious national and international institutions and countries with nuclear programmes underway, especially in the European Union, are highlighting the contribution of nuclear energy to the energy transition towards a decarbonised and sustainable world economy, we find here that the direction is the opposite,” Foro Nuclear said.

It said it is essential to have in the electrical system firm, baseload power that does not emit CO2 “such as that provided by Spanish nuclear power plants, but without the burden of the fiscal pressure they suffer, to which is added this increase in the Enresa rate”.
Foro Nuclear has repeatedly said that longer-term operation of the nuclear fleet would lead to greater financial resources being available in the Enresa fund, without having to increase the tax.
Foro Nuclear said a 2019 agreement between Enresa and the owners of Spanish nuclear power plants proposed a maximum increase of 20% in the tax, which would have taken it to about €9.58/MWh.

Foro Nuclear said: “This new increase in the Enresa tax means that, starting on July 1, an additional 130 million euros will have to be paid annually on top of the 450 million euros that the entire Spanish nuclear fleet has already contributed each year to the Enresa fund since March 2019.
“This fact, together with the disproportionate, discriminatory and suffocating fiscal burden it bears, seriously threatens the continuity of the operation of the Spanish nuclear park.”
Spain’s nuclear plants will begin shutting down from 2027. Four of its seven reactors are scheduled to close by the end of 2030, representing around 4 GW of capacity.
The nuclear phaseout was a key issue during last year’s general election campaign, with the conservative opposition People’s Party (PP) pledging to reverse the planned phaseout.

The PP won the most seats, but Socialist leader Pedro Sánchez formed a minority administration with the far-left Sumar coalition and was confirmed as prime minister. Sánchez has confirmed he wants to see “the orderly and progressive dismantling" of nuclear reactors”.
As of 2020, three nuclear units have been permanently shut down: Vandellos-1 in 1990, Jose Cabrera in 2006 and Santa Maria de Garona in 2012.
The seven that remain online are at Almaraz (2 units), Asco (2), Cofrentes (1), Trillo (1) and Vandellos (1).
Referring to Spain’s nuclear phaseout plans, Foro Nuclear president Ignacio Araluce told NucNet earlier this year that Madrid cannot go in the opposite direction of global exponential growth.
“It [Spain] is becoming isolated, so it is necessary to reconsider the future of our plants as well as the conditions that ensure their viability.”
Araluce said the notion that is being pushed that the sector does not want to pay is not true.

“However, we are not willing to accept all the extra costs not attributable to the operation of the nuclear fleet, but rather derived from changes in the waste management plan or from the lack of institutional consensus,” he said.
SPain has seven commercial nuclear plants in operation including two at Almaraz (pictured) in the west of the country.

title: Fortum Announces Completion Of First Nuclear Decommissioning Project
author: Kamen Kraev
text: FiR1 research reactor operated for 50 years near capital of Helsinki

Finland has successfully completed its first nuclear decommissioning project with the dismantling of the FiR1 research reactor, which operated for over 50 years at the VTT Technical Research Centre premises in Otaniemi, Espoo, near the capital Helsinki.
The decommissioning project was carried out by utility Fortum, which owns and operates the Loviisa nuclear station in Finland, in collaboration with VTT, the reactor’s owner.

The dismantling process, which began in June 2023 and ended in April 2024, marked a significant milestone in Finland’s nuclear industry, said Fortum. VTT received regulatory approval for decommissioning in 2021.
The company handled the full scope of the decommissioning work including planning, preparatory measures, reactor dismantling, waste management and the final disposal of radioactive waste.

Fortum said the project provided significant experience for both Fortum and VTT, particularly in preparing the extensive documentation required for the decommissioning licence. It said the experience will be valuable for future projects.

The decommissioning generated approximately 60 cubic meters of demolition waste, primarily concrete, which will be disposed of in Fortum’s Loviisa nuclear power station’s repository for low- and intermediate-level waste.
Fortum said that given the reactor’s use for research and educational purposes, the amount of decommissioning waste and its associated radioactivity were relatively small.
FiR1 was Finland’s first nuclear reactor. It was of the Triga design with a thermal output of 250 kW.
The reactor began operation in 1962 and was first used by the Helsinki University of Technology. It was permanently shut down in 2015.

According to VTT, after 1999, the FiR1 reactor was used in collaboration with the Hospital District of Helsinki for cancer therapeutic purposes until the treatment provider went out of business in 2012.
FiR1 was Finland’s first nuclear reactor. It began operation in 1962 and permanently shut down in 2015. Courtesy VTT.

title: Governor Wins Budget Battle Over $400 Million Loan For Nuclear Power Station
author: David Dalton
text: California facility had been scheduled for closure in 2025

Lawmakers in California have approved a $400m (€374m) loan to keep the two-unit Diablo Canyon nuclear power station operating until 2030 after initially expressing concerns over the cost to the taxpayer.
The state’s approved budget includes the $400m allocation, along with a requirement for the Department of Water Resources to report on how the money will be spent.

There had been criticism and concern surrounding the loan, with some arguing that taxpayers will end up footing the bill for Diablo Canyon operator Pacific Gas & Electric and that the loan will never be paid back to the general fund, putting the burden on taxpayers.

Local press reports said the approval of the loan and the decision to keep the plant open has caused friction between governor Gavin Newsom and lawmakers, with environmental and anti-nuclear advocates warning of a growing price tag to keep the plant open and ongoing legal challenges related to the environmental impacts of extending the plant’s life.

Newsom argued that Diablo Canyon is critical for maintaining grid stability during the state’s transition to clean energy, while legislative leaders questioned the necessity and cost-effectiveness of keeping the facility open.

Diablo Canyon, California’s last commercial nuclear power station, contributes roughly 9% of the state’s energy and was initially set to close in 2025 before Newsom passed a bill to extend its life to 2030.

PG&E, meanwhile, has filed a licence renewal application with the Nuclear Regulatory Commission that could eventually see Diablo Canyon’s operational lifetime extended by up to 20 years to the mid-2040s.
The current operating licences for Units 1 and 2, both Westinghouse pressurised water reactors, were set to expire in 2024 and 2025.

In 2022 the Biden administration finalised up to $1.1bn in credit payments for the continued operation of Diablo Canyon, saying nuclear power is critical in curbing climate change and it wants to keep plants open ahead of the development of next-generation reactors. Biden wants to decarbonise the power grid by 2035.
The credits are to be paid in installments until 2026, with the amount of the annual payment to be adjusted based on factors including actual costs incurred to extend the operation of Diablo Canyon.
PG&E has been quoted in press reports as saying the federal credits will help the company pay back the state loan.
Diablo Canyon, California’s last commercial nuclear power station, contributes roughly 9% of the state’s energy. Courtesy PG&E.

title: Bloc Must Implement Comprehensive Nuclear Strategy, But Challenges Remain, Says High Scientific Council
author: Kamen Kraev
text: Brussels-based group calls for ‘radical improvement’ in funding for research, development, innovation and education

The European Union must implement a comprehensive nuclear energy strategy to transition into a reliable, affordable, secure, and sovereign low-carbon energy system, but faces challenges such as securing investments and extending the operational lifetime of the current fleet, according to a position paper by the High Scientific Council (HSC) of the Brussels-based European Nuclear Society (ENS).

In the position paper, the HSC highlighted the critical role of nuclear energy in addressing Europe’s energy “trilemma”, which involves balancing climate change mitigation, energy security, and affordability.
The HSC said nuclear energy is of “strategic importance” for Europe and is needed for achieving environmental protection, enhancing energy security and ensuring affordable energy supply.

It called for the creation “as a matter of urgency” of a comprehensive European nuclear energy strategy which should align with international agreements and support the transition to a low-carbon energy system.
The strategy should also ensure Europe’s competitiveness in nuclear technology, enable the recovery of nuclear capacity and achieve strategic energy autonomy, the HSC said.
The paper noted that nuclear energy has one of the lowest greenhouse gas emissions throughout its lifecycle and uses minimal land and critical materials per unit of energy produced.
Europe has a “large autonomy” in nuclear technology, from fuel enrichment and reactor design to waste management, which minimises dependencies on other countries,” the paper said.

“It [nuclear energy] is the only clean energy source able to produce in large quantities and in a stable, dispatchable and affordable way in all the main energy vectors: electricity, heat and hydrogen.”

Publication of the paper comes as counting continues in the recent elections for the European Parliament and the nuclear industry saying support for the sector is likely to increase in the new parliament.

According to Professor Marco Ricotti, one of the HSC members and professor at Politecnico di Milano’s department of energy, nuclear energy is not a “silver bullet”, but can offer a “decisive contribution” for Europe to address and solve three key problems around energy: to electrify and decarbonise energy systems, to reduce strategic dependence on foreign suppliers, and to generate large quantities of programmable and affordable energy at a competitive, stable and predictable price.

However, the HSC warned of several challenges that need to be addressed including securing new and adequate investments, improving the nuclear industry’s delivery capabilities, integrating nuclear plants into hybrid energy systems and extending the operational lifetime of the current nuclear fleet.

The council called for a radical improvement in funding for research, development, innovation and education. They recommend the establishment of shared research-industry laboratories, new education and training programs, and facilities to prepare a large workforce for the nuclear sector.

“Effective multilateral collaboration between the nuclear sector, science and academic communities, governments, and the EU is essential to streamline efforts and accelerate nuclear programs,” the paper said.

Dr Christophe Schneidesch, another HSC member, said: “A clear message towards the private sector of a stable EU nuclear policy that supports nuclear energy in the long-term will provide the necessary stability and predictability needed for private sector investment.”

“This is also the case at national level for the governmental policies. Private stakeholders need stability in their landscape to invest in medium-long term in nuclear which by its nature, works on large timescales,” said Schneidesch, who is a technical director for reactor analysis and nuclear R&D manager at Belgium’s Tractebel Engie.

“Those clear messages can be given at policy level but also in setting financial instruments to provide guarantees or funding support. Joint ventures for nuclear projects can merge public stability and private dynamics,” Schneidesch said.

The position paper outlined several key areas for development to support Europe’s nuclear energy goals including the development of new reactor technologies and fuel technology innovation to improve efficiency, make better use of uranium and reduce nuclear waste and its radioactive lifespan.
It said there is a need for supply chain and industrial standardisation and education and training.

The HSC said nuclear energy is a “logical, long-term strategic choice for Europe” because it addresses energy needs and supports critical sectors such as healthcare through nuclear medical applications.
In March, the HSC said in another position paper that substantial efforts are needed in research, development, and innovation if nuclear power is to fulfil its vital role.
“We need a stable, long-term vision and corresponding policy and initiatives, also on the critical issue of human resources and capacity building,” lead contributor Ricotti said.

He said the demand for the possible development and deployment of nuclear technologies in Europe is impressive with organisations such as the European Nuclear Education Network and the European Human Resources Observatory for the Nuclear Energy Sector estimating that more than 100,000 people will need to be attracted and prepared within the next 10 years.”
“This represents a huge challenge as well as a tremendous acceleration required in the education and training processes,” he said.
The paper outlined key areas for development to support Europe’s nuclear energy goals including the development of new reactor technologies.
The High Scientific Council said nuclear energy is of strategic importance for Europe.

title: Cabinet Approves New Supervisory Board For State Nuclear Operator Energoatom
author: David Dalton
text: Despite war, country has ambitious plans to build new reactors
Ukraine’s cabinet has approved the makeup of the supervisory board of state nuclear power company Energoatom, consisting of five members, the energy ministry said.
Timothy John Stone was appointed as an independent member of the board.

Stone is a British businessman with interests in infrastructure, finance, nuclear power and water supply. He is a non-executive director of the Arup Group, chairman of Nuclear Risk Insurers and former non-executive director of Horizon Nuclear Power and a former senior expert non-executive director on the board of the European Investment Bank. In 2018 he was appointed chair of the UK’s Nuclear Industry Association in October 2018.

The board also includes Michael Kirst, who has held executive positions at US-based Westinghouse Electric Company. Before joining Westinghouse in 1996, he was the director of the Economic Committee of the Nato parliamentary assembly in Brussels.
Jarek Niewierowicz, a former energy minister of Lithuania and the chief advisor to the president of Lithuania on environmental and infrastructure issues, was appointed as an independent member.

The state’s representatives on the supervisory board are Tymofiy Mylovanov, Ukraine’s former minister of economic development, trade, and agriculture, now the president of the Kyiv School of Economics, and Vitaliy Petruk, state secretary of Ukraine’s economy ministry.

“We managed to attract world-class professionals as independent candidates,” said first deputy prime minister and economy minister Yulia Svyrydenko. “We expect that this composition of the supervisory board will strengthen the company's energy capabilities and help attract much-needed investments in the nuclear industry.”

The move to create the supervisory board was part of Ukraine’s plans announced in June 2023 to improve corporate governance by transforming Energoatom into a joint stock company with 100% state ownership. This structure allows for a clearer separation between government functions and commercial operations.

Energoatom operates 15 nuclear plants at all four commercial nuclear power stations in Ukraine. The four stations are Khmelnitski, Rivne, South Ukraine and Zaporizhzhia, which has been occupied by Russia since son after Moscow’s February 2022 invasion of Ukraine.

Energoatom chief executive Petro Kotin said recently that the company will begin preparations for the construction of two new Westinghouse AP1000 pressurised water reactor units at the site of the existing South Ukraine nuclear station. Kotin said Ukraine wants to have 24 GW of nuclear power capacity by 2050.

title: Framatome Gets €10 Million Towards ‘100% Sovereign Fuel’ For Russian VVER Nuclear Reactors
author: David Dalton
text: Operators looking to diversify supplies away from Moscow

French nuclear company Framatome has received financial support of €10m ($10.7m) from the European Union to accelerate the development and delivery of a 100% sovereign European fuel for Russia-designed VVER pressurised water reactors operated in Europe.

The fuel project, known as the Safe and Alternative VVER European Project, or Save, brings together 17 stakeholders to secure the mitigation of fuel supply chain risks through the development and implementation of an alternative European solution.
The partners include the four utilities that operate VVER nuclear power plants: the Czech Republic’s ČEZ, Finland’s Fortum, Hungary’s MVM Paks and Slovakia’s Slovenské Electrárne.

“Framatome welcomes this EU funding, recognizing our efforts and supporting the acceleration of our development to contribute to the diversification and security of fuel supply for VVER reactors,” said Lionel Gaiffe, senior executive vice-president of the fuel business unit at Framatome.

“Framatome is the only fuel supplier able to guarantee a 100% sovereign European technology, with a fully European design and product, and manufacturing facilities and a fuel component supply chain located and operated in the EU.”

Framatome said “the international context” has accelerated the need for a sovereign European fuel solution to avoid disruption to critical services and reduce dependency on imports from outside Europe.

Giffe said Framatome is making strides on the development of a fully European sovereign nuclear fuel product and is “strongly engaged” in supporting both the nuclear industry and the energy policy of the European countries operating VVER reactors.

According to Framatome, there are 19 VVER reactors in operation in Europe, including four VVER 1,000 MW reactors in Bulgaria and the Czech Republic, and 15 VVER 440 MW reactors in the Czech Republic, Finland, Hungary and Slovakia.

Since the onset of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, operators of VVER plants in Europe have been looking to diversify nuclear fuel supplies away from Tvel, the fuel wing of Russia’s state-owned nuclear corporation Rosatom.
In June 2023 Slovakia and Framatome signed an agreement to cooperate on nuclear energy including working towards the development of a “100% European fuel design” for the EU’s VVER reactor fleet.

Similar deals have been signed by Bulgaria, the Czech Republic and Finland with both Framatome and US-based Westinghouse Electric. Ukraine signed an exclusive fuel deal with Westinghouse for its entire fleet in June 2022.
In July 2023 a consortium led by Westinghouse was chosen by the EU in a separate agreement to develop and deliver a “secure, fully European” nuclear fuel supply to VVER plants.
The  Czech Republic operates VVER nuclear plants at Dukovany (pictured) and Temelín.Courtesy ČEZ.

title: Nuclear Waste Site Operator Pleads Guilty To Charges Over IT Security Breaches
author: David Dalton
text: UK state-owned company accepts cybersecurity‘not sufficiently adhered to’
The state-owned operator of the UK’s Sellafield nuclear waste site has pleaded guilty to criminal charges brought by the industry regulator over IT security breaches.

Lawyers acting for Sellafield told a London court on 20 June that they accepted cyber security was “not sufficiently adhered to for a period”, although they insisted there had not been a successful cyberattack and that its systems were now secure.

One of the charges to which Sellafield pleaded guilty was that it failed in March last year to “ensure that there was adequate protection of sensitive nuclear information on its information technology network”.
The other two charges related to failures to arrange “annual health checks” for its systems.

Sellafield pleaded guilty to all three charges in the prosecution brought by the Office for Nuclear Regulation under the Nuclear Industries Security Regulations 2003. Sentencing will take place on August 8.
Sellafield Ltd is owned by the UK’s Nuclear Decommissioning Authority, a UK government body set up specifically to deal with the country’s nuclear legacy.
It is in charge of cleaning up and looking after the Sellafield nuclear waste facility in Cumbria, northwest England.
In March the the UK’s nuclear energy regulator notified Sellafield Ltd that it would be prosecuted for alleged IT security offences during a four-year period between 2019 and early 2023.
The Office for Nuclear Regulation (ONR) said at the time there was no suggestion that public safety had been compromised as a result of these issues.
AN ONR spokesman said on 20 June: “We acknowledge that Sellafield Limited has pleaded guilty to all charges.
“There is no evidence that any vulnerabilities have been exploited.
“As the details of the case have yet to be heard in court, we are unable to provide further comments at this stage.”
The Sellafield site is one of the largest and most hazardous nuclear facilities in Europe.

It comprises of a range of nuclear facilities, including redundant facilities associated with early defence work, as well as operating facilities associated with the Magnox reprocessing programme, a mixed oxide fuel plant and a range of waste treatment plants.
It began life in the early 1950s making plutonium for nuclear weapons, and later that decade became the location of Calder Hall, the world’s first commercial nuclear power station.
The Sellafield site is one of the largest and most hazardous nuclear facilities in Europe.

title: Corporations Sign Agreement To Use Nuclear For Clean Hydrogen Production
author: David Dalton
text: Announcement came as president laid out plans for small modular reactor hub
South Korea is to get its first nuclear hydrogen production plant by 2027 following the signing of a cooperation agreement on Wednesday (19 June) by some of the country’s largest corporations.

Hyundai Engineering & Construction, Samsung C&T, Doosan Energy and Korea Hydro & Nuclear Power (KHNP) were among the eight companies that agreed to build the 10 MW pilot plant using $21m (€19.6m) of government funding from the Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry.

The announcement came as president Yoon Suk Yeol unveiled plans to create a small modular reactor (SMR) industrial hub in the coastal city of Gyeongju in the southeastern of the country. The government also aims to establish a hub for the hydrogen industry in the province.

Hyundai E&C said the hydrogen agreement was signed to successfully carry out a nuclear clean hydrogen production demonstration project and promote commercialisation by “bringing together companies and public institutions leading the domestic carbon neutrality and hydrogen economy revitalisation”.

The partners agreed to build and operate “a large-capacity commercial plant for the production of nuclear clean energy” and to develop “a nuclear clean hydrogen production business model for domestic and overseas export”.
A statement said the pilot will produce, store and ship more than four tonnes of clean hydrogen a day by 2027.

The statement gave no details about where the pilot would be built, or which nuclear plant will provide power to the electrolysers, but state-owned KHNP owns and operates all 26 of the country’s commercial nuclear power stations.

In his announcement, Yoon said the government will support the creation of an SMR national industrial complex worth $216m in Gyeongju so that South Korea can “preemptively secure the small module reactor and SMR manufacturing technology that is being competitively developed around the world”.

title: Junta Revokes Orano’s Operating Licence For Imouraren Uranium Mine
author: David Dalton
text: French company says move could have negative impact on region
Niger has revoked the operating licence of French company Orano at a major uranium mine, the company said on 20 June.
The move by the country’s ruling military junta targeted the Imouraren mine, which sits on one of the biggest uranium deposits in the world.
“Orano takes note of the decision by the Niger authorities to withdraw from its subsidiary Imouraren SA its licence to work the deposit,” Orano said in a statement.
It added that the move came despite its recent resumption of activities at the site in the northwest of the West African country, where France was the colonial power from 1900 to 1960.
The government had earlier warned in a statement that the site would be nationalised if mining work did not begin there by 19 June.
The company added on Thursday that infrastructure at the mine had reopened to staff from 4 June “to make progress with the work” and that dozens of people were engaged in it.
It said market conditions, with a favourable rise in the price of uranium, make it once again possible to consider bringing Imouraren into production.

“This being the case, and at the authorities’ request, Orano had submitted a concrete technical proposal to the State of Niger, enabling this development to take place as quickly as possible,” Orano said.
“To this end, the infrastructures have already been reopened since June 4, 2024, to accommodate the construction teams and move the work forward.
“Orano fears that this decision to withdraw the mining permit for the deposit will have a negative impact on the economic, social and societal development of the region.”
Orano said Imouraren would eventually provide jobs for 800 people on the project, including subcontractors.
The junta vowed to review foreign mining concessions in the country after it took power in July last year.
For more than 50 years, Orano’s Niger subsidiaries Somair and Cominak have been mining deposits in the northwest of the country.
Orano has previously said French nuclear power plants source less than 10% of their uranium from Niger.
Niger is the seventh-largest uranium producer worldwide and produced more than 2,220 tonnes last year.

Earlier this week Niger’s mines minister Ousmane Abarchi was said to have confirmed his support for Canada-based Global Atomic’s Dasa uranium project in Niger and offered assistance to streamline “administrative bottlenecks” facilitate the importation of supplies and equipment.
Global Atomic said that during a recent visit to Niger, company executives met several government officials, including Abarchi.
The Imouraren mine in northwest Niger sits on one of the biggest uranium deposits in the world. Courtesy Orano.

title: First Nuclear Steam Supply Project For Industry Begins Operation
author: David Dalton
text: ‘Heqi-1’ will use reactors at Tianwan station

China’s first nuclear-powered steam supply project for industrial use, known as Heqi-1, has been officially completed and put into operation in Jiangsu province in the east of the country, state media and China National Nuclear Corporation (CNNC) said.
Heqi-1 will use steam extracted from the secondary circuits of Units 3 and 4 of the Tianwan nuclear power station. Both units at the six-unit facility are Russian-supplied VVER-1000 plants.

After passing through multiple heat exchange stages, the steam will be transported via an insulated above-ground pipeline to the Lianyungang Petrochemical Industrial Base, a petrochemical complex that started commercial operations in 2021.
The Tianwan station has been equipped with four steam conversion devices for the project.
The main long-distance steam supply line for the project is about 23 km.
The facility is expected to supply 4.8 million tonnes of steam annually, which will reduce the burning of standard coal by 400,000 tonnes per year, CNNC said.
The project was jointly developed by CNNC subsidiary Jiangsu Nuclear Power Company and the Lianyungang Petrochemical Industry Base.

CNNC said the start of operation of the steam project shows that China’s comprehensive utilisation of nuclear energy has expanded from single power generation and meeting urban residents’ heating needs to the field of industrial steam supply. It said the Heqi-1 project “is a model of clean steam supply for the national petrochemical industry”.

China has a number  of projects to use reactors for heating. In April, a project began operation using the Generation IV Shidao Bay-1 nuclear power unit in in Shandong province, northeastern China, to generate residential nuclear heating.
The Tianwan nuclear power station has been equipped with four steam conversion devices for the project.

title: Vattenfall Announces Plans To Operate Forsmark And Ringhals Nuclear Plants For 80 Years
author: David Dalton
text: ‘In-depth investigation’ planned before final decision on investment of around $4 billion
The owners of the Forsmark and Ringhals nuclear power stations in Sweden have announced that they are planning to extend the operating lifetime of the stations’ reactors from 60 to 80 years.

Extending the operating life of the five reactors at the two stations by 20 years could provide more than 800 TWh of fossil-free electricity, roughly equivalent to today’s Swedish electricity consumption for six years, Vattenfall said.
Vattenfall owns and operates Formsark and Ringhals through its local subsidiaries Forsmarks Kraftgrupp AB and Ringhals AB.

Vattenfall said operating the two stations for 80 years would enable further fossil-free electricity into the 2060s, which favours the industry transition as well as the availability of efficient electricity supply to Swedish consumers.

“Nuclear power will play an important role in Swedish fossil-free electricity production for many decades and it is therefore of the utmost importance to invest not only in new nuclear power, but also in our existing reactors,” said Torbjörn Wahlborg, senior executive vice-president of generation in the Nordic region at Vattenfall
“After the extensive modernisations that have been carried out in the past, we see good prospects for extending the operating life up to 20 years.”
Vattenfall said there would now be “an in-depth investigation phase”, which will include more detailed cost calculations and an analysis of risks in terms of expertise and suppliers.
“After this, a final investment decision can be made,” the company said. “Most of the necessary investments are planned to take place in the 2030s.”

Björn Linde, chief executive officer of Forsmark Kraftgrupp AB and Ringhals AB, said a preliminary study that has been carried out shows that it is “efficient to utilise investments that have already been made and that contribute to a low-carbon emissions electricity system”.

He said: “Extending the operating time of existing reactors does not entail any complex licensing processes and we also believe that the additional nuclear waste can be accommodated within the system for nuclear waste from existing reactors.”
Vattenfall said investments of an estimated $3.8bn to $4.7bn (€3.5bn to €4.3bn) will be needed to replace or renovate systems and components for long-term operation at Forsmark and Ringhals.
Technical needs include maintenance, refurbishment or replacement of components such as turbines, condensers, generators, as well as modernisation of control and monitoring systems.
Investments are also needed in switchyards and power lines, plant buildings and other infrastructure.

Forsmark has three reactors with an annual production capacity of approximately 25 TWh of electricity. Vattenfall owns 66% of Forsmarks Kraftgrupp. Mellansvensk Kraftgrupp owns 25.5%, with Fortum as the largest shareholder, and Uniper (Sydkraft Nuclear Power) owns 8.5%.
Ringhals has two reactors with an annual production capacity of almost 17 TWh. Vattenfall owns 70.44% and Uniper (Sydkraft Nuclear Power) 29.56% of Ringhals AB.

Vattenfall announced earlier this month that it had shortlisted Rolls-Royce SMR and GE Hitachi’s BWRX-300 SMR designs in an ongoing evaluation to potentially deploy new small modular reactors at Ringhals.

Late last year Sweden’s parliament approved a bill allowing more commercial nuclear power reactors to be built than previously planned, scrapping the previous cap of 10, as the country seeks to increase power generation and energy security.
By 2045 the government wants to have the equivalent of 10 new reactors, some of which are likely to be SMRs.
Ringhals has two reactors with an annual production capacity of almost 17 TWh. Courtesy Vattenfall.
Forsmark has three reactors with an annual production capacity of approximately 25 TWh of electricity. Courtesy Vattenfall.

title: At China’s First CAP1000 Nuclear Plant, Revolutionary Containment Takes Shape
author: David Dalton
text: Generation III+ unit features passive containment cooling system
The three steel rings forming the walls of the main containment vessel have been hoisted into place at Unit 3 of the Sanmen nuclear power station in Zhejiang province, eastern China.
Sanmen-3 is the first CAP1000 nuclear plant under construction in China. The CAP1000 is China’s version of the Westinghouse AP1000.

Generation II pressurised water reactor unit containment buildings had a double wall with a steel liner inside and the concrete protection structure outside. Containment buildings for the Generation III+ AP1000 and CAP1000 have seen some significant changes.
According to the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission, one of the main changes is that the liner is not attached to the concrete walls in the portion above 40 metres.

The space between the inner steel vessel – made of stainless steel with a wall thickness of about 4.5 centimetres in most sections – and the outer reinforced concrete protection wall is reserved for air flow in exchange with the outside environment and a water film flow that cools the steel containment through natural convection and evaporation in case of a severe accident.
This system, called the passive containment cooling system, is designed to work in a similar way as a wet cooling tower works. It was developed by Westinghouse for the AP1000.
Installation of the three rings was completed on 5 June, the Shanghai Nuclear Engineering Research and Design Institute announced. The total hoisting weight was about 826 tonnes.
The Sanmen station is already home to two commercially operational Westinghouse AP1000 units – Sanmen-1 and Sanmen-2. They began commercial operation in 2018.
First concrete was poured for Sanmen-3 in June 2022. In March 2023, first concrete was poured for the nuclear island of Sanmen-4, also a CAP1000 unit.
According to International Atomic Energy Agency data, China has 25 nuclear plants under construction. It has 56 plants in operation that generated a 4.9% share of electricity production in 2023.
Sanmen-3 is the first CAP1000 nuclear plant under construction in China.

title: Bill Gates ‘Willing To Plow Billions’ Into Wyoming Reactor Project
author: David Dalton
text: Microsoft founder calls for US to ‘outinnovate’ adversaries on nuclear

Bill Gates said he is prepared to plow billions of dollars into a next-generation nuclear power plant project in Wyoming to meet growing US power needs and has argued that the US should be willing to “outinnovate” foreign adversaries in the nuclear energy sector.
TerraPower, a startup founded by Gates in 2008, broke ground last week for construction of its first commercial Natrium nuclear reactor in Wyoming, where a coal plant is shutting down.
“I put in over a billion, and I’ll put in billions more,” said Gates, the world’s sixth-richest person according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index.

TerraPower’s plant, which has backing by the US Department of Energy, was initially expected to be operational in 2028. But that would have meant relying on fuel from Russia, which is “unacceptable now”, Gates said on CNN. He recently said he hopes the plant will come online in 2030.

The Natrium design uses liquid sodium as a coolant rather than water and includes molten salt that can store heat to boost its output. TerraPower plans to source reactor fuel from the US and its allies, Gates said.
“Coal is being outcompeted by natural gas,” Gates told CNN. “And so what we have to do is compete effectively with natural gas.”

Gates, who also appeared on CBS News’s Face the Nation on Sunday, said he thinks Americans should value that the US needs to be a leader in nuclear energy because “you really don’t want the nuclear reactors around the world made by your adversaries”.

Americans should want nuclear energy produced in the US because “economically, it’s a huge job creator”, and the materials used in the reactors should be closely monitored and should not be “feeding into” foreign military activity.
“So, the US leadership in this space has a lot of strategic benefits,” he said, namely the amount of jobs it will take to construct the plants and get them going in the next half decade.

The Natrium reactor is a 345-MW electric sodium-cooled fast reactor with a molten salt energy storage system that is being designed to flexibly operate with renewable power generators to help decarbonise the electric grid.
Gates said ‘I put in over a billion, and I’ll put in billions more.’

title: New Nuclear Could Lower Electricity Prices By 6%, Research Suggests
author: David Dalton
text: Stockholm’s plans for reactors have gained momentum, report says

Additional Swedish nuclear capacity could lower electricity prices by 6% in the long run and save electricity consumers approximately €13bn ($13.9bn) between 2035 and 2055, analysis by Aurora Energy Research has shown.

The Stockholm-based research company said Sweden’s push towards a fossil-free economy by 2045 had gained momentum with nuclear utility Vattenfall’s potential selection of Rolls-Royce and GE Hitachi for small modular reactors at its Ringhals site.

It said additional nuclear capacity in the SE3 electricity price area is projected to “notably lower baseload prices”. SE3 covers the Stockholm metropolitan area and surrounding regions including Stockholm, Uppsala and Gotland.

According to Aurora’s analysis examining the effects of additional nuclear capacity, the commissioning of 2.5 GW of large-scale nuclear reactors in the SE3 area is projected to reduce prices by an average of €3.3/MWh between 2035 and 2055.
“While power prices are anticipated to rise ahead of 2040, they are expected to fall below €40/MWh (in real 2023 terms), following the introduction of new nuclear capacity in SE3,” Aurora said.
“While Vattenfall and the Swedish government expect the earliest operation in mid 2030s, Aurora projects a start date around 2040 due to the typical lead times of 10-15 years.”

Vattenfall announced earlier this month that it had shortlisted Rolls-Royce SMR and GE Hitachi’s BWRX-300 SMR designs in an ongoing evaluation to potentially deploy new reactors at its existing Ringhals nuclear site in southwest Sweden.

Late last year Sweden’s parliament approved a bill allowing more commercial nuclear power reactors to be built than previously planned, scrapping the previous cap of 10, as the country seeks to increase power generation and energy security.
By 2045 the government wants to have the equivalent of 10 new reactors, some of which are likely to be SMRs.
Nuclear utility Vattenfall is planning to build small modular reactors at its Ringhals site. Courtesy Vattenfall.

title: US Up To 15 Years Behind On Rolling Out Next-Gen Nuclear Power, Report Says
author: David Dalton
text: Beijing’s ‘whole-of-government’ strategy provides extensive financing and systemic coordination

The US is 10 to 15 years behind China on developing next-generation nuclear power reactors as Beijing’s state-backed technology approach and extensive low-cost financing give it the edge, a report released on Sunday said.

China has 27 commercial nuclear reactors under development*, with the average reactor taking seven years to come online – far faster than for most other countries, the Information Technology and Innovation Foundation said in the report.
According to the report, Beijing is intending to build 150 new nuclear reactors between 2020 and 2035.
The report said that although China built upon a foreign base of technology, it has become the world’s leading proponent of nuclear energy.
Chinese firms are well ahead of their Western peers, supported by a “whole-of-government” strategy that provides extensive financing and systemic coordination.

Between 2008 and 2023, China’s share of nuclear patents increased from 1.3% to 13.4% and the country now leads in the number of nuclear fusion patent applications, the Washington-based research institute said.
The world’s first so-called Generation IV high-temperature gas cooled reactor at Shidao Bay came online last December.

The China Nuclear Energy Association said that the HTR-PM (high-temperature reactor-pebble-bed modules) plant, in Shandong province, northeastern China, involved the development of more than 2,200 sets of “world-first equipment” with a total localisation rate of domestically produced materials of 93.4%.

China’s state-owned banks can offer loans as low as 1.4%, far lower than available in Western economies. Its nuclear power industry has benefited from sustained state support and localisation strategies that has allowed China to dominate sectors like renewable power and electric vehicles.

Beijing’s rapid rise in the field has been due to a “coherent national strategy” to develop nuclear power, including low-interest financing, feed-in tariffs, and streamlined regulatory approval, the institute said.
“China’s government has assigned considerable priority to domestic nuclear reactor construction as part of Beijing’s broader energy strategy,” the report said.

“China’s rapid deployment of ever-more modern nuclear power plants over time produces significant scale economies and learning-by-doing effects, and this suggests that Chinese enterprises will gain an advantage at incremental innovation in this sector going forward.”
A common narrative that China is “a copier” and the US an “innovator” has encouraged a lackadaisical attitude towards industrial policy, according to the institute.

“First, this assumption is misguided because it is possible for innovators to lose leadership to copiers with lower cost structures, as we have seen in many US industries, including consumer electronics, semiconductors, solar panels, telecom equipment, machine tools, and, as noted here, quite possibly, nuclear power. Second, it’s not clear that China is a sluggish copier and always destined to be a follower,” the report said.
* According to International Atomic Energy Agency data, China has 25 nuclear plants under construction. It has 56 plants in operation that in 2023 generated a 4.9% share of electricity production.
According to the IAEA, China has 25 commercial nuclear power plants under construction.
